2 Source rock study 2.1 Upper Jurassic Shales The source rock potential and maturity of the Upper Jurassic shales have been assessed on sidewall cores between RKB. The following results are to be emphasized (Table and Figures 2, & 4): Tau formation Excellent potential and very good organic fades, oil-prone marine organic matter of type 11 (400 HI in average), deposited in restricted and reducing environment. The anoxicity as well as the marine influence increase upwards throughout the formation as indicated by the continuous and stepwise decrease of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). The vitrinite reflectance is around % Ro (Cf. Appendix). This formation is geochemically similar to the hot shales from the top Draupne formation (Unit according to EPN subdivision). Egersund formation High source potential and fair organic facies, mainly wet gas-condensate prone mixed organic matter dominated by terrestrial influence, variable in properties, but dominantly of type ifi (180 HI in average), deposited in rather high energy environment. The continental influence and oxic conditions increase downwards as indicated by the continuous and stepwise increase of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). This formation is geochemically rather similar to the Heather formation with however clear higher input of material derived from terrestrial organic matter. The maturity is about the same as in the Tau Formation (0.63 % Ro, value at % is questionable). The source rock properties of both formations are graphically illustrated in Figure and summarized below where mean values of the main geochemical parameters are calculated based on the screening analyses (number of samples analysed indicated). TOC Tmax Si S2 +S2 HI OI EOM Yield Sat 2.2 Sandnes Formation Coals Several layers of coals and coaly shales have been sampled from the cores (2 coals and coaly shales) and analysed. These source rocks are typical of coals from the North Sea with very high S2 and EOM constituted mostly by NSO compounds. The pristane/phytane is very high and the saturates/aromatics very low. The hydrogen index is 180-240, corresponding to dominant type HI kerogen (Table and Figure 2). The potential is mainly for gas/wet gas generation. The vitrinite reflectance is around 0.64-0.67 % Ro, i.e. slightly higher than in the Upper Jurassic Tau and Egersund formations. It should be stressed that the maturity of the Jurassic section (Upper and Middle) from this well, measured by reliable vitrinite reflectance, is clearly higher than the regional trend observed so far for the northern Quadrant 25 at equivalent depths (report EP/P/EXP/GDP 94-022 RP).

question: What are the implications of a 1.14 g/cm3 Draupne gradient for hydrostatic depth estimation and overpressure trend?
answer_text: A 1.14 g/cm3 gradient indicates elevated pore pressure (overpressure) relative to normal hydrostatic, so hydrostatic depth is effectively shallower and an increasing overpressure trend exists toward the top reservoir.

4.2 DRILL STEM TESTS Two drill stem tests were carried out, one in the oil zones of each of the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formations. DST flowed oil and free gas from the Brent Group. DST flowed oil from the Sognefjord Formation. Bottom-hole sampling was carried out in DST and DST 2. Two samples were recovered from the Brent Group in DST 1, and samples were recovered from the Sognefjord formation in DST 2, for direct PVT analysis. Surface sampling was carried out in both DST's to obtain samples for recombination and PVT analysis. 4.2.1 Methodology for Interpretation The DST interpretations were carried out using the SAPHER PC interpretation package. All interpretations used the superposition method. The methodology used was: 1. Create Derivative/Log-Log plot to carry out diagnostics of the test, identify flow regions (early, middle and late time regions) and identify the reservoir and boundary models to be used in the analysis. This plot was used to identify the infinite-acting flow region and plot correct Homer straight line on the Semilog or Superposition plot. 2. Plot infinite-acting straight line on Superposition plot and identify main reservoir characteristics (permeability-thickness, skin). 3. Perform any supplementary plots that may assist in identifying character of late time flow (i.e., square-root of time plot for linear flow). 4. Return to Derivative/Log-Log plot and perform time and pressure match to dimensionless functions. Identify reservoir and boundary models to be used and generate synthetic dimensionless derivative and log-log functions for the model. Compare these with the test data. Iterate until good match is obtained. 5. Use the simulation capability to generate the synthetic pressure function from the final chosen model and the calculated reservoir parameters. Compare the synthetic pressure with the test pressure data to ensure that good match is obtained over the whole test, not just the portion being analyzed.

GEOSERVICES Well : 2/7-30 END OF PRESSURE DISCUSSION WELL REPORT Page : 111-3-1 12 SECTION 5034 ft - 10300 ft MD This section was drilled with three bits in three runs. BIT #6 DBS FM2668 drilled cement, shoetrack and 10 ft of new formation. LOT was performed giving an EMW of ppg. Drilling continued to 9540 ft when the bit was pulled due to low ROP. At 7528 ft wiper trip was done to the shoe. BIT #7 HTC ATM 03 drilled from 9540 ft to 9638 ft where it was pulled due to low ROP. BIT #6 DBS LRQ drilled from 9638 ft to section TD. The mud weight throughout this section was ppg. Starting new phase required shift of the trendline to the left, and this trendline was maintained to section TD. From the beginning of the section and onwards to 6200 ft the D'exponent is gradually decreasing indicating an increasing pore pressure. During this interval the calculated formation pressure rises from ppg to maximum ppg by 6200 ft. The D'exponent for the remainder of the section follows stable trend, with the porepressure remaining stable at to ppg. The resistivity reading throughout this section proved to be a poor parameter for pore pressure evaluation. Resistivity values at the start of the section of ohms gradually decreased to ohms by 7400 ft. These resistivity values remained at this low level for the rest of the section. peak in the readings was noted at 9960 ft this corresponded with lithological formation top not formation pressure change. The gas values only partially support the pore pressure predictions stated above. The values increased from 0.2% TO at the start of the section to maximum 1.2% TO at 5700 ft. The gas values remained 1.0% TO background level to 9440 ft where the total gas value fell to 0.04%, this was due to slower rate of penetration. From this depth and for the remainder of the section the background gas values stayed at this lower level of 0.04% to 0.08% TO, this is also due to the lower rate of penetration. The gradual increase in background gas by 5700 ft is another indicator of the increasing pore pressure mentioned above. However for the remainder of the section the values can be seen to be greatly controlled by the rate of penetration.

RELIEF WELL CONTINGENCY PLANS: WELL 217-29 Stimulation vessels Rig(s) Selection • Rig specifications • Deck layout for kill equipment • Special kill equipment Kill spools Long co-flexip hoses High pressure riser, etc. Relative Position Uncertainty One of the first steps in relief well geometry planning is to estimate the relative position uncertainty between the blowout and the proposed relief well(s). This is essential for determining the initial magnetic search depth, the number of relief wells required, and the angle of approach. Both the uncertainty in the surface positions and the borehole trajectory must be analyzed. Sulface Uncertainty More than one relief well has missed its intended target do to errors and/or misunderstanding surrounding the surface coordinates and/or azimuth reference system of the two wells. To avoid this costly mistake, redundant surveys should be taken between the blowout and the relief well wellheads using different measuring techniques. The primary objective is to assure that no gross errors exist in the primary positioning system. The secondary objective is to fix the relative distance and true north bearing between the two surface locations with an uncertainty of +/- lm, with high degree of confidence (if reasonably possible). For relief well drilling purposes only the relative position of the two wells is important (as opposed to UTM coordinates or Latitude/Longitude). Additionally, it is important to assure that common azimuth and depth reference system is being used. This has caused many directional drilling problems in the past, particularly when switching between grid systems and magnetic/true north reference systems. Normally three independent measurements are sufficient to assure reasonable confidence in relative positioning, with one using geodetic surveying techniques and sun-shots for true north reference if possible, to eliminate any remote grid errors. Borehole Uncertainty This step is essential in determining the initial magnetic search depth, the number of relief wells to start, and the angle of approach.

FORMATION EVALUATION SUMMARY Well 2/7-29 was drilled through the principal targets in the JU2 and JU7 Jurassic sand prospects. The well also penetrated the secondary target, the Permian sand in P2. The objective of the well was to establish the presence, quality and fluid content of the Jurassic sandstones via cores and wireline logs. JU2 contained hydrocarbons and had up to 50 mD core permeability. Two sands were identified in JU7. The top sand contained hydrocarbons but very poor reservoir quality (less than mD permeability). context_snippets.text: Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction On the 20th August 2005, Vertical Incidence Vertical Seismic Profile (VIVSP) was carried out for Norsk Hydro on the deviated well 31/2-N-11-H in the Troll field, offshore Norway. The objective of the survey was to obtain an accurate time depth profile and VSP image to tie to surface seismic. This report describes the time picking of the checkshot data and processing of VIVSP data which was performed using Borseis proprietary software as implemented on Geoframe commercial baseline 4.0.3. The polarity convention adopted in this report is as follows. In normal polarity an upgoing compressional wave, reflected by an increase of acoustic impedance with depth, is displayed as a white trough (negative number). A4 figures in this report are plotted at vertical time scale of 20cm/sec. The raw x,y,z, surface sensor data, raw stacked x,y,z data and migrated datasets have been provided in SEGY format on CD-ROM accompanying this document. All digital data and the processing reports is also provided on CD-ROM.

Assuming vertical ray path then 90 minus the polarisation angle (b) should be equal to the deviation angle of the borehole. Q.C. of this display is shown in Figure 8(bottom). The Horizontal MaXimum, Horizontal MiNimum, Tangent to first RaY and Normal to first RaY Components are shown in Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11 and Figure 12. A axis projection calculation is performed using HMX and axis stack with the well deviation to compute the true vertical (TV) and true horizontal (TH) wavefield. If the shotpoint is directly above the receiver TRY and TV would be the same, but in cases where the shot position is slightly off they will differ. The TRY will be used to calculate the deconvolution parameters, which again will be applied on the TV wavefield. 3.4 Preprocessing Examination of the seismic amplitudes and frequency content of the TRY component has been performed prior to the preprocessing. After careful analysis of the spectral content, zero phase third order Butterworth filter with bandpass frequency interval of 5-95Hz was applied to both the TRY and TV. The choice of bandpass was made to preserve the maximum frequency content in the data at this early stage of the processing and at the same time to remove the higher frequency noise. The data was then normalized and corrected to vertical one way travel time below MSL by subtracting the transit time from hydrophone to geophone and adding the vertical travel time using straight ray assumption and water velocity of 1480 m/s. Applying normalization turns the downgoing wavefield into plane wavefield, which later will provide more robust computations.

Commercial In Confidence 4 Sonic Calibration The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the sonic slowness log to match the vertical VSP transit times. 4.1 Compressional Sonic Calibration Prior to sonic calibration the log data (compressional & shear sonic, density, calliper, gamma ray, neutron porosity, resistivity and Photo-Electric Factor logs) were petrophysically validated (including depth-matching and environmental corrections) by Norsk Hydro. Compressional sonic was available from 1699m MD DF to 3200m MD DF. This was corrected to true vertical depth using the well deviation and bulk shifted by -35.5m to the Seismic Reference Datum, to give compressional sonic log from 1508.5m to 2085.9m TVDSS. All accompanying logs were also corrected to TVDSS. The sonic logs had some sections that were straight line interpolated where data were missing. The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the integrated sonic slowness to match the vertical VSP travel times for given reference depth. The difference in time defines the drift (Δtdrift =ΔtVSP-Δtsonic), which can be either positive or negative. postitive drift is usually caused by dispersion in the seismic wavefield with depth or distance. negative drift (too slow sonic slowness) can be due to hole rugosity where Vformation > Vborehole-fluid and is generally very local effect. In order to minimize the residual drift function, the user defined smoothed drift curve has been designed to honour the raw drift curve as closely as possible with view to generating “calibrated” sonic log that should be used for time to depth conversion only and NOT used for Acoustic Impedance generation. For AI generation, the raw sonic, correctly time indexed using the calibrated velocity function has been used for the input to the synthetic reflectivity generation. The compressional sonic was calibrated using the geometrically corrected, vertical Time/Depth relationship from the Vertical Incidence VSP survey. comparison of the sonic slowness log and the VIVSP interval velocities is shown in Figure 23 and an initial visual inspection shows the character appears similar with major lithological boundaries tying very well. The sonic, VSP interval, RMS and average velocities after calibration are shown in Figure 25 and are available as digital logs on the CD-ROM accompanying this report. The velocity information and calibrated time depth curves are tabulated in Velocity Report, Time to Depth Report and Depth to Time Report.

The main bore (P-23 Y1H) starts after this 100 and follows roughly down-dip direction, in way, that it climbs gradually upwards through the 4-series’ stratigraphy towards the main north-south trending fault (see Figure 4.2a, fault no. 5). Here, according to the model, it has reached the 5Am-sand. Fault-effects in the seismic survey around this fault cause major interpretation uncertainties, which might result in an actual well path, which runs high up in the 5Ac sand before passing the fault. After passing the fault the well is expected to be set back in the 4Cc sand. Hereafter the well is planned to follow trajectory, which runs sub- parallel to the dip direction, so that it will climb stratigraphically upwards through the overlying 4-, 5- and 6-series into the Draupne formation, where TD will be set. Confirmation of Draupne is the TD criterion for the Y1H well. The total length of the horizontal section is approx. 2450 m, from which roughly 1500 is expected to be in c-sandstone intervals, which makes 65% c-sand. The second branch (Y2H) will be kicked off within the first 100 horizontal, where the window is placed. After the kick-off point the well is planned to climb stratigraphically upwards towards the main north-south trending fault (see Figure 4.2c, fault no. 6) where it is expected to have reached the top of the 4Dc. On the eastern side of the fault the well is expected to have been set down in the middle of the 3Dc interval. RFT's in the objectives recovered mud filtrate with some solution gas. The only hydrocarbons found are in gas sand at 2385 in the Snadd Formation. The sand has good porosity but RFT pressure tests and fluid sampling indicate low permeability. A small volume of gas and mud filtrate were recovered from RFT samples. The decision was made to P&A the well without testing. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

context_snippets.text: PRCGNOSIS Well 7120/9-1 was drilled to test sandstone reservoirs of Middle to Lower Jurassic age. The structure was an east - west trending anticline plunging gently to the east. To the north and west the structure terminated against downfaulted shales. The structure was wholely within the Hammerfest Basin. Exploration Logging provided Geological Engineering Monitoring and Data Analysis System (GEINIDAS) service on 7120/9-1 from 405m to 2300m. total depth. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mud logging, automatic real-time data monitoring and recording, and pressure analyses were carried out. Continuous evaluation of pressure and drilling progress provided an aid in optimizing drilling costs, and ensuring that drilling continued with maximum safety to personnel, the well and equipment. The operator was continuously advised as to the status of these analyses, and data and results stored on magnetic disk for post-well evaluation. The printouts and plots are contained in the attachments of this report. For details of the computer programs provided, and the theory of the pressure evaluation methods used, please refer to the Program Information Book MS-144 and Pressure Log Manual MS-156. Both are available from Exploration Logg ing

For description of the deeper geology, we now turn to the three digital seismic lines. Generally there is very good correlation between these lines, the Norsk Hydro well log 7120/9-1 and the background paper entitled 'The Structural Geology of the Troms Area' (Ovrebr6 and Talleraas, Geojournal Vol 1, p. 47, 1977). Our interpretation for each of the lines is contained on the single sheet enclosed, at half the scale of the original seismic sections. The scale bar in the text (Figure 3.4) can be used to convert times to depths on these sections. Where our interpretation is based wholly or principally on the seismic data alone, we have indicated by means of (brackets) on the time sections. Depth conversion agrees well with the log of 7120/9-1. For instance, the depth of the lower marker in 7120/9- 1 is 1840 metres at one way travel time of secs. The equivalent time for 1840 metres on our depth conversion is sec, or roughly sec one way. At the marker 962 metres and seconds correspond to almost exactly seconds one way on our depth conversion. Hence we might expect errors of up to or 4%. However geological horizons at 7120/9-1 are significantly deeper than at 7120/6-1, so that there is probably an element of coincidence. Nonetheless it does suggest depth conversion is as accurate as one might expect, given the few velocity analyses available and the limitations imposed by using RMS velocities. There is also static shift of roughly 10 msecs necessary to get the water bottom to coincide with known water depths. As mentioned, full interpretation is given on the enclosed profiles. INTERPRETATION OF PROCESSES & ENVIROMLENTS The first stage in the environmental analysis has been to group together related beds or facies into units called FACIES SEQUENCES. These facies sequences reflect individual or closely related depositional events and are therefore units of genetic significance. They are usually recognized by identifying sharp boundaries followed by sequence of gradationally related beds or facies. Such sequences are commonly of fining-upward (FU) or coarsening - upward nature, but may also be of 'no-trend' type. In general the sequences of non-marine (or largely subaerial) origin, in well 7120/9-1, have fairly abundant coals and rooted horizons, and traction generated ripple laminations dominate over wave-generated ripple lamination.

question: How do the lithostratigraphic positions and formation tops of Brent, Heather, Balder, Statfjord, and Shetland GP compare in well 29/6-1?
answer_text: From shallow to deep the succession is Balder Fm above Shetland GP, then Heather Fm, then Brent Fm (top ≈ 3800 m), and then Statfjord Fm (top ≈ 4340 m).

The casing was then pressure tested to 500psi. From the 30 casing shoe to 1205 m, 24 hole was drilled in 27 drilling hours with two HTC OSC 33 bits, in three bit runs. 24 hole was drilled from 294-515 and from 515-1200 m, hole was drilled whien was subsequantly opened out to 24, prior to running the casing. The penetration rates averaged at 60 m/hr with maximum ROP of 253 m/hr and minimum ROP of m/hr. The section consisted predominantly of sand, with interbedded clay and glauconite. Towards the base of the section siltstone formed the dominant lithology. At the top of the section down to 480m, sand was drilled, the penetration rates averaged 150 m/hr to 420 and slowed to 30 t/hr at 500 where clay formation was encountered. The drill rate decreased with depth. Below this depth to 680 the lithology was loose sand,clear,subrounded and poorly sorted with intercalated clays and traces of lignite. From 680 glauconitic sand was drilled, similar to the sand described above but with coarser grain size. question: How does the operability of the Deepsea Express cement head manual override compare to the hydraulic system on well 1/3-9?
answer_text: The manual override was difficult to operate after the hydraulic system failed, indicating inferior operability compared with the hydraulic system.

context_snippets.text: The shaker room on the Maersk Jutlander filled with steam from hot mud, making it difficult to see especially with safety glasses. This was partly caused by the crew leaving the doors open and disturbing the airflow pattern, of the HVAC system. A good proportion of the Drill-Reps time was spent on logistic issues, rather than on drilling ones. dedicated offshore logistics man would remove this load, in future. If severe balling problems occur, consideration to increase the frequency of BOP Function test should be given. As it was with the riser and wellhead so balled there would have been no guarantee that the BOPs could have been used in well control situation. The MWD failed after cumulative pumping time of 154 hours in the silicate mud. This could set the limit of MWD life in silicate WBM. However anaylsis performed by technicians in town suggest that the failure was not due to the silicate WBM, but coil in the turbine had melted and short circuited parts of the turbine, resulting in power cut to the MWD. 9 5/8 Casing the use of fast developing compressive strength cemCRETE plug could have been further investigated for the kick-off plug. The extra cost due to the nature of the cemCRETE blend, could have been saved on reduced WOC time. The manual override for the Deepsea Express cement head was found to be difficult to operate, after the hydraulic system had failed - most likely due to the suction below. The manual system needs to be confirmed to be adequate. Special attention should be paid to drifting of any casing XO and its design tolerances. In preference have the X0s pre-installed on casing joint to stop them being over looked in baskets. Even if the casing is drifted in town, ensure that it is re-drifted offshore. Ensure that if the XO are to be drifted in town they are done so with solid API or special made drift (depending on the required drift ID) rather than hand-held Have taper mill for polishing any XO used, on standby as contingency - in case of design tolerance problems. 1/3-9s T2 Drilling Completion Report Rev 72

2.3 COMPARISON OF 2D AND 3D DATA There is difference in resolution between the 2D and 3D data. The higher resolution offered by the 2D data is of significant importance in the interpretation of the Pleistocene and Upper Pliocene deposits, which comprise sediments deposited during greatly varying conditions. High-resolution 2D data also increase the possibility of detecting thin features, such as sand layers and ploughmarks. The 2DHR data set is of adequate to good quality. However, the majority of the energy is reflected in the upper part. From approximately 1000ms TWT the loss of energy starts to significantly affect data quality, and below 1300ms TWT only high amplitude events can be discerned. The 3D data set TO06R06M1 was provided by Total EP Norge AS. comparison between TO06R06M1 and the 2DHR data set is presented in Figure 2.2. It can be concluded that the high- resolution 2D seismic data set displays significantly better resolution and quality in the upper sequence compared to the 3D survey TO06R06M1. High-resolution 2D data is essential for the detection of amplitude anomalies and small-scale features in the shallow part. Line: Trace: Offset: W E - TOTAL EP NORGE AS LINE NO : 02-046 - SP: Figure 2.2: 3D arbitrary line through PWL and line DA-02 showing the differences in resolution.

2.1 VSP PROCESSING 2.1.1 Velocity Survey Computations The digital VSP data were reformatted and displayed. source signature deconvolution was performed on the vertical and horizontal geophone components using operators derived from the first 600 ms of the reference hydrophone The reference hydrophone and vertical geophone components were then timed on the first trough arrival, representing the primary direct arrival from the source. The hydrophone traces were examined and the first-maximum time was picked establishing consistent reference hydrophone picks. Each downhole geophone trace was subsequently shifted by the first- maximum time value of the corresponding reference hydrophone trace. time correction of ms to account for the time from hydrophone to source, at water velocity (1500 m/sec), so that all downhole geophone traces were referenced back to the source. The downhole geophone traces for each depth level were then stacked using mean summation technique. Noisy traces were rejected prior to stacking. The stacked reference hydrophone component and stacked geophone data for all levels of each component are shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, & 7. The measured slant times were then geometrically converted to vertical times below the source and then corrected to the datum of MSL using static correction of ms, at water velocity 1500 m/sec. These time-depth pairs were then used as the input data for the final velocity survey computations to give the average, RMS and interval velocities listed in Section and displayed as Enclosure 1. Good downgoing shear energy can be seen in the horizontal components as indicated by Figures & 5. This shear arrival could be timed and used to calibrate shear log data and provide detailed VP:VS ratio. 2.1.2 Acoustic Log Calibration The acoustic log was supplied in LAS format and has been input to the calibration procedure. The depth range is – MD below DF. For the calibration, the acoustic log was integrated to produce a time-log, which is depth-indexed. The discrepancy between the corrected checkshot time of the shallowest checkshot level (within the logged interval) and the corresponding log-derived time was then computed. The time-log was next shifted by adding this value to all the time-log values, thus tying the log to the shallowest checkshot. A drift curve was then generated, showing the difference between the corrected checkshot times and the corresponding times from the shifted time-log. Calibration points fixing the drift at certain depths (including the top and bottom of the logged interval) were then chosen. Such that they divide the drift curve into intervals of approximately linear drift, and also so that they occur at velocity contrasts. The calibration points are indicated with triangular marks on the drift curve displayed on Enclosure 1. The shifts applied to the log are considered reasonable with maximum shift of 14us/m (4.3us/ft). For each interval between consecutive calibration points, the ratio between the difference in the fixed drift of these calibration points and the interval thickness was computed, and this constant was added to all acoustic log values of the interval, thus shifting the acoustic log in this interval by this amount. The whole acoustic log was calibrated by repeating this procedure for all calibration point intervals. After calibration, the calibrated time-log was computed by integrating the calibrated acoustic log and tying it to the shallowest checkshot. The residual drift curve, shown on Enclosure 1, was generated using the corrected checkshot times and the calibrated time-log. The tables in Section contain details of the acoustic log calibration, including the residual drift before and after calibration and the tabulated time-depth values listed in linear depth and linear time. The depth- indexed calibrated acoustic log and associated logs are displayed as Enclosure 2.

Apart from rutile, zircon and garnet, tourmaline is the most commonly occurring heavy mineral these samples. Tourmaline which is common to variety of metamorphic and magmatic (pegmatitic) rocks except for granulites, has been recorded in 15 sections from wells. As for the other minerals mentioned of possible importance to provenance, the distribution of tourmaline does not show any geographical trends. A mineral separation is clearly needed to concentrate the heavy minerals to produce statistically significant provenance information. Well 6407/9-1 stand out in this context. Of the detailed minerals garnet, Ti-Bt, RNQ and tourmaline samples from this well contained few grains of garnet only, and no members of the other three minerals. Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions (liquid-dominated as well as gas-dominated inclusions) have been observed hosted in overgrowth zones of both quartz and feldspar in some of the samples of this study. However, as this is point-coint study, fluid inclusion have not in any way been mapped as would have been the case in hydrocarbon fluid inclusion screening. Nevertheless, the use of microthermometry on the samples studied may well constrain the temperature (and time?) aspect of the major pore volume altering reactions which in this study are quartz overgrowth and feldspar dissolution. 41) Conclusive remarks The two overall most important diagenetic reactions responsible for pore volume alterations in the samples studied are quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) reducing porosity and (K-) feldspar dissolution which definitely is the major contributor to the formation of secondary pore volumes (PVSC). The table in Appendix shows positive correlation of quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) with depth of 0.65. K-feldspar (FSKF) shows negative correlation with depth of (feldspar dissolution). (The formation of PVSC shows positive correlation with depth of 0.34.) Though samples show grain sizes up to 500 microns practically no samples have been found to contain rock fragments as to be suitable as provenance indicators. The heavy minerals zircon and rutile are recorded in trace amounts in nearly every sample. Heavy minerals or detrital minerals (or mineral inclusions) that represent specific metamorphic facies do not give any consistent geographical distribution or clustering. Hence, no suitable provenance indicators have been recorded apart from the possible use of zircons for radiometric dating.

Possible and speculative additional reserves within the PL120 licence are dealt with in chapter 7. 6.2 Reservoir Properties The petrophysical parameters for each formation are listed in Table 5.2.1 on page 74. The Tarbert Formation, Unit II, represents lateral continuous, high quality reservoir zone of mainly clean, marine sands. The sands of the Tarbert Formation, Unit I, are also probably lateral continuous, but have some interfingering claystone intervals which may be laterally extensive, thereby creating vertical permeability barriers. The Ness Formation consists of alternating sands and shales, probably with low to moderate sand continuity. This formation is assumed to increase in thickness to the south and die out fairly rapidly northwards. The Etive Formation is assumed to exhibit very good reservoir properties, including high porosities and permeabilities, as well as extensive lateral sandbody continuity. However, this formation may show some thinning both towards south and north from the discovery well. The Rannoch Formation, Sand-unit is also generally of good reservoir quality, but deteriorates gradually towards the lower part of the unit. The lateral continuity is probably extensive.

question: What are the primary purposes and expected diagnostic indicators when choosing clean-out cement plus 3 m new hole versus staged pump/pressure buildup?
answer_text: Clean-out cement + 3 m new hole: exposes and isolates the formation by removing cement for a valid test; diagnostics are successful 3 m penetration, hole condition and absence of cement at the shoe. Staged pump/pressure buildup: determines leak‑off/fracture and safe working pressure; diagnostics are pressure‑vs‑volume build‑up, bleed‑off, surface holding pressure and sudden volume increases (mud take).

context_snippets.text: FORMATION PRESSURE TEST After drilling out casing strings the formation below the shoe will be subjected to pressure leak off test. 1. Depending on the type of formation and estimated future drilling conditions this test will be run either to predetermined pressure or to actual bleedoff. If predetermined maximum pressure is to be used, the pressure will be advised by the Stavanger Office. It will be calculated from the following: (a) Maximum mud weight anticipated to next casing point. (b) Maximum pressure anticipated when cementing the next casing string. (c) Estimated formation fracture graients. 2. Clean out cement below the shoe and make three meters of new hole. 3. Pick up into the casing and close blow out preventor. 4. Pump slowly down the drill pipe with the cementing pump pressuring up the casing and the exposed formation. Maximum pump rate is to be bbl/min. 5. The pressure is to be built up in 50 to 200 psi stages depending on the estimated fracture pressure. When the surface pressure reaches first level, shut the pump down and check for bleed off. Increase surface pressure, shut the pumps down and check again, and so on until reaching final pressure. It may be desirable to use 25 to 100 psi increments during final stages. 6. An accurate measurement of pressure build up and volume pumped is to be recorded on the form provided. If the formation begins to take mud, shut the pump down immediately and record the surface holding pressure. 7. Release the pressure, open the blow out preventor and drill ahead. 8. The results of the formation pressure test are to be reported on the Daily Drilling Report.

( HYDRO kia Depositional environments The environment of deposition is interpreted as deep marine basin. The almost constant degree of bioturbation indicates steady rate of sedimentation during the deposition of the shale intervals. The Zoophycos/Chondrites ichnofabric indicates sea depth at least 200m during deposition. The colour of the shale may reflect the quality of the bottom waters. Red colour indicates more oxygenized conditions. However, the change from red and brown colours to bluish green in well track 25/11-18T2 indicates that the colour also is influenced by diagenesis. The varicoloured nature of the shale may as whole be the result of volcanic input to the area. The thin sand beds (10-20cm) are very contorted and mixed up with clay clasts. and, as the sand also occurs in fissures in the shale, the most possible explanation is that this sand has been injected into the shale. The pore water in the sand has been trapped by the growing overburden of clay. The sand/pore water has been fluidized and this sand/water fluid has been injected into the overlying clay. The 1-2.5m thick sandstones have two possible interpretations: One interpretation is that the sand was injected into the shale due to the processes mentioned above. The clay was torn loose from the side rock and mixed into the sand. The faint lamination may be ascribed to water movement within the sand during or after injection. Another interpretation is that these sands are separate turbidites that settled between the main 40-60m thick turbidite bodies in the area, and that the - 2.5m thick sands seen in 25/11-18/T2 are the thinner outer parts of these turbidites. Then the main parts of these sands should exist between the thicker sand ridges penetrated by wells 25/11-15 and 25/11-18/T2. The faint lamination described above may then be ascribed to dewatering of the sand soon after deposition (dish structures). The lamination seen in the upper 10cm of the sand at 1721.4m in well track 25/11-18 may indicate exposure to bottom currents after the settling of turbidite, or, perhaps more likely, reworking from the dilute tail of the depositing turbidity current. The high angle of this lamination may be caused by later movements of the sandbody within the clay. 2.3.2 The Heimdal Formation (1741.5-1798 mRKB, log) The formation belongs to the Rogaland Group and is represented by cores 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 in well track 25/11-18T2. The top of the Formation was recovered in core # 16 in well track 25/11-18T2, see Enclosure 1. The entire formation consists of homogeneous sandstone almost void of sedimentary structures, except in the lower parts of cores and and also in core # 16 where very faint lamination can be seen. Above 1770.6m (core) the sand is very fine to medium grained, below the sand is fine to coarse grained. In the entire formation the sand is moderately sorted.

These geochemical differences may, regardless of origin, be mapped and used as information relating to reservoir compartmentalization. Following field filling, the major hydrocarbon homogenization process, able to erase initial geochemical differences, is diffusion. Diffusional transport in porous media is dependent upon the permeability, and low permeable layers with high tortuosities will act as barriers to diffusion. Methane is the petroleum component with the highest diffusion coefficient. This means that in reservoir sections of km lateral extension, where no diffusional barriers exist, initial differences in ?13CMethane should be erased as result of diffusive mixing over geological time scales. Significant variations in ?13CMethane over less than km distances in reservoir are therefore strong indication for the presence of diffusional barrier. These barriers to diffusion must also represent fluid flow barriers during filling and also likely production barriers.

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

Page 24 of 29 11.0 PETROPHYSICAL REPORT 11.1 Log analysis (CPI 1:200 scale attached as enclosure) All wireline logs were acquired and edited, including depth shifts, by Western Atlas. The logs used in the analysis were then borehole corrected as necessary. The Spectral Gamma was corrected for potassium content in the mud and hole size corrected, the Densilog was hole size corrected, the Dual Laterolog resistivity curves were corrected for borehole effects, and the Compensated Neutron curve was corrected for all borehole effects. The analysis of this well was done as part of multi-well study, which also included the 25/8-5S, 25/8-6, 25/8-6 T2, and the 25/8-8S, all of which are in the Elfi / Tau discovery area. The analysis focused on the Heimdal sands, as they were the only ones containing hydrocarbons, however the analysis was done over the Sele - Ty interval. All corrections and analyses were done using Logstar, the in-house Conoco evaluation program. The analysis for well 25/7-3 was not straightforward in that the upper part of the Heimdal Fm. contains shale clasts and lenses which depressed the resistivity response. Even the two primary sand units are too thin for the deep laterolog to resolve correctly. To account for this, form of resistivity forward modeling was applied. Petrophysical Model The overall petrophysical model consists of combination of several different models. Schlumberger Volan' type logic was applied in the computation of clay and silt volumes. Using information from the core analysis, porosity was computed which provided the best fit to the core data. Fluid saturation and permeability were computed using the Archie equation, capillary pressure relationships, and sound geologic reasoning. Clay and Shale Volume Computation Clay volume was computed from weighted average of non-linear transform of the gamma ray, linear transform of the gamma ray divided by bulk density, and density / neutron. The average is Hodges-Lehmann weighted average, which is described in an 1982 SPWLA paper by Coates, et al'. According to whole core descriptions of the Heimdal sands in the 25/7-3, they consist of mix of high-density turbidites, muddy sandstones, low-density turbidites, carbonate-cemented sandy shale, injected/slumped sands, and shales. They range in grain size from medium to very fine, and in sorting from well to poorly sorted'. The top five meters is heterolithic mix of each of these facies, and as such was fairly poorly resolved by the logging tools. The high sample rate density, neutron and spectral gamma tools, with their meter resolution, described the clay volume the best. detailed grain size description was used as guide in File: DEW.095.710-B3.98Rev:

question: What were the cumulative pumping hours to MWD failure for TAMBAR well 1/3-9 using silicate WBM?
answer_text: 154 hours.

context_snippets.text: The shaker room on the Maersk Jutlander filled with steam from hot mud, making it difficult to see especially with safety glasses. This was partly caused by the crew leaving the doors open and disturbing the airflow pattern, of the HVAC system. A good proportion of the Drill-Reps time was spent on logistic issues, rather than on drilling ones. dedicated offshore logistics man would remove this load, in future. If severe balling problems occur, consideration to increase the frequency of BOP Function test should be given. As it was with the riser and wellhead so balled there would have been no guarantee that the BOPs could have been used in well control situation. The MWD failed after cumulative pumping time of 154 hours in the silicate mud. This could set the limit of MWD life in silicate WBM. However anaylsis performed by technicians in town suggest that the failure was not due to the silicate WBM, but coil in the turbine had melted and short circuited parts of the turbine, resulting in power cut to the MWD. 9 5/8 Casing the use of fast developing compressive strength cemCRETE plug could have been further investigated for the kick-off plug. The extra cost due to the nature of the cemCRETE blend, could have been saved on reduced WOC time. The manual override for the Deepsea Express cement head was found to be difficult to operate, after the hydraulic system had failed - most likely due to the suction below. The manual system needs to be confirmed to be adequate. Special attention should be paid to drifting of any casing XO and its design tolerances. In preference have the X0s pre-installed on casing joint to stop them being over looked in baskets. Even if the casing is drifted in town, ensure that it is re-drifted offshore. Ensure that if the XO are to be drifted in town they are done so with solid API or special made drift (depending on the required drift ID) rather than hand-held Have taper mill for polishing any XO used, on standby as contingency - in case of design tolerance problems. 1/3-9s T2 Drilling Completion Report Rev 72

context_snippets.text: MI6 1NTEQ POST WELL ANALYSIS 2/8 S-11 & 11A Using the and rpm Fann measurements at 50°C and 80°C general rule can be derived. If the results from the 80°C test are more than one point lower than the 50°C test (irrespective of the absolute values), then the mud may have tendency for dynamic sag. Breaking circulation while tripping in The pressure sub data from previous wells confirmed that breaking circulation during the course of tripping in is critical operation in the effort to limit pressure surges on the formation. The length of time the mud stands static while out of the hole is sufficient to cool the mud to point where much greater pressures are required to break the gels at bottom if no breaks in circulation are made during the trip in. These extra pressures can be enough to fracture the formation. The following procedures should be adhered to: 1. Keep surface mud sheared 2. Break circulation at regular intervals on the trip in 3. Pick pipe out of slips 4. Start rotating the drill string at 60 rpm 5. Start circulation at 50 gpm while moving pipe in an upward direction. 6. Monitor flow line until returns are seen. 7. Increase flow rate in 50 gpm stages to 600 gpm. 8. Once flow rate is established at 600 gpm with full returns, establish drilling flow rate. Conditions should be evaluated on each hole section as to the frequency of breaking circulation. Conditions such as borehole stability, mud condition, length of time out the hole and pressure sub memory data. All these factors will need to be evaluated to define circulation intervals which will vary from well to well as conditions dictate. If the trip is round trip in an extended reach well then the lower half of the hole should be staged in with more frequent 250m intervals and washed down when approaching bottom. Staging up points in open hole should be chosen so that any large OD BHA components are placed away from any limestone stringers. If there are large number of limestone stringers at the bottom of the hole then consideration should be given to washing down from the last zone of competent formation. ECD Upper Limit A general recommended upper limit of 1.80sg (15.0ppg) ECD is recommended for Valhall wells in the overburden section. When drilling from Valhall Flanks away from the crest and known problem zones then it is possible to review each hole section in light of the DOP forecast and the FIT (after allowing significant safety margin). An upper limit for ECD in the 22 section is 1.53sg (12.8ppg) and for 16 and 12 'A section the initial target should be set point below the LOT / FIT taken unless the well path is planned to cross weaker fault zones. If so, target upper limit of 1.80sg (15.0ppg) is recommended. Prepared by: Ray Goodfellow, Cliff Kirby, 23 of 81 Ketil Inderberg, John Jelly, Gaute Grindhaug OASIS

question: How do macrofossil and foraminiferal revisions to age affect seismic–lithology correlations in cores D85-J and D85-N?
answer_text: They produced slightly revised, more accurate datings of cores D85-J and D85-N, which changed the relation between seismic sequence boundaries and lithological units.

In these two reports, further work on selected items was recommended. The present report gives the result, of this work presented in four chapters: revised palaeontology of cores D85-J and D85-N, diagenesis study of core 085-J, additional organic geochemistry analysis, and updated heat flow data. Macrofossil studies and additional foraminiferal studies of cores 085-J and D85-N have given slightly revised and more accurate dating of these cores, and the relation bet- ween seismic sequence boundaries and lithological units has been changed because of this work. The diagenesis study was concentrated on the limestone unit in core D85-J and the reason for relatively high porosity but low permeability is explained. The organic geochemistry chapter presents further analytical results and some comments on kerogen type and relationships between cores. The heat flow chapter gives comprehen- sive documentation for revision for the heat flow values previously presented, and recommendation for development of the shallow probe method as supplement to the down hole measurements. Samples of the overburden were taken on all the sites, totally of seabed cores obtained with gravity corer and 31.1 obtained downhole via the API drill string (see Chapter and App. 1). Pre-Quaternary rocks were cored on seven sites, A, J, K, N, 0, and (Fig. 2.1) of these where A, and short cores and J, K, and were respectively in, in, in and 10 long. Total accumulative length of bedrock cores was m. Including the overburden total of 510 was drilled during the 31 days of field work. In the laboratory the pre-Quaternary cores were photographed, split and described after measurements of the natural 1-radiation. Sub-samples were taken at 50 cm intervals for palaeontological datings, organic geochemical analyses, X-ray diffraction analysis and thin section microscopy (only from some intervals). Not all the sub-samples are analysed for this report. In addition to the above mentioned analyses, sound velocity of the different lithologies and porosity of two units are measured on the bedrock cores. Oedometer tests, threeaxial tests and routine geotechnical tests have been carried out on the Quaternary samples. Core C85-A consists of in of dark grey claystone and contains Paleocene palynomorphs. 5. 6507/3-3A STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The oldest sediments analysed in this well belong to the Fangst Group which were deposited in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment during Aalenian-earliest Early Bajocian times. Following transgressive event in Early Bajocian times, claystones of the Viking Group, Melke Formation accumulated in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions, becoming fully marine, inner shelf by Late Bajocian times. These sediments accumulated through to Middle Oxfordian times with apparent continuity in similar environments as sedimentation rates generally kept pace with subsidence. A flooding event at the beginning of Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones of the Spekk Formation. These sediments accumulated in marine, inner to outer shelf environment with dysaerobicianaerobic sea floor conditions from Late Oxfordian to Early Volgian times. A major stratigraphic break is present at the top of the Viking Group, Spekk Formation which is overlain by claystones of the Cromer Knoll Group, Lange Formation of Early Barremian age, which accumulated in marine, mid shelf environment. question: For intra-Brent targets, how do NIVSP, 3D seismic, and walkaway VSP compare in resolution, lateral continuity, and fault detectability?

The NH9802R99 is reprocessed data from NH9802 while NH9304 is merge of NH9304, VG91 and SH9004. The NH9802R99 data set has normal polarity display (SEG standard), i.e. an increase in acoustic impedance is represented by negative pulse (red trough on all enclosed seismic line examples). The wavelet is close to zero phase. The data quality for the survey NH9802R99 varies from good to poor. In the central parts of the field the target sequence, Middle Tarbert and Ness Formations, are clearly defined with good seismic character. In structural complicated areas, like the relay ramp area in the southeast and the drag-zone in the north-east (A-North) and the southern part of A-Main, the definition of key seismic horizons and faults are poor. In addition, the poor data quality appears to be related to shale diapirism in the Tertiary and/or the possible presence of gas in the Cretaceous and Jurassic sections. Ray-path distortion in the Terti- ary section is another factor that deteriorates the data quality. The NH9802 survey and the reprocessed NH9802R99 data set are definitely an improve- ment from the earlier data sets. The seismic reflectors are better defined, the resolution is higher and the fault definition has higher confidence. There is strong evidence for an intra-Etive fault, possibly oriented E-W, which has cut out part of the Etive interval and caused subtle structural rotation of the upper Brent relative to the lower Brent. separate structural dip (159/04°) has therefore been removed from the upper Brent. There is zone of penecontemporaneous faulting within the Ness Fm at around 4100m. There is probably fault immediately above top reservoir but the distinction between faulting and unconforrnity over this zone is difficult to establish. We would recommend that diplog data be re-displayed in the time domain to overlay large-scale seismic displays in order to resolve this. We would be pleased to work with Statoil to produce suitable plots if required. 4.2 STRESS FIELD Knowledge of stress field anisotropy and orientation can yield important tectonic insights, enable prediction of the orientation of natural and induced rock fractures and assist in the correction of core petrophysical parameters to subsurface conditions. Fracture systems and breakouts are not directly observable on diplogs (c.f. image logs, such as the CBIL) but valuable information can be obtained from calliper data alone. Boreholes in an anisotropic horizontal stress field tend to become elliptical, with the long axis of the ellipse oriented parallel to the minimum horizontal principle stress. The borehole walls will tend to fail and spall away in this direction, producing vertical grooves known as breakouts (e.g. Hillis & Williams, 1992). The four-arm diplog provides two orthogonal calliper measurements. One calliper will tend to lodge in the long-axis of the borehole ellipse, so that the callipers give an indication of the orientation of borehole elipticity, and hence an insight into the stress field. The borehole in 34/11-1 is only slightly elliptical. Data on borehole eccentricity were obtained by comparing the maximum and minimum calliper values every 0.5m, seeking eccentricities greater than 1.01, ignoring hole sections greater than out of gauge, interpreted as washouts. 1:200 plot of ellipse orientations (in-situ stress analysis) is included in Volume 2. The most obvious feature of these data is strong WNW-ENE preferred orientation (Fig. 11), indicating SSW-NNE orientation for the maximum horizontal principal stress. This orientation is consistent with regional observations on the stress field of the North Viking Graben (Cowgill et al. 1993) but is orthogonal to much of the data for the Tampen Spur (Jorgensen & Bratli, 1995). Open faults/fractures are known to cause local perturbations in the stress field (Bell et al., 1992). Such perturbations provide additional support for fault interpretations from diplogs and some insight into fault orientation. The inferred faults at 4170m and 4040m both show perturbations in the stress field consistent with approximately E-W faulting. Page 18

2 Source rock study 2.1 Upper Jurassic Shales The source rock potential and maturity of the Upper Jurassic shales have been assessed on sidewall cores between RKB. The following results are to be emphasized (Table and Figures 2, & 4): Tau formation Excellent potential and very good organic fades, oil-prone marine organic matter of type 11 (400 HI in average), deposited in restricted and reducing environment. The anoxicity as well as the marine influence increase upwards throughout the formation as indicated by the continuous and stepwise decrease of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). The vitrinite reflectance is around % Ro (Cf. Appendix). This formation is geochemically similar to the hot shales from the top Draupne formation (Unit according to EPN subdivision). Egersund formation High source potential and fair organic facies, mainly wet gas-condensate prone mixed organic matter dominated by terrestrial influence, variable in properties, but dominantly of type ifi (180 HI in average), deposited in rather high energy environment. The continental influence and oxic conditions increase downwards as indicated by the continuous and stepwise increase of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). This formation is geochemically rather similar to the Heather formation with however clear higher input of material derived from terrestrial organic matter. The maturity is about the same as in the Tau Formation (0.63 % Ro, value at % is questionable). The source rock properties of both formations are graphically illustrated in Figure and summarized below where mean values of the main geochemical parameters are calculated based on the screening analyses (number of samples analysed indicated). TOC Tmax Si S2 +S2 HI OI EOM Yield Sat 2.2 Sandnes Formation Coals Several layers of coals and coaly shales have been sampled from the cores (2 coals and coaly shales) and analysed. These source rocks are typical of coals from the North Sea with very high S2 and EOM constituted mostly by NSO compounds. The pristane/phytane is very high and the saturates/aromatics very low. The hydrogen index is 180-240, corresponding to dominant type HI kerogen (Table and Figure 2). The potential is mainly for gas/wet gas generation. The vitrinite reflectance is around 0.64-0.67 % Ro, i.e. slightly higher than in the Upper Jurassic Tau and Egersund formations. It should be stressed that the maturity of the Jurassic section (Upper and Middle) from this well, measured by reliable vitrinite reflectance, is clearly higher than the regional trend observed so far for the northern Quadrant 25 at equivalent depths (report EP/P/EXP/GDP 94-022 RP).

Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

question: What depositional processes and provenance evidence characterize NSPg140–170 gravity-flow Grid-equivalent sands from Malloy Terrace, and how do recycled taxa affect reservoir quality?
answer_text: Gravity‑flow (turbidite) sands deposited into upper‑bathyal or deeper settings, sourced from Malloy Terrace to the east; recycled taxa indicate erosion of the shelf/slope break. Recycled taxa introduce reworked detritus that increases sediment heterogeneity and can reduce reservoir quality.

CHAPTER Summary 1. The youngest strata examined are mudstones assigned to the 'Lark Formation Equivalent' of Early Oligocene age. These deposits which accumulated under upper bathyal depths rest with minor unconformity upon the Eocene 'Horda Formation Equivalent'. Throughout the Eocene and Paleocene the NSPg sequence framework of RRI has been applied to assist regional/local correlations. 2. The Late Eocene is relatively thin and is considered, at least in part, to be condensed, as reflected in the higher gamma ray mudstone unit within Sequence NSPg180. 3. The Middle Eocene comprises stacked retrogradational sequences of NSPg140 through to NSPg170. The older sequences, especially NSPg140 and NSPg150, are significantly sand- prone. Throughout the Middle Eocene progressive reduction in both sand content and thickness of the sequence is evident reflecting gross retrogradational package. The sands, equivalent to the Grid Formation and the Caran Sandstone in the UKCS, were deposited via gravity flow processes into an upper bathyal or deeper setting being sourced off the Malloy Terrace area to the east. Contemporaneous sands exist in blocks 35/3 and 35/8. Recycled taxa suggest some erosion of the shelf/slope break. 4. minor hiatus separates the Middle and Early Eocene. Within the Early Eocene part of the Hordaland Group gravity flow sands occur in Sequences NSPg120-100, being time equivalent to the Frigg Formation as seen to the south in the Viking Graben. Minor erosion of the underlying Rogaland Group is indicated in Sequence NSPg100. It is considered likely that the 35/4-1 well was located close to the westward pinch-out of Eocene sands, with little or no easterly derived sands occurring further west beyond the Marflo Ridge. 5. The Rogaland Group part of the Early Eocene comprises the Balder Formation and Sele Formation, deposited under upper bathyal depths. 6. Available biodata suggest the possibility of minor hiatus at the base of Sequence NSPg70. with Sequence NSPg60 possibly missing. 7. Sequences NSPg55 to NSPg10 comprise an essentially conformable Late - Early Paleocene section, with trace sand development. Page

context_snippets.text: 1.1 INTRODUCTION DOWNHOLE SEISMIC SERVICES (DSS) conducted Zero Offset, Vertical Incidence Vertical Seismic Profile (VSP) and Velocity Survey for SAGA PETROLEUM AS in their 34/7-23A well, located in the North Sea, Norway. The wireline was provided by Atlas Wireline Services (Stavanger). The survey began at 02:40 hours on 4th May, 1994 and was completed at 10:41 hours the next day. The weather was reported to be fair for the duration of the survey. Section of this report contains copy of the field engineer's report. All measured depths were referenced to the Kelly Bushing (KB) elevation of 25m above MSL. At the time of the survey the well had been drilled and cased to 3300 KB. Data for the survey consisted of 166 files which were recorded on magnetic tape reels and exabyte tape. Data was gathered at 135 levels from both the rig and boat sources in alternating order between 1960 in and 3295 in KB . The well was considered deviated for all data computations.

The following is summary of the levels acquired for the Rig Source VSP (in MD RKB): 34/7-23 34/7-23 From To Spacing From To Spacing 34/7-23 has depth correction on main tool level 3284 MD RKB and 34/7-23 has an extra level at 3295 MD RKB A copy of the Seismic Field Reports are included in the Section 'Field Operations Report'. Editing, stacking and timing of data The component geophone data was displayed at large scale and each component edited. The in- dividual near field monitor records were timed to the main peak, and the corresponding geophone traces shifted by this time. It was found that this system delay was not stable during the survey. The geophone data was stacked using median algorithm. summary of the traces included in the stacks at each level, the system delays and residual alignment delays are contained in the Stack Re- port. The first arrival time was taken as the top of the first peak: this corresponds to 'trough-to-trough' picking.The reader is referred to Appendix 1: First Arrival Picking for full discussion of this pro- cess. It was recorded in well 34/7-23 S,235 Rig Source VSP levels on the way up and 20 levels on the way in. 219 levels were included in data processing. 130 Rig Source VSP levels were recorded on the way up in well 34/7-23 and 15 levels on the way in. Here 125 levels were used in the data processing. VSP Processing sequence up to stack. Data in the intervals 0 MD RKB (34/7-23 S) and 0 MD R103 (34/7-23 A) were used in the Rig Source VSP processing. Fig 1. is an outline pre stack processing sequence (up to Raw stacks) described above. Saga Petroleum a.s.; 34/7-23 and

1.3.2 Acoustic Loci Calibration. Log data provided by Atlas Wireline Services (Stavanger) consisted of merged Acoustic, Density, Caliper and Gamma Ray logs over the range 2300 in to 3400 KB. These log data were first composited, edited and corrected for deviation. Calibration then proceeded as follows :- The acoustic log was integrated to convert local velocity measurements (represented as slowness in microsec/ft) to total vertical transit time. At each level, the acoustic log times were subtracted from the VSP checkshot times, thus generating the drift curve (fig. 1.4). Calibration of the log to the checkshot data proceeded as follows: point of absolute zero drift was specified at the shallowest checkshot point within the logged interval. The drift curve was analysed interactively and sectioned into intervals of approximately linear drift by placing further calibration points on or close to knee- points where the slope or trend of the drift curve changed significantly. To avoid creating false reflection coefficients, the calibration points - marked on the drift curve figures as the letter C - were positioned at velocity contrasts (i.e. formation boundaries). Using the depth difference and drift difference between successive calibration points, constant velocity correction for each interval was calculated. At each sample point of the log, fraction of the pertinent velocity correction for that interval was applied to the sample value, thus reducing the drift i.e. calibrating the log. Once completed, the calibrated log was integrated to derive corrected transit times with the residual drift also being calculated (fig.1.5). Figure displays the time-depth, interval, average and RMS velocity curves. Figure displays the drift computed from the input checkshot data and figure exhibits the drift after calibration (C-marks indicate calibration points). Enclosures and display the depth-indexed velocity log (calibrated acoustic log) and associated logs scaled at 1:500 and 1:1000 respectively. Enclosures to show the corresponding time-indexed logs. Section contains the acoustic log calibration results which details the residual drift before and after calibration and lists the calibration points. Sections and contain tabulated depth-time (linear depth) and time-depth (linear time) listings respectively.

VSP DECONVOLUTION It was not possible to achieve an inverse filter from the Rig Source VSP due to multi-path behavior. Thus an inverse filter form The Normal Incidence VSP was calculated trace by trace of the estimat- ed downgoing P-Wavefield and then stacked together to single trace operator. Desired output was a bandpass filter 12(18) - 60(24) Hz(dB/Oct) minimum phase wavelet and zero phase wavelet. The operator was then applied to all the levels on the rotated data (Display BG4 -BG5). SPHERICAL DIVERGENCE COMPENSATION The loss of energy due to spherical divergence is compensated for by applying the scalar Si to sam- ple i, where Si = (II / TO) ** and Ti is the time of sample i, TO the first arrival time, and data dependant parameter in the range to 1.5., in this case based on experience in the Snorre area. PS-WAVEFIELD SEPARATION X-T Domain Wavefield separation using time/space P- and S- angles estimated from ray-tracing were used to extract the reflected P-waves from the two components (Z,H). The rotation angles are shown in Fig. and 5. NOISE REJECTION AND RESIDUAL WAVEFIELD SUPPRESSION Residual reflected S-Wavefield was removed from the maximum reflected P-Wavefield by medi- an filter and residual reflected P-Wavefield was also removed from the maximum reflected S- Wavefield by median filter. MERGE DATA FROM 34/7-23 and 34/7-23 The two data sets were then merged to achieve an optimal coverage for 2D migration line. Fig. shows the well tracks from above. The merge point is indicated. Both data sets were also enhanced and spatial regridded separately. DATA ENHANCEMENT AND SPATIAL REGRIDDING Finally the data was regridded to spatial distance between traces and enhanced by using 5 point dip adaptive median filter in the NMO domain. VELOCITY MODEL AND MIGRATION Figure shows the final velocity model that was made when the objective was to minimize the dif- ference between first time breaks for synthetic and real data in the Normal incidence VSP case. Fig- ure shows the difference in time breaks as function of measured depth. The difference in first time break between the synthetic and real Rig Source VSP survey when this depth model, optimized for the normal incidence observations, was used to generate the synthetic Rig Source VSP was checked . The time difference indicates that velocities have to be increased in the deeper section to achieve acceptable fit with the data Rig Source observations. The only way we have managed to explain the results of this analysis is by concluding that the ve- locities must be angle-dependent (increasing towards horizontal) in the area, i.e. several or all of the layers must be regarded as anisotropic. The current algorithms for anisotropy migration assume elliptical anisotropy (transverse isotropy).

4.5 Measurement While Drilling and Wireline Logs The MWD services were provided by Sperry Sun. MWD services included directional surveys, gamma ray and resistivity measurements. The resistivity device is an electromagnetic wave type named EWR. The MWD was in use from seafloor (271 mMD RICB) to TD at 3375 mMD RICB, except for the cored intervals. question: What are the Svaneøgle TD criteria relative to the Gassum/Skagerrak reflector or HCWC, and the TD target of 3050m TVD BRT ±100m?
answer_text: TD = 50 m below the seismic Gassum/Skagerrak reflector if dry, or 50 m below HCWC in the same formation if discovery; overall TD target = 3050 m TVD BRT ±100 m.

question: For LT OBM, does an EPR-derived mud-weight schedule approximately 0.5 ppg below the recommended maximum meet kick prevention and wellbore stability criteria?
answer_text: Yes — the EPR-derived mud-weight schedule (~0.5 ppg below the recommended maximum) was selected and considered acceptable for kick prevention and wellbore stability.

This will include isolation of all hydrocarbon zones with cement plugs and or use of bridge plugs. The WH will be cut below the mudline as per NPD regulations. A more detailed P&A program will be issued at later date. Drilling Cautions These cautions apply to the 8-1/2 hole sections(OH & Sidetrack). No abnormal pressure is expected in these hole sections. The programmed mud weight is required for wellbore stability in the Hordaland shale and some deeper interbedded shale sections. These shale bodies are weak and hydratable and have history of wellbore instability problems. Shale inhibition will be provided by the low toxicity oil based mud system. The programmed mud weight schedule is based on Balder wellbore stability analysis performed by Exxon Production Research Company (EPR) in 1995. The wellbore stability study indicates that maximum mud weight of ppg is recommended for deviated well. wellbore stability chart for the Balder Area is included. Attempting to reduce the amount of overbalance, the selected mud weight is +/-.5 ppg below the recommended mud weight per EPR's wellbore stability model. Mud weights up to ppg below the recommended were successfully used in 25/8-8S/8A/8B Tau wells achieving near gauge hole wellbores. Formation pressures in the Rogaland Group range from sg to sg (8.5 ppg to ppg). The mud weight to be used to drill these formations (1.38 sg - ppg) will result in an overbalance of about 650 psi at the top of the Zone 111-4 sand. The lubricity provided by the OBM will partially mitigate the effect of this relatively high overbalance, but precautions against sticking should be taken. • Wiper trips should be used, as required, for conditioning the hole if poor hole conditions are experienced and/or significant open hole days have occurred. • The use of any High/Lo-vis sweeps or weighted sweeps should be discussed with the Operations Superintendent prior to use. • Optimal hole cleaning shall be achieved by maximizing the hydraulics and pumping at high flowrates, as specified in the hydraulics program.

context_snippets.text: General Summary This report presents an evaluation and interpretation of StethoScope675 Formation Pressure While Drilling data. Interpretation Summary 16 pressure measurement stations were evaluated and given quality grading from 1-10 as described in Section 2. Test analysis resulted in: ■ 12 good quality formation pressures (quality=10) These tests built up to stable pressure on both pretests at each station (test lost seal after stable pressure was reached). The calculated drawdown mobilities were of good quality and within range from 10 mD/cp to 452 mD/cp. ■ tests building near formation pressure (quality=7) Test 16 was building and not fully stabilized at the end of both pretests. Test did not draw down below formation pressure on pretest invest.
