All pretest interpretation plots are found in Section 5. 34/10-C-51 T2

Example of high permeability effects Anytime the pressure decreases rather than increases during buildup, the derivative curve will take sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (log of negative number -infinity). Typically, such buildup is considered un- interpretable. If this occurs for short period, then the final shut-in pressure may still be good estimate of formation pressure, depending on permeability. When the permeability is high, the total pressure changes seen during the buildup are small. The derivative calculation becomes more sensitive as the magnitude of the pressure changes gets near the resolution of the pressure gauge. The derivative curves may have the above wavy appearance. The true shape of the derivatives are often unclear. Good estimates of extrapolated formation pressure are still possible using simple straight line fit to the time function plots. Permeability estimates will be reasonable if the straight line fits reflect the true flow regime.

GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-22 & B-22 INTRODUCTION Well 25/8-B-22 was an observation well for potential horizontal oil producer. Well 25/8-B-22 was pilot hole for potential horizontal oil producer. Both wells were drilled in the Sindre Structure. The pilot hole was kicked off from B-22 at 4282m MD All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. SUMMARY This is the first time the PP/FG TM service has been used offshore Norway real-time. The well was drilled without significant problems and the reservoir pressure was close to that prognosed in the drilling programme. The PP/FG calculated pore pressure results calculated by the model can only be verified in permeable formations from formation tests and well control incidents. Pore pressure transition zones always occur in impermeable formations and here results can be contentious when compared to traditional methods of pore pressure prediction. However, the results do have value if they can aid in the prediction of pressure when entering permeable formation. There were only two depths in the well where it was possible to verify the PP/FG results: 1. possible small influx at 4387m implied that the pressure PP/FG result was close to the actual formation pressure. 2. Below the Mandal Formation we had to interpolate the resistivity through hydrocarbon-rich formations. Using this corrected resistivity curve we predicted the reservoir pressure gradient at 4500m to be 1.81g/cc. The measured pressure gradient was I.75g/cc from the MDT. A calculated pore pressure maximum of 2.09g/cc was reported during drilling of the Cromer Knoll Group. This was revised down to 2.00g/cc when the wireline data became available. The difference was mainly due to miscalibrated MWD resistivity run which was consistantly reading values 30% more conductive than the wireline, but also slightly due to the model interpreting the lithology from the gamma ray as too calcareous. The PP/FG calculated fracture pressure results were within 0.03g/cc of the actual LOT's at 13 3/8 and 7/8 shoes. This indicates that we have an accurate fracture propagation pressure gradient. Considerable valuable information and experience was gained as result of this work which will improve the PP/FG service and future pore and fracture pressure prediction in this area. It has allowed us to assess the updates and improvements to the program which have recently been added to the software, and has suggested additional improvements which are now being implemented. I. INTRODUCTION The Sperry-Sun PP/FG service is based on software model that calculates pore and fracture pressures on an incremental basis through all major lithologies in normally compacted sedimentary sequences. It requires calibration to offset wells. The two closest wells to the 2/7-29 location, 2/7-19 & 2/7-22, were studied and calibration for the real-time job was derived. This was described fully in previous report. This final report for BP Norway describes the pore and fracture pressure results using the PP/FG service on the Mmrsk Guardian for well 2/7-29. The service commenced from the 7/8 casing point at 3124m on the 16th October until the Permian at 4850m on the 21st December. Results from real- time MWD data whilst drilling arc compared to the wircline data for this post well analysis. context_snippets.text: -232- (9_ AO -INITEF. 3.6.7 Depositional environment Depositional environments for the formations are schematically outlined in Figure 3.6.30. 190.1 - m: Spekk Formation, late Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian A marine environment for the Spekk Formation is documented by the fossil records. The dominance of shale/claystone, with only minor contents of sands indicates that deposition took place in (hemi-)pelagic environment (below storm wave base). The sand may have been transported by low density turbidity currents, and deposited as thin laminae which have been mottled by bioturbation. However, an upwards shallowing trend is reflected by the coarsening upward trend, and upwards increasing bioturbation. reduction in the amount of unstructured organic material supports this suggestion. The fair content of gas-prone to inert kerogens in this part of the Spekk Formation (sub-unit 1) may suggest slightly dysoxic to oxic depositional conditions, which would agree with the generally bioturbated nature of this sub-unit. 183.5 - m: Rogn Formation, latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian The Rogn Formation (183.5 - m) appears as homogeneous sandstone bodies separated by graded, clayey sandstone and shale/claystone layers. The two different sandy facies suggest two different sediment gravity flow mechanisms. Rapid deposition of the homogeneous sandstone bodies is indicated by water escape structures. The sharp, sometimes erosive lower boundaries, and the lack of sedimentary structures and grading, indicate that they were deposited by high density turbidity currents or liquified flows. The graded, clayey sandstone layers were probably deposited by associated low density turbidity currents (Lowe, 1982). The shale/claystone beds represent the normal (hemi-)pelagic sedimentation between the frequent high and low density turbidity currents. The rich concentration of mixed marine/terrestrial type kerogens in the shales probably reflect deposition under dysoxic conditions in fairly stagnant environment. The fossil content indicate nearly normal marine conditions. ems_stlint28/Rapport/AA5/6307/07-U-02/69/19-DFC-88

The core has been sub-divided into two lithological units, which are interpreted to be lateral developments of the Spekk and Rogn Formations (Figure 3.5.1). The (mainly) Late Kimmeridgian Spekk Formation (>61 m) consists of dark grey shale/claystone, which shows increasing silt/sand content and bioturbation towards the top. Planktic microfossils document nearly normal marine environment, and the unit represents slightly regressive sequence in pelagic domain with poor bottom water circulation, especially in the lower half. The latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian Rogn Formation (>11 m, see also core 6307/07-U-02) consists of more or less massive fine grained sandstone. The unit represents sediment gravity flows in nearly normal marine environment (see discussion in Chapter 4.3.3). The distinct boundary between the two lithological units could not be related to any strong seismic reflector. Strong semi-regional reflectors within the lower unit seem to be related to cemented zones within the shale/claystone. The lower unit (Spekk Formation) posesses good potential for oil and wet gas generation. TOC values vary from to 18%. Hydrogen indices of nearly 800 mg HC/g TOC are observed. The kerogen (type I, II and III) is immature. The upper unit (Rogn Formation) showed high quality reservoir properties, with porosities of more than 30% and permeabilities which cluster at 700 mD. Here it is not evaluated whether the observed kaolinite booklets (see Chapter 3.5.3) would become problem during any hydrocarbon production.

3. GEOLOGICAL EVALUATION 3.1. Introduction Geological Setting The Draugen Field is situated in the Haltenbanken area off mid-Norway. The geological history of mid-Norway comprises Palaeozoic formative stage and Devonian to present break-up phase. Rifting and related faulting occurred from Late Carboniferous up to present day with westward moving of the axis of rifting activity. The resulting Norwegian shelf is passive cratonic margin underlain by series of continental margin basins superimposed on collapsed Palaeozoic orogeny. The Field comprises NNE/SSW trending low relief periclinal lenticular structure (20 km) with maximum vertical closure of 50 m. The main hydrocarbon accumulation is hosted by the Rogn Sandstone Formation, local Upper Jurassic composite shoreface/shelf deposit. minor, connected accumulation is hosted by the Garn Sandstone Formation, Middle Jurassic regionally extensive progradational shallow marine formation. The main reservoir facies, Rogn Formation, is enclosed to the north, south and east by butiminous claystones of the Upper and Lower Spekk Formation, time equivalent of the Rogn Formation. On the western side the Rogn Formation onlaps the Gam Formation which here rises above the field OWC. The top-seal of the Field is provided by the Upper Spekk Formation, the Lower Spekk provides seat seal over the larger part of the reservoir. Well 6407/9-B-5 was drilled from the northern water injection template to the target at top Rogn Formation, app. 1825 to the ( Fig. 1.1). The well reached TD in the sandstone's of the Garn Formation. The target was chosen to maximise on sweep of hydrocarbons as far to the north as possible. 3.2. question: How do lithological-boundary determinations compare with sampling intervals and microscopy frequency across depth ranges in well 25/8‑B‑25?
answer_text: Lithological boundaries were interpolated between neighbouring samples if drilling parameters showed no significant change; microscopic spot samples were taken every 50m MD from 1350–2700m MD, every 20m MD from 2740–3340m MD, and every 10m MD from 3340–4407m MD.

context_snippets.text: GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-25 Well 25/8-B-25 is planned to be horizontal oil producer in the Heimdal-reservoir in the Elli Structure. All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. Lithological boundaries were interpolated between two neighbouring samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and M'WD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse Cl, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. Ratios (C1/C2, Cl/C3, Cl/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of Cl. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show Cl, but very high shows of Cl are usually indicative of salt water. If the Cl/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the Cl/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If Cl/C4 is less than Cl/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the Cl Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/NON-PRODUCTIVE Cl/C5: 2-30 However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 ± C4 + Cs 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + Cs total 100 the GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LIAR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and Cs are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. Spot samples for microscopic description only, were taken every 50m MD from 1350m MD (1081.8m TVD) down to 2700m MD (1843.3m TVD). From 2740m MD (1865.5m TVD) one wet and two dry interval samples were caught every 20m down to 3340m MD (2103.1m TVD). Thereafter interval samples were caught every 10m down to TD at 4407m MD (2112.1m TVD). 3-1

question: How do TVD-scale compaction trends, blk7/12 densities, and A01 sonic data affect Eaton overlay interpretation given lithology and mud/log caveats?
answer_text: They provide the TVD-based overburden reference used for Eaton overlays, but the method is only valid for argillaceous intervals and can be compromised by mud/log caveats (mud motor effects, hole size/bit/steering, averaged/digitised wireline and unreliable density readings).

context_snippets.text: 2.1 FORMAT OF THE MUD LOG The lithologs for 7/12-A08 were drafted using the GEARHART litholog drawing and communications system. The litholog drawing system is self-contained system of hardware and software based on an Elonex PC, for the automatic drawing of lithologs from data entered by the user. On Ula the data is provided by the MWDatanet system. Plotting is carried out on Nicolet plotter with paper or sepia for field prints and high quality film for the master end of well copy. The litholog can be stored on floppy disc. The system also has the facility to transmit an image of the litholog via an internal modem to remote plotter. This facility was not used on 7/12-A08. The lithologs are plotted on vertical scale of 1:500, all depths being measured from the rotary kelly bushings (RKB). The heading sheet contains all the pertinent well information. They are divided into eight vertical columns which, from left to right, show the following information: 1. Drilling parameters: Weight on bit Mb) every metre. Bit rotary speed (RPM) Average torque (Amps) 2. Midnight depths and dates. 3. Rate of penetration (ROP) in metres/hour every metre, bit details. 4. Measured depth and true vertical depth, casing shoes. 5. Percentage cuttings lithology. 6. Interpretive lithology. 7. Hydrocarbon gas analysis of mud stream returns, including trip gas. 8. Full lithological descriptions, mud weight and ECD, directional survey data, casing point data. The scales used for drilling data, ROP and gas analysis are repeated every 200 meters and also where scale changes occur.

Bioturbated Sandstones The Ula Formation sandstones are predominantly bioturbated and range from very fine-grained wackestone to medium grained grainstones. The burrow types in the Ula Formation were classified by Kirkham and Grainge (1979) and this has subsequently been slightly modified by subsequent authors (eg. Bristow, 1988). This classification scheme is shown in Table Al. Three main burrow associations have been described from the Ula Formation (Bristow, 1988, Leonard, 1988a): 1 This association consists almost entirely of horizontal, frequently clay lined, burrows of c. lcm diameter (mainly type burrows, Table Al). This association tends to occur within fine to medium-grained, well sorted sandstones and comprises the majority of the cored Ula Formation. 2 Association is dominantly composed of and type burrows which occur within the very fine-grained, argillaceous intervals towards the top and bottom of the Ula Formation. As the grain-size of the sandstones increases from very-fine to fine-grained and they become slightly less argillaceous, and type burrows decrease in abundance at the expense of other horizontal and vertical burrows; effectively forming transition to association 1. 3 This association is dominated by small (c. lmm diameter) horizontal type burrows. It occurs within siltstone intervals. The burrow associations are clearly lithologically (substrate) controlled, as consequence they change throughout the cored interval in response to overall grain-size variations. Within the well sorted fine to medium-grained sandstones towards the top of coarsening- upwards sequences the overall degree of bioturbation decreases. Bioturbation is most intense within the finer grained, more argillaceous sandstones. The variation in the degree of bioturbation is particularly marked in association with graded and structureless beds. Within the individual fining-upwards beds the basal portion is weakly bioturbated with the degree of bioturbation increasing upwards. Only burrow association is present in the 7/12-A-08 core.

In this report most of the whole well plots are on true vertical depth scale of 1:20000 allowing the use of the transparent, condensed lithology overlay enclosed. Wireline data has been digitised at the wellsite from field prints and represents average values over an interval rather than high resolution log. Normal compaction trends have been established using data from this as well as previous wells drilled. These trends compare well with trends seen in neighbouring sections of the North Sea. The Eaton overlay method is mentioned in the appendix to this report. Emphasis is made that the technique is only suitable for argillaceous formation. The Tarbert Formation, Unit II, represents lateral continuous, high quality reservoir zone of mainly clean, marine sands. The sands of the Tarbert Formation, Unit I, are also probably lateral continuous, but have some interfingering claystone intervals which may be laterally extensive, thereby creating vertical permeability barriers. The Ness Formation consists of alternating sands and shales, probably with low to moderate sand continuity. This formation is assumed to increase in thickness to the south and die out fairly rapidly northwards. The Etive Formation is assumed to exhibit very good reservoir properties, including high porosities and permeabilities, as well as extensive lateral sandbody continuity. However, this formation may show some thinning both towards south and north from the discovery well. The Rannoch Formation, Sand-unit is also generally of good reservoir quality, but deteriorates gradually towards the lower part of the unit. The lateral continuity is probably extensive.

question: How do demultiplexing, hydrophone referencing, and pick strategy differ in their roles during VSP data processing?
answer_text: Demultiplexing separates and displays the digital channels, hydrophone referencing aligns all traces by cross‑correlating to a pilot hydrophone trace and shifting geophone traces to the effective hydrophone depth, and the pick strategy selects the first peak/extremum on the pilot and stacked traces (using up‑run picks) for travel‑time picks.

context_snippets.text: lc. DATA PROCESSING i. Velocity Survey Computations The digital data were demultiplexed and displayed. The reference hydrophone traces were examined and the arrival time of the first peak was picked on one pilot trace, against which all other reference hydrophone traces were cross-correlated, thus establishing consistent hydrophone time picks. Each downhole geophone trace was subsequently shifted by the peak arrival time value of the corresponding reference hydrophone trace, so that all downhole geophone traces were referenced to the effective hydrophone depth (i.e. the source depth plus the source-geophone distance). The downhole geophone traces for each depth level were then stacked using median summation technique. Travel times were picked from these records. Again the pick was made at the first extremum of the stacked trace which appears as peak on the recorded data. Enclosures 1A-1C display the stacked three-component seismic data for all levels. The accuracy of the depth sensor was checked by comparing wavelet arrival times of levels occupied during the down and up runs of each survey. The agreement was good. For consistency, only up run peak arrival times were used for the final calculations. The observed travel times were converted to vertical times and then referenced to Datum. These time-depth pairs form the input data for the final velocity survey computations, yielding the average, RMS and interval velocities given in Sections 2, and 5. Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

question: How do the objectives, sample states, and timing differ between single-plate capillary and FF/RI resistivity tests?
answer_text: Single-plate capillary tests measure capillary pressure versus saturation (oil displacing brine) at ambient conditions on plugs in fresh and clean states during the saturation experiment. FF/RI resistivity tests measure formation factor and resistivity index to derive the saturation exponent/cementation factor, with FF measured on clean plugs before the capillary test and RI on samples (fresh/clean) after capillary testing under 20 bar confining pressure.

Schlumberger 10.1 Procedures 10.1.1 Porosity Prior to the porosity test, the samples were dried at 60°C and 40% humidity. Grain volume was measured with Boyle's law porosimeter using helium gas. Bulk volume was measured by immersing the sample in mercury and weighing the displaced mercury. Knowing also the weight of the sample, it was possible to calculate the porosity, the pore volume and the grain density. 10.1.2 Klinkenberg Corrected Gas Permeability Gas permeability was determined by flowing nitrogen gas through the sample. moderate flow rate was used to minimize any «turbulence» effect. At steady state conditions, flow rate, back pressure and differential pressure were recorded. Thus the gas permeability and the mean pressure in the sample could be calculated. The gas permeability was determined at different back pressures allowing calculation of the Klinkenberg corrected gas permeability. During the measurements the samples were exposed to 20 bar net confining sleeve pressure. 10.1.3 Liquid Permeability The samples were exposed to net confining sleeve pressure of 20 bar to avoid water leakage along the sleeve and the sample. Liquid permeability was measured by flooding liquid through the samples at constant rate until the differential pressure stabilized. Flow rate and differential pressure were recorded, thus the permeability could be calculated. 10.1.4 Formation Resistivity Factor, Ambient Condition Each sample, saturated with simulated formation water, was placed in device specially designed for electrical measurements and exposed to known current frequency of kHz. The impedance and the phase angle were recorded, allowing calculation of the electrical sample resistivity. question: How does Overpressure Suite 7/12-A-8 apply TVD compaction trends, Eaton overlays, and formation density/sonic data?
answer_text: The suite plots TVD-based compaction trends and Eaton overlays on a TVD scale (1:20,000) using digitised wireline/drilling data; Eaton overlays are applied only to argillaceous formations, and overburden/pressure inputs use formation densities from other block 7/12 wells plus sonic densities from the 7/12 A01 sonic log.

context_snippets.text: 2.1 FORMAT OF THE MUD LOG The lithologs for 7/12-A08 were drafted using the GEARHART litholog drawing and communications system. The litholog drawing system is self-contained system of hardware and software based on an Elonex PC, for the automatic drawing of lithologs from data entered by the user. On Ula the data is provided by the MWDatanet system. Plotting is carried out on Nicolet plotter with paper or sepia for field prints and high quality film for the master end of well copy. The litholog can be stored on floppy disc. The system also has the facility to transmit an image of the litholog via an internal modem to remote plotter. This facility was not used on 7/12-A08. The lithologs are plotted on vertical scale of 1:500, all depths being measured from the rotary kelly bushings (RKB). The heading sheet contains all the pertinent well information. They are divided into eight vertical columns which, from left to right, show the following information: 1. Drilling parameters: Weight on bit Mb) every metre. Bit rotary speed (RPM) Average torque (Amps) 2. Midnight depths and dates. 3. Rate of penetration (ROP) in metres/hour every metre, bit details. 4. Measured depth and true vertical depth, casing shoes. 5. Percentage cuttings lithology. 6. Interpretive lithology. 7. Hydrocarbon gas analysis of mud stream returns, including trip gas. 8. Full lithological descriptions, mud weight and ECD, directional survey data, casing point data. The scales used for drilling data, ROP and gas analysis are repeated every 200 meters and also where scale changes occur.

Bioturbated Sandstones The Ula Formation sandstones are predominantly bioturbated and range from very fine-grained wackestone to medium grained grainstones. The burrow types in the Ula Formation were classified by Kirkham and Grainge (1979) and this has subsequently been slightly modified by subsequent authors (eg. Bristow, 1988). This classification scheme is shown in Table Al. Three main burrow associations have been described from the Ula Formation (Bristow, 1988, Leonard, 1988a): 1 This association consists almost entirely of horizontal, frequently clay lined, burrows of c. lcm diameter (mainly type burrows, Table Al). This association tends to occur within fine to medium-grained, well sorted sandstones and comprises the majority of the cored Ula Formation. 2 Association is dominantly composed of and type burrows which occur within the very fine-grained, argillaceous intervals towards the top and bottom of the Ula Formation. As the grain-size of the sandstones increases from very-fine to fine-grained and they become slightly less argillaceous, and type burrows decrease in abundance at the expense of other horizontal and vertical burrows; effectively forming transition to association 1. 3 This association is dominated by small (c. lmm diameter) horizontal type burrows. It occurs within siltstone intervals. The burrow associations are clearly lithologically (substrate) controlled, as consequence they change throughout the cored interval in response to overall grain-size variations. Within the well sorted fine to medium-grained sandstones towards the top of coarsening- upwards sequences the overall degree of bioturbation decreases. Bioturbation is most intense within the finer grained, more argillaceous sandstones. The variation in the degree of bioturbation is particularly marked in association with graded and structureless beds. Within the individual fining-upwards beds the basal portion is weakly bioturbated with the degree of bioturbation increasing upwards. Only burrow association is present in the 7/12-A-08 core.

The pore pressure increases steadily through Eocene reaching approximately 1.36sg at base Eocene (prognosed 1.39sg). The problems are mainly hole stability problems caused by sloughing shales. Another problem is the considerable variations in formation pore pressures. This will in many cases put very narrow limits on the mud weight and the margin between gaining and loosing circulation is small. The lost circulation problem is also intensivated in the lower pressure zones at the bottom of this section because of the annulus flow restriction caused by the sloughing shales above. This problem has been experienced on the previously drilled wells in the area. Efforts were now made to avoid this by better control on the hydraulics and by exercising closer control on the selecting of proper casing point. The careful control of the mud weight was primarly based on watching the mud gas, the penetration rate, the dc- exponent and the other drilling parameters. Actually no problems were recorded until 2000 m. drilling break at 1628 in was checked for flow (neg.) and high mud gas readings were occationally encountered. The mud also had to be circulated for mud rings. Overpull often occurred below 2000 in and the hole had to be reamed several times. At 2580 it was decided to stop drilling and set casing even if this depth was more than 100 in higher than the planned setting depth. This decision was made because of high mud gas, hole stability problems and the observed trend in the pore pressure. Further drilling was believed to be able to cause the same lost circulation problems as experienced in the two previously drilled wells. It was, however, later experienced that it would have been desirable to have the 5/8 casing deeper into the transition zone to be able to drill the 81/2 hole with lighter mud.

question: How does assuming an order-of-magnitude permeability ratio between Plio–Pleistocene and Paleocene–Eocene units affect reservoir flow modelling and history-matching outcomes?
answer_text: Assuming Plio–Pleistocene permeability 1–2 orders of magnitude higher allows the model to reproduce measured pore-pressure profiles by reducing overpressure in the upper loose sequence and forcing calibration of lower Paleocene–Eocene permeabilities to match deeper overpressures.

context_snippets.text: 104( I-IYDRO It ii When modelling the temperature history of sedimentary sequence one of the most important parameters to match is the heat-conductivity of the rocks. For this purpose the rock composition and porosity should be carefully analysed. In the actual case where in addition to the temperature also the pore pressure history is needed, it was also important to match the rock-permeability as close as possible. To get around this problem we had to make use of certain assumptions. In both wells modelled, the Tertiary sequence is composed at the base of thin and compact shaly Paleocen and Early Eocene sequence with some sandy stringers at Late Paleocene level. Above this sequence follows thick sandy and silty Plio- and Pleistocene sequence that evidently is fairly loose and unconsolidated. If it is assumed that this sequence has an equivalent permeability that is an order or two above what is found in the Paleocene - Eocene sequence below where overpressures start to build up, then this may be used as basis for the modelling. There has been performed one dimensional models in the area; one in each of the wells and one at shotpoint 2500 of line E-17-83 (Fig. 4). In the modelling of well 6507/2-1, the hydrostatic pressure was first subtracted from the pore pressure profile in Fig.l. This gave us the size of the over pressure in the well. Next suitable permeability value for the sediments around 1000 depth was chosen to match the measured pressure buildup at this level. The permeability of the Eocene - Paleocene sequence was then varied till good match between the measured and modelled pore pressures was obtained also for this level and down to Late Cretaceous. These permeabilities and those chosen for the remaining part of the well are shown Fig. 5; and the corresponding over pressures modelled and measured are shown in Fig. 6.

Core was cut during the drilling of side-track and represents the Ile Formation. The core starts at 3698,25m with fine-grained sandstone. Fine-grained sandstone dominates the lower and middle part of the core (up to ca. 3680m). The sandstones are strongly bioturbated (except in the lowest part of the core) and Asterozoma is the dominating trace fossil. Phosphate nodules are concentrated at 3680m, and this zone marks the top of the fine-grained sandstone interval. These sediments represent upper shoreface or delta front deposits and are part of larger coarsening upwards sequence. The phosphate nodules at 3680.3m may reflect dramatic change of the basin conditions, such as abandonment or winnowing by marine reworking (ravinement surface). question: How do claystone, sandstone, and carbonate stringer thicknesses and reservoir quality compare within the Naust Formation across wells 6305/9-1, 6506/12-11, 6407/6-4, and 6407/5-2S?
answer_text: Claystone is the dominant and thickest lithology in the Naust Formation across these wells; sandstones occur as subordinate, generally thin stringers (e.g., a ~15 m sandstone at 1142–1157 m in 6407/6-4) and carbonate (limestone/dolomite) stringers are minor and thin. Specific reservoir-quality metrics (porosity/permeability) are not provided in the context.

question: For well 30/10-A-4 Odin, with horizontal seismic, compactional overpressure, and logs present, what does gas presence indicate about vertical permeability?
answer_text: The presence of gas indicates the formation has little vertical permeability.

context_snippets.text: Of major concern must be the origin of the abnormal pressure. As has been seen, the area that the Odin field occupies has been subject to very little structural deformation as indicated on the seismic log which shows all major reflectors to be near horizontal lines. It is thought that the method of pore pressure formation here is due to the compactional effect of geostatic loading of sediment whereby the sediment is deposited far too quickly for all the water to escape during compaction. The presence of gas indicates that the formation has little vertical permeability. •

question: How do bioturbation, calcite/dolomite cementation, and chert nodules compare in occurrence and impact on reservoir quality in the Hugin Formation?
answer_text: Bioturbation is common and often strong (widespread in the units), and it interrupts good reservoir quality. Calcite/dolomite cementation (more abundant in the lower part and as thin layers upsection) likewise reduces quality to poor–fair, while chert nodules are observed throughout the middle unit but their impact on reservoir quality is not specified in the context.

context_snippets.text: 1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

4. LITHOLOGY 15/9-12 by S. Evensen The reservoir interval, the Hugin Formation of Middle Jurassic age, is devided into three units. The lowermost unit, consist in general of very fine to fine occasionally medium grained sandstones deposited in shoreface/tidal dominated enviroment. These sandstones are interbedded with few siltstone/mudstone layers, and one distinct coal layer at 3568-60 m. The lower part of the unit consist of more calcite/dolomite cemented sandstones than the upper part. The general good reservoir quality of this unit are also interrupted by strong bioturbation in some interval of the sandstones. This middle unit consist of interbedded sandstones and shales deposited in an ebb tidal delta/lower shoreface environment. The sandstones at the base of the unit are medium to coarse grained homogenous and structureless and should display good reservoir potential. To the top the sandstones are more fine-grained, laminated and strongly bioturbated. Chert nodules are observed throughout this interval. The uppermost unit consist in this well entirely of sandstones deposited in shoreface environment. The reservoir quality of the very fine to fine low-angle laminated sandstones seems to be poor (to fair) due to highly bioturbated intervals and thin calcite/dolomite layers throughout the whole unit.

All LWD memory data was dumped and logs produced as per requirements. The first wireline run became stuck at 4782m, 4720m, 4555m and 4350m whilst logging up so the second run was cancelled and wiper trip was performed before running the 5/8” casing. A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Where it is found that sliding is unavoidable towards the end of the 12 1/4” section it may be worthwhile to have Dogsub available on the Rig in case a trip is made where it could be picked up, although it would probably not be worth making special trip for it. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. The rotary BHA consisted of full gauge double nearbit roller reamer followed by float sub and variable gauge Andergauge stabilizer. This was followed by CDR, ILS stabilizer and MWD tools, as well as the ADN tool for porosity and density logs. After drilling out the float collar, shoe track and shoe, the hole was displaced to 1.32sg Versavert oil based mud. Very moderate drilling parameters were used to drill out the shoe, plugs and cement in an effort to protect the bit from excessive wear. Consequently 4.5hrs were used before drilling on new formation. The second target at TVD of 4264m had been extended to the north to take into account the significant walk rates seen in the previous 12 1/4 section. This extension allowed the 1/2 section +/- 0.5deg/30m right hand walk rate as well as 0.5/30m build or drop rate, dependant on actual walk rates experienced. Hence, ideally, maintaining the inclination and azimuth would hit the middle of the target extension.

Pressure EWL MDT was run in the 1/2” section (Tilje Fm. 3.4-Aare Fm. 6.2), and the measured formation pressures from this service were used as input to the petrophysical evaluation. No pressure measurements were taken in the Tilje Fm. 3.4, 3.3.3, 3.3.1, 3.2.2, and 1.2. The formation pressures used for these zones were estimated based on the formation pressure in adjacent zones. The measured formation pressures in the upper Tilje Fm. were about 2-2.5 bar higher than the estimated formation pressure from the RTD document. 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

context_snippets.text: 1 INTRODUCTION This report describes the sea-floor conditions and shallow geology within an approximately km area covering the Planned Well Location Idun (Figure 1.1). Potential installation and drilling hazards have been evaluated and special attention has been given to: • Seabed conditions, including water depth, sea-floor slope, seabed sediments and potential obstructions or hazards • Near-seabed sediments and likely anchoring conditions • Top hole sediments and well bore stability • Shallow water flow potential • Shallow gas • Boulders The report covers the interval from seabed down to the top of the Kai Formation at depth of 1341 meters Mean Sea Level (MSL). The report is divided into nine sections. The introduction, Section 1, is followed by summary of the main results and conclusions in Section 2. short description of the well and seismic data applied in the study is given in Section 3. In Section the criteria for horizon picking and anomaly definitions with its associated resolutions are presented. In Section description of the conditions for rig emplacement is given, including bathymetry, seabed and near-seabed sediments, potential obstructions and anchoring. Section deals with the shallow geology of the survey area, including brief geological history of the region from Miocene to present, details of the seismic interpretation and depth conversion, and geological prognosis for the well. Potential drilling hazards such as shallow gas and shallow-water flow is addressed in Section 7. Both sections, and 7, include examples from the seismic data to illustrate pertinent features. Section contains maps summarizing time structures and amplitude anomalies for the interpreted intervals. Section 8, recommendations, gives details of two possible relief well locations. V Executive Summary for well: 6507/3-7 Petroleum Indications, Type and Quality: There are three main intervals displaying hydrocarbon anomalies in this well. The sections above 1530 and at 2895-3195 consist of mostly dry gas responses, with the exception of single sample from 3201 displaying an oil-like spectrum. thin section from 2943 contains several to common, white-fluorescent, and rare, yellow-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. Inclusion abundance is marginally high enough to suggest the presence of an oil column or paleo-column at this depth. No visible petroleum inclusions are documented at 1330 or 3201 m. The section below 3546 reveals dry gas to oil-like spectra. The most significant responses are gas-condensate to oil indications noted intermittently at 3546-3600 m. Thin sections from 3549 m, 3632 m, 3717 and 3840 contain rare to several, white-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz grains. Thin sections from 3549 and 3840 also contain rare to several, blue-fluorescent, upper-moderate gravity petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. The remainder of the analyzed interval contains sub-anomalous hydrocarbon concentra- tions. No petroleum inclusions are recorded in thin sections from 1910 m, 2420 or 3339 m. Shales contain moderate amounts of gas-prone kerogen and rare to several occurrences of immature to mature oil-prone kerogen in most samples (apparently oil-mature below about 3000 m). Highest visual kerogen abundance is noted at 3339 m. Proximal Pay Indications: Anomalous concentrations of acetic acid and, in general, more prominent benzene anomalies are identified at 3546-3588 and 3651-3654 m. Samples containing acetic acid anomalies usually suggest the nearby presence of reservoired liquid petroleum (oil or condensate), while more prominent benzene anomalies can indicate nearby gas. This well is reportedly gas discovery, thus it is probable that these features are sensing penetrated charge. Anomalies within reservoirs can indicate elevated Sw (for instance in relatively tight or impermeable reservoirs). Potential Seals: Possible seals are identified at 2898 m, 3340 m, 3546 and 3690 m. Evidence for Bacterial or Thermal Alteration: Sulfur species of probable bacterial origin are noted at 1230-1250 m, 2010 and 2340 m. These compounds generally indicate migration or microseepage of light, thermogenic hydrocarbons from depth followed by bacterial sulfate reduction at temperatures below 65°C. FIS microseeps are considered encouraging for deeper liquid petroleum exploration in the vicinity, and are consistent with deeper charge in the wellbore. Other: Nothing of note.

INTERPRETATION OF FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY (FIS) DATA A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, including petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries with FIS, one can obtain valuable and unique information on three major exploration topics: 1. Petroleum migration or paleocharge 2. Seals 3. Proximity to undrilled pay and two major production topics: 1. Pay zone and bypassed pay delimitation 2. Reservoir compartmentalization. The previous discussions have concentrated on identifying spectral types in FIS data. This is necessary first interpretive step. The next task is to evaluate the significance of FIS depth trends in their own right (now knowing their spectral origins), and eventually, in light of other available information to answer specific questions, such as were enumerated above. Petrographic data from anomalous fluid inclusion zones are often critical elements of these higher order interpretations, as will be seen, which why petrographic follow-up work is conducted as routine part of every FIS analysis (see Table of Petrographic Observations). A.3.1 Significance of FIS petroleum indications The most basic question that FIS can address is Is there any evidence for present or past petroleum in this borehole Documentation of an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly generally pro- vides positive answer to this question, but could indicate other processes as well. Possible explanations for an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly are discussed in the following paragraphs. Migration without trapping A migration pathway may be indicated when FIS responses are low or moderate, when contamination and recycled inclusions can be discounted, when quoted visual petroleum inclu- sion abundances are rare or several (see Table of Petrographic Observations), and when no other petrographic or log evidence of current petroleum charge is identified in the zone. There are number of factors that influence inclusion abundance and, consequently, raw FIS response strength, including geologic setting, extent of diagenesis, rock type and permeability. However, it has been demonstrated that both visual petroleum inclusion abundance and FIS strength within many porous reservoir rocks is proportional to hydrocarbon saturation or pa- leosaturation in relative sense. Because migration occurs at average bulk-volume petroleum saturations below those encountered in charged reservoirs, FIS signal strength and visual in- clusion abundance are generally lower along migration pathways than in charged reservoirs from the same area.

question: How do the GEARHART system, MWDatanet input, and Nicolet plotting interact with RKB depth datum during depth registration?
answer_text: MWDatanet supplies the depth-tagged data to the GEARHART litholog system, which formats the logs for Nicolet plotting, and all plotted depths are registered/measured from the rotary kelly bushing (RKB).

context_snippets.text: 2.1 FORMAT OF THE MUD LOG The lithologs for 7/12-A08 were drafted using the GEARHART litholog drawing and communications system. The litholog drawing system is self-contained system of hardware and software based on an Elonex PC, for the automatic drawing of lithologs from data entered by the user. On Ula the data is provided by the MWDatanet system. Plotting is carried out on Nicolet plotter with paper or sepia for field prints and high quality film for the master end of well copy. The litholog can be stored on floppy disc. The system also has the facility to transmit an image of the litholog via an internal modem to remote plotter. This facility was not used on 7/12-A08. The lithologs are plotted on vertical scale of 1:500, all depths being measured from the rotary kelly bushings (RKB). The heading sheet contains all the pertinent well information. They are divided into eight vertical columns which, from left to right, show the following information: 1. Drilling parameters: Weight on bit Mb) every metre. Bit rotary speed (RPM) Average torque (Amps) 2. Midnight depths and dates. 3. Rate of penetration (ROP) in metres/hour every metre, bit details. 4. Measured depth and true vertical depth, casing shoes. 5. Percentage cuttings lithology. 6. Interpretive lithology. 7. Hydrocarbon gas analysis of mud stream returns, including trip gas. 8. Full lithological descriptions, mud weight and ECD, directional survey data, casing point data. The scales used for drilling data, ROP and gas analysis are repeated every 200 meters and also where scale changes occur.

Bioturbated Sandstones The Ula Formation sandstones are predominantly bioturbated and range from very fine-grained wackestone to medium grained grainstones. The burrow types in the Ula Formation were classified by Kirkham and Grainge (1979) and this has subsequently been slightly modified by subsequent authors (eg. Bristow, 1988). This classification scheme is shown in Table Al. Three main burrow associations have been described from the Ula Formation (Bristow, 1988, Leonard, 1988a): 1 This association consists almost entirely of horizontal, frequently clay lined, burrows of c. lcm diameter (mainly type burrows, Table Al). This association tends to occur within fine to medium-grained, well sorted sandstones and comprises the majority of the cored Ula Formation. 2 Association is dominantly composed of and type burrows which occur within the very fine-grained, argillaceous intervals towards the top and bottom of the Ula Formation. As the grain-size of the sandstones increases from very-fine to fine-grained and they become slightly less argillaceous, and type burrows decrease in abundance at the expense of other horizontal and vertical burrows; effectively forming transition to association 1. 3 This association is dominated by small (c. lmm diameter) horizontal type burrows. It occurs within siltstone intervals. The burrow associations are clearly lithologically (substrate) controlled, as consequence they change throughout the cored interval in response to overall grain-size variations. Within the well sorted fine to medium-grained sandstones towards the top of coarsening- upwards sequences the overall degree of bioturbation decreases. Bioturbation is most intense within the finer grained, more argillaceous sandstones. The variation in the degree of bioturbation is particularly marked in association with graded and structureless beds. Within the individual fining-upwards beds the basal portion is weakly bioturbated with the degree of bioturbation increasing upwards. Only burrow association is present in the 7/12-A-08 core.

In this report most of the whole well plots are on true vertical depth scale of 1:20000 allowing the use of the transparent, condensed lithology overlay enclosed. Wireline data has been digitised at the wellsite from field prints and represents average values over an interval rather than high resolution log. Normal compaction trends have been established using data from this as well as previous wells drilled. These trends compare well with trends seen in neighbouring sections of the North Sea. The Eaton overlay method is mentioned in the appendix to this report. Emphasis is made that the technique is only suitable for argillaceous formation. Compaction trends are based on true vertical depth and Eaton overlay plots relate to T.V.D. based data. context_snippets.text: Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, includ- ing petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries through Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS) petroleum exploration and exploitation risk tool developed at Amoco, we obtain valuable and unique information on three major top- ics relevant to exploration: 1) Hydrocarbon Migration, 2) Seals and 3) Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum and two major topics relevant to production: 1) Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimitation and 2) Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy involves the rapid, complete analysis of volatiles trapped as fluid inclusions in rock samples using quadrupole mass analyzers. The technology documents the presence and relative bulk abundance of ionized volatile fragments with mass/charge ratio of m/z 180. This includes most geologically important inorganic species as well as organic species with less than or equal to 13 carbon atoms. The resulting analysis of the petroleum fraction is comparable to the low molecular weight fraction of whole-oil gas chromatographic mass spectrometric (GCMS) analysis (without devolatilization of the gas fraction); hence, the major classes of hydrocarbons (e.g., aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins) are represented. The Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy program at FIT is unique in several ways: 1) the method- ology and theoretical framework necessary for this unique technology are the result of long-standing research and development effort, 2) the cumulative experience and database of documented case histories are the most extensive in the world and 3) the technology rep- resents the most rapid analytical capability of its kind available. In its present configuration, FIS instrumentation has the potential to analyze all available samples for 2-4 wells in 24 hr period at total cost of approximately $4000-5000 per well, thus making it one of the most inexpensive and rapid geochemical techniques available. The resulting dataset can provide nearly continuous log of paleofluid chemistries through the stratigraphic section penetrated by well, and, given adequate sample coverage, the data can be mapped in two or three dimensions. 1.1 Organization of this Report Analytical results of the FIS analysis of 34 A1 BH are presented graphically in Sections and as series of profiles each illustrating the variation of particular atomic mass (m/z) or ratio of two masses with measured depth. general discussion of the interpretation of FIS data including the significance of particular features and trends (or their absence) is provided in Section A. The remaining information provided in subsequent sections includes: 1) refer- ence spectra, collected on internal standards and used to monitor inter- and intra-analytical consistency of the quadrupole analyses which are presented and discussed in Appendix B; and 2) mass spectra for m/z 180 from all samples which are listed individually by depth in Appendix C. 1.2 Analytical Procedure Samples of rock material are freed of significant interfering contamination by washing, picking and magnetic separation to remove drilling fluids, lost circulation materials, other solid mud

3 Photomicroscopy Thin sections were prepared from 34 A1 AH samples at depths warranting further exami- nation following preliminary assessment of the FIS analytical results. The sections were then examined under petrographic microscope using variety of fluid inclusion techniques (e.g., UV-fluorescence, microthermometry, etc.) in order to verify the presence of petroleum-bearing inclusions in the rock samples and to explore textural relationships that may yield additional information on the timing of hydrocarbon migration or generation. Petrographic examina- tion is also necessary to verify that petroleum-bearing fluid inclusions present in the samples and responsible for the observed mass spectra are not relict features (i.e., that they were not already present in the mineral grains prior to deposition). Some of the calcite cemented stringers can apparently be correlated across the N1-segment. However, the calcite cemented zones in A-1 AH are probably associated with fault zones. Faulting has affected the Rannoch Formation in A-1 AH as seen from the common tectonized lamination on the cores (see Enclosure 1); hence the reduced Rannoch Formation thickness in A-1 AH, when compared to other Visund wells, is likely not fully representative for the area. The Etive Fm. on Visund mainly consists of medium-coarse sandstones (El, E3, E5), however, zones of fine-grained, micaceous Rannoch-type facies (E2, E4) occur and apparently thicken northwards on the field. The Etive zonation reflects this interlayering of coarser and finer facies. In Well A-1 AH the upper part of the Etive Formation (and likely also the lowermost Ni) is probably faulted out (possibly eroded, however, these zones appear to be present in Well A-1 BH near by). The thinning of particularly the Etive zones E4 and E3 when compared to the other Visund wells is believed to be due to condensation caused by syndepositional tectonic activity in the area (i.e. the southern triangle on the N2-segment). This is in line with the seismic which suggests thinning of the Brent isochore within the southern triangle on the N2-segment. The Ness Fm. on Visund consists for large part of sandy bay fill facies, with typical channel sandstones being rare. The Tarbert Fm. on Visund consists of very fine to fine-grained, micaceous, hummocky cross-laminated sandstones. The Ness/Torbert boundary may be difficult to pick on logs only because of often transitional facies changes. The sands were deposited after the sediment-gravity currents encountered the adverse slope associated with the western margin of the Utsira High The Ty/Heimdal Formation sands at the WING Prospect are believed to be mixture of high- density turbidites and sandy debrites deposited through feeder channel from the north. The sands can be correlated to the north (i.e. 25/8-7) of the prospect (Figure 8). The map pattern and cross-sectional geometry are seismically well defined. debris-flow origin for the majority of the sands are supported by mounded geometry of the thickest reservoir interval along the western margin of the prospect, while more sheet-like deposits to the east could be deposited by turbidity currents. The Grane Field located to the south is suitable analog with thick sandstone deposition by high-density gravity currents and high reservoir quality continuing undiminished over the mounded parts of the field. Trap Definition/Spill Point In the current interpretation the Ty/Heimdal Formation sands pinch out along the NE-SW fault trend which defines the eastern margin of the lying Terrace (Figure 9). The trap is defined based on the assumption that the sands pinch out along the mapped fault. There is some seismic evidence for this, but the quality of the Top Ty seismic pick is sometimes relatively weak, and where the Ty/Heimdal Formation gets thin interference with the Top Chalk reflector complicates the interpretation. Trap definition in the eastern part of the prospect is therefore somewhat weak (Figure 10a, and c). The oil-water contact is believed to be identical to Tau West (2091 TVDSS), as the sands at WING probably are in communication with Tau West. The current mapping of Jotun shows that the Tau West structure does not spill structurally, and therefore has to be controlled stratigraphically or by structural spill point in an older reservoir in communication with Paleocene reservoirs. Figures and are geoseismic sections of the NW-SE oriented seismic line NH9010-102 and the NE-SW oriented seismic line B-17-83. These lines illustrate the geological evolution of block 6507/2. The geological evolution of the area can be subdivided into four tectonic cycles. Each cycle started with major tectonic event which gave rise to structural relief and subsequent sedimentation controlled by tectonic lineaments. At later stage of each cycle, the sedimentation continued under tectonically quiet conditions with relief levelling, before new tectonic event initiated the next cycle. Structural elements mentioned in the text are shown in figure la. Cycle 1: Cambrian - Middle-Permian The collision of two continental plates, the Greenland/North America Plate and the Fennoscandian/Russian Plate initiated the first cycle which gave rise to the Caledonian Orogeny. Compressional episodes, combined with volcanic activity entailed deformation and metamorphism of sedimentary rocks involved in the orogeny. Early Devonian and older rocks are therefore expected to represent economic basement in the area. The Caledonian Mountain Chain is oriented in predominately NNE-SSW direction. 2.1 Classification Samples were classified using point-count results, according to the scheme of Pettijohn (1975). Quartz arenites are the dominant lithologies (Figure 2.1), with the following exceptions: lithic wacke at in the Lysing; subarkoses at m, and in the Lange; and sublitharenites at in the Lysing and and in the Tilje. It should be noted that in Jurassic samples, where feldspar dissolution is advanced, depositional arkosic component may have been diagenetically removed. Textural attributes are derived from grain size point-count data which are presented as histograms in Appendix and are summarised on Table 2.1. The Cretaceous Lysing and Lange Formation mass flow reservoirs are very fine (U) sands to coarse (L) sands, with the Lysing samples being comparatively slightly finer. In these formations sorting is moderate to moderately good and grain shapes vary from angular to rounded. Compaction is weak to moderate, which is less than would be expected under normal burial conditions for sandstones at this depth (2420-2940 below sea floor). Gam Formation sandstones are fine (U) to coarse (L) sands with good to moderately good sorting and subrounded to rounded grains. Compaction is moderate. Are/Tilje Formation sandstones comprise fine (L) to medium (L) sands, are well to moderately well sorted and subangular to subrounded. Compaction is moderately strong. Quartz, which is mostly monocrystalline and unstrained, is the dominant detrital component in Lysing/Lange samples except in the lithic wacke at m. Potassium feldspars are quite common (up to 4.0%) and generally only exhibit minor dissolution. Plagioclase feldspars and occasional microcline characterise lower Lange samples between and (3.7-5.3%). Rock fragments are widespread but generally quite minor (trace-4.3%); these comprise predominantly sedimentary clasts (mudrock, some containing calcispheres and chert fragments) with subordinate metamorphic clasts. Micas include relatively fresh muscovite (0.3-5.3%) and chloritised former biotite. Coaly carbonaceous fragments are locally common as is glauconite. Detrital illite/smectite clays are sparse but widespread, except for the uppermost lithic wacke (2822.54 m) and the subarkoses in the lower Lange (trace-2.7%). As they represent potential provenance indicators for the turbidites, heavy minerals were examined. Lysing sandstone heavy minerals comprise euhedral to rounded zircon, rutile and occasional anatase and apatite; tourmaline is absent/very rare In samples from the upper _LAPS

The performance of the TriSor OFS surface equipment during the survey was excellent, with accurate gun tuning throughout. ▪ The downhole data recorded with the Borehole VSI tool was of high quality, and good vector fidelity was recorded with high signal to noise ratio. ▪ Good first break picks were obtained in the main VSP part of the well. Estimated time picks were extended almost to seabed using the horizontal components. ▪ VSP processing was done using the component and zero phase corridor stack was obtained with bandwidth of 5-140Hz. The full bandwidth zero phase P-P corridor stack shows an increase in resolution compared to the provided surface seismic data. ▪ Compressional sonic log calibration was done with minimal drift correction and set of synthetic seismogram traces was generated for various zero phase Ricker wavelets. ▪ The full bandwidth (5-140Hz) 60ms corridor stack, along with the 5-70Hz reduced bandwidth corridor stack, tie well with the Ricker wavelet synthetic seismograms for variety of different bandwidths. ▪ good 3-way tie was made between the VSP corridor stack, Synthetics and 3D surface seismic data.

2 Acquisition A 4-level Versatile Seismic Imager (VSI) tool string (15.24m shuttle spacing) was used by Schlumberger to acquire the downhole data for the ZOVSP survey. The tools are fitted with three orthogonally opposed non-gimballed accelerometers providing flat frequency response from 2- 200Hz irrespective of the angle of tilt. A tuned array of 250cu.in Sercel G-Guns, operating at 2000psi was used as source for the survey. The guns were deployed by the rig’s crane. The guns target firing pressure was 2000 psi. Source control was provided via the use of the TriSor OFS in sea dynamic source controller and the calibrated near-field hydrophone sensor data were recorded at 1.25m below the gun cluster. The target gun depth was 5m below mean sea level (actual depth m) and the gun offset and azimuth from the wellhead were 75m and 140 degrees, respectively. The equipment was then used to acquire the main VSP survey data, at 15.24m intervals between 399.9 – 720.8m MD DF. The recording was done using the Schlumberger Maxwell acquisition system. At each level, at least five good repeatable shots were acquired and recorded. The main acquisition parameters and survey equipment are shown in Table 1. The full acquisition report can be found in the digital deliverables accompanying this report.

This applies differential correction to the sonic log where it is assumed the greatest amount of time error is caused by the lower velocity sections of the log. Over given interval the method will correct only At values which are higher than threshold, the Atmin. Values of At which are lower than the threshold are not corrected. The correction is reduction of the excess of At over Atmin ie. At - Atmin At - Atmin is reduced through multiplication by reduction coefficient which remains constant over the interval. This reduction coefficient, named G, can be defined as: G = + drift (At - Atmin) dZ Where drift is the drift over the interval to be corrected and the value (At - Atmin) dZ is the time difference between the integrals of the two curves At and Atmin, over the same interval. Hence the corrected sonic: Atmin = G(At - Atmin) + Atmin The sonic, density and Gamma ray log data are taken from the well 7221/12.
