6.3 Bathymetry The multibeam echo sounder data was processed onboard MV Fugro Meridian using Fugro Starfix suite to monitor data quality and data coverage. The data was logged in Simrad Raw format (.all) and imported into Starfix.Proc for processing. Both single beam and multibeam echo sounder data were corrected for transducer draught, acoustic velocity through sea water and vessel heave, pitch and roll, and then positioned with reference to the echo sounder transducer. 6.4 Sidescan Sonar The engineers and geophysicists examined the sidescan sonar records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks include range/scale, gains, tow fish height and position, as well as overall record quality. The sidescan sonar data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full by the geophysicist, using SonarWiz Version software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted, in which case the XTF file would be transferred to the relevant working directory for use, or, if rejected, would be flagged as potential re-run. Mosaicking of the sidescan sonar data was performed using the mosaic module, which applied slant range correction to the data and checked for full sonar coverage of the survey area. 6.5 Sub-bottom Profilers The engineers and geophysicists examined the hull-mounted pinger and mini sleeve gun records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks included sweep/scale, gains, examination of seabed pulse and penetration as well as overall record quality. The sub-bottom profiler data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full, by the geophysicist, using Starfix.Interp software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted or rejected and flagged as potential re-run. 6.6 2DHR Multichannel Seismic Quality control of the online 2DHR multichannel seismic system was undertaken by the onboard engineers, geophysicist and seismic processor. The engineers maintained an observers’ log (Appendix E.2) in which all relevant information was recorded. Typically, routine checks were made on the source and streamer; the engineers monitored the manifold pressure, gun statistics (including any dropped/mis-timed shots) as well as pulse/frequency spectra of the seismic source. Routine checks of the streamer included streamer integrity (noisy, dead or reverse polarity channels), noise (due to environmental factors or weather), and streamer depth control/feather angle. On completion of each 2DHR multichannel seismic line, the data underwent final QC. The onboard geophysicist used the RadExPro seismic processing system as well as the observers’ logs and other quality control data generated by the NTRS2 system. Shot and CMP gathers were generated, to allow the identification of bad channels/shots and noise problems, and to verify the streamer offset and depth of the gun array. Then, brute stack was generated for each line, to ascertain any swell noise and check the overall data quality. The data were processed aboard the Fugro Meridian using the OpenCPS seismic processing system. The data processing flows aim to remove noise and seismic interference from 2DHR data. Bioturbated Sandstones The Ula Formation sandstones are predominantly bioturbated and range from very fine-grained wackestone to medium grained grainstones. The burrow types in the Ula Formation were classified by Kirkham and Grainge (1979) and this has subsequently been slightly modified by subsequent authors (eg. Bristow, 1988). This classification scheme is shown in Table Al. Three main burrow associations have been described from the Ula Formation (Bristow, 1988, Leonard, 1988a): 1 This association consists almost entirely of horizontal, frequently clay lined, burrows of c. lcm diameter (mainly type burrows, Table Al). This association tends to occur within fine to medium-grained, well sorted sandstones and comprises the majority of the cored Ula Formation. 2 Association is dominantly composed of and type burrows which occur within the very fine-grained, argillaceous intervals towards the top and bottom of the Ula Formation. As the grain-size of the sandstones increases from very-fine to fine-grained and they become slightly less argillaceous, and type burrows decrease in abundance at the expense of other horizontal and vertical burrows; effectively forming transition to association 1. 3 This association is dominated by small (c. lmm diameter) horizontal type burrows. It occurs within siltstone intervals. The burrow associations are clearly lithologically (substrate) controlled, as consequence they change throughout the cored interval in response to overall grain-size variations. Within the well sorted fine to medium-grained sandstones towards the top of coarsening- upwards sequences the overall degree of bioturbation decreases. Bioturbation is most intense within the finer grained, more argillaceous sandstones. The variation in the degree of bioturbation is particularly marked in association with graded and structureless beds. Within the individual fining-upwards beds the basal portion is weakly bioturbated with the degree of bioturbation increasing upwards. Only burrow association is present in the 7/12-A-08 core.

In this report most of the whole well plots are on true vertical depth scale of 1:20000 allowing the use of the transparent, condensed lithology overlay enclosed. Wireline data has been digitised at the wellsite from field prints and represents average values over an interval rather than high resolution log. Normal compaction trends have been established using data from this as well as previous wells drilled. These trends compare well with trends seen in neighbouring sections of the North Sea. The Eaton overlay method is mentioned in the appendix to this report. Emphasis is made that the technique is only suitable for argillaceous formation. Compaction trends are based on true vertical depth and Eaton overlay plots relate to T.V.D. based data. The overburden gradient was compiled using formation densities from other wells on block 7/12 and sonic densities from the sonic log of 7/12 A01. More information on the techniques used in overpressure detection may be found in the GEARHART GEODATA manual OVERPRESSURE (1986 Internal publication).

All LWD memory data was dumped and logs produced as per requirements. The first wireline run became stuck at 4782m, 4720m, 4555m and 4350m whilst logging up so the second run was cancelled and wiper trip was performed before running the 5/8” casing. A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Where it is found that sliding is unavoidable towards the end of the 12 1/4” section it may be worthwhile to have Dogsub available on the Rig in case a trip is made where it could be picked up, although it would probably not be worth making special trip for it. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. The rotary BHA consisted of full gauge double nearbit roller reamer followed by float sub and variable gauge Andergauge stabilizer. This was followed by CDR, ILS stabilizer and MWD tools, as well as the ADN tool for porosity and density logs. After drilling out the float collar, shoe track and shoe, the hole was displaced to 1.32sg Versavert oil based mud. Very moderate drilling parameters were used to drill out the shoe, plugs and cement in an effort to protect the bit from excessive wear. Consequently 4.5hrs were used before drilling on new formation. The second target at TVD of 4264m had been extended to the north to take into account the significant walk rates seen in the previous 12 1/4 section. This extension allowed the 1/2 section +/- 0.5deg/30m right hand walk rate as well as 0.5/30m build or drop rate, dependant on actual walk rates experienced. Hence, ideally, maintaining the inclination and azimuth would hit the middle of the target extension.

question: For Unit III (Fisher Formation) at PWL, what are the lithology, measured thickness, and wells exhibiting water‑filled sands?
answer_text: Interbedded sands and clays; thickness ≈85 m; water‑filled sands reported in wells 16/1-9, 16/1-8 and 16/1-13.

context_snippets.text: Shallow Soils Shallow soil conditions across the study area have been inferred from CPT information and sub-bottom profiler interpretation. The CPT results suggest homogeneous Unit (Witch Ground Formation) composition comprising very dense silty sand, with occasional silt and clay layers. Unit is overlain by Top Seabed Layer (TSL), typically ~ to thick, of loose to dense, silty, clayey sand. Unit thickness is relatively uniform in the vicinity of the PWL, but thickens slightly south-westwards. Unit is expected to be ~13.6 thick at the PWL. Unit is underlain by Unit II deposits interpreted to represent Coal Pit Formation deposits. Unit II is expected to comprise stiff clay with clayey sand layers. Coarse material such as gravel and boulders may occur within this unit. Unit II thickness ranges from ~11 in the south-westernmost part of the study area to ~56 about km south- west of the PWL. Unit II is expected to be ~39 thick at the PWL. Potential Geohazards General The PWL is located in part of the North Sea where shallow gas is potential geohazard, especially at the Crenulate Reflector and within the Pliocene deposits. blowout occurred at 494 RKB corresponding to the Upper Unit VI level (upper part of Pliocene deposits, ‘Crenulate Reflector’) at well 16/4-1 located in the south-western part of the Luno II area. Gas was encountered at wells 16/1-6 S, 16/1-4, 16/1-8, 16/1-9, 16/1-10, 16/1-13, 16/1-14 and 16/4-5 in the Pliocene deposits. Formation gas reaching maximum of more than 3% at depths probably corresponding to the top and upper Unit VII level (Late Miocene deposits) was observed in wells 16/4-4 and 16/5-5. Shallow Gas at the PWL Shallow gas cannot be excluded at Upper Unit VI level (upper part of Pliocene deposits, ‘Crenulate Reflector’). slight gas warning is issued for the interval from Shallow Water Flow at the PWL Due to the interbedded sand/clay nature an structural complexity of the Fisher and Ling Bank Formations, there is general potential for shallow water flow in the study area. The seismic data does not indicate any particular structural closures within these deposits at the PWL. Hence, the probability of shallow water flow events at the PWL is considered to be low. Boulders at the PWL The nearest boulder (height: m) on the seabed has been identified on sidescan sonar data ~460 NNE of the PWL. Coarse material and scattered boulders may occur throughout the Quaternary deposits below Unit down to the base of Unit at the PWL (113.5 ± to 412 ± 13 MSL, 152 ms to 473 ms TWT). Faulting No major faulting has been identified in the vicinity of the PWL down to the limit of interpretation at 1203 ± 45 MSL (1238 ms TWT).

1.1 INTRODUCTION On the instructions of Lundin Norway AS, Fugro Survey AS (FSAS) performed an integrated geophysical survey over the 16\1-14 well site and extended region during the period to 16 May 2010. The survey vessel M/V Birkeland was used for the purpose of the integrated survey. The geophysical survey was required to provide information for the location, emplacement and operation of a semi-submersible drilling rig at the proposed well location and also to give an extended regional survey over the area to the east of the proposed well site. Proposed Location Co-ordinates Proposed Well Location 16\1-14 International 1924 Spheroid, ED50, UTM Zone 31N, 3°E Longitude Latitude Easting Northing This survey comprised two different types of grid. The densely spaced lines of the main survey grid consisted of km km grid orientated 359° / 179° and 089° / 269°. second larger grid covered this site survey and extended both east and west. The larger grid had the same line orientation but covered an area approximately km km. The survey programme is presented in Figure 1.1. The survey spread consists of: • Multibeam echo sounder (MBE) • Side Scan Sonar (SSS) • Sub Bottom Profiler (SBP) • Mini Air Gun (MAG) • 2D High Resolution multichannel Seismic (2DHR) The survey was performed as integrated acquisition, i.e. SSS, MBE, MAG, SBP and 2DHR simultaneously. The survey line plan consists of: • 33 lines orientated North/South • 18 cross lines orientated East/West • tie-line

Unit II (Swatchway and Coal Pit Formations) Unit II contains deposits of the Swatchway and Coal Pit Formations and comprises stiff to hard silty clay with occasional layers of dense sand and gravel. Scattered boulders may occur throughout the unit. glacial channel filled with Coal Pit Formation sediments runs from NE to SW through the north- western part of the survey area. The channel’s slope is located about 600m NW of PWL. Additionally numerous small-scale erosional channel features are observed on sub-bottom profiler data in the upper part of Unit II, some extending only few metres (Appendices and 6.5). The thickness of Unit II is expected to be about 28m at the PWL. The unit thickness varies within 2km radius around PWL between 26m in the SW and 130m within the channel in the NW. Within 2km radius around PWL the depth to the base of Unit II varies from 142m MSL in the SW to 247m MSL in the NW. Figure 4.3: 2D seismic line LN1052-313 through PWL 16/1-14 showing the Quaternary sequence (Units I to V). Unit III (Fisher Formation) The Fisher Formation is absent in the eastern part of the survey area and in the northwest, where it has been eroded by glacial channels filled with Coal Pit and Ling Bank Formation deposits. Where the Unit is present it shows parallel to sub-parallel reflectors with high amplitudes. The Fisher Formation is interpreted to comprise interbedded sands and clays. Water filled sand layers at this level were reported for wells 16/1-9, 16/1-8 and 16/1-13. Scattered boulders may occur throughout the unit. The thickness of Unit III is expected to be about 85m at the PWL. Within 2km radius of the PWL the maximum unit thickness is 87m NE of PWL. FSAS Report No. 9059.V00 Page 15

Potential Geohazards General The study area is located in part of the North Sea where shallow gas frequently occurs at the Crenulate Reflector (top of Unit VII) and in Lower Pliocene deposits (near top of Unit VIII), as results from nearby wells show. Shallow water flow is well-known problem in this region and several nearby wells have experienced this. Shallow Gas at the PWL The presence of shallow gas cannot be excluded at the PWL. slight shallow gas warning is issued at Anomaly Level (top of Unit VII), 372 ± 12 to 396 ± 13 MSL (431 to 457 ms TWT). General precautions are recommended at Anomaly Level (616 ± 21 MSL, 684 ms TWT) due to regional experience. Shallow Water Flow at the PWL Problems with shallow water flow were experienced at wells 16/1-9 (Opseth et al 2009), 16/1-13, 16/1-8 and 16/1-14 at the top of the Fisher Formation (Part of Unit IV) The vertical path of the PWL leads through interpreted channel deposits (Ling Bank and possible Fisher Formation). The seismic data suggests possible structural closure where shallow water can be trapped. Therefore moderate probability of encountering shallow water flow has to be considered at the PWL, between 203 ± MSL and 223 ± MSL (250 – 271 ms TWT). Boulders at the PWL Scattered boulders may occur within the Quaternary deposits below Unit (Units II to V,115.5 ± to 372 ± 12 m). Coarse deposits are most likely to be associated with the base of channels filled with Unit II to Unit IV deposits. Channels The PWL is located within channel, filled with Ling Bank Formation deposits (and possible Fisher Formation deposits. The base of the channel is expected to be penetrated by vertical well path at 223 ± MSL (271 ms TWT). Faulting Minor faulting has been observed within the Quaternary units associated with erosional events and sediment loading. No major fault is observed to intersect vertical path of the PWL. Environmental Considerations No environmental survey has been performed for PWL 16/1-27. Environmental investigations have been undertaken in 2012 for the near-by route surveys to the Edvard Grieg platform (FSLTD Reports No. 00911.1, and 00911.3). No indications of corals or potential protected habitats have been identified on the sidescan sonar data near PWL 16/1-27.

This is to be expected, since plug permeabilities are difficult to measure below 0.01mD, and will be biased high if any fractures at all are present in the core. We're probably seeing fracture permeability on these tests. I don't know where the perm data comes from on your 15/9-A22 summary diagram, so won't comment on its accuracy. It does not appear to be consistent with an interval dominated by Type seals. Even Type seal will have permeability in the .001-.005 rnD range. Using the oil and water density data that you supplied me, have estimated maximum column heights for the two 15/9-A22 samples. The wackestone can support an oil column of 400 ± 100 meters, while the argillaceous siltstones can support columns of 1200 ± 300 meters. Looking at your sketch, it looks like the siltstone is unstained, while the lower Hod Formation wackestones are stained. This implies one of the following: • If the siltsones are continuous over the closure, 1200m oil column (unlikely). • If the siltstones are discontinuous, 400 meter column is still necessary to stain the wackestone. Alternatively, if the staining is along fractures, the interval could have been stained with smaller oil column, and the oil would never have intruded the matrix pores. This seems more likely. Is it possible to examine the core and determine, in detail, where the staining occurs? • If the staining is in coarser-grained carbonates than the ones you sampled in this well, the stained intervals may have been fed by fractures. Depending on the underlying column height in the trap, you will see selective staining in the coarsest intervals. In this scenario, the column height can be bracketed by the entry pressures of the best stained and worst unstained seals. However, this also seems unlikely, since all Hod samples from this well appear to be Type seals. Without looking at any more data, it appears that the stain distribution in the 15/9-A22 makes the most sense if staining occurs only along fractures, or is selective and restricted to coarser-grained intervals than the ones you ssent to EPR for analysis. 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

Title: Standard Core Description, Well 25/11-22 No. 2 SEDIMENTOLOGY 2.1 Introduction A summary sheet of the core description is given in Enclosure 1. It contains the core log description with relative percentages of mud and sand. Gamma Ray curve with logger's depths is given for comparison and correlation with the graphical core log. At the left side of the summary sheet the stratigraphy is given with groups, formations and ages defined by the core facies, log patterns and biostratigraphic dating. The macro-biological content and degree of bioturbation are given according to internal Norsk Hydro procedure. The burrowing intensity scale runs from to 6, being virtually non-bioturbated, and being completely reworked by bioturbation. bathymetric curve is presented. This is an integrated interpretation based on the core description. On the right-hand side of the summary chart, comments are made on the processes and environments interpreted by the present authors. All depths on the core log are drillers depths. 2.2 Lithostratigraphy of the Palaeogene interval The Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession of the Viking Graben (Rogaland Group; lsaksen and Tonstad, 1989) comprises sandstones, mudrocks and tuffaceous deposits of highly variable thickness. In the central parts of the Viking Graben, the Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession reaches thicknesses in excess of about 1000m, whereas much thinner successions are found, for example on the Utsira High, where minimum succession thicknesses of about 100m are seen. Chalk deposits, of both autochtonous and allochtonous origin, of the Cretaceous-Danian Shetland Group, underlie the Palaeogene clastic succession. Two lithostratigraphic nomenclatures exists for the studied succession (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992). In recent studies it has been found to be most practical to use combination of the two nomenclatures, although with the main emphasis on the one by Isaksen and Tonstad (1989). lsaksen and Tonstad's subdivision of the Paleocene-Eocene into the Rogaland and Hordaland Groups is maintained, rather than the three-fold subdivision of Mudge and Copestake (1992). The Hordaland Group is not subdivided into formations, whereas the Rogaland Group consists of the Vale-, Lista-, Sele- and Balder Formations. number of other formation names were introduced by lsaksen and Tonstad in order to distinguish sandstone-rich intervals in the Palaeogene. However, as pointed out in Mudge and Copestake (1992), these refer to locally occurring sandstones, and should therefore not be given formation status. Major sandstones within the formations are seen as members, as will be discussed in the forthcoming paragraphs. The regional lithostratigraphic compilations (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992) provide set of criteria to distinguish between the four main formations. Hydro No : R-086271 ((( E&P Division F-Bergen Date Page : : 1999-11-12 31 of 38 3 SUMMARY The petrographical study from well 6305/7-1 are based on modal analyses, X-ray diffraction and SEM investigations. Samples were selected from the main types. The samples classify mostly as subarkoses in all formations with matrix content up to 7% and total cement content of approximately 5%, except in the heavily carbonate cemented samples. Quartz cement appears in all samples except in the matrix rich greywacke in Jorsalfare Formation. The clay mineral assemblage in all samples consists mainly of smectite-chlorite mixed layer clay that probably explains the high water saturation in the well. The permeability in the Egga Mbr. and Vale formation are primarily determined by their clay content, i.e. their macro/micro porosity relationship. In the Jorsalfare Formation, the cement content is the most important permeability reducing factor. The carbonate cementation are more important than the quartz cementation.

Rock Characterisation 3.3 Characteristics of the Reservoir: Summary & Discussion The following summary and discussion is based on the combined analysis of 6305/8-1, 6305/7-1 and 6305/5-1. The strength and stiffness distribution within the reservoir is governed by the lithology and facies sequences. detailed sedimentological and lithological description is given in /ref. 5, 20 & 21/ and is summarised below together with the rock mechanic properties. 3.3.1 Reservoir lithology The reservoir sequence is represented by the Jorsalfare Formation of Maastrichtian age and the informal Egga member of the Lower Paleocene Vale Formation. The Jorsalfare Formation is characterised by interbedded sandstone and mudstone facies. The sandstones are generally medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses cemented either by quartz or occasionally abundant calcite. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from to 200 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show few internal structures other than occasional parallel lamination or bioturbation near their tops. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 30%. The Egga member of the Vale Formation is dominated by sandstone but both the top and base of the sequence have significant proportion of interbedded mudstone. The sandstone units in the lower and upper part of the sequence are generally fine to medium grained (occ. coarse), fining upward, moderately to occasionally poorly sorted subarkoses to sublitharenites which are slightly to moderately cemented with quartz (2 to 8% by volume) and occasionally abundantly cemented with carbonate. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from 10 to 350 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show some primary structuring such as horizontal or cross laminations. More massive sandstones (little or no interbedded mudstone) occur in or near the middle of the sequence and are characterised by relatively featureless, fine to medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses which are poorly to slightly cemented with quartz (& occ. calcite). The beds have sharp bases and range between 50 to 700 cm in thickness. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. so-called 'pinstriped' mudstone which contains mm-thick layers of siltstone occurs near the base of the Egga member and varies in thickness across the Ormen Lange field. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 35%. 3.3.2 Strength & Stiffness of the Reservoir formation The rock strength and stiffness varies with porosity, grain size distribution, volume of cement and silt/clay/shale content and the variation in strength clearly reflects the interbedded nature of the sandstone and mudstone units (including the erosive bases to the sandstone units) and their distribution within the Egga Member and Jorsalfare Formation (figures - 3.3). Within the thicker sandstone units, slight increases in strength and/or stiffiless (note: corresponding decrease in Poisson's ratio) from the base to the top of the unit can be associated with fming upward effects and/or the influence of bioturbation. Porosity is logically associated with strength and stiffness and the weakest most compressible layers are generally observed to have the highest porosity. 2.3 Summary of the well All depths in this programme are with reference to RKB (23,5 m) unless otherwise stated. Well 6305/1-1 will be drilled with the semi-submersible drilling vessel Transocean Leader. 6305/1-1 is vertical well with an estimated TD of 4500 m. Well TD criteria is 4500 meter or drilling into rocks of Cenomanian age. The objectives of the well are to: O Test the reservoir potential within the Paleocene/Eocene and Cretaceous sequences: - Vale (Egga Mbr.) as primary target - Balder as secondary target - Lysing and Lange as third targets O Test the hydrocarbon potential and the type of hydrocarbons O Secure an optimal seismic tie to the subsurface and to understand the seismic response to the rock properties and fluid fill O Have the well approved as commitment well Drilling Strategy The basic drilling strategy for this well is to have the required safety margins in all operations. And - at the same time have the flexibility to handle the underlying uncertainties (geology, pore pressure and formation integrity). To achieve this, mud density and ECD must be controlled and maintained higher than the pore pressure, but lower than the formation fracture gradient. The mud density during drilling shall be based solely on evaluated pore pressure and not the pore pressure prognosed in this programme. Fracture gradient data will be obtained through leak-off tests (LOT). ECD will be measured by Pressure-While-Drilling sub (PWD) with real-time surface read-out. Surge & swab guidelines for tripping will be established using software for hydraulic calculations. Well design The well is deep water well with 839 water depth. Temperature at seabed is -1°C. Potential high bending loads requires an extra heavy conductor string. Pore Pressure Due to lack of relevant correlation wells the uncertainty in the pore pressure prognosis is higher than normal. Pore pressure evaluation will be highly focused during drilling. In addition to the pore pressure evaluation performed by the mudlogging company, an independent evaluation will be performed by Hydro-assigned pore pressure specialists.

1 INTRODUCTION This report is part of the research and development project “Mechanical effects of depletion of the Kristin field” carried out for Statoil. The main objective of the project is to study geomechanical issues related to the development of the Kristin field. The work consists of the following four specific topics: I. Behaviour of intact rock and faults A) Review on fault characterisation and properties B) Description and classification of core material, with focus on faults and fracture types C) Laboratory testing on reservoir and fault rock material D) Interpretation of existing laboratory tests, preliminary geomechanical analyses, and development of constitutive models for intact rock and faults II. Characterisation of shallow seismic horizons with focus on gas leakage, sand distribution and faults. III. Effects of stress changes due to production on fault properties in the reservoir and overburden. IV. Investigation of rock deformations and failure during production by geomechanical analysis. 7.2 Core Analysis A total of 11 cores were cut in well 34/7-A-4 H. The cores were cut in the Lunde Formation in the interval from to MD RKB drillers depth. The core recovery was % (recovered of m). The depth shifts to match the log depths are listed in Table 7.2.1. Conventional core analysis was carried out by GECO-PRAKLA. This including measurements of helium porosity, air permeability and grain density. The report of the conventional core analysis are distributed to the partners. The conventional core analysis are presented together with the log interpretation in Appendix and in Figure 7.1.1. The net sand averages are given in Tabel 7.1.2. 7.3 Special Core Analysis A detailed SCAL programme is being carried out on selected core samples from well 34/7-A-4 H. Resistivity Index in conjunction with oil/water capillary pressure measurements Formation Factor at reservoir pressure, permeability and pore volume changes at various confining pressures Co/Cw at simulated reservoir overburden pressure The results will be available during 1993. 7.4 Formation Pressure Measurements A Repeat Formation Tester (RFT) with HP gauge was used to obtain formation pressure measurements, see Table 7.4.1. During taking the formation pressure measurements, the HP gauge became unstable and no HP formation pressures in the water zone was obtained. The reliable HP gauge formation pressures in the oil zone are within three psi compared to the formation pressures taken in the well 34/7-1. The strain gauge pressures are plotted in Figure 7.4.1, showing an oil gradient of bar/m equivalent to an oil density of g/cc. Only one reliable formation pressure was taken in the water zone, therefore no oil water contact can be defined in the well. From the log interpretation oil is proved down to 3007m MD RKB (2583.5 TVD RKB) and water up to MD RKB (2590.3 TVD RKB). The most likely contact in the well is defined at the MD RIO (2586 TVD RKB), is assumed to be the same as defined in well 34/7-1. 7.5 Fluid Analysis No fluid sample was collected during the logging of well 34/7-A-4 H.

• 7.1.2 Log Analysis The well has been analysed using deterministic model. The effective porosity calculation is based on the density log with correction for hydrocarbon effects and shale volume. The shale volume is mainly calculated as the minimum value from the density-neutron crossplot method and the gamma ray. Water saturation is calculated from the Poupon-Leveaux (Indonesia) equation. The dip and borehole corrected deep resistivity measurement from the phasor induction log has been used as the true resistivity. The dip and borehole corrected medium resistivity reading was used in one interval where the deep, dip corrected measurement saturates. Continuous log permeabilities are estimated using the Horizon software package. The database for the permeability prediction consists of conventional core air permeabilities and log data from all the cored Upper Lunde reservoir intervals in the Snorre Field. The input parameters have been picked from log crossplots from this well and from conventional core analysis from other wells in the area. Electrical factors from special core analysis and formation water resistivity are the same as those used in the Snorre Field Development and Operating Plan (FDP). The input parameters are summarised in Table 7.1.2. The basis for the cut-off values used for net sand evaluation is as reported in the FDP. The porosity cut-off used for net sand calculation is based on the value corresponding to mD from core porosity vs. core permeability (air) crossplots. porosity cut-off of 15 % is used in the Lunde Formation, the applied shale volume cut-off is 40 %. The petrophysical net sand averages are summarised in Tables 7.1.3 and 7.1.4. The interpretation (CPI) of reservoir zones LO1 to LO7 is given in Fig. 7.1.1. and 7.1.2. The bottom of the computer processed interpretation is at mTVD RKB (3849.5 MD RKB) in reservoir zone L08. Refer to chapter for reservoir zonation. The CPI plot of the Lunde reservoirs is given in 1:500 scale in measured depth in Appendix and in true vertical depth in Appendix 4. Good reservoir properties are calculated throughout the sandstones in the oilbearing part of the reservoir zone LO2 - L05. The initial OWC was expected in the interval 4 TVD RKB in reservoir zone L06. The logs indicate oil down to mTVD RKB and water up to 2633 mTVD RKB, with the OWC most likely in the shale just at the top of reservoir zone L06. Due to pressure depletion, no OWC can be defined from formation pressures.

A rig source VSP survey was recorded in this vertical well on 3/10/94. During the survey five runs into the well were required in order to satisfactorily record 170 levels between 970 and 4400m. The source used was Bolt airgun array consisting of four 160 cu.in. guns, positioned 69m from the wellhead along bearing of 70 degrees, and at depth of 4.5m below MSL The source signature was monitored using hydrophone 2m above the array. For the purposes of trial for VSP derived synthetic sonic, data were recorded by dual receiver array positioned at intervals of the same value as the spacing between the two geophones (i.e. 15m). This has meant that there are numerous levels recorded more than once, though this is also due to levels duplicated during the different runs into the well. For the standard processing for this well, generally only the best level data recorded was selected to represent any level shot more than once, although data consistency was also aimed for in deciding which data to use. Note also that no significant timing discrepancies were encountered between such duplicated levels, implying that reasonable depth control was maintained throughout the survey. DATA TIMING AND COMPUTATIONS Noise transmitted through casing sections caused severe problems in timing the majority of the data, particularly for shallowest levels where casing noise arrivals are evident before the expected direct arrivals. In an attempt to identify direct arrivals throughout the bulk of the data, several noise attenuations were carried out. The data was first filtered using restrictive 2,5-40,45 Hz bandpass filter designed to retain most of the signal bandwidth (as seen by F-K analyses) whilst attenuating the casing noise of higher frequencies. Further to this, remaining casing noise has been attenuated through an enhacement and subtraction technique (after coarse downwave subtraction, casing noise was then estimated using a short median operator, this estimate finally being subtracted from the raw data). An automated trace alignment method was used on resultant direct arrival data, improved times generally being obtained as result. However, no usable times could be obtained for the levels at and above 2180m, these levels having to be disregarded due to the contamination from noise transmitted through the casing, nor for the level at 3944m. Final times were therefore obtained for 151 of the levels, although all those seen to be affected by casing noise should still be treated with caution. The check levels have been selected at vertical depth intervals of either 90m (for shallower levels) or 45m (for the deepest levels) in the calculation of interval velocities and for the sectional display of well geophone signals. ACOUSTIC LOG CALIBRATION The supplied acoustic log data appears to be generally of reasonable quality, but it has been edited for any erroneous values where appropriate. Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

Surface sampling was carried out in both DST's to obtain samples for recombination and PVT analysis. 4.2.1 Methodology for Interpretation The DST interpretations were carried out using the SAPHER PC interpretation package. All interpretations used the superposition method. The methodology used was: 1. Create Derivative/Log-Log plot to carry out diagnostics of the test, identify flow regions (early, middle and late time regions) and identify the reservoir and boundary models to be used in the analysis. This plot was used to identify the infinite-acting flow region and plot correct Homer straight line on the Semilog or Superposition plot. 2. Plot infinite-acting straight line on Superposition plot and identify main reservoir characteristics (permeability-thickness, skin). 3. Perform any supplementary plots that may assist in identifying character of late time flow (i.e., square-root of time plot for linear flow). 4. Return to Derivative/Log-Log plot and perform time and pressure match to dimensionless functions. Identify reservoir and boundary models to be used and generate synthetic dimensionless derivative and log-log functions for the model. Compare these with the test data. Iterate until good match is obtained. 5. Use the simulation capability to generate the synthetic pressure function from the final chosen model and the calculated reservoir parameters. Compare the synthetic pressure with the test pressure data to ensure that good match is obtained over the whole test, not just the portion being analyzed.

context_snippets.text: Structural appraisal of cores from 6406/2-1 and 6406/2-2, Lavrans Field, Haltenbanken, Norway. 151 4.5 Methodologies This section summarises the petrographic and petrophysical characterisation methodologies that were employed. 4.5.1 Petrographic characterisation techniques Polished blocks and stubs of fractured surfaces were examined with CAMSCAN CS44 high performance scanning electron microscope equipped with secondary electron (SE) detector, high resolution solid state four quadrant back-scattered electron (BSE) detector, cathodoluminescence (CL) detector and an EDAX energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS). The secondary electron (SE) signal provides topographic information and is therefore extremely useful for investigating the relationships between detrital and authigenic components and establishing their relative timing. The back-scattered electron (BSE) signal is directly proportional to the mean atomic number of the mineral; so phases of different mass have different brightness levels. The BSE signal can be combined with an image analysis system for obtaining quantitative data on mineralogical abundances, grain-sizes, porosity and cement distributions. The CL signal is extremely sensitive to trace element abundances and provides information on the growth zonations where different growth zones incorporate slightly different trace element levels. Some elements (e.g. Fe) are known to suppress the luminescence signal, whereas others (e.g. Ti and Mn) are known to enhance the signal. Therefore different mineral generations (which have very similar chemical compositions and cannot be differentiated using BSE microscopy or the EDS system) can frequently be identified using cathode luminescence. The diagenetic history of both inside and outside faults are determined and used to establish the timing of deformation in relation to the major diagenetic events. The microstructures of the deformation features were used to assess/identify the active rock deformation mechanisms (e.g. diffusive mass transfer, grain-fracturing etc.) and the history of deformation. Representative images using BSE and CL images are taken from inside and outside of the fault zone as well as traverses across the border zone areas. These images were saved in 8-bit (256 grey- levels) digital form, and then imported into an image analysis package. Processing of these images according to the philosophy and approach of Evans et al. (1994) yielded estimates of porosity and mineral abundance. This data set is then used to assess the effect of deformation on the porosity/permeability relations, and deformation/ diagenetic history of the rock. 4.5.2 Mercury Injection Porosimetry Investigation of reservoir capillary pressures was conducted using Micromeretics Autopore II 9220 mercury porosimeter. This equipment is capable of injecting mercury in step-like increments up to pressures of 60,000psi (-413MPa) into an evacuated, cleaned and dried core plug or cut sample. Capillary forces in the reservoir are functions of the surface and interfacial liquid tensions, pore size and shape, and the wetting properties of the rock. In the case of non-wetting liquid like mercury and assuming cylindrical pores this relationship is expressed by the Washburn (1921) equation: Equation 4-1 P, = -2 ycos I-, Where: P, = capillary pressure (dynes/cm2); = surface tension of Hg; = contact angle of mercury in air; rc = radius of pore aperture (pm) for cylindrical pore. The surface tension of mercury varies with purity. The accepted interfacial tension for air-Hg is 485 dynes/cm2. The contact angle between clean mercury and the solid containing the pore varies with solid composition, although a value of 140 is generally accepted. - 38 - The effect of pore geometry on petrophysical data The effect on plug-derived parameters Pore geometry data derived from thin sections can be used to predict petrophysical parameters like porosity, permeability and end point wetting phase saturation in drainage process. Ongoing research also focuses on generating capillary pressure curves. Porosity derived from BSE images is consistently lower than He-porosity (Fig. 3.10, up). This is due to resolution problem in the images acquired at relatively low magnification (X60). However, we know that abundant micro-porosity beyond the resolution in the BSE images is present in clay minerals, and in order to predict total porosity, the image porosity has to be calibrated to He-porosity by adding certain percentage of the clay content. Generally clay is quantified from the BSE images by thresholding grey levels (between the levels of pore and quartz). This works when kaolinite is the dominating authigenic clay. However, in the specimens examined in the present study chlorite predominates, and this mineral has higher grey level than quartz. good correlation with He- porosity was obtained by adding 50% of the clay (from BSE, Table 3.4) plus 50% of the chlorite content (Table 3.5) obtained by quantitative microanalysis, using both BSE and X-ray element images (Fig. 3.10, centre and down). This calibration was necessary before calculating the residual wetting phase saturation (S;) which was defined as the fraction between calculated micro-porosity and the calculated porosity (total porosity). Figure and illustrates the effect of pore geometrical parameters or parameters calculated from them on permeability measured on horizontal plugs. The image porosity, calculated total porosity and macro porosity (Fig. 3.11a-c) are all positively correlated with permeability. Macro porosity generally shows stronger correlation with permeability, since it represents the effective part of the pore network that controls fluid flow, and it is therefore applied for calculation of permeability. Image porosity and calculated porosity both contain micro-porosity that generally has negative effect on permeability. However, this expected trend is only seen for the samples from well 6406/2-2 (Fig. 3.11d). The pore size parameters median pore size, mean macro-pore area and equivalent circular diameter (Fig, 3.12a, and e) all show positive correlation with permeability. The two last are affected by the large number of small pores and were expected to have a poorer correlation than the median pore size that better accounts for the contribution from the small number of large pores. That was, however, not the case here.

• Petrologic study of Middle Jurassic sandstones 2 INTRODUCTION 0 STATOIL This study provides petrologic data for cores in the Garn, Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations in the Statoil well 6506/11-6, Kristin Field (Figure 2-1). The petrologic data include bulk chemical analyses (94 samples), modal analyses of thin sections from the same samples, photomicrographs of thin sections, and scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of fractured rock surfaces. new set of modal analyses of thin sections from the Garn Formation in well 6406/2-3T3 was also performed (24 samples) to obtain an internally consistent data set for comparing porosity development between this well and 6506/11-6. Together with routine core analyses (one-inch-diameter plugs) and wireline log profiles, these data are used to interpret the role of depositional sand quality and diagenesis in determining porosity, permeability, and net/gross distribution within these sandstone reservoirs. Comparisons are made with similar data from nearby wells in blocks 6506/11, 6506/12, and 6406/2 to develop semi-regional context for the results and to better understand sedimentologic controls and the lateral extent of porous intervals. Particular attention is given to examining the relationship of chlorite and bitumen coatings to reservoir quality and the possible factors controlling chlorite occurrence. An earlier phase of this study focused on evaluation of petrologic data provided by Saga Petroleum from wells 6406/2-1, 6406/2-2, and The goals of this study, presented at the PL 134 Exploration Committee Meeting Ni. 13 (October 1998), are as follows: • Explain observed porosity-permeability in terms of depositional & diagenetic controls. • Document and interpret patterns of grain-coating chlorite occurrence. • Study the effect of bitumen coatings on porosity-permeability. • Provide petrologic input for sedimentology studies. • Investigate the apparent westward & northward increase in chlorite coating and bulk sodium (plagioclase) content in the Garn Formation. • Document and interpret the high-permeability zone at the top of the Garn Formation. • Study the occurrence and lateral extent of interlayered porous and tight zones in the Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations.

7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

question: How do drillbreak depths at ~1303 m and 1575 m correlate with Dxc declines indicating increasing pore pressure?
answer_text: Both drillbreaks (≈1303 m and 1575 m) coincide with sharp Dxc cut‑backs, indicating rapid pore‑pressure increases beneath limestone seals.

At 1260m the Dxc derived pore pressure was estimated to be g/cc EQMW. At 1293m limestone was drilled and below this drillbreak occurred at •:. 1303m resulting in sharp cut-back in Dxc. The limestone acted as seal with a rapid pressure build-up occurring beneath it; gas levels increased sharply to a maximum of 18.29% at 1323m where oil shows were observed. The background gas increased from 0.40% to 1.00%. Pore pressure was estimated to be close to balance at g/cc EQMW and the mud weight was increased to g/cc in accordance with this resulting in the background gas immediately falling to its previous level of 0.40%. From 1340m the Dxc continued to slowly cut-back, however gas levels remained steady at between and 0.80% and at 1440m the pore pressure was estimated to be g/cc EQMW with the mud weight increased accordingly to 1.24 g/cc. Between 1440m and 1575m no change in the pore pressure was observed with gas levels remaining low and averaging 0.30%. At 1575m reverse drillbreak occurred as limestone was penetrated; on drilling into claystone below this the drillrate increased sharply resulting in cut-back in the Dxc. Gas levels also increased, the background gas rising to 2.00%. Connection gases were 1.03%, and 1.89% respectively. Since connection gases were recorded from above the limestone it was assumed that the pore pressure had been increasing steadily throughout the section above and not from just below the limestone. Balanced conditioned existed at this point with the pore pressure being calculated as g/cc EQMW. Drilling continued however without increasing the mud weight even thought the gas levels remained high. Chemical and visual checks were made to ensure complete removal of fluids. According to the program of the pre-study the cleaned core plugs were humidity dried at 60oC and 40% relative humidity or 105oC prior to further porosity and permeability analysis. 9.2.2 Helium porosity at 800 psig NCP and grain density The porosity of the samples from Batch and was determined by helium injection using a Boyle’s law porosimeter. The pore volume was determined using the He injection technique with the core plug in core holder at 800 psig net hydrostatic confining pressure. The grain volume was determined with the core plug in matrix cup with no confining pressure applied. Grain density was calculated from the recorded weight of the core plug. The bulk volume of the samples from Batch after drying at 60 degrees Celsius was calculated geometrically using the length and diameter of the sample. 9.2.3 Empirical Klinkenberg corrected gas permeability Gas permeability (horizontal, vertical plugs) was determined by flowing nitrogen gas through the samples. These estimates are lower than the permeabilities that Core Petrophysics obtained on the samples (attached). This is to be expected, since plug permeabilities are difficult to measure below 0.01mD, and will be biased high if any fractures at all are present in the core. We're probably seeing fracture permeability on these tests. I don't know where the perm data comes from on your 15/9-A22 summary diagram, so won't comment on its accuracy. It does not appear to be consistent with an interval dominated by Type seals. Even Type seal will have permeability in the .001-.005 rnD range. Using the oil and water density data that you supplied me, have estimated maximum column heights for the two 15/9-A22 samples. The wackestone can support an oil column of 400 ± 100 meters, while the argillaceous siltstones can support columns of 1200 ± 300 meters. Looking at your sketch, it looks like the siltstone is unstained, while the lower Hod Formation wackestones are stained. This implies one of the following: • If the siltsones are continuous over the closure, 1200m oil column (unlikely). • If the siltstones are discontinuous, 400 meter column is still necessary to stain the wackestone. Alternatively, if the staining is along fractures, the interval could have been stained with smaller oil column, and the oil would never have intruded the matrix pores. This seems more likely. Is it possible to examine the core and determine, in detail, where the staining occurs? • If the staining is in coarser-grained carbonates than the ones you sampled in this well, the stained intervals may have been fed by fractures. Depending on the underlying column height in the trap, you will see selective staining in the coarsest intervals. In this scenario, the column height can be bracketed by the entry pressures of the best stained and worst unstained seals. However, this also seems unlikely, since all Hod samples from this well appear to be Type seals. Without looking at any more data, it appears that the stain distribution in the 15/9-A22 makes the most sense if staining occurs only along fractures, or is selective and restricted to coarser-grained intervals than the ones you ssent to EPR for analysis. question: Which MWD/CDR failure modes are mitigated by in-line stabilizers versus roller reamers, and how do the mitigation mechanisms differ?
answer_text: In-line stabilizers mitigate high and cyclic-torque induced failures (e.g., coverplate screws backing off, exposed/stripped wiring, worn shock sleeves and detached electrical components) by reducing/damping torque transmission at the tool string; roller reamers mitigate the same rough-drilling damage by smoothing the hole and lowering aggressive bit-induced torque and cyclic loading.

CONCLUSION & RECOMMENDATIONS The MWD and CDR tool failures and damage to the MWD collars in the 12 1/4 hole section is consistent with extremely rough drilling conditions. The use of PDC bits with an aggressive cutting action and packed bottom hole assemblies produced high and cyclic torque. On both MWD runs and this caused the ten pin coverplate torx head screws to back off allowing the coverplate to fall away. The exposed MWD collar wiring was stripped away causing the real time communication failures between the MWD and CDR tools and hence the loss of real time Gamma Ray and Resistivity data. Anadrill has had previous experience of drilling in Chalk in this area, notably on well 2/11-8 where five MWD tool failures occurred in the 12 1/4 hole section. The failed tools all exhibited the following damage eaused by rough drilling: black dust on electr- ical connections, worn and loose shock sleeves and pressure activated pads and electrical components parted from circuit boards. Anadrill had recommended the use of roller reamers and the inclusion of 12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools to reduce the high and cyclic torque levels. The recommended config- uration of 12 1/4 bit-12 1/4 near bit roller reamer-8 CDR-12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer-8 MWD-12 1/4 stabilizer would have provided more protection for the CDR and MWD tools, but this was not utilised. On future vertical wells drilling in Chalk, Anadrill recommends the use of an In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools and the use of either roller reamers or turbine in the bottom hole assembly to reduce torque levels.

context_snippets.text: Weather conditions were described as good during the survey. The spacing was 10 from 2990 to 1550 MD RICB. and 20 m. Check shots were shot with A copy of the Seismic Field Reports are included in the Section 'Field Operations Report'. Editing, stacking and timing of data The component geophone data was displayed at large scale and each component edited. The in- dividual near field monitor records were timed to the main peak, and the corresponding geophone traces shifted by this time. It was found that this system delay was stable during the survey at 20 ms. The geophone data was stacked using median algorithm. summary of the traces included in the stack at each level, the system delays and residual alignment delays are contained in the Stack Report. The stacked geophone data was then timed, each level being checked interactively using blown up view of the first arrival window. The first arrival time was taken as the top of the first peak: this corresponds to `trough-to-trough' picking. The reader is referred to Appendix 1: First Arrival Pick- ing for full discussion of this process. 1 Check shot levels were recorded on the way in the hole. total of 144 zero offset levels and 16 Check Shot levels were recorded on the way up. The following levels have been edited due to noise; 2540 m, 2480 m, 2460 m, 2440 m, 2420 m, Hence 133 levels were timed and included in the check shot report, sonic calibration and the VSP data set. Check shot computations, calibration of Sonic Logs Using the first arrival values picked above, and information on survey geometry, the Check Shot Report was produced. Details of the computations and results are included in this section. The sonic and density logs were read from tape supplied from the client. After careful examination of the calculated drift between the integrated sonic log and check shot values, drift corrections were applied to the sonic log. Details of these drift corrections are given at the beginning of the Calibrat- ed Sonic Log. The logs themselves are displayed at two scales, 1:1000 (Enclosure Al) and 1:500 (Enclosure A2). These show the uncalibrated and calibrated sonic logs, density log, raw integrated sonic time, calibrated integrated sonic time and check shot information. The desired output was specified as Butterworth filter designed in the frequency domain as 12(18) - 70(24) Hz(dB/Oct) with minimum phase wavelet.For full discussion of `Deconvolution during VSP processing', see Appendix 2. After VSP deconvolution we applied enhancement of upgoing P-energy, by applying dip adaptive filtering to NMO-corrected CSG's. The CSG domain data enhancement was followed by RNMO (Reverse NMO correction). SPHERICAL DIVERGENCE COMPENSATION The loss of energy due to spherical divergence is compensated for by applying the scalar Si to sam- ple i, where Si = (Ti /TO)** and Ti is the time of sample i, TO the first arrival time, and data dependant parameter in the range to 1.5., in this case Prior to Migration we further resampled our data spatially to twice the original density (dx=12.5 m), which is preferable to our Migration algorithm. The spatial resampling was done by applying dip adaptive interpolation on NMO corrected CRG's. The pre-Migration data was finally filtered with al2 - 80Hz zero phase bandpass filter. VSP MIGRATION The finite difference depth migration algorithm is Pre-Stack Migration (shot record migration) algorithm. By assuming reciprocity, i.e. interchanging the sources and receivers the receiver wave- field is back-propagated from the surface. Modelling of the source wavefield is delayed until ex- trapolation of the receiver field reaches the depth at which the receiver is located The velocities we used for NMO correction varied only vertically, and they were derived from the Check Shot Report for the Zero Offset survey. question: How do the lithology and hardness of the Ekofisk Formation's chalky limestone (Shetland GP) compare with Tor, Hod and Blodøks?
answer_text: Ekofisk (Shetland GP): chalky off-white to light grey limestone, moderately hard; Tor: white limestone, moderately hard but becomes very hard with depth; Hod: off-white to white chalky limestone, moderately hard grading to marl with depth; Blodøks: medium–dark grey marl with argillaceous laminations (not limestone).

context_snippets.text: Lithology Description Seabed Consists of dense to very dense sands overlaying stiff clay. QUARTERNARY Clay with thin stringers of sand. Coarser material up to boulder size may occur. NORDLAND GP. - Pliocene and Pleistocene Grey claystone with thin stringers of sand and siltstone. Utsira formation Fine to medium grained, moderately well and well sorted sandstone with minor silt and limestone stringers. HORDALAND GP. - Eocene to Miocene Dominated by claystone and minor limestone/dolomite stringers with exception of the sandy Skade and Grid formations. Skade Fm. CHAPTER Summary 1. The youngest strata examined are mudstones assigned to the 'Lark Formation Equivalent' of Early Oligocene age. These deposits which accumulated under upper bathyal depths rest with minor unconformity upon the Eocene 'Horda Formation Equivalent'. Throughout the Eocene and Paleocene the NSPg sequence framework of RRI has been applied to assist regional/local correlations. 2. The Late Eocene is relatively thin and is considered, at least in part, to be condensed, as reflected in the higher gamma ray mudstone unit within Sequence NSPg180. 3. The Middle Eocene comprises stacked retrogradational sequences of NSPg140 through to NSPg170. The older sequences, especially NSPg140 and NSPg150, are significantly sand- prone. Throughout the Middle Eocene progressive reduction in both sand content and thickness of the sequence is evident reflecting gross retrogradational package. The sands, equivalent to the Grid Formation and the Caran Sandstone in the UKCS, were deposited via gravity flow processes into an upper bathyal or deeper setting being sourced off the Malloy Terrace area to the east. Contemporaneous sands exist in blocks 35/3 and 35/8. Recycled taxa suggest some erosion of the shelf/slope break. 4. minor hiatus separates the Middle and Early Eocene. Within the Early Eocene part of the Hordaland Group gravity flow sands occur in Sequences NSPg120-100, being time equivalent to the Frigg Formation as seen to the south in the Viking Graben. Minor erosion of the underlying Rogaland Group is indicated in Sequence NSPg100. It is considered likely that the 35/4-1 well was located close to the westward pinch-out of Eocene sands, with little or no easterly derived sands occurring further west beyond the Marflo Ridge. 5. The Rogaland Group part of the Early Eocene comprises the Balder Formation and Sele Formation, deposited under upper bathyal depths. 6. Available biodata suggest the possibility of minor hiatus at the base of Sequence NSPg70. with Sequence NSPg60 possibly missing. 7. Sequences NSPg55 to NSPg10 comprise an essentially conformable Late - Early Paleocene section, with trace sand development. Page

After BOP test new bit and MWD/CDR were run in the hole, and drilling continued down to 2768 mMD, where communication with the MWD was lost, again requiring trip back to surface to change the tool. The hole was backreamed to the shoe with overpull on connections necessitating the hole to be circulated clean at 2674, 2446, and 2339 mMD. The mud weight was also incresed to sg. This final BHA only changed the MWD tool from the previous run, and drilled to section TD of 3126 mMD, in the Frigg Formation. Steering was very difficult on this run and the hole angle built up to 65.2° at 3100 MD. The mud weight was increased to sg while drilling this section, and up to while circulating the hole clean prior to pulling out of the hole. Due to incresed torque and pressure the hole circulated clean at 2921, 2529, and 880 mMD. The 133/8 casing was run to and cemented at mMD, needing 100 tons of weight and working the casing to pass 2116 mMD. After performing the second stage of cementing at 977 mMD, the combo tool to do this was left in the hole, and was retrieved at the second attempt. cement squeeze was then done to ensure isolation behind the casing at 977 mMD. 121/4 HOLE SECTION The 12 IA BHA was made up including TRACS adjustable stabiliser and Security FM2943 PDC bit, and after drilling through the float collar the well was displaced to sg Carbo Sea OBM. The casing shoe was then drilled out prior to cleaning out the rat hole. No FIT was performed at this point. The hole was drilled from 7 mMD, adjusting the TRACS as necessary, and occasionally orienting to allow the hole angle to graadually drop to 54° by 3657 mMD. At 4117 mMD an attempt to change the TRACS position from 11 'A to 10 1/4 failed, and the BHA had to be pulled to surface due to dropping angle. The next assembly was rotary one, without motor or TRACS, re-running the same bit. Tight spots were worked or mMD, but ROP's were very slow and the BHA was pulled to surface, with only one minor tight spot at 3572 mMD. The hole angle did increase from 54.7° to 56.3° in this section, as planned. Another motor and TRACS were included in the next assembly, which was run in, reaming tight spots at 3560 and 3620 mMD. After drilling to 4329 mMD, in3 of mud was lost, and flow check found the annulus had dropped 98m, giving downhole emw of sg. After pulling slowly back to 4280 mMD gunk squeezes were performed, but were unsuccessful in stopping further losses. The drillstring was pulled back to surface, and diverter tool on drill pipe run in to set cement plug. No losses were noted during this operation. After BOP test new BHA was made up, without TRACS, and run in, displacing the hole to sg mud while reaming down. There was no communication with the MWD when attempting check survey at 4260 mMD, and upon tagging bottom at 4329 mMD circulation was lost again. Drilled ahead 6m, but losses incresed from 20% to 100% as did so, losing total of 94 m3. The bit was pulled back to 4308 mMD, and the mud level fell to 68m. Two LCM pills and another gunk pill set, before full returns were established after pumping back to 4199 mMD. Upon pulling back to the shoe, full circulation was achieved, the drill string run back to 4154 mMD, and then washed and reamed down to mMD, when losses reoc,cured at 10 m3/hr. Drilling recommenced, but losses were between - 18 m3/hr while drilling down to 4398 mMD, and finally increased to 30 m3/hr. After pumping back to 4328 mMD with constant losses, LCM pill was pumped, with no returns, followed by gunk squeeze at 4292 mMD. However, the pill was only partly displaced into the open hole, when the nozzles become plugged, and the bit had to pulled to surface. Open ended drill pipe was run in the hole, and the mud weight reduced to sg, while circulating the drill pipe clean at 1100 mMD. new BHA was made up and run, breaking circulation every 500m with no losses, until circulation rates were increased from 2300 to 3000 1pm, at 4340 mMD upon taking weight. After reducing flow rates to 2700 1pm, losses while reaming to bottom were - m3. depth correction of 56 was then done due correction of the length of the BHA. Drilling then recommenced at 4454 mMD and continued down to section TD of 4658 mMD, with - m3/hr mud losses. Several attempts were made to steer, but were unsuccessful due to the motor stalling out. As result the hole angle had dropped to 52.6° at 4606 mMD. The 95/8 casing was then run, losing returns at 3530 mMD, and having to work through tight hole at 4029, 4370, and 4398 mMD. It was cemented with the shoe at 4652 mMD.
