No.: Date: 13.07.01 3 Health, Safety, Environment and Quality (HSE & Q) 3.1 HSE Focus For this well, the special HSE focus will be: • Drilling shallow gas. • To avoid any spillage of oil based mud to sea. • To avoid personnel in riding belts during cement jobs. • Involve service companies in HSE campaigns. • Supervisors to be familiar with the SBP procedure. • To pay special attention to crane operations and heavy lifts on the rig. 3.2 Quality For this well, the special quality focus will be, amongst other, to plan and execute the operation of logistics and mixing of mud during the 26 section due to shallow gas. Another quality focus will be to verify HC contacts in the Rannoch Formation in M-3 H, to set the 5/8 casing shoe in the Etive Formation in M-3 AH. All down time occurred shall be report in Synergi-99. The Synergi-99 reports are to be logged on separate sheet in the Time Planner. 3.3 Risk assessments A risk evaluation for the well will be performed prior to start of 34/10-M-3 H. Live wells on template L: ref chap 3.3.1.1.

The well was drilled and steered from 1960 mMD to the TD at 3280 mMD in one run, taking hours in total. The hole angle was built up from 27.34° at 1938 mMD, to 60.53° at 2883 mMD, just above the top of the reservoir at 2887.0 mMD, and continued to build up to 68.82° at 3250 mMD. The natural build tendency of the BHA was generally sufficient to keep the wellpath on the planned line and only one short section, 1 mMD, was steered in the reservoir section. This was necessary in order to increase the build rate in Area of the reservoir, and thereby maximise the sands above the OWC. After circulating the hole clean at TD the BHA was pulled without pumping or backreaming to the shoe, where high-vis pill was pumped and the casing circulated clean. The BHA was then pulled to surface, the MWD data dumped and the tool broken down. The rest of the BHA was broken down after waiting for crane for one hour. Due to quick drilling the Western Atlas equipment only arrived onboard as the MWD was being laid down, so there was delay while the FMT tool and spear were made up and tested. The FMT was being rigged up on drillpipe when the decision came from town to run the log on wireline, so the PLC equipment was laid down and the CHT/GR/FMT combination was run on wireline. Minor hang-ups occurred at 2059, 2245, and 2415 mMD; the tool was unable to go beyond 3068 mMD. The top three pressure points were taken before, again, attempting to pass 3068 mMD, but without success. The tool was pulled to surface and rigged down. It was decided not to run in on drillpipe to take the five lower points. A 121/4 hole opening assembly was made up, including bull nose, 81/2 hole opener, followed by 121/4 hole opener 825 behind the bull nose. The well was opened up to 121/4 from 1960 - mMD, working tight spots at 3197 and 3239 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean. short wiper trip was performed back to 3100 mMD without pumping, and then the hole was backreamed from 4 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean again with 121/4 hole opener at 1955 mMD. A 95/8 liner string was run to 3272 mMD. Principal tops and comparison of prognosed and actual stratigraphic tops in the well 33/9-C17 are summarised below: Stratigraphk Top Predicted Depth 55 Actual Depth SS Difference an TVD Area 1. Brent Group. Undiff B4 Undiff B5A Area 2. Brent Group. Undiff B2 ODT TD GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY BRENT GROUP TARGET AREA 1. 2 mMD - mTVDSS The top Brent reservoir was found mTVD lower than expected, but did contain good reservoir quality sands of the Etive and Rannoch Formations, except for mMD interval of calcite cemented sandstone. The predominance of Rannoch sands was expected, and with TVT of 57.6m it must have been affected by downfaulting, thickening the better quality sands in the upper part of the Rannoch Formation.

- 28 - The 12-1/4 hole was drilled to 2716m, and after setting the 9-5/8 casing, mud weight was reduced to rd. This section coincides with carbonaceous claystones of the Viking Group, which produced significantly higher gas readings in the range - 0.30% CI to nC4. The lower part of the Draupne Formation and the entire Tarbert Formation were cored. Because of reduced returns during coring, absolute gas values were moderately, but qualitative paraffin ratios were significant. Background gas ranged from - 0.23% C1 to nC4 over this interval which represents the upper part of the Tarbert Formation. Mud weight was maintained at rd throughout the 8 1/2 hole section. In this middle to lowermost part of the Tarbert Formation, gas values were generally reduced, apart from peaks associated with coal seams. Background gas ranged from - 0.07% C1 to C3. Most significantly, nC4 values were reduced to zero, although traces were recorded on penetrating coals. Background gas averaged to - 0.08% C1 to C3 through this section, with isolated peaks of up to 1.14% C1 to nC4, corresponding to the penetration of coal seams. Generally much lower gas readings resulted from the Etive / Rannoch Formation and gas values averaged -0.04% C1 to C3.

5 FORMATION EVALUATION 5.1 Logging The logging programme included runs with wireline logs and run with CDR/CDN- tool (LWD), see Figure 4.3. The logs are of good quality and only minor problems occurred during the logging operations. Due to only minor differences between measured depth (MD) and true vertical depth (TVD), deviation corrections have not been applied. The Top Brent Group at 2455,5 mRKB (MD) is 0,1 deeper compared to the TVD, for the Top Dunlin Group the difference is 0,2 m. The logs have been analyzed using computer based model applying complex lithology method. The Brent Group net sand intervals have been defined using porosity cut-off corresponding to ml), which for the Tarbert Formation is 16 %, the Ness and Etive Formations 12 %, and the Rannoch Formation 15 %. shale volume cut-off of 40% has been applied. The main results from the preliminary log analysis are summarized in Table 5.1. For further details and final interpretation, reference is made to the Petrophysical Report. The resistivity logs indicate oil down (ODT) to 2477 mRKB and water up to (WUT) 2483 mRKB. The OWC is located within very fine grained, bioturbated and argillaceous, calcite cemented sandstone, and cannot be exactly defined from the resistivity logs. However, an OWC is from the formation pressure measurements (RFT) estimated within the Tarbert Formation at 2478 mRKB (2460 mSS). 5.2 Conventional Core Analysis A total of 10 cores were cut in the interval 1 mRKB Driller's. Core No.1 contained only marl and shaly claystone belonging to the Cromer Knoll Group and to the Heather Formation. Cores - 10 were cut in the Brent Group and 12 into the Dunlin Group. The total Brent core recovery was 186,05 (95,7%). Conventional core analysis was performed on all cores, except cores nos. 1, and 10 due to very high content of claystone. Horizontal air permeability, helium porosity and grain density were measured every 0,25 meter, while vertical permeability, summation porosity and pore saturation were measured every meter. The results are shown in Table 5.2.

4.2.2 1/2” Drilling Phase 34/10-M-4 AH T2: The section was planned as short correction run with DLS's of approximately 5.5º. With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. In the future there are two main things to be investigated further before drilling similar type of well/section. The first being the necessity of such high mud weight, which clearly initiates sticking, and drag problems. Secondly, if water based mud is to be used, clarify to what extent the graphite additives will affect Schlumberger 13 Drilling & Measurements 34/10-M-4

GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. A value of 1.38sg was obtained for the leak-off after drilling out the 13 3/8” casing and drilling 12 1/4” hole commenced. Drilling was halted at 2730 mBRT when pore pressure was seen to have reached 1.25sg and the bit was pulled into the casing shoe. In an attempt to carry on drilling an open-hole leak-off was performed that confirmed the 1.38sg value obtained earlier. Having insufficient kick tolerance to drill ahead, the decision was made to run 5/8” liner. triple-combo wireline log was run to acquire data over the drilled section. Liner was set and 1.47sg leak-off was obtained. Drilling commenced in 1/2” hole. No reservoir horizons were identified and the well was TD’d at 02:45 hrs on the 20th February at depth of 3650 mBRT. Three wireline logging runs were performed. The 6404/11-1 well was plugged and abandoned as dry hole at 22:00 hrs on the 10th March 2002 and the rig released to Norsk Hydro. RESULTS The shallowest primary target (Early Eocene T50 sandstones) was absent at the well location. Upper Cretaceous (K90 sandstones) were absent and K80 (Nise Formation) sandstones were poorly developed. The well was not extended to penetrate the deeper, K72 (Lysing Formation) secondary target.

Unfortunately also the MIXrD logging failed in this section and the litholcgy and age therefore had to be interpreted from cased hole logs and seismic. For full description of the lithology it is referred to the Sperry Sun End of Well Report. Nordland Group (1 mBRT) An undifferentiated Nordland Group is interF reted down to 2142 mBRT. The section consists of glacio-marine deposits and infilled the rifted and eroded topography at the Middle Oligocene unconformity. The interval is heavily affected by slicing and slumping. Rogaland Group (2 mBRT) The first returns were sandy and caring gave Paleocene age (Lower T30). The sandy section is interpreted to continue from the Middle Oligocene unccrr:ormity down to the Base Tertiary unconformity at 2434 mBRT based on cased and open hole logs. The biostratigraphy suggests that the entire section with returns is Paleocene (T30) in age with both the T10 and T20 missing at the base. The sandstone can be described as immature with poor sorting and detrital matrix. The section hat been assigned to the Tang Formation due to the lack of tuff. Shetland Group (2 mBRT) The Springar Formation from the Base Tertiary to Top K8C Reservoir consists of clean mudstone of Late Campanian to Maastrichtian age. The uppermost Maastrichtian is missing at the Base Tertiary unconformity (i.e. the T30 rests on intra K90). Four, metre thick sandstones define the top of the K80 Reservoir (Nise Formation) at mBRT. The high net to gross reservoir was encountered 21 below this and continued down to the Kvitnos Formation at 3810 mBRT The reservoir sandstone is Early Campanian in age and generally fine grained, moderate:y sorted and with excellent porosity and permeability characteristics. The Kvitnos Formation (3 in3RT) consists of silty mudstone with occasional carbonate cemented bands. It is Santorian to Earliest Campanian in age and spans the K70/K80 boundary at 3860 mBRT. Cromer Knoll Group (3 mBRT) A new sandstone section that continued to 4241 mBRT was encountered at 3939 mBRT. The biostratigraphic dating gave Santonian (K70.2) age, indicating that it belongs to the Lysing Formation. The sandstone is very fine grained, :lean and moderately sorted. 11 6707/10-1 Discovery Report

ROGALAND GROUP Tare Formation: 2099m(log)-2152m(log); Age: Upper Paleocene The top of this formation is picked at sharp downhole decrease in gamma ray values at 2099m(log). Mudstones recorded in the subsequent ditch cuttings samples contain the characteristic tuffaceous lithologies which are associated with the upper part of this formation. The mudstones are medium grey or medium dark grey with fine, locally prominent white 'speckle'; blocky, earthy in texture and non-calcareous. Dark brownish grey to dark grey, non-calcareous mudstones occur throughout in subequal proportions. The prominent high gamma ray log feature at c. 2120m(log) is equivalent in age to the Sele Formation which is widely developed in the Norwegian North Sea. The tuffaceous mudstones similarly equate with the Balder Formation. Tang Formation: 2152m(log)-2198m(log); Age: Upper Paleocene The upper boundary of the Tang Formation is picked at 2152m(log) where gamma ray values increase slightly downhole. The formation has moderate, serrate gamma ray log profile which increases in intensity downhole. The predominant lithology is mudstone which is variable in colour from olive to greenish grey and is locally greyish red. White to yellowish grey, microcrystalline limestone occurs in trace quantities below 2180m, probably representing thin stringers or nodules within the lower part of the unit. SHETLAND GROUP Springar Formation: 2198m(log)-2377m(log); Age: Upper Cretaceous, lower Maastrichtian to lower Campanian The downhole decrease in gamma ray values at 2198m(log) marks the top of the Springar Formation in this well. The log profile is generally smooth and moderate reflecting the homogeneity of the mudstone lithology and contrasts markedly with the overlying formation. The mudstones, which are medium light grey to light olive and olive grey, moderately hard, non-fissile, slightly to rarely moderately silty and non-calcareous, are first recorded in ditch cuttings samples at 2200m. Fine grained glauconite and finely crystalline pyrite occur rarely and traces of carbonate of possible biogenic origin or representative of thin stringers or nodules are also recorded. Nise Formation: 2377m(log)-2595m(log); Age: Upper Cretaceous, lower Campanian The top of this formation is picked tentatively on slight shift in the gamma ray log profile and decrease in gamma ray values at 2377m(log) in the absence of any sonic velocity log data for this interval. There is little discernible difference between the predominant mudstone lithologies of this unit and those of the overlying Springar Formation although the gamma ray log maximum at 2552m(log) is feature similar to those seen within the Nise Formation in numerous wells located on the Halten Terrace. The significance of this feature, seen also in type and reference wells, is not proven, although it may represent thin bentonite unit. Page

question: How do MDT/FMT and RFT pore-pressure gradients compare in the Tilje and Ror formations, and what causes discrepancies and the seal's influence?
answer_text: MDT/FMT in the Tilje show higher gradients (~1.97 s.g. declining to ~1.91 s.g., ≈2–2.5 bar above RTD estimates), while RFTs indicate distinct pressure regimes with the Ror Fm. acting as a pressure seal between Ile and Tilje. Discrepancies are due to incomplete inter‑horizon communication, formation ballooning/flushing and use of adjacent-zone estimated pressures.

Coring continued and close watch was kept on trip gas levels as these were the only available indicators of pore pressure with the d-exponent rendered useless by the sandstone formation and coring operation. The following peaks were observed: 1.62% (0.02%) at 4671m, 2.12% (0.30%) at 4699m, 4898m. Connection gas peaks were seen at 4864m and 4873m with values of 0.44% (0.29%) and 0.41% (0.29%) respectively. This time there was little doubt that these were the result of formation ballooning/flushing. Further FMT logs at 4926m confirmed maximum pore pressure gradient of 1.97sg at 4634m, declining to 1.91sg at 4926m. The actual reservoir fluid gradient was 0.044bar/m which should have produced gradient of 1.88sg at this depth, therefore it was apparent that there was not complete communication between all horizons within the reservoir. The d-exponent did not provide any useful information until the Lower Ror formation was entered at 5015m. Similarly, background gas was masked by frequent formation related peaks and provided little in the way of pressure indications in the overlying formations. close watch was kept for pump off and connection peaks since these provided the only useful pressure tool. In the event none were seen until the base of the Tofte formation. Thereafter connection gas peaks were regular feature until the end of the well. Once again these were thought to be the result of the high overbalance and not increasing pore pressure.

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION In the 12 IA section little gas was encountered and the pore pressure was assumed to stay well within the predicted range of around SG, as indicated in the Shell well programme. 8 1/2 section The pore pressure in the Hordaland group claystones varied from to maximum of SG.This remained so until the top of the Shetland group, where the pressures were at hydrostatic level of around 1.03-1.04 SG through the clays and the sands of the reservoir. Estimating the pore pressure from the Dxc was fraught with errors due to the scatter of its values. Since the trend was was largely not discernible, compromising start was made in the attempt to set trendline. From the pressure prognosis (derived from offset data) in the Hasselmus well programme, the pressure was assumed to have pressure dropped back to normal in the claystones above the reservoir, and stayed normal until TD. Two clusters of Dxc points for claystones were identified — one starting from c. 1640m to c.1700m in the Shetland Group and the other below the reservoir, from c. 1840m (Top Ror formation) to c. 1870m (Top Tilje formation) where the pressure was normal hydrostatic, as per the prognosis. Connecting these two clusters and extending the line provided the only trend. Despite the litter, Dxc points are seen to shift to the left from approximately 1150 m. From calculations, it was found that at 1300m, the pressure was SG, at c. 1350m SG, from c.1470m to 1570m it peaked to SG, at 1600m SG, and at 1625m SG, before returning to normal at 1640m. There is scatter of Dxc points even further to the left, between 1500m to 1570m which would give theoretical values of up to SG, but these have been rejected from being useful or reliable, for there were no indications from the well to suggest pressures higher than those prognosed. As the hole packed off while in the reservoir and the string got stuck there, the meachanism was believed to be differential sticking . The high overbalance/differential pressure was thought to be the cause of this, as the mud weight was SG and the ECD went up to maximum of SG. The pressure profile in the sidetrack followed the same pattern as in the original well. 8-2

context_snippets.text: Figure 2.1: Well location map (base Brent) TWT ms Fault at 4800m OVK 2938m MSL Top Brent Base Brent Figure Visund Nord, Well 34/8-B-2 HT5 Random line along drilled well path ^ Figure 2.2: Random line along the drilled path of well 34/8-B-2 HT5 3 Background Geochemical differences in oil and gas compositions related to differences in source rocks, maturity, migration pathways and/or migration distance have been documented to exist in oil fields. These geochemical differences may, regardless of origin, be mapped and used as information relating to reservoir compartmentalization. Following field filling, the major hydrocarbon homogenization process, able to erase initial geochemical differences, is diffusion. Diffusional transport in porous media is dependent upon the permeability, and low permeable layers with high tortuosities will act as barriers to diffusion. Methane is the petroleum component with the highest diffusion coefficient. This means that in reservoir sections of km lateral extension, where no diffusional barriers exist, initial differences in ?13CMethane should be erased as result of diffusive mixing over geological time scales. Significant variations in ?13CMethane over less than km distances in reservoir are therefore strong indication for the presence of diffusional barrier. These barriers to diffusion must also represent fluid flow barriers during filling and also likely production barriers.

These are the same values as used to define the Brent fluid gradients in 34/8-3A and this is consistent with the view that these two wells encounter the same fluid compartments.

Presented in the following report are the results of this study as requested by Mr. Kurt Thomas of Conoco Norway Inc. Upon receipt in the laboratory the ambient temperature saturation pressures of the bottom hole samples were determined and after discussion with Conoco it was decided to use the fluid from cylinder 8088-92 in the study. The hydrocarbon composition of the reservoir fluid was determined to decanes plus using combination of low temperature and high temperature fractional distillation. This is reported on page two of the report in terms of mol and weight percent, together with the molecular weight and density of the heptanes through decanes plus cuts. The reservoir fluid was charged to high pressure visual cell and thermally expanded to the reservoir temperature of 183°F. During constant mass expansion the fluid was found to have bubble-point of 3383 psig. The results of the pressure volume measurements at reservoir temperature may be found on pages three and four. When subjected to differential pressure depletion at the reservoir temperature the fluid evolved total of 611 cubic feet of gas at psia and 60°F. per barrel of residual oil at 60°F. The resulting relative oil volume factor was 1.316 barrels of saturated fluid per barrel of residual oil at 60°f. The oil density and the properties of the evolved gases were measured at each point during the differential pressure depletion and this data is included in the summary of the differential depletion data on page five and represented graphically on pages seventeen and eighteen.

5.1 LITHOLOGY DESCRIPTIONS . 36 HOLE SECTION As all returns were to the seabed, the lithology may only be inferred from the steady ROP with low WOB as moderately soft, uniform sequence. The relatively low torque would suggest clays with marked absence of boulder beds. 26 HOLE SECTION This section was predominantly argillaceous sequence with minor interbedded SAND horizons. The CLAYSTONE was medium to light grey,silty and was associated with abundant shell fragments and microfossils. The shell type was essentially molluscs (bivalves and gastropods) with occasional echinoids, foraminifera and bryozoa. The SAND appeared colourless or milky,although some grains were stained orange or grey.It was very coarse and angular to subround, coarse or medium grained and subround, and also fine grained. This very poorly sorted quartz was associated with abundant Lithic fragments especially black, very hard, cryptocrystalline volcanics and traces of biotite mica. Many of the coarse granular quartz grains were veined with heavy minerals and contained muscovite inclusions.There were also traces of white, fine grained SANDSTONE which was sorted and well consolidated by calcareous matrix. 17 1/2 HOLE SECTION The section commmenced as light to medium grey CLAYSTONE which was silty, finely sandy, soft and amorphous. It appeared slightly swelling, very sticky and calcareous. It was associated with traces of very fine to fine grained SAND and SHELL FRAGMENTS together with minor traces of PYRITE NODULES and LITHIC FRAGMENTS. By 500m the CLAYSTONE became increasingly silty, occasionally grading to an argillaceous SILTSTONE and also showed scattered disseminated GLAUCONITE and PYRITE. The SAND became locally consolidated into fine, sorted SANDSTONE while the loose quartz increased in size to dominantly coarse grain.

question: Which deformation indicators, dominant cement types, and their effects on porosity are observed in Balder sandstones from well 25/11-23?
answer_text: Observed deformation indicators: cataclastic/broken framework grains, brecciated appearance from squashed shale/argillaceous fragments and microfractures. Dominant cements: pore‑filling/pore‑rimming clays, kaolinite, quartz, siderite and calcite, which largely occlude intergranular pores and reduce porosity, though partial decementation of calcite locally increases microporosity.

The planned total depth of the well is Geoscience Summary The regional Balder Formation isopach is thickest on the western flank of the Balder field, which implies the presence of an Eocene Zone III sand packages. Regional Eocene depositional sand maps also suggest the transport of sand from west to east across the Balder area. This interpretation is tied to the 25/10-5 well located approximately km to the SSW. The well penetrated 19m of net oil sand and total of 28m of interbedded reservoir sand. E5 is assessed to have most likely STOOIP of 90 MBO distributed between the Zone 111-2 lower (53MBO) and Zone 111-3 (37MB0). Zone 111-4 sand is distributed sparsely and is expected to be entirely within the gas window in the E5 area. Zone 111-3 sand is also expected to be in the gas window at the proposed well location with the gas-oil contact prognosed at the base of the sand. The well is expected to find 12m of net oil pay in Zone 111-2 lower, 7m of net gas pay in Zone 111-3, and 5m of net gas pay in Zone 111-4. The key risk at E5 is encountering thin, interbedded Zone III sands with limited continuity. Zone 111-2 lower and Zone 111-3 sands map out as isolated sand bodies, suggesting potential for limited aquifer support. An additional risk is penetrating the Zone 111-2 lower reservoir above the field wide gas-oil contact. Basis for Geological Prognosis The geological prognosis is based on: 1) Depth conversion 2) Net sand prediction from attribute analysis studies on the 3D Impedance dataset. 'Seismic Interpretation The key mapping element of the Zone III sands was the use of the Balder B88s 3D seismic impedance cube to map individual sand bodies. Calibration of well control with impedance data suggest that low impedance packages correlate to sand prone intervals within the Balder formation. Seismic horizons were carried at zero-crossings at the top and base of these low impedance packages. Interval seismic attributes were then extracted and attribute analysis was performed in order to calculate net sand thickness. The impedance cube and attribute maps were used successfully in planning and drilling Zone III development wells at Mound and E2. key uncertainty for the E5 Zone III sands is the lack of local reservoir sand calibration to seismic impedance. answer_text: PHIF = φD + A × (NPHI − φD) + F·NPHI, where φD is RHOB-derived density porosity calibrated to overburden-corrected core, NPHI is neutron log (limestone units), and A and F are regression coefficients in Geolog SLEIPNER_OST (Bara ECD OBM).

1. Conclusions • Well 1/3-8 was dry because of seal failure. The vertical seal failed by fracturing induced by excess overpressure. Flexural stress caused by Tertiary halokinetic inversion may have contributed to fracturing and leakage, but this was not the primary cause. • Hydrocarbons did migrate into the 1/3-8 structure. This is evident from the shows at the top of the reservoir sands, from bulk fluid inclusion (FIS) and petrographic fluid inclusion indicators, and from the condensate that was encountered in the Lower Cretaceous. • Reservoir sandstones were encountered in the Basal Sandstone interval of the well. This was the secondary reservoir objective interval. The sands are of poor quality, but they are capable of producing and receiving oil or gas as indicated by conventional core, petrographic, and capillary pressure analyses. No sands were encountered in the younger Volgian primary reservoir objective interval. • The Kuskjell and BI5skjell prospects are no longer valid prospects because of increased risk associated with reservoir presence, reservoir quality, and seal. • The Flyndre Deep Prospect is longer valid prospect because of increased risk associated with (at the very least) seal. • The Boreskjell Prospect is no longer valid prospect based on confirmation of poor Triassic reservoir quality by the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The reservoir objective is the Triassic Skagerrak Formation, which was penetrated by both the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The formation has very poor reservoir properties in Well 1/3-8. In well 2/1-11, the formation is very sandy, but reservoir quality is poor. • The seal failure at 1/3-8 underscores the risk of seal failure at 7/11-N, similar prospect in terms of depth and predicted stratigraphy and pressure. Seal is the primary Risk at 7/11-N. Based on revised pore pressure prediction model with 1/3-8 data as calibration, the chance of seal failure (vertical or lateral) was increased significantly. This was reviewed by the PQT in January, 1998. consensus total chance of success of 18% was arrived at. This substantiated the team's concerns regarding seal failure and justified ANOC's very recent decision to try to trade or swab its interest in PL070 for an interest in more prospective acreage. • Deep Jurassic prospects can succeed. There are several examples in the UK sector of the Central Graben where commercial discoveries have been made, and several of these are being developed (e.g. Elgin, Franklin, Shearwater, Erskine). The downsides of these prospects are higher risks associated with seal failure and high drilling and production costs. The upside of high pressure Jurassic prospects is significant: higher deliverabilities even through poor reservoir rocks, greater storage capacities for given trap size, and positive impacts on porosity preservation in certain cases (up to 30% porosity at Shearwater!). To date, this play has not proven to be commercial in the Norwegian sector.

question: How do kaolinite, quartz, siderite, and calcite cements respectively affect porosity in Injection versus Balder sandstones?
answer_text: Kaolinite — strongly pore‑filling and markedly reduces porosity in injection sands and occludes pores in Balder sandstones; Quartz — presence in Balder sandstones reduces porosity (not reported in injection sands); Siderite — replacive/spindle‑shaped cement in Balder sandstones that reduces porosity; Calcite — cement reduces porosity but partial decementation in Balder sandstones can considerably increase microporosity.

The planned total depth of the well is Geoscience Summary The regional Balder Formation isopach is thickest on the western flank of the Balder field, which implies the presence of an Eocene Zone III sand packages. Regional Eocene depositional sand maps also suggest the transport of sand from west to east across the Balder area. This interpretation is tied to the 25/10-5 well located approximately km to the SSW. The well penetrated 19m of net oil sand and total of 28m of interbedded reservoir sand. E5 is assessed to have most likely STOOIP of 90 MBO distributed between the Zone 111-2 lower (53MBO) and Zone 111-3 (37MB0). Zone 111-4 sand is distributed sparsely and is expected to be entirely within the gas window in the E5 area. Zone 111-3 sand is also expected to be in the gas window at the proposed well location with the gas-oil contact prognosed at the base of the sand. The well is expected to find 12m of net oil pay in Zone 111-2 lower, 7m of net gas pay in Zone 111-3, and 5m of net gas pay in Zone 111-4. The key risk at E5 is encountering thin, interbedded Zone III sands with limited continuity. Zone 111-2 lower and Zone 111-3 sands map out as isolated sand bodies, suggesting potential for limited aquifer support. An additional risk is penetrating the Zone 111-2 lower reservoir above the field wide gas-oil contact. Basis for Geological Prognosis The geological prognosis is based on: 1) Depth conversion 2) Net sand prediction from attribute analysis studies on the 3D Impedance dataset. 'Seismic Interpretation The key mapping element of the Zone III sands was the use of the Balder B88s 3D seismic impedance cube to map individual sand bodies. Calibration of well control with impedance data suggest that low impedance packages correlate to sand prone intervals within the Balder formation. Seismic horizons were carried at zero-crossings at the top and base of these low impedance packages. Interval seismic attributes were then extracted and attribute analysis was performed in order to calculate net sand thickness. The impedance cube and attribute maps were used successfully in planning and drilling Zone III development wells at Mound and E2. key uncertainty for the E5 Zone III sands is the lack of local reservoir sand calibration to seismic impedance. answer_text: 30/2-3: Early–Late Toarcian; 30/3-9: Early Toarcian through Late Toarcian into Aalenian?–Early Bajocian; 34/11-2: Early–Late Toarcian.

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 30/2-3 is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. Deposition was interrupted during mid Callovian times, possibly because of regional regressive phase. Subsidence and sedimentation of the Heather Formation resumed during late Callovian?-Early Oxfordian times although further, major unconformity separates the Early Oxfordian Heather Formation sensu stricto from the overlying Draupne Formation. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. Sedimentation continued through to Middle Volgian times in similar environmental conditions, although major unconformity is present at the top of the Draupne Formation. The Early Cretaceous sequence is characterised by major condensation and unconformities. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of Early Hauterivian calcareous claystones assigned to the Valhall Formation which accumulated in marine, inner shelf setting. These sediments are overlain unconformably by Early Barremian calcareous claystones of the Tuxen Formation following regional transgressive phase. further unconformity separates the Tuxen Formation from the overlying Early Albian Sola Formation. The Soia Formation accumulated in marine, mid shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Following period of non deposition, transgressive phase during Late Albian times resulted in the deposition of calcareous claystones of the Rodby Formation in marine, outer shelf setting. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group, Formation 'A' were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest samples analysed are sands of the DuniIn Group, Cook Formation of Late Pliensbachian?-?Early Toarcian and Early Toarclan age, which were deposited in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment with the accumulation of Drake Formation claystones during Early Toarcian, Late Toarcian and Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times. A regional regressive event during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group, Broom?-Ness formations. Deposition of the Brent Group continued through Late Bajocian, Late Bajocian?-?Early Bathonian and Early-Middle Bathonian times with the deposition of the Ness and Ness?-Tarbert formations. During Early-Middle Bathonian times sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. stratigraphic break occurs at the top of the Early-Middle Bathonian interval. Heather Formation deposition continued during early Callovian through to Middle Oxfordian times in marine, inner shelf setting. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Late Oxfordian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in an inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. An unconformity exists within the Draupne Formation resulting from the absence of early Kimmeridglan to Early Volgian aged sediments. Accumulation of Draupne Formation sediments resumed during Middle-latest Middle Volgian times in marine, mid to outer shelf setting with dysaerobic to anaerobic bottom conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment throughout Early-Late Ryazanian times. Deposition continued, without apparent unconformity, with Cromer Knoll Group sediments of latest Late Ryazanian age. Deposition occurred in marine, inner to mid shelf environment and continued thorough Late Valanginian-Early Hauterivian times. Following period of erosion or non deposition during Late Hauterivian to Late Aptlan times, deposition of Cromer Knoll Group sediments resumed briefly during Early Albian times in marine, mid shelf setting. further unconformity at the top of Cromer Knoll Group sediments indicates period of erosion or non deposition during Middle and Late Albian times. Deposition resumed with transgression at the beginning of Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Early Cenomanian through to Late Maastrichtlan age. A period of erosion and/or non deposition during Early Palaeocene times possibly resulted in the absence of Rogaland Group, Vale Formation sediments. Deposition resumed with calcareous and non calcareous claystone of the Rogaland Group, Lista Formation which accumulated in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment during Early to Late Palaeocene times. In particular, wells 30/9-3, 3A, 30/9-4 and 30/9-7 have provided the basis for the more detailed geological prognosis for this well. Regional geological framework The Triassic-Jurassic sequence in general shows depositional history from widespread continental environment (M.Norian-L.Rhaetian) through nearly continuous sealevel rise during the Early Rift Phase of Late Rhaetian-Oxfordian age, to the more deeper marine conditions during the Main Rift Phase of Oxfordian-Rhyazanian times. The Jurassic stratigraphy expected in this well is listed below: 1) Early-Late Toarcian: Marine shales of the Drake Fm. 2) Late Toarc-Aalenian: Marine alluvial fan-delta sands of the Oseberg Fm. 3) Aalen-Earliest Bathonian: Regressive/transgressive sand, shale and coal of the Rannoch, Etive, Ness and Tarbert Fms. 4) Latest Bathonian-Callovian-Middle Volgian: Marine shales of the Heather Fm.

question: How do lithology, calcareousness, and pyrite/siderite/glauconite occurrences compare between Sele (2953–3026 m) and Lista (3026–3096 m)?
answer_text: Both formations are dominated by interbedded shale and clay; Sele (2953–3026 m) has firmer, mostly non‑calcareous shales with occasional calcareous clay, few sandstone/silt stringers and thin limestone streaks, while Lista (3026–3096 m) has softer, sticky, more variably colored clays/shales with a thick sand lens and partly slightly calcareous clay. Pyrite is frequent in Sele, whereas pyrite, siderite and glauconite occur only in minor amounts in Lista.

Sele Formation (2953 - 3026 m) This formation is dominated by interbedded shale and clay. The shales, represented mostly in the upper part, vary in colour from light grey to light green and are generally firm to hard and non-calcareous. The clay resembles the clay described from the Balder Formation, but is occasionally calcareous. Few stringers of fine to medium grained sandstone (clear - white subrounded grains) and siltstone has also been encountered, together with rather thin streaks of white to yellow-brown limestone. Pyrite occursfrequently within this interval. Lista Formation (3026 - 3096 m) The main lithology in this formation is shale and clay, with slight changes in colour. In the upper part of the interval soft and sticky light grey clay dominates, only intersected by thick sand lense, consisting of clear to white medium grained quartz grains (from 3 m). From 3037 light brown to redish brown clay occurs, which . is partly silty and slightly calcareous. This clay is interbedded with vary-coloured shales and light grey clay in the lower part of the interval. The shales are light green, light to medium grey and brown to brownish red, firm and fissile and have varying content of silt. Thin limestone streaks (white to light brown) occur through- out the interval. Pyrite, siderite and glauconite occur only in minor amounts.

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

3.7 REFERENCE WELLS Several wells have been considered for extrapolation with the play concept. These are essentially situated in the Hammerfest Basin northeast of the licence area. Data from these wells were used to constrain predictions of the petrophysical characteristics of the inferred reservoir sandstones of the Realgrunnen Group and, to lesser extent, of the Lower Basal Clastics in the Gamma Prospect. They comprise conventional wells drilled in the quadrants 7119, 7120, 7121, 7122 and 7219, as well as IKU shallow drilling 7018/05-U- 06 at the margin of the Troms-Finnmark Platform some 25 km southwest of the licence area. Thermal and kinetic input parameters derived from some of the considered wells were used to calibrate the modelling of hydrocarbon generation and expulsion from the principal source rock of the Hekkingen Formation in the Tromso Basin. Hydrocarbon characteristics were mainly extrapolated from data representative for the discoveries in the Hammerfest Basin, namely 7122/6-1 (oil and gas), Snohvit (oil and gas), Albatross (oil and gas), Askeladden (oil and gas), and Alke (gas). 3.8 OPERATIONAL GEOLOGY WELL PROGRAM 3.8.1 SAMPLING PROGRAM The standard cuttings sampling intervals will be as follows (Fig. 3.8.1): every 10 from 30 csg shoe (after return of drilling fluid) down to thel3 3/8 casing shoe at 2000 m. every from the 5/8 casing shoe down to T.D. at 3009 m. Wet samples will be collected at each interval and sent onshore periodically for splitting. The wellsite geologist will instruct the mud loggers in order to get sufficient samples to fulfil the dispatching requirements (see data distribution chart). Storage and distribution of samples to partners and the NPD will be handled as per later instruction. Extra samples will be taken on wellsite geologists request. Samples will be continuously examined under microscope and fluoroscope, and calcimetry will be performed with spacing decided upon by the wellsite geologist. One set of washed and dried samples will be kept on the rig until the well is finished. The geochemical samples (an additional unwashed set) will be collected on request from the Norsk Agip Exploration department.

Division of Biarofcl Corp.AS Common for all the jobs: - 60 feet corebarrel length - Aluminium innertubes - CD 93 corehead - Water based mud - Upper cretaceous Ekofisk formation The only difference between the jobs are the hole angle. Our investigation shows that the results becomes poorer with increasing hole angle. Enclosed you will find sketch which describes the relative force required to push the core upwards when coring in high angle wells. This curve is compared with the same force when coring in vertical wells. Whenever stringer or fracturated formation enters the innertube at 50 degrees angle, the stringer will bee in more physical contact with the innertube than normal. This is due to the fact that the force pushing the core upwards will be decomposed into two forces. One vertical and one horizontal. It is the horizontal force that force the stringer into physical contact with the innertube. This creates more friction inside the innertube, and the more friction the more force is required to push the core up. At certain point the compressive force becomes to high for the formation to withstand. The formation will then collapse with jammed core as the result. In this job the hole angle was only degrees, and this may have contributed to better result compared with other jobs in the Ekofisk field. ILj

question: How do anisotropy parameters delta=0.05 and epsilon=0.07 influence traveltime accuracy in a 3D Eikonal VSP migration splice?

context_snippets.text: time over the logged interval can be obtained. This is not usually adequate, however, for detailed studies and the log requires calibration. The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmitted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognized, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attributed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the borehole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Checkshot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time with the check shot time at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate, the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. The different types of shifts are discussed in more detail in chapter 4.2.

3. Extraction of N.I. VSP from the 2D WA data The Normal Incidence traces were extracted from the 2D Walkaway VSP after binning. Navigation data processing and binning are described in detail in the 2D Walkaway VSP report. total time shift for each trace included: system delay of approximately 20 ms, derived by detecting the peak of each near-field hydrophone measurement, geometry static and time shift due to distance between actual shot position and center of bin cell. After the binning, the extracted Normal Incidence VSP is just an one-fold dataset (one trace per level), in opposite to traditional N.I. VSP with several shots per each level before stack. The data is shown in Display Group R1. The first arrival time was taken at the top of the first peak: this corresponds to trough-to- trough picking. The reader is referred to Appendix 1: First Arrival Picking for full discussion of this process.

Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. However, Appendix: VSP Deconvolution - Page of 2. Mod. 09.11.00

as many of the multiples are in fact short period and generated in the near surface region, where the ray paths are not significantly different, applying deterministic deconvolution with short input window may prove effective. An alternative is predictive deconvolution. This process, while effective on surface seismic data, is for VSP inferior to the deterministic method described above. This is because no assumptions are made in the deterministic method about the nature of the source or the reflectors. In predictive deconvolution, the assumptions made are that the reflection series is white, and that the source signature is minimum phase. The method is applicable to situations where the up- and downgoing ray paths differ significantly, and may be used in combination with deterministic approach. Software to perform both these types of deconvolution, together with sophisticated wavelet analysis package, is available at RWS. The software is sufficiently flexible to allow deconvolution operators to be designed, processed independently and stored for use as required in either other stages of the VSP processing, or on other data sets. RWS has experience in the reprocessing of surface seismic data employing VSP derived deconvolution operators.

context_snippets.text: 1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

4. LITHOLOGY 15/9-12 by S. Evensen The reservoir interval, the Hugin Formation of Middle Jurassic age, is devided into three units. The lowermost unit, consist in general of very fine to fine occasionally medium grained sandstones deposited in shoreface/tidal dominated enviroment. These sandstones are interbedded with few siltstone/mudstone layers, and one distinct coal layer at 3568-60 m. The lower part of the unit consist of more calcite/dolomite cemented sandstones than the upper part. The general good reservoir quality of this unit are also interrupted by strong bioturbation in some interval of the sandstones. This middle unit consist of interbedded sandstones and shales deposited in an ebb tidal delta/lower shoreface environment. The sandstones at the base of the unit are medium to coarse grained homogenous and structureless and should display good reservoir potential. To the top the sandstones are more fine-grained, laminated and strongly bioturbated. Chert nodules are observed throughout this interval. The uppermost unit consist in this well entirely of sandstones deposited in shoreface environment. The reservoir quality of the very fine to fine low-angle laminated sandstones seems to be poor (to fair) due to highly bioturbated intervals and thin calcite/dolomite layers throughout the whole unit.

Seawater was used as the drilling fluid, with high viscous pills being pumped on every connection to aid hole cleaning. The hole was displaced to s.g. mud prior to running casing. Dxc data was widely scattered, most likely due to the hydraulic action on the unconsolidated sediments, and as consequence could not be used in estimating the pore pressure regime. No shallow gas was observed. With the absence of any hole problems the 36 section was considered to be normally pressured. This section was originally drilled as 7/8 pilot hole to 1100m with returns to seabed. This hole section was drilled using sea water, with high Viscous pills being pumped every connection to aid hole cleaning. The hole was displaced to sg mud prior to running the 13 3/8 casing. A Dxc trend was established from 500m (1.00) and 1050m (1.45), this indicated normally compacting sequence. Dxc scatter and changes from the trend line were the result of hydraulic action and lithological variations. No shallow gas was observed in this section. Given small variations in Dxc normal compaction trend was established. This section was considered to be normally pressured at 1.03 s.g. This section was drilled with six bit runs using bits, including an Eggbeater PDC bit. The lithology comprised primarily of mudstones with minor limestone stringers to depth of 3010m where tuffaceous mudstones and minor sandstones were encountered. At 3110m the lithology changed to limestone and mudstone with massive limestones at 3220m A KCL/Polymer based mud was used with an initial density of sg. pressure was increasing, with the Dxc trend continually shifting (k=0.2609, a=0.0003363). The mud weight increases affected the Dxc values and this was taken into account when estimating pore pressure. Background gas was between to 0.30% down to 1450m with only one swab gas at 1410m. From 1500m more swab gases were seen and continued to appear down to 1700m; background gas increased noticably at 1630m to 0.50%. From 1763m, an egg-beater bit was run, which gave very poor Dxc response because of the cutting action. However, with still increasing background gas and the continual presence of swab gas from 1973m onwards, the formation pressure was estimated to be sg EQMW. The next run, from 2178m, used rock bit which gave an excellent Dxc response, and trend, (k=0.914,a=0.0004303) representing sg EQMW, was quickly established. This trend shifted sinistrally at 2590m and quickly stabilised to sg EQMW trend, (k=0.3601,a=0.0001837). Gas values were steadily decreased from 2430m, with the background falling from 0.10% to 0.04%. Any further shifts in the Dxc trend were due to bit change or formation, and the pore pressure was assumed to remain at sg EQMW, due to the occurrence of relatively substantial trip gases; 0.54% at 3060m and 0.57% at 3162m. Its existence is linked to the presence of seismic marker between the Top Reservoir and Tpp C2 markers. Extension of this Intra Reservoir marker, and consequently of the extra sedimentary layer, is limited to the northern part of the 1/3-3 structure without calibration at wells. The Extra Package is well developed and thicker in the northern part of the structure, pinching out towards the 1/3-3 well. Since it seems to onlap the unit towards the 1/3-3 (pinch out) in the south, with probable complete erosion of in the north, it is believed to be younger sedimentary layer (Early Volgian) trapped along the Ula faults (see above play concept) and corresponding to new trangressive pulse. SUMMARY: This shallow drilling project has been run in the Skagerrak area, northeast of the Farsund Subbasin. In September 1988, 667 km of shallow seismic data were collected. Subcropping bedrock units and Quaternary thickness were mapped and potential drillsites selected. Four holes have been drilled: 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88 and 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 on line IKU-0822SK-88. The drilling was carried out with M/S Bucentaur in May 1989. The water depth for the localities varied from 505 to 525 and the Quaternary overburden from to m. The holes were drilled from 90 to below sea bed (603.7 to 817.5 below sea level). The four cores comprise about 420 of diamond (piggyback) drilling in bedrock of Paleozoic and Mesozoic age. The coring yielded 370 of samples representing 88.5% recovery in average. This report presents seismic interpretation, sedimentology, petrophysical logs and core measurements, biostratigraphy and organic geochemistry. In addition, special studies have been made including trace fossil analyses, thermal conductivity, oedo- meter and apatite fission track analysis. The depositional environment, bedrock subcrop distribution, stratigraphy, regional correlations and burial history are discussed. KEYWORDS: Shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin North Sea Paleozoic Skagerrak Mesozoic SkOries

- 11- SINTEF-ORUPPIEN 3. FISSION TRACK ANALYSIS Apatite fission track analyses were run on the Mesozoic cores in the main project (Appendix A.10). As they give information about maximum temperature and timing, another two samples were picked from core 13/2-U-2 and submitted to Geotrack International, Australia. Even if the most promising intervals of the core were selected, the two samples did not yield single grain of apatite or zircon. Unfortunately, it was therefore not possible to proceed further with the fission track analysis. 4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Good bathymetric maps are of great help in interpreting the outcropping geology between seismic lines. On Figure the previous geological inter- pretation is combined with the new bathymetric map. The steep slope in southwest along the - fault is very striking. On the SW - NE line IKU- 101SK-88, sp 3000-3200, topographic high of about 50 was found and the form was discussed in the Main Report. From the bathymetric map it is clear that the high is not local dome but more the easternmost seen extension of WNW - ESE trending ridge. This trend can also be seen on the three dimensional perspective view (Figure 2.3). The bathymetric map has thus limited the discussion about volcanic intrusions by showing that dome structure probably does not exist. No clear evidence of outcropping volcanic rocks is seen near the drill site. In combination with the seismic evidence of possible subcropping volcanic rocks (e. g. the strong disturbance and loss of reflection continuity on line IKU-0822SK-88, sp 2700-2900) there might be subcropping dike system in the area as indicated on Figure 4.1. From the shallow drilling program in 1989 it seems probable that also the Paleozoic rocks found outcropping east of 9°E in the Skagerrak area is of mainly Cambro-Silurian age. Core 13/2-U-2 was postmature, but evaluating the above suggested existence of volcanic dike, we still find it very probable that this was caused by later Paleozoic intrusions. This is also supported by the supposed migrated hydrocarbon content in the core. We therefore find it highly valuable to continue the investigation of the Paleozoic rocks in the Skagerrak area. INTRODUCTION 5_Eg , _INTEF-GRUPPEN The joint industrial research and development program SHALLOW DRILLING FARSUND SUBBASIN 1988/89 had the objective to carry out shallow seismic, shallow drilling and laboratory examination of the subcropping bedrock in the Skagerrak area northeast of the Farsund Subbasin and to evaluate these data. The main target was to collect high quality bedrock cores from selected intervals of the Mesozoic and Paleozoic strata in the area. The program of shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin was initiated from near- shore bedrock mapping project in the coastal Norwegian North Sea areas. This study was based on existing data, mainly conventional seismic, and was carried out by IKU in cooperation with NPD (Oljedirektoratet) and Statoil (Rokoengen et al. 1988). proposal for shallow drilling program was put forward to several companies of which seven supported the program as Early Participants. One company joined as an Early Late Participant before drilling started (and increased the budget) and one company has, so far, joined as Late Participant after drilling. NPD had observer status in the project. Following the intentions of the inaugural meeting in Stavanger on 19th August 1988, shallow seismic survey with 667 km of digital (2.5 sec.) and analog equipment was run in September 1988 (Figure 1.1). The data were collected and processed by A/S Geoteam. Based on the new seismic data, revised bedrock and Quaternary thickness maps were presented and possible coring sites proposed in February 1989 (Lippard and Rokoengen 1989). Dril- ling program and priorities were discussed and decided on Steering Committee meeting at Oppdal and applications sent to NPD in March 1989. First priority was given to the two drillsites 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 (Figure 1.1) located on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate Base Cretaceous and cover most of the Jurassic section in the area. Second priority was given to the drill- sites 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 located on the shallow seismic line IKU-0822SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate the oldest Mesozoic sediments (of supposed Triassic age) and give information from the Paleozoic rocks in the area. The drillings were done on the platform northeast of the Farsund Subbasin (Figure 1.2), where the drilled strata can be tied into the basin itself.

These geochemical differences may, regardless of origin, be mapped and used as information relating to reservoir compartmentalization. Following field filling, the major hydrocarbon homogenization process, able to erase initial geochemical differences, is diffusion. Diffusional transport in porous media is dependent upon the permeability, and low permeable layers with high tortuosities will act as barriers to diffusion. Methane is the petroleum component with the highest diffusion coefficient. This means that in reservoir sections of km lateral extension, where no diffusional barriers exist, initial differences in ?13CMethane should be erased as result of diffusive mixing over geological time scales. Significant variations in ?13CMethane over less than km distances in reservoir are therefore strong indication for the presence of diffusional barrier. These barriers to diffusion must also represent fluid flow barriers during filling and also likely production barriers.

question: Can helium porosimetry, mercury immersion, and nitrogen adsorption on cleaned core plugs reliably determine porosity, grain density, and permeability?
answer_text: Yes. Helium porosimetry (Boyle’s law) and mercury immersion are used to calculate porosity and grain density, and nitrogen (air) permeability measurements (with Klinkenberg correction) are used to determine permeability.

Nevertheless, the use of microthermometry on the samples studied may well constrain the temperature (and time?) aspect of the major pore volume altering reactions which in this study are quartz overgrowth and feldspar dissolution. 41) Conclusive remarks The two overall most important diagenetic reactions responsible for pore volume alterations in the samples studied are quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) reducing porosity and (K-) feldspar dissolution which definitely is the major contributor to the formation of secondary pore volumes (PVSC). (The formation of PVSC shows positive correlation with depth of 0.34.) Though samples show grain sizes up to 500 microns practically no samples have been found to contain rock fragments as to be suitable as provenance indicators. The heavy minerals zircon and rutile are recorded in trace amounts in nearly every sample. Heavy minerals or detrital minerals (or mineral inclusions) that represent specific metamorphic facies do not give any consistent geographical distribution or clustering. Hence, no suitable provenance indicators have been recorded apart from the possible use of zircons for radiometric dating.

Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were.used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.
