STOOlP and EUR Assessment PROBABILISTIC DISTRIBUTION P90 Mean P10 STOOIP 91 155 222 R.F. 40 46 60 EUR 44 74 117 WELL OBJECTIVES AND LOCATION SELECTION CRITERIA Two wells are planned to appraise the Ringhorn field reserves and to enhance the confidence in the resource base for future development planing. The vertical section of the well is proposed at the southern nose of the main Ringhorn horst block and the sidetrack well is located at about 420m to the east (Figure-3 & 4) 25/8-12S Well The objectives of the vertical well are to test the reservoir quality and continuity of primarily the Zone-2 & Zone-3 sandstone, encountered in the 25/8-11 well (Figure-5). The well will penetrate the Zone-2 sandstone and is anticipated to encounter oil on rock in the Zone-3 sandstone. Seismically, this well is located at about 190m to the west of the normal fault separating the Ringhorn main fault block and the up-thrown block (Figure-1 & 3). Coring is planned in this well, with the objective to gather detailed reservoir parameters, primarily for the Zone-2 and Zone-3 sandstone 25/8-12A Side-track Well RISK The proposed sidetrack well is planned on the up-thrown fault block (F/B4) southeast of the Ringhorn main horst block (F/B3). Based on seismic, the well is located about 200m from the two bounding faults to the east and west. The main objective of this sidetrack well, is to prove up the resource base attributed to the Triassic sandstone in this untested fault block, which is interpreted to separated from the Ringhorn main fault block by normal fault to the west. The well will also test the Triassic reservoir quality, its continuity and the fluid system. The current interpretation shows that the Lower Jurassic Statfjord sand in the main fault block (F/B3) is juxtaposed against the Triassic sandstone in the up-thrown block (F/B4). Thus, the Triassic sandstone is anticipated to share the same fluid system as Ringhorn (Figure-5). However, chemical precipitation and the thick Lower Jurassic shale trapped on the fault plane may hamper this interpretation. Another objective of the well is to test the Lower Jurassic shale thickness for validation of reservoir architecture and reservoir model. The current structural model has excluded large amount of shale volume in this up-thrown block from the reserves assessment. The result of the well will also help in reservoir depletion planing, as the reservoir depletion model does not have water injection well within the upthrown fault block. The uncertainties associated with the resource size are the quality of the reservoir sand, the fluid system and the shale thickness primarily in the up-thrown fault block. Uncertainty in time depth conversion is expected due to the variation of chalk thickness as the base is seismically unresolvable.

The Paleocene sands below 2000 are normally pressured. From the top of the cretaceous at ca. 2355 the pore pressure increases rapidly from SG eq. to SG eq. at 3000 m. The pore pressure below 3000 is estimated to remain constant towards the base of the Cretaceous. rise in pore pressure is estimated at the base of the Cretaceous to SG at depth of 3695 m. The 5/8 casing shoe will be set just below this in the top of the Jurassic, Kimmeridge Clay formation, but it could be set as high as 3670 if hole conditions dictate. At the top of the Brent sandstone the pore pressures is estimated to be SG. From this maximum value at ca. 3800 the pore pressure decreases slightly due to gas/water column in the Brent. The liner will be set just below the Brent sand in the Dunlin formation and the well completed to TD in hole. The pore pressure is expected to continue its gradual decline and value of SG eq. has been estimated in the top of the Statfjord formation at ca. 4340 m. The pore pressure decreases slightly through the Triassic shales except for slightly over pressured section around 4700 if the well is penetrated this deep.

42 A. INTERPRETATION OF FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY (FIS) DATA A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, including petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries with FIS, one can obtain valuable and unique information on three major exploration topics: 1. Petroleum migration or paleocharge 2. Seals 3. Proximity to undrilled pay and two major production topics: 1. Pay zone and bypassed pay delimitation 2. Reservoir compartmentalization. The previous discussions have concentrated on identifying spectral types in FIS data. This is necessary first interpretive step. The next task is to evaluate the significance of FIS depth trends in their own right (now knowing their spectral origins), and eventually, in light of other available information to answer specific questions, such as were enumerated above. Petrographic data from anomalous fluid inclusion zones are often critical elements of these higher order interpretations, as will be seen, which why petrographic follow-up work is conducted as routine part of every FIS analysis (see Table of Petrographic Observations). A.3.1 Significance of FIS petroleum indications The most basic question that FIS can address is Is there any evidence for present or past petroleum in this borehole? Documentation of an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly generally pro- vides positive answer to this question, but could indicate other processes as well. Possible explanations for an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly are discussed in the following paragraphs. Migration without trapping A migration pathway may be indicated when FIS responses are low or moderate, when contamination and recycled inclusions can be discounted, when quoted visual petroleum inclu- sion abundances are rare or several (see Table of Petrographic Observations), and when no other petrographic or log evidence of current petroleum charge is identified in the zone. There are number of factors that influence inclusion abundance and, consequently, raw FIS response strength, including geologic setting, extent of diagenesis, rock type and permeability. However, it has been demonstrated that both visual petroleum inclusion abundance and FIS strength within many porous reservoir rocks is proportional to hydrocarbon saturation or pa- leosaturation in relative sense. Because migration occurs at average bulk-volume petroleum saturations below those encountered in charged reservoirs, FIS signal strength and visual in- clusion abundance are generally lower along migration pathways than in charged reservoirs from the same area. Fluid Inclusion Technologies (FIT), Inc., is laboratory-based petroleum service or- ganization established in 1997 and offering variety of analytical services including some previously proprietary technologies. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. The procedure has major impact in the areas of both Petroleum Production and Exploration Applications providing informa- tion unattainable via more traditional methods and, has been instrumental in the discovery of significant petroleum reserves, influenced exploration and acreage acquisition decisions and provided innovative options for resource estimation, petroleum production and enhanced oil recovery operations. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphic Analysis, often in combination with other patented techniques, emerging geochemical methodologies and standard microscopic methods, all available through Fluid Inclusion Technologies, Inc., provides unique and un- equaled industry product boasting an impressive list of proven applications including deter- mination of Product Type, Hydrocarbon Migration, Seals and Seal Integrity, Fluid Contacts, Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum, Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimi- tation, Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization and Fluid Pressure Compartments. Further information regarding the application of FIS Analysis and the other technical ser- vices we provide to problems in petroleum exploration and production is available elsewhere in this report and on our website:www.fittulsa.com. 4.1 General Logistics of Initiating an FIS Analysis To Initiate an FIS Analysis: contact FIT' directly to discuss goals of the study, sample requirements, turnaround time, pricing, and other related aspects. When sampling for FIS Analysis: the technique is equally applicable to cuttings, core and outcrop samples, but all samples will ultimately be reduced to cuttings-sized rock ma- terial. Wells drilled with any mud system can be analyzed (including oil-based systems), as can samples of any age (i.e., fresh cuttings or those warehoused for many years). Our suggested sampling interval for general well studies is 30 ft (10 m). Pay-delineation studies, reservoir-scale studies or other applications involving rapidly changing fluid chemistries should be sampled at the tightest possible spacing, depending on sample availability (e.g., 1-3 ft). A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 43 gas) and the relative abundance of these inclusions will influence the bulk spectra. Addi- tionally, total inclusion abundance will affect the spectra insofar as higher molecular weight species represent smaller volumetric proportion of petroleum and are also less volatile, hence decrease below instrumentation detection limits before low molecular weight species. Conse- quently, some samples with low oil inclusion abundance generate wet gas mass spectra, for instance. Optical inclusion abundance and characteristics should be consulted, where pro- vided, to verify the interpreted petroleum type (see Table of Petrographic Observations). With the above limitations in mind, the following petroleum types are identified on the basis of spectral characteristics: Dry gas: mostly C1 with lesser C2-C3 and no higher hydrocarbons. Wet gas: C1-C9 may be present, but C6+ species are in minimal abundance. The alkane slope is extreme. Gas-condensate: C1-C11 may be present. The alkane slope is quite steep, reflecting very gas- enriched phase. Volatile oil: C1-C13 present. Slight gas-range enrichment is observed and the alkane slope is mod- erate to steep. Oil: C1-C13 is present. The alkane slope may be flat to moderate. Biodegradation is suggested if sulfur compounds such as H2S, COS, CS2, S2 (+/- SO2) and/or thiols are present in addition to petroleum species. Ratios of paraffins to naphthenes may be low as well, as bacteria typically prefer to metabolize alkanes compared to other classes of petroleum compounds. Petrographic data may provide further evidence for biodegradation in the form of low-gravity petroleum inclusions. Bacterial activity is generally restricted to maximum burial temperatures below 65-70°C; hence FIS evidence of biodegradation is most commonly observed in rocks that are currently below this temperature. Thermal alteration of liquid petroleum species can produce spectra very similar to those generated from biodegraded hydrocarbons, because the products of two common processes, bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR) and thermochemical sulfate reduction (TSR), are essentially identical. The best distinction is made from current bottom-hole temperature data, which, if above 140°C or so may be indicative of TSR, and if below 70°C or so is more consistent with BSR. Potential interpretive problems arise in the intervening temperature range, when deeply buried sediments are unroofed or when petroleum altered at shallow depths becomes buried to greater depth. Petrographic data may help, as pyrobitumen frequently accompanies TSR, while low-gravity liquid petroleum inclusions often occur in association with bacteri- ally altered oils. Additional temperature or thermal maturity data (including fluid inclusion homogenization temperatures) may also be useful. The presence of significant amounts of sulfur species can indicate sour petroleum phase, where the souring process may in some cases be reflection of the source rock, but could also reflect BSR or TSR. study of TSR sour gas pools in Canada suggests that evaluating the relative proportion of products and reactants can provide measure of sour gas potential. As TSR progresses, long-chain alkanes decrease while low molecular weight petroleum species increase along with CO2, aromatics organic acids and the various sulfur compounds enumer- ated above. Ironically, H2S alone may not be as accurate an indicator of H2S content, as it is scavenged naturally (e.g., to form pyrite in iron-rich rocks) and by the metallic internal surfaces of the analytical system.

The primary objective for running StethoScope 675 in the in section of the well was to evaluate reservoir pressure and mobility profiles in the identified zones where screens would be planned to be located. A total of Sixteen (16) tests were performed resulting in five (5) valid high-quality formation pressures, one (1) valid medium quality formation pressure, three (3) valid low quality formation pressures, three (3) dry tests and four (4) tight tests. Pressure Acquisition Sequence: All pretests were performed while pulling out of hole (POOH) in run with mud pumps on. Thirteen (13) pretests were performed while POOH post TD while the remaining three (3) were performed post re-logging of the section after acquiring initial tests. 2 Interpretation Summary 2.1 Run Summary Run Run Dates: 26th to 30th of April 2020 Mud Type: Baroid BaraECD (OBM), g/cc. Hermod oil and simulated brine were used on both fresh and cleaned core plugs (8 in all). Temperature and net confining pressure during experiments were 112 bar and 76°C respectively, and results from the first drainage are considered good. Raw data are presented in table 5.4.4 In figure 5.4.5, capillary pressures are converted to height above the FWL, and corresponding water saturations are plotted against the log derived equivalent from well 25/11-15. As seen from the figure, the spread in measured water saturations is most pronounced where capillary pressures are low (towards the bottom of the oil zone). When moving up through the oil column, differences become less, and irreducible water saturations vary between s.u. and s.u. The relation between depth and capillary pressure is based on the difference in density of g/cc between water and oil (oil density from PVT-analysis of bottom hole sample = g/cc, water density from formation pressure gradient = g/cc. No conversion from laboratory to reservoir conditions has been performed as reservoir pressure and temperature have been applied to system containing Hermod oil and simulated brine. Reservoir properties of applied plugs are fairly constant, and no clear relation between water saturation and permeability can be derived. Buckley-Leverett type approach would therefore not help in unifying the data. Through trial and error the function Sw* = BhA has been found to provide reasonable fits with the available dataset. Here Sw* is given by Sw* = (Sw-Sw,)/(1-Sw,), and is height above the FWL. and are constants. On figure 5.4-5, Sw vs. height from core and Sw-curves based on three sets of constants in the above equation are shown. The A's and B's were found using linear regression on crossplot of selected pairs of the log of Sw* and the log of h. Based on the equation: log Sw* = log + Alogh, B then becomes the intercept and the slope of the regression line. The functions, as given below define mean, optimistic and pessimistic water saturations for use in volume calculations and reservoir simulation.

The petrophysical interpretation comprises shaly sand model giving effective porosity and effective water saturation as output. Shale volumes are derived from the Gamma Ray log, while porosities are determined from the Density log. Porosities show only minor variations throughout the Utsira Formation, and no permeability cutoff is hence applied. A clay volume cutoff of 40% is applied to delineate sands both in the Utsira and Paleocene Formations. A CPI-plot of the Utsira sands is given as figure 8.2. question: For well 6507/5-2, what are the objectives and expected outputs of MDT pressure profiling versus MDT fluid sampling?
answer_text: MDT pressure profiling: obtain pressures in all permeable zones to assess overpressure, compartmentalisation, inter-well communication and fluid gradients (output: pressure measurements/profiles). MDT fluid sampling: collect water and oil samples to verify fluid type and compare oils with offset wells and underlying Jurassic (output: fluid samples, not necessarily PVT quality).

context_snippets.text: Geoservices Saga Petroleum A further drilling break was flowchecked at 4526m but proved negative. From this point there was no further evidence of increasing pore pressure gradient with both the d-exponent and background gas indicating, if anything, decreasing trend. At 4593m another drilling break occurred which was flowchecked at 4596m. The well was found to be flowing and total of 8m' was allowed into the trip tank before the well was shut in. Post kick analysis of the drilling data failed to yield any valid indicators that might have predicted this overpressured zone. The elapsed time from the drill break until the flow check was about four minutes and there were no indications of influx during this period. It was only after the pumps were shut down for the flowcheck that an increase in volume was noted. Following the kick an attempt was made to establish the bottom hole pressure but this failed due to breakdown of the formation. It was later determined that the well was flowing from TD and leaking out to the formation at between 3970 and 3950m. The hole packed off around the string at 3800m and it was necessary to back it off after setting cement plug on bottom. With the string free circulation was established with difficulty and the kick circulated out. Extremely high gas values were recorded while circulating. Gas composition showed large proportion of heavier components and good fluorescence was obtained from fluid samples suggesting that reservoir formation had been encountered. Later in the circulation the returns were seen to consist entirely of slightly brackish water for several minutes. It is therefore possible that the migrating gas bubble reduced the hydrostatic enough to produce water from one of the porous sand formations. Once well control had been re-established it was determined that the hole was in extremely poor condition with large, unstable washed out sections. It was therefore plugged back to below the 13 3/8 casing shoe prior to sidetracking. Following evaluation of the VSP log run in the 5/8 casing at the end of the 121/4 section of 6406/2- 3T2 it was determined that the kick originated in the Aptian sandstone of the Intra Lange formation and not in the Gam formation as had been originally thought.

1. Conclusions • Well 1/3-8 was dry because of seal failure. The vertical seal failed by fracturing induced by excess overpressure. Flexural stress caused by Tertiary halokinetic inversion may have contributed to fracturing and leakage, but this was not the primary cause. • Hydrocarbons did migrate into the 1/3-8 structure. This is evident from the shows at the top of the reservoir sands, from bulk fluid inclusion (FIS) and petrographic fluid inclusion indicators, and from the condensate that was encountered in the Lower Cretaceous. • Reservoir sandstones were encountered in the Basal Sandstone interval of the well. This was the secondary reservoir objective interval. The sands are of poor quality, but they are capable of producing and receiving oil or gas as indicated by conventional core, petrographic, and capillary pressure analyses. No sands were encountered in the younger Volgian primary reservoir objective interval. • The Kuskjell and BI5skjell prospects are no longer valid prospects because of increased risk associated with reservoir presence, reservoir quality, and seal. • The Flyndre Deep Prospect is longer valid prospect because of increased risk associated with (at the very least) seal. • The Boreskjell Prospect is no longer valid prospect based on confirmation of poor Triassic reservoir quality by the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The reservoir objective is the Triassic Skagerrak Formation, which was penetrated by both the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The formation has very poor reservoir properties in Well 1/3-8. In well 2/1-11, the formation is very sandy, but reservoir quality is poor. • The seal failure at 1/3-8 underscores the risk of seal failure at 7/11-N, similar prospect in terms of depth and predicted stratigraphy and pressure. Seal is the primary Risk at 7/11-N. Based on revised pore pressure prediction model with 1/3-8 data as calibration, the chance of seal failure (vertical or lateral) was increased significantly. This was reviewed by the PQT in January, 1998. consensus total chance of success of 18% was arrived at. This substantiated the team's concerns regarding seal failure and justified ANOC's very recent decision to try to trade or swab its interest in PL070 for an interest in more prospective acreage. • Deep Jurassic prospects can succeed. There are several examples in the UK sector of the Central Graben where commercial discoveries have been made, and several of these are being developed (e.g. Elgin, Franklin, Shearwater, Erskine). The downsides of these prospects are higher risks associated with seal failure and high drilling and production costs. The upside of high pressure Jurassic prospects is significant: higher deliverabilities even through poor reservoir rocks, greater storage capacities for given trap size, and positive impacts on porosity preservation in certain cases (up to 30% porosity at Shearwater!). To date, this play has not proven to be commercial in the Norwegian sector.

A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. A Interpretation of Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS) Data A.1 FIS Analysis A.1.1 Introduction to FIS Analysis Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy involves the rapid, complete analysis of volatiles trapped as fluid inclusions in rock samples using quadrupole mass analyzers attached to an automated, high- vacuum sample introduction system. The technique documents the presence and relative bulk abundance of ionized volatile fragments with mass/charge ratio of m/z 180 that have been released from fluid inclusions by crushing of natural samples. This includes most geologically important inorganic species as well as organic species with less than or equal to 13 carbon atoms. The resulting analysis of the petroleum fraction is comparable to the low molecular weight fraction of whole-oil gas chromatographic - mass spectrometric (GCMS) analysis (without devolatilization of the gas fraction); hence, the major classes of hydrocarbons (e.g., aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins) are represented. Unlike GCMS, where the quadrupole is front-ended with GC, boiling point separation is not achieved and all species are analyzed simultaneously. Hence, significant interference can occur among species with the same mass to charge ratio. However, what FIS lacks in compound specificity, it makes up for in sensitivity and speed, allowing detection of petroleum in samples that are well beyond the reach of standard GCMS methodologies. Prior to analysis, samples of rock material are freed of significant interfering contamina- tion by washing, picking and magnetic separation as necessary to remove drilling fluids, lost circulation materials, other solid mud additives such as gilsonite, and metallic particles from the drillstring. Cleaned samples are loaded with appropriate standards into specially designed autosamplers and are heated in vacuum oven for minimum of 24 hours. This is done to remove adsorbed organic and inorganic volatile material that could interfere with the analysis. The autosampling device is placed in the vacuum system and evacuated to appropriate high vacuum. Bulk fluid inclusion volatiles are afterwards instantaneously released from each sam- ple in sequential manner by automated mechanical crushing. Volatile organic and inorganic species are dynamically pumped through quadrupole mass analyzers where they are ionized, separated according to their mass/charge and recorded. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy is unique in several ways: 1) the methodology and theoretical framework are the result of long-standing research and development effort, 2) the cumulative experience and database of documented case histories are the most extensive in the world and 3) the technology represents the most rapid analytical capability of its kind available. The resulting dataset can provide nearly continuous log of present and past pore fluid chemistry through the stratigraphic section penetrated by well, and, given adequate sample coverage, the data can be mapped in two or three dimensions. This methodology was followed in preparing the annotated depth plots found at the front of this report and is adequate for most circumstances. Nevertheless, the use of microthermometry on the samples studied may well constrain the temperature (and time?) aspect of the major pore volume altering reactions which in this study are quartz overgrowth and feldspar dissolution. 41) Conclusive remarks The two overall most important diagenetic reactions responsible for pore volume alterations in the samples studied are quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) reducing porosity and (K-) feldspar dissolution which definitely is the major contributor to the formation of secondary pore volumes (PVSC). The table in Appendix shows positive correlation of quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) with depth of 0.65. K-feldspar (FSKF) shows negative correlation with depth of (feldspar dissolution). (The formation of PVSC shows positive correlation with depth of 0.34.) Though samples show grain sizes up to 500 microns practically no samples have been found to contain rock fragments as to be suitable as provenance indicators. The heavy minerals zircon and rutile are recorded in trace amounts in nearly every sample. Heavy minerals or detrital minerals (or mineral inclusions) that represent specific metamorphic facies do not give any consistent geographical distribution or clustering. Hence, no suitable provenance indicators have been recorded apart from the possible use of zircons for radiometric dating.

CONCLUSION & RECOMMENDATIONS The MWD and CDR tool failures and damage to the MWD collars in the 12 1/4 hole section is consistent with extremely rough drilling conditions. The use of PDC bits with an aggressive cutting action and packed bottom hole assemblies produced high and cyclic torque. On both MWD runs and this caused the ten pin coverplate torx head screws to back off allowing the coverplate to fall away. The exposed MWD collar wiring was stripped away causing the real time communication failures between the MWD and CDR tools and hence the loss of real time Gamma Ray and Resistivity data. Anadrill has had previous experience of drilling in Chalk in this area, notably on well 2/11-8 where five MWD tool failures occurred in the 12 1/4 hole section. The failed tools all exhibited the following damage eaused by rough drilling: black dust on electr- ical connections, worn and loose shock sleeves and pressure activated pads and electrical components parted from circuit boards. Anadrill had recommended the use of roller reamers and the inclusion of 12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools to reduce the high and cyclic torque levels. The recommended config- uration of 12 1/4 bit-12 1/4 near bit roller reamer-8 CDR-12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer-8 MWD-12 1/4 stabilizer would have provided more protection for the CDR and MWD tools, but this was not utilised. On future vertical wells drilling in Chalk, Anadrill recommends the use of an In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools and the use of either roller reamers or turbine in the bottom hole assembly to reduce torque levels.

MEASUREMENTS: AIR PERMEABILITY Standard air permeability is measured with nitrogen gas as net confining sleeve pressure of 15 bar. The gas flow rate, the pressure drop, p, over the plug sample, and the back pressure, P2, is measured. The air permeability, Kg, is then calculated using Darcy's law. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability value, -el, is determined empirically for each sample. Our empirical correction is based on permeability measurements using different back pressures. Our statistical measurements have been performed on sandstone samples from different fields in the North Sea area with different lithologi. The permeameters used are designed by GECO Petroleum Laboratory. To get complete permeability curve, we also report the Ka-value, defined as the extrapolated air permeability at 1/Pm = (see figure), together with the Klinkenberg corrected permeability, Kal. Measured air permeability, Kg, and 1/Pm (where Pm is average pressure in the sample) for each measurement are also reported. WELL: 2/11-8

Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were.used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

STOOlP and EUR Assessment PROBABILISTIC DISTRIBUTION P90 Mean P10 STOOIP 91 155 222 R.F. 40 46 60 EUR 44 74 117 WELL OBJECTIVES AND LOCATION SELECTION CRITERIA Two wells are planned to appraise the Ringhorn field reserves and to enhance the confidence in the resource base for future development planing. The vertical section of the well is proposed at the southern nose of the main Ringhorn horst block and the sidetrack well is located at about 420m to the east (Figure-3 & 4) 25/8-12S Well The objectives of the vertical well are to test the reservoir quality and continuity of primarily the Zone-2 & Zone-3 sandstone, encountered in the 25/8-11 well (Figure-5). The well will penetrate the Zone-2 sandstone and is anticipated to encounter oil on rock in the Zone-3 sandstone. Seismically, this well is located at about 190m to the west of the normal fault separating the Ringhorn main fault block and the up-thrown block (Figure-1 & 3). Coring is planned in this well, with the objective to gather detailed reservoir parameters, primarily for the Zone-2 and Zone-3 sandstone 25/8-12A Side-track Well RISK The proposed sidetrack well is planned on the up-thrown fault block (F/B4) southeast of the Ringhorn main horst block (F/B3). Based on seismic, the well is located about 200m from the two bounding faults to the east and west. The main objective of this sidetrack well, is to prove up the resource base attributed to the Triassic sandstone in this untested fault block, which is interpreted to separated from the Ringhorn main fault block by normal fault to the west. The well will also test the Triassic reservoir quality, its continuity and the fluid system. The current interpretation shows that the Lower Jurassic Statfjord sand in the main fault block (F/B3) is juxtaposed against the Triassic sandstone in the up-thrown block (F/B4). Thus, the Triassic sandstone is anticipated to share the same fluid system as Ringhorn (Figure-5). However, chemical precipitation and the thick Lower Jurassic shale trapped on the fault plane may hamper this interpretation. Another objective of the well is to test the Lower Jurassic shale thickness for validation of reservoir architecture and reservoir model. The current structural model has excluded large amount of shale volume in this up-thrown block from the reserves assessment. The result of the well will also help in reservoir depletion planing, as the reservoir depletion model does not have water injection well within the upthrown fault block. The uncertainties associated with the resource size are the quality of the reservoir sand, the fluid system and the shale thickness primarily in the up-thrown fault block. Uncertainty in time depth conversion is expected due to the variation of chalk thickness as the base is seismically unresolvable.

SUMMARY Most of the samples in this well, at least in the lower part of the well consist of sidewall cores or cores. Continuous lithologies were not available. The lowermost sample examined is at 2565m and consists of soft white limestone of Early Paleocene (Dan Ian) or possibly Late Cretaceous age and was deposited in shelf environment. Uphole there is transition to mixed sandy-silty and limestone lithologies, again laid down in shallow shelf environment. An Early Paleocene age can be confirmed for these deposits from the lowermost sidewall core at 2549.1m upto 2515.8m. These deposits are overlain by series of Late Paleocene deposits of the Rogaland Group (Lista and Ileimdal Formations). The lowermost part of the sequence at 2495.0m consists of medium to coarse and fine to medium sandstones but uphole from 2478.0m the lithologies consist primarily of claystone and sandstone. Reworked material of Late Jurassic age is abundant at several levels in the Late Paleocene. Reworked early Middle or Early Jurassic and occasionally older materials have also been identified at all levels in the \ veil. There was deepening of the basin; these deposits were laid down in an outer shelf or bathyal environment, probably with good circulation though there may have been periods of restricted circulation. This is most marked in the uppermost sample at 2030m(dcs). This thick sequence of claystones and sandstones extends uphole for almost 500m and tops at about 2030m (dcs). This is coincident with the top of the Lista Formation (2028m, clients data). In the uppermost parts of the well section there are indications of one or more condensed or non-sequences. Palynozone Tp5a is represented by only one sample (2030m dcs) and palynozone Tp4b has not been identified. The Late Paleocene is overlain by deposits of Early Eocene-Late Paleocene age. The lowermost part of this sequence is assigned to the Sele Formation and the upper part to the Balder Formation (Balder/Sele boundary is at 1991m, clients data). Lithologies consist of grey and greenish grey claystones. These deposits were laid down in bathyal or outer shelf environment, probably with some restriction in circulation. Early Eocene deposits are identified uphole of 1956.5m at which level there is major change in the assemblages. The depositional environment was outer shelf to bathyal but marine event is recognised between 1870-1900m; the deposits around this level were probably outer shelf. The Balder Formation continues uphole to 1939m (clients data) and the top is coincident in this well with palynozone Tp6a2 (= top Deflandrea oebisfeldensis). Lithologies of the available Balder samples consisted of dark grey claystone. Stratlab a.s/ P904/2/95 Esso Norway Well 25/8-6: Main hole and 12 sidetrack

NORSK PETROPHYSICAL FIELD STUDY, HERMOD AREA, Page: 16 4 GEOLOGY AND STRATIGFtAPHY 4.1 Structural framework and tectonic setting Blocks 25/11 and 25/8 lie on the western flank of the Utsira High along the eastern flank of the Southern Viking Graben. The Utsira High has been positive feature since the initial opening of the Southern Viking Graben in Permian times. During the Middle to Late Jurassic, large scale, extensional block faulting resulted in extensive erosion of the high and the removal of large volumes of earlier deposited sediments. The Statfjord Fm. was heavily eroded but appears to be present over most of the licence area and pinches out to the south of the 25/11-17 well. transgression in the Late Jurassic resulted in the formation of shallow marine platform and the deposition of shallow marine sandstones which can be correlated over large part of the high. During the early Cretaceous the area remained positive feature and received only thin deposits which were probably exposed and eroded during low-stand times. During the late Cretaceous the area received little clastic input and thick sequence of limestones were deposited on shallow marine platform. From the Late Cretaceous to the present day the Southern Viking Graben has been characterised by regional subsidence. During the Paleocene the East Shetland Platform was raised in response to the spreading period which had commenced in the Norwegian Greenland sea. This combined with number of relative sea-level changes resulted in the erosion of the Shetland Platform and the deposition of a number of large submarine fans in the Southern Viking Graben. Since deposition of the Paleocene and early Eocene sands the Utsira High has been stable and the deposits appear only to have been affected by compactional effects in the shales and associated sliding, slumping and small scale faulting. The sands appear to have been isolated as a result rapid deposition resulting in retention of high volumes of pore water. Compaction and possibly early emplacement of hydrocarbons causing pressure build up within the sands probably shortly after deposition. This pressure appears to have exceeded the strength of the surrounding shales resulting in injection of the sand into the shales. The extent of this injection is not well defined at present, but large number of wells in the Hermod, Balder and Jotun area exhibit various amounts of sand injections into the surrounding shales. 4.2 Depositional environment An overview of the depositional environment of the Rogaland Group is presented here. more detailed description can be found in Ref. /4.1/. Vale Fm The Vale Fm. marks the return to clastic deposition after the shallow marine chalk deposition of the Shetland Group. The Vale Fm. lies unconformably on the calcareous Tor Fm. or the Ekofisk Fm depending on the amount of erosion of the Chalk. The lower few meters of the formation are strongly calcareous reflecting the mixing of the hemi-pelagic/pelagic clays with the underlying chalk. There is sharp but conformable break between the lower calcareous part of the formation and the upper non-calcareous part.

LITHOLOGY SUMMARY Well 25/8-B-7 was kicked off at 290m MD below the 26 casing shoe. 17 1/2 HOLE SECTION: 290m — 1230m MD ( 3m TVD) No sampling. The sampling commenced at 3250m MD (1895.9m TVD). Spot samples were taken every 50m from 1230m - 3464m MD: This section consists of claystone and stringers of limestone and dolomite, down to the top of the tuffaceous section. In the interval 1571 -1659m MD sandstone was encountered. Sandstone: The sand stone consists of fine grained, well sorted, transparent quartz grains. The grains are rounded and spherical. The matrix consists of light olive grey argillaceous cement which is soft and non-calcareous. There are traces of glauconite. Claystone: The claystone is dusky yellowish brown becoming olive black to dark grey from 2000 MD downwards. It is generally firm to hard, blocky, commonly with faint lamination but else homogeneous. It is occasionally slightly silty and occasionally micropyritic. The claystone is non- calcareous. Dolomite/Limestone: The limestone is generally dark yellowish brown dolomitic limestone. The colour varies between olive grey, light brown, dark yellowish orange to dark yellowish brown. It is moderate hard to hard, occasionally brittle, locally angular, and generally microcrystalline to cryptocrystalline. The limestone is blocky and towards the end of this section it becomes soft to firm and crumply. 3 0m MD: This section consists of Tuff, claystone and stringers of dolomite and limestone. Tuff: The tuff is medium dark grey, light grey to medium light grey or medium blue grey. It is firm, brittle, blocky and commonly faintly laminated. It is speckled with varied clasts of claystone and rock fragments and it is occasionally micropyritic. The tuff is interbedded with the claystone, it is very Claystone: The claystone is olive black, blocky, non-calcareous, occasionally micropyritic and generally homogeneous. It is occasionally slightly silty and disseminated carbonaceous material is present occasionally. It becomes increasingly greenish in colour downwards to an olive grey, greenish grey and dark greenish grey colour. Glauconite occurs occasionally, particularly in the lowermost part of the section where the colour may be greenish black and the claystone hard to very hard. 3 2m MD: This section consists of claystone and downwards increasing content of sandstone. Claystone: The claystone is greenish black to olive grey. It is firm to hard, blocky, homogeneous, micropyritic and contains finely dessiminated carbonaceous material. It is non-calcareous, slightly silty and occasionally glauconitic. 3-2

Well 33/9-14 was the third well on the Statfjord Nord structure and was drilled to appraise the Upper Jurassic Volgian Sand. An oil column of 46m was expected in the well with the oil-water contact at 2741m. The previous well, 33/9-8, was drilled approximately km tO the north- east, penetrating full oil column in the Volgian Sand and discovered an oil- water contact for the Middle Jurassic Brent Group. Well 33/913 was drilled in the northern part of the structure and proved full oil column in the Brent Group. However, it was not expected to find oil the Brent reservoir on this well. Exploration Logging provided Geological Engineering Monitoring and Data Analysis System (GEMDAS) service on 33/9-14 from 271m to 2982m total depth. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mud logging, automatic real- time data monitoring and recording, and pressure analyses were carried out. Continuous evaluation of pressure and drilling progress provided an aid in optimising drilling costs, and ensuring that drilling continued with maximum safety to personnel, the well and equipment. The operator was continuously advised as to the status of these analyses, and data and results stored on magnetic tape for post-well evaluation. The printouts and plots are contained in the attachments of this report. For details of the computer programs provided, and the theory of the pressure evaluation methods used, refer to the Software Information Sheets and Pressure Log Manual MS-156. Both are available from Exploration Logging.

Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

context_snippets.text: 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. 1 SUMMARY Petroleum geochemical analyses of Isotube mud gas and drill cuttings samples from the interval 499m to 797m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7322/7-1 have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. Drill cuttings samples from the Nordland Group (484m to 540m) mainly poor to minor source potential, mainly for gas. The shallowest sample 499m has good organic carbon content and marginally good source potential, mainly for gas, but is unlikely to have generated significant hydrocarbons in attaining the present level of maturity. Drill cuttings samples from the Kolmule Formation (540m to 661m), the Kolje Formation (661m to 677m) and the unspecified reservoir section (677m to 797mTD) have mainly poor to marginally fair source potential, mainly for gas. Extracts of selected samples the Nordland Group and unspecified reservoir are dominated by polar fractions, attributed mainly to polyglycols from the drilling fluid. Alkane fractions include suspected base oil, possibly from the drilling fluid. Biomarker ratios indicate that all extracted samples are immature for oil generation with vitrinite reflectance no more than 0.6%. The regional unconformity at the base Nordland Group is not evident from the data. Most biomarker ratios indicate slightly lower maturation level for the two deeper samples 763m and 790m from the unspecified reservoir than for the three shallower samples 499m, 505m and 517m form the Nordland Group. This may be related to combination of organic facies variation and reworking of organic material into the shallower section. The 763m and 790m samples contain mainly terrestrial higher plant derived organic material consistent with the rather low HI values throughout the interval. The 499m, 505m and 517m samples contain mainly marine organic material and type II or mixed type II/type III kerogen. The rather low HI values throughout the Nordland Group could be related to oxidation during reworking of the organic material. Isotube mud gas samples are dominated by N2 and also O2+Ar with N2/(O2+Ar) ratios indicative of air and with low CO2 concentrations. Samples from 690m, 750m and 790m comprise thermogenic gas generated from gas mature source rock with vitrinite reflectance around 1%. Samples from 510m and 530m are suggested to have leaked, indicated by low gas wetness and anomalously heavy carbon isotope ratios. Interpretation of samples from 550m, 590m and 630m is less clear but these do not appear to have leaked. Relatively heavy C2 and C3 carbon isotope ratios could suggest biodegradation, although this is not supported by molecular composition ratios, and it is unclear why biodegradation should affect shallow gases within the claystones of the Kolmule Formation but not the underlying unspecified reservoir section.

8.5” HOLE SECTION S-11 Hole Section Summary BHA#9 (2864m-3778m) was steering assembly with an AIM mudmotor and rockbit at the end. The top of cement was tagged at 2820m and while the cement was drilled out, the hole was displaced to drill out mud. The section started with build section and the hole was geosteered horizontally into the reservoir. BHA#10 (3778m-3861m) was rotary steerable assembly incorporating Anadrills Powerdrive tool. This drilled to depth of 3861m where an increase in Gamma Ray and seperation in resistivity readings indicated drilling into the Våle / Lista when MWD tool passed 3648m This was also indicated in returns from this depth and so it was decided to pull back and perform an open hole sidetrack from 3648m MD. Directional Objective Drill 1/2” horizontal hole to TD in Tor, obtaining LWD for geosteering of perforations. Main build section from 65 to 96 deg, BUR deg. L.O.T./F.I.T. An extended L.O.T. was performed after drilling 96m of formation to 2960mMD (2687.2TVD)into the Hod Fm. The string was pulled out to the 5/8” shoe at 2861.8m MD/ 2663.5m TVD and the result of the LOT was SG EQMD (15.2ppg) Lithology The major part of this setion was drilled in chalk with the Tor Fm at the very start. The Hod Fm came in at 2942m MD/ 2685.9m TVD and then the Tor reservoir was encountered at 3021m MD/ 2682.9m TVD. The last part of the section (3842-3861m) was drilled through Ekofisk, Våle, Lista Fm claystone. Drilling Fluid Density The hole was displaced from1.77 SG oilbased mud to SG while drilling out the cement and was kept at the same weight to the end of the section. Cavings No cavings observed. Hole Condition/Cleaning Hole cleaning was generally good but the hole was circulated clean due to high ecd readings once at 3265m and at 3726m due to increasing drag. Gas Gas levels were high in this sction while drilling in the TOR chalk, but were relatively low while drilling in the HOD formation 0-03 – 17.6% with an avarage of - 5%. 10.2% maximum observed at 3339m MD. Casing No casing was run as an open hole sidetrack was performed. Cementing N/A Section Page 11

FLUIDS 7.3 DRILLING FLUIDS SECTION SUMMARY Section Summary Sat and cemented the 13 3/8” casing. Ran in hole with 12 1/4” BHA to drill float and drill through cement (TOC +/-1258m MD). While drilling through cement, the highest pH recorded was 11.5. Returns were diverted into separate pit which was treated and re-used. Fluid loss was controlled by adding Mil-Pac LV and Permalose-HT. Drilled directly through cement and three metres into new formation and performed an LOT 1313 MD. While drilling through the Lista formation, KCl was maintained at 150 kg/m3 and Glycol of 3% by additions of Aquacol D. The mud weight was relatively easy to control at SG with no severe screen blinding at shakers while drilling through sands. While drilling through clays +/- 1500m MD, the dilution rate was increased and the centrifuge was run intermittently on solids removal. All four shakers were dressed with 230 mesh screens. 10 minute gels increased towards the high end of section and were hard to maintain at < 20 Pa. Before reaching TD, 1974m, +/- 90 m3 of fresh Aqua drill mud was introduced into the system. At TD, circulated bottoms up and pulled out of hole while pumping. Mechanical cavings were observed on shakers in small quantities as consequence of low mud weight. The mud weight remained at SG throughout the section. Ran in hole with the 5/8” riser to 1968m MD. While running casing, new mud for the %2” interval was prepared. Cemented the casing but bumped the plug 900 strokes early. decision was made to run in hole with an %2” assembly, tag top of cement in the 5/8” liner and drill out cement and three metres into formation and perform an LOT. Mud Properties/ Drilling Fluid Technical Performance KCl content was maintained at 150+ kg/m3 throughout the drilling of the12 1/4” section. The mud weight was SG with Glycol 3%. Some mechanical cavings were observed at shakers while taking B/U. As the whole section was drilled with the same mud weight, with an increasing pore pressure curve from start section through the Lista/Våle formations, section was drilled with “low” mud weight. This caused the mechanical cavings on shakers. There were no recorded down hole losses during the section and no significant problems with hole cleaning recorded. Mud Rheology Mud rheology was on the spec., but on the higher side of spec. The reason was the LGS picked up by the mud system while drilling through clays. As we got control of solids control with the help of shakers and the centrifuges running, we got control of the higher end of rheology. Section Page 12

PROGRAM FOR CONDITIONING MUD, BULLHEADING, PERORATING AND REFRACTURING WELL 2/8A-17 OBJECTIVE: To condition the mud, bullhead the mud, add perforation interval in the Upper Hod and perform new stimulation job to obtain production from the Tor Formation. BACKGROUND: Having been unsuccessful in cleaning the wellbore by bullheading, the well has been surged to attempt to unplug the perforation without success. Further, an attempt to RIH to perforate failed due to the diesel/mud interface. The wellbore contains diesel from the packer to surface and mud from the perforation to the packer. The SCSSV is open and connected to handpump. Drilling is in charge of the operation. The steps referred to in the below procedure are in the General Completion Program. A preliminary wellbore schematic is attached. (Attachment I). PROCEDURE: 1. Leave the well with psi at surface for six hours to test the plugged perforations as barrier. 2. Rig up the Gray BPV lubricator assembly and test to 5000 psi and test the BPV by measuring bleed back volume. 3. Nipple down Xmas-tree and install dart in the BPV. 4. Nipple up drilling riser and BOP with 3/8 pipe ram. Test the riser BOP against the dart as specified in the General Drilling Program. Pull dart and BPV.

INTRODUCTION After the Well 2/8A-17 ceased flowing on 20 May 1985, the Upper Hod perforations were isolated by dumping marbles, glass-beads and sand. Further the well was perforated and stimulated in the Tor Formation on 26 May 1985. Below is report of the preparation for and execution of the Tor fracture stimulation treatment. WELL HISTORY PRIOR TO FRAC Well 2/8A-17 was stimulated third time in the Upper Hod lbs of 20/40 mesh sand was pumped during the treatment. However, the stimulation did not provide adequate communication with the Tor Formation. In an attempt to flow the well, it produced solids and ceased flowing on 20 May 1985. In an attempt to kill the well 140 bbls of mud was bullheaded into it. As this kill-mud was bullheaded with no problems it was immediately followed by 400 bbls of diesel leaving only diesel in the tubing thus avoided clean-up operation. The denser Tor interval 8m MD RKB was perforated three times with 90° phasing, spf, 7/8 gun. The well schematic is attached as Attachment 1. FRAC DESIGN A very conservative pump schedule was designed. Similar to the last refrac job in the Upper Hod Formation, pad of 55,000 gallons was chosen. Further, the first seven sand stages were extended to ensure some proppant to enter the formation prior to possible premature screen-out. The proppant chosen was 20/40 mesh sand. Attachment details the designed stimulation including volumes and proppant addition schedules.

Figure 4.4f shows correlation panel of the nearby wells. Target Sands The well is planned to land in the base of the 4Cc-sand. The first 100 meters will be reserved for the ITBS. The main bore (P-23 Y1H) starts after this 100 and follows roughly down-dip direction, in way, that it climbs gradually upwards through the 4-series’ stratigraphy towards the main north-south trending fault (see Figure 4.2a, fault no. 5). Here, according to the model, it has reached the 5Am-sand. Fault-effects in the seismic survey around this fault cause major interpretation uncertainties, which might result in an actual well path, which runs high up in the 5Ac sand before passing the fault. After passing the fault the well is expected to be set back in the 4Cc sand. Hereafter the well is planned to follow trajectory, which runs sub- parallel to the dip direction, so that it will climb stratigraphically upwards through the overlying 4-, 5- and 6-series into the Draupne formation, where TD will be set. Confirmation of Draupne is the TD criterion for the Y1H well. The total length of the horizontal section is approx. 2450 m, from which roughly 1500 is expected to be in c-sandstone intervals, which makes 65% c-sand. The second branch (Y2H) will be kicked off within the first 100 horizontal, where the window is placed. After the kick-off point the well is planned to climb stratigraphically upwards towards the main north-south trending fault (see Figure 4.2c, fault no. 6) where it is expected to have reached the top of the 4Dc. On the eastern side of the fault the well is expected to have been set down in the middle of the 3Dc interval. The remaining of the well is planned to follow gradual climb in stratigraphy through the entire 4-, 5- and 6-series sands until the Draupne formation is reached. high number of normal faults can be expected along the way. Confirmation of Draupne is again the TD criterion for the well. The total length of the horizontal section is approx. 2830 m, from which roughly 1950 is expected to be in c-sandstone intervals, which makes 70% c-sand. question: How do Kyrre FM depositional environments and sequence‑stratigraphic traits differ between wells showing outer‑shelf/upper‑bathyal facies and wells with shelfal facies and unconformities?
answer_text: Outer‑shelf/upper‑bathyal wells: Kyrre FM is mudstone‑dominated, deposited at upper‑bathyal depths with abundant planktonic microfauna/dinocyst assemblages and preserved maximum‑flooding surfaces (e.g. MFS at ~1472 m and ~1745 m). Shelfal/unconformity wells: Kyrre FM records shallower shelf deposition with episodes of erosion and major unconformities (Kyrre resting unconformably on Heather FM or overlain by younger Nordland deposits), indicating sequence truncation.

context_snippets.text: 7. BIOSTRATIGRAPHY LATE CRETACEOUS A. Interval: 2,500m - 2,560m; Early Santonian (top not seen). Lithostratigraphic Units: Shetland Group, Kyrre Formation. Environment: Marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal. The top and age of this interval are based on: the top occurrence of consistently common Cenosphaera spp. at 2,500m, and Stensioeina polonica at 2,560m, indicating Zone LKM7 of Early Santonian age. the top occurrence of Heterosphaeridium difficile at 2,520m, indicating the Early Santonian LKP5c subzone. Micropalaeontology Microfaunas are moderately abundant and diverse, consisting of radiolaria, diatoms and planktonic, agglutinating and calcareous benthonic foraminifera. Events of note include prominent Coscinodiscus sp. and common Coscinodiscus sp.9 at 2,500m and Globotruncana linneiana at 2,560m. A marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment is indicated. 2) Palynology Assemblages are abundant and diverse with dinocysts predominating and subordinate pollen. The dinocyst component is characterised by Chatangiella spp., Heterosphaeridium? heteracanthum, Palaeoperidinium pyrophorum, Trithyrodinium suspect urn and Spiniferitesspp. In addition to the taxa listed above, ,the record of common Chatangiella bondarenkoi and prominent Trithyrodinium suspecta at 2,500m, indicate the LKP4b subzone or older. The records of prominent Chatangiella niiga and prominent Heterosphaeridium? heteracanthum at 2,500m, ?Chatangiella 'spinosa' and common Chatangiella granulifera at 2,510m, Chatangiella 'spinosa', Chatangiella tripartita, Raphidodinium 'furcatum' and several specimens of R. fucatum at 2,520m, Xiphophoridium alatum and Tanyosphaeridium variecalamus at 2,530m, relatively common Raphidodinium fucatum at 2,540m, R. 'multifurcata' at 2,550m and Odontochitina Triangulata' at 2,560m are all of significance. 3 ) Stratigraphic Comments A major unconformity is present at the base of the interval.

CHAPTER Summary 1. Youngest strata examined comprise arenaceous deposits assigned to the Nordland Group of ranging Pleistocene - Pliocene age. It is noteworthy that the normally distinctive Early Pliocene palynofloras are lacking, hence the interval may be of post-Early Pliocene age. 2. The Nordland Group rests unconformably upon Hordaland Group deposits of Oligocene age. These strata are laterally correlative with the Lark Formation, as defined in the UKCS. Following an initial phase of upper bathyal deposition, sediments above 1050m accumulated under shelfal conditions. 3. The Early Oligocene rests with marked unconformity upon thin development of the Early Eocene Balder Formation. No evidence is encountered to indicate the presence of Hordaland Group sediments of Eocene age. 4. The Early Eocene Balder Formation rests with an intra-Rogaland Group hiatus upon slightly truncated Lista Formation as there is no positive biodata for palynofloral Subzones PP4D, PP4C, PP5B or PP5A. 5. The Paleocene comprises both the Lista and Vale Formations, with earliest Paleocene (equivalent to microfaunal Zone MP[I] and palynofloral Zone PP1) strata absent. The regionally recognised improvement in open marine conditions in the Early Paleocene is evident. It is noteworthy that within sediments attributable to palynofloral Subzones PP3D (part)-PP3A significant input of reworking is evident. This may reflect the proximity to gravity flow fan systems. Erosion of Jurassic and Cretaceous material was probably via shelf edge incision. Recycling becomes less prominent in the Early Paleocene. 6. The Early Paleocene rests with significant, erosional unconformity upon the Kyrre Formation of early Campanian age. This relationship of Tertiary and Mesozoic strata is characteristic of most wells between 62°N and 63° 25'N along the edge of the Norwegian shelf. 7. The Kyrre Formation comprises the early Campanian and most of the late Santonian and is represented by mudstones deposited under upper bathyal depths. Microfaunal data from 1480m substantiate the inferred maximum flooding surface (MFS) at 1472m(log). The near base Campanian event is probably correlative with the Ma flooding event of Haq et al. (1987). Close to the base of the Kyrre Formation further MFS is inferred at 1745m(log), occurring in proximity to the late/early Santonian boundary. This surface is correlated to the 86 Ma MFS of Haq et al. (1987). Page

question: How were depth-shifted density logs and porosity–permeability crossplots used to set Dunlin GP net-sand cutoffs in well 34/7-8?
answer_text: Cores were depth‑shifted to match the density log (CDL), and porosity versus horizontal air‑permeability crossplots were used to define the Dunlin GP net‑sand cutoffs (Table 5.2).

context_snippets.text: - 48 - 5. FORMATION EVALUATION 5.1 Petrophysical Analysis The petrophysical interpretation of well 34/7-8 is based on available log, core and test data. 5.1.1 Conventional Core Analysis A total of cores were cut in the Upper Jurassic reworked sand, Dunlin Group, Statfjord Formation and Upper Lunde Unit (Fig 4.3). The cores have been depth shifted to match the density log (CDL) depth (Table 5.1). Conventional core analyses have been carried out by Corelab and consist of measurements of porosity, air-permeability, grain density and fluid saturation. complete list of core analysis data is given in the Petrophysical Report well 34/7-8 (Ref. 1). To define the net sand averages, the porosities have been plotted versus horizontal air permeabilities (Fig. a-d). Based on this analysis net sand cutoffs have been defined (Table 5.2). 5.1.2 Log Analysis Methods The well 34/7-8 has been analysed using modified version of Logcalc CAM model. This model calculates porosity from the neutron-density crossplot, with correction for hydrocarbon effects. Shale volume is defined as the minimum value calculated from the GR and the neutron-density crossplot.

question: If glycol-contaminated cuttings (830–2813 m, well 7124/4-1) were not acid-treated, how would geochemical headspace GC results differ?

context_snippets.text: Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. Figures 1a-c show the Rock-Eval pyrolysis trace and the thermal extraction GC and pyrolysis-GC of Kolmule formation shale which has been washed with water only. Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

4. LITHOLOGY 15/9-12 by S. Evensen The reservoir interval, the Hugin Formation of Middle Jurassic age, is devided into three units. The lowermost unit, consist in general of very fine to fine occasionally medium grained sandstones deposited in shoreface/tidal dominated enviroment. These sandstones are interbedded with few siltstone/mudstone layers, and one distinct coal layer at 3568-60 m. The lower part of the unit consist of more calcite/dolomite cemented sandstones than the upper part. The general good reservoir quality of this unit are also interrupted by strong bioturbation in some interval of the sandstones. This middle unit consist of interbedded sandstones and shales deposited in an ebb tidal delta/lower shoreface environment. The sandstones at the base of the unit are medium to coarse grained homogenous and structureless and should display good reservoir potential. To the top the sandstones are more fine-grained, laminated and strongly bioturbated. Chert nodules are observed throughout this interval. The uppermost unit consist in this well entirely of sandstones deposited in shoreface environment. The reservoir quality of the very fine to fine low-angle laminated sandstones seems to be poor (to fair) due to highly bioturbated intervals and thin calcite/dolomite layers throughout the whole unit.
