question: For FIS versus low-MW GCMS, how do their sample sources, analyte range (≤13C/m/z180), and resolved hydrocarbon classes compare?
answer_text: FIS analyzes volatiles trapped in rock fluid inclusions (ionized fragments up to m/z 180, organic species ≤13 C), while low‑MW GCMS analyzes the low‑molecular‑weight fraction of whole oil (including the gas fraction) and is comparable in analyte range. Both methods represent the same major hydrocarbon classes: aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins.

context_snippets.text: Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, includ- ing petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries through Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS) petroleum exploration and exploitation risk tool developed at Amoco, we obtain valuable and unique information on three major top- ics relevant to exploration: 1) Hydrocarbon Migration, 2) Seals and 3) Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum and two major topics relevant to production: 1) Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimitation and 2) Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy involves the rapid, complete analysis of volatiles trapped as fluid inclusions in rock samples using quadrupole mass analyzers. The technology documents the presence and relative bulk abundance of ionized volatile fragments with mass/charge ratio of m/z 180. This includes most geologically important inorganic species as well as organic species with less than or equal to 13 carbon atoms. The resulting analysis of the petroleum fraction is comparable to the low molecular weight fraction of whole-oil gas chromatographic mass spectrometric (GCMS) analysis (without devolatilization of the gas fraction); hence, the major classes of hydrocarbons (e.g., aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins) are represented. The Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy program at FIT is unique in several ways: 1) the method- ology and theoretical framework necessary for this unique technology are the result of long-standing research and development effort, 2) the cumulative experience and database of documented case histories are the most extensive in the world and 3) the technology rep- resents the most rapid analytical capability of its kind available. In its present configuration, FIS instrumentation has the potential to analyze all available samples for 2-4 wells in 24 hr period at total cost of approximately $4000-5000 per well, thus making it one of the most inexpensive and rapid geochemical techniques available. The resulting dataset can provide nearly continuous log of paleofluid chemistries through the stratigraphic section penetrated by well, and, given adequate sample coverage, the data can be mapped in two or three dimensions. 1.1 Organization of this Report Analytical results of the FIS analysis of 34 A1 BH are presented graphically in Sections and as series of profiles each illustrating the variation of particular atomic mass (m/z) or ratio of two masses with measured depth. general discussion of the interpretation of FIS data including the significance of particular features and trends (or their absence) is provided in Section A. The remaining information provided in subsequent sections includes: 1) refer- ence spectra, collected on internal standards and used to monitor inter- and intra-analytical consistency of the quadrupole analyses which are presented and discussed in Appendix B; and 2) mass spectra for m/z 180 from all samples which are listed individually by depth in Appendix C. 1.2 Analytical Procedure Samples of rock material are freed of significant interfering contamination by washing, picking and magnetic separation to remove drilling fluids, lost circulation materials, other solid mud

3 Photomicroscopy Thin sections were prepared from 34 A1 AH samples at depths warranting further exami- nation following preliminary assessment of the FIS analytical results. The sections were then examined under petrographic microscope using variety of fluid inclusion techniques (e.g., UV-fluorescence, microthermometry, etc.) in order to verify the presence of petroleum-bearing inclusions in the rock samples and to explore textural relationships that may yield additional information on the timing of hydrocarbon migration or generation. Petrographic examina- tion is also necessary to verify that petroleum-bearing fluid inclusions present in the samples and responsible for the observed mass spectra are not relict features (i.e., that they were not already present in the mineral grains prior to deposition). Some of the calcite cemented stringers can apparently be correlated across the N1-segment. However, the calcite cemented zones in A-1 AH are probably associated with fault zones. Faulting has affected the Rannoch Formation in A-1 AH as seen from the common tectonized lamination on the cores (see Enclosure 1); hence the reduced Rannoch Formation thickness in A-1 AH, when compared to other Visund wells, is likely not fully representative for the area. The Etive Fm. on Visund mainly consists of medium-coarse sandstones (El, E3, E5), however, zones of fine-grained, micaceous Rannoch-type facies (E2, E4) occur and apparently thicken northwards on the field. The Etive zonation reflects this interlayering of coarser and finer facies. In Well A-1 AH the upper part of the Etive Formation (and likely also the lowermost Ni) is probably faulted out (possibly eroded, however, these zones appear to be present in Well A-1 BH near by). The thinning of particularly the Etive zones E4 and E3 when compared to the other Visund wells is believed to be due to condensation caused by syndepositional tectonic activity in the area (i.e. the southern triangle on the N2-segment). This is in line with the seismic which suggests thinning of the Brent isochore within the southern triangle on the N2-segment. The Ness Fm. on Visund consists for large part of sandy bay fill facies, with typical channel sandstones being rare. The Tarbert Fm. on Visund consists of very fine to fine-grained, micaceous, hummocky cross-laminated sandstones. The Ness/Torbert boundary may be difficult to pick on logs only because of often transitional facies changes. question: How do Tor FM and Ekofisk FM lithologies (quartz, clay, calcite proportions) differ and what are the reservoir quality implications?
answer_text: Ekofisk FM has significantly higher quartz (up to ~39%) and clay (trace to ~10%) and correspondingly lower calcite than Tor FM (calcite commonly 70–98%); consequently Ekofisk lithologies generally exhibit poorer reservoir quality (reduced porosity/permeability) than the purer Tor chalk.

context_snippets.text: Netwint 3. STRATIGRAPHY The lithostratigraphic nomenclature used in this report follows that of Deegan and Scull (1977) and Isaksen and Tonstad (1989). The Cenozoic micropalaeontological zonation scheme utilised is based broadly on King (1989), but subsequently modified as response to the publications of Gradstein et al. (1992) and Gradstein and Backstrom (1996) as well as more detailed studies in the southern Norwegian offshore, Greater Ekofisk area, by Network Stratigraphic Consulting Limited scientific staff (See Figure 1). The Late Cretaceous micropalaeontological zonation scheme utilised is based on King et al (1989), but subsequently modified as response to more detailed chalk studies in the Central North Sea area carried out by Network Stratigraphic Consulting Limited scientific staff. The Late Cretaceous nannoplankton zonation scheme broadly follows Mortimer (1987), with modifications based on Burnett (1990, 1996), Burnett et al (1998) and detailed chalk studies in the Central North Sea area carried out by Network Stratigraphic Consulting Limited scientific staff. A micropalaeontological (microfauna/nannoplankton) review study of the chalk sections of Valhall Field wells (Gallagher and Bailey 1993) has resulted in the construction of Combined Zonation Scheme (refer to the Wellsite Manual') for the Tor and Hod Formations of this area. Comprehensive revision of this zonation based on recent horizontal well data has resulted in more refined scheme for the Tor and Hod Formations (see Figures - 3). The gamma ray log signature over the Tor Formation in these well tracks was unusually high in places (although such responses have been previously recorded elsewhere on the field). It was decided to isolate lithology from the high gamma intervals to more closely determine biostratigraphy and lithology at these levels. LITHOLOGY AND LITHOFACIES LITHOLOGIC CHARACTER General. The core materials from Maastrichtian- and Danian-aged reservoir sections in the North Sea, Norway, are composed primarily of yellowish brown to very light gray chalk. The major components of these chalks are micrograined. calcareous, coccolithophorid material and traces to very common quartz. The chalks also contain, macrograined skeletal debris, chalk clasts, and trace amounts to very rare (typically less than 5%) clay minerals and pyrite. Primary bedding, although commonly indistinct, ranges from thin to very thick and frequently exhibits low-angle (10-20 degrees) inclination. Bedding-parallel planar lamination and wavy lamination are the most common primary sedimentary structures. The more common massive chalks, those that contain no primary internal structure, typically contain weak to moderate mottling representative of bioturbation and burrowing. Recognizable burrow forms include Chondrites, Planolites, and Zoophycos. The cored sections described to date exhibit only minor stylolitization. Phillips 2/7 4X. The cored interval in the 2/7 4X is yellowish gray, light-gray, and greenish gray chalk composed mainly of micron-size coccolithophorid debris and microcrystalline calcite cement. Calcite content, determined by x-ray diffraction analysis, ranges from 52 to 100 percent; most commonly, however, the calcite content is in the range of 70 to 98 percent. The quartz content in the 2/7 4X chalk section ranges from to 39 percent. Clay minerals occur in trace amounts (<1%) to 10 percent. Quartz and clay-mineral content are significantly greater in the Ekofisk Formation (the upper one- half of the cored interval in this well) than in the underlying chalks of the Tor Formation (Figure 1). LITHOFACIES These studies indicate that North Sea chalk sequences can be subdivided into eleven reccurring lithofacies types (Table II) that are likely to be important in terms of the tectonic, stratigraphic, sedimentologic, diagenetic history of the chalk section and that are also likely have significance in terms of their reservoir behavior. summary of the defining character of these eleven lithofacies, as determined from wells studied to date (and subject to revision as additional wells are included in the study), is provided here.

Some of the major points are summarised below: - The youngest sediments analysed at 1600m are of Early Oligocene age. - The Rogaland Gp (Balder Fm) was penetrated at 2111m. - The Shetland Gp (Tor Fm) was penetrated at 2431m. Latest Maastrichtian sediments (Ekofisk Fm) are not recognised in this well, implying an unconformity at the CfT boundary. - There is major unconformity at 3185m(log) where Cenomanian sits directly on Early Barremian sediments. A thin Early Barremian section (approximately 2,5m) sits directly on Middle Volgian sediments, implying another major unconformity at 3191,5m (log). - The Late Jurassic section is less than 20m in thickness, represented by sediments of Middle Volgian, Middle Oxfordian and Early Oxfordian ages, separated by hiati. The age of the reservoir interval is indicated by biostratigraphical events above and below. No age significant events are recorded within the reservoir interval. - The fault zone penetrated within the interval 9m has probably cut out parts of the Ness and ORE Fms and may partly be the reason for difficulties in interpreting the biostratigraphy of the lowermost part of the Middle Jurassic.

The problems are mainly hole stability problems caused by sloughing shales. Another problem is the considerable variations in formation pore pressures. This will in many cases put very narrow limits on the mud weight and the margin between gaining and loosing circulation is small. The lost circulation problem is also intensivated in the lower pressure zones at the bottom of this section because of the annulus flow restriction caused by the sloughing shales above. This problem has been experienced on the previously drilled wells in the area. Efforts were now made to avoid this by better control on the hydraulics and by exercising closer control on the selecting of proper casing point. The careful control of the mud weight was primarly based on watching the mud gas, the penetration rate, the dc- exponent and the other drilling parameters. Actually no problems were recorded until 2000 m. drilling break at 1628 in was checked for flow (neg.) and high mud gas readings were occationally encountered. The mud also had to be circulated for mud rings. Overpull often occurred below 2000 in and the hole had to be reamed several times. At 2580 it was decided to stop drilling and set casing even if this depth was more than 100 in higher than the planned setting depth. This decision was made because of high mud gas, hole stability problems and the observed trend in the pore pressure. Further drilling was believed to be able to cause the same lost circulation problems as experienced in the two previously drilled wells. question: For well 7321/8-2 how does the vitrinite-derived 600±90 m erosion estimate compare with the regional ~1500 m estimate, and what causes explain the difference?
answer_text: The vitrinite-derived estimate (600 ± 90 m) is much lower than the regional estimate (~1500 m). This difference is attributed to the well’s limited drilled section and absence of shallow samples (notably the upper Kolmule Fm) and likely removal of any Torsk Fm plus part of the Kolmule Fm.

context_snippets.text: 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. 1 SUMMARY Petroleum geochemical analyses of Isotube mud gas and drill cuttings samples from the interval 499m to 797m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7322/7-1 have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. Drill cuttings samples from the Nordland Group (484m to 540m) mainly poor to minor source potential, mainly for gas. The shallowest sample 499m has good organic carbon content and marginally good source potential, mainly for gas, but is unlikely to have generated significant hydrocarbons in attaining the present level of maturity. Drill cuttings samples from the Kolmule Formation (540m to 661m), the Kolje Formation (661m to 677m) and the unspecified reservoir section (677m to 797mTD) have mainly poor to marginally fair source potential, mainly for gas. Extracts of selected samples the Nordland Group and unspecified reservoir are dominated by polar fractions, attributed mainly to polyglycols from the drilling fluid. Alkane fractions include suspected base oil, possibly from the drilling fluid. Biomarker ratios indicate that all extracted samples are immature for oil generation with vitrinite reflectance no more than 0.6%. The regional unconformity at the base Nordland Group is not evident from the data. Most biomarker ratios indicate slightly lower maturation level for the two deeper samples 763m and 790m from the unspecified reservoir than for the three shallower samples 499m, 505m and 517m form the Nordland Group. This may be related to combination of organic facies variation and reworking of organic material into the shallower section. The 763m and 790m samples contain mainly terrestrial higher plant derived organic material consistent with the rather low HI values throughout the interval. The 499m, 505m and 517m samples contain mainly marine organic material and type II or mixed type II/type III kerogen. The rather low HI values throughout the Nordland Group could be related to oxidation during reworking of the organic material. Isotube mud gas samples are dominated by N2 and also O2+Ar with N2/(O2+Ar) ratios indicative of air and with low CO2 concentrations. Samples from 690m, 750m and 790m comprise thermogenic gas generated from gas mature source rock with vitrinite reflectance around 1%. Samples from 510m and 530m are suggested to have leaked, indicated by low gas wetness and anomalously heavy carbon isotope ratios. Interpretation of samples from 550m, 590m and 630m is less clear but these do not appear to have leaked. Relatively heavy C2 and C3 carbon isotope ratios could suggest biodegradation, although this is not supported by molecular composition ratios, and it is unclear why biodegradation should affect shallow gases within the claystones of the Kolmule Formation but not the underlying unspecified reservoir section.

question: What are the geological ages and depositional environments of the Sleipner, Hugin, Heather, and Draupne formations?
answer_text: Sleipner — Early–Mid Callovian: virtually non‑marine deposition; Hugin — Mid–Late Callovian: restricted marine (shoreface/tidal to ebb‑tidal delta sandstones); Heather — Mid to latest Oxfordian: claystone with limestone stringers and interbedded sandstones (marine clay/limestone facies); Draupne — Early Berriasian: open marine, periodically anoxic, organic‑rich claystone.

These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

4. LITHOLOGY 15/9-12 by S. Evensen The reservoir interval, the Hugin Formation of Middle Jurassic age, is devided into three units. The lowermost unit, consist in general of very fine to fine occasionally medium grained sandstones deposited in shoreface/tidal dominated enviroment. These sandstones are interbedded with few siltstone/mudstone layers, and one distinct coal layer at 3568-60 m. The lower part of the unit consist of more calcite/dolomite cemented sandstones than the upper part. The general good reservoir quality of this unit are also interrupted by strong bioturbation in some interval of the sandstones. This middle unit consist of interbedded sandstones and shales deposited in an ebb tidal delta/lower shoreface environment. The sandstones at the base of the unit are medium to coarse grained homogenous and structureless and should display good reservoir potential. To the top the sandstones are more fine-grained, laminated and strongly bioturbated. Chert nodules are observed throughout this interval. The uppermost unit consist in this well entirely of sandstones deposited in shoreface environment. The reservoir quality of the very fine to fine low-angle laminated sandstones seems to be poor (to fair) due to highly bioturbated intervals and thin calcite/dolomite layers throughout the whole unit.

question: How do Hugin FM lithology and reservoir quality compare between wells 15/9-12 and 15/9-F-1B; what are the key similarities and differences?
answer_text: Both wells’ Hugin Formation is dominantly sandstone ranging from very fine to very coarse and moderately to well sorted. Well 15/9‑12 is described in three units with variable reservoir quality (good potential in basal medium–coarse sands but overall poor–fair upsection due to strong bioturbation, calcite/dolomite cement, chert nodules and a coal layer), whereas 15/9‑F‑1B is simply noted as very fine–very coarse, moderately–well sorted with rare claystone stringers and no detailed reservoir problems reported.

context_snippets.text: GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. context_snippets.text: • Petrologic study of Middle Jurassic sandstones 2 INTRODUCTION 0 STATOIL This study provides petrologic data for cores in the Garn, Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations in the Statoil well 6506/11-6, Kristin Field (Figure 2-1). The petrologic data include bulk chemical analyses (94 samples), modal analyses of thin sections from the same samples, photomicrographs of thin sections, and scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of fractured rock surfaces. new set of modal analyses of thin sections from the Garn Formation in well 6406/2-3T3 was also performed (24 samples) to obtain an internally consistent data set for comparing porosity development between this well and 6506/11-6. Together with routine core analyses (one-inch-diameter plugs) and wireline log profiles, these data are used to interpret the role of depositional sand quality and diagenesis in determining porosity, permeability, and net/gross distribution within these sandstone reservoirs. Comparisons are made with similar data from nearby wells in blocks 6506/11, 6506/12, and 6406/2 to develop semi-regional context for the results and to better understand sedimentologic controls and the lateral extent of porous intervals. Particular attention is given to examining the relationship of chlorite and bitumen coatings to reservoir quality and the possible factors controlling chlorite occurrence. An earlier phase of this study focused on evaluation of petrologic data provided by Saga Petroleum from wells 6406/2-1, 6406/2-2, and The goals of this study, presented at the PL 134 Exploration Committee Meeting Ni. 13 (October 1998), are as follows: • Explain observed porosity-permeability in terms of depositional & diagenetic controls. • Document and interpret patterns of grain-coating chlorite occurrence. • Study the effect of bitumen coatings on porosity-permeability. • Provide petrologic input for sedimentology studies. • Investigate the apparent westward & northward increase in chlorite coating and bulk sodium (plagioclase) content in the Garn Formation. • Document and interpret the high-permeability zone at the top of the Garn Formation. • Study the occurrence and lateral extent of interlayered porous and tight zones in the Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations.

The primary sedimentary lamination is defined by concentrations of strongly orientated micas and carbonaceous fragments (Plate 1A). Micaceous laminae also contain relatively high amounts of clay matrix. Detrital mineralogy consists predominantly of quartz, K-feldspar, low grade argillites, clay lithics and mica, and the sample is classified as subarkosic arenite (Figure 2.1). Micas consist of both muscovite and biotite (brown/green coloured) and are variably altered to authigenic clay (kaolinite) or are splayed. Authigenic pore- occluding minerals comprise minor quartz overgrowths and trace amounts of ferroan calcite. Pyrite is dominantly grain or matrix replacive component. The cleaner sandstone laminae are generally poorly compacted and have moderately good visible porosity preserved within an open grain framework (Plate 1B). Overall reservoir quality is, however, predicted to be moderate to poor, and is strongly controlled by the tight micaceous lamination which is expected to have strong directional influence on permeability.

3. GEOLOGICAL EVALUATION 3.1. Introduction Geological Setting The Draugen Field is situated in the Haltenbanken area off mid-Norway. The geological history of mid-Norway comprises Palaeozoic formative stage and Devonian to present break-up phase. Rifting and related faulting occurred from Late Carboniferous up to present day with westward moving of the axis of rifting activity. The resulting Norwegian shelf is passive cratonic margin underlain by series of continental margin basins superimposed on collapsed Palaeozoic orogeny. The Field comprises NNE/SSW trending low relief periclinal lenticular structure (20 km) with maximum vertical closure of 50 m. The main hydrocarbon accumulation is hosted by the Rogn Sandstone Formation, local Upper Jurassic composite shoreface/shelf deposit. minor, connected accumulation is hosted by the Garn Sandstone Formation, Middle Jurassic regionally extensive progradational shallow marine formation. The main reservoir facies, Rogn Formation, is enclosed to the north, south and east by butiminous claystones of the Upper and Lower Spekk Formation, time equivalent of the Rogn Formation. On the western side the Rogn Formation onlaps the Gam Formation which here rises above the field OWC. The top-seal of the Field is provided by the Upper Spekk Formation, the Lower Spekk provides seat seal over the larger part of the reservoir. Well 6407/9-B-5 was drilled from the northern water injection template to the target at top Rogn Formation, app. 1825 to the ( Fig. 1.1). The well reached TD in the sandstone's of the Garn Formation. The target was chosen to maximise on sweep of hydrocarbons as far to the north as possible. 3.2. Sample Collection The only samples collected were ditch cuttings, no cores or sidewall samples were taken. SEPOT-1012.E 13

Technical Memorandum (John Cater and Andrew Taylor, lchron Limited) Introduction Slabbed core from wells 6507/7-3, 6507/7-A17 and 6507/7-A35 was logged at ResLab Laboratories, Stavanger, by John Cater and Andrew Taylor (lchron Limited), on March 25th-27th 2003. For each well, copy of the hand-drawn 1:50 scale core log and written log comments are presented here. Illustrative core photographs are shown on Plates to 5. The sedimentology of the cored intervals is summarised below. Detailed descriptions are contained in the log comments. The depositional environments recorded by the cored intervals are interpreted below. Recommendations for future work to investigate the likely distribution and facies of Late Cretaceous sandstones in the Heidrun area are made at the end of this memorandum. Note that the most recent biostratigraphic data are not available for this memorandum. All depths quoted are core depths. Summary of core descriptions and interpreted depositional environments The cored section comprises mid to late Coniacian siltstones of the Kvitnos Formation overlying 2.51m of medium grained sandstones of the mid-Coniacian Lysing Formation (2367.55m-2370.06m), which in turn overlie fine grained sandstones of the late Aalenian Garn Formation. 2360.00m - 2367.55m This interval is dominated by laminated siltstones displaying local, weak bioturbation by pyritised Chondrites and sand-filled Sabularia (Plate 1A and 1B). The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

context_snippets.text: 5 Summary Summarised below are the key points and conclusions drawn from the acquisition and processing of the Zero Offset Vertical Seismic Profile for well 7221/12-1in the Svanefjell field. ▪ The survey acquisition was successful. The performance of the TriSor OFS surface equipment during the survey was excellent, with accurate gun tuning throughout. ▪ The downhole data recorded with the Borehole VSI tool was of high quality, and good vector fidelity was recorded with high signal to noise ratio. ▪ Good first break picks were obtained in the main VSP part of the well. Estimated time picks were extended almost to seabed using the horizontal components. ▪ VSP processing was done using the component and zero phase corridor stack was obtained with bandwidth of 5-140Hz. The full bandwidth zero phase P-P corridor stack shows an increase in resolution compared to the provided surface seismic data. ▪ Compressional sonic log calibration was done with minimal drift correction and set of synthetic seismogram traces was generated for various zero phase Ricker wavelets. ▪ The full bandwidth (5-140Hz) 60ms corridor stack, along with the 5-70Hz reduced bandwidth corridor stack, tie well with the Ricker wavelet synthetic seismograms for variety of different bandwidths. ▪ good 3-way tie was made between the VSP corridor stack, Synthetics and 3D surface seismic data.

2 Acquisition A 4-level Versatile Seismic Imager (VSI) tool string (15.24m shuttle spacing) was used by Schlumberger to acquire the downhole data for the ZOVSP survey. The tools are fitted with three orthogonally opposed non-gimballed accelerometers providing flat frequency response from 2- 200Hz irrespective of the angle of tilt. A tuned array of 250cu.in Sercel G-Guns, operating at 2000psi was used as source for the survey. The guns were deployed by the rig’s crane. The guns target firing pressure was 2000 psi. Source control was provided via the use of the TriSor OFS in sea dynamic source controller and the calibrated near-field hydrophone sensor data were recorded at 1.25m below the gun cluster. The target gun depth was 5m below mean sea level (actual depth m) and the gun offset and azimuth from the wellhead were 75m and 140 degrees, respectively. The equipment was then used to acquire the main VSP survey data, at 15.24m intervals between 399.9 – 720.8m MD DF. The recording was done using the Schlumberger Maxwell acquisition system. At each level, at least five good repeatable shots were acquired and recorded. The main acquisition parameters and survey equipment are shown in Table 1. The full acquisition report can be found in the digital deliverables accompanying this report.

2. Delta Minimum In the case of negative drift second method is used, called At minimum. This applies differential correction to the sonic log where it is assumed the greatest amount of time error is caused by the lower velocity sections of the log. Over given interval the method will correct only At values which are higher than threshold, the Atmin. Values of At which are lower than the threshold are not corrected. The correction is reduction of the excess of At over Atmin ie. At - Atmin At - Atmin is reduced through multiplication by reduction coefficient which remains constant over the interval. This reduction coefficient, named G, can be defined as: G = + drift (At - Atmin) dZ Where drift is the drift over the interval to be corrected and the value (At - Atmin) dZ is the time difference between the integrals of the two curves At and Atmin, over the same interval. Hence the corrected sonic: Atmin = G(At - Atmin) + Atmin The sonic, density and Gamma ray log data are taken from the well 7221/12. Absent values in the sonic log were filled using linear interpolation. depth interval of – 705.2306m MD DF (439.3518m-674.8098m TVDSS) was available for sonic calibration and synthetics generation. The gap in the density log was filled using constant value of g/cm3. A comparison between the VSP interval velocity and the raw sonic derived velocity is shown in Figure 40 and show match between velocities in the deeper section unaffected by casing noise prior to sonic calibration. Figure 41 shows the Sonic Calibration results. The reference level for the computed raw drift is set at 446.16m TVDSS in the good quality VSP data interval. The maximum raw drift observed for the target interval is +2ms. The sonic curve is calibrated using knee points. After calibration the residual drift over the good VSP interval is less than +/- 1ms. The calibrated sonic was extended to MSL using the sea bed depth and velocity. The extended sonic is then integrated and used as the time-depth relation for the well. The calibrated sonic will be used for depth-time conversion only. For synthetics generation, the raw sonic, correctly time- indexed using the calibrated sonic, will be used. Figure 42 shows the calibrated velocity logs compared with the interval velocity from the VSP.

6.3 Bathymetry The multibeam echo sounder data was processed onboard MV Fugro Meridian using Fugro Starfix suite to monitor data quality and data coverage. The data was logged in Simrad Raw format (.all) and imported into Starfix.Proc for processing. Both single beam and multibeam echo sounder data were corrected for transducer draught, acoustic velocity through sea water and vessel heave, pitch and roll, and then positioned with reference to the echo sounder transducer. 6.4 Sidescan Sonar The engineers and geophysicists examined the sidescan sonar records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks include range/scale, gains, tow fish height and position, as well as overall record quality. The sidescan sonar data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full by the geophysicist, using SonarWiz Version software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted, in which case the XTF file would be transferred to the relevant working directory for use, or, if rejected, would be flagged as potential re-run. Mosaicking of the sidescan sonar data was performed using the mosaic module, which applied slant range correction to the data and checked for full sonar coverage of the survey area. 6.5 Sub-bottom Profilers The engineers and geophysicists examined the hull-mounted pinger and mini sleeve gun records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks included sweep/scale, gains, examination of seabed pulse and penetration as well as overall record quality. The sub-bottom profiler data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full, by the geophysicist, using Starfix.Interp software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted or rejected and flagged as potential re-run. 6.6 2DHR Multichannel Seismic Quality control of the online 2DHR multichannel seismic system was undertaken by the onboard engineers, geophysicist and seismic processor. The engineers maintained an observers’ log (Appendix E.2) in which all relevant information was recorded. Typically, routine checks were made on the source and streamer; the engineers monitored the manifold pressure, gun statistics (including any dropped/mis-timed shots) as well as pulse/frequency spectra of the seismic source. Routine checks of the streamer included streamer integrity (noisy, dead or reverse polarity channels), noise (due to environmental factors or weather), and streamer depth control/feather angle. On completion of each 2DHR multichannel seismic line, the data underwent final QC. The onboard geophysicist used the RadExPro seismic processing system as well as the observers’ logs and other quality control data generated by the NTRS2 system. Shot and CMP gathers were generated, to allow the identification of bad channels/shots and noise problems, and to verify the streamer offset and depth of the gun array. Then, brute stack was generated for each line, to ascertain any swell noise and check the overall data quality. The data were processed aboard the Fugro Meridian using the OpenCPS seismic processing system. The data processing flows aim to remove noise and seismic interference from 2DHR data. question: Compute gas rate and assess if 2718 psia confirms reservoir pressure given DST oil rate 3250 STB/D and GOR 235 scf/stb?
answer_text: Gas rate = 3250 STB/D × 235 scf/STB = 763,750 scf/day (~763.8 MSCF/D). Yes, 2718 psia matches the reported initial reservoir pressure (2718 psia @ 1882 m TVDSS) and is confirmed by the DST.

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

STRUCTURAL GEOLOGY GROUP IG,UiB/NRSC REPORT NO.: REVISION NO: TITLE: Cap-rock qualities of the Teistengrunnen Group, southwestern Barents Sea with emphasis on its fracture pattern AUTHORS(S): Roy H. Gabrielsen NUMBER OF PAGES: 129 NUMBER OF COPIES: DISTRIBUTION: Norsk Hydro a.s.; restricted ABSTRACT: The cap rocks of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations in wells 7321/9-1, 7219/9-1, 7120/2-2, 7120/6-1, 7120/12-1, 7228/2-1, 7228/9-1 and 7125/1-1 have been investigated from structural geological and rock mechanical point of view. The study has demonstrated that the fracture geometry and fracture frequency vary within the study area. The following preliminary conclusions are drawn: 1) The shales of the Fuglen Formation reveal higher vertical shear strengths (16-40 MPa) than the shales of the Hekkingen Formation (7-22 MPa). If erosion of approximately 1000 metres of rocks is assumed, the bulk of the cap rock may have been fractured. The present data, however indicate that the fracture frequency attributed to this deformation, is low. 2) The wells in the western part of the study area are characterized by high fracture frequencies and low-angle fractures. This deformation is probably associated with post early Tertiary compressional reactivation of some of the master fault complexes. Accordingly, the master fault complexes associated with the large basins in the west (Tromso Basin and Bjornoya Basins) are potentially most exposed to leakage through microfractures. However, since the shales of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations seem to have different rock mechanical properties the continuity of these units should be mapped in detail, and the problems with diffusion characteristcs of the units should be addressed.

A-13 4 PETROPHYSICAL EVALUATION 4.1 General The aim of this section is to present the petrophysical evaluation results of the Sognefjord Formation in well 31/2-M-42. The 13 3/8 casing shoe was located at 835 MD and the 5/8 casing at 1521 MD. The well has been plugged and permanently abandoned. Log Data Well 31/2-M-42 was logged with Schlumberger wireline and MWD logs. The following logs are recorded and used in the interpretation of the Sognefjord formation: Table A-6 Logs used for computation. Log quality and corrections The well was drilled with (water based) Anco 2000 KCI mud. Hole conditions are good and the overall log quality is good. The HALS laterologs are the only deep resistivity devices run in this well. The accuracy of these logs may be less in the water zone where the resistivity is low. For comments on the MDT data, see section 4.2 Evaluation Method True vertical depths and thicknesses are calculated with Recall algorithms correcting for the well path penetrating the formation. The petrophysical evaluation is done with the Recall program Prototype and the calculation parameters including parameter sources are listed in Table A-7. Litholoqy Calcite cemented sections are determinated by cut off density log and in addition visual inspection of logs. In these sections porosity is set to zero and water saturation to 1. The GR log is used to calculate the shale volume as fraction of the total bulk volume. The OR minimum has been choosen to give clean sandstone also in the micaceous part of the reservoir section.

A-13 When drilling with water based mud the lack of microresistivity device might introduce great errors in porosity calculation due to reduced possibility of hydrocarbon correction. The method used to correct for invasion effects is described in section below. The logs used in the computation have been corrected for environmental effects by the service company. The natural gamma ray was calibrated to MWD-API units, corrected for mud radiation. The navigator resistivity was normalized for tool size, borehole size, formation dielectric properties, and mud resistivity. The density was calibrated to gauge hole. Correction curve was presented by use of dual spaced detectors and 'spine and ribs' algorithm. 4.2 Evaluation Method True vertical depths and thickness' are calculated with Recall algorithms correcting for the well path penetrating the formation. The petrophysical evaluation is done with the Recall program Prototype and the calculation parameters including parameter sources are listed in Table A-5. The formation temperature is estimated from the temperature gradient for the Troll Field. Water saturation is calculated from the Poupon - Leveaux equation using the MHz phase resistivity log. (as the calculated shale values in the Sognefjord fm. are zero, the Poupon- Leveaux reduces to the Archie eq.) Porosity is calculated from the density log. This log may be heavily affected by hydrocarbons present. To apply hydrocarbon correction to the porosity pseudo MSFL (microresistivity) has been computed. The relation assumed was the following: SXO = SW (UK) For detailed information and equations of porosity, water saturation and formation temperature please refer 'Final well report, well 31/5-H-6H', Norsk Hydro 1996. • Definition of Net Reservoir To obtain the best values for net sand in the well the calcite's have been manually picked on the density log (BDCM) and by applying cut off on the density log. 4.4 Petrophysical log interpretation results Table A-6 and figures A-4 - A-6 presents the petrophysical interpretation results (CPI) for the pilot hole in well 31/2-Y-24 and the build up and horizontal section of well 31/2-Y-24 AH. The net sand log average table A-6 covers only the horizontal section from the 10 3/4 casing shoe to end interpretation at MD RKB. The OWC was picked at ND MSL (1789.5 MD RKB) in good C-sand in well Y-24 H. The OWC was not penetrated neither in the landing nor the horizontal part of the well Y-24 AH.

context_snippets.text: Structural core description - Well 15/9-19SR 33 At MD RKB in the Triassic, fracture with oil patches was encountered in an otherwise dry Skagerrak Formation. This is probably fracture of dilatational nature, possibly late fracture. The same phenomenon has been seen in the Pismo Formation of California, where fractures are observed in_the field as both barriers and (more rarely) conduits. Brace (1978) showed that pore-volume increase, or dilitancy, accompanies failure of intact rock in the laboratory. Antonelli et al. (1993) found that dilatation is found in an early stage of deformation band development. (Furthermore, it should be noted that en echelon open induced fractures were encountered in thin section at MD RKB.) a2. Decreased porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis The thin section from MD RKB (Skagerrak Fm.) exhibits compaction in the fracture, but no grain crushing. At mesoscopic scale, the fracture is filled with grey material, and is probably syn-sedimentary. It is surrounded by some rotated bedding and clay clasts and may well be associated with slumping at low mean stress levels. a3. Unchanged porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis Such band was found at MD RKB (Triassic). This type seems to be easier to recognize at core scale that in the thin-section. b. Deformation bands with cataclasis In most thin sections the deformed zone has decreased porosity relative to the host rock. This is mainly due to tighter packing, grain size reduction (Figure 1, Appendix B) and possible pore-filling illite (Figures B5/B6, Appendix B). This type is represented in most of the thin sections. Porosity is decreased typically by one order of magnituded, from (roughly speaking) 20 % to 0-2 %. 6.3 Comparison of meso and micro scale observations The number of thin sections (15) is bit too small to make complete analysis of micro/meso scale relationships. question: How do Hi‑Vis bentonite mud and seawater‑gel mud differ in composition, typical drilling uses, and suitable drilled-hole sections?
answer_text: Hi‑Vis bentonite mud is bentonite pre‑hydrated at 99–113 Kg/m3 and flocculated with seawater (2:1) and lime for a high‑viscosity cleaning/displacement fluid (used to clean holes and before running 30" casing); seawater‑gel mud is seawater thickened to about 1.04–1.38 sg used for drilling the 36" and 26" hole sections.

(Data in Table A6a-b) Predictions of the compositional kinetic models concerning the physical properties (GOR, saturation pressure, formation volume factor Bo) of the fluids generated as function of primary cracking are shown in Figure and Table A7. The observations made based on activation energy distributions and carbon chain length distributions from pyrolysis are generally supported by the results shown. P-N-A low wax petroleum type was predicted, thus the fluids generated fall within the black oil class. They reach saturation pressures of >200 bars (approximately begin of volatile oil) only at highest kerogen conversion levels (90% TR) where secondary cracking reactions might have already set in under closed-system pyrolysis conditions. Saturation pressures of both samples gradually evolve from ~150 bar for sample and ~100 bar for sample to values between 200 and 250 bar with maturity. Similarily, GOR values evolve from 155 respectively 89 Sm3/Sm3 to 504 respectively 352 Sm3/Sm3 at highest maturity levels (90% TR). GOR values of the Hekkingen Fm sample from the Krill Member are higher at all kerogen conversion levels. Both samples show systematics of GOR evolution which reflect the earlier results from kinetics and pyrolysis GC: In concordance with moderatley broad Ea distribution and the aromatic and phenolic signature observed under open-system pyrolysis conditions GORs as well as saturation pressures and formation volume factors show relatively steep gradients. Increasing GORs and saturation pressures with increasing maturity very well reproduce the natural behaviour of mixed terrestrial-marine organic matter derived fluids. In contrast, rather uniform GORs and saturation pressures would reproduce the natural behaviour of aquatic, mainly algal, homogeneous Type organic matter derived fluids. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

Data from these wells were used to constrain predictions of the petrophysical characteristics of the inferred reservoir sandstones of the Realgrunnen Group and, to lesser extent, of the Lower Basal Clastics in the Gamma Prospect. They comprise conventional wells drilled in the quadrants 7119, 7120, 7121, 7122 and 7219, as well as IKU shallow drilling 7018/05-U- 06 at the margin of the Troms-Finnmark Platform some 25 km southwest of the licence area. Thermal and kinetic input parameters derived from some of the considered wells were used to calibrate the modelling of hydrocarbon generation and expulsion from the principal source rock of the Hekkingen Formation in the Tromso Basin. Hydrocarbon characteristics were mainly extrapolated from data representative for the discoveries in the Hammerfest Basin, namely 7122/6-1 (oil and gas), Snohvit (oil and gas), Albatross (oil and gas), Askeladden (oil and gas), and Alke (gas). 3.8 OPERATIONAL GEOLOGY WELL PROGRAM 3.8.1 SAMPLING PROGRAM The standard cuttings sampling intervals will be as follows (Fig. 3.8.1): every 10 from 30 csg shoe (after return of drilling fluid) down to thel3 3/8 casing shoe at 2000 m. every from the 5/8 casing shoe down to T.D. at 3009 m. question: If Hugin core data show a strong porosity–Kh correlation, is the 2 mD/15 PU permeability–porosity cutoff still appropriate for reservoir selection?
answer_text: No — the 2 mD / 15 PU cutoff was arbitrary and based mainly on Sleipner data, so a Hugin-specific permeability/porosity cutoff should be derived from the Hugin porosity–Kh correlation.

context_snippets.text: Core porosity versus horizontal permeability relationship: To establish the relationship, RCA from Hugin and Sleipner formations has been utilized. Porosity volume was determined by helium injection at net confining sleeve pressure of 15 bar. Standard air permeability was measured with nitrogen gas at net confining sleeve pressure of 17 bar. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability correlation was used (Figure 16). Porosity in percentage, permeability in mD The porosity-Kh relationship was derived mainly from Sleipner Formation data, since the majority of the points from the Hugin Formation presented very poor relationship between porosity and Kh. For average porosity calculations, an arbitrary permeability cut-off of 2mD was used, which corresponds to porosity cut-off of 15 PU. 40% clay cut-off is also used for average calculations. Water Saturation Computation: Minimum shows were seen in drill cuttings and sidewall cores from the top of the Hugin Formation. Traces of dark brown tarry dead oil stains together with weak, dull yellow flouresence were described at the top of the Hugin Formation at 2318 mBRT. Rw (OHMM) Rw Temp. (°C) 0.04 82 Table 5.3.5. Water saturation parameters No special core analysis were performed to determine the cementation exponent or resistivity index. value of for was derived from the Pickett plot. True resistivity of the formation (RT) was derived from DLL/MLL after borehole correction. Saturation was calculated using the Archie equation. The logs and formation pressure data indicate that the Ty and Hugin formations are water bearing.

OUTLINE TEST PROCEDURES FOR CONVENTIONAL CORE ANALYSIS STUDIES PERFORMED ON WELL NUMBER 15/6-8S A. CORE RECEIPT Schlumberger received approx. metres of core material from the subject well in our Stavanger laboratory. The core was recovered using fluted aluminium barrel and was inches in diameter. It was cut into one metre long sections and preserved at the wellsite by capping each end (no resin injection was required). On arrival, the state of preservation of the core was good. There was one core in total (indicated as Hugin/Triassic age), which comprised the following: B. CORE GAMMA On receipt of the core in the laboratory the natural gamma radiation was measured using Na (TI) crystal scintillator, and the natural Gamma emission intensity of the core was plotted as log against core depth on scale of to 200. This is supplemented by simultaneous measurement of the spectrum of gamma rays naturally emitted from the core. As the radioactive elements emit gamma rays of characteristic energies it is possible to isolate the contributions made by each element from the total core gamma count by performing spectral analysis in the energy domain. A multi channel analyser provides the raw gamma spectrum, quantitative analysis of this spectrum is accomplished using computer techniques. log of the intensities of potassium, uranium and thorium is obtained in this way. Core gamma measurements were made with the core contained in the barrel. The core was assessed by the Operator, from the core gamma, to need correction to wireline log of minus metre (see section 5). C. PLUG CUTTING Following core gamma measurements the core was carefully removed from the barrel and wiped clean before being measured and marked up. Plug samples, of one inch in diameter by approximately one inch in length, were then cut. This involved drilling samples parallel to the apparent bedding every 25 cm in sand sections (every 50 cm from - core regarded by Operator as tight, therefore plugging program reduced) to represent the horizontal data and additional samples, perpendicular to apparent bedding to represent the vertical data. The horizontal plugs had permeability, porosity and grain density measurements made while the vertical plugs had permeability only. Simulated formation brine, constructed to required concentration of 50,000 ppm with sodium chloride, was used as the drill bit lubricant. The end faces were lightly brushed using the same fluid to remove any fines induced by trimming. Plug offcuts were retained and labelled for possible future use. DEMINEX 1516-8S

STATOIL 1 INTRODUCTION Two Drill Stem Tests were planned in well 34/11-2S in the hydrocarbon bearing Brent Group. The tests were performed in the period 20/4-12/5-96, and the objectives were to: • collect pressure and temperature data for determination of reservoir properties and productivity • obtain representative fluid samples • investigate lateral boundary effects • determine the minimum horizontal stress (minifrac test) The first test was two stage test designed to investigate the productivity of the low permeability Etive Formation and the lower part of the Ness Formation. The second test was performed in Tarbert/Ness Formation. Figure shows the location of well 34/11-2S. The well was drilled with an average deviation of 27° through the reservoir section. 2 SUMMARY DST IA, 1B and DST were designed to collect pressure and temperature data for transient pressure analysis for determination of the reservoir productivity, and to obtain representative fluid samples. The Etive Formation (DST 1A) was perforated from to MD RKB, and the well was opened on 16/64 adjustable choke. The choke was increased several times, and the well produced mud to surface after approximately three hours. After hours the annulus pressure was lost and the PCT (Pressure Controlled Tester) valve shut in the well dovvnhole. The loss of annulus pressure was most likely caused by the packer not withstanding the big differential pressure across the elements. The test was aborted when communication between tubing and annulus was discovered. The well was killed and the test string was pulled out of hole. No analysis was performed from the pressure data from DST 1A, and no fluid sample was collected. The test objectives were not fulfilled for the Etive Formation, but the pressure response clearly shows that the productivity is very low. FADATMAMIPROU41123.SAM

Data acquisition and production control Downhole pressure gauges: 2 ELS LMR 1000, 15K and ELS MQGX 16K gauges to be run in one MWS/Halliburton gauge carrier. 4 ea Schlumberger Unigage Quartz 18K gauges to be run in DGA gauge adaptor. Surface data acquisition: In addition to Schlumberger manual registration, the ELS electronic surface data acquisition system will be used to monitor wellhead data at the choke manifold (including signals from the sand detector) and separator data. Chemical injection: - Glycol will be injected on the upstream side of the choke manifold and at the sub sea test tree to prevent hydrate formation during production startup. Injection for hydrate inhibition is not required after surface temperature has reached 30 'C. If water is produced it may become necessary to inject emulsion breaker. The emulsion breaker should be injected on the upstream side of the Choke Manifold. Injection rate should be adjusted to give the recommended concentration of approx. 10 ppm. If during oil production foaming causes problems for the separating process required defoamers may be injected on the upstream side of the Choke Manifold to give concentration of approx. ppm. If viscous oil and/or oil with high vax content is being produced addition of vax inhibitior may be required. Particularly prior to shutting in the well for pressure buildup(s). In this case inject wax inhibitor at the sub sea test tree. Sand production: In the event of sand production monitor development and quantity by: 7. oY Electronic sand detector (continuous monitoring). B.S.&W. performed by test crew at regular intervals after well startup and following choke changes. Erosion probe in standpipe to be monitored at regular intervals by test company operator on the rig floor.

Test objectives: 'lest procedures The main object for the test was to collect pressure and temperate data for transient pressure analysis for determination of the upper Brent Gp. reservoir productivity and to obtain representative fluid samples. Test procedures: 1. Perforation / Clean-up flow: The well was perforated underbalanc.ed, utilising 5/8 TCP guns with DP BMX charges, 12 shoot per foot, 30 deg phasing at 11:40 on 8th May 96.11e well was open on mm (16/64) adjustable choke lined through the separator to the burners. At 12:53 the adjustable choke was opened up to mm (20/64), further opened to mm (24/64) at 13:32 and diverted to mm fixed choke at 14:20. At 14:35 flow was diverted through mm (24/64) adjustable choke which was increased to mm (32/64) at 14:36 and finally flow was diverted through mm find choke at 14:45 where it stayed for the remainder of the flow period. Gas rate measurement was started at 15:40. 2. Clean up build up: The well was shut in at the PCT tester valve on 9th May 96 at 14:14 hr and the pressure upstream of the choke manifold bled off to 31 bar. This pressure increased slowly indicating possible leak at the PCT, and after investigation it was decided to flow the well again to achieve stable flow conditions before re-shutting in the well at the choke manifold. 3. Main flow. The well was opened on 9th May 96 at 20:46 on mm (16/64) adjustable choke which was increased in steps reaching mm (32/64) at 22:38. Flow was then diverted through mm fixed choke at 22:42 and gas rate measurement started at 23:50. 4. Main build up. The well was shut in at the choke manifold on 10th May 96 at 05:20. 5. Mini frac / kill well: After the build up was finished, mini frac was performed to find the minimum horizontal stress in the formation. After completion, the well was killed as per STATOIL program.

question: What are the two TVD MSL ranges used for seismic drift linear-shift calibration in VSP well 7/11-11?

context_snippets.text: The raw VSP data were supplied in SEGY format. The vertical component accelerometer and reference hydrophone data were timed to their first maxima. This corresponds to “trough to trough” picking. The data quality was generally good, although the levels at 1300, 1200 and 700m were of poor quality due to casing arrival interference. The picked times were optimised using regressive smoothing algorithm, and these were used to calculate set of vertical travel times below datum. Well velocity computations have been produced and are shown as Appendix 1. Time-depth, average and interval velocity curves are shown as Appendix 2, Figures 1-3. The VSP interval velocity curve is not compatible with the sonic velocities due to the variable ray travel paths through different near surface formations. The VSP times give correct average velocities to the receivers, but the log data should be referred to for accurate interval velocities. 3.2 Sonic Log Calibration Sonic, density, caliper, gamma ray and other logs were supplied over the interval – 4695.3m MDDF. Corrected vertical travel times have been used to calibrate the sonic log. The seismic drift curve was computed as follows: 3212.8 – 3940.6m TVD MSL us/ft linear shift 3940.6 – 4412.6m TVD MSL us/ft linear shift The calibration drift is not considered to be representative of the true formation interval velocities as the ray travel paths pass through laterally variable structure. The log calibration drift curve is displayed in Appendix Figure 4. The calibrated and uncalibrated sonic logs are plotted at linear depth scale of 1:500 as Enclosure 1, together with checkshot data, formation tops, computed acoustic impedance and other available log data. 3.3 Synthetic Seismograms The uncalibrated sonic log has been stretched to times defined by the log calibration. P- wave synthetic seismogram responses were created from the sonic and density logs. The synthetic reflection coefficient series was created at sample interval of 2ms two-way time. The time indexed data listing is shown as Appendix 3. The synthetic reflection coefficient series was convolved with maximum bandwidth 5- 45Hz zero phase filter. This is shown as Figure 1.3.

The stacked three component non-gimballed , and component data aligned at one- way corrected times are shown as Figures 4.1, & 4.4. Figure shows an FK display of the vertical component data The optimum upgoing P-wave has been derived using the vertical component data. 5- 100Hz zero phase preliminary bandpass filter, spherical divergence compensation (T**2.4) and transmission loss compensation (by normalising the direct arrival amplitudes within 40ms window) were applied to the data. The data were shifted to align at 100ms (Figure 4.5) and the downgoing wavefield was calculated by use of 9:1 spatial median (Figure 4.6). The residual energy after downgoing wavefield subtraction is displayed as Figure 4.7. The residual wavefield was aligned at two-way times below MSL (Figure 4.8). Spiking deconvolution operators were designed from the downgoing P-wavefield on trace-by- trace basis. The deconvolution operator design window was 0-500ms. After filter tests the data were output with maximum bandwidth 5-45Hz zero phase bandpass filter (Figure 4.9). Figure shows an FK display of the aligned deconvolved upgoing wavefield prior to the application of any band limiting filters. The deconvolved upgoing wavefield was enhanced by use of spatial 9:1 median filter enhancing dips of +/-0.2ms/m and is displayed with maximum bandwidth 5-45Hz zero phase filter as Figure 4.11. The data has been imaged using VSP-CMP transform with 2D velocity model with dips of 10 degrees (Figure 4.12). The enhanced deconvolved upgoing wavefield has been transposed such that data recorded at the first arrival curve is repositioned to trace 1, by taking series of small windows from each input trace. Subsequent corridors are composed of windows parallel to the first window looking further into the data. The VSP corridor stack has been generated by stacking traces to of the transposed VSP to derive single trace best estimate along the time-depth curve (Figure 4.13). The stacked data was analysed to investigate spectral and attenuation changes over the survey. Figure shows the total amplitude losses. Figure shows spectral analyses and Figure shows the downgoing wavefield in FZ space. The complete processing sequence is listed in Section 4.2.

Geophysical Review The seismic coverage over PL172 is extensive. There are over 4000 kilometers of seismic data on the license, which include the Statfjord Nord, Statfjord Ost, Statfjord and Murchison 3D surveys. Most of the early vintages of 2D seismic are of poor to fair quality and were not used in this interpretation. The data interpreted for this prospect consisted of Mobil reprocessed Nopec NOD8-87 2D lines (310 kilometers), Mobil proprietary MN91 2D lines (85 kilometers), and the reprocessed Statfjord Nord (E86R93) 3D survey. All of the seismic data used was wavelet processed/reprocessed to zero phase. The data quality of both the 2D and 3D seismic was good to excellent. The horizons that have been interpreted and/or mapped over PL172 are summarized below: Horizon Color Top Rogaland Group brown Top Shetland Group yellow Base Cretaceous Unconformity red Base Munin sandstone yellow Top Brent Group green Top Dunlin Group orange Top Statfjord Formation blue The Base Cretaceous Unconformity, Base Munin and Top Brent reflectors were completely remapped across the entire license prior to choosing drilling location. The Base Cretaceous Unconformity is easily recognized throughout the area. The reflector is high-amplitude peak caused by the high acoustic impedance Mime Formation limestones overlying the much lower impedance sandstones and shales of the Upper and Middle Jurassic. The Volgian-age Munin sandstone unit, where present, immediately underlies the Base Cretaceous Unconformity as observed in wells 33/9-8, 33/9-14, 33/9-15 and 33/9-16. The acoustic impedance of the upper Munin is similar to that of the Draupne and Heather shales. The impedance of the lower Munin is somewhat higher, which results in seismic reflector that can be recognized as distinct from that of the more widespread Upper Jurassic shales. This characteristic Base Munin reflector is peak which can be followed with confidence on the 3D seismic data. The seismic character of the Top Brent is variable and can be difficult to interpret. This is caused by the variable nature of the upper Brent acoustic impedance and the low impedance contrast with the overlying Upper Jurassic sands and shales. In the Prospect area, downthrown from the Murchison-Snorre Ridge, the horizon is seen as weak trough.

Page As mentioned earlier, the recorded well geophone data shows an inconsistency in the downgoing wevefield. This is seen as clear step in the bubble period after the first arrival at trace 10 in the recorded data. plot of the recorded gun signature shows similar step at the same trace number with similar periodicity. For this reason we believe that the inconsistency in the recorded downgoing wavefield results from an inconsistency in the input source signature. This could be caused by faulty airgun, or it may simply be result of change in pressure at which the airgun was operating. The significance of this inconsistency in the downgoing wavefield .is that it creates difficulties in separating the downgoing and upgoing wavefields. This results in . small portion of the downwave, for the deepest 10 traces being residual in the data after wavefield separation. This portion of the downgoing wavefield remains in the final upgoing wavefield displays, and has the appearance of steeply dipping reflected event. It should not be interpreted as such. Attempts were made to completely remove this residual portion of the transmitted energy.This was done at two stages. Firstly, we attempted to achieve better wavefield separation. This was done in two ways. The first method tried was to shorten the length of the median operator used to smooth the downgoing uavefield for wavefield separation. This allows for greater variation in the downgoing wavefield. This did not produce significantly bettor result than the original wavefield separation. The second method attempted was to use sloping median for the uavefield separation. Against it was hoped that this would allow for the step in the downgoing wavefield. Unfortunately, this method was also unsuccessful. Finally, an attempt was made to suppress this residual part of the dounuave after uavefield separation. Although this was to some extent successful in removing the residual event, it was considered to be more damaging to the data set than the event itself. For this reason the event remains in the final upgoing uctiefiEld displays. The event can be clearly seen in the unmedianed displays. In the displays with nine point median, the median process should have rejected the event, and it should therefore not effect the final result. In the case of the five point median, the event uill not be rejected so well. Care should therefore be te.;:en when making interpretations of this region of the data on these displays. The stabilized doungoine wavefield has been used to design the VSP deconvelutien operator (250 as application window). This has been applied as appropriate during processing. The deconvolved downgoing uavefield, display shows the effectiveness of collapsing the multiple tail after the downgoing first arrival within the deconvolution window.
