ANALYSIS PROCEDURES PREPARATION: Laboratory core handling and sampling, The plug samples for analyses were collected by drilling with one inch bore, using brine as cooling agent. The samples were cut to one inch lengths and subsequently cleaned in soichlet extractor using alternating sequences of methanol and toluene. Finally the samples were dried under controlled conditions at 60 °C and 40 % relative humidity for at least 48 hours prior to the measurements. MEASUREMENTS Spectral core gamma log A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of charac- teristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by WE, Institutt For Energitelcnildc, Kjeller. The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentra- tions of thorium and uranium in ppm. Gas Permeability Gas permeability (horizontal and vertical core plugs) was determined flowing nitrogen gas through the samples. At steady state conditions, the gas flow rate, the pressure drop over the plug sample and the upstream pressure were recorded. The confining pressure applied during the measurement was 20 bar. The gas permeability Kn2 was then calculated using Darcy's law. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability value, K1, was determined empirically.

With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. question: For Hugin and Sleipner core analyses, what net confining sleeve pressures were used for helium porosity and nitrogen permeability measurements?

context_snippets.text: Core porosity versus horizontal permeability relationship: To establish the relationship, RCA from Hugin and Sleipner formations has been utilized. Porosity volume was determined by helium injection at net confining sleeve pressure of 15 bar. Standard air permeability was measured with nitrogen gas at net confining sleeve pressure of 17 bar. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability correlation was used (Figure 16). Porosity in percentage, permeability in mD The porosity-Kh relationship was derived mainly from Sleipner Formation data, since the majority of the points from the Hugin Formation presented very poor relationship between porosity and Kh. CORE RECEIPT Schlumberger received approx. metres of core material from the subject well in our Stavanger laboratory. The core was recovered using fluted aluminium barrel and was inches in diameter. It was cut into one metre long sections and preserved at the wellsite by capping each end (no resin injection was required). On arrival, the state of preservation of the core was good. There was one core in total (indicated as Hugin/Triassic age), which comprised the following: B. CORE GAMMA On receipt of the core in the laboratory the natural gamma radiation was measured using Na (TI) crystal scintillator, and the natural Gamma emission intensity of the core was plotted as log against core depth on scale of to 200. This is supplemented by simultaneous measurement of the spectrum of gamma rays naturally emitted from the core. As the radioactive elements emit gamma rays of characteristic energies it is possible to isolate the contributions made by each element from the total core gamma count by performing spectral analysis in the energy domain. A multi channel analyser provides the raw gamma spectrum, quantitative analysis of this spectrum is accomplished using computer techniques. log of the intensities of potassium, uranium and thorium is obtained in this way. Core gamma measurements were made with the core contained in the barrel. The core was assessed by the Operator, from the core gamma, to need correction to wireline log of minus metre (see section 5). C. PLUG CUTTING Following core gamma measurements the core was carefully removed from the barrel and wiped clean before being measured and marked up. Plug samples, of one inch in diameter by approximately one inch in length, were then cut. This involved drilling samples parallel to the apparent bedding every 25 cm in sand sections (every 50 cm from - core regarded by Operator as tight, therefore plugging program reduced) to represent the horizontal data and additional samples, perpendicular to apparent bedding to represent the vertical data. The horizontal plugs had permeability, porosity and grain density measurements made while the vertical plugs had permeability only. Simulated formation brine, constructed to required concentration of 50,000 ppm with sodium chloride, was used as the drill bit lubricant. All depths on the core log are drillers depths. 2.2 Lithostratigraphy of the Palaeogene interval The Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession of the Viking Graben (Rogaland Group; lsaksen and Tonstad, 1989) comprises sandstones, mudrocks and tuffaceous deposits of highly variable thickness. In the central parts of the Viking Graben, the Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession reaches thicknesses in excess of about 1000m, whereas much thinner successions are found, for example on the Utsira High, where minimum succession thicknesses of about 100m are seen. Chalk deposits, of both autochtonous and allochtonous origin, of the Cretaceous-Danian Shetland Group, underlie the Palaeogene clastic succession. Two lithostratigraphic nomenclatures exists for the studied succession (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992). In recent studies it has been found to be most practical to use combination of the two nomenclatures, although with the main emphasis on the one by Isaksen and Tonstad (1989). lsaksen and Tonstad's subdivision of the Paleocene-Eocene into the Rogaland and Hordaland Groups is maintained, rather than the three-fold subdivision of Mudge and Copestake (1992). The Hordaland Group is not subdivided into formations, whereas the Rogaland Group consists of the Vale-, Lista-, Sele- and Balder Formations. number of other formation names were introduced by lsaksen and Tonstad in order to distinguish sandstone-rich intervals in the Palaeogene. However, as pointed out in Mudge and Copestake (1992), these refer to locally occurring sandstones, and should therefore not be given formation status. Major sandstones within the formations are seen as members, as will be discussed in the forthcoming paragraphs. The regional lithostratigraphic compilations (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992) provide set of criteria to distinguish between the four main formations. Samples were selected from the main types. The samples classify mostly as subarkoses in all formations with matrix content up to 7% and total cement content of approximately 5%, except in the heavily carbonate cemented samples. Quartz cement appears in all samples except in the matrix rich greywacke in Jorsalfare Formation. The clay mineral assemblage in all samples consists mainly of smectite-chlorite mixed layer clay that probably explains the high water saturation in the well. The permeability in the Egga Mbr. and Vale formation are primarily determined by their clay content, i.e. their macro/micro porosity relationship. Rock Characterisation 3.3 Characteristics of the Reservoir: Summary & Discussion The following summary and discussion is based on the combined analysis of 6305/8-1, 6305/7-1 and 6305/5-1. The strength and stiffness distribution within the reservoir is governed by the lithology and facies sequences. detailed sedimentological and lithological description is given in /ref. 5, 20 & 21/ and is summarised below together with the rock mechanic properties. 3.3.1 Reservoir lithology The reservoir sequence is represented by the Jorsalfare Formation of Maastrichtian age and the informal Egga member of the Lower Paleocene Vale Formation. The Jorsalfare Formation is characterised by interbedded sandstone and mudstone facies. The sandstones are generally medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses cemented either by quartz or occasionally abundant calcite. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from to 200 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show few internal structures other than occasional parallel lamination or bioturbation near their tops. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 30%. The Egga member of the Vale Formation is dominated by sandstone but both the top and base of the sequence have significant proportion of interbedded mudstone. The sandstone units in the lower and upper part of the sequence are generally fine to medium grained (occ. coarse), fining upward, moderately to occasionally poorly sorted subarkoses to sublitharenites which are slightly to moderately cemented with quartz (2 to 8% by volume) and occasionally abundantly cemented with carbonate. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from 10 to 350 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show some primary structuring such as horizontal or cross laminations. More massive sandstones (little or no interbedded mudstone) occur in or near the middle of the sequence and are characterised by relatively featureless, fine to medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses which are poorly to slightly cemented with quartz (& occ. calcite). The beds have sharp bases and range between 50 to 700 cm in thickness. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. so-called 'pinstriped' mudstone which contains mm-thick layers of siltstone occurs near the base of the Egga member and varies in thickness across the Ormen Lange field. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 35%. 3.3.2 Strength & Stiffness of the Reservoir formation The rock strength and stiffness varies with porosity, grain size distribution, volume of cement and silt/clay/shale content and the variation in strength clearly reflects the interbedded nature of the sandstone and mudstone units (including the erosive bases to the sandstone units) and their distribution within the Egga Member and Jorsalfare Formation (figures - 3.3). Within the thicker sandstone units, slight increases in strength and/or stiffiless (note: corresponding decrease in Poisson's ratio) from the base to the top of the unit can be associated with fming upward effects and/or the influence of bioturbation. Porosity is logically associated with strength and stiffness and the weakest most compressible layers are generally observed to have the highest porosity. The objectives of the well are to: O Test the reservoir potential within the Paleocene/Eocene and Cretaceous sequences: - Vale (Egga Mbr.) as primary target - Balder as secondary target - Lysing and Lange as third targets O Test the hydrocarbon potential and the type of hydrocarbons O Secure an optimal seismic tie to the subsurface and to understand the seismic response to the rock properties and fluid fill O Have the well approved as commitment well Drilling Strategy The basic drilling strategy for this well is to have the required safety margins in all operations. context_snippets.text: BSD/VSP/VC.2 DISPLAY VC Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display describes the primary and multiple reflection responses of the subsurface at the borehole location, within and below the depth range of the VSP. This data is filtered using the 'maximum bandwidth' filter designed after F-K analysis to determine the usable bandwidth of the upgoing wavefield. In marine data, if source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the input wavelet is zero phase and the wavelet contained in the data is zero phase modified by earth absorption and transmission loss effects (ie mixed phase). Events that reach the time-depth curve are primary and their lithologic significance can be established unequivocally by reference to the calibrated velocity log. Multiples having their last bounce from primary within the range of the VSP may be identified by observing their termination in the data at the same depth point at which the primary cuts the time-depth curve. From this display, any dip across the well location can be recognised by moveout of the primary event to shorter time, as the geophone moves up the well and away from the lithology creating the reflection. No azimuth of dip can be computed from this display but true dip can be computed from measurement of the AT against vertical depth increment. Unconformities may be recognised by an abrupt change of moveout of adjacent primary events. Topographical features up-dip away from the well may be recognised by an increase in the AT or in the termination of an event away from the time-depth curve. Dip increasing up-dip away from the well can be observed in the data; however, if dip is decreasing up-dip (ie crest of an anticline) then the event in question will disappear from the data. Dip can be calculated using the method described in the Appendix contained in this report. DISPLAY VC(FK) F-K Display of Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display is used in the design of the 'maximum bandwidth' filter in conjunction with the F-K display of the deconvolved upgoing wavefield and filter trials. It shows the data from the upgoing wavefield at two-way time transformed into F-K space. Any filter applied to the data before transformation is noted on the display. Since the upgoing wavefield is aligned horizontally, or near horizontally, in T-X space (unless there is steep dip across the well location) it is aligned vertically, through zero wavenumber, in F-K space. The 'maximum bandwidth' filter is the least restrictive filter that can be applied to the upgoing wavefield to remove noise whilst retaining resolution of the data in the zone of interest. The F-K analysis is therefore performed on data within window around the zone of interest. Additionally, the data is windowed in time so that data analysed is close to the time-depth curve, where we would expect better resolution. If the zone of interest is not known, it is assumed to be just above T.D. of the well.

S Abstract The dipmeter from the Jurassic and part of Cretaceous of 33/9-18 is of high quality and only degraded in sections of irregular borehole. Irregular borehole sections are found in brecciated, fractured or strongly sheared zones, often subhorizontal. The mode of drilling is not related to quality of hole. The absence of borehole breakout indicates low horizontal stress anisotropy. This can only be explained by low macroscopic strength due to densely spaced dislocation planes. The Jurassic is of extreme complexity but can be understood if it is subdivided into four structural domains: 1) huge block of lower Jurassic sliding off the Statiford crest during early rifting in Upper Jurassic collapses under its own weight. Albeit strongly deformed internally, the gross stratigraphy is preserved 2) series of smaller slides are emplaced, forming pile of imbrication sheets with varying internal bedding orientation 3) turbidites are deposited on strongly sculptured surface, enclosing occasional allochthonous slide blocks, and sliding into local swales to form slightly reoriented sheets or wedges 4) deposition of Draupne shale as the basin floor rotates due to continued main fault activity. Changes in the plunge of deformation axes are ascribed to syndepositional activity of large transverse fault. Gravitational instability of the talus wedge led to the formation of low angle thrusts, thought to affect also the Cretaceous, causing minor reorientation of lamination.

question: If a manometer records 30 MPa at collapse, does that equal the specimen's triaxial compressive strength?
answer_text: Not exactly — the specimen's triaxial compressive strength equals the manometer reading corrected by the piston/sample area factor (strength = 30 MPa × Ccorr).

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 15

5 CT SCANNING CT-scanning The analytical programme required CT (Computer Tomography) of core material from this well. The resolution for the CT-Scan,s are 512 512 pixels. 5.1 CT Scanning Whole Core CT scanning visualises representative homogeneous sections for possible further studies. The CT scan also helps locating any fractured areas of the core, identify density variations and can be used as tool for orientation of the core prior to slabbing or subsequent plug sampling. The core still in unopened core inner barrels was CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One overview picture (topogram) and four slice pictures were produced every 100-cm of core. The topogram is standard X-ray photo taken from above, covering 100 cm of core. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. 5.2 CT Scanning Seal Peels All Seal Peels (preserved whole core) from this well were CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One (topogram) overview picture, two radial and two axial slice pictures were produced for each seal peel. The topogram is standard X-ray Scan taken from above, covering the length of the preserved core sample. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. The slice pictures are reading of radiation passing through the core. An X-ray source is sending pulses of energy through the core and set of detectors rotating around the core detects the passing signals. The readings are used for making computer produced slice picture of the core. When seal peels are CT scanned, print of the CT scan is mounted along with the core B-cut representing the removed whole core. A total of fifty-one SWC samples and eight 1,5” Horizontal plugs were also CT-Scanned. The CT scans are presented as separate report. Restricted 11

The oldest samples analysed are sands of the DuniIn Group, Cook Formation of Late Pliensbachian?-?Early Toarcian and Early Toarclan age, which were deposited in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment with the accumulation of Drake Formation claystones during Early Toarcian, Late Toarcian and Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times. A regional regressive event during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group, Broom?-Ness formations. Deposition of the Brent Group continued through Late Bajocian, Late Bajocian?-?Early Bathonian and Early-Middle Bathonian times with the deposition of the Ness and Ness?-Tarbert formations. During Early-Middle Bathonian times sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. stratigraphic break occurs at the top of the Early-Middle Bathonian interval. Heather Formation deposition continued during early Callovian through to Middle Oxfordian times in marine, inner shelf setting. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Late Oxfordian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in an inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. An unconformity exists within the Draupne Formation resulting from the absence of early Kimmeridglan to Early Volgian aged sediments. Accumulation of Draupne Formation sediments resumed during Middle-latest Middle Volgian times in marine, mid to outer shelf setting with dysaerobic to anaerobic bottom conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment throughout Early-Late Ryazanian times. Deposition continued, without apparent unconformity, with Cromer Knoll Group sediments of latest Late Ryazanian age. Following period of erosion or non deposition during Late Hauterivian to Late Aptlan times, deposition of Cromer Knoll Group sediments resumed briefly during Early Albian times in marine, mid shelf setting. further unconformity at the top of Cromer Knoll Group sediments indicates period of erosion or non deposition during Middle and Late Albian times. Deposition resumed with transgression at the beginning of Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. WELL SEISMIC EDIT The raw data are edited to remove bad traces, and the hydrophone break times are evaluated to be used as timing reference for the downhole data. The break time is defined as the time at which tangent to the first downward deflection crosses the zero line. PLOT (STACKED DATA) shows the median stacked downhole data from the vertical axis only. The break time of each trace is recomputed on the vertical component after stacking and displayed as TRANSIT TIME, which is now the transit time from surface sensor to the first compressional arrival.

question: How does KRISTIN-specific mudlogging differ from standard mudlogging regarding recording organic contaminants and using gas scales up to C5?
answer_text: KRISTIN mudlogging must record first instances of organic contaminants (including glycol) in addition to normal mud logs, and use gas scales capable of displaying all gas up to C5 (a separate scale may be used).

question: For 2/11-S-11 Valhall overburden, specify the recommended ECD upper limit (sg, ppg).
answer_text: Recommended ECD upper limit: 1.80 sg (15.0 ppg).

context_snippets.text: MI6 1NTEQ POST WELL ANALYSIS 2/8 S-11 & 11A Using the and rpm Fann measurements at 50°C and 80°C general rule can be derived. If the results from the 80°C test are more than one point lower than the 50°C test (irrespective of the absolute values), then the mud may have tendency for dynamic sag. Breaking circulation while tripping in The pressure sub data from previous wells confirmed that breaking circulation during the course of tripping in is critical operation in the effort to limit pressure surges on the formation. The length of time the mud stands static while out of the hole is sufficient to cool the mud to point where much greater pressures are required to break the gels at bottom if no breaks in circulation are made during the trip in. These extra pressures can be enough to fracture the formation. The following procedures should be adhered to: 1. Keep surface mud sheared 2. Break circulation at regular intervals on the trip in 3. Pick pipe out of slips 4. Start rotating the drill string at 60 rpm 5. Start circulation at 50 gpm while moving pipe in an upward direction. 6. Monitor flow line until returns are seen. 7. Increase flow rate in 50 gpm stages to 600 gpm. 8. Once flow rate is established at 600 gpm with full returns, establish drilling flow rate. Conditions should be evaluated on each hole section as to the frequency of breaking circulation. Conditions such as borehole stability, mud condition, length of time out the hole and pressure sub memory data. All these factors will need to be evaluated to define circulation intervals which will vary from well to well as conditions dictate. If the trip is round trip in an extended reach well then the lower half of the hole should be staged in with more frequent 250m intervals and washed down when approaching bottom. Staging up points in open hole should be chosen so that any large OD BHA components are placed away from any limestone stringers. If there are large number of limestone stringers at the bottom of the hole then consideration should be given to washing down from the last zone of competent formation. ECD Upper Limit A general recommended upper limit of 1.80sg (15.0ppg) ECD is recommended for Valhall wells in the overburden section. When drilling from Valhall Flanks away from the crest and known problem zones then it is possible to review each hole section in light of the DOP forecast and the FIT (after allowing significant safety margin). An upper limit for ECD in the 22 section is 1.53sg (12.8ppg) and for 16 and 12 'A section the initial target should be set point below the LOT / FIT taken unless the well path is planned to cross weaker fault zones. If so, target upper limit of 1.80sg (15.0ppg) is recommended. Prepared by: Ray Goodfellow, Cliff Kirby, 23 of 81 Ketil Inderberg, John Jelly, Gaute Grindhaug OASIS

question: For B-cut slabbed, epoxy-mounted samples photographed white and UV (1:4), what deliverables and separate report components are required?
answer_text: Digital core images (Corimag) — white‑light and UV‑light photographs of the epoxy‑mounted B‑cut at 1:4 scale — delivered as separate core photo reports.

context_snippets.text: Porosity and grain density Grain volume was measured by helium injection using Boyle's law porosimeter. Bulk volume was determined by immersing the sample in mercury (the weight balance/ buoyancy technique). Porosity and grain density were calculated from the recorded weight of the samples. Slabbing and mounting of core cuts After all samples had been taken, the cores were slabbed using long bed saw with water cooled diamond saw blade. The whole core length (except seal peels) was slabbed into four parts (A,B,C and cut). After slabbing, the B-cut (reference cut) was mounted in plastic trays, by casting in epoxy resin. Core photos Digital core images ( Corimag ), white and UV-light were taken of the entire well. Standard core photo scale 1:4 was taken of the B-cut both white and UV-light. The core photos are delivered as separate reports.

PREPARATION: Laboratory core handling and sampling. The plug samples for analyses were collected by drilling with one inch bore, using simulated formation brine (constructed to standard concentration of 50 000 ppm NaCl) as cooling agent. Horizontal samples, taken every 25 cm, were drilled parallel to the bedding and the vertical samples, were taken approximately every 50 cm, normal on the bedding. The samples were cut to one inch lengths and the end faces were lightly brushed using the same fluid, to remove any fines induced by trimming. The plug samples were then cleaned in soxhlet extractor using alternating sequences of methanol and toluene. Toluene was used to remove any residual hydrocarbons and methanol to remove water and residual salts. The plug samples were dried in heating cabinet between the toluene and methanol extraction to avoid mixing of the solvents. Chemical and visual checks were made to ensure complete removal of all the pore contaminants. Finally the samples were dried under controlled conditions at 60 °C and 40 % relative humidity for at least 48 hours prior to the measurements.

A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 gas) and the relative abundance of these inclusions will influence the bulk spectra. Addi- tionally, total inclusion abundance will affect the spectra insofar as higher molecular weight species represent smaller volumetric proportion of petroleum and are also less volatile, hence decrease below instrumentation detection limits before low molecular weight species. Conse- quently, some samples with low oil inclusion abundance generate wet gas mass spectra, for instance. Optical inclusion abundance and characteristics should be consulted, where pro- vided, to verify the interpreted petroleum type (see Table of Petrographic Observations). With the above limitations in mind, the following petroleum types are identified on the basis of spectral characteristics: Dry gas: mostly C1 with lesser C2-C3 and no higher hydrocarbons. Wet gas: C1-C9 may be present, but C6+ species are in minimal abundance. The alkane slope is extreme. Gas-condensate: C1-C11 may be present. The alkane slope is quite steep, reflecting very gas- enriched phase. Volatile oil: C1-C13 present. Slight gas-range enrichment is observed and the alkane slope is mod- erate to steep. Oil: C1-C13 is present. The alkane slope may be flat to moderate. Biodegradation is suggested if sulfur compounds such as H2S, COS, CS2, S2 (+/- SO2) and/or thiols are present in addition to petroleum species. Ratios of paraffins to naphthenes may be low as well, as bacteria typically prefer to metabolize alkanes compared to other classes of petroleum compounds. Petrographic data may provide further evidence for biodegradation in the form of low-gravity petroleum inclusions. Bacterial activity is generally restricted to maximum burial temperatures below 65-70°C; hence FIS evidence of biodegradation is most commonly observed in rocks that are currently below this temperature. Thermal alteration of liquid petroleum species can produce spectra very similar to those generated from biodegraded hydrocarbons, because the products of two common processes, bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR) and thermochemical sulfate reduction (TSR), are essentially identical. The best distinction is made from current bottom-hole temperature data, which, if above 140°C or so may be indicative of TSR, and if below 70°C or so is more consistent with BSR. Potential interpretive problems arise in the intervening temperature range, when deeply buried sediments are unroofed or when petroleum altered at shallow depths becomes buried to greater depth. Petrographic data may help, as pyrobitumen frequently accompanies TSR, while low-gravity liquid petroleum inclusions often occur in association with bacteri- ally altered oils. Additional temperature or thermal maturity data (including fluid inclusion homogenization temperatures) may also be useful. The presence of significant amounts of sulfur species can indicate sour petroleum phase, where the souring process may in some cases be reflection of the source rock, but could also reflect BSR or TSR. study of TSR sour gas pools in Canada suggests that evaluating the relative proportion of products and reactants can provide measure of sour gas potential. As TSR progresses, long-chain alkanes decrease while low molecular weight petroleum species increase along with CO2, aromatics organic acids and the various sulfur compounds enumer- ated above. Ironically, H2S alone may not be as accurate an indicator of H2S content, as it is scavenged naturally (e.g., to form pyrite in iron-rich rocks) and by the metallic internal surfaces of the analytical system.

question: What operational and data-quality implications arise when spectral GR is acquired separately and logged more than three days after other measurements?
answer_text: Delayed acquisition (spectral GR run >3 days after other logs) causes logging delays, reduced operational efficiency and non-compliance with the DAP. It also risks inconsistent or incomplete data that may require re-running logs or late integration.

The performance of the TriSor OFS surface equipment during the survey was excellent, with accurate gun tuning throughout. ▪ The downhole data recorded with the Borehole VSI tool was of high quality, and good vector fidelity was recorded with high signal to noise ratio. ▪ Good first break picks were obtained in the main VSP part of the well. Estimated time picks were extended almost to seabed using the horizontal components. ▪ VSP processing was done using the component and zero phase corridor stack was obtained with bandwidth of 5-140Hz. The full bandwidth zero phase P-P corridor stack shows an increase in resolution compared to the provided surface seismic data. ▪ Compressional sonic log calibration was done with minimal drift correction and set of synthetic seismogram traces was generated for various zero phase Ricker wavelets. ▪ The full bandwidth (5-140Hz) 60ms corridor stack, along with the 5-70Hz reduced bandwidth corridor stack, tie well with the Ricker wavelet synthetic seismograms for variety of different bandwidths. ▪ good 3-way tie was made between the VSP corridor stack, Synthetics and 3D surface seismic data.

2 Acquisition A 4-level Versatile Seismic Imager (VSI) tool string (15.24m shuttle spacing) was used by Schlumberger to acquire the downhole data for the ZOVSP survey. The tools are fitted with three orthogonally opposed non-gimballed accelerometers providing flat frequency response from 2- 200Hz irrespective of the angle of tilt. A tuned array of 250cu.in Sercel G-Guns, operating at 2000psi was used as source for the survey. The guns were deployed by the rig’s crane. The guns target firing pressure was 2000 psi. Source control was provided via the use of the TriSor OFS in sea dynamic source controller and the calibrated near-field hydrophone sensor data were recorded at 1.25m below the gun cluster. The target gun depth was 5m below mean sea level (actual depth m) and the gun offset and azimuth from the wellhead were 75m and 140 degrees, respectively. The equipment was then used to acquire the main VSP survey data, at 15.24m intervals between 399.9 – 720.8m MD DF. The recording was done using the Schlumberger Maxwell acquisition system. At each level, at least five good repeatable shots were acquired and recorded. The main acquisition parameters and survey equipment are shown in Table 1. The full acquisition report can be found in the digital deliverables accompanying this report.

2. Delta Minimum In the case of negative drift second method is used, called At minimum. This applies differential correction to the sonic log where it is assumed the greatest amount of time error is caused by the lower velocity sections of the log. Over given interval the method will correct only At values which are higher than threshold, the Atmin. Values of At which are lower than the threshold are not corrected. The correction is reduction of the excess of At over Atmin ie. At - Atmin At - Atmin is reduced through multiplication by reduction coefficient which remains constant over the interval. This reduction coefficient, named G, can be defined as: G = + drift (At - Atmin) dZ Where drift is the drift over the interval to be corrected and the value (At - Atmin) dZ is the time difference between the integrals of the two curves At and Atmin, over the same interval. Hence the corrected sonic: Atmin = G(At - Atmin) + Atmin The sonic, density and Gamma ray log data are taken from the well 7221/12. 6.3 Bathymetry The multibeam echo sounder data was processed onboard MV Fugro Meridian using Fugro Starfix suite to monitor data quality and data coverage. The data was logged in Simrad Raw format (.all) and imported into Starfix.Proc for processing. Both single beam and multibeam echo sounder data were corrected for transducer draught, acoustic velocity through sea water and vessel heave, pitch and roll, and then positioned with reference to the echo sounder transducer. 6.4 Sidescan Sonar The engineers and geophysicists examined the sidescan sonar records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks include range/scale, gains, tow fish height and position, as well as overall record quality. The sidescan sonar data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full by the geophysicist, using SonarWiz Version software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted, in which case the XTF file would be transferred to the relevant working directory for use, or, if rejected, would be flagged as potential re-run. Mosaicking of the sidescan sonar data was performed using the mosaic module, which applied slant range correction to the data and checked for full sonar coverage of the survey area. 6.5 Sub-bottom Profilers The engineers and geophysicists examined the hull-mounted pinger and mini sleeve gun records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks included sweep/scale, gains, examination of seabed pulse and penetration as well as overall record quality. The sub-bottom profiler data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full, by the geophysicist, using Starfix.Interp software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted or rejected and flagged as potential re-run. 6.6 2DHR Multichannel Seismic Quality control of the online 2DHR multichannel seismic system was undertaken by the onboard engineers, geophysicist and seismic processor. The engineers maintained an observers’ log (Appendix E.2) in which all relevant information was recorded. Typically, routine checks were made on the source and streamer; the engineers monitored the manifold pressure, gun statistics (including any dropped/mis-timed shots) as well as pulse/frequency spectra of the seismic source. Routine checks of the streamer included streamer integrity (noisy, dead or reverse polarity channels), noise (due to environmental factors or weather), and streamer depth control/feather angle. On completion of each 2DHR multichannel seismic line, the data underwent final QC. The onboard geophysicist used the RadExPro seismic processing system as well as the observers’ logs and other quality control data generated by the NTRS2 system. Shot and CMP gathers were generated, to allow the identification of bad channels/shots and noise problems, and to verify the streamer offset and depth of the gun array. Then, brute stack was generated for each line, to ascertain any swell noise and check the overall data quality. The data were processed aboard the Fugro Meridian using the OpenCPS seismic processing system. The data processing flows aim to remove noise and seismic interference from 2DHR data. context_snippets.text: Structural core description - Well 15/9-19SR 33 At MD RKB in the Triassic, fracture with oil patches was encountered in an otherwise dry Skagerrak Formation. This is probably fracture of dilatational nature, possibly late fracture. The same phenomenon has been seen in the Pismo Formation of California, where fractures are observed in_the field as both barriers and (more rarely) conduits. Brace (1978) showed that pore-volume increase, or dilitancy, accompanies failure of intact rock in the laboratory. Antonelli et al. (1993) found that dilatation is found in an early stage of deformation band development. (Furthermore, it should be noted that en echelon open induced fractures were encountered in thin section at MD RKB.) a2. Decreased porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis The thin section from MD RKB (Skagerrak Fm.) exhibits compaction in the fracture, but no grain crushing. At mesoscopic scale, the fracture is filled with grey material, and is probably syn-sedimentary. It is surrounded by some rotated bedding and clay clasts and may well be associated with slumping at low mean stress levels. a3. Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time with the check shot time at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod. mercury immersion technique. Samples with large holes require special attention. Special tests such as com- pressive strength or static moduli require additional plugs (see Special Testing). Velocities are measured using the Pulse Transmission Technique (Schreiber, et al. 1973) with nominal frequencies of 300-500 KHz. Dry velocities are measured first, samples are then saturated with 25,000 ppm NaC1 brine for the saturated velocity measurements. Saturation is performed in separate pressure chamber where samples are main- tained at 1000 psi for 12 hours. Velocities are recorded to effective pressures equivalent to conditions corre- sponding to the depths from which the samples came. Specifically, with normal hydrostatic gradient of psi/ft, sample from depth of 10,000 feet would be subjected to maximum effective stress of 5,000 psi. Since we report on measurements on series of pressures up to this value and give the best fitting quadratic for each data set, you can calculate the velocities at any pressure below the maximum. This of course would be necessary if the reservoir of interest were over pressured. The data presented in the tables which follow has been subjected to number of quality control checks but when data, i.e. the raw information, appears sound but generates inconsistencies we elect to report the data. The inconsistencies are flagged in the tabular reports. An explanation of the data symbols and abbreviations used in the tables is given in Chapter 2. The velocity tables consist of measurements of Vp, Vsi and Vs2 for three possible saturation states; native, wet and dry. Vsi and Vs2 refer to two shear velocities having com- mon propagation direction. The particle motion or polarization used to measure Vsi is orthogonal to that used to measure Vs2. Thus the difference between Vsi and Vs2 at specific pressure reflects the amount of shear wave anisotropy or shear wave birefringence. It is quite common for both the horizontal and diagonal core plugs to display large differences. Velocities are reported in either ft/sec or rn/sec while effective pres- sure control points are reported in psi {14503 psi — 1Kbar — 100 MPa). April 21, 1995

question: How do draw‑work rim bolt failures (3–4 mm) compare with iron roughneck jaw failures in causes, repair methods, and typical downtime?
answer_text: Draw-work rim bolt failures (3–4 mm) were due to loose/missing bolts and were fixed by installing/torquing new bolts, drilling alignment holes and tack‑welding with ~4 hours downtime; iron roughneck jaw/clamp failures were mechanical breakages repaired or replaced (or awaited spares) with typical downtimes of about 10–38.5 hours.

It is valid for both oil and gas reservoirs but to certain extent limited to those cases where the difference in pressure inside the fracture and reservoir fluid pressure is sufficient to establish fluid loss rate that is inversely proportional to the square root of time. An 1/2 Sinor liner bit was run in on 108 joints of 5/8 liner. This bit drilled from 2645m to 2654m MD where the top drive stalled out at 18 kft/lbs torque and mud returns were completely lost. While drilling the liner 15-20% mud returns were recorded. After losing the returns the well was stabilized and the liner hanger and TSP packer was set, and the running string pulled out of hole. mud weight was retained at ppg throughout this hole section before being raised to ppg before pumping out to the casing window from 2645m to 1472m. The drilling assembly was then tripped out of hole. While drilling the liner 15%-20% mud returns were recorded, and total of 372 bbls of mud was lost while drilling the liner into Tor formation. After complete loss of returns the annulus was filled with base oil, and 10 ppg mud was pumped to reduce the losses. This interval consisted predominantly of claystone and tuff from the balder formation, claystone from the Sele formation and claystone with limestone stringers from the Lista formation of the Rogaland group prior to entering the depleted Tor formation.

However, the density log is uncertain/poor at top Vale level which can explain the difference between VSP and synthetic seismogram at this level. At Top Egga Formation both the velocity and density log show large, but gradual increase. Synthetic seismogram generated by relative high frequent wavelet (figure 4.2-7), dominant frequency of around 35-38Hz, result in two separated peaks within the Egga Formation. There is good match between the synthetic seismogram and the VSP corridor stack. However to check the tie to the HSP data somewhat lower frequency wavelet is required. The synthetic seismograms on figure 4.2-8 is generated by wavelet extracted from the 35/40Hz high pass filtered VSP corridor stack resulting in one combined broad peak within the Egga Formation. Except for static shift of around 12-15ms this in more in accordance with the HSP data. On figure 4.2-9 which is focused around the reservoir section, the corridor stack has been generated in order to have the same wavelet as the HSP data for the Jorsalfar - Balder interval. This has been done by generating filter which convert the wavelet from the VSP data to the wavelet in the HSP data. The filter has then been convolved with the high frequent corridor stack in order to be comparable with the HSP data. The most important observation is that in this water filled Egga reservoir setting, the TVALE trough is actually corresponding to near top Egga Formation. Actually the top Egga Formation will be 2-3ms shallower than the maximum amplitude of the TVALE trough on the synthetic seismogram and the VSP corridor stack (Fig.4.2-9). While the top Vale Formation ties to the crossover from minor trough to peak above the main trough . This trough is distinct on the VSP corridor stack, but less distinct and show relatively low continuity on the HSP data. The seismic event TJOR has been picked on strong trough related to gradual density and velocity increase around the geological boundary Top Jorsalfar. There is good tie between the synthetic seismogram and VSP corridor stack at this level. However, there is timeshift of around 14-15ms to the HSP data, which show a very broad and asymmetrical trough at this level. Comparison of mid- and faroffset data show that the seismic response is delayed on faroffset compared to midoffset (fig.4.2-10). This is probably due to use of to high stacking velocities at this level. By interpreting the TJOR event on both mid (1100-2500m) and faroffset (2500-3800m) data an local anomaly of around 300m 800m, where TJOR is between 15 and 25ms deeper on far than on midoffset data, has been identified. This offset dependant response can explain the broad and asymmetrical waveform of this trough. The stacking velocity anomaly is probably not identified by the velocity picking due to grid size of 600 600m. For the deeper events, TKYR (near top Kyrre Formation) and TLYSING (near top Lysing Formation) the tie to the HSP data becomes somewhat more complicated due to lower frequencies and the deviated well path. The seismic event TKYR is picked at peak related to decrease in impedance around 15m into the Kyrre Formation. It should be noted however that these latter strength profiles are in part calibrated with respect to the MSWC data thus resulting in some bias. Counter to this, is the argument that no UCS below MPa has been measured and that due to the apparent field wide uniformity of the overburden sequence it should be anticipated that 6305/7-1 will have similar formation strength distribution to 6305/8-1. This is partly confirmed by the fact that common strength trend is identifiable in all Ormen Lange wells based on the semi-calibrated sonic and gamma-ray log analysis (equations & 2.2). It was stated earlier (section 2.3.3) that for the mudstone sequence below the reservoir, the gamma-ray based UCS trend should be taken as the base case. While this argument is still held true, the difference in the lithlogies of the mudstone above and below the reservoir (section 2.4.1) should be noted - the mudstones of the Kyrre Formation are generally described as being more dense and fissile and one could therefore expect greater strength. The scatter in the MSWC data indicates that the strength does indeed vary between the lower and upper limits defined by the gamma-ray and sonic log based UCS trends but common trend is difficult to define. The bilinear trend for the Young's modulus and constrained modulus reflects the apparent increase in the stiffness which occurs just above the reservoir as identified from the MSWC data (table 2.1) and sonic velocity data (equation & 2.4). The change in stiffness appears to be related to gradual increase in density in the mudstone immediately above the reservoir. The gamma-ray based stiffness profile and that generated from the plasticity index do not show this bilinearity as they are less sensitive to density changes unlike the sonic log based data. And as sonic velocity is fundamentally coupled to density and elastic properties the stiffness profile determined from this data is probably the more correct and is recommended as the base case (although this is subject to the limitations in the MSWC data set, section 2.1). Title: Well Programme 36/7-3 Page 24 of 58 Revision: Date: 05.12.01 Viking Group Depth interval :2930 - TD (2940) mMSL Age :Bathonian The Heather Formation is expected to be present beneath an unconformity separating the Jurassic from the Cretaceous sequence. Heather Formation The Heather Formation in well 36/7-1 comprises siltstone with traces of sandstone and limestone. The siltstone is brown black/grey, olive grey to grey black and slightly calcare- ous. It contains traces of limestone and medium to very coarse sand. 5.3 Depth conversion Mapping All interpretation was performed on Charisma work station and detailed maps have been made for the main events. The time interpretation was gridded in IRAP using grid increment of 100x100m. To correct for static shift, -4ms were applied to all the horizons prior to depth conversion. The time maps were depth converted by making use of gridded stacking velocities from the processing. layer cake depth conversion was applied to eleven interpreted horizons for the establishment of stratigraphic framework. Individual correction factors in the range from to were applied to each horizon from the calibration of velocities in nearby wells. For the Top C3 reservoir, the calibration factor 0,9321 was used. The mean sea level was used as the datum for the average velocity calculations. Prognosis and uncertainties The 36/7-3 prognosis is based on an analysis of both the stacking velocities from the 3D survey and on comparison of interval velocities from nearby wells. The high resolution site survey was used for the seabed estimation and the Quaternary sequence prognosis. Table 5.3.1 shows the prognosed times and depth values for the main events for well 36/7-3. Uncertainties from the depth conversion and from picking each horizon have been analyzed separately and added for the cumulative error estimation for the main events. The interval velocity prognosis for well 36/7-3 has been compared with the velocities from the nearest wells 35/9-3 T2, 35/9-1 and 36/7-1. The best correlation is observed towards well 35/9-3 T2. The Quaternary and Tertiary thicknesses and stratigraphy are similar in the wells and interval velocities in these sequences are prognosed to be very similar. In the lower Kyrre Formation, however, the seismic record indicates velocity increase towards well 36/7-3, which may be caused by greater concentration of carbonif- erous sediments. The increased velocities in the lower part of the Upper Cretaceous introduces the greatest uncertainty in the prognosis. The uneven Lower Cretaceous velocity trend in well 35/9-3 is shown in Figure 5.3.1, and compared with the prognosed velocities for each main sequence in well 36/7-3.

The planned total depth of the well is Geoscience Summary The regional Balder Formation isopach is thickest on the western flank of the Balder field, which implies the presence of an Eocene Zone III sand packages. Regional Eocene depositional sand maps also suggest the transport of sand from west to east across the Balder area. This interpretation is tied to the 25/10-5 well located approximately km to the SSW. The well penetrated 19m of net oil sand and total of 28m of interbedded reservoir sand. E5 is assessed to have most likely STOOIP of 90 MBO distributed between the Zone 111-2 lower (53MBO) and Zone 111-3 (37MB0). Zone 111-4 sand is distributed sparsely and is expected to be entirely within the gas window in the E5 area. Zone 111-3 sand is also expected to be in the gas window at the proposed well location with the gas-oil contact prognosed at the base of the sand. The well is expected to find 12m of net oil pay in Zone 111-2 lower, 7m of net gas pay in Zone 111-3, and 5m of net gas pay in Zone 111-4. The key risk at E5 is encountering thin, interbedded Zone III sands with limited continuity. Zone 111-2 lower and Zone 111-3 sands map out as isolated sand bodies, suggesting potential for limited aquifer support. An additional risk is penetrating the Zone 111-2 lower reservoir above the field wide gas-oil contact. Basis for Geological Prognosis The geological prognosis is based on: 1) Depth conversion 2) Net sand prediction from attribute analysis studies on the 3D Impedance dataset. 'Seismic Interpretation The key mapping element of the Zone III sands was the use of the Balder B88s 3D seismic impedance cube to map individual sand bodies. Calibration of well control with impedance data suggest that low impedance packages correlate to sand prone intervals within the Balder formation. Seismic horizons were carried at zero-crossings at the top and base of these low impedance packages. Interval seismic attributes were then extracted and attribute analysis was performed in order to calculate net sand thickness. The impedance cube and attribute maps were used successfully in planning and drilling Zone III development wells at Mound and E2. key uncertainty for the E5 Zone III sands is the lack of local reservoir sand calibration to seismic impedance. 1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

This data was presented along with the estimated formation pressure gradient and leak off test results. Drilling Exponent If hole was drilled through good thickness of uniform 'normally' pressured shales, holding parameters of bit size, weight on bit (WOB), rotary speed (RPM) and mud weight constant, gradual reduction in the rate of penetration would be expected, due to the increasingly compacted nature of the sediments encountered and to the increasing differential bottom hole pressure (BHP). If subsequently an overpress- ured zone was encountered, reversal of the 'normal' rate of penetration trend would be seen. This is explained in terms of variation in differential BHP, i.e. if formation pore pressure is greater than bottom hole hydrostatic pressure, then shales will tend to explode into the hole - thus making the overpressured formation comparatively more drillable. In practice, it is not feasible to hold the independent variables of WOB, RPM, bit size and mud weight constant through more than very short section of the hole. Jordan and Shirley (19bb) produced an equation aimed at normalising rate of penetration, with respect to the variables of RPM, WOB, and bit size. The product was known as the 'd' exponent. Hole Stability A formation breakout analysis carried out for this area shows that there is dominant NW - SE trend for the maximum horizontal rock stress direction (Ref. Gyda - Breakout Analysis, Addis & McLean, 1989, which also applies for the Ula Field). In practical terms, this implies that an inclined well drilled at 90° to the maximum horizontal stress direction would be more stable than well of similar inclination drilled parallel to that stress direction. Well AO7B will be drilled along an azimuth of 322°N from the top of the Ekofisk Formation and will be quasi parallel to the direction of maximum horizontal stress for length of over 1800m MD. This will result in risk of increased wellbore instability from the top of the Ekofisk Formation to approximately 5100m MD, where the well is turned to the west. The planned mud weight of sg will exert sufficient overbalance over the expected pore pressure and should counteract instability resulting from the effects of maximum horizontal stress. The 9-5/8 casing shoe will be set within the uppermost part of the reservoir and an FIT is not planned. Leak off tests performed in adjacent wells have returned values close to sg EMW. question: How do Mandal FM lithofacies, biostratigraphy, and gas signatures compare across wells 2/1-5, 1/6-6, 7/12-9, and 2/7-29, and what depositional differences are inferred?
answer_text: 2/1‑5: organic‑rich "hot" Kimmeridge‑Clay mudstones with Early Portlandian–Late Kimmeridgian dinocysts (marine); 1/6‑6: mixed limestone and massive claystone with marl and thin sands, carbonate‑rich (Ca 30–70%) and ditch gas 0.02%–18.2% (avg ~0.8%–2.8%); 7/12‑9: dominantly claystone with dolomite/limestone stringers and rare sandstones; 2/7‑29: brown‑black carbonaceous, calcareous, pyritic mudstones with an interbedded sandstone member. Depositional inference: 2/1‑5 and 2/7‑29 indicate deeper, more anoxic basinal marine deposition, whereas 1/6‑6 and 7/12‑9 reflect more proximal, carbonate‑influenced and sand‑influenced shelf environments.

4. JURASSIC STRATIGRAPHY The uppermost 3900 metres of well 2/1-5 yielded no surprises, geologically, and thus call for no further evaluation here. The remainder of the well section, from the hot shale of the Upper Jurassic Mandal Formation to T.D. at 4458 mBRT, was in contrast quite different from forecast. Clarifying the stratigraphy of this pre-Cretaceous sequence was seen as major concern of the present study. In the following sections it will be explained how the understanding of Jurassic stratigraphy has progressed, leading in the end to a profound revision of the earlier interpretation. 4.1 Biostratigraphy As soon as the well site geological reports began to indicate deviations from the well prognosis, procedure was set up for monitoring the age of the strata being drilled, through rapid biostratigraphical analysis of wellbore cuttings material. This effort was successful only in part, owing to the absence of diagnostic microfossils over critical intervals of the drilled section. It was thus necessary to terminate the well without the support of age determinations to testify that Top Triassic had been reached. Subsequently, the Stratigraphy Branch of BP Sunbury undertook follow-up study on sidewall core material, their final results being presented in report by Lowe et al. (1983). These results essentially confirm the earlier findings and are incorporated in Figs. and as well as summarized below. a. typical hot shale palynofacies prevails in the interval 3875-4046 mBRT. This interval is devoid of age-diagnostic microfaunas or microfloras, but the palynological organic residue is typical of the upper part of the Kimmeridge Clay, i.e. Mandel Formation. b. The interval 4050-4109 mBRT yielded dinoflagellate cysts of Early Portlandian to Late Kimmeridgian age. Among the species reported were Glossodinium dimorphum with latest appearance at 4050 mBRT. This species was used by Duxbury to define extinction line NOR-S3 in his scheme for stratigraphic correlation in blocks 7/12 and 2/1, Duxbury (1981). The presence of dinocysts indicates marine environment of deposition for this interval. report/213 -12-

Limestones were white becoming dirty grey white, bluish grey, firm, locally very hard, blocky, massive, homogeneous. They were microcrystalline (mudstone- wackestone), locally argillaceous, commonly grading to sandy Limestones, rarely dolomitic. Porosity was moderate. At the top of the section the Claystones were medium to dark grey, soft to firm, waxy, blocky to platy, rarely sticky and amorphous. They were slightly calcareous, locally very pyritic, micromicaceous and hydroturgid. Towards the middle of the section the clays became more firm, brittle with an angular break. Mottled blue green clays, locally earthy brown appeared with the beginning of the Mandal formation at 4847m (+ve drill break). At the bottom of the section the clays became brittle, slightly micaceous, and slightly silty. Marl stringers were common throughout the section. dominant characteristic was their tendancy to form elongate, tabular cuttings.They were pale grey, firm, massive, locally platy with smooth, waxy texture. Towards the end of the section they became brittle, slightly micaceous, slightly silty. The Sandstones occurred in thin beds within the top 60m of the section. They were very fine grading to fine, firm, brittle, subblocky to angular, moderate to very well rounded, moderate sphericity, well sorted, calcareous with moderate porosity. SECTION I: 956 TO 2766 in, NORDLAND - HORDALAND GROUPS This section consisted of claystone with minor dolomite/limestone stringers and rare traces of sandstone. The claystone was generally medium to dark grey and occasionally olive grey or brown grey, becoming varicoloured below 2570 in. The cuttings were firm, sometimes moderately soft, sub-blocky to amorphous and non to slightly swelling. The claystone ranged from non to slightly calcareous and graded to silty claystone in parts of the 17 1/2 hole. There were also traces of disseminated pyrite down to 1030 m. The dolomite was pale cream to pale brown/buff, hard to very hard, brittle, generally blocky, amorphous in parts, dominantly cryptocrystalline and occasionally found with black argillaceous microlaminations. There is no doubt that compaction seriously have modifi- cated the original framework of all samples studied. The main features observed were: - grain deformation - deformation of ductiles - pressure solution Crushing of brittle grains, especially micas, feldspars and lithic fragments is common in most of the studied samples. (Plate 51) Feldspars break easily, whereas micas are more commonly bent and squeezed between more rigid grains. More ductile grains such as intraclasts, shale fragments and organic matter, are plastic deformed and flow between harder fragments, resulting in almost complete loss of porosity and permeability. (Plate 52.) Pressure solution at grain contacts (Plate 24) seem to be one of the important factors in pore reduction in many samples. There is considerable variation in the extent of pressure solution, although the overpressured sandstones in 35/3-2 seem to be less affected. However, quartz overgrowth due to fresh water flushing has probably played an important role too, and the relative amount of quartz cement from pressure solution and fresh water flushing can not be determined.

4. GEOLOGY AND SHOWS 33 A. WELL 35/a-3, Seabed to 900m. The interval from seabed (284m) to the 30 casing point (450m) was drilled without returns. The rate of penetration averaged ,6m/hr. Little can be deduced from the drilling parameters as to the nature of the formation. The lithology is assumed to be similar to that found immediately below the 30 casing shoe. This was almost equal amounts of clay and sand/sandstone, as seen in the cuttings samples. The clay was grey, soft and sticky, and slightly to non-calcareous, with traces of shell fragments and pyrite. The sand was of clear loose quartz grains, medium to coarse grained, subangular to subrounded, moderately sorted, with traces of metamorphic rock fragments. Just below the casing shoe extremely high ROP's of 200m/hr or more were experienced. The drill bit was taking only minimal weight, thus the high ROE' was attributed to very soft unconsolidated formation being washed away by the impact of the drilling fluid at the bit. From 450-610m the lithology was of varying proportions of clay and sand, as described above. The sand was also found with grey to brown, fine grained, friable sandstone, grading to siltstone. small amount of white, hard, blocky limestone was found in the sample at 510m. From 610-800m the sand/sandstone was found in association with siltstone, this being brown to red-brown, firm, glauconitic and grading to siltstone. Glauconite became common, up to 20% of the cuttings sample, dark green to black in colour, moderately hard and globular in habit. From 800m to 900m the lithology was predominantly grey, green grey to brown, soft, sticky, non-calcareous clay. ROP's over the interval 450-900m averaged at 19m/hr. There was however consid- erable fluctuation in the rate throughout. Background gas values ranged between was the only constituent of the gas. The age of these formations is assumed to range from Quaternary to U. Tertiary.

The poroperm values are closely related to the grain size variations and the original mineralogy. Medium grained sandstones have highest poroperm values while finer grained sandstones with high mica content have low values. The vertical permeability is often lower than the horizontal because of high mica content. Diagenetic quartz and feldspar have to certain extent reduced poroperm values, but this effect seems minor in relation to the grain size and primary mineralogy. Sandstones with predominantly intergranular porosity have high permeabilities and Sw of <25%. Sandstones with mostly intragranular and microporosity have relatively low permeabilities and Sw >25%. The major factors controlling the pore types is the presence or absence of microquartz cement, clay matrix and the grain size. 6.9 The Ula Formation has been divided into poroperm units which are comparable with the reservoir zones in other 7/12 wells. 6.10 There is close correspondence between the poroperm zones and the coarsening and fining upwards depositional units. Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time with the check shot time at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod.
