Velocities are measured using the Pulse Transmission Technique (Schreiber, et al. 1973) with nominal frequencies of 300-500 KHz. Dry velocities are measured first, samples are then saturated with 25,000 ppm NaC1 brine for the saturated velocity measurements. Saturation is performed in separate pressure chamber where samples are main- tained at 1000 psi for 12 hours. Velocities are recorded to effective pressures equivalent to conditions corre- sponding to the depths from which the samples came. Specifically, with normal hydrostatic gradient of psi/ft, sample from depth of 10,000 feet would be subjected to maximum effective stress of 5,000 psi. Since we report on measurements on series of pressures up to this value and give the best fitting quadratic for each data set, you can calculate the velocities at any pressure below the maximum. This of course would be necessary if the reservoir of interest were over pressured. The data presented in the tables which follow has been subjected to number of quality control checks but when data, i.e. the raw information, appears sound but generates inconsistencies we elect to report the data. The inconsistencies are flagged in the tabular reports. An explanation of the data symbols and abbreviations used in the tables is given in Chapter 2. The velocity tables consist of measurements of Vp, Vsi and Vs2 for three possible saturation states; native, wet and dry. Vsi and Vs2 refer to two shear velocities having com- mon propagation direction. The particle motion or polarization used to measure Vsi is orthogonal to that used to measure Vs2. Thus the difference between Vsi and Vs2 at specific pressure reflects the amount of shear wave anisotropy or shear wave birefringence. It is quite common for both the horizontal and diagonal core plugs to display large differences. Velocities are reported in either ft/sec or rn/sec while effective pres- sure control points are reported in psi {14503 psi — 1Kbar — 100 MPa). April 21, 1995

context_snippets.text: - E9 - NET CONFINING PRESSURE MEASUREMENTS The samples, 100% saturated with simulated formation water, were mounted in core holders specially designed for high hydrostatic pressures. Prior to the analyses the net confining pressure was set to 20 bar in order to displace water from the sample surface and to avoid leakage along the rubber sleeve and the sample. The following net confining pressure levels were applied: 40 bar, 75 bar, 100 bar, 150 bar and 200 bar. At each confining pressure level the samples were measured for water permeability, porosity and formation resistivity factor. Pore pressure and temperature were at room conditions during the measurements. Stability time at each pressure level was set to hour. a) Water permeability, (kw) Water permeability was measured by pumping simulated formation water (filtered and degassed) through the samples at constant flowrate until the differential pressure stabilized. Differential pressure and flowrate were recorded, thus the permeability could be calculated. b) Porosity, (0) It is assumed that the porosity at 20 bar net confining pressure is equal to the porosity determined initially in the analysis program i.e. the helium porosity measured with Boyle's law porosimeter (applying no confining pressure). graduated pipette was used to collect expelled water when the net confining pressure was increased, thus the reduction in pore volume could be recorded. c) Formation Resistivity Factor, (I+) The two end pieces of the core holder were used as separate electrodes for electrical measurements. Steel nets were placed at the end faces of the sample to ensure good electrical contact. The samples were exposed to known current of frequency of kHz. The impedance and the phase angle were recorded for each sample, allowing calculation of the electrical sample resistivity. Knowing the resistivity of the simulated formation water, formation resistivity factor was calculated for each sample. question: What are the Fangst Group coring aims, minimum core runs, and stopping criteria (water/shale/base)?
answer_text: Aims: to gather petrophysical and geological core data (including water saturation) from the Fangst Group reservoir units. Minimum: one core in both the Middle Jurassic and the Lower Jurassic sandstones (one per unit); stop coring when water contact, shale, or the base of the reservoir section is reached.

question: Across wells 2/1-5, 2/5-6, 2/7-29, 1/6-6, and 7/12-9, what consistent and contrasting lithology, palynology/biostratigraphy, and geochemical trends occur in Mandal FM?
answer_text: Mandal FM is consistently dominated by carbonaceous brown‑black mudstone/claystone (pyritic, locally calcareous) with intermittent limestone/dolomite stringers and occasional thin sandstone beds. Palynology shows a hot‑shale palynofacies often barren of diagnostic fossils but locally yields Early Portlandian–Late Kimmeridgian dinocysts (e.g. Glossodinium dimorphum at ~4050 m), and geochemistry shows variable carbonates (calcite ~30–70% in upper parts down to ~6% lower, dolomite up to ~23%) with formation gas ~0.02%–18.2% (average ~0.8%–2.8%) and pervasive pyrite.

4. JURASSIC STRATIGRAPHY The uppermost 3900 metres of well 2/1-5 yielded no surprises, geologically, and thus call for no further evaluation here. The remainder of the well section, from the hot shale of the Upper Jurassic Mandal Formation to T.D. at 4458 mBRT, was in contrast quite different from forecast. Clarifying the stratigraphy of this pre-Cretaceous sequence was seen as major concern of the present study. In the following sections it will be explained how the understanding of Jurassic stratigraphy has progressed, leading in the end to a profound revision of the earlier interpretation. 4.1 Biostratigraphy As soon as the well site geological reports began to indicate deviations from the well prognosis, procedure was set up for monitoring the age of the strata being drilled, through rapid biostratigraphical analysis of wellbore cuttings material. This effort was successful only in part, owing to the absence of diagnostic microfossils over critical intervals of the drilled section. It was thus necessary to terminate the well without the support of age determinations to testify that Top Triassic had been reached. Subsequently, the Stratigraphy Branch of BP Sunbury undertook follow-up study on sidewall core material, their final results being presented in report by Lowe et al. (1983). These results essentially confirm the earlier findings and are incorporated in Figs. and as well as summarized below. a. typical hot shale palynofacies prevails in the interval 3875-4046 mBRT. This interval is devoid of age-diagnostic microfaunas or microfloras, but the palynological organic residue is typical of the upper part of the Kimmeridge Clay, i.e. Mandel Formation. b. The interval 4050-4109 mBRT yielded dinoflagellate cysts of Early Portlandian to Late Kimmeridgian age. Among the species reported were Glossodinium dimorphum with latest appearance at 4050 mBRT. This species was used by Duxbury to define extinction line NOR-S3 in his scheme for stratigraphic correlation in blocks 7/12 and 2/1, Duxbury (1981). The presence of dinocysts indicates marine environment of deposition for this interval. report/213 -12-

question: For dilatational fractures (oil patches), en echelon fractures, and compaction-filled fractures (no cataclasis), how do porosity, degree of cataclasis, and fill compare?
answer_text: Dilatational fractures (oil patches): increased porosity (dilatancy), no cataclasis, oil‑patch/open fill; En echelon fractures: open/increased porosity, no cataclasis, open (may contain oil); Compaction‑filled fractures (no cataclasis): decreased porosity relative to host, no cataclasis, filled with grey syn‑sedimentary/compaction material.

context_snippets.text: Structural core description - Well 15/9-19SR 33 At MD RKB in the Triassic, fracture with oil patches was encountered in an otherwise dry Skagerrak Formation. This is probably fracture of dilatational nature, possibly late fracture. The same phenomenon has been seen in the Pismo Formation of California, where fractures are observed in_the field as both barriers and (more rarely) conduits. Brace (1978) showed that pore-volume increase, or dilitancy, accompanies failure of intact rock in the laboratory. Antonelli et al. (1993) found that dilatation is found in an early stage of deformation band development. (Furthermore, it should be noted that en echelon open induced fractures were encountered in thin section at MD RKB.) a2. Decreased porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis The thin section from MD RKB (Skagerrak Fm.) exhibits compaction in the fracture, but no grain crushing. At mesoscopic scale, the fracture is filled with grey material, and is probably syn-sedimentary. It is surrounded by some rotated bedding and clay clasts and may well be associated with slumping at low mean stress levels. a3. Unchanged porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis Such band was found at MD RKB (Triassic). This type seems to be easier to recognize at core scale that in the thin-section. b. Deformation bands with cataclasis In most thin sections the deformed zone has decreased porosity relative to the host rock. This is mainly due to tighter packing, grain size reduction (Figure 1, Appendix B) and possible pore-filling illite (Figures B5/B6, Appendix B). This type is represented in most of the thin sections. Porosity is decreased typically by one order of magnituded, from (roughly speaking) 20 % to 0-2 %. 6.3 Comparison of meso and micro scale observations The number of thin sections (15) is bit too small to make complete analysis of micro/meso scale relationships. However, the following may be stated: i. No relationship between infill colour and microstructure seems to exist.

question: What was the peak MBT (ppb) recorded for Well 3/7-4, and was PDC-bit powdered cuttings hydration identified as the primary cause?
answer_text: Peak MBT was 38 ppb, and yes—PDC-bit powdered cuttings hydration was identified as the primary cause.

context_snippets.text: OPERATOR A/S Norske Shell WELL 3/7-4 SECTION 17 1/2 Hole The cement was drilled with seawater, then the hole was displaced with sg mud. The leak off test gave sg mud weight equivalent. When drilling commenced, it was necessary to dump the header tank on each connection as it was full of cuttings. From 892 to 1011 meters, the formation consisted of very soft clays. The string tended to hydraulic; that is to say it was lifted by pump pressure from the bottom of the hole. The soft clays were extremely hydratable and the MBT showed that the clay content of the mud rose sharply. This problem was compounded by the use of PDC bit. PDC bits produce cuttings that are powder size. This powder is difficult to remove from the system. After being circulated second time, the clay particles are dispersed and begin to affect rheology. Drilled ahead to 1182 meters. The string continued to hydraulic in the soft clays. At 1182 mete-L's it was necessary to pump the string out of the hole. Drilled ahead to 1853 meters. The MBT continued to rise, and eventually reached 38 ppb. This again was due to the powdered cuttings that hydrated and made extraction with the solids control equipment impossible. Prior to this point, the centrifuge was being run to reduce solids. Only the high rpm machine was available for use, so that barite was being dumped in addition to clay solids. That barite was being dumped in addition to solids created other problems. The mixing equipment could not maintain the required weight in the active so the centrifuge was eventually stopped. The barite mixing system was monitored and mixed approximately 10 metric tonnes per hour. Speeds in excess of this caused blockages in the screw conveyor troughs or the drive belts to break. Reducing clay content in the mud is also achievable through dilution with premix. This was difficult on the Hunter. Mixing 50 cubic meters of premix required hours. Weighting up the premix to 1,5 sg required an additiond hours. During this time it was not possible to add barite to the active system as required.

question: For the Lomond field, what are the wet gas initially-in-place (Bcm) and recovery factor (%) versus estimated reserves (Bcm)?
answer_text: Wet gas initially-in-place ≈25 Bcm; recovery factor ≈70%; estimated reserves ≈17 Bcm.

context_snippets.text: per cent. This is compatible with core measurements. Ranges of petrophysical parameters are presented in Table 5.4. 5.3.3 Reservoir Engineering The formation fluid is lean gas condensate with gas to liquid ratio of 188 m3/MMscm. An oil rim is encountered within one of the wells (Robertson ERC, 1990b). Pressure data show that each well lies in separate compartment. This is supported by log data which shows different hydrocarbon water contacts in each well. Many tests prove difficult to interpret unambiguously due to poor formation permeability, multiphase flow and the presumed isolated nature of the sands. However, two of the wells showed good flow rates and permeability thickness values. Test permeabilities averaged between - 10 mD with core data averaging 10 mD. 5.3.4 Volumetrics and Reserves A wet gas initially in place of approximately 25 Bcm has been established for Lomond and an approximate recovery factor of 70 per cent. applied, giving reserves of the order of 17 Bcm. As Lomond is relatively lean gas condensate, liquid dropout may be small and condensate recoveries of around 35 per cent. are therefore expected. 5.4 Conclusions On the basis of the descriptions above, the following key points can be made, which are of direct relevance to the inferred Well 1/3-6 reservoir model. • Intrafield shale out of reservoir sandstones can be used to model the distribution of fluids and contacts. • Top structure mapping and pressure data indicate that the reservoirs at Cod and Lomond are possibly faulted. • Complex fluid and contact distribution may therefore be controlled by one or combination of reservoir sand shale outs and faulting. • Gross reservoir thickness in the nearest analogue (Cod Field) is directly related to structural position, whereas at Lomond it is not. • Net to gross ratio variation tends to parallel gross thickness trends and is controlled by the detailed distribution of reservoir sandstones facies. • Porosity variations are controlled by primary facies type and depth of burial. question: For well 7321/7-1 Snadd gas sand at 2385 m, what are porosity, permeability and RFT/fluid observations?
answer_text: Good porosity; low permeability; RFTs and fluid sampling recovered small volumes of gas and mud filtrate (solution gas).

context_snippets.text: 8 PETROPHYSICAL EVALUATION SUMMARY The petrophysical evaluation of the well shows the primary and secondary objectives have low porosity, poor permeability and are wet. RFT's in the objectives recovered mud filtrate with some solution gas. The only hydrocarbons found are in gas sand at 2385 in the Snadd Formation. The sand has good porosity but RFT pressure tests and fluid sampling indicate low permeability. A small volume of gas and mud filtrate were recovered from RFT samples. The decision was made to P&A the well without testing. WELL DATA The petrophysical evaluation was performed using logs recorded on intermediate logging run (1 m) and the final logging run (1425 - TD). The sections of hole logged above 1425 do not have hydrocarbon potential. Log quality is generally. good with two exceptions, both on the final logging run. The first is the result of poor hole conditions which complicate the evaluation of the interval from 2450-2800 m. The second is an SFL tool failure that occurred at 2478 m. Logging run 5A has good SFL recorded from 1425-2450 m. The result is 28 meter gap in SFL data. It was decided not to relog as the missing data was not in a critical zone and several hours would have been required to relog. Conventional cores were taken in the StO Formation and the Snadd gas sand. The grain densities measured on core plugs are high in the gas sand apparently due to the presence of heavy minerals. A sand/shale model was used for lithology identification and porosity calculation. Density, neutron, sonic and gamma-ray logs were the primary input for the model. The matrix density used to calculate porosity is gm/cc in the primary objective, in the Snadd gas sand, and in the Carnian sands. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Petrologic analyses demonstrate that the Sto displays all the characteristics of deeply buried, highly compacted sandstone. The period of maximum burial prior to uplift must have been long enough for the rock to reach equilibrium with its subsurface en- vironment. When the Snadd Formation is plotted on the porosity-depth curve, it departs from the normal compaction trendline, instead deviating toward the higher porosities (Fig. 12). Such elevated porosities in deeply buried sandstones are characteristic of reservoirs with secondary porosity (Schmidt and McDonald, 1979). The petrographic evidence of secondary porosity further confirms this interpretation. SUMMARY: IMPLICATIONS FOR EXPLORATION IN THE BARENTS SEA Petrologic examination of the cored reservoirs in the 7321/7-1 well identified two types of sandstone with dissimilar reservoir properties. The Sto Formation represents compositionally mature sandstone with mostly primary porosity. Deep burial of the rock resulted in highly reduced porosity and permeabil- ity. Diagenetic processes influencing this rock, including chemical and mechanical compaction, are depth-sensitive. Exploration should be confined to areas experiencing minimum amounts of uplift when the Sto and similar compositionally mature sandstones are the primary reservoir objectives. Unfortu- nately, the trend of eastward decreasing uplift, as interpreted by MENI , is accompanied by concurrent decrease in the thickness of the Sto and other units (Gjelberg and others, 1987; Snedden and others, 1989). However, there may be central fairways where the reservoir thickness and estimated maximum burial depths fall within acceptable limits.

context_snippets.text: PRCGNOSIS Well 7120/9-1 was drilled to test sandstone reservoirs of Middle to Lower Jurassic age. The structure was an east - west trending anticline plunging gently to the east. To the north and west the structure terminated against downfaulted shales. The structure was wholely within the Hammerfest Basin. Exploration Logging provided Geological Engineering Monitoring and Data Analysis System (GEINIDAS) service on 7120/9-1 from 405m to 2300m. total depth. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mud logging, automatic real-time data monitoring and recording, and pressure analyses were carried out. Continuous evaluation of pressure and drilling progress provided an aid in optimizing drilling costs, and ensuring that drilling continued with maximum safety to personnel, the well and equipment. The operator was continuously advised as to the status of these analyses, and data and results stored on magnetic disk for post-well evaluation. The printouts and plots are contained in the attachments of this report. For details of the computer programs provided, and the theory of the pressure evaluation methods used, please refer to the Program Information Book MS-144 and Pressure Log Manual MS-156. Both are available from Exploration Logg ing

Generally there is very good correlation between these lines, the Norsk Hydro well log 7120/9-1 and the background paper entitled 'The Structural Geology of the Troms Area' (Ovrebr6 and Talleraas, Geojournal Vol 1, p. 47, 1977). Our interpretation for each of the lines is contained on the single sheet enclosed, at half the scale of the original seismic sections. The scale bar in the text (Figure 3.4) can be used to convert times to depths on these sections. INTERPRETATION OF PROCESSES & ENVIROMLENTS The first stage in the environmental analysis has been to group together related beds or facies into units called FACIES SEQUENCES. These facies sequences reflect individual or closely related depositional events and are therefore units of genetic significance. They are usually recognized by identifying sharp boundaries followed by sequence of gradationally related beds or facies. Such sequences are commonly of fining-upward (FU) or coarsening - upward nature, but may also be of 'no-trend' type. In general the sequences of non-marine (or largely subaerial) origin, in well 7120/9-1, have fairly abundant coals and rooted horizons, and traction generated ripple laminations dominate over wave-generated ripple lamination.

question: How do basal FIS boundaries' PTP signal shifts and inclusion decline distinguish present fluid contacts from paleo fluid contacts?
answer_text: Present-day contact: the petroleum-dominant FIS leg is replaced by water‑soluble PTP signals at the base and visual petroleum inclusion abundance decreases in parallel. Paleo contact: high inclusion abundance in the petroleum zone without corresponding PTP signals in the water leg.

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 51 A.3.4 Seals FIS seals are inferred at boundaries marking abrupt changes in FIS species strength or chem- istry. The underlying assumption is that detected fluids are more or less synchronous on either side of the boundary and that some process has prevented free mixing of species across this barrier. In detail the boundary may represent change in lithology, poroperm or structural element. In the case of in-situ generated petroleum the boundary might represent transi- tion from poor to better source rock, or immature to mature source intervals. In the case of migrated petroleum the boundary might represent the extent of petroleum migration through porous rock, or the top seal to present or past petroleum column. Basal compartment limits may represent seals or, in some cases, fluid contacts or paleocontacts (see below). In general, only the tops of FIS compartments are identified on interpreted FIS depth plots. If fluids were not synchronous on either side of the compartment boundary (e.g. post-migration unconformity) then the seal interpretation would be in error. Seals may be selective or chro- matographic, in which case low molecular weight species may migrate across the boundary, while higher molecular weight species do not. A.3.5 Microseepage FIS microseeps are analogous to gas chimneys seen in seismic data, and surface manifestations of deeper charge identified in surface geochemical surveys. They are interpreted to result from near-vertical migration of light hydrocarbons followed by bacterial alteration in the shallow subsurface at temperature-depth conditions permissible for bacterial activity. Most bacteria are restricted to temperatures below 65-70°C; hence, anomalies may be observed in the up- per 1-3 km of rock column, depending on the prevailing geothermal gradient. Key indictor species include light hydrocarbons, CO2, possibly organic acids and aromatic compounds, and sulfurous volatiles, including H2S, COS, CS2, S2 ( /- SO2) and in some cases thiols. H2S is often sequestered within pyrite in iron-rich siliciclastics, hence is less common in shale-bearing lithologies. Inclusion formation in such low temperature environments may be aided by pre- cipitation of bacterial carbonate. FIS microseeps are geometrically distinct, often beginning at the surface and abruptly disappearing at the appropriate temperature-controlled depth. The presence of an FIS microseep appears to be good indicator of deeper charge in the immediate vicinity, although weak seeps may represent regional signals within shallow aquifers. Data suggest that these anomalies overlie 75-80% of productive reservoirs, while only 10% of non-productive areas display similar signals. Hence, the presence of strong seep within dry hole might indicate deeper or nearby lateral charge in the area. A.3.6 Fluid Contacts The basal boundary (abrupt or transitional) of any strong FIS compartment is candidate for present or past fluid contact, although the interpretation is often equivocal. The most compelling evidence for present day contact occurs where hydrocarbon-dominant FIS signals (the petroleum leg) give way to water-soluble dominant signals (PTP in the water leg) and where visual petroleum inclusion abundance displays parallel decrease. When inclusion abundance is high in the petroleum zone but PTP signals are not present in the water leg, it is possible that paleo-charge is recorded. SHALLOW GEOLOGY AND WELL PROGNOSIS 6.1 Background The proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location is situated in NCS block 7219/8. The interpreted stratigraphy is based on information from tie wells. Interpretation is limited to the top Cretaceous, 1847m MSL (1646ms TWT) at the PWL. Two figures are presented, figures and 6.2, illustrating the geological profiles at the proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location. Time-Depth conversion is based upon velocities derived from seismic processing of the 2D data (figure 10.1). All depths are quoted in metres MSL and two way time in milliseconds at the proposed location. The time-depth conversion is expected to be accurate to ±2m at seabed increasing to around ±10m at second TWT. 6.2 Sub-seabed Conditions The geological section to the top Cretaceous has been split into units as tied to offset wells, previous surveys (section 3.4) and in accordance with interpretation provided by Statoil. Quaternary - Nordland Group (Unit 1): Unit is expected to comprise very soft to firm clay with rare gravel becoming firm clay with sand layers and silt with depth. The base is marked by moderate amplitude, phase reversed, approximately sub-horizontal reflector reaching 458 to 506m MSL (589 to 639ms TWT) across the site, deepening gently to the north. The base of Unit represents sand layer and gas level (section 7) and is an angular unconformity. At this horizon slight risk of gas is assigned at the PWL (section 7). Within unit several possibly erosional events are observed. At 426m MSL (555ms TWT) at the PWL weak possibly reverse phase horizon is seen possibly representing sand layer. Possible boulders may be expected throughout this unit and specifically at the base as seen in offset wells. Well 7220/8-1 confirms the base of Unit as sand layer and also encountered boulders. Problems with boulders are also reported at the base Quaternary in the 7219/9-1 well (section 7.4); this is referenced from the 7220/7-1 drilling program and the problems are not specified. The 7220/5-1 well also encountered boulders at the base Quaternary. Tertiary (Palaeocene to Eocene) - Sotbakken Group (Units and 3): Unit forms thick sequence, the upper part is seismically well layered, with horizons dipping to the northwest, while the lower part is possibly less so though it becomes obscured by the seabed multiple. question: What are the depths and magnitudes of torque spikes, standpipe pressure drops, washouts, and twist‑offs recorded in well 2/4-18?

Initially the weight was 1.45sg but as hole problems developed throughout the section this was increasd to 1.50sg. number of different formations were encountered during the drilling of this section and each posed its own problems. The Balder is known as lost circulation zone and both the Sele and the Lista can become unstable if left exposed for long periods of time. A formation integrity test was performed at the 13 3/8 casing shoe which gave minimum fracture gradient of 1.65sg EMW. Initially drilling proceeded with no problems. There were no cavings seen in the returns, the torque and drag indicators were normal and hole cleaning did not appear to be problem. No drag was seen during the trips at 2043m and 2186m and there was no fill on returning to bottom after these trips. The well was circulated clean and the mud conditioned prior to entering the Balder Formation as this is known as potential loss zone. However no losses were experienced. During the trip at 2628m the first indications of tight hole were observed with tight spots at 2494m and 2446m. However these were not serious and no tight hole was seen on the trip back in. While drilling at 2850m the first indications of more serious hole problems were seen with the appearence of cavings which appeared to originate in the Lista. formation. In response to this the mud weight was allowed to drift up from 1.45sg to 1.47sg. This mud weight was maintained throughout the drilling of the chalk. Although initially the amount of cavings did reduce, it then increased once more to between 10% and 30% of the returns. The mud weight was then increased at the base of the chalk prior to entering the Cromer Knoll Group, first to 1.48sg and then to 1.5sg. The hole condition was seen to have deteriorated considerably when it packed off while drilling at 3229m and there was 60 bar increase in stand pipe pressure. Whilst circulation was reestablished and there were no losses as result, it was clear that problems were developing and it was thought these were caused by the Lista formation from which large amounts of cavings were being seen along with gas peak of 0.9% (over previous background level of 0.1%) which originated at about 2400m. The trip out at 3237m encountered tight spots in the chalk at 3071m and 2966m and, more seriously, in the Hordaland formation between 2210m and 2180m. On the trip back in hole tight spot was seen at 2160m and the bit had to be washed down to 2180m. The well packed off and 12m3 of mud was lost to the formation. Once circulation had been reestablished half of this mud was returned along with large volumes of cavings and gas peak of 1.6%. In total some 32m3 of cuttings were circulated out of the hole whilst tying to clean up the blockage. The background gas varied throughout the section depending upon both formation and drilling rate. Initially levels of between 0.3% and 0.6% were seen from the start of the section down to 1480m. The gas then rose quite rapidly to between 1.5% and % until 1550m when it then dropped back to previous levels. From 2130m to 2450m the gas reduced further to between 0.1% and 0.3% and throughout most of the chalk section it did not rise above 0.1%. At the base of the section it rose to between 0.1% and 0.3%. The mud temperature increased steadily throughout the section from 43° to 67° at TD. However it did remain very steady at around 60° throughout the chalk section.

question: Do the sonic increases (163→190→213 µs/ft) and a coincident resistivity peak indicate progressive pore-pressure increase and hydrocarbon presence?
answer_text: Yes; the sonic increases (163→190→213 µs/ft) indicate a progressive pore-pressure increase, and the coincident high resistivity peak suggests hydrocarbons at the top of the Mandal.

context_snippets.text: Formation Pressures affecting the temperature out readings. The temperature data showed continuation of the previously established geothermal gradient of degC/100m. The temperature gradient exhibits slight negative trend from 3450m to 3530m and then increases at the normal geothermal gradient to TD. Sonic data shows compactional trend to the top of the chalk when the data shows trend of 163 usecs/ft. As the chalk grades to mudstones the travel time increases to 190 usecs/ft by 3400m. Between 3400m and 3520m the data shows an increasing trend in mudstones suggesting an increase in pore pressure. Sonic data shows rapid increase in travel time at the top of the Mandal Formation reaching 213 usecs/ft, the values gradually decrease fromthis point to TD. Resistivity data indicates normally compacting sequence to the top of the chalk with values then becoming scattered. As mudstones are encountered the trend decreases to TD. An anomaly to this trend is high resistivity peak at the top of the Mandal suggesting the presence of hydrocarbons. No significant hole problems were observed on tripping and connections. In conclusion, with all pore pressure prediction methods there was no evidence to suggest any changes in pore pressure between 2730m and 3400m, the estimate remaining at sg. Between 3400m and TD; Dxc, gas, temperature and to lesser extent, wireline data indicated gradual increase in the pore pressure regime. This data provided an estimate of sg which continued to TD.

3.2 THE PRESSURE LOG — DISCUSSION Formation pressures were continuously evaluated from the 18 5/8 casing shoe until T.D. at 3710m. The following measured and calculated parameters were used in the pore pressure evaluation:- Corrected Drilling exponent Shale Density Mud Temperature In/Out MWD Tool Temperature Total Gas Observations of hole condition, cavings, trip gas and connection gas also furnished valuable data for overpressure evaluation, as did data obtained from wireline logs. The pore pressure profile encountered during the drilling of 7/12 - Al0 was basically normal'. However three zones of increasing formation pressure were encountered: 1) 1400m - 2050m : From just above the 13 3/8 casing shoe in the 12 1/4 section, the pore pressure increased to maximum of - SG. 2) 2200m - 2650m : This was in the 12 1/4 hole section and the pore pressure increased to maximum of SG. 3) 3405m : At the end of the 12 1/4 section, where the top of the Kimmeridgian Mandal formation was encountered the pore pressure rose to SG. The well can be divided pressure profile :- into the following sections with regard to the pore 1. 547m to 1400m Normal pore pressure (possible transition zone below 1000m) 2. 1400m to 1650m Rise in pore pressure to SG. 3. 1650m to 2050m Stable pressure SG. 4. 2250m to 2500m Rise in pore pressure to SG 5. 2500m to 3405m Stable or slight reduction in pressure 6. 3405m to T.D. Rapid rise stabilizing at SG.

- 23 -_ DISCUSSION OF THE PRESSURE LOG ( continued ) Flowline temperature was not available through this section due to the sensor being continuously buried in cuttings in section of the shaker box not readily accessible for maintenance. Gas levels were generally low to moderate in this section, ranging between 0.3% - 1.0%, with only occasional isolated peaks above the background level. Trip gases were all in the range - % (total) which were only slightly above the drilled gas levels. Overpull of 75 Klbs was encountered whilst reaming at 1700m, mainly due to packing of cuttings in the annulus during periods of continual very fast drilling; however the mud weight was raised from 1.28 sg to sg prior to drilling ahead. Through most of this section, data from logs of previous wells in the field was used in aiding in the estimation the pore pressure gradient. SECTION : 1/2 HOLE FROM 3203 TO 4375 I. The lithology in this section was variable; initially tuffaceous mudstone before small sandstone section, then siltstone, limestone and mudstone sections before the main body of hard chalky limestone with chert nodules. The base of the interval from about 4030m onwards consisted of calcareous mudstone. The lithology being so variable and the use of PDC bits in this section meant that no usable DXc Exp- onent trend was obtained although slight cutback was observed in the mudstone at the base of the section which was judged to be indicative of an increase in formation pore pressure. Drilling gas levels were very low, generally below %, down to 4200m where tenfold increase in background level was seen. This increased background level plus connection gases of up to % and wiper trip gases of up to % also were indicative of increased pore pressure in the section from 4200m to 4375m. Mud temperatures were not available over the first part of the interval due to the sensor being buried by accumulated cuttings, and the short bit runs made after clearing the sensor gave highly variable values. From 3800m stable trend was seen with slight cutback shown from 4100m. Delta temperature showed an increasing trend from 4200m. The pore pressure estimate was maintained at sg down to 4050m where indications from gas, temperature and DXc trends led to this being raised to sg in the MANDAL formation after 4300m. SECTION : HOLE FROM 4375 TO 4550 The lithology in this section consisted of the bottom part of the MANDAL formation and the main GYDA SANDSTONE reservoir. Most of the section was cored so no useful formation pore pressure evaluation information was recorded. The pore pressure estimate of sg seen in the MANDAL formation was maintained until the top of the GYDA sandstone was encountered where it was lowered to sg.

Authority J. Gamblen The pore and fracture pressures in this section are primarily based on the Gyda wells. Normal pore pressure (1.04 SG) will be evident until c. 1300m where it gradually increases to SG at c. 1700m. It gradually increases to 1.45 SG by section TD at 3200m. The 5/8 LOT at 3200m is expected around SG EMW. The 1/2 hole will be drilled to top reservoir, and possibly to well TD (4523m BRT) if mud weights allow. If the Mandal formation is not overpressured, the mud weight in use at top reservoir is SG or below, and there are no indications of hole problems, drilling/coring will continue to well TD, provided the error bar on top salt remains deeper than TD. If the Mandal formation is overpressured, the liner will be committed having tagged top sand, and the reservoir interval will be drilled in hole. The 1/2 hole will be initially drilled in the Chalk group. The upper Chalk, in the top Ekofisk formation, is expected to contain chert. The amount of chert is difficult to predict, however the lithology logs produced following 1/3-3 and 2/1-6 both indicated chert in the Ekofisk formation. Also, traces of blue grey chert were reported in the upper and mid Tor formations from well 1/3-3. Occasional pyrite was reported in the lower Tor formations on well 2/1-6. This cherty limestone is difficult to drill and will require conical insert drilling bits to efficiently drill the interval. As well as the hard drilling conditions in the Chalk Group there is also the possibility of stuck pipe due to differential sticking in the Tor. Careful attention will be made to monitoring mud properties and minimising overbalance. BP's extensive stuck pipe guidelines will be strictly adhered to throughout this section. of BP Norway Limited U.A.

SUMMARY This is the first time the PP/FG TM service has been used offshore Norway real-time. The well was drilled without significant problems and the reservoir pressure was close to that prognosed in the drilling programme. The PP/FG calculated pore pressure results calculated by the model can only be verified in permeable formations from formation tests and well control incidents. Pore pressure transition zones always occur in impermeable formations and here results can be contentious when compared to traditional methods of pore pressure prediction. However, the results do have value if they can aid in the prediction of pressure when entering permeable formation. There were only two depths in the well where it was possible to verify the PP/FG results: 1. possible small influx at 4387m implied that the pressure PP/FG result was close to the actual formation pressure. 2. Below the Mandal Formation we had to interpolate the resistivity through hydrocarbon-rich formations. Using this corrected resistivity curve we predicted the reservoir pressure gradient at 4500m to be 1.81g/cc. The measured pressure gradient was I.75g/cc from the MDT. A calculated pore pressure maximum of 2.09g/cc was reported during drilling of the Cromer Knoll Group. This was revised down to 2.00g/cc when the wireline data became available. The difference was mainly due to miscalibrated MWD resistivity run which was consistantly reading values 30% more conductive than the wireline, but also slightly due to the model interpreting the lithology from the gamma ray as too calcareous. The PP/FG calculated fracture pressure results were within 0.03g/cc of the actual LOT's at 13 3/8 and 7/8 shoes. This indicates that we have an accurate fracture propagation pressure gradient. Considerable valuable information and experience was gained as result of this work which will improve the PP/FG service and future pore and fracture pressure prediction in this area. It has allowed us to assess the updates and improvements to the program which have recently been added to the software, and has suggested additional improvements which are now being implemented. I. INTRODUCTION The Sperry-Sun PP/FG service is based on software model that calculates pore and fracture pressures on an incremental basis through all major lithologies in normally compacted sedimentary sequences. It requires calibration to offset wells. The two closest wells to the 2/7-29 location, 2/7-19 & 2/7-22, were studied and calibration for the real-time job was derived. This was described fully in previous report. This final report for BP Norway describes the pore and fracture pressure results using the PP/FG service on the Mmrsk Guardian for well 2/7-29. The service commenced from the 7/8 casing point at 3124m on the 16th October until the Permian at 4850m on the 21st December. Results from real- time MWD data whilst drilling arc compared to the wircline data for this post well analysis. Offshore PP/FG Engineers Gaute Grindhaug Donald MacDonald George Irvine Karl Gunnar Tjeliveit (Trainee) Sperry-Sun Drilling Services PP/FG report for BP Norway Well 2/7-29

Solids control: The shakers were initially dressed with 52 mesh screens to handle the cold fluid after diplacement. As the circulating temperature increased, finer 165 and 200 mesh screens were fitted. The centrifuge or desilters were not run.

121/4 Drilling Phase BHA 8, similar in specification to the eventual drilling assembly, was run in hole to drill out the 13 3/8 shoe, but at 750m the cross-over between the drill collars and HWDP backed out and the BHA plunged 2000m to its death on top of the float collar. BHA was therefore standard fishing assembly and successfully retrieved the drilling BHA in the first run. Although there was no visible damage to the assembly, all tools were laid down for inspection as precaution. BHA 10 was therefore the first assembly to drill formation and it should be noted that the (back-up) motor utilised was of specification designed for use at higher temperatures deeper in the hole. The rotor/stator fit therefore, was not ideal for this run but good differential pressure was in any case maintained whilst drilling. This replacement motor also had stabiliser sleeve fixed on the bent housing rather than the rotating bit-box model that is the preferred option for serious orientation. Notwithstanding the above, any disappointment with regard to ROP was perhaps as much function of bit choice as motor design, though pump problems with their associated low flow rates undoubtedly played part. Security FM2943DR was chosen for this section and comparisons drawn between this location and nearby Asgard show that in the latter field, somewhat more aggressive (Hycalog) bits are used above the Lysing formation. Interestingly, use of this type of bit on Asgard does not appear to compromise steerability but even with the bit chosen, orientation on this location was found to be difficult and may be an indication that formations here are somewhat different to those on Asgard, at least in their steerability. In the 17Y2 phase the borehole had been allowed to drift towards the southwest corner of the target and it was deemed prudent to nudge the well back towards target centre prior to drilling into the Lysing (the barrier on Asgard between steerable and difficult formations). This was attempted on two occasions with BHA 10 but with little success, tool face tending to be erratic and difficult to control. Poor MWD signals (the tool was later to fail) may have been part of the problem but the claystone found on this location is undoubtedly less steerable than that on Asgard. Combined with the fact that the bend on the motor was set at the minimum 0.39°, little effect was seen from the orientation. At 3223m the MWD failed and the assembly pulled to replace the tool. On surface. little wear was seen on the bit that was therefore re-run and as well as changing the MWD. the opportunity was taken to increase the bend on the motor to 0.78° so that orientation would have more effect. Steering was attempted as soon as the BHA was run to bottom but again, tool face control was difficult and steering ineffective. Fortunately, the path of the well at this point continued to drift towards the northeast, making further time-consuming attempts at correction unnecessary. steady but slow increase in angle was noted throughout this run but no specific disadvantage was seen in increasing the bend of the motor and overall, good pendulum effect was maintained despite the use of relatively aggressive drilling parameters in order to improve the rate of penetration. Little was seen of the Lysing sandstone expected to dull the bit and despite continued pump problems, an overall improvement in ROP over the previous run was noted. At 4200m planned BHA change took effect and although from purely directional point of view packed assembly would have been the preferred option in order to keep the well straight, the motor was replaced with rotary pendulum

ASGARD UNIT - SMORBUKK SC* 12 1/4 Hole Section The 12 1/4 section was drilled using bit runs. The 13 3/8 casing shoe track and 3m new formation were drilled out using 12 1/4 bit to 2655 mMD. The hole was circulated clean and FIT was performed to SG EMW. Unintentional, higher pressure was applied, equivalent to SG, when performing the FIT breaking the formation. However, no problems related to leak off' was experienced throughout the section. Displacement to 1.75 sg Versa Vert oil based mud was carried out during drilling the cement. This mud was used in rest of the section to section ID at 5555 mMD. The 121/4 hole was then drilled and oriented to 3800 mMD. From 3800 to 4275 rotary drilling found place. After several attempt to steer below Lysing Fm, the BHA was pulled out of hole at 4299 mMD. A motor assembly with extra strong motor with bend, MWD-CDR, and less aggressive PDC bit was then run in hole to drill and orient second turn. Drilled from 4299 to 4306 MD, drilled and oriented from 4306 to 4329 MD. Pulled out due to poor drilling rate even in rotation. Changed bit back to the aggressive BX447, else same BHA. Ran in hole and drilled and oriented from 4329 MD. Problems holding tool face and to feed stable weight down to bit. Excellent ROP in rotation (30-40 m/hr). Drilled with this assembly down to 4645 MD. Steering was difficult and did not achieve enough turn. It was decided to pull out to run in with turbine. Ran in with 1° bend turbine and Smith MGR35DHS bit, this was short gauge medium aggressive bit, and new MWD tool. The inclination remained around 45° - 47°, and the well was turned approximately 35° through this bit run - from 347° to 312°. Penetration rates were in the order of - m/hr while orienting and - 20 m/hr while rotating. The bit was pulled at 5000 mMD; this was planned trip to change assembly for the build in inclination. A rotary assembly with TRACS tool and new MWD (including ISONIC) was run in the hole. The Lysing formation was reamed for ISONIC data on the way the hole; the first stand with circulation for real-time data, then without circulation for memory data only. The MWD tool stopped transmitting data at approximately 5026 mMD, and the assembly was pulled at 5035 mMD. The rotary assembly was rerun with new MWD tool. There was no communication with this tool when it was tested at 500 m, so the assembly was pulled. The backup MWD tool was run with the old CDR. This assembly drilled to section I'D at 5555 m. The penetration rate was much higher than expected at an average m/hr for the run, with ROPs of 20 - 30 m/hr between slower dolomite stringers. The Garn Formation was seen on the MWD log, and returns were circulated at 5528 mMD. The returns contained mainly claystone with siltstone and some sandstone, and in view of the relatively high GR values, drilling continued to 5555 mMD where returns were circulated again. The returns contained sandstone, confirming the Garn Formation. The 5/8 casing was run to 5540 mMD. The Lange sandstones caused some problems, with tight hole from 4880 m, but the casing was landed successfully. The casing was cemented with approximately 40% returns. gyro survey was run in casing prior to drilling out the shoe.

question: How do cuttings parameters correlate with mud parameters and lithological descriptions in the 16/1-3 mud log?
answer_text: Cuttings percentages and lithological descriptions are plotted adjacent to ROP, gas (API), mud weight (in/out) and mud temperatures, so lithology changes correlate with contemporaneous variations in ROP, gas responses and mud weight/temperature on the 16/1-3 mud log.

context_snippets.text: GEARHART GEODATA SERVICES LTD. -9- THE MUD LOG - Introduction The mud log is plotted on 1:500 vertical depth scale from the rotary table to total depth at 3498 metres. The depths are given from Rotary Kelly Bushings at mean sea level. The mud log consists of (from the left) column with bit run data, followed by histogram type rate of penetration (ROP) plot measured in minutes per metre. This is followed by depth scale and percentage cuttings lithology column. Then follows a logarithmic plot of gas measured in API units. Next are mud temperatures (in and out) and mud weights (in and out). The space on the right hand side of the log is used for lithological descriptions and mud data. Cuttings were sampled at predetermined intervals, or at specific intervals and depths as requested by the rig geologist. The lag time was continuously updated and frequently checked by means of calcium carbide lag tests. Field prints of the log were sent onshore at regular intervals.

context_snippets.text: The marine Jurassic sequences from the northern North Sea show several major changes in the general characteristics of the palynological constituents, represented essentially by an alternation of two types of preservation. Certain intervals are characterised by the relatively well preserved appearance of their constituents and include the common occurrence of material comparable to palynomacerals and 3, or in some cases structureless (sapropelic) organic matter, but with only infrequent blade- shaped palynomaceral 4. Such intervals are believed to represent relatively enclosed areas where energy conditions at the sea bottom may be relatively low because current activity from tides or open oceanic conditions is limited. Conversely, other intervals subject to higher oxygenation and current activity are characterised by poorly preserved constituents which are frequently darkened or bleached and dominated by high proportions of blade-shaped palynomaceral 4. These intervals can be correlated, using dinocysts, across the northern North Sea and appear to be relatively isochronous, and thus most likely reflect regional changes of depositional setting.

Number of copies Abstract Trace fossil analysis has been conducted for the cored interval in well 15/12-A8 within the Varg field area. This consists of lower, sandrich Upper Jurassic' succession, and overlying shale dominated Heather Formation. Seven discrete ichnofabrics, all similar to ichnofabrics identified previously from the Varg field area, has been identified. For the lower sand- dominated succession, three broad' groups can be assembled based on their palaeoenvironment association: I. range of trace fossils characterised by combination of Ophiomorplui irregulaire and Ophiomorpha nodosa, which commonly interfinger with ichnofabric eight 'Burrow mottled ichnofabric' associated with middle to upper shoreface conditions. 2. combination of ichnofabrics Ophiomorpha irregulaire and Palaeophycus heberti associated with lower shoreface to upper offshore transitional. 3. combination of Palaeophycus heberti-Phycosiphon and Phycosiphon-Teichichnus that is associated with middle to lower shoreface conditions. In the upper shale dominated succession two trace fossil assemblages are particularly apparent: I. number of Phycosiphon dominated ichnofahrics that are associated with the lower end of offshore storm deposits. 2. Chondrites-Phycosiphon assemblages that is associated with offshore shelf conditions. Utilising the detailed information from the ichnofabric analysis, high-resolution sequence swatigraphy based on the ichnofabric-stacking pattern has been established. This suggests that the sand dominated reservoir succession can be divided into two depositional sequences. marked basinward shift at the base of the two sequences suggests that sand initially was brought out due to relative fall of sea-level or forced regression. This was followed by relative rise of sea level foming thick transgressive package and thin highstand package. The transgression continued in the lower part of the Heather Formation, forming thick transgressive succession. However as the rate of relative sea level rise slowed thin regressive succession or high stand formed in the middle of the cored Heather Formation. On top of this renewed drowning followed with the establishment of offshore shelf conditions. Distribution: 7 Saga Petroleum ASA 3 Smedvig Technologies as. However, observed cross bedding within the coarser intervals interfingering with the finer, more bioturbated intervals, probably reflect depositional environment closer to normal wave-base activity. However, care most is taken in assigning one specific environment to this ichnofabric 'blindly' since it may resemble both ichnofabrics 5, 6, and even 7, without carefully analysing the trace fossils, sediment grain-size and what ever appears of the original lamination. This ichnofabric commonly occurs above the Ophiomorpha nodosa ichnofabric (Ichnofabric 7) in what appears to be in the upper part of prograding succession where the high degree of biogenetic reworking suggests reduced or slow accumulation of sediments. Martin and Pollard (1996) do not assign any particular environment to this ichnofabric, however the more clear observations of traces in addition to sediment grain-size and preserved lamination suggests middle lower- to-upper shoreface setting for this ichnofabric. Martin and Pollard (1996) describes the similar ichnofabric from the Kittiwake Field (UKCS) as rare and points out that some of the poorly outlined ellipsoidal burrows may in fact be de- watering structures. It should be noted however that 'classical' definition of lower upper to middle shoreface environments describes low angle lamination to cross- bedding as observed sparsely within the less bioturbated intervals of this ichnofabric. Together with grain-size and trace fossils assemblage support an interpretation of middle to lower-upper shoreface setting for this ichnofabric. Smedvig Technologies as. 25

question: How do mud-loss events compare to MWD-decoding failures in Lange FM regarding causes, operational impacts, and mitigations?
answer_text: Mud-losses in the Lange FM were due to loss zones/formation communication (manifesting as system gains and lost m3) and required flow reduction, shut-ins and mud‑weight adjustments; MWD decoding failures were caused by massive valve/noise, high downhole torque and oil‑based mud signal attenuation. Operational impacts differed: mud‑losses forced circulation cutbacks, bleeding off pressure and mud‑weight changes to stabilize the well, whereas MWD failures reduced real‑time data density and were mitigated by reducing RPM/WOE/flow, switching to X3 data rate, using adaptive equalizer/forced decoding and relying on memory logs.

A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Where it is found that sliding is unavoidable towards the end of the 12 1/4” section it may be worthwhile to have Dogsub available on the Rig in case a trip is made where it could be picked up, although it would probably not be worth making special trip for it. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. The rotary BHA consisted of full gauge double nearbit roller reamer followed by float sub and variable gauge Andergauge stabilizer. This was followed by CDR, ILS stabilizer and MWD tools, as well as the ADN tool for porosity and density logs. After drilling out the float collar, shoe track and shoe, the hole was displaced to 1.32sg Versavert oil based mud. Very moderate drilling parameters were used to drill out the shoe, plugs and cement in an effort to protect the bit from excessive wear. Consequently 4.5hrs were used before drilling on new formation. The second target at TVD of 4264m had been extended to the north to take into account the significant walk rates seen in the previous 12 1/4 section. This extension allowed the 1/2 section +/- 0.5deg/30m right hand walk rate as well as 0.5/30m build or drop rate, dependant on actual walk rates experienced. Phillips Petroleum Company Norway Egdar, 2/7-30 SUMMARY This report presents the results of structural core goniometry analysis of the vertical well 2/7-30 (Egdar prospect). The interval of interest was the Chalk Group from which six cores (10302-10748 ft) were recovered and examined using an electromagnetic goniometer (Phillips Petroleum Company) to determine the orientation of structural and sedimentological features. The overall objectives of this study were to detail the core fracture description (styles, density, distribution), present fracture orientation data and provide structural interpretation. Core goniometry was completed on all six cores. None of the cores were oriented therefore core data were rotated to subsurface orientation using supplied FMS data. Features recorded from the core comprise range of bedding types (including moderately common siliceous hurls) and tectonic, irregular, healed and stylolite-associated fractures (also bedding parallel fractures, slump-fractures). In addition to the standard Phillips Petroleum fracture classification, fracture types were further classified into open and closed categories. Fracture densities have been calculated for all fracture types on per foot basis. Tectonic tilt analysis suggests that relatively consistent structural dip can be applied for the whole well. value of 9°/245 is calculated for the Tor Formation (locally SSW at base of the cored interval) and this decreases to 4°/271 for the Ekofisk Formation. Most low angle bedding planes show moderate azimuth scatter about the sub-horizontal axis and are therefore sensitive to local tilting or warping. NW-SE palaeoslope trend is inferred from measured Slump-fold axes, probably reflecting mass transport of material off the Eldfisk structure. Tectonic fractures are poorly developed in this well (maximum fractures/ft at 10663 ft and 10680 ft) and have relatively consistent NNW-SSE to NW-SE fracture strike trends, dipping at 45-80° towards the east and west (55/253; 47-80/065). Greatest development of tectonic fractures occurs within the uppermost cored interval (clay sealed conjugate shear fractures; 10302-20 ft) and also locally within the Tor Formation (10660-10685 ft). Subordinate NE-SW and E-W tectonic fracture strike trends also occur; the E-W trend is largely confined to the Tor Formation. Tectonic fractures have unusually high percentage fracture fills (53% of fractures are completely/partially filled), dominantly comprising clay, stylolitic material and calcite. Due to poor tectonic fracture definition in this well, the distribution of observed fractures is apparently largely function of differential mechanical compaction and the strong slump/rotational slide signature. Stylolite-associated fractures (57% of total fractures) are the most abundant fracture type in this well. They occur as discrete though pervasive fracture swarms, up to 55 fractures/ft (10500-10502 ft). Stylolite-associated fractures in this well are unusual in that they are commonly associated with micro-stylolitic to high amplitude stylolites and are most abudant within the Ekofisk rather than the Tor Formation. Development is apparently strongly controlled by resedimented chalk masses. Healed fractures (26% of total fractures) show similar dominant fracture strike trends (71°/256; 74°/087) to the tectonic set although have water scatter in dip directions within the slumped intervals. Irregular fractures (8% of total fractures) do not have consistent orientations and this is attributed to their close association with heavily deformed, slumped intervals and with siliceous intervals. These fractures are short, discontinuous and dominantly cemented (68% fractures complete/partially filled) with fill type reflecting locally sourced, remobilised material (siliceous, clay/carbonaceous fines and calcite). The Top Heimdal Formation has therefore been picked on weak indications on the seismic combined with isopaching of the Heimdal sequence. Top Ekofisk Formation (fig. 6.) The purpose of the well was to test the hydrocarbon potential within the Maastrichtian Tor Formation and the Danian Ekofisk Formation in the Swrimne prospect. DATA PROCESSING Image data has been speed corrected for the effect of stick and pull. Then the images have been oriented, that is the left hand side of the image is aligned to magnetic north. The resistivity image has been dynamically filtered using meter window and sample step length. The quality of the image is good, there is just 5-10 % affected by the effect of stick and pull. The resolution of the acoustic image is much better than the one of the resistivity image. IMAGE INTERPRETATION Images have been interpreted using the software of Western Atlas, by means of the program named VISION. The main visible features have been picked. context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 30/3-9 is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest samples analysed are sands of the DuniIn Group, Cook Formation of Late Pliensbachian?-?Early Toarcian and Early Toarclan age, which were deposited in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment with the accumulation of Drake Formation claystones during Early Toarcian, Late Toarcian and Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times. A regional regressive event during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group, Broom?-Ness formations. Deposition of the Brent Group continued through Late Bajocian, Late Bajocian?-?Early Bathonian and Early-Middle Bathonian times with the deposition of the Ness and Ness?-Tarbert formations. During Early-Middle Bathonian times sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. stratigraphic break occurs at the top of the Early-Middle Bathonian interval. Heather Formation deposition continued during early Callovian through to Middle Oxfordian times in marine, inner shelf setting. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Late Oxfordian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in an inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. An unconformity exists within the Draupne Formation resulting from the absence of early Kimmeridglan to Early Volgian aged sediments. Accumulation of Draupne Formation sediments resumed during Middle-latest Middle Volgian times in marine, mid to outer shelf setting with dysaerobic to anaerobic bottom conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment throughout Early-Late Ryazanian times. Deposition continued, without apparent unconformity, with Cromer Knoll Group sediments of latest Late Ryazanian age. Deposition occurred in marine, inner to mid shelf environment and continued thorough Late Valanginian-Early Hauterivian times. Following period of erosion or non deposition during Late Hauterivian to Late Aptlan times, deposition of Cromer Knoll Group sediments resumed briefly during Early Albian times in marine, mid shelf setting. further unconformity at the top of Cromer Knoll Group sediments indicates period of erosion or non deposition during Middle and Late Albian times. Deposition resumed with transgression at the beginning of Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Early Cenomanian through to Late Maastrichtlan age. A period of erosion and/or non deposition during Early Palaeocene times possibly resulted in the absence of Rogaland Group, Vale Formation sediments. Deposition resumed with calcareous and non calcareous claystone of the Rogaland Group, Lista Formation which accumulated in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment during Early to Late Palaeocene times. 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 34/11-2S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The stratigraphic succession observed in 34/11-2S is complicated by repeated faulting of Brent Group and Viking Group, Heather Formation sediments. Details of these fault repeats are discussed in the biostratigraphy and lithostratigraphy chapters of this report. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine to coarse grained sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marine, inner shelf environment during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian times. Following marine transgression during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian to Late Pliensbachian times, deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen and Burton Formation occurred in marine, inner shelf conditions. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachian and Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of beginning of Aalenian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Broom Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Aalenian?- Early Bajocian times continued deposition of the Rannoch Formation was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian, Bajocian and Bajocian-?Bathonian and Early Bathonian times. The Early Bathonian, Middle? Bathonian and Late? Bathonian sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu stricto accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition of claystones continued through to early Callovian times in similar environmental setting. Deposition was interrupted, possibly because of regional regressive phase, resulting in the absence of middle and late Callovian aged sediments. Heather Formation deposition continued during Early Oxfordian times and was followed by period of erosion or non deposition. Following renewed subsidence, the Late Jurassic transgressive phase resumed during Kimmeridgian?-?Ryazanian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of calcareous claystones of Early? Albian age and are succeeded, following short period of erosion or non deposition, by Late Albian sediments. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Cenomanian age through to Late Maastrichtian age. A period of erosion and/or non deposition during Early Palaeocene times resulted in the absence of Montrose Group, Vale Formation sediments. -3- INTRODUCTION Norsk Hydro's well 7117/9-2 is the second well drilled on main structure called the Senja Ridge, situated in the north-western parts of the Troms-1 exploration area. The first well, 7117/9-1, was also operated by Norsk Hydro, with IKU as biostratigraphic consultant. The biostratigraphy of well 7117/9-2 is based on the analysis of cuttings, sidewalls and core samples. Fossil material obtained from the first set of sidewall cores does not seem to match the fossil material obtained from cuttings. This is particularly evident across the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary and in the Paleocene/Eocene, though difficult to demonstrate in the thick sequence of Albian deposits. Sidewall cores down to 1695 are therefore considered unreliable. We have documented this in the text and, as sidewall analysis was well underway before discovering the anomaly, we have plotted out the SWC results on the log sheets. Analyses carried out during drilling (hot shots) indicated an unusually thick sequence of Albian and Aptian deposits. Following consultation with the client it was decided that some reduction in the density of analyses should be made. Fairly complete palynological analysis were to be carried out, based primarily on sidewall cover, but with sample density somewhat less than the standard detailed palynology (1 sample/15 m). Micropaleontological analyses should also be reduced though the primary net should be supplemented if results warrented this. In the lower part of the well most samples analysed for micropaleontology were barren. Preservation of palynological material is also extremely poor (below ca 3400 m). In view of the interest expressed in this part of the section we have nevertheless attempted to locate workable samples. These are few and far between, though an assemblage recorded at 4798 gave reliable Barremian or younger age. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. There is no doubt that compaction seriously have modifi- cated the original framework of all samples studied. The main features observed were: - grain deformation - deformation of ductiles - pressure solution Crushing of brittle grains, especially micas, feldspars and lithic fragments is common in most of the studied samples. (Plate 51) Feldspars break easily, whereas micas are more commonly bent and squeezed between more rigid grains. More ductile grains such as intraclasts, shale fragments and organic matter, are plastic deformed and flow between harder fragments, resulting in almost complete loss of porosity and permeability. (Plate 52.) Pressure solution at grain contacts (Plate 24) seem to be one of the important factors in pore reduction in many samples. There is considerable variation in the extent of pressure solution, although the overpressured sandstones in 35/3-2 seem to be less affected. However, quartz overgrowth due to fresh water flushing has probably played an important role too, and the relative amount of quartz cement from pressure solution and fresh water flushing can not be determined.

Offshore transition mudstone and sandstone. This facies association is seen in the lower meters of the cored section and comprises inter bedded well burrowed mudstones (Lithofacies and very fine grained wave rippled to micro hummocky cross-stratified sandstones (Lithofacies C). The bed thickness is typically to 15 cm. Burrows of chondrites type are recognized. The alternating lithology probably represent alternation of fair weather mud layers and storm sands within an offshore transition zone, e.g. deposition close to the storm weather wave base. Palynofacies characteristics are consistent with this interpretation. Lower shoreface sandstone and minor mudstone. The cored section from 3976,5m to 3967,25m can be subdivided into four minor fining upward sub units. Each unit consists of massive cross stratified fine grained sandstone (Lithofacies and minor C) with an erosive base which passes upward to burrowed, very fine grained sandstone and inter bedded sandstone/mudstone similar to the bedding in the lower meter of the cored section. The massive cross strata, hummocky or swaly, are typical of high energy middle shoreface setting. The interbedded sandstone and mudstone beds suggest more quiet or protected shoreface environment. The four units can also be seen defined as four parasequences within lower order (4th or 6th order) sequences. The gradual increase of mudstone in the two upper units may also indicate that this part of the cored section represents retrograding parasequence sets. question: For OSEBERG FM sandstones, what are the documented lithofacies, depositional setting, and evidence for Aalenian timing?

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 30/2-3 is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. Deposition was interrupted during mid Callovian times, possibly because of regional regressive phase. Subsidence and sedimentation of the Heather Formation resumed during late Callovian?-Early Oxfordian times although further, major unconformity separates the Early Oxfordian Heather Formation sensu stricto from the overlying Draupne Formation. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. Sedimentation continued through to Middle Volgian times in similar environmental conditions, although major unconformity is present at the top of the Draupne Formation. The Early Cretaceous sequence is characterised by major condensation and unconformities. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of Early Hauterivian calcareous claystones assigned to the Valhall Formation which accumulated in marine, inner shelf setting. These sediments are overlain unconformably by Early Barremian calcareous claystones of the Tuxen Formation following regional transgressive phase. further unconformity separates the Tuxen Formation from the overlying Early Albian Sola Formation. The Soia Formation accumulated in marine, mid shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Following period of non deposition, transgressive phase during Late Albian times resulted in the deposition of calcareous claystones of the Rodby Formation in marine, outer shelf setting. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group, Formation 'A' were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment.
