question: How should the MWGT decrease from 1.82 to 1.80 sg after a 2872 m LOT with 1.96 sg EMW in well 6406/2-3 be interpreted?
answer_text: The 2872 m LOT showed formation integrity to 1.96 sg EMW, so lowering the mud from 1.82 sg to 1.80 sg was a conservative, safe reduction remaining below the tested fracture/LOT pressure.

context_snippets.text: 6406 - follow the trends established in the original well but the effects of the fluid migration as result of crossflow from 4596m to 3970m in the original well were unknown. Based on data from the kick the pore pressure gradient at 4596m was estimated to be sg and the possibility of fractured and/or charged fonnations could not be discounted. The mud weight was therefore raised to 1.82sg prior to kicking off but was reduced to 1.80sg following leak-off test at 2872m which gave result of I.96sg EMW. After initiating the kick off bit number was replaced with steerable motor assembly and PDC bit. The result of this was highly erratic penetration rate of between 20m/hr and 50m/hr with consequent poor quality d.-exponent data. Throughout the Kvitnos formation it was not possible to use the d- exponent as pressure evaluation tool and gas values were relied on to provide warning of any pressure increase. In the event there were no such indications with no connection gas and background levels remaining steady at between 0.2% and 0.4%. Based on estimates from the previous well track it was assumed that the pore pressure gradient remained constant at 1.40sg down to 3200m before beginning gradual rise through the lower Kvitnos and into the Lysing and Lange formations. The estimated pressure gradient in the Lysing formation was 1.48sg. Once into the Lysing the penetration rate became less erratic and d-exponent quality improved. Background gas in the Lysing remained at between 0.2% and 0.4%, dropping to 0.2% at the transition to the Lange formation at 3570m. The d-exponent indicated that the pressure gradient within the Lysing was either stable or increasing only slightly. Again there were no connection gas or other evidence to suggest otherwise. Due to the high overbalance the likelihood of connection gas was, in fact, remote unless formation charging had taken place. At this time the only useful pressure tool, apart from the d- exponent, was the background gas level. At 3591m new formation integrity test was carried out to 1.92sg EMW. The bit was then changed but the steerable motor assembly was rerun. Only minor trip gas of 0.47% (0.20%) was reported. This biogenic fabric is well seen as the mudrocks transform to green colour and clean medium grained sand-filled burrows are preserved, presumably piping down sand from the overlying unconformity surface of the Skalmen Formation. This uppermost green mudrock contains glauconite /chlorite and phosphatic shell fragments (Fig. 3A,D), whilst the mudrocks as whole appear to be of mixed clay composition (illite with subordinate smectite or chlorite-smectite and kaolinite; Fig. 3E). The more kaolinitic nature of the clay-fraction in the single Skalmen sample analysed by XRD (Plug 2; Fig. 3E) adds weight to the argument that the mudrock interval may be of different provenance. Interpretation: as with the Skalmen sandstones, the combination of glauconite/chlorite and burrowing (especially the Chondrites-type) suggests a marine setting. The association of reddening, intense bioturbation and sand-filled burrows piping down from the overlying unconformity all point to reduced sedimentation rates and the existence of submarine hiatal surface at the mudrock /sandstone interface. Collectively therefore sand- starved site below wave base is implied, arguably associated with depositional high. However, the thrust of this interpretation would be undermined if all the burrowing were associated with the hiatal surface; this would open up other possibilities for the mudrock origin (see End. 1). question: How does vertical resolution of 2DHR compare to 3D TO06R06M1 for resolving thin sands, ploughmarks, and amplitude anomalies at well PWL25/5-7?

2.3 COMPARISON OF 2D AND 3D DATA There is difference in resolution between the 2D and 3D data. The higher resolution offered by the 2D data is of significant importance in the interpretation of the Pleistocene and Upper Pliocene deposits, which comprise sediments deposited during greatly varying conditions. High-resolution 2D data also increase the possibility of detecting thin features, such as sand layers and ploughmarks. The 2DHR data set is of adequate to good quality. However, the majority of the energy is reflected in the upper part. From approximately 1000ms TWT the loss of energy starts to significantly affect data quality, and below 1300ms TWT only high amplitude events can be discerned. The 3D data set TO06R06M1 was provided by Total EP Norge AS. comparison between TO06R06M1 and the 2DHR data set is presented in Figure 2.2. It can be concluded that the high- resolution 2D seismic data set displays significantly better resolution and quality in the upper sequence compared to the 3D survey TO06R06M1. High-resolution 2D data is essential for the detection of amplitude anomalies and small-scale features in the shallow part. 2.1 VSP PROCESSING 2.1.1 Velocity Survey Computations The digital VSP data were reformatted and displayed. source signature deconvolution was performed on the vertical and horizontal geophone components using operators derived from the first 600 ms of the reference hydrophone The reference hydrophone and vertical geophone components were then timed on the first trough arrival, representing the primary direct arrival from the source. The hydrophone traces were examined and the first-maximum time was picked establishing consistent reference hydrophone picks. Each downhole geophone trace was subsequently shifted by the first- maximum time value of the corresponding reference hydrophone trace. time correction of ms to account for the time from hydrophone to source, at water velocity (1500 m/sec), so that all downhole geophone traces were referenced back to the source. The downhole geophone traces for each depth level were then stacked using mean summation technique. Noisy traces were rejected prior to stacking. The stacked reference hydrophone component and stacked geophone data for all levels of each component are shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, & 7. The measured slant times were then geometrically converted to vertical times below the source and then corrected to the datum of MSL using static correction of ms, at water velocity 1500 m/sec. These time-depth pairs were then used as the input data for the final velocity survey computations to give the average, RMS and interval velocities listed in Section and displayed as Enclosure 1. Good downgoing shear energy can be seen in the horizontal components as indicated by Figures & 5. This shear arrival could be timed and used to calibrate shear log data and provide detailed VP:VS ratio. 2.1.2 Acoustic Log Calibration The acoustic log was supplied in LAS format and has been input to the calibration procedure. The depth range is – MD below DF. For the calibration, the acoustic log was integrated to produce a time-log, which is depth-indexed. The discrepancy between the corrected checkshot time of the shallowest checkshot level (within the logged interval) and the corresponding log-derived time was then computed. The time-log was next shifted by adding this value to all the time-log values, thus tying the log to the shallowest checkshot. A drift curve was then generated, showing the difference between the corrected checkshot times and the corresponding times from the shifted time-log. Calibration points fixing the drift at certain depths (including the top and bottom of the logged interval) were then chosen. Such that they divide the drift curve into intervals of approximately linear drift, and also so that they occur at velocity contrasts. The calibration points are indicated with triangular marks on the drift curve displayed on Enclosure 1. The shifts applied to the log are considered reasonable with maximum shift of 14us/m (4.3us/ft). For each interval between consecutive calibration points, the ratio between the difference in the fixed drift of these calibration points and the interval thickness was computed, and this constant was added to all acoustic log values of the interval, thus shifting the acoustic log in this interval by this amount. The whole acoustic log was calibrated by repeating this procedure for all calibration point intervals. After calibration, the calibrated time-log was computed by integrating the calibrated acoustic log and tying it to the shallowest checkshot. The residual drift curve, shown on Enclosure 1, was generated using the corrected checkshot times and the calibrated time-log. The tables in Section contain details of the acoustic log calibration, including the residual drift before and after calibration and the tabulated time-depth values listed in linear depth and linear time. The depth- indexed calibrated acoustic log and associated logs are displayed as Enclosure 2.

question: How do toluene Dean–Stark extraction and methanol Soxhlet cleaning differ in their effects on measured fluid saturation in saturation analysis?
answer_text: Dean–Stark with toluene yields direct water-volume readings but leaves dissolved salts in the core (so water volumes must be corrected for salt), while methanol Soxhlet cleaning removes salt deposits (and residual hydrocarbons) allowing salt-correction of measured water.

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Well 2/8A-10 Net fracturing pressures were heavily influenced by friction (on the order of 200 psig), which can be attributed to an axial fracture in communication with the Tor Formation through small passage. However, the net fracturing pressures, which should be interpretable since the pump rate was kept constant, are indicative of fracture growing to the top of the Tor Formation and into the overlying claystone. The fracture was probably capable of penetrating the claystone since the Tor was not significantly depleted. The apparent communication with the Tor Formation was confirmed by the fluid loss rate of ft/(min)i compared to ft/(min)1 obtained in the subsequent Tor Formation frac job, by relatively high post-frac production, and by pressure transient analysis of the post-frac flow test suggesting Tor Formation properties. Tor Formation The net fracturing pressures, on the order of 300 psig, indicate continuous, radially-propagating fracture which, according to the theoretical fracture radius of about 150 ft, penetrated the claystone above the Tor Formation. context_snippets.text: GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. A value of 1.38sg was obtained for the leak-off after drilling out the 13 3/8” casing and drilling 12 1/4” hole commenced. Drilling was halted at 2730 mBRT when pore pressure was seen to have reached 1.25sg and the bit was pulled into the casing shoe. In an attempt to carry on drilling an open-hole leak-off was performed that confirmed the 1.38sg value obtained earlier. Having insufficient kick tolerance to drill ahead, the decision was made to run 5/8” liner. triple-combo wireline log was run to acquire data over the drilled section. Liner was set and 1.47sg leak-off was obtained. Drilling commenced in 1/2” hole. No reservoir horizons were identified and the well was TD’d at 02:45 hrs on the 20th February at depth of 3650 mBRT. Three wireline logging runs were performed. The 6404/11-1 well was plugged and abandoned as dry hole at 22:00 hrs on the 10th March 2002 and the rig released to Norsk Hydro. RESULTS The shallowest primary target (Early Eocene T50 sandstones) was absent at the well location. Upper Cretaceous (K90 sandstones) were absent and K80 (Nise Formation) sandstones were poorly developed. The well was not extended to penetrate the deeper, K72 (Lysing Formation) secondary target.

context_snippets.text: 1.1 INTRODUCTION Well 2/8 F-14 was planned to supplement and eventually replace production from well 2/8A-1A. The plan was to drill vertically through the reservoir section with entry 200m NNW of the original well, with planned TD in the Hod Formation. Cores and wireline logs were planned in the reservoir section. As reference for future subsidence and compaction studies, radioactive markers were to be placed in the Tor Formation by wireline. The well plan was to build to 27° at the 13-3/8 shoe and then vertically to TD. The Tor Formation was planned to be drilled with 9-5/8 drilling liner. Three cores were originally planned for the Tor formation. Wireline logs were also planned in the reservoir section. This well was drilled with Versaport synthetic oil based mud system from 354m. The cuttings were slurrified in the MSD unit and injected into the Valhall disposal well. SERVICE PROVIDED Baker Hughes INTEQ provided Drillbyte service using software version 2.3.0RO from an INTEQ combined SLS and MWD logging unit on well 2/8 F-14, from 354m to total depth of 2635m. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mudlogging, automatic real-time data acquisition, monitoring, recording and pore pressure analyses were carried out. Continuous evaluation of pore pressure and drilling progress provided an aid in optimising drilling performance and ensured that drilling operations continued with maximum safety to personnel, the well and equipment. The operator was continually advised as to the status of these analyses and data, and the results were stored on magnetic media for post well evaluation. The printouts and plots are contained in the appendices and attachments of this report.

The objective of this report is to provide detailed description of the wireline operation and data acquisition for the Aker BP 2/8-F-18A well in the Valhall field. The service provider for the wireline operations was Schlumberger and the QA/QC witnessing was carried out by Dave Hardy and Lindsay Herbert of One&Zero. This report focuses on the wireline data acquisition in relation to the section. The 2/8-F-18 is slanted pilot hole dedicated for data acquisition to inform later decisions of the Lower Hod development. The project currently carries producers and injector; however, the test injector (2/8-F-18 B) along with core data and wireline logs will be used to assess the feasibility of further infill injector placement. The primary target is the Hod package, although hydrocarbons are present throughout Hod to Hod 5/6. Wireline logs will be acquired throughout the entire open hole interval, which also includes Tor formation above. This is potentially water flooded by sea water, and will thus provide information regarding residual oil saturation (Sor) behind the flood-front. Geological background and expected formation properties 2/8-F-18 will only have chalk exposed, consisting of Tor, Magne and Hod formation. The expected porosity range between 20-45 p.u with associated permeability ranging between 0.01-6 mD. The Hod layer is assumed to be tight zone acting as baffle between Tor/Magne and Lower Hod, which consists of Hod 3, Hod and Hod 5/6. Water saturation (Sw) is expected to range between 30-100 %. Water salinity is likely 55 ppk; however, Tor formation may have lower salinity due to sea water injection

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

Halliburton Geo Consultants Limited IV. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

Cretaceous and Tertiary times provided period of relative tectonic quiescence. The basin-fill was primarily affected by regional basin downwarp, resulting in gently westward thickening wedge of Cretaceous and Tertiary strata. Reactivation along the pre-Cretaceous fault systems, resulting from an Alpine N-S compressional field during early Tertiary times, and continuing salt movements, generated some inversion features and localised thickening of the overlying stratigraphic sequence. Halokinetic movements have occurred from Triassic times onwards, with particularly important episode coinciding with, and possibly triggered by, the Late Kimmerian tectonic event. 2.2 Regional Stratigraphy and Basinal Development (Fig. 4) The oldest sedimentary strata penetrated in the area are coarse clastic sediments of the Rotliegendes Formation (Lower Permian in age). Volcanic intercalations are found in the basinal area (well 3/7-2). Marine incursions during late Permian times led to the deposition of thick evaporites (salt together with anhydrite and carbonates) in the subsiding SOgne Basin. After the sea receded thick Triassic sequence was deposited over the Zechstein evaporites and carbonates. This phase of sedimentation continued into Late Triassic/Early Jurassic times: possible Lower Jurassic strata have been reported only from the well 3/5-2. At the end of Early Jurassic times rifting phase took place. Block faulting, accompanied by drop in sea level and subsequent erosion of the emerged blocks, led to the deposition of fluvio-deltaic sediments of Aalenian to Bathonian age (the Bryne Formation, within the Vestland Group). These comprise alternating shales and sandstones with occasional laterally persistent coals. The potential sediment source areas were the Mandel High and the Southern Vestland Arch. A second phase of uplift and non-deposition occurred at the end of the Middle Jurassic, expressed in the Callovian Unconformity. This

Sedimentation during Palaeocene and Eocene times is characterised by series of marine transgressions and regressions. Claystones and limestones constitute the greater part of the Paleogene sequence, with locally well developed sandstones at the base. Volcanic tuffs and tuffaceous shales of the Balder Formation indicate widespread volcanic event at the Palaeocene - Eocene boundary. Subsidence in the North Sea continued at an uniform rate in Neogene times, resulting in the deposition of fine grained marine clastics. thin Quaternary cover completes the stratigraphic column. 2.3 Previous Exploration Results (Fig. 1) Within PL 147, the wells 3/7-1, -2 and -3 were all dry. question: How does Draupne source-rock potential (TOC, kerogen type, depositional environment) compare with Hugin sandstone reservoir quality and depositional characteristics?
answer_text: Draupne: TOC ~3.90±1.90 wt%, kerogen type II, deposited in a reducing open‑marine, periodically anoxic environment. Hugin: Middle Jurassic sandstones (very fine to very coarse) deposited in shoreface/tidal and ebb‑tidal delta settings with variable reservoir quality from good (medium–coarse homogeneous units) to poor–fair (very fine, bioturbated and calcite/dolomite‑cemented intervals).

context_snippets.text: 1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

4. LITHOLOGY 15/9-12 by S. Evensen The reservoir interval, the Hugin Formation of Middle Jurassic age, is devided into three units. The lowermost unit, consist in general of very fine to fine occasionally medium grained sandstones deposited in shoreface/tidal dominated enviroment. These sandstones are interbedded with few siltstone/mudstone layers, and one distinct coal layer at 3568-60 m. The lower part of the unit consist of more calcite/dolomite cemented sandstones than the upper part. The general good reservoir quality of this unit are also interrupted by strong bioturbation in some interval of the sandstones. This middle unit consist of interbedded sandstones and shales deposited in an ebb tidal delta/lower shoreface environment. The sandstones at the base of the unit are medium to coarse grained homogenous and structureless and should display good reservoir potential. To the top the sandstones are more fine-grained, laminated and strongly bioturbated. Chert nodules are observed throughout this interval. The uppermost unit consist in this well entirely of sandstones deposited in shoreface environment. The reservoir quality of the very fine to fine low-angle laminated sandstones seems to be poor (to fair) due to highly bioturbated intervals and thin calcite/dolomite layers throughout the whole unit.

context_snippets.text: VERTICAL SEISMIC PROFILE REPORT APPENDIX Description of V.S.P. Displays Vertical Well: Source at Well Head Display VA (Stacked Geophone Data at one-way time) This display indicates the quality of the data used in the subsequent VSP processing. The trace displayed for each geophone position is the result of editing, as appropriate, and summing common depth traces; the common depth traces having undergone trace alignment procedure (based on cross correlation) in order to obtain accurate alignment prior to summation. Source signature deconvolution will have been applied to marine data, unless otherwise stated, using the gun hydrophone signal as source signature. Wavelet stabilisation may optionally have been applied to the data to remove variations in source character due to changing source conditions, (particularly onshore) and/or variation in geophone coupling. A broad band filter will have been applied to this data in order to remove noise without compromising the usable bandwidth of the data. The polarity of this display is such that the first downgoing arrival is plotted as black peak. (SEC normal polarity) Display VA(FK) (F-K Display of Stacked Geophone Data at One-Way Time) This display shows the stacked geophone data (after source signature deconvolution, if appropriate) at one-way time transformed into F-K space. This data is displayed as wave number (K) against frequency, with variation in colour indicating amplitude in dB below the maximum amplitude. A velocity alignment in T-X space transforms to an alignment in F-K space, rotated through 90°; the various wavefields (i.e. velocity alignments) commonly observed in T-X space transform into F-K space as illustrated in Fig.1 The strongest wavefield will normally be the Downgoing wavefield and this transforms into an alignment from zero wave number, zero frequency sloping in the positive wave number direction. Significant velocity changes in wavefield will result in multiple alignments in F-K space; although in practice it may not be possible to differentiate between the different F-K alignments and the resulting event may be smeared. /Cont'd....

Displays VC and VD (Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time; before and after enhancement) These displays show the Primary and Multiple activity observed at the borehole location from the shallowest VSP geophone position to some way below the deepest VSP geophone position (and therefore, normally, some way below Total Depth of the borehole). The data shown on Display VD is that of Display VC after application of spatial filter; this spatial filter will be the result of various trials and will have been chosen to give the best enhancement of the upgoing events (horizontal and/or dipping) observed in the data. In marine data, if source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the input wavelet will be zero-phase and the wavelet contained in the data will be zero phase modified by earth absorption and transmission loss effects (i.e. mixed phase). In the case of onshore data, if neither wavelet stablisation nor source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the source signature remains in the data. Wavelet stabilisation can be carried out by shaping to any given wavelet; we would recommend, however, that all geophone data is transformed to the waveform of shallow geophone level. In this case then the source signature effectively remains in the data but is made consistent from level to level. Events that reach the time-depth curve are primary and their lithologic significance can be established unequivocally by reference to the calibrated velocity log. This comparison can be made using Display VG1 which contains the data from Display VF and the calibrated velocity log at the scale(s) of the seismic section. Multiples having their last bounce from primary within the range of the VSP may be identified by observing their termination in the data at the same depth point at which the primary cuts the time-depth curve. From this display, any dip across the well location can be recognised by move- out of the primary event to shorter time, as the geophone moves up the well and away from the lithology creating the reflection. No azimuth of dip can be computed from this display but true-dip can be computed from measurement of the LT against vertical depth increment. Unconformity may be recognised by an abrupt change of moveout of adjacent primary events. Topographical features up-dip away from the well may be recognised by an increase in the LT or in the termination of an event away from the time-depth curve. Dip increasing 'up-dip' away from the well can be observed in the data; however, if dip is decreasing 'up-dip' (i.e. crest of an anticline) then the event in question will disappear from the data. This data will normally have been filtered using the 'optimum' filter designed after F-K analysis to determine the usable bandwidth of the upgoing wavefield. /Cont'd...

6.3 Top and Fault Seal Top seal at the prospect is provided by the Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous shales overlying the Bryne Formation. In two nearby wells, 10/8-1 and 9/12-1, this shale interval is 331 in and 487 thick respectively. Within these wells the shale is generally silty with occasional interbedded claystone and limestone. Northwestward, toward to the basin center, the silt content of the interval decreases. At the TOTT prospect well location this interval is estimated to be 556 thick and to provide adequate top seal for the prospect. Esso's technique for fault seal analysis is based on the study of the vertical displacement of the stratigraphic sections along fault plane, the sealing characteristics of the resultant fault gouge and the changes in these factors laterally along fault. Displaced section analysis models have been constructed based on two wells, 9/2-1 and 10/8-1, providing range from sand-prone to shale-prone nature for the Jurassic section, respectively. These models suggest, in general, that for fault throws between 50 and 150 meters there will be cross leak only from the low-side to the high-side of fault. For fault throws less than 50 there will be cross leak whereas for throws greater than 150 the fault will be sealing. Fault plane profiles along the critical faults to the north of the prospect indicate that migration of hydrocarbons into the prospect from this direction is feasible (section 6.4). Fault plane profiles along the crestal faults on the prospect indicate that cross leak is probable, resulting in reservoir communication across the structure. Although these crestal faults cut through the top seal, they are not interpreted to have caused dip leakage. 6.4 Source The predicted source for hydrocarbons in the TOTT prospect is the Kimmeridgian Tau Formation. The formation was deposited on shallow-marine shelf. Restricted circulation in the Egersund Basin led to the deposition of organic-rich shales in the deep portions of the basin. In the vicinity of Block 9/5 the formation is 37 to 105 thick with 27 to 55 thick zone of high total organic carbon (TOC), the hot shale, in the upper part of the formation. The formation laps out on the basin margins and is absent in wells near Block 10/7, such as 10/8-1 and 9/12-1.

The last window for output trace will extend to the end of the data on the deepest input trace; for output trace the last window will extend to the end of data on the next to deepest input trace and so on. question: How should the GR-picked resistivity trend for well 7121/1-1 be adjusted for overpressure, RFT/DST, and drilling indicators?
answer_text: Shift the GR-picked resistivity trend downward (lower resistivity/ohm·m) where overpressure is indicated; calibrate/replace the normal trend using RFT/DST-measured points; and use drilling indicators (d‑exponent/ROP, cavings, trip gas, torque/overpull, hole fill, pump pressure) as early warnings or confirmation to apply the downward adjustment.

context_snippets.text: • Using the resistivity-log and picking shale points (from the gamma ray log) plot resistivity (ohm7m) on .a log scale. and depth on natural scale to set up a tread line. However, overpressured shales are more conductive to electricity (lower resistivity) because they contain larger volumes of salt water than would normal shale at the same depth. Overpressures are not the only variable to the normal trends. Shifts from the normal trend can also be caused by salinity, mineralogy, temperature and mud properties. By using the formation density log (FOG) normal trend for bulk densities can be established (both density and depth on natural scale). Any movement into overpressure will show as reduction in bulk density because of the increasing amount of pore fluids. The tool sends out gamma rays and sensor records the amount of back scattering. This depends on the bulk density of the formation. RFT and DST results can be used to calculate normal trends for those plots. In addition, any information pertinent to pressure detection such as hole condition during trips, cavings, trip gas and connection gas were also noted on the pressure log. This data was presented along with the estimated formation pressure gradient and leak off test results. Drilling Exponent If hole was drilled through good thickness of uniform 'normally' pressured shales, holding parameters of bit size, weight on bit (WOB), rotary speed (RPM) and mud weight constant, gradual reduction in the rate of penetration would be expected, due to the increasingly compacted nature of the sediments encountered and to the increasing differential bottom hole pressure (BHP). If subsequently an overpress- ured zone was encountered, reversal of the 'normal' rate of penetration trend would be seen. This is explained in terms of variation in differential BHP, i.e. if formation pore pressure is greater than bottom hole hydrostatic pressure, then shales will tend to explode into the hole - thus making the overpressured formation comparatively more drillable. In practice, it is not feasible to hold the independent variables of WOB, RPM, bit size and mud weight constant through more than very short section of the hole. Jordan and Shirley (19bb) produced an equation aimed at normalising rate of penetration, with respect to the variables of RPM, WOB, and bit size. The product was known as the 'd' exponent. 'd' = LOG Penetration Rate in Ft/Hr b0 (rev/min) 12 Weight On Bit (lbs) Bit Diameter (ins) 10 A corrected 'd' exponent value related to the mud weight and 'normal' pore pressure, is used to allow for reasonably accurate pore pressure prediction 'dc' normal gradient (ppg) 'd' actual mud weight (ppg) Disadvantages are that not all parameters affecting penetration rate are included in the equation, but these are outweighed by the advantages. Dc exponents are particularly useful in dealing with long transition zones and also bit life can be closely estimated by the use of drilling trends.

Pit Monitor Program A third online program was the Pit Monitor Program which gave graphical display of the state of chosen mud pit on one of the channels of the VT220 video screen. Usually the active pit was monitored with this program but occasionally the total of all the pits or the trip tank was displayed, -for instance when several pits were being used during cement job or when pipe was being tripped in or out of the hole. The data was displayed as horizontal relative histogram with absolute values in two columns on the right hand side of the screen. Swab/Surge Pressure Program This program calculated the hydrostatic fluctuations produced by motion of the drill string during trips or casing runs. Two options were available , either a table of effective mud density for variety of pipe speeds or the effective mud density and pressure increment at point of particular interest. The mud system was basically made up using fresh water, 40 ppb KCL, 1/2 ppb KOH and Soda Ash, ppb DEXTRID, 1/2 ppb PAC-R and 1/2 ppb XCD Polymer. Small additions of PAC-L and Stockopol EM 35 was necessary to control fluid loss and clay encapsulation. While drilling ahead, the mud weight was increased from initial to sg at 1951 meters. During this operation some rheology problems occured because we were not able to maintain necessary dilution, and the solids control equipment unfortuneately removed too much barite resulting in problems maintaining the mud weight at sg. These rheology problems disappeared when lost circulation occured at 2058 meters, resulting in cutting back mud weight to sg. Dilution with fresh premix was used during this operation and the theology, 10 min gels and MBT decreased to acceptable values. Two LCM pills were pumped on bottom with some success followed by total losses when back on bottom. A total of days were spent on combating the lost circulation problems. Several LCM pills with mica F/C, Wall Nut F/C and Diaseal-M were used with some success. Also cement was pumped and squeezed down hole to seal off the loss zone. Mud weight was again reduced to sg at 2082 meters and sg at 2108 meters. At 2108 meters full returns were regained and no further mud losses were recorded. total of 2227 barrels mud and LCM pills were lost and squeezed down hole. The LCM pills and cement did not affect the mud, exept for an increase in pH and small periodical losses of mud on shaker when circulating out the LCM material. While drilling ahead to 2238 meters tight hole was experienced on trips with maximum overpull 50 000 lbs. At 2252 it was decided to run Schlumberger RFT-tool to determine the formation pressure. The RFT results showed normal pressure equal to sg MW from the 13 3/8 casing shoe and down to 2252. The mud weight was reduced to sg in sg stages. total of 2050 barrels fresh mud was made up for this operation, and 2440 barrels old mud dumped because of lack of pit space.

question: For well 6507/3-7, how do shallow gas and boulder hazards compare in depth ranges, risk levels, and affected stratigraphic units?
answer_text: Shallow gas: medium risk within the Kai Formation (around the Kai top at ~1341 m MSL). Boulder hazard: cobbles/boulders reported in Undifferentiated Naust T/Naust A at ~421–522 m MSL (reported intervals 421–423, 430–431, 447, 461–463, 504–522 MSL).

context_snippets.text: 1 INTRODUCTION This report describes the sea-floor conditions and shallow geology within an approximately km area covering the Planned Well Location Idun (Figure 1.1). Potential installation and drilling hazards have been evaluated and special attention has been given to: • Seabed conditions, including water depth, sea-floor slope, seabed sediments and potential obstructions or hazards • Near-seabed sediments and likely anchoring conditions • Top hole sediments and well bore stability • Shallow water flow potential • Shallow gas • Boulders The report covers the interval from seabed down to the top of the Kai Formation at depth of 1341 meters Mean Sea Level (MSL). The report is divided into nine sections. The introduction, Section 1, is followed by summary of the main results and conclusions in Section 2. short description of the well and seismic data applied in the study is given in Section 3. In Section the criteria for horizon picking and anomaly definitions with its associated resolutions are presented. In Section description of the conditions for rig emplacement is given, including bathymetry, seabed and near-seabed sediments, potential obstructions and anchoring. Section deals with the shallow geology of the survey area, including brief geological history of the region from Miocene to present, details of the seismic interpretation and depth conversion, and geological prognosis for the well. Potential drilling hazards such as shallow gas and shallow-water flow is addressed in Section 7. Both sections, and 7, include examples from the seismic data to illustrate pertinent features. Section contains maps summarizing time structures and amplitude anomalies for the interpreted intervals. Section 8, recommendations, gives details of two possible relief well locations. Section contains full list of references. All positional data is referenced to ED50, Zone 32, Central Meridian 9° East. All depths are relative to Mean Sea Level (MSL), unless stated otherwise.

During the drilling of Well 6507/3-3 boulders were reported within Unit from 30 to 32 below seabed (421 to 423 MSL) and also at 56 below seabed (447 MSL). Completion report for Well 6507/3-3 reported slow interval during drilling within Unit 2, from 113 to 131 below seabed (504 m to 522 MSL), caused by boulders. During the drilling of Well 6507/3-7 boulders were reported within Unit from 53 to 54 below seabed (430 to 431 MSL), with possible boulders also reported between 84 and 86 below seabed (461 to 463 MSL). V Executive Summary for well: 6507/3-7 Petroleum Indications, Type and Quality: There are three main intervals displaying hydrocarbon anomalies in this well. The sections above 1530 and at 2895-3195 consist of mostly dry gas responses, with the exception of single sample from 3201 displaying an oil-like spectrum. thin section from 2943 contains several to common, white-fluorescent, and rare, yellow-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. Inclusion abundance is marginally high enough to suggest the presence of an oil column or paleo-column at this depth. No visible petroleum inclusions are documented at 1330 or 3201 m. The section below 3546 reveals dry gas to oil-like spectra. The most significant responses are gas-condensate to oil indications noted intermittently at 3546-3600 m. Thin sections from 3549 m, 3632 m, 3717 and 3840 contain rare to several, white-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz grains. Thin sections from 3549 and 3840 also contain rare to several, blue-fluorescent, upper-moderate gravity petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. The remainder of the analyzed interval contains sub-anomalous hydrocarbon concentra- tions. No petroleum inclusions are recorded in thin sections from 1910 m, 2420 or 3339 m. Shales contain moderate amounts of gas-prone kerogen and rare to several occurrences of immature to mature oil-prone kerogen in most samples (apparently oil-mature below about 3000 m). Highest visual kerogen abundance is noted at 3339 m. Proximal Pay Indications: Anomalous concentrations of acetic acid and, in general, more prominent benzene anomalies are identified at 3546-3588 and 3651-3654 m. Samples containing acetic acid anomalies usually suggest the nearby presence of reservoired liquid petroleum (oil or condensate), while more prominent benzene anomalies can indicate nearby gas. This well is reportedly gas discovery, thus it is probable that these features are sensing penetrated charge. Anomalies within reservoirs can indicate elevated Sw (for instance in relatively tight or impermeable reservoirs). Potential Seals: Possible seals are identified at 2898 m, 3340 m, 3546 and 3690 m. Evidence for Bacterial or Thermal Alteration: Sulfur species of probable bacterial origin are noted at 1230-1250 m, 2010 and 2340 m. These compounds generally indicate migration or microseepage of light, thermogenic hydrocarbons from depth followed by bacterial sulfate reduction at temperatures below 65°C. FIS microseeps are considered encouraging for deeper liquid petroleum exploration in the vicinity, and are consistent with deeper charge in the wellbore. Other: Nothing of note.

3 Discussion 3.1 Hydrocarbon quantity The hydrocarbon detection limit or threshold for the HCSTM is set to 800 counts which is comparable to concentration of ≈ 100 ppm HC. At the opposite end of the scale, wells with an Imax higher than 10,000 counts have been known to produce commercially elsewhere. Hydrocarbon contents are rather regularly distributed as shown in Figure 3, fluctuating between Imax 2000 – 6000 counts, only rarely up to Imax 6000-12000 counts. 3.2 Hydrocarbon quality Comparison with API gravity using range of reference petroleums gives correlation with HCSTM Q580 of R2 = (90 different oils) and (112 different oils) for CUSC. (HCSTMQ580 = Figure 1, lower insert, unpublished data and CUSC Q580 = Figure 2.) Hydrocarbon HCSTM measurements of the cored section show variation in Q580 within the range – corresponding to light oil to heavy oil compositions. The restricted presence of Q580 scattering is indicative of overall good vertical fluid communication. However, there are three depths that stand out in this respect: 3557.3 Discrete shift from light to medium oil compositions 3565.3 Local shift medium-heavy-medium oil compositions 3580.3 Overall shift from medium to heavy oil compositions. The shift close to is readily observable, whereas the other shifts are subtle accompanied by an overall decrease in grain size with depth. However, even below 3600 m, in those few segments were poro-perm performance suddenly shifts from poor to good medium oils can be detected in an otherwise heavy oil environment (Figure 6). Overall there seems to be good vertical fluid communication, from the top of the cored section down to approximately 3608 m, the shifts from light through medium to heavy oil composition possibly due to gravitative segregation. In this respect the HCSTM spectral information (Figure 5) from light/medium oil at 3549 (Q580 0.27) to light/medium oil some 20 deeper at 3568 (Q580 0.24) is pointing towards common source for this petroleum. The light to medium oil compositions occurring above 3580 correspond to API values close to 35-40. Q580 values of to reflect predominantly PAH of 2-3 ring isomers (Lakowitz, 1991; Parr & Hanson-Parr, 1988, Khorasani 1987; Dumke & Teschner 1988; Barker & Kopp 1991; Kihle 1995; Zhu & Mullins 1992; Stasiuk & Snowdon, 1997). question: How do kaolinite aggregates compare to illite/illite-smectite grain coats in occluding intergranular macroporosity?
answer_text: Kaolinite occurs as irregular aggregates that more commonly occlude intergranular macroporosity, while illite/illite‑smectite more often form thinner, rarer grain coats that less extensively occlude porosity.

question: What was the initial mud density (sg) between 278–350 m in well 34/10-32, and were any mud-weight adjustments noted?
answer_text: Initial mud density was 1.15 sg; a later adjustment increased mud weight from 1.185 sg to 1.20 sg.

context_snippets.text: 36 HOLE SECTION 167-278m As expected, the pore pressure remained normally pressured throughout the 36 hole section. The section was drilled using seawater with high viscosity pills being pumped at every connection. 26 HOLE SECTION 278-350m A shallow gas-charged sand was expected in this hole section. Consequently shallow gas BOP stack was run and 12 1/4 pilot hole was drilled with an MWD tool in the BHA. The MWD indicated possible gas zone at 331m. Despite the possible shallow gas-charged zone, no abnormal pore pressure was noted in the 26 hole section. The section was drilled using mud density -of 1.15sg. The majority .of this section was normally pressured. While drilling, connection gas was noted between 550m and 6.00m, and the mud weight was increased from 1.185g to 1.20sg to counteract this problem. However, none of the other pressure indicators showed any sign of pore pressure increase in this interval, so the gas was probably being swabbed in from the gas sand below the 20 casing shoe. There is large shift in the corrected D-Exponent curve in the interval 720-830m. This seems to be entirely due to increasing WOB to maintain penetration rate as the bit dulls. There is corresponding shift in the IDEL Drill Strength curve in this same interval. The interval 830-1400m was drilled using very low WOB (2-5 kkg). This makes computer-generated pore pres- sure indicators such as IDEL and D-Exponent extremely unreliable. However, apart from 2% trip gas peak at 831m, there are no indications of abnormal pressure in this interval. The general increase in background gas levels can be accounted for by the increasing sand and silt content of the formation being drilled. After 1750m there are signs of increasing pore pressure; We begin to see connection gas, and the corrected D-exponent and IDEL Drill Strength curves show a change in slope. At 1960m there is rapid increase in gas levels, indicating that the mud column is no longer overbalancing the formation fluid pressure. By the end of the 17 1/2 section at 1981m, the IDEL pore pressure was 1.18sg(E).

INTRODUCTION The present report gives the results of PVT analysis and compositional analysis of two bottom hole samples from well 34/10-32R, Dst 2.1. The quality of the samples was checked by determining the bubble point at reservoir temperature, which was found to be and 385.8 bar at 127 respectively. Based on the information available to LAB there is no compelling reason to choose one bottom hole sample over the other. One possible explanation for the difference in observed bubble point could be that one of the samples had lost some gas during transfer from the tool to the bottle. The sample with the highest bubble point, called BHS #1, was therefore choosen for PVT study. The composition of both samples was determined by single flash to atmospheric conditions followed by gaschromatographic analysis of the stabilized oil and gas. Mathematical recombination of the oil and gas compositions according to the measured gas oil ratio then gave the final reservoir fluid composition. Separate portions of the sample were transferred to PVT cell and rolling ball viscosimeter for differential liberation studies and viscosity measurements respectively. An extended reservoir fluid composition to C20 plus is calculated for BHS #1 from single flash data and additional C10 - C20 plus data reported in the destillation report.

Both samples were well consolidated and the tests were accomplished for the requested plugs. PREPARATION : The plugs were cleaned by extraction using first methanol, then toluene and finally with methanol. Prior to the analyses, the plugs were dried at 600C and 40% relative humidity under controlled conditions. MEASUREMENTS: POROSITY AND GRAIN DENSITY Grain volume was measured by Boyles law porosimeter using helium. Bulk volume was obtained by mercury displacement. Knowing also the weight of the sample, porosity and grain density were calculated on both samples. AIR PERMEABILITY Both samples were installed in Hassler holder for air permeability measurements. The sleeve pressure used was 15 bar. Air permeability was measured using N2 gas at four different pressures. These values were the basis for calculating the Klinkenberg corrected permeability. Both tabular and graphic compilations of data have been enclosed in this report. WATER SATURATION Both plugs were saturated as close as possible to 100 % by using first vacuum and then injecting simulated formation water into desicator which contained the samples. They were afterwards exposed to pressure of 50 bar for 24 hours of duration to ensure good saturation. STATOIL 34/10-32

PROGRAM FOR CONDITIONING MUD, BULLHEADING, PERORATING AND REFRACTURING WELL 2/8A-17 OBJECTIVE: To condition the mud, bullhead the mud, add perforation interval in the Upper Hod and perform new stimulation job to obtain production from the Tor Formation. BACKGROUND: Having been unsuccessful in cleaning the wellbore by bullheading, the well has been surged to attempt to unplug the perforation without success. Further, an attempt to RIH to perforate failed due to the diesel/mud interface. The wellbore contains diesel from the packer to surface and mud from the perforation to the packer. The SCSSV is open and connected to handpump. Drilling is in charge of the operation. The steps referred to in the below procedure are in the General Completion Program. A preliminary wellbore schematic is attached. (Attachment I). PROCEDURE: 1. Leave the well with psi at surface for six hours to test the plugged perforations as barrier. 2. Rig up the Gray BPV lubricator assembly and test to 5000 psi and test the BPV by measuring bleed back volume. 3. Nipple down Xmas-tree and install dart in the BPV. 4. Nipple up drilling riser and BOP with 3/8 pipe ram. Test the riser BOP against the dart as specified in the General Drilling Program. Pull dart and BPV.

INTRODUCTION After the Well 2/8A-17 ceased flowing on 20 May 1985, the Upper Hod perforations were isolated by dumping marbles, glass-beads and sand. Further the well was perforated and stimulated in the Tor Formation on 26 May 1985. Below is report of the preparation for and execution of the Tor fracture stimulation treatment. WELL HISTORY PRIOR TO FRAC Well 2/8A-17 was stimulated third time in the Upper Hod lbs of 20/40 mesh sand was pumped during the treatment. However, the stimulation did not provide adequate communication with the Tor Formation. In an attempt to flow the well, it produced solids and ceased flowing on 20 May 1985. In an attempt to kill the well 140 bbls of mud was bullheaded into it. As this kill-mud was bullheaded with no problems it was immediately followed by 400 bbls of diesel leaving only diesel in the tubing thus avoided clean-up operation. The denser Tor interval 8m MD RKB was perforated three times with 90° phasing, spf, 7/8 gun. The well schematic is attached as Attachment 1. FRAC DESIGN A very conservative pump schedule was designed. Similar to the last refrac job in the Upper Hod Formation, pad of 55,000 gallons was chosen. Further, the first seven sand stages were extended to ensure some proppant to enter the formation prior to possible premature screen-out. The proppant chosen was 20/40 mesh sand. Attachment details the designed stimulation including volumes and proppant addition schedules.

question: For the Skade Formation, summarize grain size, sorting, and cement type occurrence frequency.
answer_text: Medium-grained, moderately sorted sandstone; calcareous cement occurs occasionally.

SPERRY - SUN PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) Sonic log: Can be used to calculate pore pressures, using Eaton’s formula, and subsequently confirm and/or revise any pore pressure calculations made whilst drilling. 6608/10-D-1 AH/BH

The first to be checked was the thermal conductivity, and from theoretical calculations based on input of mineral composition, water content and gas voids (in some cores) it was found that the originally used values for thermal conductivity should have been multiplied by factor of about 1.81. Further analyses of the needle probes used for the field measurements showed that the correct factor is 1.799, which therefore should be applied to all values given in the first report. Other effects which were investigated were possible changes in thermal conductivity due to pressure and temperature changes from in situ conditions to the laboratory, gas influence, anisotropy and possible influences on the temperature gradient due to Quaternary glaciations. Objective The objective for well 15/5-6 was to appraise the 15/5-5 discovery (Heimdal Fm) primarily by confirming oil filled Intra Lista Sandstone, and secondarily by reducing the uncertainty in the Heimdal volume estimates i.e. seismic pick and depth conversion. Geoservices Mudlogging A standard North Sea Geoservices Mudlogging unit running ALS2 Level 5 software was used for this well. The unit was manned at all times by data engineer, with mudloggers present during the sampled intervals. Real time depth data was collected at lm intervals throughout the well. Additionally, the entire time database for the well (4 second storage interval) was backed up to magnetic tape and is available for analysis. Other functions performed by Geoservices included hydraulic and swab/surge simulations, pore pressure estimation, gas component analysis and day to day reporting of operational parameters. The mudloggers were responsible for cuttings sample collection and analysis including shale density readings. During coring operations the mudloggers assisted.

The well was planned to test a Lower Cretaceous/Upper Jurassic wedge play immediately to the south of the Loppa High, and drilled to total depth of 2630 in bdf in rocks of Triassic age. The upper of the two seismically-defined wedges was found to comprise silts and shales of Early to Middle Albian age (Wedge In), whilst the lower wedge consisted of two contrasting clastic packages of Valanginian to latest Ryazanian (Wedge IIa) and Early Volgian (Wedge IIb) age respectively. Oil was recovered from RFT's at in (Wedge ha) and in (an isolated sand in the Kimmeridgian Hekkingen Formation). In addition, well-log interpretation revealed low hydrocarbon saturations in sands of the Triassic Fruholmen Formation. Subsequent testing revealed the Fruholmen to be tight and the hydrocarbons to be immovable, but total of 1600 litres light 31°API (0.87 g/cm3 ) oil was recovered from the hydrocarbon-bearing interval in Wedge ha. Evaluation of the test results was hampered by technical problems encountered during the testing. However, RFT pressures together with the petrophysical evaluation suggest single oil column of approximately 90 in in Wedge IIa (Valanginian) with an oil-water contact at about 1970 in bdf. Reservoir parameters in the hydrocarbon-bearing zone are generally poor, with extensive quartz overgrowth and calcite cementation resulting in an average porosity of only 13% and net/gross of 8%. question: Which petrographic indicators best distinguish textural, grain‑size, and diagenetic features in 25/11‑23 injection sands?
answer_text: Abundant induced clay matrix/pore‑filling clays, good sorting and fine–to–medium grain size, shale/argillaceous fragments and brecciation, cataclastic broken feldspar/quartz and microfractures, and diagenetic cements (kaolinite, quartz, siderite, calcite) with organic pore‑fill.

The well is expected to find 12m of net oil pay in Zone 111-2 lower, 7m of net gas pay in Zone 111-3, and 5m of net gas pay in Zone 111-4. Basis for Geological Prognosis The geological prognosis is based on: 1) Depth conversion 2) Net sand prediction from attribute analysis studies on the 3D Impedance dataset. 'Seismic Interpretation The key mapping element of the Zone III sands was the use of the Balder B88s 3D seismic impedance cube to map individual sand bodies. Calibration of well control with impedance data suggest that low impedance packages correlate to sand prone intervals within the Balder formation. Seismic horizons were carried at zero-crossings at the top and base of these low impedance packages. Interval seismic attributes were then extracted and attribute analysis was performed in order to calculate net sand thickness. The impedance cube and attribute maps were used successfully in planning and drilling Zone III development wells at Mound and E2. key uncertainty for the E5 Zone III sands is the lack of local reservoir sand calibration to seismic impedance. Our investigation shows that the results becomes poorer with increasing hole angle. Enclosed you will find sketch which describes the relative force required to push the core upwards when coring in high angle wells. This curve is compared with the same force when coring in vertical wells. Whenever stringer or fracturated formation enters the innertube at 50 degrees angle, the stringer will bee in more physical contact with the innertube than normal. This is due to the fact that the force pushing the core upwards will be decomposed into two forces. One vertical and one horizontal. It is the horizontal force that force the stringer into physical contact with the innertube. This creates more friction inside the innertube, and the more friction the more force is required to push the core up. At certain point the compressive force becomes to high for the formation to withstand. The formation will then collapse with jammed core as the result. Example of high permeability effects Anytime the pressure decreases rather than increases during buildup, the derivative curve will take sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (log of negative number -infinity). Typically, such buildup is considered un- interpretable. If this occurs for short period, then the final shut-in pressure may still be good estimate of formation pressure, depending on permeability. When the permeability is high, the total pressure changes seen during the buildup are small. The derivative calculation becomes more sensitive as the magnitude of the pressure changes gets near the resolution of the pressure gauge. The derivative curves may have the above wavy appearance. The true shape of the derivatives are often unclear. Good estimates of extrapolated formation pressure are still possible using simple straight line fit to the time function plots. Permeability estimates will be reasonable if the straight line fits reflect the true flow regime.

The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. 3.6.3 Potential Sensitive Habitats and Species Submarine Structures Made by Leaking Gases ‘Submarine structures made by leaking gases’ are defined by the EC Habitats Directive as comprising ‘methane derived authigenic carbonate’ (MDAC) that forms rock-like slabs, pavements and pillars formed through process of precipitation where the carbonate cements the sand (Judd, 2001). They have restricted distribution in European waters, due-in-part, to their relationship to sources of shallow gas. MDAC is often found in conjunction with pockmarks, and are protected as Annex habitats within the EC Habitats Directive. While Norway is not party to the EC Habitats Directive and these habitats are not protected by other Norwegian legislation, it was still considered important to establish whether any MDAC occurred within the survey area. As result, of the original 10 proposed transects were located over pockmarks, hard contacts and areas of high reflectivity. Further information on these features is provided in Appendix B. Possible shallow gas accumulations close to seabed, with hard contacts within seabed depressions above them, were identified across the survey site from geophysical data. Environmental groundtruthing supported this assertion, with visual identification of potential structures indicative of MDAC. These structures were found on the camera transects ES1 and ES3, and were accompanied by bacterial mats growing on the surface of the surrounding sediment. The presence of potential MDAC indicates that hydrocarbon seep is currently active or has occurred in the past; while the presence of the bacterial mats suggests that seeping of hydrocarbon-rich water may be currently active. It is possible that other hard contacts in similar pockmark depressions across the site represent MDAC structures. 3.6.4 Conclusion General Habitats / Biotopes A review of the geophysical and environmental data suggested that three habitats occurred within the survey area. These habitats were defined by the EUNIS habitat classification as ‘circalittoral mixed sediments’ (A5.44), ‘circalittoral muddy sand’ (A5.26), and MDAC which is analogous to ‘communities on soft circalittoral rock’ (A4.23). These habitats were characterised by fine to medium silty sand with varying densities of shell fragment mosaics. Potentially Sensitive Habitats and Species Potential MDAC structures with associated Beggiatoa sp. bacterial mats and cold-water seeps were found in two locations. These findings indicate the likely presence of these structures elsewhere. MDAC structures are noteworthy as they are protected by the EC Habitats Directive. However these habitats are not described under any legislation relevant to the Norwegian Sea. No Norwegian Red List species or other vulnerable environmental resource (as defined by Section 51 of ‘The Activities Regulations’) were recorded within the survey area.
