Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were.used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

STOOlP and EUR Assessment PROBABILISTIC DISTRIBUTION P90 Mean P10 STOOIP 91 155 222 R.F. 40 46 60 EUR 44 74 117 WELL OBJECTIVES AND LOCATION SELECTION CRITERIA Two wells are planned to appraise the Ringhorn field reserves and to enhance the confidence in the resource base for future development planing. The vertical section of the well is proposed at the southern nose of the main Ringhorn horst block and the sidetrack well is located at about 420m to the east (Figure-3 & 4) 25/8-12S Well The objectives of the vertical well are to test the reservoir quality and continuity of primarily the Zone-2 & Zone-3 sandstone, encountered in the 25/8-11 well (Figure-5). The well will penetrate the Zone-2 sandstone and is anticipated to encounter oil on rock in the Zone-3 sandstone. Seismically, this well is located at about 190m to the west of the normal fault separating the Ringhorn main fault block and the up-thrown block (Figure-1 & 3). Coring is planned in this well, with the objective to gather detailed reservoir parameters, primarily for the Zone-2 and Zone-3 sandstone 25/8-12A Side-track Well RISK The proposed sidetrack well is planned on the up-thrown fault block (F/B4) southeast of the Ringhorn main horst block (F/B3). Based on seismic, the well is located about 200m from the two bounding faults to the east and west. The main objective of this sidetrack well, is to prove up the resource base attributed to the Triassic sandstone in this untested fault block, which is interpreted to separated from the Ringhorn main fault block by normal fault to the west. The well will also test the Triassic reservoir quality, its continuity and the fluid system. The current interpretation shows that the Lower Jurassic Statfjord sand in the main fault block (F/B3) is juxtaposed against the Triassic sandstone in the up-thrown block (F/B4). Thus, the Triassic sandstone is anticipated to share the same fluid system as Ringhorn (Figure-5). However, chemical precipitation and the thick Lower Jurassic shale trapped on the fault plane may hamper this interpretation. Another objective of the well is to test the Lower Jurassic shale thickness for validation of reservoir architecture and reservoir model. The current structural model has excluded large amount of shale volume in this up-thrown block from the reserves assessment. The result of the well will also help in reservoir depletion planing, as the reservoir depletion model does not have water injection well within the upthrown fault block. The uncertainties associated with the resource size are the quality of the reservoir sand, the fluid system and the shale thickness primarily in the up-thrown fault block. Uncertainty in time depth conversion is expected due to the variation of chalk thickness as the base is seismically unresolvable.

BORDALARD GROUP 905 mie - 1901 WID 904.9 mTVD - mTVD This group consisted of major claystones with some loose sand and limestone stringers (close to the group base). Claystone: Dark brownish black, olive black, dark grey, brownish black, soft to firm, occasionally brittle, blocky, non calcareous to slightly calcareous, occasional traces of sand and limestone. Traces of glauconite, micromica and micropyrite were also present. Average background gas from 1110m to 1270m was 852 ppm and from 1270m to the base of this group it averaged 1600 ppm. Thin sand beds with oil was encountered in the Heimdal Formation and an oil sample was recovered at mBRT (2078.1 mTVD SS). representative water sample was recovered at mBRT (2088.0 TVD SS), however no test was carried out due to the limited production potential. From the top of the Heimdal reservoir to the Oil-Down-To (ODT) there is m. The upper section of the Heimdal Formation consists of interbedded sandstone and claystone, with low permeability (less than mD) and expected low oil production potential. The water sample recovered is above the Oil-Water-Contact (OWC) on the Jotun Field (2092 mTVD SS). The OWC is estimated in this well at 2080 mTVD SS. CONCLUSIONS 25/8-9 slope setting but the catastrophic nature of the main sand beds plus the prevalence of debris flows suggests slope setting or basin floor site in which there is considered topographic irregularity. • the main sand delivery system remains unknown. • sand connectivity and architecture are the main concerns with the Heimdal reservoir. • the Heimdal Formation comprises texturally and mineralogically diverse sediments. The sampled sandstones are dominantly sublithic arenites and wackes, with variable grain sizes (silt-fsU) and detrital clay abundances (5.5-38.5%). Diagenetic overprinting is largely restricted to replacive pyrite and locally significant quartz overgrowths. • reservoir quality is variable (0 = 6.0-30.7%, Kh = 0.03-1350mD), reflecting the observed textural and mineralogical variability of the cored interval. The best reservoir quality is observed in the clean, fine grained sands of lithotype Sd-d, where dewatering has remobilised detrital clay. Increasing ductile contents (especially detrital clay) and finer grain sizes in lithotypes DF and Si/Sr impart lower reservoir quality to these samples. Patchy solid cements (quartz in the single cemented sample examined) degrade porosities, but have less impact on permeabilities as pore throats generally remain open. VESTLAND GROUP The main conclusions related to the Vestland Group are: • in 25/8-9 the Vestland Group comprises relatively thick (86.0m It), heterogeneous but sand-prone succession that can be readily divided into a series of discrete, genetically-related depositional packages and subpackages. The sedimentology of these suggests that the entire Vestland Group belongs to the Hugin Formation. • the genetically-defined depositional packages range in nature from fluvial sandstones through bay-fill deposits to estuarine deposits to marine shoreface sandstones. The stratal arrangements however, favour these deposits infilling series of stacked incised valleys, the contacts between which have the characteristics of (candidate) sequence boundaries. The depositional evolution of the Vestland Group is pulsed rather than progressive therefore with each incised valley fill representing discrete, 'detached' series of depositional subenvironments separate from those above and below. • whilst the Vestland Group succession is 'layered' in 25/8-9 both the nature of some of the facies, and the probable existence of incised valleys means that the layering may well be breached within the scale of the prospect. • the Vestland Group comprises texturally variable, quartz-dominated sandstones whose detrital clay content is <16.5%. Mica is also relatively abundant in these sandstones (≤7.0%). Authigenic phases are essentially replacive and are dominated by kaolinite and pyrite although locally ferroan carbonate cement is abundant (eg. core 2). • reservoir characteristics in the cored Vestland interval are highly variable (7.8-42.5%, Kh 0.32-16000mD), reflecting the textural variability. The best overall reservoir quality is encountered in the cleaner and overall coarser grained fluvial sandstones (packages Al and B2), whilst the generally fine grained and argillaceous nature of the lagoonal mudrock (subpackage C2) means that they are of non-reservoir quality. question: Does the Spekk Formation in well 6307/7-U-3 represent a (hemi-)pelagic below storm-wave-base setting with low-density turbidites and dysoxic–oxic conditions?
answer_text: Yes — in well 6307/7-U-3 the Spekk Formation was deposited in a (hemi-)pelagic below storm-wave-base setting with low‑density turbidity laminae and slightly dysoxic to oxic conditions.

context_snippets.text: -232- (9_ AO -INITEF. 3.6.7 Depositional environment Depositional environments for the formations are schematically outlined in Figure 3.6.30. 190.1 - m: Spekk Formation, late Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian A marine environment for the Spekk Formation is documented by the fossil records. The dominance of shale/claystone, with only minor contents of sands indicates that deposition took place in (hemi-)pelagic environment (below storm wave base). The sand may have been transported by low density turbidity currents, and deposited as thin laminae which have been mottled by bioturbation. However, an upwards shallowing trend is reflected by the coarsening upward trend, and upwards increasing bioturbation. reduction in the amount of unstructured organic material supports this suggestion. The fair content of gas-prone to inert kerogens in this part of the Spekk Formation (sub-unit 1) may suggest slightly dysoxic to oxic depositional conditions, which would agree with the generally bioturbated nature of this sub-unit. 183.5 - m: Rogn Formation, latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian The Rogn Formation (183.5 - m) appears as homogeneous sandstone bodies separated by graded, clayey sandstone and shale/claystone layers. The two different sandy facies suggest two different sediment gravity flow mechanisms. Rapid deposition of the homogeneous sandstone bodies is indicated by water escape structures. The sharp, sometimes erosive lower boundaries, and the lack of sedimentary structures and grading, indicate that they were deposited by high density turbidity currents or liquified flows. The graded, clayey sandstone layers were probably deposited by associated low density turbidity currents (Lowe, 1982). The shale/claystone beds represent the normal (hemi-)pelagic sedimentation between the frequent high and low density turbidity currents. The rich concentration of mixed marine/terrestrial type kerogens in the shales probably reflect deposition under dysoxic conditions in fairly stagnant environment. The fossil content indicate nearly normal marine conditions. ems_stlint28/Rapport/AA5/6307/07-U-02/69/19-DFC-88

-115- :Bag -INTEF-GRUPPEN 3.5.1 Summary Totally of Late Jurassic sediments (in the southern part of the Hitra Basin) were penetrated between and below seabed, with core recovery of 99% of the cored section (see comment below). The core has been sub-divided into two lithological units, which are interpreted to be lateral developments of the Spekk and Rogn Formations (Figure 3.5.1). The (mainly) Late Kimmeridgian Spekk Formation (>61 m) consists of dark grey shale/claystone, which shows increasing silt/sand content and bioturbation towards the top. Planktic microfossils document nearly normal marine environment, and the unit represents slightly regressive sequence in pelagic domain with poor bottom water circulation, especially in the lower half. The latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian Rogn Formation (>11 m, see also core 6307/07-U-02) consists of more or less massive fine grained sandstone. The unit represents sediment gravity flows in nearly normal marine environment (see discussion in Chapter 4.3.3). The distinct boundary between the two lithological units could not be related to any strong seismic reflector. Strong semi-regional reflectors within the lower unit seem to be related to cemented zones within the shale/claystone. The lower unit (Spekk Formation) posesses good potential for oil and wet gas generation. TOC values vary from to 18%. Hydrogen indices of nearly 800 mg HC/g TOC are observed. The kerogen (type I, II and III) is immature. The upper unit (Rogn Formation) showed high quality reservoir properties, with porosities of more than 30% and permeabilities which cluster at 700 mD. Here it is not evaluated whether the observed kaolinite booklets (see Chapter 3.5.3) would become problem during any hydrocarbon production.

3. GEOLOGICAL EVALUATION 3.1. Introduction Geological Setting The Draugen Field is situated in the Haltenbanken area off mid-Norway. The geological history of mid-Norway comprises Palaeozoic formative stage and Devonian to present break-up phase. Rifting and related faulting occurred from Late Carboniferous up to present day with westward moving of the axis of rifting activity. The resulting Norwegian shelf is passive cratonic margin underlain by series of continental margin basins superimposed on collapsed Palaeozoic orogeny. The Field comprises NNE/SSW trending low relief periclinal lenticular structure (20 km) with maximum vertical closure of 50 m. The main hydrocarbon accumulation is hosted by the Rogn Sandstone Formation, local Upper Jurassic composite shoreface/shelf deposit. minor, connected accumulation is hosted by the Garn Sandstone Formation, Middle Jurassic regionally extensive progradational shallow marine formation. The main reservoir facies, Rogn Formation, is enclosed to the north, south and east by butiminous claystones of the Upper and Lower Spekk Formation, time equivalent of the Rogn Formation. On the western side the Rogn Formation onlaps the Gam Formation which here rises above the field OWC. The top-seal of the Field is provided by the Upper Spekk Formation, the Lower Spekk provides seat seal over the larger part of the reservoir. Well 6407/9-B-5 was drilled from the northern water injection template to the target at top Rogn Formation, app. 1825 to the ( Fig. 1.1). The well reached TD in the sandstone's of the Garn Formation. The target was chosen to maximise on sweep of hydrocarbons as far to the north as possible. 3.2. Sample Collection The only samples collected were ditch cuttings, no cores or sidewall samples were taken. SEPOT-1012.E 13

question: How do km walkaway acquisition parameters differ from those of 140 6-level offset seismic profiles in shot spacing, receiver spacing, and fold?
answer_text: Shot spacing: walkaway = 25 m; receiver spacing: walkaway recorded two downhole levels simultaneously (dual-tool) versus six levels per offset in the 6‑level profiles; fold/traces: walkaway produced ~832 traces (~840 = 140×6), i.e. essentially the same.

context_snippets.text: Schlumberger SONIC CALIBRATION - GEOGRAM PROCESSING REPORT • COMPANY HYDRO WELL : 7120/2-1 FIELD : WILDCAT COUNTRY : OFFSHORE NORWAY LOGGED : 18 SEP 85 ANALYST J.M. Smidt PROCESSED : 19 OCT 85 This binder contains the results of the WSC/GEO processing from the above well. ; CHECK-SHOT DATA - First-break times computed in the VSP processing (see VSP Processing Report) have been used. 62 out of 66 check shot levels have been used. Pseudo-shots are generated at the top and bottom of the Sonic log. Results are Listed in the Geophysical Airgun Report. 2 ; DRIFT COMPUTATIONS - The drift (seismic time - sonic time) data computed for the check shot levels used are listed in the Drift Computation Report. After examination of the open hole logs, knee points were selected at formation boundaries. The imposed correction to the sonic was kept close to the amount computed for all levels included, and is documented in the Sonic Adjustment Parameter Report. Knee-points were chosen in order not to create false reflections.

Page WALKANAY SEISMIC PROFILE The km walkaway seismic profile was traversed over vertical borehole with shot spacing of 25 metres (fig 1). The line was shot into successive levels of the downhole tool. The data set is equivalent to shooting 140 6-level offset seismic profiles. The survey was shot using two 200 cubic inch air guns. A dual tool geophone was used during the data acquisition; hence two levels of data were recorded simultaneously as the shot positions were moved along the profile. The geophone depths range from 1265 to 1165 metres measured from the logging datum. total nf 832 traces were recorded during the acquisition which was used as the started point for the processing. However prior to the processing, the raw data, i.e the surface (hydrophone) traces and the downhole (geophone) traces have been evaluated and bad traces deleted. SURFACE SENSOR RECORDS Figure contains the surface sensor data which are used to establish the downhole geophone break times. In the figure the LEVEL number varies with aeophone position in the borehole, the level number commences at the deepest location and increases to the shallowest location. The data are displayed in the form of common receiver gathers such that there is only one level or one geophone position for each display. The measured depth of the geophone relative to the logging datum is listed under DEPTH. TIME denotes the break time of each sensor trace relative to the start of digitisation. Each trace is scaled to its maximum amplitude and the value of the excursion from highest peak to lowest trough is displayed as PEAK/PEAK. DOWNHOLE SENSOR RECORDS Figure comprises the dnwnhole geophone records corresponding to the surface sensor monitors displayed earlier. LEVEL, DEPTHS, and PEAK/PEAK on each heading have the same meaning as for the surface breaks. TIME now displays the time of the geophone breaks relative to the start of recording. The definition of the break time on both surface and downhole sensors is that time indicated by picking the zero crossing preceding the malor downwards movement of the trace under reverse S.E.G. polarity. On the traces at the end of the line it's sometimes difficult to pick the break times accurately because of low siqnal to noise ratio. STATIC CORRECTION AND BAND PASS FILTER SURFACE SENSOR RECORDS

The site survey for the 7120/2-1 was performed between 25 March and 17 April 1985, by A/S Geoteam using the survey vessel M/V Geo Scanner. The coordinates for the well were given as 710 58' 57,7 200 28' 33,8 The area of the survey was km square centred on the provisional well location, and the object was to investigate the shallow geology and seabed features of the location using echosounder and side scan sonar and to delineate possible seabed and sub seabed hazards. The results of the site survey can be summarized as follows: - Water depth at the location was 387 MSL - Seabed was dominated by pockmarks having diameters less than 25 metres, at density of approximately 260/km2. Coral ridges oriented NE-SW protruded up to 45 metre above seabed of soft well laminated silty clay. - The seabed had dip of 0,9% towards NE. 1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group. context_snippets.text: FORMATION PRESSURE TEST After drilling out casing strings the formation below the shoe will be subjected to pressure leak off test. 1. Depending on the type of formation and estimated future drilling conditions this test will be run either to predetermined pressure or to actual bleedoff. If predetermined maximum pressure is to be used, the pressure will be advised by the Stavanger Office. It will be calculated from the following: (a) Maximum mud weight anticipated to next casing point. (b) Maximum pressure anticipated when cementing the next casing string. (c) Estimated formation fracture graients. 2. Clean out cement below the shoe and make three meters of new hole. 3. Pick up into the casing and close blow out preventor. 4. Pump slowly down the drill pipe with the cementing pump pressuring up the casing and the exposed formation. Maximum pump rate is to be bbl/min. 5. The pressure is to be built up in 50 to 200 psi stages depending on the estimated fracture pressure. When the surface pressure reaches first level, shut the pump down and check for bleed off. Increase surface pressure, shut the pumps down and check again, and so on until reaching final pressure. It may be desirable to use 25 to 100 psi increments during final stages. 6. An accurate measurement of pressure build up and volume pumped is to be recorded on the form provided. If the formation begins to take mud, shut the pump down immediately and record the surface holding pressure. 7. Release the pressure, open the blow out preventor and drill ahead. 8. The results of the formation pressure test are to be reported on the Daily Drilling Report.

Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time (TI) with the check shot time (Tc)at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate, the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. The different types of shifts are discussed in more detail in chapter 4.2. Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod. June 30, 1993

4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( TVD vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. • From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

Sigyn 16/7-A-2 & 16/7-A-2 HT2 BAT Sonic Final Logging Report Summary The Halliburton BAT LWD SONIC tool was used to log the 12 1/4” section in well 16/7-A-2 and 1/2” section in 16/7-A-2 HT2 in Statoil & ExxonMobil’s Sigyn field. In 16/7-A-2 H, the 8” BAT tool was run in memory mode behind Geopilot drilling assembly. The data was obtained in four runs, run 500-800. In 16/7-A-2 HT2, the 3/4” BAT tool was run in recorded mode in combination with MRIL-WD behind Anadrill. The log was recorded in one run, run 1600. The tool ran out of waveform memory at m for high frequency and at 4227 for low frequency. Still, it was recording downhole calculated computed picks for both high and low frequency to TD. The analyses of the recorded waveform data and computed picks from both wells are detailed in this report. Log Review Discussion – Sigyn 16/7-A-2 Compressional Log The high frequency compressional data is in general of good quality throughout the entire well. An example of compressional signal is shown in figure 1. There is also log example in figure 5. The compressional curve was processed using 13 kHz high frequency pass filter, minimum slowness of 40 µs/ft and maximum slowness of 250 µs/ft. There were no particular problems of interpreting this log. Shear Log The final shear log is composite of refracted shear, which generally exists when the shear velocity is faster than the fluid velocity, and interface mode derived shear, which is used when no direct shear is present. When the shear velocity is slower than the fluid velocity, shear delta is determined by applying dispersion correction to the low frequency interface mode arrival (detailed in the background discussion, appendix 3). These zones are indicated on the final log plot by filled curve “Shear Flag”, which is (filled) when refracted shear was used and otherwise. In this well we have just short section of slow shear. The fast shear curve was processed using 13 kHz high frequency pass filter, minimum slowness of 40 µs/ft and maximum slowness of 250 µs/ft. The slow shear curve was processed using 5-15 kHz band-pass filter, minimum slowness of 50 us/ft and maximum slowness of 600 us/ft. There were no particular problem interpreting the shear log. But in the areas where there was difficult to obtain shear value, there was an alias of the compressional value, which could look like true shear value. question: In Upper Lunde (Rhaetian), how do calcite, dolomite and quartz cements in silt/sand/conglomerate lithologies affect porosity and permeability in wells w34/4-4 and w34/4-7?
answer_text: Calcite, dolomite and quartz cements (with intergranular clays) greatly reduce pore connectivity and permeability: well 34/4-4 has pores ~20–82p with microporosity ~1,9% and permeability "severely restricted", while well 34/4-7 has pores ~82–177p (up to 82–350p in sandstone) with microporosity ~n,13% (and ~ft,7% in parts) and permeability restricted.

question: What is the Spekk Formation lithology and depositional (hemi-pelagic) setting, and what is the inferred origin of its sand laminae?
answer_text: Spekk Formation is dominantly shale/claystone to sandy shale deposited in a (hemi-)pelagic marine setting below storm wave base. Its sand laminae are inferred to have been transported and deposited by low‑density turbidity currents.

context_snippets.text: -232- (9_ AO -INITEF. 3.6.7 Depositional environment Depositional environments for the formations are schematically outlined in Figure 3.6.30. 190.1 - m: Spekk Formation, late Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian A marine environment for the Spekk Formation is documented by the fossil records. The dominance of shale/claystone, with only minor contents of sands indicates that deposition took place in (hemi-)pelagic environment (below storm wave base). The sand may have been transported by low density turbidity currents, and deposited as thin laminae which have been mottled by bioturbation. However, an upwards shallowing trend is reflected by the coarsening upward trend, and upwards increasing bioturbation. reduction in the amount of unstructured organic material supports this suggestion. The fair content of gas-prone to inert kerogens in this part of the Spekk Formation (sub-unit 1) may suggest slightly dysoxic to oxic depositional conditions, which would agree with the generally bioturbated nature of this sub-unit. 183.5 - m: Rogn Formation, latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian The Rogn Formation (183.5 - m) appears as homogeneous sandstone bodies separated by graded, clayey sandstone and shale/claystone layers. The two different sandy facies suggest two different sediment gravity flow mechanisms. Rapid deposition of the homogeneous sandstone bodies is indicated by water escape structures. The sharp, sometimes erosive lower boundaries, and the lack of sedimentary structures and grading, indicate that they were deposited by high density turbidity currents or liquified flows. The graded, clayey sandstone layers were probably deposited by associated low density turbidity currents (Lowe, 1982). The shale/claystone beds represent the normal (hemi-)pelagic sedimentation between the frequent high and low density turbidity currents. The rich concentration of mixed marine/terrestrial type kerogens in the shales probably reflect deposition under dysoxic conditions in fairly stagnant environment. The fossil content indicate nearly normal marine conditions. ems_stlint28/Rapport/AA5/6307/07-U-02/69/19-DFC-88

-115- :Bag -INTEF-GRUPPEN 3.5.1 Summary Totally of Late Jurassic sediments (in the southern part of the Hitra Basin) were penetrated between and below seabed, with core recovery of 99% of the cored section (see comment below). The core has been sub-divided into two lithological units, which are interpreted to be lateral developments of the Spekk and Rogn Formations (Figure 3.5.1). The (mainly) Late Kimmeridgian Spekk Formation (>61 m) consists of dark grey shale/claystone, which shows increasing silt/sand content and bioturbation towards the top. Planktic microfossils document nearly normal marine environment, and the unit represents slightly regressive sequence in pelagic domain with poor bottom water circulation, especially in the lower half. The latest Kimmeridgian - earliest Volgian Rogn Formation (>11 m, see also core 6307/07-U-02) consists of more or less massive fine grained sandstone. The unit represents sediment gravity flows in nearly normal marine environment (see discussion in Chapter 4.3.3). The distinct boundary between the two lithological units could not be related to any strong seismic reflector. Strong semi-regional reflectors within the lower unit seem to be related to cemented zones within the shale/claystone. The lower unit (Spekk Formation) posesses good potential for oil and wet gas generation. TOC values vary from to 18%. Hydrogen indices of nearly 800 mg HC/g TOC are observed. The kerogen (type I, II and III) is immature. The upper unit (Rogn Formation) showed high quality reservoir properties, with porosities of more than 30% and permeabilities which cluster at 700 mD. Here it is not evaluated whether the observed kaolinite booklets (see Chapter 3.5.3) would become problem during any hydrocarbon production.

3. GEOLOGICAL EVALUATION 3.1. Introduction Geological Setting The Draugen Field is situated in the Haltenbanken area off mid-Norway. The geological history of mid-Norway comprises Palaeozoic formative stage and Devonian to present break-up phase. Rifting and related faulting occurred from Late Carboniferous up to present day with westward moving of the axis of rifting activity. The resulting Norwegian shelf is passive cratonic margin underlain by series of continental margin basins superimposed on collapsed Palaeozoic orogeny. The Field comprises NNE/SSW trending low relief periclinal lenticular structure (20 km) with maximum vertical closure of 50 m. The main hydrocarbon accumulation is hosted by the Rogn Sandstone Formation, local Upper Jurassic composite shoreface/shelf deposit. minor, connected accumulation is hosted by the Garn Sandstone Formation, Middle Jurassic regionally extensive progradational shallow marine formation. The main reservoir facies, Rogn Formation, is enclosed to the north, south and east by butiminous claystones of the Upper and Lower Spekk Formation, time equivalent of the Rogn Formation. On the western side the Rogn Formation onlaps the Gam Formation which here rises above the field OWC. The top-seal of the Field is provided by the Upper Spekk Formation, the Lower Spekk provides seat seal over the larger part of the reservoir. Well 6407/9-B-5 was drilled from the northern water injection template to the target at top Rogn Formation, app. 1825 to the ( Fig. 1.1). The well reached TD in the sandstone's of the Garn Formation. The target was chosen to maximise on sweep of hydrocarbons as far to the north as possible. 3.2. Sample Collection The only samples collected were ditch cuttings, no cores or sidewall samples were taken. SEPOT-1012.E 13

question: How do moldic porosity, cementation/remineralization, and diagenesis affect the reservoir quality of the D85-J limestone?
answer_text: Moldic porosity produces locally high porosity but does not improve permeability, while cementation/remineralization and diagenetic pore occlusion destroy pore interconnectivity; overall the D85-J limestone has very low permeability and little reservoir potential.

Because of the surprisingly low heat flow values that were calculated quite some effort was put into investigations to look for any errors in the heat flow calculation. Calibration of the log to the checkshot data proceeded as follows: point of absolute zero drift was specified at the shallowest checkshot point within the logged interval. The drift curve was analysed interactively and sectioned into intervals of approximately linear drift by placing further calibration points on or close to knee- points where the slope or trend of the drift curve changed significantly. To avoid creating false reflection coefficients, the calibration points - marked on the drift curve figures as the letter C - were positioned at velocity contrasts (i.e. formation boundaries). Using the depth difference and drift difference between successive calibration points, constant velocity correction for each interval was calculated. At each sample point of the log, fraction of the pertinent velocity correction for that interval was applied to the sample value, thus reducing the drift i.e. calibrating the log. question: How do texture, bulk density, and coarse fraction compare between the Holocene veneer and Viking Bank (upper and lower), Cape Shore, and Ferder?
answer_text: Holocene veneer: very loose–medium dense silty sand with shell fragments (finest texture, lowest bulk density, low coarse fraction); Viking Bank (upper): interbedded soft–firm sandy clay and loose–medium dense sand (variable texture/density, occasional gravel); Viking Bank (lower)/Tampen/Sperus: medium–very dense sand interbedded with firm–stiff sandy clay and gravel/boulders (coarser texture, higher bulk density, high coarse fraction); Cape Shore: sandy clay with occasional coarse deposits (clay-rich, firmer than veneer, occasional coarse fraction); Ferder: hard gravelly sandy clay over stiff sandy clay with occasional gravel (coarsest, highest bulk density and coarse fraction).

Holocene Veneer A Holocene veneer (generally less than thick) of very loose to medium dense silty sand with shell fragments is expected to be present across the entire survey area. Viking Bank Formation (upper unit) The Holocene veneer is underlain by the upper unit of the Viking Bank Formation. The depth to the base of the unit across the survey area is presented in Appendix B.3. The unit, which has well-layered seismic character, infills series of predominantly north/south orientated iceberg ploughmarks which incise into the underlying unit. The unit thickness is highly variable across the survey area due to the ploughmarked basal surface, but generally thins from east to west, becoming very thin or absent in the extreme west of the site. The unit is interpreted to comprise interbedded soft to firm sandy clay and loose to medium dense sand with occasional gravel. Geotechnical testing suggests large variability in the distribution of clay and sand layers within the unit across the site (Reference 4). Occasional diffraction hyperbolae observed on seismic data are likely to indicate the presence of boulders within the unit. Viking Bank (lower unit), Tampen and Sperus Formations The upper unit of the Viking Bank Formation is expected to be underlain by an undifferentiated unit comprising the lower unit of the Viking Bank Formation, the Tampen Formation and the Sperus Formation. The individual formations were not distinguishable from the seismic data and are therefore grouped together for the purposes of this report. The lower unit of the Viking Bank Formation overlies the Tampen Formation, which in turn overlies the Sperus Formation. The thickness of the unit increases from south-west to north-east. PAGE 11 OF 73 3:5 UNSTEADY-STATE WATERFLOODS AND OILFLOODS 1. Restoration A series of waterflood tests were performed on samples and 2. These were initiated upon completion of the air-brine capillary pressure tests. In accordance with the specifications for the work, the level of saturation at the final point of the capillary pressure test (13.8 bars) was used as the connate water saturation (Swir 1) for the first waterfloods. Restoration for these tests was thus achieved by saturating the voided pore space with de-aired,depolarised mineral oil. The oil had been blended to have viscosity of approximately times that of the simulated formation brine in order to emulate the reservoir oil-water viscosity ratio. The saturation of the voided space was achieved by carefully performed vacuuming and flooding technique. The freezing point of the simulated formation brine was first determined and then the desaturated samples placed in precisely controlled freezer set to few degrees above this freezing point. The samples were left to cool for about 24 hours along with batch of the appropriate oil- blend and then vacuumed under oil inside the cooling apparatus. Each sample was rapidly warmed back to room temperature allowing saturation to take place under atmospheric pressure. After about hours the samples were removed from the oil, weighed and then checked for complete saturation by material balance. 2. Constant Flow Rate, Unsteady-State Waterflood. question: For DST 25/8-8S, what were initial pressure, peak and stabilized flow rates, and were any sand-control issues observed?
answer_text: Initial reservoir pressure 2842.0 psia; peak flow ~5000 STB/D; stabilized flow 3950 STB/D; sand production observed (continuous >1% at 5000 STB/D, traces ±1% during stabilized flow).

context_snippets.text: PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

PORE PRESSURE EVALUATION , 25/8-B-12 & B-12 12 VI HOLE SECTION A Leak Off Test was performed at the top of the section at 1348m MD/1071m TVD to g/cc EMW. During the drilling all normal parameters for pore pressure were monitored. This hole section was drilled highly overbalanced with s.g. mud in order to maintain hole stability in the Hordaland shales. The d-Exponent showed minor variations in the trend line throughout the section. Cut backs in the trend line could be explained by lithological changes e.g. at approximately 1560m TVD the cut back corresponds to dolomitic limestone stringer The gas level developed as normal for this section. The drilled and background gas was low throughout the entire section with readings of 2-6 units API. It increased to maximum of 13 units at 4618m in claystone. No signs of connection gas were present, and no drag on connections, presence of cavings or increasing mud temperature out indicated any increase in pore pressure. In addition, no hole problems were experienced throughout the section which could be an indication of overpressure. The wiper trip from TD produced trip gas of only 10 units which was only marginally above drilled gas levels, even after lowering the mud weight to g/cc. Despite variations in the d-Exponent, the other qualifiers suggest normally pressured section. 8 1/2 HOLE SECTION Prior to drilling out the 5/8 casing shoe the mud weight was lowered to SG as there were no longer wellbore stability concerns associated with the Hordaland shale. After drilling the shoe, 3m of new formation were drilled to 4748m MD, 2122m TVD. Here formation integrity test was performed to g/cc equivalent mud weight. Gas levels remained relatively low with maximum of approx. 20 units. There were no signs of connection gas throughout the section and the low figure for trip gas of 15 units following the wiper trip would also suggest normally pressured formation. As the Dexponent relies on homogenous shale, it could not be used as reliable indication of overpressure in the reservoir section of sandstone, with limestone and siltstone. Hole problems were absent during the drilling of the section. This would also support the view of normally pressured formation. question: How do gas, wet-gas, and oil generation potentials compare for the Callovian (Middle Jurassic) shale in well 36/1-2?
answer_text: Gas and wet‑gas potential is VERY GOOD, while oil (liquid) generation potential is minor/limited.

context_snippets.text: TS 9499CC INTRODUCTION One set of core chips (Core No. 1, 2987-3005 m) from the Saga 36/1-2 well were submitted for source rock evaluation by Amoco Norway. High acoustic velocities recorded in this interval indicate low porosities and suggest that rocks in this area may have been buried deeper than present subsurface depth. Therefore, the stage of diagenesis is of special importance for this study. Duplicate samples were analyzed of the M. Jurassic shale to check for variability among the core fragments. CONCLUSIONS* The M. Jurassic (Callovian) shale has VERY GOOD hydrocarbon generation capability for GAS and WET GAS. The EARLY - EARLY PEAK diagenetic level of these effective GAS source beds is not unusual for the present depth. DISCUSSION Organic carbon weight percents of and indicate VERY GOOD hydrocarbon generation capability (Table 1). Visual kerogen analyses (Table 3) indicate potential for GAS and WET GAS generation by approximately equal proportions of structured and amorphous kerogen. H/C ratios (Table 2) suggest greater capacity for oil gener- ation than visual analyses. However, low extractable organic/total organic carbon ratios and strong odd-carbon predominance of the extracts (CPI 1.4-1.6) suggest that these shales have only minor liquid genera- tion capability.

CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS On the evidence of the data submitted for analysis this study CONCLUDS that:- . The 36/1-2 well penetrated Jurassic section with the following fades and environments:- INTERVAL(m) PA 0128 MIRO:M:1E14T Laminated Subwave base 2375-3147 claystone marine 3147-3193 Carbonaceous sand distal deltaic 3193-3233 Carbonaceous claystone prodelta 3233-3237 Glauconitic transgressive sand marine 3237-TD. Foliated metamorphic biotite gneiss basement 2. The poor petrophysical properties of the middle Jurassic sand (the only potential reservoir) are due to com- bination of low primary porosity (textural immaturity), combined with minor carbonate cementation. Porosity in this sand may increase eastwards, but is unlikely to increase westwards into the basin. 3. An upper Jurassic sand may be developed to the east of this location, but is unlikely to be present to the west in the direction of the basin centre.

- - At the request of Saga Petroleum A/S and Company, synthetic seismogram study of Norwegian North Sea Well 36/1-2 was undertaken. Synthetics had already been calculated by G.S.I. and, although their calculation did not apparently take into account the migration effects of dip unconformities, their primaries-only synthetic for the standard 'compression as white' polarity showed quite good match with their unmigrated processed section at the well. However, when multiple reflections were included, the match became far from satisfactory. When compared with the BP processed section the reverse situation held; the primaries-only 'compression as white' showed very little similarity, whilst including the multiples improved the match. Conclusions were made still more difficult to draw by the ambiguity in polarity of recording, this having been omitted from the descriptive annotation of the acquisition parameters. When the synthetics based on convention of 'compression as black' were included in the comparisons, the order of qualities of the matches were reversed again. This variability was perhaps surprising in view of the fact that applying a simple time delay of about 20 msec to the BP processed section makes it appear very similar to the G.S.I. processed data, apart from exhibiting reduced legginess in character. Data from an earlier survey carried out by Western was also to hand and this exhibited other differences. Here the G.S.I. synthetics fitted best under the compression as black' convention, though from previous experience we believe the convention used by this contractor is also compression as white'. question: In the HANZ formation, how do calcareous Jurassic sands compare to subarkoses/arkosic arenites in carbonate cement, porosity, and permeability versus depth?
answer_text: Calcareous Jurassic sands contain 10–43% carbonate cement and become more cemented with depth, generally exhibiting lower porosity and permeability than subarkoses/arkosic arenites, which have porosities of 26–33% and permeabilities of 2000–8000 mD.

Subarkoses of both wells are of similar mineral composition and texture. The reservoir quality, namely porosity, is governed by detrital clays, authigenic quartz and feldspar overgrowth and authigenic kaolinite. The intergranular, primary porosity ranges from 11 to 22%, and the secondary porosity averages 8%. Permeability reductions are mainly caused by detrital clay ranging to 14%. Reservoir quality of Upper Jurassic sandstones: The sampled interval covers core material over 64 meters. Upper Jurassic sands comprise variety of lithofacies: Limestones and marls, laminated argillaceous sands, calcareous sands, subarkoses and arkosic arenites. The high content of glauconite in all lithofacies allows confident separation from Middle Jurassic sands. The limestones and marls are tight with few moldic, isolated pores. The laminated, argillaceous sands are fine grained and have high proportions of feldspar. The lamination is caused by clayrich - claypoor alternating beds. The clayrich beds are almost tight and presumably non-permeable. The claypoor layers are composed of siliclastic framework grains in calcitic matrix_ Detrital feldspar grains are partially altered, dissolved and replaced by occluding kaolinite, which has caused abundant microporosity. The rocks with the best reservoir quality are subarkoses to arkosic arenites, which have permeabilities from 2000 to 8000mD. Porosities of these lithofacies range from 26 to 33%. Porosity reductions are caused by detrital clays and more importantly by carbonate cements. Sandstones with 10 to 43% carbonate cement are defined as calcareous sandstones. The reservoir appears more cemented with increasing depth. This is probably result of higher proportions of carbonaceous shell debris. The porosity/permeability cross-plot for the clean sands displays very poor correlation, which is thought to originate from carbonate decementation. Streaks with high permeability occur in particular at the base of the analyzed section, where calcareous sandstones predominate. A confident correlation of Upper Jurassic sands in wells 25/10-8 and 25/10-8A was not possible, because the samples of 25/10-8 were too disintegrated. Only one sample allowed the identification of cuttings from calcareous sandstone. Reservoir quality of Middle Jurassic/Triassic sandstones: The dense sampling, with one sample per meter, allows detailed reservoir zonation with tight sandstone types at the base and highly permeable subarkoses to lithic arenites at the top. In-between a thick section of fine grained, well sorted, feldspatic sandstones occurs. The Triassic base comprises tight calcarenaceous sands passing into limestones with combined calcite/dolomite contents of more than 60%. These are overlain by Middle Jurassic calcareous sands with total calcite contents of 23 to 39%. These rocks have only few isolated. moldic pores and permeabilities of less than mD. The feldspatic sandstones attain permeabilities up to 260 mD and porosities up to 27%. Porosity reductions are caused by: detritral clays, secondary quartz, calcite cement, kaolinite and abundant finely disseminated pyrite. The overlying subarkoses show the highest variability in permeabilities, from to 3500 mD. PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

The Spectral Gamma was corrected for potassium content in the mud and hole size corrected, the Densilog was hole size corrected, the Dual Laterolog resistivity curves were corrected for borehole effects, and the Compensated Neutron curve was corrected for all borehole effects. Even the two primary sand units are too thin for the deep laterolog to resolve correctly. To account for this, form of resistivity forward modeling was applied. Petrophysical Model The overall petrophysical model consists of combination of several different models. Schlumberger Volan' type logic was applied in the computation of clay and silt volumes. Using information from the core analysis, porosity was computed which provided the best fit to the core data. Fluid saturation and permeability were computed using the Archie equation, capillary pressure relationships, and sound geologic reasoning. Clay and Shale Volume Computation Clay volume was computed from weighted average of non-linear transform of the gamma ray, linear transform of the gamma ray divided by bulk density, and density / neutron. The average is Hodges-Lehmann weighted average, which is described in an 1982 SPWLA paper by Coates, et al'. According to whole core descriptions of the Heimdal sands in the 25/7-3, they consist of mix of high-density turbidites, muddy sandstones, low-density turbidites, carbonate-cemented sandy shale, injected/slumped sands, and shales. They range in grain size from medium to very fine, and in sorting from well to poorly sorted'. HYDRO TROLL OLJE / TROLL WEST GAS PROVINCE Grading : Internal Title: Well Programme 31/2-K-21 H/AY1H/AY2H Revision : Page : 37 of 95 Date : 2000-12-14 4 FORMATION DATA 4.1 Main objectives The objective of the observation well 31/2-K-21 is to determine the depth, quality and thickness of the reservoir sand intervals down to the Top 3-series. It is anticipated that the top reservoir will be encountered within the oil zone and that the GOC could be difficult to interpret as it is probably within the 5Am sand. The main objective of the 31/5-K-21 AY1H/AY2H well is to penetrate and drain the area north east of the K2-template which is located in the southern part of TWGP. The main branch (AY1H) will be the shorter of the two branches and is planned to drain the 4Dc subcrop. The secondary branch (AY2H) will kick off to the west and is planned to drain the older 4-series sands. 4.2 Geophysical prognosis and uncertainties Only minor possible faults can be interpreted in the Hordaland and Rogaland Groups, and the top of the Green Clay interval is typically irregular surface. Still, none of the faults in the upper sections are expected to cause any drilling problems, see Figure 4.5. The pilot, buildup section and heel of 31/2-K-21 are located in compartment with scattered minor faults. The wellpaths have been optimized as far as possible to avoid faults. However drilling through some deformed/fractured zones is unavoidable, and awareness is suggested concerning ECD and mud weight. Several faults have been interpreted in the horizontal reservoir section from seismic coherency data (Fig. 4.1a). Two faults have been interpreted and marked on the seismic section along the horizontal wellpath for 31/2-K-21 AY1H (Fig. 4.1b). In this area the wellpath actually goes parallel to possible, minor fault, but it is belived that if this fault is real, it will only have stratigraphic consequence and will not cause drilling problems. Several faults have also been interpreted along the horizontal section of 31/2-K-21 AY2H, see Fig. 4.1c, but none of these faults are expected to cause any drilling problems due to small offsets. Even though none of the faults along the horizontal sections are expected to cause drilling problems, awareness is suggested concerning ECD and mud weight. Strucural maps for the seismically interpreted reservior horizons (Top Sognefjord, Top 4-series and Top 3-series) are shown in Figures 4.2a, 4.2b and 4.2c. Along the horizontal section several intervals of high acoustic impedance are evident which may indicate calcite cemented zones. These are common in the whole area and are unavoidable with respect to well track planing. In general the extent and depth of possible calcite cemented zones are difficult to predict from the seismic data. All drilled wells are used as calibration pionts in the velocity model for depth conversion of the reservior horizons. The influence range is weighted and the nearest wells have dominant effect. The 31/2-K-23 well to the west and the 31/2-2 well in the toe end area, have most influence on the depth- and isochore maps.

The vessel MV Fugro Meridian, operated by Fugro Survey Ltd, carried out the survey in November 2012. The final geophysical survey program covered one km large template area (PWL 2/9-5 Alt 1). It consisted of 37 integrated survey lines, including one tie line towards existing well 2/9-3 which is the tie well for this survey. On all integrated lines data were acquired with multibeam echo sounders, dual- frequency side scan sonar (120 kHz and 400 kHz), hull-mounted pinger (sub-bottom profiler), mini air gun and 2DHR digital multichannel seismic system. The geotechnical Survey comprised Cone Penetration Tests at 10 locations at and around the PWL (Figure 2.1). question: Did well 25/8‑B‑12 in the Hordaland shale exhibit connate gas shows, significant cavings, or d‑exponent indications of overpressure?
answer_text: No — there were no connection/connate gas shows, no significant cavings, and only minor d‑exponent variations that did not indicate overpressure.

context_snippets.text: PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

This hole section was drilled highly overbalanced with s.g. mud in order to maintain hole stability in the Hordaland shales. The d-Exponent showed minor variations in the trend line throughout the section. Cut backs in the trend line could be explained by lithological changes e.g. at approximately 1560m TVD the cut back corresponds to dolomitic limestone stringer The gas level developed as normal for this section. In addition, no hole problems were experienced throughout the section which could be an indication of overpressure. Despite variations in the d-Exponent, the other qualifiers suggest normally pressured section. 8 1/2 HOLE SECTION Prior to drilling out the 5/8 casing shoe the mud weight was lowered to SG as there were no longer wellbore stability concerns associated with the Hordaland shale. After drilling the shoe, 3m of new formation were drilled to 4748m MD, 2122m TVD. Here formation integrity test was performed to g/cc equivalent mud weight. Gas levels remained relatively low with maximum of approx. 20 units. Hole problems were absent during the drilling of the section. This would also support the view of normally pressured formation. FEASIBILITY OF SHALLOW-PROBE HEAT FLOW SURVEYS IN THE BARENTS SEA Gary W. Zielinski, Omegalink International Ltd. ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. The latter application suggests an operational and interpretational advantage in performing combined heat flow/surface geochemical surveys in the Barents Sea and elsewhere. INTRODUCTION As part of the 1985 IKU Barents Sea heat flow program, reconnaissance shallow-probe heat flow measurements were performed at nine site locations, Saettem et al (1985). Corresponding thermal conductivity measurements were performed on gravity-core samples covering similar depth intervals (0 - meters). The intent of these measurements was to combine the shallow thermal data with the deeper downhole data to assess the feasibility and limitations of future shallow-probe surveys in the Barents Sea as cost effective means of increasing data density. The main problem associated with shallow penetration (less than 10 meters) heat flow measurements in shallow water areas is due to periodic fluctuation in bottom water temperature. These fluctuations propagate into the sediment and generally constitute serious disturbance to the background heat flow. This disturbing effect is generally absent in abyssal plain areas where most marine heat flow measurements are confined. question: Should we subtract hydrophone-to-geophone transit time or add straight-ray vertical travel time (1480 m/s) when converting hydrophone first-breaks to geophone times?
answer_text: Subtract the hydrophone‑to‑geophone transit time and add the straight‑ray vertical travel time using water velocity 1480 m/s.

context_snippets.text: Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction On the 20th August 2005, Vertical Incidence Vertical Seismic Profile (VIVSP) was carried out for Norsk Hydro on the deviated well 31/2-N-11-H in the Troll field, offshore Norway. The objective of the survey was to obtain an accurate time depth profile and VSP image to tie to surface seismic. This report describes the time picking of the checkshot data and processing of VIVSP data which was performed using Borseis proprietary software as implemented on Geoframe commercial baseline 4.0.3. The polarity convention adopted in this report is as follows. In normal polarity an upgoing compressional wave, reflected by an increase of acoustic impedance with depth, is displayed as a white trough (negative number). A4 figures in this report are plotted at vertical time scale of 20cm/sec. The raw x,y,z, surface sensor data, raw stacked x,y,z data and migrated datasets have been provided in SEGY format on CD-ROM accompanying this document. All digital data and the processing reports is also provided on CD-ROM.

The Horizontal MaXimum, Horizontal MiNimum, Tangent to first RaY and Normal to first RaY Components are shown in Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11 and Figure 12. A axis projection calculation is performed using HMX and axis stack with the well deviation to compute the true vertical (TV) and true horizontal (TH) wavefield. If the shotpoint is directly above the receiver TRY and TV would be the same, but in cases where the shot position is slightly off they will differ. The TRY will be used to calculate the deconvolution parameters, which again will be applied on the TV wavefield. 3.4 Preprocessing Examination of the seismic amplitudes and frequency content of the TRY component has been performed prior to the preprocessing. After careful analysis of the spectral content, zero phase third order Butterworth filter with bandpass frequency interval of 5-95Hz was applied to both the TRY and TV. The choice of bandpass was made to preserve the maximum frequency content in the data at this early stage of the processing and at the same time to remove the higher frequency noise. The data was then normalized and corrected to vertical one way travel time below MSL by subtracting the transit time from hydrophone to geophone and adding the vertical travel time using straight ray assumption and water velocity of 1480 m/s. Applying normalization turns the downgoing wavefield into plane wavefield, which later will provide more robust computations.

Commercial In Confidence 4 Sonic Calibration The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the sonic slowness log to match the vertical VSP transit times. 4.1 Compressional Sonic Calibration Prior to sonic calibration the log data (compressional & shear sonic, density, calliper, gamma ray, neutron porosity, resistivity and Photo-Electric Factor logs) were petrophysically validated (including depth-matching and environmental corrections) by Norsk Hydro. Compressional sonic was available from 1699m MD DF to 3200m MD DF. This was corrected to true vertical depth using the well deviation and bulk shifted by -35.5m to the Seismic Reference Datum, to give compressional sonic log from 1508.5m to 2085.9m TVDSS. All accompanying logs were also corrected to TVDSS. The sonic logs had some sections that were straight line interpolated where data were missing. The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the integrated sonic slowness to match the vertical VSP travel times for given reference depth. The difference in time defines the drift (Δtdrift =ΔtVSP-Δtsonic), which can be either positive or negative. postitive drift is usually caused by dispersion in the seismic wavefield with depth or distance. negative drift (too slow sonic slowness) can be due to hole rugosity where Vformation > Vborehole-fluid and is generally very local effect. In order to minimize the residual drift function, the user defined smoothed drift curve has been designed to honour the raw drift curve as closely as possible with view to generating “calibrated” sonic log that should be used for time to depth conversion only and NOT used for Acoustic Impedance generation. For AI generation, the raw sonic, correctly time indexed using the calibrated velocity function has been used for the input to the synthetic reflectivity generation. The compressional sonic was calibrated using the geometrically corrected, vertical Time/Depth relationship from the Vertical Incidence VSP survey. comparison of the sonic slowness log and the VIVSP interval velocities is shown in Figure 23 and an initial visual inspection shows the character appears similar with major lithological boundaries tying very well. The sonic, VSP interval, RMS and average velocities after calibration are shown in Figure 25 and are available as digital logs on the CD-ROM accompanying this report. The velocity information and calibrated time depth curves are tabulated in Velocity Report, Time to Depth Report and Depth to Time Report.

question: How do lost-circulation incidence and subsequent squeeze-job frequency compare between drilling operations and casing/cementing stages?

context_snippets.text: 1.1 INTRODUCTION Well 2/8 F-14 was planned to supplement and eventually replace production from well 2/8A-1A. The plan was to drill vertically through the reservoir section with entry 200m NNW of the original well, with planned TD in the Hod Formation. Cores and wireline logs were planned in the reservoir section. As reference for future subsidence and compaction studies, radioactive markers were to be placed in the Tor Formation by wireline. The well plan was to build to 27° at the 13-3/8 shoe and then vertically to TD. The Tor Formation was planned to be drilled with 9-5/8 drilling liner. Three cores were originally planned for the Tor formation. Wireline logs were also planned in the reservoir section. This well was drilled with Versaport synthetic oil based mud system from 354m. The cuttings were slurrified in the MSD unit and injected into the Valhall disposal well. SERVICE PROVIDED Baker Hughes INTEQ provided Drillbyte service using software version 2.3.0RO from an INTEQ combined SLS and MWD logging unit on well 2/8 F-14, from 354m to total depth of 2635m. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mudlogging, automatic real-time data acquisition, monitoring, recording and pore pressure analyses were carried out. Continuous evaluation of pore pressure and drilling progress provided an aid in optimising drilling performance and ensured that drilling operations continued with maximum safety to personnel, the well and equipment. The operator was continually advised as to the status of these analyses and data, and the results were stored on magnetic media for post well evaluation. The printouts and plots are contained in the appendices and attachments of this report.

The objective of this report is to provide detailed description of the wireline operation and data acquisition for the Aker BP 2/8-F-18A well in the Valhall field. The service provider for the wireline operations was Schlumberger and the QA/QC witnessing was carried out by Dave Hardy and Lindsay Herbert of One&Zero. This report focuses on the wireline data acquisition in relation to the section. The 2/8-F-18 is slanted pilot hole dedicated for data acquisition to inform later decisions of the Lower Hod development. The project currently carries producers and injector; however, the test injector (2/8-F-18 B) along with core data and wireline logs will be used to assess the feasibility of further infill injector placement. The primary target is the Hod package, although hydrocarbons are present throughout Hod to Hod 5/6. Wireline logs will be acquired throughout the entire open hole interval, which also includes Tor formation above. This is potentially water flooded by sea water, and will thus provide information regarding residual oil saturation (Sor) behind the flood-front. Geological background and expected formation properties 2/8-F-18 will only have chalk exposed, consisting of Tor, Magne and Hod formation. The expected porosity range between 20-45 p.u with associated permeability ranging between 0.01-6 mD. The Hod layer is assumed to be tight zone acting as baffle between Tor/Magne and Lower Hod, which consists of Hod 3, Hod and Hod 5/6. Water saturation (Sw) is expected to range between 30-100 %. Water salinity is likely 55 ppk; however, Tor formation may have lower salinity due to sea water injection
