answer_text: Transmitted VSP frequency range observed: 5–90 Hz; zero-phase response reliable up to at least 60 Hz.

context_snippets.text: The 15/12-16s deviated well VSP was recorded by Schlumberger on 14th March 2006 and the data were provided to Zebra Geosciences Ltd in SEGY format-1. The stated objectives of the VSP survey were as follows: 1. To provide detailed compression wave time-depth relationship over the complete well. 2. To provide clear match between the zero phase multiple free VSP and the surface seismic data 3. To provide high resolution zero phase image of the reservoir. It is felt that the survey has been reasonably successful in achieving these objectives. Rig source data were recorded by Schlumberger with levels at separation suitable for VSP processing between 2955.0m and 2004m MDbDF. Above this depth, checkshot data were recorded at depths of After timing, the data were processed by Zebra Geosciences to yield P-wave reflection image. An FK plot of the raw data shows frequency content in the transmitted arrival of at least 5-90Hz with only very low levels of random noise and unwanted coherent arrivals evident in the raw data. The frequency content in the reflected wavefield is lower and final data have been filtered at 5,10-50,70Hz. The upgoing wavefield data, are shown before deconvolution with preliminary 3,5-100,120Hz filter as Figure 1.1, after deconvolution with the 5,10-50,70Hz filter as Figure and then after the application of trace median tracking filter ms/trc dip as Figure 1.3. The seismic line L905 was provided to Zebra geosciences in SEGY-1 format. The VSP corridor and synthetic seismogram filtered with 5,10-50,70Hz have been inserted into this line and are displayed in Figures 1.4, & 1.5. There is good match between the VSP and synthetic data and the borehole data shows good match to the surface seismic line. The VSP is thought to be good estimate of the zero phase multiples free seismic response at the well location up to frequencies of at least 60Hz. This is supported by the match of the VSP to the synthetic seismogram which is generated from the logs recorded in the borehole. A calibrated velocity log has been computed using the corrected vertical times from the VSP data and the available log data. The calibrated acoustic log is provided on linear 1:1000 depth scale as Enclosure and on linear time scale together with the VSP, synthetic seismogram and other log data as Enclosure 2. Normal polarity: An upgoing compressional wave is recorded as negative number and plotted as white trough (i.e. for upgoing wavefields: an increase in acoustic impedance is represented by white trough.) Recommendations from the lessons learned can be found under Lessons Learned A system for drilling and under-reaming at the same time during directional work was utilized for the first on Valhall (and the North Sea) in this well. The system called Steerable Reaming While Drilling (SRWD) was used in the first part of the reservoir section with positive results and is therefor recommended for use in future wells where underreaming is required to get casing/liner to bottom. Lesson: Magnetic interference was experienced from MD even though the directional plan indicated that no wells should be close enough to cause interference. With magnetic interference causing problems with MWD surveys, and also with cement in samples, gyro was run to confirm the 20 tie-in and to check well center coordinates. The pressures in the adjacent wells were monitored. Proximity calculations were run and MWD surveys were compared to the gyro. Recommendation: contingency plan for well collision, double checking of directional plans with respect to the tie-in, slot and platform center coordinates, and check that all adjacent wells and sidetracks are identified and taken into account when making directional/anti-collision programs should be developed. Lesson: leak in the injection line to A-3 on Valhall DP caused injection shutdown and six hours of rig time. After the injection was shut down at Valhall, drilling continued until the MSD holding tank was full. It was decided that cuttings were not to be dumped overboard because removing/installing the conveyors to dump cuttings would require several hours, and because disconnecting transfer lines would cause slurry to be spilled on WP platform.

context_snippets.text: GEOLABil NOR distribution is more like that expected for light oil than condensate. condensate would be expected to have lesser amount of biomarkers than observed and an even lighter distribution. The observed fragmentograms of the saturated fraction indicate marine source rock, likely to be of Jurassic origin, most likely Upper Jurassic. The fragmentograms of the aromatic fraction support the above maturity estimates. The density of the sample was found to be API 40°, typical of light oils. Condensates would usually have an API value of 45° or more. This fits well with the other data for the oil. The Rock-Eval data for the cuttings samples show strong dominance of oil based mud additives in the samples. Also the samples were, even after considerable effort to wash them, very dirty with mud clearly adsorbed to the particle surfaces. As result, the Rock-Eval data are not considered to show any real variation or trend in the cuttings samples. The TOC results are probably more close to reality, but any detailed interpretation on the basis of these is also considered to be futile. The TOC content of the normally very rich Mandal Formation could indicate that the samples are past peak oil generation. That the maturity is high can be seen from vitrinite data (see tables and histograms from IFE, Appendix IV). On the basis of the vitrinite data the top of the oil window (0.6 % Ro) is entered at about 3200 m, base oil window (1.0 % Ro) at about 4100 ( very tentative since samples around this depth lack identifiable vitrinite) and base condensate window (1.3 % Ro at about 4600 m). The thermal extract chromatogram of the 4531 cuttings sample (dark grey marl) shows dominantly drill mud signature. The thermal extract from sandstone core sample might also be influenced by the drill mud, but this sample might also contain hydrocarbons derived from in-situ oil. It is not possible to give any more details about the source or maturity based on these data. The extraction data are also very affected by the oil based drilling mud. This is also shown in the saturated hydrocarbons chromatograms of the two analysed samples. It cannot be excluded that other hydrocarbons are present as well, but this is reduced to speculation due to the dominance of the oil based mud signature which masks the in-situ signature.

question: For well 6407/8-6, can you confirm CT deliverables: topograms, four slice images per 100 cm, 51 SWC, and eight 1.5" plugs?
answer_text: Yes — CT deliverables include topograms with four slice images every 100 cm, and 51 SWC samples plus eight 1.5" horizontal plugs were CT-scanned.

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 15

5 CT SCANNING CT-scanning The analytical programme required CT (Computer Tomography) of core material from this well. The resolution for the CT-Scan,s are 512 512 pixels. 5.1 CT Scanning Whole Core CT scanning visualises representative homogeneous sections for possible further studies. The CT scan also helps locating any fractured areas of the core, identify density variations and can be used as tool for orientation of the core prior to slabbing or subsequent plug sampling. The core still in unopened core inner barrels was CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One overview picture (topogram) and four slice pictures were produced every 100-cm of core. The topogram is standard X-ray photo taken from above, covering 100 cm of core. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. 5.2 CT Scanning Seal Peels All Seal Peels (preserved whole core) from this well were CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One (topogram) overview picture, two radial and two axial slice pictures were produced for each seal peel. The topogram is standard X-ray Scan taken from above, covering the length of the preserved core sample. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. The slice pictures are reading of radiation passing through the core. An X-ray source is sending pulses of energy through the core and set of detectors rotating around the core detects the passing signals. The readings are used for making computer produced slice picture of the core. When seal peels are CT scanned, print of the CT scan is mounted along with the core B-cut representing the removed whole core. A total of fifty-one SWC samples and eight 1,5” Horizontal plugs were also CT-Scanned. The CT scans are presented as separate report. Restricted 11

question: In Cook Fm, how does MSFL, LLS, induction and laterolog reliability differ between water-bearing and oil zones?
answer_text: In the Cook Fm: MSFL is degraded by wash‑outs (less reliable), LLS reads deeper and is less affected (more reliable), induction logs give better readings in water‑bearing zones, and laterologs are preferred in oil zones.

Analysis methods The well is analysed using computer model based on the complex lithology method. question: What is the justification for using only up-run peak picks after comparing down- and up-arrival picks in sonic arrival analysis?
answer_text: Because down- and up-run arrival times agreed well and, for consistency, only the up-run peak arrival times were used for the final calculations.

context_snippets.text: lc. DATA PROCESSING i. Velocity Survey Computations The digital data were demultiplexed and displayed. The reference hydrophone traces were examined and the arrival time of the first peak was picked on one pilot trace, against which all other reference hydrophone traces were cross-correlated, thus establishing consistent hydrophone time picks. Each downhole geophone trace was subsequently shifted by the peak arrival time value of the corresponding reference hydrophone trace, so that all downhole geophone traces were referenced to the effective hydrophone depth (i.e. the source depth plus the source-geophone distance). The downhole geophone traces for each depth level were then stacked using median summation technique. Travel times were picked from these records. Again the pick was made at the first extremum of the stacked trace which appears as peak on the recorded data. Enclosures 1A-1C display the stacked three-component seismic data for all levels. The accuracy of the depth sensor was checked by comparing wavelet arrival times of levels occupied during the down and up runs of each survey. The agreement was good. For consistency, only up run peak arrival times were used for the final calculations. The observed travel times were converted to vertical times and then referenced to Datum. These time-depth pairs form the input data for the final velocity survey computations, yielding the average, RMS and interval velocities given in Sections 2, and 5. Figure shows the plot of time-depth, interval, average and RMS velocity.

Since an error in the time pick reduces the interval time of one unit and increases the interval time of the adjacent unit correspondingly these errors do not cumulate in the deeper layers. context_snippets.text: 7. BIOSTRATIGRAPHY LATE CRETACEOUS A. Interval: 2,500m - 2,560m; Early Santonian (top not seen). Lithostratigraphic Units: Shetland Group, Kyrre Formation. Environment: Marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal. The top and age of this interval are based on: the top occurrence of consistently common Cenosphaera spp. at 2,500m, and Stensioeina polonica at 2,560m, indicating Zone LKM7 of Early Santonian age. the top occurrence of Heterosphaeridium difficile at 2,520m, indicating the Early Santonian LKP5c subzone. Micropalaeontology Microfaunas are moderately abundant and diverse, consisting of radiolaria, diatoms and planktonic, agglutinating and calcareous benthonic foraminifera. Events of note include prominent Coscinodiscus sp. and common Coscinodiscus sp.9 at 2,500m and Globotruncana linneiana at 2,560m. A marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment is indicated. 2) Palynology Assemblages are abundant and diverse with dinocysts predominating and subordinate pollen. CHAPTER Summary 1. Youngest strata examined comprise arenaceous deposits assigned to the Nordland Group of ranging Pleistocene - Pliocene age. It is noteworthy that the normally distinctive Early Pliocene palynofloras are lacking, hence the interval may be of post-Early Pliocene age. 2. The Nordland Group rests unconformably upon Hordaland Group deposits of Oligocene age. These strata are laterally correlative with the Lark Formation, as defined in the UKCS. Following an initial phase of upper bathyal deposition, sediments above 1050m accumulated under shelfal conditions. 3. The Early Oligocene rests with marked unconformity upon thin development of the Early Eocene Balder Formation. No evidence is encountered to indicate the presence of Hordaland Group sediments of Eocene age. 4. The Early Eocene Balder Formation rests with an intra-Rogaland Group hiatus upon slightly truncated Lista Formation as there is no positive biodata for palynofloral Subzones PP4D, PP4C, PP5B or PP5A. 5. The Paleocene comprises both the Lista and Vale Formations, with earliest Paleocene (equivalent to microfaunal Zone MP[I] and palynofloral Zone PP1) strata absent. The regionally recognised improvement in open marine conditions in the Early Paleocene is evident. It is noteworthy that within sediments attributable to palynofloral Subzones PP3D (part)-PP3A significant input of reworking is evident. This may reflect the proximity to gravity flow fan systems. Erosion of Jurassic and Cretaceous material was probably via shelf edge incision. Recycling becomes less prominent in the Early Paleocene. 6. The Early Paleocene rests with significant, erosional unconformity upon the Kyrre Formation of early Campanian age. This relationship of Tertiary and Mesozoic strata is characteristic of most wells between 62°N and 63° 25'N along the edge of the Norwegian shelf. 7. The Kyrre Formation comprises the early Campanian and most of the late Santonian and is represented by mudstones deposited under upper bathyal depths. Microfaunal data from 1480m substantiate the inferred maximum flooding surface (MFS) at 1472m(log). The near base Campanian event is probably correlative with the Ma flooding event of Haq et al. (1987). Close to the base of the Kyrre Formation further MFS is inferred at 1745m(log), occurring in proximity to the late/early Santonian boundary. This surface is correlated to the 86 Ma MFS of Haq et al. (1987). Page

121/4 Drilling Phase BHA 8, similar in specification to the eventual drilling assembly, was run in hole to drill out the 13 3/8 shoe, but at 750m the cross-over between the drill collars and HWDP backed out and the BHA plunged 2000m to its death on top of the float collar. BHA was therefore standard fishing assembly and successfully retrieved the drilling BHA in the first run. Although there was no visible damage to the assembly, all tools were laid down for inspection as precaution. BHA 10 was therefore the first assembly to drill formation and it should be noted that the (back-up) motor utilised was of specification designed for use at higher temperatures deeper in the hole. The rotor/stator fit therefore, was not ideal for this run but good differential pressure was in any case maintained whilst drilling. This replacement motor also had stabiliser sleeve fixed on the bent housing rather than the rotating bit-box model that is the preferred option for serious orientation. Notwithstanding the above, any disappointment with regard to ROP was perhaps as much function of bit choice as motor design, though pump problems with their associated low flow rates undoubtedly played part. Security FM2943DR was chosen for this section and comparisons drawn between this location and nearby Asgard show that in the latter field, somewhat more aggressive (Hycalog) bits are used above the Lysing formation. Interestingly, use of this type of bit on Asgard does not appear to compromise steerability but even with the bit chosen, orientation on this location was found to be difficult and may be an indication that formations here are somewhat different to those on Asgard, at least in their steerability. In the 17Y2 phase the borehole had been allowed to drift towards the southwest corner of the target and it was deemed prudent to nudge the well back towards target centre prior to drilling into the Lysing (the barrier on Asgard between steerable and difficult formations). This was attempted on two occasions with BHA 10 but with little success, tool face tending to be erratic and difficult to control. Poor MWD signals (the tool was later to fail) may have been part of the problem but the claystone found on this location is undoubtedly less steerable than that on Asgard. Combined with the fact that the bend on the motor was set at the minimum 0.39°, little effect was seen from the orientation. At 3223m the MWD failed and the assembly pulled to replace the tool. On surface. little wear was seen on the bit that was therefore re-run and as well as changing the MWD. the opportunity was taken to increase the bend on the motor to 0.78° so that orientation would have more effect. Steering was attempted as soon as the BHA was run to bottom but again, tool face control was difficult and steering ineffective. Fortunately, the path of the well at this point continued to drift towards the northeast, making further time-consuming attempts at correction unnecessary. steady but slow increase in angle was noted throughout this run but no specific disadvantage was seen in increasing the bend of the motor and overall, good pendulum effect was maintained despite the use of relatively aggressive drilling parameters in order to improve the rate of penetration. Little was seen of the Lysing sandstone expected to dull the bit and despite continued pump problems, an overall improvement in ROP over the previous run was noted. At 4200m planned BHA change took effect and although from purely directional point of view packed assembly would have been the preferred option in order to keep the well straight, the motor was replaced with rotary pendulum

The hole was circulated clean and FIT was performed to SG EMW. Unintentional, higher pressure was applied, equivalent to SG, when performing the FIT breaking the formation. However, no problems related to leak off' was experienced throughout the section. Displacement to 1.75 sg Versa Vert oil based mud was carried out during drilling the cement. This mud was used in rest of the section to section ID at 5555 mMD. The 121/4 hole was then drilled and oriented to 3800 mMD. From 3800 to 4275 rotary drilling found place. After several attempt to steer below Lysing Fm, the BHA was pulled out of hole at 4299 mMD. A motor assembly with extra strong motor with bend, MWD-CDR, and less aggressive PDC bit was then run in hole to drill and orient second turn. Drilled from 4299 to 4306 MD, drilled and oriented from 4306 to 4329 MD. Pulled out due to poor drilling rate even in rotation. Changed bit back to the aggressive BX447, else same BHA. Ran in hole and drilled and oriented from 4329 MD. Problems holding tool face and to feed stable weight down to bit. Excellent ROP in rotation (30-40 m/hr). Drilled with this assembly down to 4645 MD. Steering was difficult and did not achieve enough turn. It was decided to pull out to run in with turbine. Ran in with 1° bend turbine and Smith MGR35DHS bit, this was short gauge medium aggressive bit, and new MWD tool. The inclination remained around 45° - 47°, and the well was turned approximately 35° through this bit run - from 347° to 312°. Penetration rates were in the order of - m/hr while orienting and - 20 m/hr while rotating. The bit was pulled at 5000 mMD; this was planned trip to change assembly for the build in inclination. A rotary assembly with TRACS tool and new MWD (including ISONIC) was run in the hole. The Lysing formation was reamed for ISONIC data on the way the hole; the first stand with circulation for real-time data, then without circulation for memory data only. The MWD tool stopped transmitting data at approximately 5026 mMD, and the assembly was pulled at 5035 mMD. The rotary assembly was rerun with new MWD tool. There was no communication with this tool when it was tested at 500 m, so the assembly was pulled. The backup MWD tool was run with the old CDR. This assembly drilled to section I'D at 5555 m. The penetration rate was much higher than expected at an average m/hr for the run, with ROPs of 20 - 30 m/hr between slower dolomite stringers. The Garn Formation was seen on the MWD log, and returns were circulated at 5528 mMD. The returns contained mainly claystone with siltstone and some sandstone, and in view of the relatively high GR values, drilling continued to 5555 mMD where returns were circulated again. The returns contained sandstone, confirming the Garn Formation. The 5/8 casing was run to 5540 mMD. The Lange sandstones caused some problems, with tight hole from 4880 m, but the casing was landed successfully. The casing was cemented with approximately 40% returns. gyro survey was run in casing prior to drilling out the shoe.

They were exposed to vacuum and saturated with simulated formation water. The pore pressure were loaded to 10 bar and then unloaded to atmospheric pressure. Prior to the analyses the ionic equilibrium between the brine and the rock were allowed to be reached. The following net confining pressure levels were applied: 50 bar, 100 bar, 200 bar, 300 bar and 400 bar. At each confining pressure level the samples were measured for water permeability, porosity and formation resistivity factor. Pore pressure and temperature were at room conditions during the measurements. Stability time at each pressure level was 24 hours. For each step of increasing confining pressure, the measurements were done according to the following procedure: creeping time 15 min. 30 min. 60 min. 2 hours 4 hours 8 hours 24 hours pore volume variation >0000004 electrical resistance >00004XX brine permeability a) Water permeability, (K) Water permeability was measured by pumping simulated formation water (filtered and degassed) through the samples at constant flowrate until the differential pressure stabilized. Differential pressure and flowrate were recorded, thus the permeability could be calculated. The permeability measurements were performed within from to 30 minutes due to the permeability of the samples. The permeability measurments started after hours and the pore volume variation was almost stopped at that time. b) Porosity, (0) A graduated pipette was used to collect expelled water when the net confining pressure was increased, thus the reduction in pore volume could be recorded. c) Formation Resistivity Factor, (FP) The two end pieces of the core holder were used as separate electrodes for electrical measurements. Steel nets were placed at the end faces of the sample to ensure good electrical contact. The samples were exposed to known current of frequency of kHz. The impedance and the phase angle were recorded for each sample, allowing calculation of the electrical sample resistivity. Knowing the resistivity of the simulated formation water, formation resistivity factor was calculated for each sample. question: For the Hekkingen, Snadd, and Kobbe formations, how do TOC, kerogen type, and oil versus gas potential compare?
answer_text: Hekkingen: rich TOC (up to 7.8%), kerogen type II, mainly oil‑prone (marine with some terrestrial input); Snadd: highly variable TOC (0.03–12.67%, average ~1%), mainly kerogen type III and predominantly gas‑prone with locally oil‑prone intervals. Kobbe: TOC up to 3.27%, kerogen type not explicitly stated but terrestrially influenced, with mixed oil‑and‑gas potential producing predominantly waxy oil.

(Data in Table A6a-b) Predictions of the compositional kinetic models concerning the physical properties (GOR, saturation pressure, formation volume factor Bo) of the fluids generated as function of primary cracking are shown in Figure and Table A7. The observations made based on activation energy distributions and carbon chain length distributions from pyrolysis are generally supported by the results shown. P-N-A low wax petroleum type was predicted, thus the fluids generated fall within the black oil class. They reach saturation pressures of >200 bars (approximately begin of volatile oil) only at highest kerogen conversion levels (90% TR) where secondary cracking reactions might have already set in under closed-system pyrolysis conditions. Saturation pressures of both samples gradually evolve from ~150 bar for sample and ~100 bar for sample to values between 200 and 250 bar with maturity. Similarily, GOR values evolve from 155 respectively 89 Sm3/Sm3 to 504 respectively 352 Sm3/Sm3 at highest maturity levels (90% TR). GOR values of the Hekkingen Fm sample from the Krill Member are higher at all kerogen conversion levels. Both samples show systematics of GOR evolution which reflect the earlier results from kinetics and pyrolysis GC: In concordance with moderatley broad Ea distribution and the aromatic and phenolic signature observed under open-system pyrolysis conditions GORs as well as saturation pressures and formation volume factors show relatively steep gradients. Increasing GORs and saturation pressures with increasing maturity very well reproduce the natural behaviour of mixed terrestrial-marine organic matter derived fluids. In contrast, rather uniform GORs and saturation pressures would reproduce the natural behaviour of aquatic, mainly algal, homogeneous Type organic matter derived fluids. The physical properties of fluids generated from both samples can therefore be described as typically mixed terrestrial-marine. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

3.7 REFERENCE WELLS Several wells have been considered for extrapolation with the play concept. These are essentially situated in the Hammerfest Basin northeast of the licence area. Data from these wells were used to constrain predictions of the petrophysical characteristics of the inferred reservoir sandstones of the Realgrunnen Group and, to lesser extent, of the Lower Basal Clastics in the Gamma Prospect. They comprise conventional wells drilled in the quadrants 7119, 7120, 7121, 7122 and 7219, as well as IKU shallow drilling 7018/05-U- 06 at the margin of the Troms-Finnmark Platform some 25 km southwest of the licence area. Thermal and kinetic input parameters derived from some of the considered wells were used to calibrate the modelling of hydrocarbon generation and expulsion from the principal source rock of the Hekkingen Formation in the Tromso Basin. Hydrocarbon characteristics were mainly extrapolated from data representative for the discoveries in the Hammerfest Basin, namely 7122/6-1 (oil and gas), Snohvit (oil and gas), Albatross (oil and gas), Askeladden (oil and gas), and Alke (gas). 3.8 OPERATIONAL GEOLOGY WELL PROGRAM 3.8.1 SAMPLING PROGRAM The standard cuttings sampling intervals will be as follows (Fig. 3.8.1): every 10 from 30 csg shoe (after return of drilling fluid) down to thel3 3/8 casing shoe at 2000 m. every from the 5/8 casing shoe down to T.D. at 3009 m. Wet samples will be collected at each interval and sent onshore periodically for splitting. The wellsite geologist will instruct the mud loggers in order to get sufficient samples to fulfil the dispatching requirements (see data distribution chart). Storage and distribution of samples to partners and the NPD will be handled as per later instruction. Extra samples will be taken on wellsite geologists request. Samples will be continuously examined under microscope and fluoroscope, and calcimetry will be performed with spacing decided upon by the wellsite geologist. One set of washed and dried samples will be kept on the rig until the well is finished. The geochemical samples (an additional unwashed set) will be collected on request from the Norsk Agip Exploration department.

121/4 Drilling Phase BHA 8, similar in specification to the eventual drilling assembly, was run in hole to drill out the 13 3/8 shoe, but at 750m the cross-over between the drill collars and HWDP backed out and the BHA plunged 2000m to its death on top of the float collar. BHA was therefore standard fishing assembly and successfully retrieved the drilling BHA in the first run. Although there was no visible damage to the assembly, all tools were laid down for inspection as precaution. BHA 10 was therefore the first assembly to drill formation and it should be noted that the (back-up) motor utilised was of specification designed for use at higher temperatures deeper in the hole. The rotor/stator fit therefore, was not ideal for this run but good differential pressure was in any case maintained whilst drilling. This replacement motor also had stabiliser sleeve fixed on the bent housing rather than the rotating bit-box model that is the preferred option for serious orientation. Notwithstanding the above, any disappointment with regard to ROP was perhaps as much function of bit choice as motor design, though pump problems with their associated low flow rates undoubtedly played part. Security FM2943DR was chosen for this section and comparisons drawn between this location and nearby Asgard show that in the latter field, somewhat more aggressive (Hycalog) bits are used above the Lysing formation. Interestingly, use of this type of bit on Asgard does not appear to compromise steerability but even with the bit chosen, orientation on this location was found to be difficult and may be an indication that formations here are somewhat different to those on Asgard, at least in their steerability. In the 17Y2 phase the borehole had been allowed to drift towards the southwest corner of the target and it was deemed prudent to nudge the well back towards target centre prior to drilling into the Lysing (the barrier on Asgard between steerable and difficult formations). This was attempted on two occasions with BHA 10 but with little success, tool face tending to be erratic and difficult to control. Poor MWD signals (the tool was later to fail) may have been part of the problem but the claystone found on this location is undoubtedly less steerable than that on Asgard. Combined with the fact that the bend on the motor was set at the minimum 0.39°, little effect was seen from the orientation. At 3223m the MWD failed and the assembly pulled to replace the tool. On surface. little wear was seen on the bit that was therefore re-run and as well as changing the MWD. the opportunity was taken to increase the bend on the motor to 0.78° so that orientation would have more effect. Steering was attempted as soon as the BHA was run to bottom but again, tool face control was difficult and steering ineffective. Fortunately, the path of the well at this point continued to drift towards the northeast, making further time-consuming attempts at correction unnecessary. steady but slow increase in angle was noted throughout this run but no specific disadvantage was seen in increasing the bend of the motor and overall, good pendulum effect was maintained despite the use of relatively aggressive drilling parameters in order to improve the rate of penetration. Little was seen of the Lysing sandstone expected to dull the bit and despite continued pump problems, an overall improvement in ROP over the previous run was noted. At 4200m planned BHA change took effect and although from purely directional point of view packed assembly would have been the preferred option in order to keep the well straight, the motor was replaced with rotary pendulum

The Lysing formation was reamed for ISONIC data on the way the hole; the first stand with circulation for real-time data, then without circulation for memory data only. The MWD tool stopped transmitting data at approximately 5026 mMD, and the assembly was pulled at 5035 mMD. The rotary assembly was rerun with new MWD tool. There was no communication with this tool when it was tested at 500 m, so the assembly was pulled. The backup MWD tool was run with the old CDR. This assembly drilled to section I'D at 5555 m. The penetration rate was much higher than expected at an average m/hr for the run, with ROPs of 20 - 30 m/hr between slower dolomite stringers. The Garn Formation was seen on the MWD log, and returns were circulated at 5528 mMD. The returns contained mainly claystone with siltstone and some sandstone, and in view of the relatively high GR values, drilling continued to 5555 mMD where returns were circulated again. The returns contained sandstone, confirming the Garn Formation. The 5/8 casing was run to 5540 mMD. The Lange sandstones caused some problems, with tight hole from 4880 m, but the casing was landed successfully. The casing was cemented with approximately 40% returns. gyro survey was run in casing prior to drilling out the shoe.

question: For well 35/11-15 ST2, if preserved seal-peel cores are retested, which porosity and bulk-volume determination methods should be used?
answer_text: Measure grain volume/porosity by helium injection using a Boyle's-law porosimeter and determine bulk volume by mercury immersion using the weigh-balance/buoyancy technique.

context_snippets.text: Porosity and grain density Grain volume was measured by helium injection using Boyle's law porosimeter. Bulk volume was determined by immersing the sample in mercury, using the weigh balance/ buoyancy technique. Porosity and grain density were calculated by recording the weight of the samples, PRESERVATION: Preserved whole core samples Twenty one whole core samples (seal peels) for preservation were cut from the cores and preserved in Ergoseal wax. A list over preserved samples is included in section of this report. Core photos Digital core photos ( Corimag ) were taken of the A-cut, both white and UV-light. The core photos are delivered as separate report. Slabbing and mounting of core cuts After all samples had been taken, the cores were slabbed using long bed saw with water cooled diamond saw blade. The whole core length (except seal peels) was slabbed into four parts (A,B,C and D-cut). After slabbing, the B-cut (reference cut) was mounted in plastic trays by casting in epoxy resin. 3 Geological Programme 3.1 Purpose of the Well The vertical exploration well 2/6-5 will be drilled on the Chalk Prospect which is situated in the central eastern part of PL 008 (Figs. and 3.2). The main purpose of well 2/6-5 is to test the presence of hydrocarbons and the reservoir properties within the Shetland Group in the Chalk Prospect. The planned TD of the well is 25 into Basement, or prognosed TD at 3185 mRKB. The well will be planned as possible future producer. Secondary purpose of the well is to test possible sediment fill in the interval between the Shetland Group and the basement topography. For well 2/6-5 the primary target of Cretaceous age is prognosed at 2843 mRKB, below approx. 40 of the Ekofisk Tight zone causing the laterally consistent seismic reflector mapped as the Top Shetland horizon. The primary target interval consists of the total Shetland package below the tight zone mentioned above. Target interval belongs to the Ekofisk-, Tor- and Hod Formations (or their time equivalents). Reservoir zones are expected in several intervals, some in pressure communication and some not. A distinct change in ROP is expected when drilling from the Ekofisk Formation tight zone into the primary target of prognosed highly porous carbonates. The porosity in the Shetland Group is expected to be more than 35%, locally more than 50%. Open reservoir structure and or zones with large number of small fractures are expected. Secondary target is the section mapped below the Shetland Group. This interval is of unknown age, but probably belonging to Jurassic/Triassic infill of the faulted basement topography of the Mandal High. However, the interval might show up as only representing intra basement reflectivity within metamorphic rocks. The well is located high on structural closure defined on Top Shetland Group (Figs. and 3.2). The trapping mechanism is partly caused by structuring reflecting the Paleotopography of the underlying crystalline Mandal High, and partly due to stratigraphical component within the Shetland Group (Fig. 3.3). The latter is supported by the observation of anomally low seismic stacking velocities for parts of this interval draping the Mandal High. A possible seismic direct hydrocarbon indicator (flatspot) is observed in the Shetland Group at approx. 2965 mRKB (2.855 sec TWT.). The total depth of the well is estimated to 3185 mRKB (with an uncertainty of +/- 175 m), or 25 m within basement, whatever comes first. 1:\FELLESTORINGLETEBOR\2_6_5\PROGRAM\265WP.DOC 17

Following transgressive event in Early Bajocian times, claystones of the Viking Group, Melke Formation accumulated in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions, becoming fully marine, inner shelf by Late Bajocian times. These sediments accumulated through to Middle Oxfordian times with apparent continuity in similar environments as sedimentation rates generally kept pace with subsidence. The stacked reference hydrophone component and stacked geophone data for all levels of each component are shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, & 7. The measured slant times were then geometrically converted to vertical times below the source and then corrected to the datum of MSL using static correction of ms, at water velocity 1500 m/sec. The depth range is – MD below DF. For the calibration, the acoustic log was integrated to produce a time-log, which is depth-indexed. The discrepancy between the corrected checkshot time of the shallowest checkshot level (within the logged interval) and the corresponding log-derived time was then computed. The time-log was next shifted by adding this value to all the time-log values, thus tying the log to the shallowest checkshot. A drift curve was then generated, showing the difference between the corrected checkshot times and the corresponding times from the shifted time-log. Calibration points fixing the drift at certain depths (including the top and bottom of the logged interval) were then chosen. Such that they divide the drift curve into intervals of approximately linear drift, and also so that they occur at velocity contrasts. The calibration points are indicated with triangular marks on the drift curve displayed on Enclosure 1. The shifts applied to the log are considered reasonable with maximum shift of 14us/m (4.3us/ft). For each interval between consecutive calibration points, the ratio between the difference in the fixed drift of these calibration points and the interval thickness was computed, and this constant was added to all acoustic log values of the interval, thus shifting the acoustic log in this interval by this amount. The whole acoustic log was calibrated by repeating this procedure for all calibration point intervals. After calibration, the calibrated time-log was computed by integrating the calibrated acoustic log and tying it to the shallowest checkshot. The residual drift curve, shown on Enclosure 1, was generated using the corrected checkshot times and the calibrated time-log. Stewart (1987) in an important paper on the stratigraphy of S the Early Paleogene of the central North Sea documents series of depositional sequences providing valuable framework that, combined with lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data allow detailed stratigraphic analysis of the sedimentary basin. Somewhat similar studies have also been carried out on the Frigg Field (Conort 1986). Stewart (0p.cit.) recognised total of 10 seismically defined sequences based on study of over 300 wells. Each depositional sequence (Stewart p. 559) is regarded as an essentially chronostratigraphic unit that can be correlated on regional scale. The sequence boundaries are frequently associated with characteristic wireline log responses which locally permit recognition of the sequence by well data alone.

Observed amounts of fine sandstone increase in the lower part of the well section making up 30 - 40% of the lithologies and often 50%. The sandstones are micaceous, with occasional coaly streaks. There are traces of glauconite or chlorite and pyrite throughout most of the interval. Towards the base of the well section claystones are again predominant and some limestones are observed. The base of this interval is set at the uppermost core sample at 2682m. See comment (2) under Bathonian to Bajocian interval.

1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

question: Which measurements and setups are specified for well 6407/8-6 (include plug prep/CT, D&S moisture, Specγ, and STT parameters)?
answer_text: Plug prep/plug handling: horizontal plugs drilled (including 1.5″ noted), cut with an air‑driven plug drill using Clarisol lubricant and immediately wrapped in cling film, aluminium foil and ProtecCore laminate; CT: 512×512 pixel CT scans — whole core: one topogram + four slice pictures every 100 cm; seal peels: one topogram, two radial and two axial slices; 51 SWC and eight 1.5″ horizontal plugs CT‑scanned; D&S moisture: Dean‑Stark on plugs using Clarisol, water extracted with toluene (bp ≈110°C), methanol Soxhlet to remove salts, brine correction applied, samples dried at 60°C for 48 h; Specγ: NaI scintillator spectral core gamma, total gamma in c/min, K in %, Th and U in ppm, calibrated with IFE standards and plotted at 1:200; STT: simplified triaxial on 1×2″ vertical natural‑moisture samples with constant radial confining pressure 2 MPa and axial hydraulic loading to failure, failure read on manometer in MPa with a correction factor applied.

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 15

5 CT SCANNING CT-scanning The analytical programme required CT (Computer Tomography) of core material from this well. The resolution for the CT-Scan,s are 512 512 pixels. 5.1 CT Scanning Whole Core CT scanning visualises representative homogeneous sections for possible further studies. The CT scan also helps locating any fractured areas of the core, identify density variations and can be used as tool for orientation of the core prior to slabbing or subsequent plug sampling. The core still in unopened core inner barrels was CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One overview picture (topogram) and four slice pictures were produced every 100-cm of core. The topogram is standard X-ray photo taken from above, covering 100 cm of core. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. 5.2 CT Scanning Seal Peels All Seal Peels (preserved whole core) from this well were CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One (topogram) overview picture, two radial and two axial slice pictures were produced for each seal peel. The topogram is standard X-ray Scan taken from above, covering the length of the preserved core sample. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. The slice pictures are reading of radiation passing through the core. An X-ray source is sending pulses of energy through the core and set of detectors rotating around the core detects the passing signals. The readings are used for making computer produced slice picture of the core. When seal peels are CT scanned, print of the CT scan is mounted along with the core B-cut representing the removed whole core. A total of fifty-one SWC samples and eight 1,5” Horizontal plugs were also CT-Scanned. The CT scans are presented as separate report. Restricted 11

context_snippets.text: Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. Figures 1a-c show the Rock-Eval pyrolysis trace and the thermal extraction GC and pyrolysis-GC of Kolmule formation shale which has been washed with water only. Figures 1d-f show the Rock-Eval pyrolysis trace and the thermal extraction GC and pyrolysis-GC of

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

context_snippets.text: 8 PETROPHYSICAL EVALUATION SUMMARY The petrophysical evaluation of the well shows the primary and secondary objectives have low porosity, poor permeability and are wet. RFT's in the objectives recovered mud filtrate with some solution gas. The only hydrocarbons found are in gas sand at 2385 in the Snadd Formation. The sand has good porosity but RFT pressure tests and fluid sampling indicate low permeability. A small volume of gas and mud filtrate were recovered from RFT samples. The decision was made to P&A the well without testing. WELL DATA The petrophysical evaluation was performed using logs recorded on intermediate logging run (1 m) and the final logging run (1425 - TD). The sections of hole logged above 1425 do not have hydrocarbon potential. Log quality is generally. good with two exceptions, both on the final logging run. The first is the result of poor hole conditions which complicate the evaluation of the interval from 2450-2800 m. The second is an SFL tool failure that occurred at 2478 m. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

The top of the formation, down to 1220, is marked by an increase of the gas show with C1=6000 ppm, C2=180 ppm and C3-05 <10ppm. like the Sto. Plots of reservoir properties versus present burial depth do not exhibit the same depth-related linear trend, instead displaying general scatter in the 1000 to 2000 range (Fig. 11). The lack of well-defined porosity (permeability)-depth trend confirms the importance of adjusting present burial depths for removed section. Interestingly, the Sto Formation in 7321/7-1 displays the greatest maximum burial depth and the lowest average porosity and permeability (Fig. 10). Petrologic analyses demonstrate that the Sto displays all the characteristics of deeply buried, highly compacted sandstone. The period of maximum burial prior to uplift must have been long enough for the rock to reach equilibrium with its subsurface en- vironment. When the Snadd Formation is plotted on the porosity-depth curve, it departs from the normal compaction trendline, instead deviating toward the higher porosities (Fig. 12). Such elevated porosities in deeply buried sandstones are characteristic of reservoirs with secondary porosity (Schmidt and McDonald, 1979). The petrographic evidence of secondary porosity further confirms this interpretation. SUMMARY: IMPLICATIONS FOR EXPLORATION IN THE BARENTS SEA Petrologic examination of the cored reservoirs in the 7321/7-1 well identified two types of sandstone with dissimilar reservoir properties. The Sto Formation represents compositionally mature sandstone with mostly primary porosity. Deep burial of the rock resulted in highly reduced porosity and permeabil- ity. Diagenetic processes influencing this rock, including chemical and mechanical compaction, are depth-sensitive. Exploration should be confined to areas experiencing minimum amounts of uplift when the Sto and similar compositionally mature sandstones are the primary reservoir objectives. Unfortu- nately, the trend of eastward decreasing uplift, as interpreted by MENI , is accompanied by concurrent decrease in the thickness of the Sto and other units (Gjelberg and others, 1987; Snedden and others, 1989). However, there may be central fairways where the reservoir thickness and estimated maximum burial depths fall within acceptable limits.

3.2 Well 34/7-19 The interpretation has been performed interactively by correlation on normalized images generated from conductivity curves of the FMS tool. For the following description, the reader is referred to the Composite Log (Enclosure 2). The Composite Log provides the following tracks; Petrophysical log (GR), depth annotation with formation tops and cores implemented (depthshifts included), dip-azimuth tadpoles, correlation lines superimposed on normalized images, and conductivity raw-curves. The interpretation is further supported by detailed sections where important features are described and examplified, and Schmidt stereograms projected to the upper sphere in order to evaluate the structural orientations throughout the Brent Group. Hole quality has been evaluated from caliper logs to be fair to good for the entire investigated section. The Rannoch Formation, as expressed in this well, mainly consists of parallel laminated, fine to medium grained coarsening upwards sequence. The FMS interpretation generated from correlated surfaces within the Rannoch Formation is shown in Figure 3.2.1. The lower, fine grained (silty) part of the section displays nearly uniform structural trend of laminae. For the interval between 2605.00m and 2640.00m the calculated mean orientation equals 268/4.8 (Fig. 3.2.2). The close clustering of poles seen from the Schmidt plot reflects the parallel nature of the laminae which probably was close to horisontal during deposition, and therfore is considered to represent the present structural rotation for this part of the Brent Group. The upper part of the Rannoch Formation (above 2605.00m) is characterised by larger spread of tadpoles which is partly caused by an increased occurrence of steep dipping laminations. The mean dip of the planar structures between 2595.00m and 2604.50m is calculated to be 286/5.2. From Figure 3.2.3 the spread of poles due to cross-lamination is obvious. In spite of the orientation variations, the mean structural orientation for this interval is close to the interval below 2605.00m. In addition, tadpoles are present which display dips in excess of 30 - 40 degrees (Fig. 3.2.1). With the exception of the surface at ca 2585.00m which is interpreted to represent carbonate cemented lense, these steep dipping surfaces are related to fractures (faults and joints). The two lowermost of these tadpoles at 2604.50m represent the carbonate cemented joints at core depth 2600.80m (Fig. 3.2.4). At approximately 2590.00m another pair of tadpoles which relate to steep dipping surfaces appear. These are correlated to the faults observed in the cores at 2585.30m - 2586.30m (core depth). Based on core observations (thin fault surfaces within the same lithology which do not affect the orientation of the layering within the sequence), this faulting is regarded unimportant with respect to throw. These fault surfaces dip at 72 degrees towards northeast. Structural Dipmeter Interpretation of Wells 34/7-12, 19 and 20

INTRODUCTION The report presents the results of petrographical evaluation of the cored section in Well 7122/2-1, that was drilled by Norsk Hydro within the PL179 licence during the Autumn 1992. Well 7122/2-1 provided eight cores from the depth intervals 1771-1784m (core to 3), 1812-1824m (core 4) and 1833-1932m (core to 8). The upper four cores represent the Early to Middle Barremian Kolje Formation, whilst the lower four represent the Valanganian to Heuterivian Knurr Formation. main objective of the present study is to provide detailed petrographical characterization of these cored intervals. Furthermore, an attempt is maid to decipher the diagenetic evolution in order to comment on the effect of rock composition and diagenetic evolution on the reservoir quality of the sandstones. The report presents 1) the results of standard petrographical analyses based on thin- section and XRD-analyses, and 2) the results of some more detailed mineralogical and textural analyses emphasising the diagenetic evolution of the sandstones. The discussion on the diagenetic evolution includes detailed modal analyses, fluid inclusion thermometry on inclusions in quartz cements and Cathodo-Luminescence (CL) and Back Scatter Electron Imaging (BSE) using Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). The report is organized as follows: The standard petrographical analyses of samples from the cored sections are presented in Part 2, and the results of the more detailed diagenetic analyses on the samples are presented in Part 3. summary of the findings of the present study and some recommendations for further work is given in Part 4. In order to support planning of South End development special wavelet processing and subsequent band-limited inversion has been applied to sub cube of the 3-D dataset. METHODOLOGY Interpretation of the seismic data and the mapping of those data has been done without preconceived geologic models. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

2 Source rock study 2.1 Upper Jurassic Shales The source rock potential and maturity of the Upper Jurassic shales have been assessed on sidewall cores between RKB. The following results are to be emphasized (Table and Figures 2, & 4): Tau formation Excellent potential and very good organic fades, oil-prone marine organic matter of type 11 (400 HI in average), deposited in restricted and reducing environment. The anoxicity as well as the marine influence increase upwards throughout the formation as indicated by the continuous and stepwise decrease of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). The vitrinite reflectance is around % Ro (Cf. Appendix). This formation is geochemically similar to the hot shales from the top Draupne formation (Unit according to EPN subdivision). Egersund formation High source potential and fair organic facies, mainly wet gas-condensate prone mixed organic matter dominated by terrestrial influence, variable in properties, but dominantly of type ifi (180 HI in average), deposited in rather high energy environment. The continental influence and oxic conditions increase downwards as indicated by the continuous and stepwise increase of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). This formation is geochemically rather similar to the Heather formation with however clear higher input of material derived from terrestrial organic matter. The maturity is about the same as in the Tau Formation (0.63 % Ro, value at % is questionable). The source rock properties of both formations are graphically illustrated in Figure and summarized below where mean values of the main geochemical parameters are calculated based on the screening analyses (number of samples analysed indicated). TOC Tmax Si S2 +S2 HI OI EOM Yield Sat 2.2 Sandnes Formation Coals Several layers of coals and coaly shales have been sampled from the cores (2 coals and coaly shales) and analysed. These source rocks are typical of coals from the North Sea with very high S2 and EOM constituted mostly by NSO compounds. The pristane/phytane is very high and the saturates/aromatics very low. The hydrogen index is 180-240, corresponding to dominant type HI kerogen (Table and Figure 2). The potential is mainly for gas/wet gas generation. The vitrinite reflectance is around 0.64-0.67 % Ro, i.e. slightly higher than in the Upper Jurassic Tau and Egersund formations. It should be stressed that the maturity of the Jurassic section (Upper and Middle) from this well, measured by reliable vitrinite reflectance, is clearly higher than the regional trend observed so far for the northern Quadrant 25 at equivalent depths (report EP/P/EXP/GDP 94-022 RP).

Several gas peaks were observed, few of them quite large, but all gas is believed to be drilled gas associated with very high penetration rates. slight increase in drag on connections was recorded from approximately 1750 metres. but the increase is probably result of high hole inclination. No close to balance indicators, such as trip gas or connection gas were observed. Thus, interpretation of given data suggests normal pore pressure throughout the entire hole section.
