context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 51 A.3.4 Seals FIS seals are inferred at boundaries marking abrupt changes in FIS species strength or chem- istry. The underlying assumption is that detected fluids are more or less synchronous on either side of the boundary and that some process has prevented free mixing of species across this barrier. In detail the boundary may represent change in lithology, poroperm or structural element. In the case of in-situ generated petroleum the boundary might represent transi- tion from poor to better source rock, or immature to mature source intervals. In the case of migrated petroleum the boundary might represent the extent of petroleum migration through porous rock, or the top seal to present or past petroleum column. Basal compartment limits may represent seals or, in some cases, fluid contacts or paleocontacts (see below). In general, only the tops of FIS compartments are identified on interpreted FIS depth plots. If fluids were not synchronous on either side of the compartment boundary (e.g. post-migration unconformity) then the seal interpretation would be in error. Seals may be selective or chro- matographic, in which case low molecular weight species may migrate across the boundary, while higher molecular weight species do not. A.3.5 Microseepage FIS microseeps are analogous to gas chimneys seen in seismic data, and surface manifestations of deeper charge identified in surface geochemical surveys. They are interpreted to result from near-vertical migration of light hydrocarbons followed by bacterial alteration in the shallow subsurface at temperature-depth conditions permissible for bacterial activity. Most bacteria are restricted to temperatures below 65-70°C; hence, anomalies may be observed in the up- per 1-3 km of rock column, depending on the prevailing geothermal gradient. Key indictor species include light hydrocarbons, CO2, possibly organic acids and aromatic compounds, and sulfurous volatiles, including H2S, COS, CS2, S2 ( /- SO2) and in some cases thiols. H2S is often sequestered within pyrite in iron-rich siliciclastics, hence is less common in shale-bearing lithologies. Inclusion formation in such low temperature environments may be aided by pre- cipitation of bacterial carbonate. FIS microseeps are geometrically distinct, often beginning at the surface and abruptly disappearing at the appropriate temperature-controlled depth. The presence of an FIS microseep appears to be good indicator of deeper charge in the immediate vicinity, although weak seeps may represent regional signals within shallow aquifers. Data suggest that these anomalies overlie 75-80% of productive reservoirs, while only 10% of non-productive areas display similar signals. Hence, the presence of strong seep within dry hole might indicate deeper or nearby lateral charge in the area. A.3.6 Fluid Contacts The basal boundary (abrupt or transitional) of any strong FIS compartment is candidate for present or past fluid contact, although the interpretation is often equivocal. The most compelling evidence for present day contact occurs where hydrocarbon-dominant FIS signals (the petroleum leg) give way to water-soluble dominant signals (PTP in the water leg) and where visual petroleum inclusion abundance displays parallel decrease. When inclusion abundance is high in the petroleum zone but PTP signals are not present in the water leg, it is possible that paleo-charge is recorded. SHALLOW GEOLOGY AND WELL PROGNOSIS 6.1 Background The proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location is situated in NCS block 7219/8. The interpreted stratigraphy is based on information from tie wells. Interpretation is limited to the top Cretaceous, 1847m MSL (1646ms TWT) at the PWL. Two figures are presented, figures and 6.2, illustrating the geological profiles at the proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location. Time-Depth conversion is based upon velocities derived from seismic processing of the 2D data (figure 10.1). All depths are quoted in metres MSL and two way time in milliseconds at the proposed location. The time-depth conversion is expected to be accurate to ±2m at seabed increasing to around ±10m at second TWT. 6.2 Sub-seabed Conditions The geological section to the top Cretaceous has been split into units as tied to offset wells, previous surveys (section 3.4) and in accordance with interpretation provided by Statoil. Quaternary - Nordland Group (Unit 1): Unit is expected to comprise very soft to firm clay with rare gravel becoming firm clay with sand layers and silt with depth. The base is marked by moderate amplitude, phase reversed, approximately sub-horizontal reflector reaching 458 to 506m MSL (589 to 639ms TWT) across the site, deepening gently to the north. The base of Unit represents sand layer and gas level (section 7) and is an angular unconformity. At this horizon slight risk of gas is assigned at the PWL (section 7). Within unit several possibly erosional events are observed. At 426m MSL (555ms TWT) at the PWL weak possibly reverse phase horizon is seen possibly representing sand layer. Possible boulders may be expected throughout this unit and specifically at the base as seen in offset wells. Well 7220/8-1 confirms the base of Unit as sand layer and also encountered boulders. Problems with boulders are also reported at the base Quaternary in the 7219/9-1 well (section 7.4); this is referenced from the 7220/7-1 drilling program and the problems are not specified. The 7220/5-1 well also encountered boulders at the base Quaternary. Tertiary (Palaeocene to Eocene) - Sotbakken Group (Units and 3): Unit forms thick sequence, the upper part is seismically well layered, with horizons dipping to the northwest, while the lower part is possibly less so though it becomes obscured by the seabed multiple. Sediments are expected to comprise predominantly silty claystone. Sand layers may be present in the upper part, as suggested by seismic character.

question: In well 6406/2-2 for the 409 m core, what are the prescribed protocols for handling (1 m sections capped), gamma, plug-cutting, SEM, and Hg-injection?
answer_text: Cores: cut into 1 m sections and capped at both ends at the wellsite; Gamma: measure natural gamma with a Na(Tl) scintillator and perform spectral analysis (K, U, Th) plotted vs depth; Plug‑cutting: cut 1 in. diameter × ≈1 in. length plugs — every 25 cm parallel to bedding (horizontal) and every 1 m perpendicular to bedding (vertical); SEM: use CAMSCAN CS44 with SE, BSE, CL detectors and EDAX EDS, save 8‑bit images for image analysis; Hg‑injection: use Micromeritics Autopore II 9220 on evacuated, cleaned, dried samples, inject mercury in steps up to 60,000 psi, using γ=485 dynes/cm2 and contact angle = 140°.

context_snippets.text: Structural appraisal of cores from 6406/2-1 and 6406/2-2, Lavrans Field, Haltenbanken, Norway. 151 4.5 Methodologies This section summarises the petrographic and petrophysical characterisation methodologies that were employed. 4.5.1 Petrographic characterisation techniques Polished blocks and stubs of fractured surfaces were examined with CAMSCAN CS44 high performance scanning electron microscope equipped with secondary electron (SE) detector, high resolution solid state four quadrant back-scattered electron (BSE) detector, cathodoluminescence (CL) detector and an EDAX energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS). The secondary electron (SE) signal provides topographic information and is therefore extremely useful for investigating the relationships between detrital and authigenic components and establishing their relative timing. The back-scattered electron (BSE) signal is directly proportional to the mean atomic number of the mineral; so phases of different mass have different brightness levels. The BSE signal can be combined with an image analysis system for obtaining quantitative data on mineralogical abundances, grain-sizes, porosity and cement distributions. The CL signal is extremely sensitive to trace element abundances and provides information on the growth zonations where different growth zones incorporate slightly different trace element levels. Some elements (e.g. Fe) are known to suppress the luminescence signal, whereas others (e.g. Ti and Mn) are known to enhance the signal. Therefore different mineral generations (which have very similar chemical compositions and cannot be differentiated using BSE microscopy or the EDS system) can frequently be identified using cathode luminescence. The diagenetic history of both inside and outside faults are determined and used to establish the timing of deformation in relation to the major diagenetic events. The microstructures of the deformation features were used to assess/identify the active rock deformation mechanisms (e.g. diffusive mass transfer, grain-fracturing etc.) and the history of deformation. Representative images using BSE and CL images are taken from inside and outside of the fault zone as well as traverses across the border zone areas. These images were saved in 8-bit (256 grey- levels) digital form, and then imported into an image analysis package. Processing of these images according to the philosophy and approach of Evans et al. (1994) yielded estimates of porosity and mineral abundance. This data set is then used to assess the effect of deformation on the porosity/permeability relations, and deformation/ diagenetic history of the rock. 4.5.2 Mercury Injection Porosimetry Investigation of reservoir capillary pressures was conducted using Micromeretics Autopore II 9220 mercury porosimeter. This equipment is capable of injecting mercury in step-like increments up to pressures of 60,000psi (-413MPa) into an evacuated, cleaned and dried core plug or cut sample. Capillary forces in the reservoir are functions of the surface and interfacial liquid tensions, pore size and shape, and the wetting properties of the rock. In the case of non-wetting liquid like mercury and assuming cylindrical pores this relationship is expressed by the Washburn (1921) equation: Equation 4-1 P, = -2 ycos I-, Where: P, = capillary pressure (dynes/cm2); = surface tension of Hg; = contact angle of mercury in air; rc = radius of pore aperture (pm) for cylindrical pore. The surface tension of mercury varies with purity. The accepted interfacial tension for air-Hg is 485 dynes/cm2. The contact angle between clean mercury and the solid containing the pore varies with solid composition, although a value of 140 is generally accepted. However, we know that abundant micro-porosity beyond the resolution in the BSE images is present in clay minerals, and in order to predict total porosity, the image porosity has to be calibrated to He-porosity by adding certain percentage of the clay content. Generally clay is quantified from the BSE images by thresholding grey levels (between the levels of pore and quartz). This works when kaolinite is the dominating authigenic clay. The image porosity, calculated total porosity and macro porosity (Fig. 3.11a-c) are all positively correlated with permeability. Macro porosity generally shows stronger correlation with permeability, since it represents the effective part of the pore network that controls fluid flow, and it is therefore applied for calculation of permeability. However, this expected trend is only seen for the samples from well 6406/2-2 (Fig. 3.11d). The pore size parameters median pore size, mean macro-pore area and equivalent circular diameter (Fig, 3.12a, and e) all show positive correlation with permeability. • Petrologic study of Middle Jurassic sandstones 2 INTRODUCTION 0 STATOIL This study provides petrologic data for cores in the Garn, Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations in the Statoil well 6506/11-6, Kristin Field (Figure 2-1). The petrologic data include bulk chemical analyses (94 samples), modal analyses of thin sections from the same samples, photomicrographs of thin sections, and scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of fractured rock surfaces. new set of modal analyses of thin sections from the Garn Formation in well 6406/2-3T3 was also performed (24 samples) to obtain an internally consistent data set for comparing porosity development between this well and 6506/11-6. Together with routine core analyses (one-inch-diameter plugs) and wireline log profiles, these data are used to interpret the role of depositional sand quality and diagenesis in determining porosity, permeability, and net/gross distribution within these sandstone reservoirs. Comparisons are made with similar data from nearby wells in blocks 6506/11, 6506/12, and 6406/2 to develop semi-regional context for the results and to better understand sedimentologic controls and the lateral extent of porous intervals. Particular attention is given to examining the relationship of chlorite and bitumen coatings to reservoir quality and the possible factors controlling chlorite occurrence. An earlier phase of this study focused on evaluation of petrologic data provided by Saga Petroleum from wells 6406/2-1, 6406/2-2, and The goals of this study, presented at the PL 134 Exploration Committee Meeting Ni. 13 (October 1998), are as follows: • Explain observed porosity-permeability in terms of depositional & diagenetic controls. • Document and interpret patterns of grain-coating chlorite occurrence. • Study the effect of bitumen coatings on porosity-permeability. • Provide petrologic input for sedimentology studies. • Investigate the apparent westward & northward increase in chlorite coating and bulk sodium (plagioclase) content in the Garn Formation. • Document and interpret the high-permeability zone at the top of the Garn Formation. • Study the occurrence and lateral extent of interlayered porous and tight zones in the Ile, Tofte, and Tilje Formations.

The oldest core, 7230/05-U-06, is of early Early Anisian age and consists of regressive shallow storm-influenced subtidal clayey siltstones, barrier shoreface/tidal inlet sandstones and lagoonal clayey siltstones uncon- formably overlain by subtidal channel filling sandstones, tidal flats and stacked tidal flat-bay fill and coastal plain associations. Core 7230/05-U-05 of Early Ladinian age consists of stacked tidal flat-bay fill and coastal plain clayey/silty sandstones. They are abruptly overlain by barrier shoreface sandstones and subtidal lagoon deposits. Core 7230/05-U-04 of Late Ladinian age consists of shallow storm influenced shoreface clayey and sandy siltstones. It is unconformably overlain by regressive shallow subtidal, intertidal and coastal plain clayey and sandy siltstones. Marine flooding of the coastal plain caused deposition of regressive stacked shallow subtidal to coastal plain sandy and clayey siltstones. Core 7230/05-U-03 consists of three units separated by unconformities. The lower (Norian) unit consists of marginal marine to coastal plain sandstones and sandy siltstones. It is abruptly overlain by Late Norian-Rhaetian predominately fining upward sandstones (85 %) and sandy siltstones deposited in a braided river deltaic environments. The rocks in this unit are considered to have certain reservoir potential. The unit is unconformably overlain by (Hettangian/Sinemurian) marginal marine siltstones and sandstones. Core 7230/05-U-02 contains marine siltstones in the lower part which continue from the underlying core (U-03). The Sinemurian-Middle to Late Toarcian sandstones were deposited in mouth bars/distributary channels, sandy bays and on delta plains. The sandstones have fair reservoir potential, and they may be lateral equivalent to the Nordmela Formation. They are unconformably overlain by Bajocian-Aalenian to Early Callovian-Late Bathonian transgressive shoreface sandstones to shallow shelf silty claystones which may be lateral equivalent to the Ste Formation. glauconitic con- glomerate (condensation) separates the Late Oxfordian to Late Kimmeridgian black anoxic shales. and an unconformity above this separates the Early and Late Kimmeridgian black shales. which may be lateral equivalent to the Teistengrunnen Group. -307- -INTEF-GRUPPEN Although these units seem promising with respect to reservoir potential, significant compositional differences may discriminate them. In core U-03 lithic to feldspatic arenites of Unit are overlain by the quartz arenites of Unit C. In core U-02 Unit A, which is interpreted as continuation of Unit of core U-03, shows interbedding of quartz arenites and feldspatic arenites with clayey and silty matrix as an important component and/or rooted beds. The overlying Unit contains significant amounts of glaucony and pelletoids which reduces the permeability. There are many similarities in the diagenesis of the different units such as early precipitation of siderite, pyrite and titanium oxide, some mechanical compaction, kaolinitization and/or illitization of matrix, micas and feldspars and precipitation of potassium feldspar, quartz and kaolinite. The extent of the diagenetic processes is, however, controlled by the original elastic composition of the units or beds thereby introducing different reservoir properties. A porosity - permeability plot of Late Triassic and Jurassic sandstones is shown in Figure 4.10. The porosity partly exceeds 25 % and the permeability is usually higher than 10 mD. Lower porosity and permeability were mainly caused by high primary.mairix content (Jurassic sandstones) or high content of late diagenetic calcite in the Triassic sandstones). The well sorted Late Triassic sandstones in core U-03 have in general lower po,cosity, and particularly lower permeability than the well sorted Jurassic sandstone. This is probably caused by the higher content of authigenic clay minerals in the Triassic sandstones. Despite the lower permeability of Late Triassic sandstones, they have higher reservoir potential than the Jurassic sandstone. This is due to the high content of well sorted sandstones (85 %) in Unit in U-03 and that the braided river deltaic sandstones bodies are more likely to be stacked upon each other both laterally and vertically. The Jurassic deltaic sandstones consist of isolated well sorted sandstone bodies in bioturbated and/or rooted clayey/silty sandstones. The chance for the different sandstone bodies to have direct contact is lower than for the Triassic braided river deltaic sandstone. However, the permeability of some of the bioturbated/rooted sandstones may be high enough to allow hydrocarbon migration during production. AB7/shall.drilling 87/hoved/307/ems/19-MAR-88

context_snippets.text: Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. Figures 1a-c show the Rock-Eval pyrolysis trace and the thermal extraction GC and pyrolysis-GC of Kolmule formation shale which has been washed with water only. Figures 1d-f show the Rock-Eval pyrolysis trace and the thermal extraction GC and pyrolysis-GC of

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

Clays quantified by this method may not always be directly comparable to quantification by separation of the clay fraction because of the following factors: - - clays may have preferred orientation in the whole rock preparation - the presence of size fractions greater than microns - whole rock analysis of illite may be influenced by mica in samples 8.2 Clay Fraction XRD Analysis Ten plug end trims from core no were selected by OMV for XRD analysis. Information with regard to any unusual clays which may be present e.g. Palygorskite, Corrensite Although clay minerals are evident in whole rock diffractograms, the most satisfactory method for their quantification is to extract and separately analyse the clay fraction. Separating the <2 micron fraction is achieved by ultrasound, shaking and centrifugation. The total weight of clay extracted is obtained by removing 20ml of the clay suspension and evaporating to dryness. Size fractions other than <2 micron (e.g. 2-16 micron) are obtained by varying the centrifuge speed and time. The clay XRD mount is obtained by filtering the clay suspension through Millipore filter and drying the filtrate on the filter paper. The samples are analysed as an untreated clay, after ‘glycolation ’overnight and following ‘heating’ at 380°C for hours and 550°C for one hour. The highest Imax counts occur throughout Core #3, peaking at mere counts, typical for residual oils. As reference, cores from oil legs and live condensates frequently record Imax values in the region of 100,000 to 700,000 counts. Core #3 provides continuous section of former oil leg, now comprising residual oils only, of light to medium oil signatures without trend of gravitational segregation. However, presence of OBM with a quite heavy Q580 signature close to 4315m suggests that the cores, at least in proximity of the depth of the OBM reference sample, might have been contaminated by OBM. This contamination would have caused core petroleum compositions to shift to too heavy signatures, i.e., shifting former condensate signature to light oil signature. In other words, the HCSTM detected residual oil leg might represent former condensate where signatures are shifted towards light oil because of OBM invasion. horizontal high-resolution scan through e.g., 4315.15m is therefore recommended for quantifications on OBM invasion. A detailed set of GC-MS analyses is recommended for further documentation of the trending compositions within the 4313 – 4331.22m interval. No distinct OGC or OWC/paleo-OWC contacts were identified. Additionally, for the origin of the HC signatures not (only) being sorbed HC along grain boundaries but potentially also occurring in the form of liquid HC in fluid inclusions, fluid inclusion study for the identification and timing of trapped hydrocarbon fluid inclusions in authigenic quartz is recommended.

Compensated Dual Resistivity (CDR) - The CDR tool provides borehole compensated MHz electromagnetic wave resistivity with two depths of investigation derived from measurements of phase shift and amplitude. question: In well 35/11-2, which formation—contrasting Brent's producible hydrocarbons—was tight, low net/gross and untested?
answer_text: The Sognefjord Formation.

context_snippets.text: 2.8 PETROPHYSICS 2.8.1 Introduction The 35/11-2 well encountered hydrocarbons in the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formation. Evaluation with RFT's and log data indicated the Brent contained producible hydrocarbons. The Sognefjord Formation has low net/gross, is tight and was not tested. 2.8.2 Summary The petrophysical evaluation for well 35/11-2 was performed using open hole wireline logs. Matrix parameters were established using core data when possible (Figure 2.10).The dual laterolog was used for resistivity, and the LDT calibrated to core was used to calculate porosity. Net sands were picked where the Dual Laterolog-Micro SFL log indicated permeable zones. Core data further indicated 10% porosity cutoff should be applied to the net sands. The petrophysical results along with the parameters used in the evaluation are summarized in Figure 2.11. For reserves and mapping purposes the upper Ness and the Tarbert are grouped into one unit, the lower Ness is in separate unit. The Etive and Oseberg are each separate units. The Archie parameters and apparent Rw used to calculate water saturation were determined using Pickett plots. The above method compensates for errors which could result from using incorrect Rw. The Rw obtained from analysis of a fluid sample from DST is ohm/m. The reference temperature for the Rw value is 130°C.

S 4.3 PORE PRESSURE Introduction Figure is composite plot of formation pressures against depth for well 35/11-3. Wireline pre-test data (FMT pressures) were obtained in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. Over the remainder of the well the pore pressure profile has been derived from empirically calculated data. Figure is composite plot of drilling exponent (Dxc), wireline and gas data for the well. Shale factor data for the Tertiary interval has been included to llustrate the influence of clay mineralogy changes on the data plots. The interpretation of pore pressures has been largely based upon the Dxc and Delta data plots, supplemented by gas data and well bore conditions. However, for the most part, the 35/11-3 well was drilled with significant overbalance which has minimized the use of these parameters. Well Summary Normal pore pressures equivalent to ppg EMW (equivalent mud weight) are assumed for the top hole section of Quaternary to Tertiary (Pliocene) age claystones and sandstones. There was no evidence of shallow gas as was tentatively interpreted at 479 to 497m and 573 to 634m on the shallow site survey. The Miocene Utsira Formation sandstones ( m) are overpressured to ppg EMW, and resulted in salt water flow into the well. Similar overpressured environments were encountered in the Utsira Formation in the Mobil operated 35/11-1 and 35/11-2 wells, and in the adjacent Gulf operated block, 35/8. Both of the previous Mobil wells in block 35/11 were drilled on, or adjacent to, seismically disturbed zones in the basal Nordland and uppermost Hordaland

Group sediments. This chaotic seismic character has been interpreted as being result of plastic deformation and/or slumping of the sediments. If is believed to have genetic link with the origin of the abnormal pore pressures in the Utsira Formation (see Well 35/11-2, Final Well Report, section 4.3). The 35/11-3 well, however, was drilled at location free from disrupted zones with only slight chaotic seismic structure, yet was still overpressured. This questions the previously argued causitive link between the disrupted zones and the development of abnormal pore pressures. Below the base of the Utsira Formation, pore pressure is believed to return to normal in the claystones and sandstones of the Nordland Group, and to remain so down to approximately 1400m in the Hordland Group. Below this depth the Dxc and wireline data plots indicate an increase in pore pressure up to maximum of to ppg at approximately 1660m. It should be noted however, that the observed shifts in the data plots are coincident with change from mixed layer to smectite clays and it is difficult to quantify accurately how much of the shift is due to changes in clay mineralogy and how much to increased pore pressure. I Below 1700m, the data plots indicate regression in pore pressure to normal (i.e approximately ppg BMW) by 1800m. Pressure remains close to normal throughout the Upper Cretaceous Shetland Group to 2600m. Below this depth, the data plots suggest that pore pressure increases slowly with depth down into the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Group, reaching maximum overpressure of around 9.5ppg BMW by the base Cretaceous. A marked shift in the compaction data plots, together with an increase in gas levels, marks the transition to higher pore pressures at the top of the Jurassic Viking Group at 2821m. •

- 204 - GAFFNEY, CLINE & ASSOCIATES CASED HOLE DST-2 Perforations 3 5m Commentary The zone perforated for this test was in the lower section of the Upper Jurassic Heather Formation. Log interpretation carried out by Schlumberger and Gulf had indicated that hydrocarbons could be present within the section though only limited intervals of moveables were postulated, water saturations seemingly being high and hydrocarbons possibly being reduced to residual for the most part. The log interpretation was hampered by lack of information pertaining to water resistivity and also by problems of mineralisation and therefore was considered only in semi-quantitative fashion. It was understood that sidewall core analysis had supported the view that hydrocarbons were present, possibly in the liquid phase. Prior to testing, the mud weight was taken down from ppg to 12.7 ppg in order to reduce the differential pressure across the APR-N tester . valve to an acceptable level, internal pressure being provided by only partial water cushion of some 2133 metres. full water cushion was not used since reservoir pressure of around 5300 psig was expected from RFT data and it was considered necessary to maintain an underpressure of around 0 psig if the formation was to be given fair chance to flow. The well began to clean up very quickly when opened for the main flow period and some 45 bbl of water cushion was recovered in 40 minutes. However, another 15 minutes were required to seemingly recover bbl of viscous gel that had been spotted above the APR-N valve and with all other flowing conditions unaltered this seemed to indicate more recovery than could be accounted for.

• The density and neutron logs show small gas effect in the Ness Formation and in some thin, clean sand stringers in the Etive. The gas effect is not seen in the other formations due to the thin sand and shale sequences. The increased liquid yield as seen in DST in the Tarbert Formation could reduce the gas effect on the density and neutron logs in this part of the well. The logs were reviewed to identify potential gas/oil contact in the Tarbert,but no contact is apparent. 2.8.4 Sognefjord Formation 2 The Sognefjord Formation was found to have of net reservoir rock. Log data indicate the formation has thin sand/shale laminations and low porosity. Core data from the base of the zone shows it to be micaceous. Fourteen RFT pressure readings were attempted in the Sognefjord Formation. Figure is summary of the RFT results. A segregated RFT sample taken from this interval required 2 hours, 41 minutes to fill the and gallon chambers. Gas with mud filtrate was recovered from both chambers. test was not conducted in this interval due to the poor reservoir characteristics. 2.8.3 BRENT GROUP 1 The evaluation of the Brent Group indicates pay section with an average porosity of 16.7%, and an average water saturation of 32.7%. Drill stem tests produced oil, gas and condensate at various rates from zones between 3370-3542 m.

question: How do grain size, porosity, and mineralogy compare between Unit 10 (10590') and Unit 23 (10473')?

END OF GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY WELL REPORT Page : II-1-1 17 SECTION 1545 ft - 5034 ft MD 1545 ft - 5032 ft TVD All of this section is part of the Nordland group. It primarily consists of CLAYSTONE with some minor interbedded SAND and rare minor LIMESTONE stringers. The CLAYSTONE is light grey to dark grey, soft and sticky, but increasingly firmer with depth. It is sandy and silty, and micaceous in almost the whole section, and it varies between calcareous to non calcareous, becoming less to non calcareous, less to non micaceous and less sandy towards section TD. It also becomes darker with depth. Occasionally some Glauconite and Pyrite is present within the CLAYSTONE and there is trace of shell fragments and LIMESTONE. SAND is present in short intervals down the section, the amount varying from traces to 20 % and is comprised of clear translucent loose Quartz. The grains vary from very fine to medium fine grained, angular to rounded, moderate sphericity and are very well sorted. No cementation is seen. The SAND becomes increasingly rare with depth and from 3840 ft no SAND is seen. The LIMESTONE is milky white to very light brown, firm, argil- laceous and cryptocrystalline. The shell fragments occur mainly in the upper part of the section. Background gas throughout this section remained between % and % total hydrocarbon gas equivalent with the highest background gas around 3000 ft, and peak of % Total gas at 2230 ft.

Bedding and fracture dip data have been presented on separate dip tracks on the composite summary log (Enclosure 1) and their classifications are summarised below: o Bedding: This occurs as alternating lighter and darker beds or laminae (Plate 5) according to the relative proportions of micritic calcite versus fine grained terriginous siliceous material, and the effects of bioturbation. True bedding of this type is visible throughout much of the core except within debris flow units. Slumped bedding planes have been included in the bedding classification. Where noted, siliceous rich beds have been distinguished from bedding and shale bedding (Plates 11, 15) • Shale bedding: Shale bedding occurs as distinct and individual dark grey to black shale laminations and beds ranging in thickness from 3-4 mm to greater than cm (Plate 6). They display very sharp contacts with the adjacent chalk lithologies and locally appear to occur at regularly spaced intervals. • Zoophycos burrows: Several horizons contain these characteristic pelagic-hemipelagic feeding traces (Plate 2). They generally comprise bedding-parallel and slightly discordant, frequently discontinuous traces of up to mm in thickness with well developed spreiten. The traces trend to be clay enriched and thus also defined by colour. It is relatively common for these traces to depart from the plane of bedding and consequently they have only been used to define the bedding orientation where other bedding types are absent. Burrows (other): Indeterminate bedding parallel to discordant burrows, frequently clay enriched. o Stylolites: Stylolites are common feature within the cored interval. They comprise sub- mm to sub-cm thick, near black, sub-planar, meandering to strongly sutured dissolution planes (Plate 4) that are generally parallel to near-parallel to bedding (Plate 1). They are used to define bedding attitude in the absence of well defined bedding or shale bedding. Z&S Geology Ltd. ZSL-95-227

DATE : 27/05/91 (SIDETRACK 04/06/91) DATE RIG OFF HIRE : 18/06/91 5.6. PETROPHYSICS 5.6.1 INTRODUCTION The 24/9-4 Well encountered hydrocarbons in sands of Lower Eocene age. The evaluation of the RFT and the log data indicated that the zone between 1766 and 1830 BRT contained sandstone beds and stringers which were partly hydrocarbon filled. 5.6.2. FORMATION EVALUATION The petrophysical evaluation for the well was performed using open hole wireline logs (Fig. 9). The Dual Laterolog was used for evaluating above 1800 BRT while the Dual Induction log was used Only three very thin laminae (10 cm or less) of sand were observed in the cored section. It has therefore not been possible to calibrate log porosity with measured porosity in cores. The Archie parameters used to calculate Rw were taken from the thick water-bearing sand between 1864.5 and 1906 BRT, where formation resistivity of ohmm was obtained from the MWD Dual resistivity tool. The assumed porosity in the same sand is 30 % . This gives an Rw (free water resistivity) of ohmzn at 55°C. A saturation model using the Indonesian equation was preferred. A 12% porosity cutoff and 50% shale cutoff were used when evaluating net sand. The effective water saturation cut-off was set at 50 % when calculating the net pay. LOGGING A7.1 MWD Logs 17 Yz hole section A MWD service (Anadrill Schlumberger) including gamma ray sensor for picking the sandstone intervals, and survey measurements was run over the 17 Y2 section. Sand (Utsira Fm.) was detected at 405 with corresponding increase in penetration rate. At 600 severe shocks were recorded which led to failure of the gamma ray sensor (fractured crystal). Further increase in shock rate at 725 eventually led to the failure of the direction and inclination sensor package at 920 m. 12 '4 hole section The MWD tool over this section included gamma ray, resistivity and survey measurements package. The tool indicated the presence of unexpected sand packages in the upper part of the Hordaland Gp. from 1750 to 1850 m, shallower than the potential Frigg Fm. MWD failures were recorded over this section. The MWD stopped pulsing at 2708 due to seal problem in silicate(high pH) mud, and this caused significant amount of non-productive time as magnetic single shot survey had to be run to comply with internal surveying procedures. The second tool failure was related to the same mud related problems. Picking the next section TD for the 5/8 casing had to be done without the gamma ray support and the thinner than expected Cromer Knoll interval which was targeted as the casing seat was missed. Casing was set within the Upper Jurassic Draupne shale. 8 Y2 hole section Drilling continued with no response from the GST (geosteering motor with resistivity at the bit). Real time resistivity was critical for coring point selection so the GST tool was recovered for evaluation, with no problem identified at surface. The backup GST tool was picked up and attempts to shallow test were inconclusive (because of difficulties in transmitting the signal via mud rather than formation). GST#2 was run in the hole and drilling resumed with no response of the tool. These tool failures were due to insulation problems on some wires that are not regularly checked prior to tool dispatch. The bottom hole assembly was recovered to install MWD/CDR configured in rotary mode to bring the resistivity sensor as close to the bit as possible. Another MWD failure was recorded, related to the silicate mud, and magnetic single shot survey was attempted with no success. A7.2 Wireline Logs 12 'A hole section A transparent sand (not seen on seismic) had been penetrated in the Hordaland Gp. and to supplement the MWD log, suite of GR-CNL-LDL-AS was logged across the 0 section. This intermediate logging was added to the initial formation evaluation programme. 8 V2 hole section Based upon little encouragement from hydrocarbon shows and MWD resistivity response, the dry case scenario was decided for further formation evaluation. The initial wireline programme for dry hole scenario consisted of runs: 1/ Supercombo: NGS/Resistivity/Micro-Resistivity/Array Sonic/Density 2/ Repeat Formation Tester (RFT) for pressure measurements only 3/ Vertical Seismic Profile (VSP) 4/ Sidewall Samples (CST) optional. No L.O.T. was conducted on this sidetrack but on the original well an L.O.T. at the shoe (2806m MD, 2411m TVD) was conducted to 1.80SG EQMW using 1.58SG mud and 52 bar pressure. The hole was displaced to 1.43SG mud while drilling cement from 2756m to 2790m MD and was maintained at that level throughout the section. Claystones with limestone stringers of the Shetland group to 3027m MD (2486.1m TVD) underlain by Cromer Knoll (claystone with limestone interbeds) to 3107m MD (2502.3m TVD). This was underlain to TD by the Lunde formation (predominantly sandstone, interbedded with mudstone and minor limestone stringers). From 2810m MD to the top of the Lunde formation at 3107m MD (2502.3m TVD) gas values ranged from 0.03% to 0.19%. Beneath 3107m MD gas values ranged from 0.1% to 3.6% with maximum formation gas seen of % at 3117m MID. No connection, trip or swab gases were seen. No Dxc trend could be discerned due to the short vertical length of the section drilled. The prognosed pore pressure indicated 1.53SG at the 5/8 casing shoe rising to I.57SG at the top of the reservoir. The reservoir has depleted pore pressure of 1.24SG in the short length of section drilled in this well. Although the overlying formations have pore pressure in excess of the mud weight, the impermeable nature of these formations means that no cavings or connection/trip gasses were observed. There was no data from the drilling of the well which contradicted the prognosis.

3.5.1 Overburden The shale collapse gradient in the overburden has been calculated from: • Initial pore pressure gradient • Overburden and least horizontal stress gradient • Stassi d’ Alia failure criterion The fracture gradient, FG, is based on: • Formation integrity and leak-off tests from neighbour wells • Loss incidents and operational experience Normal hydrostatic pressure is seen down to the lower part of the Hordaland Gp. An increasing trend is seen towards the Rogaland Gp., and as confirmed by measurements in several wells pressure gradient (EMW) of about g/cc is expected in the Lista Fm. in the Rogaland Gp. In the lower part of the Rogaland Gp., decreasing pressure is seen, continuing into the upper part of the Shetland Gp., the minimum EMW value is about g/cc. In the lower part of the Shetland Gp., the pressure is increasing again to an EMW value of about g/cc at BCU. 3.5.2 Reservoir Vigdis Øst (horst); see also section Factors adding uncertainties to the bore hole stability prognosis are: • Shale thickness (initial pressure or not) • Formation strength calculation (model, data input quality etc.) • Presence and maturity of palaeosols • Well inclination effects • Time factor • Faults and lineaments • Inter bedding effects (angle between well path and bedding, angle of attack) The fracture gradient (FG) in the reservoir is estimated by use of the following formula: FG = 1.85sg – * (PP initial – PP depleted) The fracture gradient in the reservoir is directly related to the pore pressure, which is an uncertainty factor. Also, the uncertainty of the fracture gradient estimation increases when drilling horizontal wells along planes of weakness in complex depleted reservoirs. 3.5.3 Exploration target Vigdis Nordøst Well 34/7-B-1 was drilled into the Statfjord Fm. in the Vigdis Nordøst structure in March 1997. As these pressure points coincided with the initial Snorre water gradient curve (App G), we have strong reasons to believe that Vigdis Nordøst was not depleted at the time of drilling in 1997, and thus Snorre production is not considered to have any influence on Vigdis Nordøst. However, since Vigdis Nordøst lies adjacent to the Vigdis st structure and Vigdis st has been pressure depleted from 2004 until today (2007) with some 20 bar, it is prudent to define this as the expected pressure scenario for Vigdis Nordøst. 340 bar @datum 2300 TVD MSL (1.45 SG) is probably the most likely situation in the Vigdis Nordøst. context_snippets.text: GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-25 Well 25/8-B-25 is planned to be horizontal oil producer in the Heimdal-reservoir in the Elli Structure. All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. Lithological boundaries were interpolated between two neighbouring samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and M'WD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse Cl, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. Ratios (C1/C2, Cl/C3, Cl/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of Cl. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show Cl, but very high shows of Cl are usually indicative of salt water. If the Cl/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the Cl/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If Cl/C4 is less than Cl/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the Cl Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/NON-PRODUCTIVE Cl/C5: 2-30 However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 ± C4 + Cs 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + Cs total 100 the GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LIAR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and Cs are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. Spot samples for microscopic description only, were taken every 50m MD from 1350m MD (1081.8m TVD) down to 2700m MD (1843.3m TVD). From 2740m MD (1865.5m TVD) one wet and two dry interval samples were caught every 20m down to 3340m MD (2103.1m TVD). Thereafter interval samples were caught every 10m down to TD at 4407m MD (2112.1m TVD). 3-1

A rig source VSP survey was recorded in this vertical well on 3/10/94. During the survey five runs into the well were required in order to satisfactorily record 170 levels between 970 and 4400m. The source used was Bolt airgun array consisting of four 160 cu.in. guns, positioned 69m from the wellhead along bearing of 70 degrees, and at depth of 4.5m below MSL The source signature was monitored using hydrophone 2m above the array. For the purposes of trial for VSP derived synthetic sonic, data were recorded by dual receiver array positioned at intervals of the same value as the spacing between the two geophones (i.e. 15m). This has meant that there are numerous levels recorded more than once, though this is also due to levels duplicated during the different runs into the well. For the standard processing for this well, generally only the best level data recorded was selected to represent any level shot more than once, although data consistency was also aimed for in deciding which data to use. Note also that no significant timing discrepancies were encountered between such duplicated levels, implying that reasonable depth control was maintained throughout the survey. DATA TIMING AND COMPUTATIONS Noise transmitted through casing sections caused severe problems in timing the majority of the data, particularly for shallowest levels where casing noise arrivals are evident before the expected direct arrivals. In an attempt to identify direct arrivals throughout the bulk of the data, several noise attenuations were carried out. The data was first filtered using restrictive 2,5-40,45 Hz bandpass filter designed to retain most of the signal bandwidth (as seen by F-K analyses) whilst attenuating the casing noise of higher frequencies. Further to this, remaining casing noise has been attenuated through an enhacement and subtraction technique (after coarse downwave subtraction, casing noise was then estimated using a short median operator, this estimate finally being subtracted from the raw data). An automated trace alignment method was used on resultant direct arrival data, improved times generally being obtained as result. However, no usable times could be obtained for the levels at and above 2180m, these levels having to be disregarded due to the contamination from noise transmitted through the casing, nor for the level at 3944m. Final times were therefore obtained for 151 of the levels, although all those seen to be affected by casing noise should still be treated with caution. The check levels have been selected at vertical depth intervals of either 90m (for shallower levels) or 45m (for the deepest levels) in the calculation of interval velocities and for the sectional display of well geophone signals. ACOUSTIC LOG CALIBRATION The supplied acoustic log data appears to be generally of reasonable quality, but it has been edited for any erroneous values where appropriate. The edited log has been re-integrated prior to calibration. The calibration is well controlled by the check level data. contd....

Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. GEOPHYSICAL MAPPING GENERAL For general discussion on seismic data quality, geophysical setting and acoustic properties of the Valhall Chalk reservoir please refer to; 1990 VALHALL GEOLOGIC AND GEOPHYSICAL RE ANALYSIS AND RESERVE REASSESSMENT Text 2/2. A subsequent map revision based on the 2-D seismic database was released in March 1992. Since then the seismic data base has been upgraded by 3-D seismic dataset covering the field. METHODOLOGY Interpretation of the seismic data and the mapping of those data has been done without preconceived geologic models. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

question: For well 33/9-18 VSP, which combination of time-depth curve, F-K/max-band filtering, and calibrated logs/3D ties best distinguishes primaries from multiples?
answer_text: Use the two‑way time–depth curve display of the upgoing wavefield (VC) combined with F‑K analysis using the 'maximum bandwidth' filter, tied to calibrated velocity logs and 3D seismic ties.

context_snippets.text: BSD/VSP/VC.2 DISPLAY VC Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display describes the primary and multiple reflection responses of the subsurface at the borehole location, within and below the depth range of the VSP. This data is filtered using the 'maximum bandwidth' filter designed after F-K analysis to determine the usable bandwidth of the upgoing wavefield. In marine data, if source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the input wavelet is zero phase and the wavelet contained in the data is zero phase modified by earth absorption and transmission loss effects (ie mixed phase). Events that reach the time-depth curve are primary and their lithologic significance can be established unequivocally by reference to the calibrated velocity log. Multiples having their last bounce from primary within the range of the VSP may be identified by observing their termination in the data at the same depth point at which the primary cuts the time-depth curve. From this display, any dip across the well location can be recognised by moveout of the primary event to shorter time, as the geophone moves up the well and away from the lithology creating the reflection. No azimuth of dip can be computed from this display but true dip can be computed from measurement of the AT against vertical depth increment. Unconformities may be recognised by an abrupt change of moveout of adjacent primary events. Topographical features up-dip away from the well may be recognised by an increase in the AT or in the termination of an event away from the time-depth curve. Dip increasing up-dip away from the well can be observed in the data; however, if dip is decreasing up-dip (ie crest of an anticline) then the event in question will disappear from the data. Dip can be calculated using the method described in the Appendix contained in this report. DISPLAY VC(FK) F-K Display of Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display is used in the design of the 'maximum bandwidth' filter in conjunction with the F-K display of the deconvolved upgoing wavefield and filter trials. It shows the data from the upgoing wavefield at two-way time transformed into F-K space. Any filter applied to the data before transformation is noted on the display. Since the upgoing wavefield is aligned horizontally, or near horizontally, in T-X space (unless there is steep dip across the well location) it is aligned vertically, through zero wavenumber, in F-K space. The 'maximum bandwidth' filter is the least restrictive filter that can be applied to the upgoing wavefield to remove noise whilst retaining resolution of the data in the zone of interest. The F-K analysis is therefore performed on data within window around the zone of interest. Additionally, the data is windowed in time so that data analysed is close to the time-depth curve, where we would expect better resolution. If the zone of interest is not known, it is assumed to be just above T.D. of the well.

S Abstract The dipmeter from the Jurassic and part of Cretaceous of 33/9-18 is of high quality and only degraded in sections of irregular borehole. Irregular borehole sections are found in brecciated, fractured or strongly sheared zones, often subhorizontal. The mode of drilling is not related to quality of hole. The absence of borehole breakout indicates low horizontal stress anisotropy. This can only be explained by low macroscopic strength due to densely spaced dislocation planes. The Jurassic is of extreme complexity but can be understood if it is subdivided into four structural domains: 1) huge block of lower Jurassic sliding off the Statiford crest during early rifting in Upper Jurassic collapses under its own weight. Albeit strongly deformed internally, the gross stratigraphy is preserved 2) series of smaller slides are emplaced, forming pile of imbrication sheets with varying internal bedding orientation 3) turbidites are deposited on strongly sculptured surface, enclosing occasional allochthonous slide blocks, and sliding into local swales to form slightly reoriented sheets or wedges 4) deposition of Draupne shale as the basin floor rotates due to continued main fault activity. Changes in the plunge of deformation axes are ascribed to syndepositional activity of large transverse fault. Gravitational instability of the talus wedge led to the formation of low angle thrusts, thought to affect also the Cretaceous, causing minor reorientation of lamination.

question: If a centrifuge continuously dumps barite at ~10 t/h, what are the expected impacts on MBT, mud weight, and solids-control performance?
answer_text: MBT will rise (observed up to ~38 ppb), mud weight will become difficult to control/unstable (mixing could not maintain required weight), and solids‑control performance will deteriorate as the centrifuge becomes ineffective and dumps barite and fine solids.

context_snippets.text: OPERATOR A/S Norske Shell WELL 3/7-4 SECTION 17 1/2 Hole The cement was drilled with seawater, then the hole was displaced with sg mud. The leak off test gave sg mud weight equivalent. When drilling commenced, it was necessary to dump the header tank on each connection as it was full of cuttings. From 892 to 1011 meters, the formation consisted of very soft clays. The string tended to hydraulic; that is to say it was lifted by pump pressure from the bottom of the hole. The soft clays were extremely hydratable and the MBT showed that the clay content of the mud rose sharply. This problem was compounded by the use of PDC bit. PDC bits produce cuttings that are powder size. This powder is difficult to remove from the system. After being circulated second time, the clay particles are dispersed and begin to affect rheology. Drilled ahead to 1182 meters. The string continued to hydraulic in the soft clays. At 1182 mete-L's it was necessary to pump the string out of the hole. Drilled ahead to 1853 meters. The MBT continued to rise, and eventually reached 38 ppb. This again was due to the powdered cuttings that hydrated and made extraction with the solids control equipment impossible. Prior to this point, the centrifuge was being run to reduce solids. Only the high rpm machine was available for use, so that barite was being dumped in addition to clay solids. That barite was being dumped in addition to solids created other problems. The mixing equipment could not maintain the required weight in the active so the centrifuge was eventually stopped. The barite mixing system was monitored and mixed approximately 10 metric tonnes per hour. Speeds in excess of this caused blockages in the screw conveyor troughs or the drive belts to break. Reducing clay content in the mud is also achievable through dilution with premix. This was difficult on the Hunter. Mixing 50 cubic meters of premix required hours. Weighting up the premix to 1,5 sg required an additiond hours. During this time it was not possible to add barite to the active system as required.

question: How does the source-rock potential of Upper Jurassic sandstones compare between wells 2/5-10 and 2/5-10A?
answer_text: Both wells’ Upper Jurassic sandstones have no source‑rock potential.

context_snippets.text: Schlurnbenger GEOLABFINOR been higher. The present petroleum potential is fair to rich (2.5 to mcl HC/g rock). The original potential is thought to have been mainly rich to very rich for mainly oil generation. The four sandstone samples have low S2 and TOC values ;and have no source rock potential. A comparison was made of the Farsund Formation claystones in wells 2/E-10 and 2/5- 10A. Unfortunately many of the cuttings samples in well 2/5-10 from the Farsund Formation were dominated by barite and the amount of analysis that could be performed was limited. It is difficult to see any correlation between the Gamma Log and the hydrogen index. It is also diffioult to see direct correlation between the 2/5-10 well and the 2/5-10A well. It is possible that this lack of correlation is due to the samples being cuttings samples. These are not from specific depth (as are the log readings) but from depth range. What material is actually analyzed might hence not come from 1he same depth as given by the log. Also there is probably difference in logger depth and driller's depth. The differences in the hydrogen indices between the two wells at the same depth could also possibly be attributed to the difficulty of establishing the exact depth from which the cuttings are really from and how much of the ma erial is from different parts of the depth range which the cuttings represent. Gyda - Breakout Analysis, Addis & McLean, 1989, which also applies for the Ula Field). In practical terms, this implies that an inclined well drilled at 90° to the maximum horizontal stress direction would be more stable than well of similar inclination drilled parallel to that stress direction. Well AO7B will be drilled along an azimuth of 322°N from the top of the Ekofisk Formation and will be quasi parallel to the direction of maximum horizontal stress for length of over 1800m MD. This will result in risk of increased wellbore instability from the top of the Ekofisk Formation to approximately 5100m MD, where the well is turned to the west. The planned mud weight of sg will exert sufficient overbalance over the expected pore pressure and should counteract instability resulting from the effects of maximum horizontal stress. 3 Geological Programme 3.1 Purpose of the Well The vertical exploration well 2/6-5 will be drilled on the Chalk Prospect which is situated in the central eastern part of PL 008 (Figs. and 3.2). The main purpose of well 2/6-5 is to test the presence of hydrocarbons and the reservoir properties within the Shetland Group in the Chalk Prospect. The planned TD of the well is 25 into Basement, or prognosed TD at 3185 mRKB. The well will be planned as possible future producer. Secondary purpose of the well is to test possible sediment fill in the interval between the Shetland Group and the basement topography. For well 2/6-5 the primary target of Cretaceous age is prognosed at 2843 mRKB, below approx. 40 of the Ekofisk Tight zone causing the laterally consistent seismic reflector mapped as the Top Shetland horizon. The primary target interval consists of the total Shetland package below the tight zone mentioned above. Target interval belongs to the Ekofisk-, Tor- and Hod Formations (or their time equivalents). Reservoir zones are expected in several intervals, some in pressure communication and some not. A distinct change in ROP is expected when drilling from the Ekofisk Formation tight zone into the primary target of prognosed highly porous carbonates. The porosity in the Shetland Group is expected to be more than 35%, locally more than 50%. Open reservoir structure and or zones with large number of small fractures are expected. Secondary target is the section mapped below the Shetland Group. This interval is of unknown age, but probably belonging to Jurassic/Triassic infill of the faulted basement topography of the Mandal High. However, the interval might show up as only representing intra basement reflectivity within metamorphic rocks. The well is located high on structural closure defined on Top Shetland Group (Figs. and 3.2). The trapping mechanism is partly caused by structuring reflecting the Paleotopography of the underlying crystalline Mandal High, and partly due to stratigraphical component within the Shetland Group (Fig. 3.3). A possible seismic direct hydrocarbon indicator (flatspot) is observed in the Shetland Group at approx. 2965 mRKB (2.855 sec TWT.). This biogenic fabric is well seen as the mudrocks transform to green colour and clean medium grained sand-filled burrows are preserved, presumably piping down sand from the overlying unconformity surface of the Skalmen Formation. This uppermost green mudrock contains glauconite /chlorite and phosphatic shell fragments (Fig. 3A,D), whilst the mudrocks as whole appear to be of mixed clay composition (illite with subordinate smectite or chlorite-smectite and kaolinite; Fig. 3E). Interpretation: as with the Skalmen sandstones, the combination of glauconite/chlorite and burrowing (especially the Chondrites-type) suggests a marine setting. The association of reddening, intense bioturbation and sand-filled burrows piping down from the overlying unconformity all point to reduced sedimentation rates and the existence of submarine hiatal surface at the mudrock /sandstone interface. Collectively therefore sand- starved site below wave base is implied, arguably associated with depositional high. However, the thrust of this interpretation would be undermined if all the burrowing were associated with the hiatal surface; this would open up other possibilities for the mudrock origin (see End. 1).
