Most critical is to define the oil volume in the Garn Formation. • reservoir parameters : porosity, permeability, sedimentology, diagenesis (petrology). • pressure and pressure gradients. • fluid samples gas , oil and water. • biostratigraphic information for correlation. • data necessary for tying seismic to the subsurface. a). Prove oil in the Gam Formation (This is the most important of all objectives listed): In addition the aim is to gather sufficient information to be able to quantify the volume of oil in the Gam Formation in the structure. • Well Location - Location is selected to give the best possible chance of placing an oil leg in the Gam Formation. It is placed downdip on the block within the amplitude anomaly in position where, even with the possible errors in depth conversion, there is the best chance of placing the Gam in the oil leg. The location should not be below the structural spill to the east. (note: this is achieved on some of the depth map versions but not all). This means that the well location does NOT specifically target the Gas oil contact or the Oil water contact . • Be able to sidetrack updip or downdip, 1000 laterally. • Prove oil in Gam based on shows, logs, MDT/RFT pressure b). Define gas/oil contact in Gam • If gas/oil contact present or can be confidently calculated from MDT/RFT then requirements are met. • If gas/oil contact uncertain - optional sidetrack c). Define oil/water contact in Gam • If oil/water contact present or can be calculated from MDT/RFT then requirements are met. • If oil/water contact uncertain - optional sidetrack d). Quality fluid samples • Obtain good quality PVT fluid samples for reservoir engineering, facilities design, marketing. e). Collect data required for future field development and reservoir characterization: cores, logs, MWD, sidewall cores.

BP Amoco Norge AS Report No. 8321/Id 6.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY SUMMARY 6.4.1 Melke Formation The Melke Formation is uncored in the 6507/5-2 well and has no si___ nificant reservoir potential in the Skary area. The Melke is dominated by mudstones, possibly with minor component of very fine grained argillaceous sandstones, and forms regionally extensive seal to reservoirs in the underlying succession. To the north of the Skary area lower parts of the Melke locally contain progradational wedges of sandstone which were derived from the north. These sandstones do not, however, extend much further south than the Nome Field. Wealdy progradational log signatures within lower parts of the Melke Formation in the Skary area may be distal equivalent of these progradational wedges. 6.4.2 Garn Formation The Gam Formation as whole in the 6507/5-2 well has mean porosity of 19.03%, an arithmetic mean permeability of 1529.75mD and geometric mean permeability of 944.3mD. This formation is by far the best quality reservoir encountered in the 6507/5-2 well, but is marginally poorer than the equivalent interval in the 5-1 well. Although of good quality throughout, the Garn is internally heterogeneous with some marked internal variations in reservoir characteristics associated with changes in depositional facies. Detailed facies description and correlation of the Garn Formation suggests that the interval as whole is likely to be laterally extensive with sheetform external geometry, although there is some potential for significant thickness variations over distances of few tens of kilometres, particularly in response to syn-depositional variations in subsidence rate. In addition, there is potential for lateral pinch-out of the upper parts of the Gam Formation to the south of the Skary area, although the minimal variation between the 5-1 and 5-2 wells suggests that this may occur over significantly greater distance than the well spacing and potentially at some location beyond the licence boundary. The local presence of bitumen stain within the Gam Formation may suggests relatively complex history of hydrocarbon emplacement. It is possible that relatively early hydrocarbon charge could be partially responsible for the preservation of excellent reservoir quality. The greatest uncertainty concerning the reservoir potential of the Gam Formation at the field scale is possible variations in the degree of cementation rather than continuity of the sandbody. 6.4.3 Not Formation The Not Formation has mean core analysis porosity of 10% and an arithmetic mean permeability of 69.38mD with low geometric mean permeability of only 1.43mD. Reservoir quality is highly variable and is primarily controlled by the depositional facies of the sediment, being at maximum in the coarsest parts of the formation and specifically in the unit of 'Gam facies' corresponding to the lower part of Reservoir Subzone JS11. In this interval the arithmetic mean permeability is 208mD (geometric mean 69.3mD) with mean porosity of 14.3%. Local carbonate cementation in this part of the Not Formation has detrimental effect on reservoir quality and in large part accounts for the difference between the rock quality of this unit and the overlying sandstones of the Gam Formation. Carbonate cementation, in the form of irregular diagenetic nodules, was also noted at similar level in the 6507/5-1 well but the discrete nature of these 'doggers' in the previous well suggests they that are unlikely to have significant effect on the overall permeability of the units which contain them. The more diffuse cements in the 'Gam facies' unit appear to have greater overall impact on reservoir quality, although the presence of sandstones in this interval with permeabilities in excess of 1000mD indicates the potentially excellent reservoir quality that might be expected in the absence of carbonate cements. Page 82

1.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY The Garn Formation and uppermost Not Formation represent the primary reservoir in the 6507/5-4 well. good visible oil stain was observed in the core with probable gas cap in the upper part of the Garn. The cored interval of the Garn Formation in 6507/5-4 has mean porosity of 17.89%, with a relatively low standard deviation of 2.41, but has wide range of permeability values with maximum of 9870 mD and minimum of mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is 1739.33 mD, with slightly lower geometric mean permeability of mD, and relatively high standard deviation of highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals only weak positive correlation. There is moderate relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Reservoir quality is influenced by variations in the abundance of kaolinite, the main authigenic mineral. Although quartz overgrowth cement has reduced porosity, it does not appear to control variations in reservoir quality. The cored interval of the Tilje Formation is in the water leg and has poor to only rarely moderate reservoir quality. In view of the broad similarity in terms of depositional character between the Tilje Formation between Skarv wells, diagenetic influence on this reduction in reservoir quality needs to be considered. The Tilje Formation has mean measured porosity of 16.01%, with standard deviation of 0.35, and limited range of permeability values with minimum of mD and maximum of 1290 mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is mD, with geometric mean permeability of only mD, and standard deviation of 198.33, highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals positive correlation and there is good relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Authigenic kaolinite has significant deleterious effect on reservoir quality. Other authigenic minerals have also reduced reservoir quality, as has compaction, which is likely to be most important in the less well sorted and ductile-rich sandstones. significant proportion of the macroporosity in the Tilje is of secondary, grain dissolution origin and secondary porosity tends to be common in sandstones rich in detrital albite and lithic grains. The reservoir geology of the remaining Jurassic succession is variable but is generally lower than that in either the Garn or Tilje Formation. Moderately good quality sandstones occur in the upper part of the Not Formation whereas much poorer quality is prevalent in the micaceous, very fine sandstones in the lower part of the formation. The micaceous sandstones also tend to be rich in kaolinite and carbonate cements. The Ile Formation is sand prone relative to the enclosing Ror and Not Formations but is particularly thin and condensed in the 6507/5-4 well. The highly bioturbated and typically argillaceous nature of these sandstones results in generally poor reservoir quality. 1.5 ZONATION AND CORRELATION The Lower to Middle Jurassic sediments examined in the study well contain complete succession of the constituent formations recognised in earlier wells (6507/5-1 and 6507/5-2) which penetrated this interval in the Skarv area (see RRI Reports Nos. 8150/Id and 8321/Id, respectively). As result of regional work in the Mid Norway area, Robertson erected broadly chronostratigraphic zonation scheme for the entire Lower to Middle Jurassic which was defined in ‘The Lower to Middle Jurassic reservoirs of Mid Norway’ study (RRI Report No. EM079, 1997). This zonation scheme has been extended into the 6507/5-4 well as part of this report, the zones being given the appropriate suffixes (e.g. Tilje 1, Ror 4, etc.). All of the constituent zones are recognised in the present study well although, in common with the successions in these earlier wells, subdivision of the Melke Formation is difficult and the usable wireline log data terminate in the upper part of the Åre Formation, making correlations below this depth impossible.

1 Executive Summary This report presents an evaluation and interpretation of StethoScope Formation Pressure While Drilling data from well 33/9-A-38 in the Statfjord field. 33/9-A-38 is sidetrack well from well 33/9-A-38 to the target ADU01 in Cook. The objective of well 33/9-A-38 is to produce undrained oil from the Cook Fm. and Cook Fm. 1B reservoirs. A total of tests were performed resulting in valid pressures and dry pretests. Pressure Acquisition Sequence: All tests were performed while POOH after reaching the total depth. 2 Interpretation Summary 2.1 Run Summary Run Dates: 30th of July – 03rd of August 2015 Mud Type: Versatec (OBM) with specific gravity of 1.54. question: For depth conversion from Top Chalk, which constant interval velocity (in/sec) should be used when Cretaceous two-way time exceeds 20 msec?
answer_text: Use a constant interval velocity of 3500 in/sec.

context_snippets.text: Depth conversion was achieved by isopaching down from Top Chalk. Nine wells were analyzed for velocity information and the following methodology was applied. Where the Cretaceous interval is greater than 20 msecs constant interval velocity of 3500 in/sec was used. Where the interval was less than 20 msecs the following formula was applied Cretaceous Isopach (m) = *Cretaceous Isochron (m sec) + 4357 The proposed well intersects the Base Cretaceous just east and outside of nearby closure. The closure has previously been intersected by the 25/11-5 well. The Lower Jurassic, Statfjord Formation sands intersected in this well are water wet with no shows. 5.3 RESERVOIR 5.3.1 Summary Seismic interpretation and well log correlations provide the framework for the reservoir mapping. The Balder Field sands are interpreted to have been deposited in deep water submarine fan environment by high-density turbidity currents. All mounds penetrated to date contain both massive and some thinner sands. High-relief mounded geometries are believed to have been caused by complex interaction between deposition and syn- and post- depositional deformation processes. Associated sand injections into overlying shales occurred during the soft-sediment deformation processes which predominantly took place during early Eocene. The lower Tertiary section is split into main reservoir zones. (Eocene Zone III, Paleocene Zones II, D3 and IA2). The definition of the main biostratigraphic zones established in 1991 is anchored in top/base occurrence of palynomorphs from cores and sidewall cores (Figure 13). The sandbody geometry is complex and total sand thickness can vary from few to over 100 meters. Reservoir properties are excellent with average porosity of 33%, permeability of 1-10 Darcies and 85-90% average oil saturation. MOOIRPM.DOC - 23.02.95 / Pg 13

This report discusses the theory and processing of DSI* Array Sonic data for well 25/11-16 as run lA on 16th July 1992. Acquisition was made using five modes: Lower and Upper Dipole, Low frequency monopole for Stoneley, High frequency monopole for P&S and Compressional First Motion Detection. Details of acquisition of the first four modes are contained in the section on operating modes included in the Appendix A. The field-computed FMD compressional slowness was not reprocessed but is included in the final display of the results. The Digital Sonic waveforms were processed with the Slowness-Time Co- herence method to determine the sonic Compressional, Shear and Stoneley wave velocities. 2.1 Log Quality Control The waveforms from the receivers of the sonic array were checked visu- ally for frequency content and apparent correct functioning of the tool, at intervals of 50m along the logged interval. It immediately appeared that all modes were affected by waveforms ac- quisition problem above 1,425 m: from this depth up to the casing shoe the transmission from the downhole tool appears intermittent and the acquisi- tion was locked on the same waveform for several meters at the time. For this upper interval any further computation produced stepping slow- ness profile, with the exception of the compressional FMD slowness, which is computed indipendently from the transmitted waveform. The lower section presents data of generally good quality, although some- times largely attenuated by the very soft formation.

4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( TVD vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

context_snippets.text: FLUIDS 7.3 DRILLING FLUIDS SECTION SUMMARY Section Summary The surface volume of Carbo-Sea IOE mud left from the 12 1/4” interval, was centrifuged to cut the weight from SG to the required SG. In addition, about 30 m3 of premix were added to build additional volume of SG mud and to lower the mud rheology. After running in hole with the 1/2” bit to top of cement at 2309m, the hole was displaced from to SG mud whilst drilling the shoetrack from 2309m to the shoe at 2356m. Prior to drilling out of the shoe, additions of the Max-Bridge bridging and fluid loss control system commenced to establish an adequate starting concentration in the active system in preparation for drilling into the reservoir. The rat hole was cleaned out to 2361m and metres of new formation were drilled before carrying out an LOT. The well was pressured up to 148 bars – equal to SG mud weight. Due to problem with the ZoneTrak logging tool, the string was pulled to surface and the ZoneTrak replaced with back-up tool. The assembly was then again re-run to bottom and drilling continued from 2363m. drilling break at 2384m indicated top of the reservoir, which was confirmed by the ZoneTrak resistivity tool. Consequently, the string was pulled to surface and the coring program could commence. Cut cores, each core barrel filled with 27 metres of formation, in the interval from 2385m to 2521.4m. Max-Bridge chemicals were added continuously throughout the interval according to the recommended mixing rate. The mud weight was controlled between and SG with the addition of premixed base oil with emulsifiers. After the completion of core run decision was made to drill an additional 104 metres to allow enough rathole for testing and logging operations. Section TD was taken at 2625 m. Run and Cementing 7” Liner After the completion of logging operations clean up run was performed prior to running the 7” liner. The liner was run and the top set 100 metres inside the 5/8” casing shoe, and the 7” liner shoe at 2623m. On the first attempt at cementing the liner, there was rapid increase in pressure to 100 bars at 100 LPM as the spacer was pumped. Suspected pack off round the hanger area. The cement job was aborted, with downhole losses recorded at 1m3/hr. In order to establish even pressure and stem losses, the well was circulated with 500 LPM, 50-90 bars, and 20 RPM with addition of the LCM chemical LC-Lube, LC Lube fine, Soluflake Med/Fine and Fordacal 36 over one full circulation. Max-shield borehole sealant in base oil was bled via slug pit into the active. This was effective in reducing the losses. The first cement job was carried out, but it was not possible to set the packer. In order to check for cement integrity behind the 7” liner Segmented Bond tool log was performed on wireline. The log showed no cement behind the liner. new cement job was required to secure the liner. An EZSV packer was set at 2550m and the well perforated under the packer, from 2280 to 2282m, in order that circulation could be established between the 7” liner and 1/2”annulus. The remedial cement job was carried out behind the 7” liner. In order to confirm cement segmented bond log was again performed. This showed that there was no cement from the bottom of the perforation depth, 2551 to 2383m, but good cement from 2383m to top of the perforation depth at 2280m. Section Page 13

2) Background, connection and trip gas were continuously monitored by the Raroid Hot Wire gas detector. Mud gas samples were prepared, steam distilled and analyzed at regular intervals for contect of indi- vidual hydrocarbon gases and reported in parts per million, methane, ethane, propane, butane, and pentane. 3) Shale factor and shale density of samples were recorded and plotted. 4) Mud volums in pits and flow in and out were continuously monitored to detect either an influx of formation fluid or lost circulation. 5) Mud densities in and out were continuously monitored by electronic transducing devices. 6) Surge pressures were calculated for trips. 7) Surge pressures at various running speeds were calculated for casing strings. 8) Pressure drop calculations were run daily or as requested. This data was used to select proper jet sizes and hydraulics and maintaining minimum annular velocity in the riser. 9) The minimum cost drilling program was used in conjunction with drill rate data to optimise weight on bit and rotary speed. 10) Bit contant programs were run on the 316 computer in an effort to predict tooth and bearing wear prior to each bit run. These programs have given close enough predictions on most sections of the hole. Continuously monitored torque has also been valuable aid, in deter- mining bit wear. 11) Bit run summary reports were printed after each bit run and sent to the STAVANGER office.

The section was drilled successfully within budget time in one run, penetrating several sedimentary rock groups, including the tuffaceous Balder formation, without problems. The Carbo-Sea oil based mud system proved once more to be of high quality, contributing to excellent hole cleaning and an effective drilling operation. Also, being able to run casing continuously to bottom with miniscule problems, reflects good quality in regards to hole cleaning. The 500 kg salt sacks appeared well sealed, resulting in dry salt that was easily added via hopper to the active system. Emphasis must be made on continuous quality control of the mentioned salt sacks, to avoid shipment of flocculated salt which has devastating effect on salt hopper equipment. Focus should be set on improving measuring devices on bulk tanks, as these have proven inaccurate at times.

answer_text: Monitored variables (with units): depth (m); rate of penetration, heave-and-tide compensated (m/hr and min/m); modified "d" exponent (dimensionless); total and chromatographic gas (%); formation bulk density (SG); mud temperature (°C, suction & flowline); mud weight (SG, suction & flowline); rotary speed (RPM); weight on bit and total hookload (metric tonnes); cumulative bit revolutions on bottom; torque (amps); cumulative pump strokes and strokes/min; totalised active & reserve pit volumes (barrels); trip tank volume (barrels); pump pressure (psi); flowrate (L/min, suction & flowline); mud conductivity (ppm NaCl, suction & flowline); shale factor (meq/100g); and H2 in mud (ppm) at discrete intervals. 4.6.6 Drilling fluids Ref. appendix D, drilling fluid program. This section will be drilled with Novatec POBM. Condition the received mud to the specified properties. Displace to sg POBM while drilling the shoe track. It is critical that all the mud has been sheared on surface prior to displacement. Condition the mud as required prior to drilling formation. If possible all premixes should be sheared prior to usage to get maximum yield from the clay and chemicals. Monitor and evaluate cuttings quality regarding condition, texture and amount. Maintain stable a- level and avoid fluctuations. If there are indications of poor hole cleaning, stop drilling and circulate the hole clean. Rotate the string with as high RPM as possible to aid hole cleaning. Perform at least 00C tests each day when circulating. Limestone stringers in the Balder Fm. has experienced losses at fracture pressures equal to 1.66 - sg in this sequence. TD of the 12 1/4 section will be into top Ty Fm., which is depleted gas reservoir. Due to depletion, the fracture pressure is reduced compared to initial pressure. With respect to both sequences, there will be high focus on ECD and clean hole all time during drilling. In addition, strategy pumping LCM to prevent losses will be performed. Highest ECD observed in A-4 when loosing returns was sg. The following recommendations are made to avoid lost returns: • Monitor mud weight and mud properties carefully throughout the section. • Pumping LCM pills will start above the Balder Fm. or latest when top Balder Fm. is penetrated and continued until TD of the section. detailed procedure containing final recipe will be sent to the rig in advance of the operations. • Make sure the hole is clean prior to drilling the Balder Fm. and the Ty Fm. Control ECD while drilling the Balder Fm. It is important to be able to pull out to the casing shoe without having to circulate. • Monitor ECD data, torque and drag, and data from cuttings flow meters for signs of poor hole cleaning. • Be careful when bringing up pumps, reaming and tripping. Control reaming speed, and wait one minute prior to changing reaming direction when reaming prior to connections. Perform surge and swab analysis to evaluate tripping speed. • Page 32 of 56

INTRODUCTION Logging unit T.C. 1054 was constructed and supplied to meet the special requirements of Statoil, according to D.N.V. regulations. The logs produced were: 1. Total concept log to special format for Statoil, sent in to the office on weekly basis. 2. Well completion log to special format for Statoil, sent in at the end of the well. 3. Supplementary sheets of bit data, mud data and deviation survey data for the well, forming section of this well completion report. As drilling progressed, the following data was telexed twice daily, or as appropriate to Statoil base at metre intervals: - depth(metres), heave and tide compensated rate of penetration (metres/hour, minutes/ metre ), modified 'd' exponent, gas (percent), formation bulk density (specific gravity), mud temperature in the flowline (degrees centigrade), mud weight in the suction pit (specific gravity), rotary revolutions per minute and the weight on the bit (metric tonnes). The parameters monitored in the logging unit were:- depth (metres), metre), total hookload and the weight on the bit (metric tonnes), cumulative bit revolutions on bottom and rotary revolutions per minute, torque (amps), cumulative pump strokes and stroke per minute function, totalised active and reserve,pit volumes (barrels), trip tank volume (barrels), pump pressure (p.s.1.), continuous total gas (percent), chromatographic gas analysis (percent), mud temperature- suction and flowline (degrees centigrade), mud weight - suction and flowline (specific gravity), flowrate - suction and flowline (litres per minute), mnd conductivity suction and flowline (p.p.m. Na Cl), formation bulk density (specific gravity), shale factor (milliequivalents per 100 grams), H2 present as gaseous phase in the mPd (p.p.m.) at dis- crete intervals.

The drilling of this final section did not go as smoothly as it might have done. Drill rates were generally rather low, even allowing for the high overbalance of the mud weight. This was due to rather hard, abrasive formations which were drilled using somewhat inadequate bits. Bit wear was rather high, two bits having 100 % bearing wear on one cone, and were, in fact, pulled just in time before any cones were lost. The last bit was 1/8 out of gauge. Excessive bit torque was also problem which resulted in the bits being off bottom on numerous occasions while the hole was reamed. chert band at 2675-76 caused excessively high torque and bit no. 17 was pulled early as result of very low drill rates at this stage (1.5 m/hr). EXcessive metal content was found in cuttings while bit no. 18 was on bottom. As this bit was in good condition when pulled it was assumed that the HWDP was wearing on the casing shoe and this was replaced with S135 drill pipe. This appeared to solve the problem, however, high torque and relatively low drill rates continued to be problem right to TD. The increase in mud weight from to SG at 2850 appeared to exaggerate the problem of slow drilling. Reducing the rotary speed and increasing the WOB showed some initial improvement in ROP but the bit wear was still rather high. The hole had to be reamed from 2845-50 several times before bit no. 20 could get to bottom without torquing up. iii, - - . 4.4,, .. • .

This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. Deposition was interrupted during mid Callovian times, possibly because of regional regressive phase. Subsidence and sedimentation of the Heather Formation resumed during late Callovian?-Early Oxfordian times although further, major unconformity separates the Early Oxfordian Heather Formation sensu stricto from the overlying Draupne Formation. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. Sedimentation continued through to Middle Volgian times in similar environmental conditions, although major unconformity is present at the top of the Draupne Formation. The Early Cretaceous sequence is characterised by major condensation and unconformities. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of Early Hauterivian calcareous claystones assigned to the Valhall Formation which accumulated in marine, inner shelf setting. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group, Formation 'A' were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. context_snippets.text: 2.3 Formation Multi Tester (FMT) In the Jurassic/Triassic sandstones the FMT log was run twice in an attempt to establish pressure gradients and to obtain reservoir fluid samples. The first FMT run was in combination with HP crystal pres- sure/temperature gauge. A total of four single reservoir fluid samples were taken. Run no.1 In run no.1, 11 out of 17 attempts to take pressure points were successful. 1.2 Purpose of the well The main objective of well 6608/10-7 was to test the extent of hydrocarbons in Upper to Lower Jurassic sandstones in the Melke- and Åre Formation, downflanks of well 6608/10-6, and if possible prove fluid contacts. Another objective, originally designated to possible sidetrack of well 6608/10-7, was to perform an interference test in the Åre Formation towards well 6608/10-6. side track was to be drilled if analysis of formation water samples confirmed high content of Barium. This would demand information about communication towards 6608/10-6 from a position further downflanks than the 6608/10-7 position. 1.3 Result of the well The well was spudded in water depth of 408 and drilled to total depth of 2319 mMD. No shallow gas was observed by the ROV at the wellhead. Two reservoir zones were penetrated, the Melke Formation Sandstone member and the Åre Formation. silty/sandy Not Formation was also encountered, but it did not have the same reservoir quality as the two previously mentioned. The sandstone sequence of the Melke Formation proved to be oil bearing. The main part of the oil bearing reservoir zone was cored. No oil-water contact was encountered. Oil was observed down to 2007 mMD in the Melke Formation. Weak hydrocarbon shows were seen in core chips from the Not Formation. The Åre Formation proved to be water filled up to 2018 mMD. The water samples proved to have Barium content lower than the limit set for requiring the sidetrack to be drilled. The observed formation tops were not in accordance with the prognosis. The difference between the prognosis and the observations for Tertiary and Cretaceous formation tops seem to vary bit. Typically, the Tertiary and Cretaceous formation tops, as well as the base Cretaceous unconformity were encountered deeper than prognosed. The top of the Melke Formation sandstone sequences, the Not Formation and the Åre Formation were encountered shallower than prognosed, but within the given uncertainties. (Ref. Fig. 4.3)

INTRODUCTION During shallow drilling cruise in the Barents Sea in 1987 (Appendix 1) samples were obtained from the Quaternary sediments covering the pre Quaternary rocks in the area. The purpose of this sampling was to document the conditions of the drilled Quaternary formation and to provide some regional data on general geotechnical conditions and glacial geology of the area. These were initiated upon completion of the air-brine capillary pressure tests. In accordance with the specifications for the work, the level of saturation at the final point of the capillary pressure test (13.8 bars) was used as the connate water saturation (Swir 1) for the first waterfloods. Restoration for these tests was thus achieved by saturating the voided pore space with de-aired,depolarised mineral oil. The oil had been blended to have viscosity of approximately times that of the simulated formation brine in order to emulate the reservoir oil-water viscosity ratio. The saturation of the voided space was achieved by carefully performed vacuuming and flooding technique. The freezing point of the simulated formation brine was first determined and then the desaturated samples placed in precisely controlled freezer set to few degrees above this freezing point. The samples were left to cool for about 24 hours along with batch of the appropriate oil- blend and then vacuumed under oil inside the cooling apparatus. Each sample was rapidly warmed back to room temperature allowing saturation to take place under atmospheric pressure. This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. Subsidence and sedimentation of the Heather Formation resumed during late Callovian?-Early Oxfordian times although further, major unconformity separates the Early Oxfordian Heather Formation sensu stricto from the overlying Draupne Formation. PROGRAM FOR CONDITIONING MUD, BULLHEADING, PERORATING AND REFRACTURING WELL 2/8A-17 OBJECTIVE: To condition the mud, bullhead the mud, add perforation interval in the Upper Hod and perform new stimulation job to obtain production from the Tor Formation. BACKGROUND: Having been unsuccessful in cleaning the wellbore by bullheading, the well has been surged to attempt to unplug the perforation without success. Further, an attempt to RIH to perforate failed due to the diesel/mud interface. The wellbore contains diesel from the packer to surface and mud from the perforation to the packer. The SCSSV is open and connected to handpump. Drilling is in charge of the operation. The steps referred to in the below procedure are in the General Completion Program. A preliminary wellbore schematic is attached. (Attachment I). PROCEDURE: 1. Leave the well with psi at surface for six hours to test the plugged perforations as barrier. 2. Rig up the Gray BPV lubricator assembly and test to 5000 psi and test the BPV by measuring bleed back volume. 3. Nipple down Xmas-tree and install dart in the BPV. 4. Nipple up drilling riser and BOP with 3/8 pipe ram. Test the riser BOP against the dart as specified in the General Drilling Program. Pull dart and BPV.

INTRODUCTION After the Well 2/8A-17 ceased flowing on 20 May 1985, the Upper Hod perforations were isolated by dumping marbles, glass-beads and sand. Further the well was perforated and stimulated in the Tor Formation on 26 May 1985. Below is report of the preparation for and execution of the Tor fracture stimulation treatment. WELL HISTORY PRIOR TO FRAC Well 2/8A-17 was stimulated third time in the Upper Hod lbs of 20/40 mesh sand was pumped during the treatment. However, the stimulation did not provide adequate communication with the Tor Formation. In an attempt to flow the well, it produced solids and ceased flowing on 20 May 1985. In an attempt to kill the well 140 bbls of mud was bullheaded into it. As this kill-mud was bullheaded with no problems it was immediately followed by 400 bbls of diesel leaving only diesel in the tubing thus avoided clean-up operation. The denser Tor interval 8m MD RKB was perforated three times with 90° phasing, spf, 7/8 gun. The well schematic is attached as Attachment 1. FRAC DESIGN A very conservative pump schedule was designed. Similar to the last refrac job in the Upper Hod Formation, pad of 55,000 gallons was chosen. Further, the first seven sand stages were extended to ensure some proppant to enter the formation prior to possible premature screen-out. The proppant chosen was 20/40 mesh sand. Attachment details the designed stimulation including volumes and proppant addition schedules.

context_snippets.text: 2.8 PETROPHYSICS 2.8.1 Introduction The 35/11-2 well encountered hydrocarbons in the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formation. Evaluation with RFT's and log data indicated the Brent contained producible hydrocarbons. The Sognefjord Formation has low net/gross, is tight and was not tested. 2.8.2 Summary The petrophysical evaluation for well 35/11-2 was performed using open hole wireline logs. Matrix parameters were established using core data when possible (Figure 2.10).The dual laterolog was used for resistivity, and the LDT calibrated to core was used to calculate porosity. Net sands were picked where the Dual Laterolog-Micro SFL log indicated permeable zones. Core data further indicated 10% porosity cutoff should be applied to the net sands. The petrophysical results along with the parameters used in the evaluation are summarized in Figure 2.11. For reserves and mapping purposes the upper Ness and the Tarbert are grouped into one unit, the lower Ness is in separate unit. The Etive and Oseberg are each separate units. The Archie parameters and apparent Rw used to calculate water saturation were determined using Pickett plots. The above method compensates for errors which could result from using incorrect Rw. The Rw obtained from analysis of a fluid sample from DST is ohm/m. The reference temperature for the Rw value is 130°C.

S 4.3 PORE PRESSURE Introduction Figure is composite plot of formation pressures against depth for well 35/11-3. Wireline pre-test data (FMT pressures) were obtained in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. Over the remainder of the well the pore pressure profile has been derived from empirically calculated data. Figure is composite plot of drilling exponent (Dxc), wireline and gas data for the well. Shale factor data for the Tertiary interval has been included to llustrate the influence of clay mineralogy changes on the data plots. The interpretation of pore pressures has been largely based upon the Dxc and Delta data plots, supplemented by gas data and well bore conditions. However, for the most part, the 35/11-3 well was drilled with significant overbalance which has minimized the use of these parameters. Well Summary Normal pore pressures equivalent to ppg EMW (equivalent mud weight) are assumed for the top hole section of Quaternary to Tertiary (Pliocene) age claystones and sandstones. There was no evidence of shallow gas as was tentatively interpreted at 479 to 497m and 573 to 634m on the shallow site survey. The Miocene Utsira Formation sandstones ( m) are overpressured to ppg EMW, and resulted in salt water flow into the well. Similar overpressured environments were encountered in the Utsira Formation in the Mobil operated 35/11-1 and 35/11-2 wells, and in the adjacent Gulf operated block, 35/8. Both of the previous Mobil wells in block 35/11 were drilled on, or adjacent to, seismically disturbed zones in the basal Nordland and uppermost Hordaland

Group sediments. This chaotic seismic character has been interpreted as being result of plastic deformation and/or slumping of the sediments. If is believed to have genetic link with the origin of the abnormal pore pressures in the Utsira Formation (see Well 35/11-2, Final Well Report, section 4.3). The 35/11-3 well, however, was drilled at location free from disrupted zones with only slight chaotic seismic structure, yet was still overpressured. This questions the previously argued causitive link between the disrupted zones and the development of abnormal pore pressures. Below the base of the Utsira Formation, pore pressure is believed to return to normal in the claystones and sandstones of the Nordland Group, and to remain so down to approximately 1400m in the Hordland Group. Below this depth the Dxc and wireline data plots indicate an increase in pore pressure up to maximum of to ppg at approximately 1660m. It should be noted however, that the observed shifts in the data plots are coincident with change from mixed layer to smectite clays and it is difficult to quantify accurately how much of the shift is due to changes in clay mineralogy and how much to increased pore pressure. I Below 1700m, the data plots indicate regression in pore pressure to normal (i.e approximately ppg BMW) by 1800m. Pressure remains close to normal throughout the Upper Cretaceous Shetland Group to 2600m. Below this depth, the data plots suggest that pore pressure increases slowly with depth down into the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Group, reaching maximum overpressure of around 9.5ppg BMW by the base Cretaceous. A marked shift in the compaction data plots, together with an increase in gas levels, marks the transition to higher pore pressures at the top of the Jurassic Viking Group at 2821m. •

- 204 - GAFFNEY, CLINE & ASSOCIATES CASED HOLE DST-2 Perforations 3 5m Commentary The zone perforated for this test was in the lower section of the Upper Jurassic Heather Formation. Log interpretation carried out by Schlumberger and Gulf had indicated that hydrocarbons could be present within the section though only limited intervals of moveables were postulated, water saturations seemingly being high and hydrocarbons possibly being reduced to residual for the most part. The log interpretation was hampered by lack of information pertaining to water resistivity and also by problems of mineralisation and therefore was considered only in semi-quantitative fashion. It was understood that sidewall core analysis had supported the view that hydrocarbons were present, possibly in the liquid phase. Prior to testing, the mud weight was taken down from ppg to 12.7 ppg in order to reduce the differential pressure across the APR-N tester . valve to an acceptable level, internal pressure being provided by only partial water cushion of some 2133 metres. full water cushion was not used since reservoir pressure of around 5300 psig was expected from RFT data and it was considered necessary to maintain an underpressure of around 0 psig if the formation was to be given fair chance to flow. The well began to clean up very quickly when opened for the main flow period and some 45 bbl of water cushion was recovered in 40 minutes. However, another 15 minutes were required to seemingly recover bbl of viscous gel that had been spotted above the APR-N valve and with all other flowing conditions unaltered this seemed to indicate more recovery than could be accounted for.

The gas effect is not seen in the other formations due to the thin sand and shale sequences. The logs were reviewed to identify potential gas/oil contact in the Tarbert,but no contact is apparent. 2.8.4 Sognefjord Formation 2 The Sognefjord Formation was found to have of net reservoir rock. Log data indicate the formation has thin sand/shale laminations and low porosity. Core data from the base of the zone shows it to be micaceous. A segregated RFT sample taken from this interval required 2 hours, 41 minutes to fill the and gallon chambers. Technical Memorandum (John Cater and Andrew Taylor, lchron Limited) Introduction Slabbed core from wells 6507/7-3, 6507/7-A17 and 6507/7-A35 was logged at ResLab Laboratories, Stavanger, by John Cater and Andrew Taylor (lchron Limited), on March 25th-27th 2003. For each well, copy of the hand-drawn 1:50 scale core log and written log comments are presented here. Illustrative core photographs are shown on Plates to 5. The sedimentology of the cored intervals is summarised below. Detailed descriptions are contained in the log comments. The depositional environments recorded by the cored intervals are interpreted below. Recommendations for future work to investigate the likely distribution and facies of Late Cretaceous sandstones in the Heidrun area are made at the end of this memorandum. Note that the most recent biostratigraphic data are not available for this memorandum. All depths quoted are core depths. Summary of core descriptions and interpreted depositional environments The cored section comprises mid to late Coniacian siltstones of the Kvitnos Formation overlying 2.51m of medium grained sandstones of the mid-Coniacian Lysing Formation (2367.55m-2370.06m), which in turn overlie fine grained sandstones of the late Aalenian Garn Formation. 2360.00m - 2367.55m This interval is dominated by laminated siltstones displaying local, weak bioturbation by pyritised Chondrites and sand-filled Sabularia (Plate 1A and 1B). The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

SUMMARY This is the first time the PP/FG TM service has been used offshore Norway real-time. The well was drilled without significant problems and the reservoir pressure was close to that prognosed in the drilling programme. The PP/FG calculated pore pressure results calculated by the model can only be verified in permeable formations from formation tests and well control incidents. Pore pressure transition zones always occur in impermeable formations and here results can be contentious when compared to traditional methods of pore pressure prediction. However, the results do have value if they can aid in the prediction of pressure when entering permeable formation. There were only two depths in the well where it was possible to verify the PP/FG results: 1. possible small influx at 4387m implied that the pressure PP/FG result was close to the actual formation pressure. 2. Below the Mandal Formation we had to interpolate the resistivity through hydrocarbon-rich formations. Using this corrected resistivity curve we predicted the reservoir pressure gradient at 4500m to be 1.81g/cc. The measured pressure gradient was I.75g/cc from the MDT. A calculated pore pressure maximum of 2.09g/cc was reported during drilling of the Cromer Knoll Group. This was revised down to 2.00g/cc when the wireline data became available. The difference was mainly due to miscalibrated MWD resistivity run which was consistantly reading values 30% more conductive than the wireline, but also slightly due to the model interpreting the lithology from the gamma ray as too calcareous. The PP/FG calculated fracture pressure results were within 0.03g/cc of the actual LOT's at 13 3/8 and 7/8 shoes. This indicates that we have an accurate fracture propagation pressure gradient. Considerable valuable information and experience was gained as result of this work which will improve the PP/FG service and future pore and fracture pressure prediction in this area. It has allowed us to assess the updates and improvements to the program which have recently been added to the software, and has suggested additional improvements which are now being implemented. I. INTRODUCTION The Sperry-Sun PP/FG service is based on software model that calculates pore and fracture pressures on an incremental basis through all major lithologies in normally compacted sedimentary sequences. It requires calibration to offset wells. The two closest wells to the 2/7-29 location, 2/7-19 & 2/7-22, were studied and calibration for the real-time job was derived. This was described fully in previous report. This final report for BP Norway describes the pore and fracture pressure results using the PP/FG service on the Mmrsk Guardian for well 2/7-29. The service commenced from the 7/8 casing point at 3124m on the 16th October until the Permian at 4850m on the 21st December. Results from real- time MWD data whilst drilling arc compared to the wircline data for this post well analysis. question: Which wells reported RFT, MDT, or FMT formation pressure measurements in the Fangst Group?

context_snippets.text: III1.6 Summary of Pore Pressure The pore pressure, overburden and fracture gradients are presented in enclosed figure, together with the mud weight gradient used in the well. The pore pressure is evaluated using drilling parameters, DXC, and sonic log and measured formation pressures (FMT's). The pore pressure gradient was equal to the normal gradient (1.03 g/cc) from seabed down to the Kai Formation (1245 m) as prognosed. Due to relatively thiner section of the Kai Formation (which was expected to have abnormal pressure) and relatively more sandy lithology it was difficult to see clear trend both on DXC and sonic measurements. However, by taking into consideration other drilling parameters especially gas readings which started to increase below the top Kai Formation, the pore pressure was estimated to be increasing from below the top Kai Formation. Background gas values increased from % to 1-3 % from 1250 m. The pore pressure gradient started to increase from about 1250 and reached its maximum value g/cc at 1300 m, g/cc lower than prognosed. It remained the same down to the top Jurassic (Melke Formation) at 1352 m and decreased abruptly to normal gradient again. FMT's (5 points) were taken at the top reservoir section (Fangst Group) from 1361 to 1395 in. pore pressure gradient of g/cc was calculated from the FMT's in the top section of reservoir which estimated to be continued the same throughout the rest of the reservoir and to the TD. 40 letk89102013r

Comments to some of the parameters are given below. Pressure EWL MDT was run in the 1/2” section (Tilje Fm. 3.4-Aare Fm. 6.2), and the measured formation pressures from this service were used as input to the petrophysical evaluation. No pressure measurements were taken in the Tilje Fm. 3.4, 3.3.3, 3.3.1, 3.2.2, and 1.2. The formation pressures used for these zones were estimated based on the formation pressure in adjacent zones. The measured formation pressures in the upper Tilje Fm. were about 2-2.5 bar higher than the estimated formation pressure from the RTD document. Therefore, in the Fangst Group formations Garn and Ile, formation pressure bars higher than the estimated formation pressure from the RTD document was used. The formation pressures in the Not Fm. and in the Ror Fm. were estimated based on formation pressures in adjacent zones. Temperature No temperature curve were available, and the representative bottom hole temperature for each formation was based on an assumption of the annular temperature being equal to the formation temperature (desribed below). The formation temperature is in the petrophysical evaluation model derived from the standard field wide temperature model (Chapter in the “Full field update – Petrophysics” document [2]). GR scaling and shift GR scaling and GR shift, which are used to normalize the gamma-ray curve, were set manually. The parameters were tuned so that VSH from the gamma-ray method are in accordance with field averages based on high case (Ror Fm. 1) and low case (Garn Fm.). question: For well 30/6‑E‑15 AT3, what are the MD values of the 18 5/8″ casing shoe and the 16″ section TD?
answer_text: 18 5/8″ casing shoe: 1212 m MD; 16″ section TD: 2900 m MD.

context_snippets.text: WELL SUMMARY Objective and Result Well 30/6-E-15 / E-15 was the fourteenth well to be drilled from the Oseberg Øst platform. The well was designed to be horizontal tubing oil producer in the Etive Formation on the Beta Saddle structure, with Ness and Oseberg Formations as possible additional objectives. Operations Summary Activity on well 30/6-E-15 / E-15 continued 2001-04-22 after the conductor was installed on 2000-10-02. 34 Hole Section The 34” hole section was drilled in one run from 222m to 354m MD. The section was drilled as vertical hole with inclination between 0.0° and 0.8°. No tight hole or instability was observed. The conductor shoe was set at 350m MD. 24 Hole Section The cement and conductor shoe was drilled from 351-356m MD. Prepared to run Gyro for 24 hole section. After drilling through the conductor shoe, the 24 hole was drilled and oriented down to 1217m MD. No hole problems encountered during drilling, or when pulling out of hole. The 24” hole was circulated clean, and the 18 5/8 casing was set with the casing shoe @ 1212m MD. The casing point was reached in one run. No FIT was taken. 16 Hole Section The cement plugs and float were drilled from 1196-1197m MD. Then drilled out cement and shoe to 1211m MD. After drilling to 1220m MD FIT to sg. was performed at 1212m MD. The 16 section was drilled without incident, in one run, to TD at 2900m MD. Hole conditions were good. However extensive circulating at TD was required to fully clean the hole from cuttings. The casing shoe was set at 2898m MD. First 12 1/4 Hole Section Cement wiper plug was tagged at 2860m MD. The wiper plugs, float and cement in the shoe track were drilled from 2860-2898m MD. Rathole and three meters of new formations were drilled out from 2898-2903m MD. After circulating the well, FIT test was performed to sg. at 2903m MD. The 12 1/4 pilot hole was drilled in runs, due to MWD-tool failure on the two first run. TD was reach at 6228m MD. From 6045-6228m MD the hole was drilled without a working logging-tool. Regarding hole conditions, there were some problems when running in Run # due to tight hole. When running Run # the hole was tight all the way. Lot of coal and carbonaceous clay were observed when reaming down on last run. The hole was cleaned before logging. PEX, MDT and GPIT were run on wire-line.

The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

Two reservoir zones were penetrated, the Melke Formation Sandstone member and the Åre Formation. silty/sandy Not Formation was also encountered, but it did not have the same reservoir quality as the two previously mentioned. The sandstone sequence of the Melke Formation proved to be oil bearing. The main part of the oil bearing reservoir zone was cored. No oil-water contact was encountered. Oil was observed down to 2007 mMD in the Melke Formation. Weak hydrocarbon shows were seen in core chips from the Not Formation. The Åre Formation proved to be water filled up to 2018 mMD. The top of the Melke Formation sandstone sequences, the Not Formation and the Åre Formation were encountered shallower than prognosed, but within the given uncertainties. (Ref. Fig. 4.3)

Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

For this purpose the rock composition and porosity should be carefully analysed. In the actual case where in addition to the temperature also the pore pressure history is needed, it was also important to match the rock-permeability as close as possible. To get around this problem we had to make use of certain assumptions. In both wells modelled, the Tertiary sequence is composed at the base of thin and compact shaly Paleocen and Early Eocene sequence with some sandy stringers at Late Paleocene level. Above this sequence follows thick sandy and silty Plio- and Pleistocene sequence that evidently is fairly loose and unconsolidated. If it is assumed that this sequence has an equivalent permeability that is an order or two above what is found in the Paleocene - Eocene sequence below where overpressures start to build up, then this may be used as basis for the modelling. There has been performed one dimensional models in the area; one in each of the wells and one at shotpoint 2500 of line E-17-83 (Fig. 4). In the modelling of well 6507/2-1, the hydrostatic pressure was first subtracted from the pore pressure profile in Fig.l. This gave us the size of the over pressure in the well. Next suitable permeability value for the sediments around 1000 depth was chosen to match the measured pressure buildup at this level. The permeability of the Eocene - Paleocene sequence was then varied till good match between the measured and modelled pore pressures was obtained also for this level and down to Late Cretaceous. These permeabilities and those chosen for the remaining part of the well are shown Fig. 5; and the corresponding over pressures modelled and measured are shown in Fig. 6.

question: For well 7122/7-2, what are the formulas, computational steps, and physical meanings distinguishing average velocity (SRD→GEO) versus RMS velocity?
answer_text: Average velocity (SRD→GEO): Vavg = vertical depth / (TWT/2) = 2·Depth / TWT, computed by dividing the vertical depth from SRD by half the two‑way travel time. RMS velocity: Vrms = sqrt(Σ(νi^2·Δti) / ΣΔti) with νi the velocity in each ms interval, computed as the root‑mean‑square of interval velocities over time; Vavg is the bulk mean velocity to depth, Vrms is the energy/time‑weighted velocity used for NMO and seismic propagation.

than on the 3D seismic data. However the complete coverage of the 3D seismic data in map view allows the shapes of the amplitude anomalies to be imaged. The Plio-Quaternary Unconformity is seen on seismic data as reflector of laterally variable amplitude. This is to be expected, as the unconformity brings different lithologies in contact with each other and the tuning effects on seismic amplitudes will vary from place to place. In addition, there are some anomalous areas which show indications of gas in the sediments. These indications are: reverse phase top reflector, normal phase basal reflector, highest amplitudes in subtle structural highs, phase reversed lateral truncation, localised edge diffractions, acoustic masking and velocity pull-down of deeper reflectors. The proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are both on the edge of an amplitude anomaly at the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity which is likely to be due to gas in the sediments. linear feature, which may be buried iceberg ploughmark with sandy infill, links the western and eastern parts of the anomaly. The thickness of the possible gas bearing interval is estimated to be less than 21 at the proposed 7122/7-2 location and less than 16 at the relief well location. There is no lithology or velocity data from the previous well 7122/7-1 at such shallow level, but realistic velocities would place the top of the possible gas bearing zone at somewhere between 55 and 75 below seabed (432 and 452 MSL). At such shallow level, any gas bearing sandy layer is likely to be normally pressured. The gas may not be moveable. The seismic data do not indicate the gas saturation and moderate to high seismic amplitudes can be produced by only or 10% gas saturation. None the less, due caution should be taken while drilling through the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity. Reference is made to the Askeladden West well 7120/7-1 which had gas bearing sand interval in the Quaternary, from 375 to 392 m. The Base Tertiary Unconformity is of variable seismic amplitude within the site survey area. These lateral changes are interpreted as mostly due to lithological variations and seismic tuning effects. The amplitudes at the proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are not anomalously high and the chance of shallow gas at the Base Tertiary Unconformity is assessed as low. The interval in question is less than 10 thick. pilot hole will be drilled through this level and appropriate shallow gas procedures will be followed. Conclusions At the proposed location of well 7122/7-2 there may be boulders in the glacial sediments down to maximum of 100 below seabed. In the lower half of the same interval there may be gas in sandy layer up to 21 thick. The gas is likely to be normally pressured and the saturation may be low. The chance of gas at the Plio- Quaternary Unconformity level is assessed as high. Between 580 and 600 MSL there may be thin layer of gas bearing sand at the Base Tertiary Unconformity. context_snippets.text: 4.0 VSP Processing The VSP has been processed for 74 levels between 1410 and 465 metres MD below KB. Figures to 14 in Appendix summarize the VSP processing. 4.1 Band-Pass Filtering, True Amplitude Recovery and Normalisation After analysing the VSP power spectrum, zero-phase Butterworth filter (sixth order harmonic). with band pass of - 90 Hz is applied initially. Whole trace equalization has been achieved by normalizing the RMS amplitude of the first breaks to correct for transmission losses of the direct wave, so the data now simulates plane wavefield. static time shift of ms has been applied to each trace to correct transit times for the location of the surface sensor with respect to mean sea level. The Geophysical airgun report enclosed in this binder shows the Time and Depth relationship for each VSP level. Figure 6 shows the data after Band Pass Filtering, Static time shift and Normalisation. 4.2 Down and Upgoing Wavefield Separation by Velocity Filter Figures 7, 8, and 10 show the data after wavefield separation. than on the 3D seismic data. However the complete coverage of the 3D seismic data in map view allows the shapes of the amplitude anomalies to be imaged. The Plio-Quaternary Unconformity is seen on seismic data as reflector of laterally variable amplitude. This is to be expected, as the unconformity brings different lithologies in contact with each other and the tuning effects on seismic amplitudes will vary from place to place. In addition, there are some anomalous areas which show indications of gas in the sediments. These indications are: reverse phase top reflector, normal phase basal reflector, highest amplitudes in subtle structural highs, phase reversed lateral truncation, localised edge diffractions, acoustic masking and velocity pull-down of deeper reflectors. The proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are both on the edge of an amplitude anomaly at the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity which is likely to be due to gas in the sediments. linear feature, which may be buried iceberg ploughmark with sandy infill, links the western and eastern parts of the anomaly. The thickness of the possible gas bearing interval is estimated to be less than 21 at the proposed 7122/7-2 location and less than 16 at the relief well location. There is no lithology or velocity data from the previous well 7122/7-1 at such shallow level, but realistic velocities would place the top of the possible gas bearing zone at somewhere between 55 and 75 below seabed (432 and 452 MSL). At such shallow level, any gas bearing sandy layer is likely to be normally pressured. The gas may not be moveable. The seismic data do not indicate the gas saturation and moderate to high seismic amplitudes can be produced by only or 10% gas saturation. None the less, due caution should be taken while drilling through the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity. Reference is made to the Askeladden West well 7120/7-1 which had gas bearing sand interval in the Quaternary, from 375 to 392 m. The Base Tertiary Unconformity is of variable seismic amplitude within the site survey area. These lateral changes are interpreted as mostly due to lithological variations and seismic tuning effects. The amplitudes at the proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are not anomalously high and the chance of shallow gas at the Base Tertiary Unconformity is assessed as low. The interval in question is less than 10 thick. pilot hole will be drilled through this level and appropriate shallow gas procedures will be followed. Conclusions At the proposed location of well 7122/7-2 there may be boulders in the glacial sediments down to maximum of 100 below seabed. In the lower half of the same interval there may be gas in sandy layer up to 21 thick. The gas is likely to be normally pressured and the saturation may be low. The chance of gas at the Plio- Quaternary Unconformity level is assessed as high. Between 580 and 600 MSL there may be thin layer of gas bearing sand at the Base Tertiary Unconformity. The chance of gas at this level is assessed as low 3.5.13.2 Possible Drilling Hazards choosing suitable anchor positions. • At the proposed location of well 7122/7-2 there may be boulders in the glacial sediments down to maximum of 100 below seabed

context_snippets.text: Geoservices Saga Petroleum A further drilling break was flowchecked at 4526m but proved negative. From this point there was no further evidence of increasing pore pressure gradient with both the d-exponent and background gas indicating, if anything, decreasing trend. At 4593m another drilling break occurred which was flowchecked at 4596m. The well was found to be flowing and total of 8m' was allowed into the trip tank before the well was shut in. Post kick analysis of the drilling data failed to yield any valid indicators that might have predicted this overpressured zone. The elapsed time from the drill break until the flow check was about four minutes and there were no indications of influx during this period. It was only after the pumps were shut down for the flowcheck that an increase in volume was noted. Following the kick an attempt was made to establish the bottom hole pressure but this failed due to breakdown of the formation. It was later determined that the well was flowing from TD and leaking out to the formation at between 3970 and 3950m. The hole packed off around the string at 3800m and it was necessary to back it off after setting cement plug on bottom. With the string free circulation was established with difficulty and the kick circulated out. Extremely high gas values were recorded while circulating. Gas composition showed large proportion of heavier components and good fluorescence was obtained from fluid samples suggesting that reservoir formation had been encountered. Later in the circulation the returns were seen to consist entirely of slightly brackish water for several minutes. It is therefore possible that the migrating gas bubble reduced the hydrostatic enough to produce water from one of the porous sand formations. Once well control had been re-established it was determined that the hole was in extremely poor condition with large, unstable washed out sections. It was therefore plugged back to below the 13 3/8 casing shoe prior to sidetracking. Following evaluation of the VSP log run in the 5/8 casing at the end of the 121/4 section of 6406/2- 3T2 it was determined that the kick originated in the Aptian sandstone of the Intra Lange formation and not in the Gam formation as had been originally thought.

question: How do offshore plug-drilling and Dean-Stark plug preparation differ in drilling method, lubricant used, and preservation/treatment?
answer_text: Offshore plug‑drilling used an air‑driven plug drill with refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant and plugs were wrapped in cling film, aluminium foil and sealed with ProtecCore laminate immediately; Dean–Stark plugs were drilled onshore with Clarisol oil as cooling agent and then subjected to toluene Dean–Stark extraction, Soxhlet methanol cleaning for salts and dried at 60°C for 48 hours.

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 15
