The resolution for the CT-Scan,s are 512 512 pixels. 5.1 CT Scanning Whole Core CT scanning visualises representative homogeneous sections for possible further studies. The CT scan also helps locating any fractured areas of the core, identify density variations and can be used as tool for orientation of the core prior to slabbing or subsequent plug sampling. The core still in unopened core inner barrels was CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One overview picture (topogram) and four slice pictures were produced every 100-cm of core. The topogram is standard X-ray photo taken from above, covering 100 cm of core. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. 5.2 CT Scanning Seal Peels All Seal Peels (preserved whole core) from this well were CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One (topogram) overview picture, two radial and two axial slice pictures were produced for each seal peel. The topogram is standard X-ray Scan taken from above, covering the length of the preserved core sample. It shows larger structures and fractures in the core, and is used for selection of detailed slice pictures. The slice pictures are reading of radiation passing through the core. An X-ray source is sending pulses of energy through the core and set of detectors rotating around the core detects the passing signals. The readings are used for making computer produced slice picture of the core. When seal peels are CT scanned, print of the CT scan is mounted along with the core B-cut representing the removed whole core. A total of fifty-one SWC samples and eight 1,5” Horizontal plugs were also CT-Scanned. The CT scans are presented as separate report. Restricted 11

42 A. INTERPRETATION OF FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY (FIS) DATA A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, including petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries with FIS, one can obtain valuable and unique information on three major exploration topics: 1. Petroleum migration or paleocharge 2. Seals 3. Proximity to undrilled pay and two major production topics: 1. Pay zone and bypassed pay delimitation 2. Reservoir compartmentalization. The previous discussions have concentrated on identifying spectral types in FIS data. This is necessary first interpretive step. The next task is to evaluate the significance of FIS depth trends in their own right (now knowing their spectral origins), and eventually, in light of other available information to answer specific questions, such as were enumerated above. Petrographic data from anomalous fluid inclusion zones are often critical elements of these higher order interpretations, as will be seen, which why petrographic follow-up work is conducted as routine part of every FIS analysis (see Table of Petrographic Observations). A.3.1 Significance of FIS petroleum indications The most basic question that FIS can address is Is there any evidence for present or past petroleum in this borehole? Documentation of an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly generally pro- vides positive answer to this question, but could indicate other processes as well. Possible explanations for an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly are discussed in the following paragraphs. Migration without trapping A migration pathway may be indicated when FIS responses are low or moderate, when contamination and recycled inclusions can be discounted, when quoted visual petroleum inclu- sion abundances are rare or several (see Table of Petrographic Observations), and when no other petrographic or log evidence of current petroleum charge is identified in the zone. There are number of factors that influence inclusion abundance and, consequently, raw FIS response strength, including geologic setting, extent of diagenesis, rock type and permeability. However, it has been demonstrated that both visual petroleum inclusion abundance and FIS strength within many porous reservoir rocks is proportional to hydrocarbon saturation or pa- leosaturation in relative sense. Because migration occurs at average bulk-volume petroleum saturations below those encountered in charged reservoirs, FIS signal strength and visual in- clusion abundance are generally lower along migration pathways than in charged reservoirs from the same area. FIS#FI150639a - 6406/12-3S - www.fittulsa.com

Fluid Inclusion Technologies (FIT), Inc., is laboratory-based petroleum service or- ganization established in 1997 and offering variety of analytical services including some previously proprietary technologies. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. The procedure has major impact in the areas of both Petroleum Production and Exploration Applications providing informa- tion unattainable via more traditional methods and, has been instrumental in the discovery of significant petroleum reserves, influenced exploration and acreage acquisition decisions and provided innovative options for resource estimation, petroleum production and enhanced oil recovery operations. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphic Analysis, often in combination with other patented techniques, emerging geochemical methodologies and standard microscopic methods, all available through Fluid Inclusion Technologies, Inc., provides unique and un- equaled industry product boasting an impressive list of proven applications including deter- mination of Product Type, Hydrocarbon Migration, Seals and Seal Integrity, Fluid Contacts, Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum, Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimi- tation, Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization and Fluid Pressure Compartments. Further information regarding the application of FIS Analysis and the other technical ser- vices we provide to problems in petroleum exploration and production is available elsewhere in this report and on our website:www.fittulsa.com. 4.1 General Logistics of Initiating an FIS Analysis To Initiate an FIS Analysis: contact FIT' directly to discuss goals of the study, sample requirements, turnaround time, pricing, and other related aspects. New clients are particularly encouraged to consult with our staff during the early stages of project development to optimize sample selection, preparation and shipment. Rock materials for FIS Analysis are shipped directly to FIT for sample preparation including any necessary crushing/sieving, subsampling and washing. When sampling for FIS Analysis: the technique is equally applicable to cuttings, core and outcrop samples, but all samples will ultimately be reduced to cuttings-sized rock ma- terial. Wells drilled with any mud system can be analyzed (including oil-based systems), as can samples of any age (i.e., fresh cuttings or those warehoused for many years). Our suggested sampling interval for general well studies is 30 ft (10 m). Pay-delineation studies, reservoir-scale studies or other applications involving rapidly changing fluid chemistries should be sampled at the tightest possible spacing, depending on sample availability (e.g., 1-3 ft). A maximum of 575 samples can be analyzed for given well. Approximately gm of clean rock material is needed for each sample. In most cases, some amount of additional washing is required - even for washed samples, thus, it is best to send enough to ensure ample material after final wash. A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 43 gas) and the relative abundance of these inclusions will influence the bulk spectra. Addi- tionally, total inclusion abundance will affect the spectra insofar as higher molecular weight species represent smaller volumetric proportion of petroleum and are also less volatile, hence decrease below instrumentation detection limits before low molecular weight species. Conse- quently, some samples with low oil inclusion abundance generate wet gas mass spectra, for instance. Optical inclusion abundance and characteristics should be consulted, where pro- vided, to verify the interpreted petroleum type (see Table of Petrographic Observations). With the above limitations in mind, the following petroleum types are identified on the basis of spectral characteristics: Dry gas: mostly C1 with lesser C2-C3 and no higher hydrocarbons. Wet gas: C1-C9 may be present, but C6+ species are in minimal abundance. The alkane slope is extreme. Gas-condensate: C1-C11 may be present. The alkane slope is quite steep, reflecting very gas- enriched phase. Volatile oil: C1-C13 present. Slight gas-range enrichment is observed and the alkane slope is mod- erate to steep. Oil: C1-C13 is present. The alkane slope may be flat to moderate. Biodegradation is suggested if sulfur compounds such as H2S, COS, CS2, S2 (+/- SO2) and/or thiols are present in addition to petroleum species. Ratios of paraffins to naphthenes may be low as well, as bacteria typically prefer to metabolize alkanes compared to other classes of petroleum compounds. Petrographic data may provide further evidence for biodegradation in the form of low-gravity petroleum inclusions. Bacterial activity is generally restricted to maximum burial temperatures below 65-70°C; hence FIS evidence of biodegradation is most commonly observed in rocks that are currently below this temperature. Thermal alteration of liquid petroleum species can produce spectra very similar to those generated from biodegraded hydrocarbons, because the products of two common processes, bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR) and thermochemical sulfate reduction (TSR), are essentially identical. The best distinction is made from current bottom-hole temperature data, which, if above 140°C or so may be indicative of TSR, and if below 70°C or so is more consistent with BSR. Potential interpretive problems arise in the intervening temperature range, when deeply buried sediments are unroofed or when petroleum altered at shallow depths becomes buried to greater depth. Petrographic data may help, as pyrobitumen frequently accompanies TSR, while low-gravity liquid petroleum inclusions often occur in association with bacteri- ally altered oils. Additional temperature or thermal maturity data (including fluid inclusion homogenization temperatures) may also be useful. The presence of significant amounts of sulfur species can indicate sour petroleum phase, where the souring process may in some cases be reflection of the source rock, but could also reflect BSR or TSR. study of TSR sour gas pools in Canada suggests that evaluating the relative proportion of products and reactants can provide measure of sour gas potential. As TSR progresses, long-chain alkanes decrease while low molecular weight petroleum species increase along with CO2, aromatics organic acids and the various sulfur compounds enumer- ated above. Ironically, H2S alone may not be as accurate an indicator of H2S content, as it is scavenged naturally (e.g., to form pyrite in iron-rich rocks) and by the metallic internal surfaces of the analytical system.

question: How do recorded loss rates (m3/hr) during 7" liner cementing compare with segmented bond log results?

question: How do the lithologies of Heimdal, Nordland, Utsira, and Hordaland compare regarding sand versus shale/clay stringers?
answer_text: Heimdal and Utsira are predominantly sand reservoirs, whereas Nordland is mainly claystone with sandstone stringers and Hordaland is chiefly shale/claystone (with occasional dolomite stringers).

context_snippets.text: GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-25 Well 25/8-B-25 is planned to be horizontal oil producer in the Heimdal-reservoir in the Elli Structure. All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. Lithological boundaries were interpolated between two neighbouring samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and M'WD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse Cl, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. Ratios (C1/C2, Cl/C3, Cl/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of Cl. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show Cl, but very high shows of Cl are usually indicative of salt water. If the Cl/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the Cl/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If Cl/C4 is less than Cl/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the Cl Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/NON-PRODUCTIVE Cl/C5: 2-30 However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 ± C4 + Cs 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + Cs total 100 the GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LIAR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and Cs are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. The conventional core analysis are presented together with the log interpretation in Appendix and in Figure 7.1.1. The net sand averages are given in Tabel 7.1.2. 7.3 Special Core Analysis A detailed SCAL programme is being carried out on selected core samples from well 34/7-A-4 H. Resistivity Index in conjunction with oil/water capillary pressure measurements Formation Factor at reservoir pressure, permeability and pore volume changes at various confining pressures Co/Cw at simulated reservoir overburden pressure The results will be available during 1993. 7.4 Formation Pressure Measurements A Repeat Formation Tester (RFT) with HP gauge was used to obtain formation pressure measurements, see Table 7.4.1. During taking the formation pressure measurements, the HP gauge became unstable and no HP formation pressures in the water zone was obtained. The reliable HP gauge formation pressures in the oil zone are within three psi compared to the formation pressures taken in the well 34/7-1. The strain gauge pressures are plotted in Figure 7.4.1, showing an oil gradient of bar/m equivalent to an oil density of g/cc. Only one reliable formation pressure was taken in the water zone, therefore no oil water contact can be defined in the well. From the log interpretation oil is proved down to 3007m MD RKB (2583.5 TVD RKB) and water up to MD RKB (2590.3 TVD RKB). The most likely contact in the well is defined at the MD RIO (2586 TVD RKB), is assumed to be the same as defined in well 34/7-1. 7.5 Fluid Analysis No fluid sample was collected during the logging of well 34/7-A-4 H.

• 7.1.2 Log Analysis The well has been analysed using deterministic model. The effective porosity calculation is based on the density log with correction for hydrocarbon effects and shale volume. The shale volume is mainly calculated as the minimum value from the density-neutron crossplot method and the gamma ray. Water saturation is calculated from the Poupon-Leveaux (Indonesia) equation. The dip and borehole corrected deep resistivity measurement from the phasor induction log has been used as the true resistivity. The dip and borehole corrected medium resistivity reading was used in one interval where the deep, dip corrected measurement saturates. Continuous log permeabilities are estimated using the Horizon software package. The database for the permeability prediction consists of conventional core air permeabilities and log data from all the cored Upper Lunde reservoir intervals in the Snorre Field. The input parameters have been picked from log crossplots from this well and from conventional core analysis from other wells in the area. Electrical factors from special core analysis and formation water resistivity are the same as those used in the Snorre Field Development and Operating Plan (FDP). The input parameters are summarised in Table 7.1.2. The basis for the cut-off values used for net sand evaluation is as reported in the FDP. The porosity cut-off used for net sand calculation is based on the value corresponding to mD from core porosity vs. core permeability (air) crossplots. porosity cut-off of 15 % is used in the Lunde Formation, the applied shale volume cut-off is 40 %. The petrophysical net sand averages are summarised in Tables 7.1.3 and 7.1.4. The interpretation (CPI) of reservoir zones LO1 to LO7 is given in Fig. 7.1.1. and 7.1.2. The bottom of the computer processed interpretation is at mTVD RKB (3849.5 MD RKB) in reservoir zone L08. Refer to chapter for reservoir zonation. The CPI plot of the Lunde reservoirs is given in 1:500 scale in measured depth in Appendix and in true vertical depth in Appendix 4. Good reservoir properties are calculated throughout the sandstones in the oilbearing part of the reservoir zone LO2 - L05. The initial OWC was expected in the interval 4 TVD RKB in reservoir zone L06. The logs indicate oil down to mTVD RKB and water up to 2633 mTVD RKB, with the OWC most likely in the shale just at the top of reservoir zone L06. Due to pressure depletion, no OWC can be defined from formation pressures.

The performance of the TriSor OFS surface equipment during the survey was excellent, with accurate gun tuning throughout. ▪ The downhole data recorded with the Borehole VSI tool was of high quality, and good vector fidelity was recorded with high signal to noise ratio. ▪ Good first break picks were obtained in the main VSP part of the well. A tuned array of 250cu.in Sercel G-Guns, operating at 2000psi was used as source for the survey. The guns were deployed by the rig’s crane. The guns target firing pressure was 2000 psi. This applies differential correction to the sonic log where it is assumed the greatest amount of time error is caused by the lower velocity sections of the log. Over given interval the method will correct only At values which are higher than threshold, the Atmin. Values of At which are lower than the threshold are not corrected. The correction is reduction of the excess of At over Atmin ie. At - Atmin At - Atmin is reduced through multiplication by reduction coefficient which remains constant over the interval. This reduction coefficient, named G, can be defined as: G = + drift (At - Atmin) dZ Where drift is the drift over the interval to be corrected and the value (At - Atmin) dZ is the time difference between the integrals of the two curves At and Atmin, over the same interval. 6.3 Bathymetry The multibeam echo sounder data was processed onboard MV Fugro Meridian using Fugro Starfix suite to monitor data quality and data coverage. The data was logged in Simrad Raw format (.all) and imported into Starfix.Proc for processing. Both single beam and multibeam echo sounder data were corrected for transducer draught, acoustic velocity through sea water and vessel heave, pitch and roll, and then positioned with reference to the echo sounder transducer. 6.4 Sidescan Sonar The engineers and geophysicists examined the sidescan sonar records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks include range/scale, gains, tow fish height and position, as well as overall record quality. The sidescan sonar data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full by the geophysicist, using SonarWiz Version software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted, in which case the XTF file would be transferred to the relevant working directory for use, or, if rejected, would be flagged as potential re-run. Mosaicking of the sidescan sonar data was performed using the mosaic module, which applied slant range correction to the data and checked for full sonar coverage of the survey area. 6.5 Sub-bottom Profilers The engineers and geophysicists examined the hull-mounted pinger and mini sleeve gun records online as the survey progressed. Routine checks included sweep/scale, gains, examination of seabed pulse and penetration as well as overall record quality. The sub-bottom profiler data from all completed survey lines were viewed offline in full, by the geophysicist, using Starfix.Interp software. On completion of this review, the geophysicist would update the Analogue Data QC Log accordingly (Appendix E.4). Lines would either be accepted or rejected and flagged as potential re-run. 6.6 2DHR Multichannel Seismic Quality control of the online 2DHR multichannel seismic system was undertaken by the onboard engineers, geophysicist and seismic processor. The engineers maintained an observers’ log (Appendix E.2) in which all relevant information was recorded. Typically, routine checks were made on the source and streamer; the engineers monitored the manifold pressure, gun statistics (including any dropped/mis-timed shots) as well as pulse/frequency spectra of the seismic source. Routine checks of the streamer included streamer integrity (noisy, dead or reverse polarity channels), noise (due to environmental factors or weather), and streamer depth control/feather angle. On completion of each 2DHR multichannel seismic line, the data underwent final QC. The onboard geophysicist used the RadExPro seismic processing system as well as the observers’ logs and other quality control data generated by the NTRS2 system. Shot and CMP gathers were generated, to allow the identification of bad channels/shots and noise problems, and to verify the streamer offset and depth of the gun array. Then, brute stack was generated for each line, to ascertain any swell noise and check the overall data quality. The data were processed aboard the Fugro Meridian using the OpenCPS seismic processing system. The data processing flows aim to remove noise and seismic interference from 2DHR data. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

They comprise conventional wells drilled in the quadrants 7119, 7120, 7121, 7122 and 7219, as well as IKU shallow drilling 7018/05-U- 06 at the margin of the Troms-Finnmark Platform some 25 km southwest of the licence area. The pressure log commences with the establishment of returns at the 30 casing shoe. These sediments may be assumed to be in full communication with the seabed, therefore showing normal pore pressure gradient of 1.03/1.04 SG equivalent mud weight (EMW). DXc trends over this section tend to be unreliable, since as measure of drillability of the formation, values are misleadingly low. In such unconsolidated sequences, drill rate is very strongly affected by the 'jetting' action of the bit nozzles. Hence DXc shows decreasingly negative anomaly until the formation is sufficiently lithified so as to be unaffected by bit washing. Gas levels are high, and relatively constant at 50 to 100 units, with occasional peaks from the minor sand horizons. These gas levels represent the immature, shallow gas zones commonly present in such sediments. Mud temperature readings show normal trends i.e. steadily increasing with depth although there is temporary but inconclusive increase in delta from 600 to 670 metres. Electric log plots of deep resistivity and sonic time show normal trends, although the resistivity plot displays negative trend from 600 to 800 metres. This is assumed to reflect the increasing sand content of the formation. In summary, the recent Pliocene sediments are interpreted as having constant 'normal' pore pressure gradient of 1.03/1.04 SG EMW. Miocene ( metres) This section comprises clays and claystones with major sand sequence, the Utsira formation, from 847 to 1062 metres. The pressure log for this sequence is characterised by major cutback in DXc, with corresponding increase in background gas. Both these changes are result of the Utsira sand member, and are not attributed to an increase in pore pressure gradient. Mud temperature plots show the normal trend established over long bit runs, as previously discussed. Sonic delta also displays normal trend, that is, a steady decrease with depth. Resistivity shows similar trend, although shifted negatively (but with the same gradient) across the sand sequence. Pore pressure gradient through the Miocene is assumed to be normal at 1.03/1.04 SG EMW.

context_snippets.text: Differential sticking problems were encountered during this section (both during the drilling and logging runs). This was thought in part to be due to the high overbalance. The mud density was reduced to minimum of 1.23sg to combat these problems. Formation pressures over this interval where measured with the Schlumberger wireline MDT tool and found to be in the order of sg. It should be noted that this overbalance (approximately 1000psi) is not significantly different to that used during the drilling of the original hole, where such severe hole problems were not encountered (however this well was deviated, giving increased BHA contact with the low side of the hole). Summary Increases in formation pressure inferred from trends in the modified exponent indicate that the top section of this well is not normally pressured. Using the Eaton method, formation pressure estimates were made up to maximum of 1.5sg. The modified exponent proved to be useful well-site pore pressure indicator, whilst drilling through thick mudstone sections in the 12 1/4” hole section. Two principal cutbacks in the trend were observed and attributed to increases in formation pressure. This method was not applicable to the 8.5” hole section. Wireline MDT measurements showed the formation pressure to be 1.05sg in the reservoir. No significant trip, connection or swab gases were observed, indicating that the drilling mud provided a sufficient overbalance. However the volume of cavings produced whilst circulating for short time with mud density of 1.52sg, in the 12 1/4” hole section, suggests that 1.55sg is minimum requirement to to provide sufficient overbalance in this hole section.

The procedure for calculation of PP from porosity log and, where possible, calibration using actual pressure values, is as follows: - Where good gamma ray or spontaneous potential log data are available they are used for determination of shale intervals. series of shale baselines is drawn on the lithology log and shale determination analysis run to create dataset of shale points (prefix SHPT) which are applied to the porosity logs to define all shale intervals on the porosity logs. - The porosity shale points are then filtered using boxcar filter to produce continuous shale porosity trend dataset (called for example 'DT shale f39') for each porosity log. Special phase behavior measurements with injection gases (PVT and core-flow tests), providing important information to evaluate gas injection recovery mechanisms. Measurements of type (1)-(4) are always needed. The amount of type (2)-(5) data will vary, but the engineering disciplines Reservoir, Production, Flow Assurance, and Process should be able (forced) to specify specifically the number and type of measurements required at any given phase of exploration, delineation, and field development. From reservoir point-of-view, most sample information can be obtained immediately and does not require “wait-and-see”; with one exception. Special gas-injection measurements (5) may be needed, but the design and interpretation of such studies are not usually needed until relatively late stage in field development. It is almost impossible to obtain too much type (1) “basic” compositional data and, sometimes, saturation pressures. These data are also inexpensive and can be measured almost immediately after the samples are obtained. Furthermore, such basic data is always used as basis for deciding whether to use the samples in other measurements (2)-(5). A limited number of samples should be stored long-term, for (a) unexpected and “confirmation” data requirements, and (b) for studying processes which may first be defined later in field development, e.g. type (5) data. Recommendation – Cost-Effective Sample Storage The recommended practice for cost-effective sample storage is based on the observations that: 1. Storing large number of samples for extended periods of time has high associated cost while providing little or no information. 2. Only limited number of samples are usually required for long-term storage – i.e. for “later” usage (usage dependent on longer-term assessment of the field development). 3. Most samples can provide useful and timely information “immediately” at cost significantly less than “wait-and-see” long-term storage practice. 4. “Immediate” basic analysis of all samples provides: a. basis for whether the sample should be used for further testing (few samples), or whether the sample should be discarded (most samples). b. Information which can be used for on-going engineering, including correlation of statistically-significant data base. 5. Each engineering discipline (reservoir, production, flow assurance, and process) should be forced to define the type and number of samples required for their needs, and time-frame for usage.

context_snippets.text: ESSO NORGE AS Ng«) 34 ol 73 4 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Reservoir quality of Paleocene sandstones: The analyzed interval in well 25/10-7S comprises series of inhomogeneous, coarse- to medium grained subarkoses to lithic arenites, whereas the samples from well 25/10-8 are classified as subarkoses. Subarkoses of both wells are of similar mineral composition and texture. The reservoir quality, namely porosity, is governed by detrital clays, authigenic quartz and feldspar overgrowth and authigenic kaolinite. The intergranular, primary porosity ranges from 11 to 22%, and the secondary porosity averages 8%. Permeability reductions are mainly caused by detrital clay ranging to 14%. Reservoir quality of Upper Jurassic sandstones: The sampled interval covers core material over 64 meters. Upper Jurassic sands comprise variety of lithofacies: Limestones and marls, laminated argillaceous sands, calcareous sands, subarkoses and arkosic arenites. The high content of glauconite in all lithofacies allows confident separation from Middle Jurassic sands. The limestones and marls are tight with few moldic, isolated pores. The laminated, argillaceous sands are fine grained and have high proportions of feldspar. The lamination is caused by clayrich - claypoor alternating beds. The clayrich beds are almost tight and presumably non-permeable. The claypoor layers are composed of siliclastic framework grains in calcitic matrix_ Detrital feldspar grains are partially altered, dissolved and replaced by occluding kaolinite, which has caused abundant microporosity. The rocks with the best reservoir quality are subarkoses to arkosic arenites, which have permeabilities from 2000 to 8000mD. Porosities of these lithofacies range from 26 to 33%. Porosity reductions are caused by detrital clays and more importantly by carbonate cements. Sandstones with 10 to 43% carbonate cement are defined as calcareous sandstones. The reservoir appears more cemented with increasing depth. This is probably result of higher proportions of carbonaceous shell debris. The porosity/permeability cross-plot for the clean sands displays very poor correlation, which is thought to originate from carbonate decementation. Streaks with high permeability occur in particular at the base of the analyzed section, where calcareous sandstones predominate. A confident correlation of Upper Jurassic sands in wells 25/10-8 and 25/10-8A was not possible, because the samples of 25/10-8 were too disintegrated. Only one sample allowed the identification of cuttings from calcareous sandstone. Reservoir quality of Middle Jurassic/Triassic sandstones: The dense sampling, with one sample per meter, allows detailed reservoir zonation with tight sandstone types at the base and highly permeable subarkoses to lithic arenites at the top. In-between a thick section of fine grained, well sorted, feldspatic sandstones occurs. The Triassic base comprises tight calcarenaceous sands passing into limestones with combined calcite/dolomite contents of more than 60%. These are overlain by Middle Jurassic calcareous sands with total calcite contents of 23 to 39%. These rocks have only few isolated. moldic pores and permeabilities of less than mD. The feldspatic sandstones attain permeabilities up to 260 mD and porosities up to 27%. Porosity reductions are caused by: detritral clays, secondary quartz, calcite cement, kaolinite and abundant finely disseminated pyrite. The overlying subarkoses show the highest variability in permeabilities, from to 3500 mD. The permeability is controlled mainly by calcite cement and subordinated detrital clays and authigenic quartz. PETIVINGRAPHICAL COffillitlfANCY

question: What were Farmand Survey's responsibilities compared to Dia‑Team and Fugro‑McClelland during 7316/6‑U‑2 coring operations?
answer_text: Farmand Survey was the main contractor responsible for the drilling operation; Dia‑Team supplied the diamond coring staff, and Fugro‑McClelland operated the seabed template with the pipe clam.

context_snippets.text: -A. 3. 7- A.3.2 Drilling General Main contractor for the drilling operation was A/S K/S Farmand Survey in Oslo, using the Norwegian built drill ship M/S Bucentaur (Figure A.3.3). The bedrock coring was based on the piggyback coring concept as described below. Farmand Survey had subcontracted Dia-Team in Trondheim for diamond coring staff and Fugro-McClelland BV in Holland to operate the seabed template with the pipe clam. IKU had subcontracted A/S Geoteam in Oslo for the positioning (see Appendix A.4 below) and British Plaster Board Instruments (BPB) Ltd in U.K. to carry out downhole logging. Boundaries between lithozones and foraminifera assemblage zones are rarely penetrated by cored sample and the exact location of these boundaries is uncertain. In cases where log response or information from the drilling suggest more accurate boundary depth this level has been chosen. 6.1 Core 7317/10-U-01 6.1.1 Lithology and structures The stratigraphy of this borehole is summarized in Figure 6.2. The samples from this site generally comprise nonstratified, very silty clay with varying, but low content of sand and fine gravel. The clay content is typically 40-50% and the silt content typically 35%. The remaining constituent is sand and fine gravel. It has been noted that clasts of rounded clays tone observed in bulk samples is absent in the coarse fractions of the split sample. These clasts are mechanically weak and are apparently worn down during sample splitting. The clast content is therefore underestimated in the recorded grain size parameters. The main exceptions are samples between and which partly comprise sands, and samples between and which comprise silty clays. The content of coarse sand and gravel is lower in the latter interval and comprises pyritized burrows (30% of the gravel fraction at m). Eight lithozones, named Li - L8, are distinguished in this borehole based on variations in colour, petrography, structures and grain size variation. Some of the variations are rather faint. Statistical work on the petrography is not done, and comments given below are limited to particular observations that appear diagnostic for the different intervals. background content of rock fragments throughout most of the hole comprises various undifferentiated angular - subrounded sedimentary rocks dominated by mudstones and sandstones. Rounded to well rounded clasts form very common constituent of most of the samples. The roundedness of these clasts is striking. They disintegrate, however, when the samples are disperged for grain size analysis (causing an error in grain size analysis) and appear mechanically weak. question: If Ty Fm is encountered, should we expect very fine–medium sandstone with moderate–poor sorting and claystone/siltstone interbeds?
answer_text: Yes — Ty Fm is very fine to medium‑grained sandstone, moderately to poorly sorted, with interbedded claystone and siltstone.

question: For BALDER 25/8-12 A after coring, what are the 8 1/2 hole TD (RKB) and the shut-in location?
answer_text: TD = 2119 RKB; shut-in location = the BOP stack.

context_snippets.text: After coring operations are completed, drill the 8'/2 hole to the well TD of 2119 RKB. At If flow is encountered while drilling this section, the well will be shut-in at the BOP stack. Plug and Abandonment of Well After the prescribed logging program has been completed the well will be & A'd. This will include isolation of all hydrocarbon zones with cement plugs and or use of bridge plugs. The WH will be cut below the mudline as per NPD regulations. A more detailed P&A program will be issued at later date. Drilling Cautions These cautions apply to the 8-1/2 hole sections(OH & Sidetrack). No abnormal pressure is expected in these hole sections. The programmed mud weight is required for wellbore stability in the Hordaland shale and some deeper interbedded shale sections. These shale bodies are weak and hydratable and have history of wellbore instability problems. Shale inhibition will be provided by the low toxicity oil based mud system. The programmed mud weight schedule is based on Balder wellbore stability analysis performed by Exxon Production Research Company (EPR) in 1995. The wellbore stability study indicates that maximum mud weight of ppg is recommended for deviated well. wellbore stability chart for the Balder Area is included. Attempting to reduce the amount of overbalance, the selected mud weight is +/-.5 ppg below the recommended mud weight per EPR's wellbore stability model. Mud weights up to ppg below the recommended were successfully used in 25/8-8S/8A/8B Tau wells achieving near gauge hole wellbores. Formation pressures in the Rogaland Group range from sg to sg (8.5 ppg to ppg). The mud weight to be used to drill these formations (1.38 sg - ppg) will result in an overbalance of about 650 psi at the top of the Zone 111-4 sand. The lubricity provided by the OBM will partially mitigate the effect of this relatively high overbalance, but precautions against sticking should be taken. • Wiper trips should be used, as required, for conditioning the hole if poor hole conditions are experienced and/or significant open hole days have occurred. • The use of any High/Lo-vis sweeps or weighted sweeps should be discussed with the Operations Superintendent prior to use. • Optimal hole cleaning shall be achieved by maximizing the hydraulics and pumping at high flowrates, as specified in the hydraulics program.

question: In plug-drilling core handling, how do 50,000 ppm NaCl cooling and Soxhlet (toluene/methanol) cleaning compare in preserving porosity and permeability?
answer_text: Both are used to preserve porosity/permeability: 50,000 ppm NaCl brine is used as the drilling coolant and Soxhlet cleaning (toluene/methanol) is used to remove hydrocarbons and salts before measurements.

context_snippets.text: Porosity and grain density Grain volume was measured by helium injection using Boyle's law porosimeter. Bulk volume was determined by immersing the sample in mercury (the weight balance/ buoyancy technique). Porosity and grain density were calculated from the recorded weight of the samples. Slabbing and mounting of core cuts After all samples had been taken, the cores were slabbed using long bed saw with water cooled diamond saw blade. The whole core length (except seal peels) was slabbed into four parts (A,B,C and cut). After slabbing, the B-cut (reference cut) was mounted in plastic trays, by casting in epoxy resin. Core photos Digital core images ( Corimag ), white and UV-light were taken of the entire well. Standard core photo scale 1:4 was taken of the B-cut both white and UV-light. The core photos are delivered as separate reports.

PREPARATION: Laboratory core handling and sampling. The plug samples for analyses were collected by drilling with one inch bore, using simulated formation brine (constructed to standard concentration of 50 000 ppm NaCl) as cooling agent. Horizontal samples, taken every 25 cm, were drilled parallel to the bedding and the vertical samples, were taken approximately every 50 cm, normal on the bedding. The samples were cut to one inch lengths and the end faces were lightly brushed using the same fluid, to remove any fines induced by trimming. The plug samples were then cleaned in soxhlet extractor using alternating sequences of methanol and toluene. Toluene was used to remove any residual hydrocarbons and methanol to remove water and residual salts. The plug samples were dried in heating cabinet between the toluene and methanol extraction to avoid mixing of the solvents. A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 gas) and the relative abundance of these inclusions will influence the bulk spectra. Addi- tionally, total inclusion abundance will affect the spectra insofar as higher molecular weight species represent smaller volumetric proportion of petroleum and are also less volatile, hence decrease below instrumentation detection limits before low molecular weight species. Conse- quently, some samples with low oil inclusion abundance generate wet gas mass spectra, for instance. Optical inclusion abundance and characteristics should be consulted, where pro- vided, to verify the interpreted petroleum type (see Table of Petrographic Observations). With the above limitations in mind, the following petroleum types are identified on the basis of spectral characteristics: Dry gas: mostly C1 with lesser C2-C3 and no higher hydrocarbons. Wet gas: C1-C9 may be present, but C6+ species are in minimal abundance. The alkane slope is extreme. Gas-condensate: C1-C11 may be present. The alkane slope is quite steep, reflecting very gas- enriched phase. Volatile oil: C1-C13 present. Slight gas-range enrichment is observed and the alkane slope is mod- erate to steep. Oil: C1-C13 is present. The alkane slope may be flat to moderate. Biodegradation is suggested if sulfur compounds such as H2S, COS, CS2, S2 (+/- SO2) and/or thiols are present in addition to petroleum species. Ratios of paraffins to naphthenes may be low as well, as bacteria typically prefer to metabolize alkanes compared to other classes of petroleum compounds. Petrographic data may provide further evidence for biodegradation in the form of low-gravity petroleum inclusions. Bacterial activity is generally restricted to maximum burial temperatures below 65-70°C; hence FIS evidence of biodegradation is most commonly observed in rocks that are currently below this temperature. Thermal alteration of liquid petroleum species can produce spectra very similar to those generated from biodegraded hydrocarbons, because the products of two common processes, bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR) and thermochemical sulfate reduction (TSR), are essentially identical. The best distinction is made from current bottom-hole temperature data, which, if above 140°C or so may be indicative of TSR, and if below 70°C or so is more consistent with BSR. Potential interpretive problems arise in the intervening temperature range, when deeply buried sediments are unroofed or when petroleum altered at shallow depths becomes buried to greater depth. Petrographic data may help, as pyrobitumen frequently accompanies TSR, while low-gravity liquid petroleum inclusions often occur in association with bacteri- ally altered oils. Additional temperature or thermal maturity data (including fluid inclusion homogenization temperatures) may also be useful. The presence of significant amounts of sulfur species can indicate sour petroleum phase, where the souring process may in some cases be reflection of the source rock, but could also reflect BSR or TSR. study of TSR sour gas pools in Canada suggests that evaluating the relative proportion of products and reactants can provide measure of sour gas potential. As TSR progresses, long-chain alkanes decrease while low molecular weight petroleum species increase along with CO2, aromatics organic acids and the various sulfur compounds enumer- ated above. Ironically, H2S alone may not be as accurate an indicator of H2S content, as it is scavenged naturally (e.g., to form pyrite in iron-rich rocks) and by the metallic internal surfaces of the analytical system.

Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time (TI) with the check shot time (Tc)at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate, the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. The different types of shifts are discussed in more detail in chapter 4.2. Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod. June 30, 1993

4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( TVD vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. • From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

context_snippets.text: 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

The well was planned to test a Lower Cretaceous/Upper Jurassic wedge play immediately to the south of the Loppa High, and drilled to total depth of 2630 in bdf in rocks of Triassic age. The upper of the two seismically-defined wedges was found to comprise silts and shales of Early to Middle Albian age (Wedge In), whilst the lower wedge consisted of two contrasting clastic packages of Valanginian to latest Ryazanian (Wedge IIa) and Early Volgian (Wedge IIb) age respectively. Oil was recovered from RFT's at in (Wedge ha) and in (an isolated sand in the Kimmeridgian Hekkingen Formation). In addition, well-log interpretation revealed low hydrocarbon saturations in sands of the Triassic Fruholmen Formation. Subsequent testing revealed the Fruholmen to be tight and the hydrocarbons to be immovable, but total of 1600 litres light 31°API (0.87 g/cm3 ) oil was recovered from the hydrocarbon-bearing interval in Wedge ha. From analogy with similar environments elsewhere it was postulated that this surface may have been the site of soil development and possibly related cementation. On logs the surface coincided with thick tight zone (figure 4), and in order to match both pressures and water cut it was found necessary to make the surface a complete barrier to vertical permeability in all updip areas, where maximum erosion of the lower unit had taken place (figure 5). Thus, in this case, the cross section was used to test geological hypotheses such as the existence of permeability barriers and possible Kv/KH ratios, which were then used in full field simulation. 4. Full Field Modelling The use of full field modelling is natural extension of the cross-section work described above. However, layers are coarser, and due to the size of the model, changes are more difficult and more expensive to make. However, certain facets of the reservoir model such as areal variability can be tested. In the field under study the net/gross ratio shows marked changes areally. This is caused by the natural feature of fluviatile systems where zones located on, or near, the major axis of the drainage system tend to be sand rich, while those on the periphery are sand poor. Figure shows diagramatically this relationship. In sand-rich zones, where channels erode into one another, the overall transmissibility is good, as is the vertical permeability. However, in sand-poor zones both these parameters are drastically lowered. In order to account for this effect, the net/gross ratio was introduced as multiplier for the two horizontal gridblock permeabilities. It was found that for an effective match, the vertical grid block permeability had to be multiplied by power of the net/gross ratio because the interbedded shales parallel to reservoir layers will always have more pronounced impact on vertical fluid movement (figure 7). Research is continuing into more realistic ways of modelling such parameters as the effective vertical permeability, but it is hoped that the above discussion indicates that it is possible to improve reservoir modelling by iterative use of simulation models. CONDENSATE FIELD WITH NO PRODUCTION DATA. One of the major exploration plays in the North Sea currently is for condensate in Mesozoic sandstone reservoirs of the Central and Northern North Sea. Clearly, development of reservoirs of this type could involve markedly different development programmes from those currently in operation on the oilfields. Compositional changes, gas/liquid relative relationships and the possibility of cycling are important factors that require consideration and, as this paper demonstrates, the system becomes very complex making the prediction of the optimum configuration for maximum liquid recovery difficult. In order to analyse the problem, simple model was built using realistic reservoir properties. The model was then used to test various production strategies and the sensitivity of these to the reservoir geological model. Geological Model The geological model is illustrated in figure and represents an average Brent Sand package with three layers of high permeability representing the Etive Formation, low permeability layer at the Rannoch/Etive boundary and four layers of intermediate permeability representing the Rannoch and Broom Formations. Since this was preliminary study the model was kept as simple as realism allowed, and such features as very high permeability zones in the Etive Formation were not introduced.

3.2 Well 34/7-19 The interpretation has been performed interactively by correlation on normalized images generated from conductivity curves of the FMS tool. For the following description, the reader is referred to the Composite Log (Enclosure 2). The Composite Log provides the following tracks; Petrophysical log (GR), depth annotation with formation tops and cores implemented (depthshifts included), dip-azimuth tadpoles, correlation lines superimposed on normalized images, and conductivity raw-curves. The interpretation is further supported by detailed sections where important features are described and examplified, and Schmidt stereograms projected to the upper sphere in order to evaluate the structural orientations throughout the Brent Group. Hole quality has been evaluated from caliper logs to be fair to good for the entire investigated section. The Rannoch Formation, as expressed in this well, mainly consists of parallel laminated, fine to medium grained coarsening upwards sequence. The FMS interpretation generated from correlated surfaces within the Rannoch Formation is shown in Figure 3.2.1. The lower, fine grained (silty) part of the section displays nearly uniform structural trend of laminae. For the interval between 2605.00m and 2640.00m the calculated mean orientation equals 268/4.8 (Fig. 3.2.2). The close clustering of poles seen from the Schmidt plot reflects the parallel nature of the laminae which probably was close to horisontal during deposition, and therfore is considered to represent the present structural rotation for this part of the Brent Group. The upper part of the Rannoch Formation (above 2605.00m) is characterised by larger spread of tadpoles which is partly caused by an increased occurrence of steep dipping laminations. The mean dip of the planar structures between 2595.00m and 2604.50m is calculated to be 286/5.2. From Figure 3.2.3 the spread of poles due to cross-lamination is obvious. In spite of the orientation variations, the mean structural orientation for this interval is close to the interval below 2605.00m. In addition, tadpoles are present which display dips in excess of 30 - 40 degrees (Fig. 3.2.1). With the exception of the surface at ca 2585.00m which is interpreted to represent carbonate cemented lense, these steep dipping surfaces are related to fractures (faults and joints). The two lowermost of these tadpoles at 2604.50m represent the carbonate cemented joints at core depth 2600.80m (Fig. 3.2.4). At approximately 2590.00m another pair of tadpoles which relate to steep dipping surfaces appear. These are correlated to the faults observed in the cores at 2585.30m - 2586.30m (core depth). Based on core observations (thin fault surfaces within the same lithology which do not affect the orientation of the layering within the sequence), this faulting is regarded unimportant with respect to throw. These fault surfaces dip at 72 degrees towards northeast. Structural Dipmeter Interpretation of Wells 34/7-12, 19 and 20

Due to rather poor seismic data in the eastern part of the wellpath the prognosis was uncertain, but it was expected that the wellpath would penetrate the Ness, Etive and Rannoch Fms. before entering the Southern Triangle Area after crossing the Tordis Main Fault east of Tordis. During drilling, no evidence of the fault could be seen, even though the well length was increased with 100 MD. The general trend with thinning Etive Fm. from SW towards NE seems to continue, and no certain Etive Fm. is interpreted in the well. Dating of cuttings during the drilling phase indicated lower part of the Rannoch Fm. without any sign of Upper Jurassic sediments all the way below the Ness Fm. sediments. revised interpretation (see chapter 6) dates the upper part of the reservoir as Ness Fm. and the lower part as ?Tarbert Fm. The sand quality in the distal part was better than prognosed based on description of cuttings and log evaluation. The data acquisition programme in the reservoir section was conducted according to the plan. VSP was run to TD in addition to MWD/LWD logs. JASDRAJ16201WWRI2AH.DOC

context_snippets.text: 36 HOLE SECTION : 89 - 160m This section was originally drilled as 7/8 pilot hole down to 1100m. Returns were to the seabed. Seawater was used as the drilling fluid, with high viscous pills being pumped on every connection to aid hole cleaning. The hole was displaced to s.g. mud prior to running casing. Dxc data was widely scattered, most likely due to the hydraulic action on the unconsolidated sediments, and as consequence could not be used in estimating the pore pressure regime. No shallow gas was observed. With the absence of any hole problems the 36 section was considered to be normally pressured. This section was originally drilled as 7/8 pilot hole to 1100m with returns to seabed. This hole section was drilled using sea water, with high Viscous pills being pumped every connection to aid hole cleaning. The hole was displaced to sg mud prior to running the 13 3/8 casing. A Dxc trend was established from 500m (1.00) and 1050m (1.45), this indicated normally compacting sequence. Dxc scatter and changes from the trend line were the result of hydraulic action and lithological variations. No shallow gas was observed in this section. Given small variations in Dxc normal compaction trend was established. This section was considered to be normally pressured at 1.03 s.g. This section was drilled with six bit runs using bits, including an Eggbeater PDC bit. The lithology comprised primarily of mudstones with minor limestone stringers to depth of 3010m where tuffaceous mudstones and minor sandstones were encountered. At 3110m the lithology changed to limestone and mudstone with massive limestones at 3220m A KCL/Polymer based mud was used with an initial density of sg. This was increased gradually to sg by 1700m and this mudweight was maintained to the end of the section. A Dxc trend (k=0.7028,a=0.0001178), representing sg EQMW was established between 1100m and 1170m. From here down to 1750m the pore

pressure was increasing, with the Dxc trend continually shifting (k=0.2609, a=0.0003363). The mud weight increases affected the Dxc values and this was taken into account when estimating pore pressure. Background gas was between to 0.30% down to 1450m with only one swab gas at 1410m. From 1500m more swab gases were seen and continued to appear down to 1700m; background gas increased noticably at 1630m to 0.50%. From 1763m, an egg-beater bit was run, which gave very poor Dxc response because of the cutting action. However, with still increasing background gas and the continual presence of swab gas from 1973m onwards, the formation pressure was estimated to be sg EQMW. From 2088m swab gases were much more frequent though the background gas fell and remained at steady 0.18%. At 2050m, rough correlation of Dxc data was discernible despite the irregular scatter still persisting. trend (k=0.3429, a=0.002512) was denoted as sg EQMW. The next run, from 2178m, used rock bit which gave an excellent Dxc response, and trend, (k=0.914,a=0.0004303) representing sg EQMW, was quickly established. This trend shifted sinistrally at 2590m and quickly stabilised to sg EQMW trend, (k=0.3601,a=0.0001837). Gas values were steadily decreased from 2430m, with the background falling from 0.10% to 0.04%. Any further shifts in the Dxc trend were due to bit change or formation, and the pore pressure was assumed to remain at sg EQMW, due to the occurrence of relatively substantial trip gases; 0.54% at 3060m and 0.57% at 3162m. Wireline data shows slow decrease in resistivity from 1400m with this trend reaching its lowest point at 1750m, to ohmm, indicating pore pressure increase with pore fluids causing conductivity increase. Sonic data does not display the expected decrease associated with compaction disequilibrium over this interval, however it does cut back markedly at 1840m, 160 to 130 micsecs. At 1900m, the resistivity also begins to decrease from to ohmm, but remains static from 1980m. Sonic data decreases again over the The next wireline indications of abnormal pressures are at 2420m, where the resistivity begins to decrease again, to minimum at 2600m, 0.80 to ohmm; sonic data, although erratic, also slows down at 2600m, 140 to 115 micsecs. From this depth on, the data reflects formation changes rather than pressure. Shale density data showed no compactional trend from the start of returns and cut back from an initial g/cc to g/cc at 1760m. Below this point compaction trend is discernible with the values increasing again to final g/cc. Numerous additions were made to the mud system throughout this hole section which caused the temperature data to be ambiguous. An initial EXIOG Well Report - BP 2/1-10

1/3-3 Discovery - Evaluation and Appraisal Proposal September 1996 311D1d/Rep8-96/kr Page 18 Sequence stratigraphy and biostratigraphy give correlation between the 1/3-3 Upper Jurassic sands and the same reservoir level in well 2/1-6 (Gyda area) and 7/12-8 (Ula area) (Fig.3.8). The thickness variations of the reservoir series are mainly due to variation of fault activity during deposition. Average core porosity of the 2/1-6 reservoir (northern Gyda Field) (Fig.3.9) ranges from 8.6% to 18.4% and permeability from to 27 mD. The best layer is the 43 Zone III where average core porosity reaches 18.4% and permeability inD which is correlated with the 1/3-3 CI layer. The 1/3-3 Cl layer is correlated to the 26 Zone of the 2/1-10 well where mean core porosity is 17.8%, reaching maximum of 23.3%. Mean permeability is m13 (maximum 86 inD) (Fig.3.10). An evolution of porosity and permeability along the structure has been estimated taking into account the results of the mentioned wells and the sandstone deposition direction (along the faults). Nevertheless, possible degradation of the reservoirs between the northern and the southern culminations by facies changes or diagenetic barrier has not to be excluded. • EXTRA SEDIMENTARY LAYER In addition to the proven reservoir layers, the 1995/96 seismic interpretation shows possible extra sedimentary unit referred to as the Extra Package for the accumulation/reserves estimations discussed and illustrated Anther below. Its existence is linked to the presence of seismic marker between the Top Reservoir and Tpp C2 markers. Extension of this Intra Reservoir marker, and consequently of the extra sedimentary layer, is limited to the northern part of the 1/3-3 structure without calibration at wells. The Extra Package is well developed and thicker in the northern part of the structure, pinching out towards the 1/3-3 well. Since it seems to onlap the unit towards the 1/3-3 (pinch out) in the south, with probable complete erosion of in the north, it is believed to be younger sedimentary layer (Early Volgian) trapped along the Ula faults (see above play concept) and corresponding to new trangressive pulse. Even though this new package was never reached by well in the 1/3-3 vicinity, sedimentological interpretation in terms of new trangressive pulse is favourable to sandprone layer, with possible porosities of 15 - 18 - 21% and permeabilities of - 10 inD. 3.4 Prospect Mapping A new interpretation has been performed in 1995/96 using 3D seismic data. It is based on the merge of the BPN9202 and Gyda 3D data performed in mid 95. The post-stack merge processing includes zero phasing of the data. Quality of the seismic data is very goal (Fig.3.3) and picking does not present any difficulty over most of the structure.

Authority J. Gamblen The pore and fracture pressures in this section are primarily based on the Gyda wells. Normal pore pressure (1.04 SG) will be evident until c. 1300m where it gradually increases to SG at c. 1700m. It gradually increases to 1.45 SG by section TD at 3200m. The 5/8 LOT at 3200m is expected around SG EMW. The 1/2 hole will be drilled to top reservoir, and possibly to well TD (4523m BRT) if mud weights allow. If the Mandal formation is not overpressured, the mud weight in use at top reservoir is SG or below, and there are no indications of hole problems, drilling/coring will continue to well TD, provided the error bar on top salt remains deeper than TD. If the Mandal formation is overpressured, the liner will be committed having tagged top sand, and the reservoir interval will be drilled in hole. The 1/2 hole will be initially drilled in the Chalk group. The upper Chalk, in the top Ekofisk formation, is expected to contain chert. The amount of chert is difficult to predict, however the lithology logs produced following 1/3-3 and 2/1-6 both indicated chert in the Ekofisk formation. Also, traces of blue grey chert were reported in the upper and mid Tor formations from well 1/3-3. Occasional pyrite was reported in the lower Tor formations on well 2/1-6. This cherty limestone is difficult to drill and will require conical insert drilling bits to efficiently drill the interval. As well as the hard drilling conditions in the Chalk Group there is also the possibility of stuck pipe due to differential sticking in the Tor. Careful attention will be made to monitoring mud properties and minimising overbalance. BP's extensive stuck pipe guidelines will be strictly adhered to throughout this section. of BP Norway Limited U.A.

question: What contiguous porosity (phi) ranges classify very-good, reasonable-good, and poor reservoir quality?
answer_text: Very-good: phi > 32%; Reasonable–good: 24% < phi < 32%; Poor: phi < 24%.

context_snippets.text: -43- 7. Petrophysical Evaluation General A petrophysical evalution has been made from the top of the Jurassic sand at m. Above this depth no zones of particular interest were encountered. The interpretation is based on suite of Schlum- berger logs with listing of the different logging runs given in table I/7.1. The reservoir is interpreted to be gas bearing from to ca. 1574 m. This is confirmed by the graph of RFT pressures versus depth shown as figure 1/8.2 and from separation between porosity logs in the cleaner sand intervals. Below 1574 m, the clean sands, where log interpretation is most reliable, appear to be water bearing. In the less clean zones between 1574 and 1622 some oil saturation exists as seen in cores. The hydrocarbon saturation as estimated from log data varies between a maximum of 40% and zero in the interval 1574 to 1622 m. This would be consistent with the presence of residual oil. The oil bleeding from cores as noted at surface could be interpreted as extremely low formation permeability rather than the presence of producible oil. An RFT sample taken at 1597 in permeable interval recovered no hydrocarbons although it was heavily contaminated with mud filtrate. Core analysis shows that some intervals between 1574 and 1622 contained high percentages of mica which may affect standard log interpretation. However, the presence of mica in these quantities re- sults in very low permeabilities and the net effect would be that any hydrocarbons would be non-producible. When developing the porosity/permeability relationship from core ana- lyses shown as fig. 7.2, it was found that shale and mica have similar effect. It is important to note that this relationship is proba- bly pessimistic as an average trend since it is indicative of the tighter intervals and not the cleaner sands which were too unconsoli- dated to be analysed. Evaluation of the Gas Zone - 1574 Porosities have been determined from the fdc log applying correct- ion for gas and were found to be in agreement with measurements made on cores, even in shalier or more micaceous intervals. Based on the distinct relationship between porosity and permeability as mea- sured on cores (see fig. 7.2) permeabilities of mD (corresponding to ca. 24% porosity) and 100 mD (corresponding to ca. 32% porosity) have been used as boundary values for rock classification as follows: 0 >32% : very good reservoir rock 24% < <32% : reasonable to good reservoir 0 <24% : poor to non reservoir

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.
