Gabrielsen NUMBER OF PAGES: 129 NUMBER OF COPIES: DISTRIBUTION: Norsk Hydro a.s.; restricted ABSTRACT: The cap rocks of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations in wells 7321/9-1, 7219/9-1, 7120/2-2, 7120/6-1, 7120/12-1, 7228/2-1, 7228/9-1 and 7125/1-1 have been investigated from structural geological and rock mechanical point of view. The study has demonstrated that the fracture geometry and fracture frequency vary within the study area. The following preliminary conclusions are drawn: 1) The shales of the Fuglen Formation reveal higher vertical shear strengths (16-40 MPa) than the shales of the Hekkingen Formation (7-22 MPa). If erosion of approximately 1000 metres of rocks is assumed, the bulk of the cap rock may have been fractured. The present data, however indicate that the fracture frequency attributed to this deformation, is low. 2) The wells in the western part of the study area are characterized by high fracture frequencies and low-angle fractures. This deformation is probably associated with post early Tertiary compressional reactivation of some of the master fault complexes. Accordingly, the master fault complexes associated with the large basins in the west (Tromso Basin and Bjornoya Basins) are potentially most exposed to leakage through microfractures. However, since the shales of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations seem to have different rock mechanical properties the continuity of these units should be mapped in detail, and the problems with diffusion characteristcs of the units should be addressed.

The sections above 1530 and at 2895-3195 consist of mostly dry gas responses, with the exception of single sample from 3201 displaying an oil-like spectrum. thin section from 2943 contains several to common, white-fluorescent, and rare, yellow-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. Inclusion abundance is marginally high enough to suggest the presence of an oil column or paleo-column at this depth. No visible petroleum inclusions are documented at 1330 or 3201 m. The section below 3546 reveals dry gas to oil-like spectra. The most significant responses are gas-condensate to oil indications noted intermittently at 3546-3600 m. Thin sections from 3549 m, 3632 m, 3717 and 3840 contain rare to several, white-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz grains. Thin sections from 3549 and 3840 also contain rare to several, blue-fluorescent, upper-moderate gravity petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. The remainder of the analyzed interval contains sub-anomalous hydrocarbon concentra- tions. No petroleum inclusions are recorded in thin sections from 1910 m, 2420 or 3339 m. Shales contain moderate amounts of gas-prone kerogen and rare to several occurrences of immature to mature oil-prone kerogen in most samples (apparently oil-mature below about 3000 m). Highest visual kerogen abundance is noted at 3339 m. Proximal Pay Indications: Anomalous concentrations of acetic acid and, in general, more prominent benzene anomalies are identified at 3546-3588 and 3651-3654 m. Samples containing acetic acid anomalies usually suggest the nearby presence of reservoired liquid petroleum (oil or condensate), while more prominent benzene anomalies can indicate nearby gas. This well is reportedly gas discovery, thus it is probable that these features are sensing penetrated charge. Anomalies within reservoirs can indicate elevated Sw (for instance in relatively tight or impermeable reservoirs). Potential Seals: Possible seals are identified at 2898 m, 3340 m, 3546 and 3690 m. Evidence for Bacterial or Thermal Alteration: Sulfur species of probable bacterial origin are noted at 1230-1250 m, 2010 and 2340 m. INTERPRETATION OF FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY (FIS) DATA A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, including petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries with FIS, one can obtain valuable and unique information on three major exploration topics: 1. Petroleum migration or paleocharge 2. Seals 3. Proximity to undrilled pay and two major production topics: 1. Pay zone and bypassed pay delimitation 2. Reservoir compartmentalization. The previous discussions have concentrated on identifying spectral types in FIS data. This is necessary first interpretive step. The next task is to evaluate the significance of FIS depth trends in their own right (now knowing their spectral origins), and eventually, in light of other available information to answer specific questions, such as were enumerated above. Petrographic data from anomalous fluid inclusion zones are often critical elements of these higher order interpretations, as will be seen, which why petrographic follow-up work is conducted as routine part of every FIS analysis (see Table of Petrographic Observations). A.3.1 Significance of FIS petroleum indications The most basic question that FIS can address is Is there any evidence for present or past petroleum in this borehole Documentation of an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly generally pro- vides positive answer to this question, but could indicate other processes as well. Possible explanations for an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly are discussed in the following paragraphs. Migration without trapping A migration pathway may be indicated when FIS responses are low or moderate, when contamination and recycled inclusions can be discounted, when quoted visual petroleum inclu- sion abundances are rare or several (see Table of Petrographic Observations), and when no other petrographic or log evidence of current petroleum charge is identified in the zone. There are number of factors that influence inclusion abundance and, consequently, raw FIS response strength, including geologic setting, extent of diagenesis, rock type and permeability. However, it has been demonstrated that both visual petroleum inclusion abundance and FIS strength within many porous reservoir rocks is proportional to hydrocarbon saturation or pa- leosaturation in relative sense. Because migration occurs at average bulk-volume petroleum saturations below those encountered in charged reservoirs, FIS signal strength and visual in- clusion abundance are generally lower along migration pathways than in charged reservoirs from the same area.

Fluid Inclusion Technologies (FIT), Inc., is laboratory-based petroleum service or- ganization established in 1997 and offering variety of analytical services including some previously proprietary technologies. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. The procedure has major impact in the areas of both Petroleum Production and Exploration Applications providing informa- tion unattainable via more traditional methods and, has been instrumental in the discovery of significant petroleum reserves, influenced exploration and acreage acquisition decisions and provided innovative options for resource estimation, petroleum production and enhanced oil recovery operations. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphic Analysis, often in combination with other patented techniques, emerging geochemical methodologies and standard microscopic methods, all available through Fluid Inclusion Technologies, Inc., provides unique and un- equaled industry product boasting an impressive list of proven applications including deter- mination of Product Type, Hydrocarbon Migration, Seals and Seal Integrity, Fluid Contacts, Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum, Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimi- tation, Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization and Fluid Pressure Compartments. Further information regarding the application of FIS Analysis and the other technical ser- vices we provide to problems in petroleum exploration and production is available elsewhere in this report and on our website:www.fittulsa.com. 1.1 General Logistics of Initiating an FIS Analysis To Initiate an FIS Analysis: contact FIT' directly to discuss goals of the study, sample requirements, turnaround time, pricing, and other related aspects. New clients are particularly encouraged to consult with our staff during the early stages of project development to optimize sample selection, preparation and shipment. Rock materials for FIS Analysis are shipped directly to C&M Storage2, our sample handling facility, for sample preparation including any necessary crushing/sieving, subsampling and washing. The turnaround time for typical FIS Analysis is preliminary data in 1-2 weeks time following receipt of samples by C&M and final report 1-2 weeks following preliminary analysis. These times are approximate and depend on the amount of sample preparation required, job size and analytical backlog. At the time of issue of this report, the cost for obtaining an FIS Analysis was $5,500 U.S. for full-well analysis (up to 575 samples) and $3,000 U.S. for short-well analysis (up to 180 samples). The cost includes the automated mass spectrometric analysis, preparation of and fluid inclusion petrography on selected thin-sections sampled throughout the well, and interpretation in the form of annotated depth plots (see Figure 1). When sampling for FIS Analysis: the technique is equally applicable to cuttings, core and outcrop samples, but all samples will ultimately be reduced to cuttings-sized rock ma- terial. context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 Current Charge A zone that displays strong FIS hydrocarbon indications and high visual petroleum in- clusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) may reflect penetrated pay, but could also indicate paleo-charge or, in some cases, migration pathway (e.g., where inclusion abundance is enhanced by extensive microfracturing). provisional interpretation of current charge is strengthened if residual petroleum (especially live oil stain) is identified in thin section, and particularly if water-soluble petroleum species (so-called proximal pay indicators; see below) are recorded in FIS data (e.g., in the seal overlying the anomaly, in the water leg underlying the anomaly, or in low permeability zones within the reservoir section itself). Any independent indications (e.g., from electric logs or mudlog gas shows) provide further encouragement. Paleo-charge Intervals of strong FIS response, high visual inclusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) and significant bitumen (e.g., dead oil stain or asphaltic residue) without accompanying water-soluble anomalies or independent evidence of current charge, may represent paleo-column, but could also represent current charge or in rare cases migration pathway. The interpretation of paleo-charge is favored if valid DST has shown the interval to be currently wet. Recycled inclusions Very rarely, detritus that is generated from previous sedimentary rock may contain inher- ited petroleum inclusions. These inclusions must be recognized, as they clearly do not provide any useful information about the current petroleum system(s). Petrographic or microther- mometric criteria can often be used to argue the origin of these inclusions, for instance, the presence of petroleum inclusions along recycled quartz overgrowths, or measured homogeniza- tion temperatures that are too high to have been produced during the current burial history. Associated FIS depth trends are usually erratic and poorly compartmentalized, and inclusion abundance is typically low. Inherited inclusions may be restricted to specific geologic units that derived detritus from particular provenance, and are not found in intercalated chemical precipitates (e.g. bedded carbonates or diagenetic cements). Heavy bitumen stain In some instances, pore-occluding bitumen may contribute to FIS signals. Here, solid petroleum behaves as any other cement, and is capable of trapping residual hydrocarbons as bitumen-hosted fluid inclusions. These may be invisible due to the opacity of the solid petroleum host. Petroleum species may also desorb from pore-occluding bitumen during crush- ing, much as they do from mature kerogen (see below). Bitumen-sourced FIS responses may be inferred when strongly anomalous zones contain low visible petroleum inclusion abundance but have significant amounts of bitumen (e.g., common, abundant or extremely abundant). Abundant pore-filling bitumen in porous rock implies significant petroleum saturation at some time, so low visual petroleum inclusion abundance is unexpected (and not commonly encoun- tered). In such cases it is possible either that the size of the inclusions are below the resolution of the light microscope (< micron), that grain surface conditions (e.g., wettability) did not favor trapping of inclusions, or that the section was diagenetically quiescent during and after charging (i.e., little or no cementation or microfracturing).

A.4 Individual Track Plots A.4.1 Explanation and Significance of Individual Track Plots The following is synopsis of the significance of the different patterns of mass abundances and abundance ratios shown in Tracks 1-25. Note that not all species are quantified using their parent or molecular peaks (e.g., methane at m/z = 15) in order to minimize interfering contributions from other species. A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. Track 2: m/z = 44 Dominant peak for carbon dioxide (CO+2 ), with possible minor contribution from C+3 hydrocarbon fragments and acetic acid. A.2 FIS Mass Spectra 43 is inferred (but not demonstrated) only in the presence of other sulfur species. The m/z 32 would appear to be good one for indicating sulfur presence; however, this ion location suffers major potential interference from atmospheric oxygen (O+2 ). Care must be taken when interpreting sulfur-enriched FIS spectra, because at first glance they resemble the water-soluble enriched spectra. Ideally, the distinction lies in the location of CS2 at m/z 76 (as opposed to benzene at 78), H2S at m/z 34 and S+2 and/or SO2 at m/z 64. SO2 presence can be verified by the presence of paired anomaly at 64 and 48. In practice, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between sulfur-enrichment and water-soluble species enrichment when these species are not strongly anomalous, and combinations of the two spectra occur as well. A.2.3 Summary of the Five Spectral Types The above is relatively detailed account of the characteristics of the five major classes of FIS mass spectra. In the end, however, the best way to recognize and distinguish among spectral types is to compare them to the end-member examples presented herein and categorize them by eye. After examining few examples of each, pattern recognition will become easy. Understanding the complexities outlined in the previous sections is important, but usually unnecessary for first-order interpretation of FIS mass spectra. To summarize: Non-hydrocarbon Spectra: Characterized by four peak clusters centered on m/z 15, 28, 42 and 55; the first three being dominant. Most peaks are attributable to water and carbon dioxide. Gas-range enriched: Characterized by strong responses on C1-C5 (m/z 12-72) and lesser intensities on higher molecular weight ion locations. Peak clusters may be more broad at m/z 12-30 and 37-46. Predominance of masses 15 and 16, and high 57/55 ratios is possible. Liquid-range enriched: Characterized by the presence of C7-C13+ species as regularly-spaced peak clusters in the m/z 95-180 range, which are dominated by ions from paraffinic and naph- thenic compounds. Aromatic species contribute subordinate peak clusters between the paraffin- naphthene peaks (although, typically only benzene, toluene and xylenes are resolved). Water-soluble enriched: Characterized by methane, ethane, organic acids, benzene and toluene. Acetic Acid (m/z 60) and aromatic peak clusters (m/z 78, 91, 105) attain intensities near or greater than those of adjacent paraffin-naphthene peak clusters. Sulfur-compound enriched: Characterized by the presence of H2S, COS, CS2 and SO2 and/or native sulfur gas as indicated by anomalies on some combination of the m/z peaks 34, 48, 60, 64 and 76. A.2.4 Combinations of Spectral Types Combined FIS spectra are common, and appear as superimposed end member types. Although combinations of all end member spectra have been noted, the most common are gas + liquids and liquids + water-solubles. Recall that FIS is bulk technique and samples the entire fluid history of the pore system. Hence, mixed FIS spectra might be expected if the sample has experienced temporally distinct charges of petroleum (or brine) types or contained heterogeneous (immiscible) fluid in the pore system at some time.

Four sets of unwashed and sealed samples at 10 intervals from 1500 to 3670 (the top of the Lower Carbonaceous Mudstone), and every from 3670 to TD. One mineralogical/petrographical sample (washed), every 100 from 1000 in and every 50 from 2300 to 2950 m. One biostratigraphical and two geochemical samples all unwashed and sealed, every 10 from the base of the chalk group 3420 to 3637 in (the top of the Mandal formation), and every from there to TD. Total gas was measured as percent equivalent methane in air. Chromatographic breakdown of the total gas was in the range Cl through to C5, also quoted in percent. The lithology in well 7/12-9 could be divided into seven sections. SECTION I: 956 TO 2766 in, NORDLAND - HORDALAND GROUPS This section consisted of claystone with minor dolomite/limestone stringers and rare traces of sandstone. The claystone was generally medium to dark grey and occasionally olive grey or brown grey, becoming varicoloured below 2570 in. The cuttings were firm, sometimes moderately soft, sub-blocky to amorphous and non to slightly swelling. The claystone ranged from non to slightly calcareous and graded to silty claystone in parts of the 17 1/2 hole. There were also traces of disseminated pyrite down to 1030 m. The dolomite was pale cream to pale brown/buff, hard to very hard, brittle, generally blocky, amorphous in parts, dominantly cryptocrystalline and occasionally found with black argillaceous microlaminations. The limestone was light buff/brown, firm to hard, blocky, brittle, microcrystalline, and commonly dolomitic. The sandstone occurred in small traces from 956 down to 1120 in, quartz grains were clear, white, translucent, hard, medium to coarse and loose. The rate of penetration (ROP), averaged 24 m/hour in the 17 1/2 section and below 2350 averaged 56 m/hour, (when 12 1/4 PDC bit was run). In the 17 1/2 section the maximum ROP was 90 m/hour (1531 m) in the claystone, and the minimum m/hour (1800 and 2182 m) in the dolomite/limestone stringers, which were generally distinguished by an ROP of less than m/hour. V PA LAE °ENVIRONMENTAL SUMMARY Throughout the Eocene present and the majority of the Oligocene restricted outer shelf to bathyal conditions operated with shale and clays representing the dominant lithologies. In the upper part of the Oligocene, above 1950m, the microfaunas indicate transition to slightly shallower, inner to outer shelf conditions which persisted through the Lower and Middle Miocene. Shales continued to dominate the lithologies of the Oligocene, Lower Miocene and lower part of the Middle Miocene. Above 1310m, however, these are superseded by clays which dominate the lithology to the top of the well. Fine to coarse sand becomes important in the top 175m of the sequence. In the Upper Miocene shallowing of the environment continued with sediments being deposited under generally restricted inner shelf conditions. Similar conditions prevailed throughout the Pliocene and Pleistocene - Recent intervals. - 13 - RESEARCH

Sele Formation (2953 - 3026 m) This formation is dominated by interbedded shale and clay. The shales, represented mostly in the upper part, vary in colour from light grey to light green and are generally firm to hard and non-calcareous. The clay resembles the clay described from the Balder Formation, but is occasionally calcareous. Few stringers of fine to medium grained sandstone (clear - white subrounded grains) and siltstone has also been encountered, together with rather thin streaks of white to yellow-brown limestone. Pyrite occursfrequently within this interval. Lista Formation (3026 - 3096 m) The main lithology in this formation is shale and clay, with slight changes in colour. In the upper part of the interval soft and sticky light grey clay dominates, only intersected by thick sand lense, consisting of clear to white medium grained quartz grains (from 3 m). From 3037 light brown to redish brown clay occurs, which . is partly silty and slightly calcareous. This clay is interbedded with vary-coloured shales and light grey clay in the lower part of the interval. The shales are light green, light to medium grey and brown to brownish red, firm and fissile and have varying content of silt. Thin limestone streaks (white to light brown) occur through- out the interval. Pyrite, siderite and glauconite occur only in minor amounts.

During constant oompositicn expansicns at this terper- ature, the fluids were found to have bubble point pressures of 842 psig, 857 psig and 853 psig for cylinder numbers 811514, 810822 and 811513 respectively. The results of pressure-volume measurements recorded above the saturaticn pressure pressure for cylinder numbers 811514 and 810822 respectively may be found an pages three and four. As requested sample from cylinder number 811513 was utilized for the remainder of the study. The hydrocarbon composition of the subsurface fluid was determined by low te4;erature fractianal distillaticn. The results of this distillation in terms of both mol percent and weight percent are presented cn page two. The results of the pressure-volume measurements at reservoir temperature, recorded whilst determining the saturation pressure, may be found an page six. When subjected to differential pressure depletion at the reservoir temperature, the fluid evolved total of 395 cubic feet of gas at psia and 60°F. per barrel of residual oil at 60°F. The resulting relative oil volume factor being 1.298 barrels of saturated fluid per barrel of residual oil. The oil density and the properties of the evolved gases were measured at each point during the differential pressure depleticn and these data are included in the summary of the differential depletion data on page seven.

3.4 Reservoir Geology The Rogn Formation in the Draugen Field is subdivided in sequence stratigraphic zones (Ref 6) which all have been identified in cores and/or logs of well 6407/9-A-2. Correlation of cores and electric logs from 6407/9-A-2 with those of the nearlying well 6407/9-1, shows that Rogn Fm is an equally good reservoir in the A-2 location. However, 6407/9-A-2 has retained sedimentary structures while cores from 6407/9-1 and other Draugen wells are more disturbed. Permeabilities are high and uniform throughout, - D, apart from near the base where the permeability rapidly decreases. No significant vertical barriers, shales or tight streaks are observed. The absolute values of the estimates are therefore only an indication. For 6407/9-A-2 the pore pressure was around hydrostatic down to 1250m TVDBDF (Fig. 3.1). From this point (base of Hordaland Gp) and through the Tare formation the pore pressure rose to peak of SG in top of the Tang Fm, somewhat above the prognosed SG. Then the pressure decreased to slightly above hydrostatic, SG, at the base of the Tang and reaching hydrostatic within the Upper Spekk Fm. Well 6407/9-A-2 was sidetracked as A-2 below the 13 3/8 casing shoe. At this point the pressure had decreased to around hydrostatic and remained at this level to TD in the sidetrack hole. No connection gases were observed at any stage, which might have indicated near-balance situation. FLOWLINE TEMPERATURE Mud temperature out and delta temperature plots were of little value as indicators of overpressured zones. This was primarily due to the cooling effect of the long marine riser, and the frequent additions of mud in order to maintain volume. Bit runs in the latter part of the well were also of short duration. WIRELINE LOGS The DELTA shale plot confirms the presence of an undercompacted/ overpressured zone between 800m and 1500m. question: If Brent reservoir is 80 bar depleted, how would ECD limits impact HXT open-hole gravelpack?
answer_text: ECD must be kept below the reduced fracture gradient (~1.77 SG EMW) to avoid mud loss; otherwise there is a high risk of losing mud during the HXT open‑hole gravelpack.

context_snippets.text: OPERATOR A/S Norske Shell WELL 3/7-4 SECTION 17 1/2 Hole The cement was drilled with seawater, then the hole was displaced with sg mud. The leak off test gave sg mud weight equivalent. When drilling commenced, it was necessary to dump the header tank on each connection as it was full of cuttings. From 892 to 1011 meters, the formation consisted of very soft clays. The string tended to hydraulic; that is to say it was lifted by pump pressure from the bottom of the hole. The soft clays were extremely hydratable and the MBT showed that the clay content of the mud rose sharply. This problem was compounded by the use of PDC bit. PDC bits produce cuttings that are powder size. This powder is difficult to remove from the system. After being circulated second time, the clay particles are dispersed and begin to affect rheology. Drilled ahead to 1182 meters. The string continued to hydraulic in the soft clays. At 1182 mete-L's it was necessary to pump the string out of the hole. Drilled ahead to 1853 meters. The MBT continued to rise, and eventually reached 38 ppb. This again was due to the powdered cuttings that hydrated and made extraction with the solids control equipment impossible. Prior to this point, the centrifuge was being run to reduce solids. Only the high rpm machine was available for use, so that barite was being dumped in addition to clay solids. That barite was being dumped in addition to solids created other problems. The mixing equipment could not maintain the required weight in the active so the centrifuge was eventually stopped. The barite mixing system was monitored and mixed approximately 10 metric tonnes per hour. Speeds in excess of this caused blockages in the screw conveyor troughs or the drive belts to break. Reducing clay content in the mud is also achievable through dilution with premix. This was difficult on the Hunter. Mixing 50 cubic meters of premix required hours. Weighting up the premix to 1,5 sg required an additiond hours. During this time it was not possible to add barite to the active system as required.

As consequence, the fracture gradient in top Statfjord Formation is reduced to 1,77 SG EMW (worst case). However, the pressure points which are taken in well 34/104-414 will also be valid for H-4H. Well J-4H will be drilled prior to H-4H. If the results from J-411 proves the reservoir to be depleted with 80 bar, the risk of loosing mud to the formation is high. Therefore, focusing on ECD limitations is important in this section. • The decision of mudweight in this section will be based on the pressure points taken in J-4H. Hence, no value for the FIT below 5/8 shoe has been calculated. The 1/2 section will be redrilled from Deepsea Trym (34/10-L-3T2 H). If the well does not fulfil the requirements, the whole 12 1/4 section will be plugged back to the 13 3/8 casing shoe (Ref. 4.7). In this case, the 12 1/4 and 1/2 section will be re-drilled from Deepsea Trym. 150 meter of 13Cr110 5/8 casing will be installed in the lower part of 5/8 casing, since it is not planned to sting the production tubing into the gravel packer. A separate program for re-drilling, gravelpacking and completing the well will be issued. 5.3 Completion Strategy It is planned to install the Horizontal X-mas Tree System after the 5/8 casing is installed and pressure tested. This allows for pulling the BOP with only one shallow set plug. The open hole section will be re-drilled through the HXT. This has been successfully done on several wells on the Gullfaks Satellites. The reservoir section will be re-drilled using drill-in fluid optimised with respect to the gravelpack operation. Well 34/10-L-3T2H will be completed with an open-hole gravelpack installed in the 1/2 reservoir section. The gravelpack operations will be performed using Schlumberger's AIIPACTM system with shunt tubes and viscous carrier fluid. This system will reduce the risk of experiencing an early screen out during the gravelpacking operation. The production tubing will then be run into the well in heavy brine. The tubing hanger will be run on WOR, and after landing the hanger tubing and annulus will be displaced to packer fluid. To set the production packer, ball will be dropped and seated in the pre-installed Halliburton Monolock plug. The packer is set by pressuring up the tubing string against the plug. Page of

context_snippets.text: The 15/12-16s deviated well VSP was recorded by Schlumberger on 14th March 2006 and the data were provided to Zebra Geosciences Ltd in SEGY format-1. The stated objectives of the VSP survey were as follows: 1. To provide detailed compression wave time-depth relationship over the complete well. 2. To provide clear match between the zero phase multiple free VSP and the surface seismic data 3. To provide high resolution zero phase image of the reservoir. It is felt that the survey has been reasonably successful in achieving these objectives. Rig source data were recorded by Schlumberger with levels at separation suitable for VSP processing between 2955.0m and 2004m MDbDF. Above this depth, checkshot data were recorded at depths of After timing, the data were processed by Zebra Geosciences to yield P-wave reflection image. An FK plot of the raw data shows frequency content in the transmitted arrival of at least 5-90Hz with only very low levels of random noise and unwanted coherent arrivals evident in the raw data. The frequency content in the reflected wavefield is lower and final data have been filtered at 5,10-50,70Hz. The upgoing wavefield data, are shown before deconvolution with preliminary 3,5-100,120Hz filter as Figure 1.1, after deconvolution with the 5,10-50,70Hz filter as Figure and then after the application of trace median tracking filter ms/trc dip as Figure 1.3. The seismic line L905 was provided to Zebra geosciences in SEGY-1 format. The VSP corridor and synthetic seismogram filtered with 5,10-50,70Hz have been inserted into this line and are displayed in Figures 1.4, & 1.5. There is good match between the VSP and synthetic data and the borehole data shows good match to the surface seismic line. The VSP is thought to be good estimate of the zero phase multiples free seismic response at the well location up to frequencies of at least 60Hz. This is supported by the match of the VSP to the synthetic seismogram which is generated from the logs recorded in the borehole. A calibrated velocity log has been computed using the corrected vertical times from the VSP data and the available log data. The calibrated acoustic log is provided on linear 1:1000 depth scale as Enclosure and on linear time scale together with the VSP, synthetic seismogram and other log data as Enclosure 2. Normal polarity: An upgoing compressional wave is recorded as negative number and plotted as white trough (i.e. for upgoing wavefields: an increase in acoustic impedance is represented by white trough.) This report may contain suggestions as to the manner in which the data processed by Zebra Geosciences Ltd might be interpreted. These suggestions are the opinions of Zebra Geosciences Ltd, are based upon the limited information available to the company and should not be regarded as definitive. They are provided at no cost as courtesy to the client and Zebra Geosciences Ltd can accept no responsibility for any loss or damage resulting from their use.

Recommendations from the lessons learned can be found under Lessons Learned A system for drilling and under-reaming at the same time during directional work was utilized for the first on Valhall (and the North Sea) in this well. The system called Steerable Reaming While Drilling (SRWD) was used in the first part of the reservoir section with positive results and is therefor recommended for use in future wells where underreaming is required to get casing/liner to bottom. Lesson: Magnetic interference was experienced from MD even though the directional plan indicated that no wells should be close enough to cause interference. With magnetic interference causing problems with MWD surveys, and also with cement in samples, gyro was run to confirm the 20 tie-in and to check well center coordinates. The pressures in the adjacent wells were monitored. Proximity calculations were run and MWD surveys were compared to the gyro. Recommendation: contingency plan for well collision, double checking of directional plans with respect to the tie-in, slot and platform center coordinates, and check that all adjacent wells and sidetracks are identified and taken into account when making directional/anti-collision programs should be developed. Lesson: leak in the injection line to A-3 on Valhall DP caused injection shutdown and six hours of rig time. After the injection was shut down at Valhall, drilling continued until the MSD holding tank was full. It was decided that cuttings were not to be dumped overboard because removing/installing the conveyors to dump cuttings would require several hours, and because disconnecting transfer lines would cause slurry to be spilled on WP platform.

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

3.7 REFERENCE WELLS Several wells have been considered for extrapolation with the play concept. These are essentially situated in the Hammerfest Basin northeast of the licence area. Data from these wells were used to constrain predictions of the petrophysical characteristics of the inferred reservoir sandstones of the Realgrunnen Group and, to lesser extent, of the Lower Basal Clastics in the Gamma Prospect. They comprise conventional wells drilled in the quadrants 7119, 7120, 7121, 7122 and 7219, as well as IKU shallow drilling 7018/05-U- 06 at the margin of the Troms-Finnmark Platform some 25 km southwest of the licence area. Thermal and kinetic input parameters derived from some of the considered wells were used to calibrate the modelling of hydrocarbon generation and expulsion from the principal source rock of the Hekkingen Formation in the Tromso Basin. Hydrocarbon characteristics were mainly extrapolated from data representative for the discoveries in the Hammerfest Basin, namely 7122/6-1 (oil and gas), Snohvit (oil and gas), Albatross (oil and gas), Askeladden (oil and gas), and Alke (gas). 3.8 OPERATIONAL GEOLOGY WELL PROGRAM 3.8.1 SAMPLING PROGRAM The standard cuttings sampling intervals will be as follows (Fig. 3.8.1): every 10 from 30 csg shoe (after return of drilling fluid) down to thel3 3/8 casing shoe at 2000 m. every from the 5/8 casing shoe down to T.D. at 3009 m. The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. Looking at your sketch, it looks like the siltstone is unstained, while the lower Hod Formation wackestones are stained. This implies one of the following: • If the siltsones are continuous over the closure, 1200m oil column (unlikely). • If the siltstones are discontinuous, 400 meter column is still necessary to stain the wackestone. Alternatively, if the staining is along fractures, the interval could have been stained with smaller oil column, and the oil would never have intruded the matrix pores. This seems more likely. Is it possible to examine the core and determine, in detail, where the staining occurs? • If the staining is in coarser-grained carbonates than the ones you sampled in this well, the stained intervals may have been fed by fractures. Depending on the underlying column height in the trap, you will see selective staining in the coarsest intervals. This treatment was performed on 19 March 1982 through the perforated interval 2540-2565 (TVD), as shown on Figure 19. Conclusions 1) The results from the diesel injection test, pump-in/flowback tests and also the mini-frac (pump-in/shut-in test) gave closure stress on the order of 7100 psig. context_snippets.text: 3.4 Rig Location Survey The rig site investigation survey was performed by Gardline Surveys using the vessel M.V. L'Espoir. The survey took place between 20th. and 30th. June 1996. Site survey interpretation was performed by Britsurvey between the 15th. and 26th. July 1996. Seismic 3D data (SG-9508) were integrated with the acquired high resolution 2D data set(SG-9610) for the site survey interpretation. The purpose of the survey was to examine the seabed and shallow geology to identify any features which may prove hazardous to the drilling operation. 6. RESERVE CALCULATIONS 6.1 Introduction All reserve calculations in this report are limited to the Brent Group reservoir of the A-South structure as outlined in chapter 4.3. Possible and speculative additional reserves within the PL120 licence are dealt with in chapter 7. 6.2 Reservoir Properties The petrophysical parameters for each formation are listed in Table 5.2.1 on page 74. The Tarbert Formation, Unit II, represents lateral continuous, high quality reservoir zone of mainly clean, marine sands. The sands of the Tarbert Formation, Unit I, are also probably lateral continuous, but have some interfingering claystone intervals which may be laterally extensive, thereby creating vertical permeability barriers. The Ness Formation consists of alternating sands and shales, probably with low to moderate sand continuity. This formation is assumed to increase in thickness to the south and die out fairly rapidly northwards. The Etive Formation is assumed to exhibit very good reservoir properties, including high porosities and permeabilities, as well as extensive lateral sandbody continuity. However, this formation may show some thinning both towards south and north from the discovery well. The Rannoch Formation, Sand-unit is also generally of good reservoir quality, but deteriorates gradually towards the lower part of the unit. The lateral continuity is probably extensive.

The intention being that cement returns from any top-up job would be confirmed by visual observations from the ROV, and thus saving rigtime by not having to run dedicated 1/2 DP grouting stinger. The 13 3/8 casing cementing was planned with cement returns planned back to the seabed. The 5/8 casing cementation was planned with the T.00 at 300 above the shoe to leave 690 window in the unlikely event of having to sidetrack below the 13 3/8 casing shoe.

context_snippets.text: 1 INTRODUCTION This report describes the sea-floor conditions and shallow geology within an approximately km area covering the Planned Well Location Idun (Figure 1.1). Potential installation and drilling hazards have been evaluated and special attention has been given to: • Seabed conditions, including water depth, sea-floor slope, seabed sediments and potential obstructions or hazards • Near-seabed sediments and likely anchoring conditions • Top hole sediments and well bore stability • Shallow water flow potential • Shallow gas • Boulders The report covers the interval from seabed down to the top of the Kai Formation at depth of 1341 meters Mean Sea Level (MSL). The report is divided into nine sections. The introduction, Section 1, is followed by summary of the main results and conclusions in Section 2. short description of the well and seismic data applied in the study is given in Section 3. In Section the criteria for horizon picking and anomaly definitions with its associated resolutions are presented. In Section description of the conditions for rig emplacement is given, including bathymetry, seabed and near-seabed sediments, potential obstructions and anchoring. Section deals with the shallow geology of the survey area, including brief geological history of the region from Miocene to present, details of the seismic interpretation and depth conversion, and geological prognosis for the well. Potential drilling hazards such as shallow gas and shallow-water flow is addressed in Section 7. Both sections, and 7, include examples from the seismic data to illustrate pertinent features. Section contains maps summarizing time structures and amplitude anomalies for the interpreted intervals. Section 8, recommendations, gives details of two possible relief well locations. Section contains full list of references. All positional data is referenced to ED50, Zone 32, Central Meridian 9° East. All depths are relative to Mean Sea Level (MSL), unless stated otherwise.

During the drilling of Well 6507/3-3 boulders were reported within Unit from 30 to 32 below seabed (421 to 423 MSL) and also at 56 below seabed (447 MSL). V Executive Summary for well: 6507/3-7 Petroleum Indications, Type and Quality: There are three main intervals displaying hydrocarbon anomalies in this well. The sections above 1530 and at 2895-3195 consist of mostly dry gas responses, with the exception of single sample from 3201 displaying an oil-like spectrum. thin section from 2943 contains several to common, white-fluorescent, and rare, yellow-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. Inclusion abundance is marginally high enough to suggest the presence of an oil column or paleo-column at this depth. No visible petroleum inclusions are documented at 1330 or 3201 m. The section below 3546 reveals dry gas to oil-like spectra. The most significant responses are gas-condensate to oil indications noted intermittently at 3546-3600 m. Thin sections from 3549 m, 3632 m, 3717 and 3840 contain rare to several, white-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz grains. Thin sections from 3549 and 3840 also contain rare to several, blue-fluorescent, upper-moderate gravity petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. The remainder of the analyzed interval contains sub-anomalous hydrocarbon concentra- tions. No petroleum inclusions are recorded in thin sections from 1910 m, 2420 or 3339 m. Shales contain moderate amounts of gas-prone kerogen and rare to several occurrences of immature to mature oil-prone kerogen in most samples (apparently oil-mature below about 3000 m). Highest visual kerogen abundance is noted at 3339 m. Proximal Pay Indications: Anomalous concentrations of acetic acid and, in general, more prominent benzene anomalies are identified at 3546-3588 and 3651-3654 m. Samples containing acetic acid anomalies usually suggest the nearby presence of reservoired liquid petroleum (oil or condensate), while more prominent benzene anomalies can indicate nearby gas. This well is reportedly gas discovery, thus it is probable that these features are sensing penetrated charge. Anomalies within reservoirs can indicate elevated Sw (for instance in relatively tight or impermeable reservoirs). Potential Seals: Possible seals are identified at 2898 m, 3340 m, 3546 and 3690 m. Evidence for Bacterial or Thermal Alteration: Sulfur species of probable bacterial origin are noted at 1230-1250 m, 2010 and 2340 m. These compounds generally indicate migration or microseepage of light, thermogenic hydrocarbons from depth followed by bacterial sulfate reduction at temperatures below 65°C. FIS microseeps are considered encouraging for deeper liquid petroleum exploration in the vicinity, and are consistent with deeper charge in the wellbore. Other: Nothing of note.

At the opposite end of the scale, wells with an Imax higher than 10,000 counts have been known to produce commercially elsewhere. Hydrocarbon contents are rather regularly distributed as shown in Figure 3, fluctuating between Imax 2000 – 6000 counts, only rarely up to Imax 6000-12000 counts. 3.2 Hydrocarbon quality Comparison with API gravity using range of reference petroleums gives correlation with HCSTM Q580 of R2 = (90 different oils) and (112 different oils) for CUSC. (HCSTMQ580 = Figure 1, lower insert, unpublished data and CUSC Q580 = Figure 2.) Hydrocarbon HCSTM measurements of the cored section show variation in Q580 within the range – corresponding to light oil to heavy oil compositions. The restricted presence of Q580 scattering is indicative of overall good vertical fluid communication. However, there are three depths that stand out in this respect: 3557.3 Discrete shift from light to medium oil compositions 3565.3 Local shift medium-heavy-medium oil compositions 3580.3 Overall shift from medium to heavy oil compositions. The shift close to is readily observable, whereas the other shifts are subtle accompanied by an overall decrease in grain size with depth. However, even below 3600 m, in those few segments were poro-perm performance suddenly shifts from poor to good medium oils can be detected in an otherwise heavy oil environment (Figure 6). Overall there seems to be good vertical fluid communication, from the top of the cored section down to approximately 3608 m, the shifts from light through medium to heavy oil composition possibly due to gravitative segregation. In this respect the HCSTM spectral information (Figure 5) from light/medium oil at 3549 (Q580 0.27) to light/medium oil some 20 deeper at 3568 (Q580 0.24) is pointing towards common source for this petroleum. SUMMARY: This shallow drilling project has been run in the Skagerrak area, northeast of the Farsund Subbasin. In September 1988, 667 km of shallow seismic data were collected. Subcropping bedrock units and Quaternary thickness were mapped and potential drillsites selected. Four holes have been drilled: 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88 and 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 on line IKU-0822SK-88. The drilling was carried out with M/S Bucentaur in May 1989. The water depth for the localities varied from 505 to 525 and the Quaternary overburden from to m. The holes were drilled from 90 to below sea bed (603.7 to 817.5 below sea level). The four cores comprise about 420 of diamond (piggyback) drilling in bedrock of Paleozoic and Mesozoic age. The coring yielded 370 of samples representing 88.5% recovery in average. This report presents seismic interpretation, sedimentology, petrophysical logs and core measurements, biostratigraphy and organic geochemistry. In addition, special studies have been made including trace fossil analyses, thermal conductivity, oedo- meter and apatite fission track analysis. The depositional environment, bedrock subcrop distribution, stratigraphy, regional correlations and burial history are discussed. KEYWORDS: Shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin North Sea Paleozoic Skagerrak Mesozoic SkOries

As they give information about maximum temperature and timing, another two samples were picked from core 13/2-U-2 and submitted to Geotrack International, Australia. Even if the most promising intervals of the core were selected, the two samples did not yield single grain of apatite or zircon. Unfortunately, it was therefore not possible to proceed further with the fission track analysis. 4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Good bathymetric maps are of great help in interpreting the outcropping geology between seismic lines. On Figure the previous geological inter- pretation is combined with the new bathymetric map. The steep slope in southwest along the - fault is very striking. On the SW - NE line IKU- 101SK-88, sp 3000-3200, topographic high of about 50 was found and the form was discussed in the Main Report. From the bathymetric map it is clear that the high is not local dome but more the easternmost seen extension of WNW - ESE trending ridge. This trend can also be seen on the three dimensional perspective view (Figure 2.3). The bathymetric map has thus limited the discussion about volcanic intrusions by showing that dome structure probably does not exist. No clear evidence of outcropping volcanic rocks is seen near the drill site. In combination with the seismic evidence of possible subcropping volcanic rocks (e. g. the strong disturbance and loss of reflection continuity on line IKU-0822SK-88, sp 2700-2900) there might be subcropping dike system in the area as indicated on Figure 4.1. From the shallow drilling program in 1989 it seems probable that also the Paleozoic rocks found outcropping east of 9°E in the Skagerrak area is of mainly Cambro-Silurian age. Core 13/2-U-2 was postmature, but evaluating the above suggested existence of volcanic dike, we still find it very probable that this was caused by later Paleozoic intrusions. This is also supported by the supposed migrated hydrocarbon content in the core. We therefore find it highly valuable to continue the investigation of the Paleozoic rocks in the Skagerrak area. Our recommendation is to acquire shallow seismic data between 9° and 10° and then continue with shallow drilling based on the results of the seismic.

INTRODUCTION 5_Eg , _INTEF-GRUPPEN The joint industrial research and development program SHALLOW DRILLING FARSUND SUBBASIN 1988/89 had the objective to carry out shallow seismic, shallow drilling and laboratory examination of the subcropping bedrock in the Skagerrak area northeast of the Farsund Subbasin and to evaluate these data. The main target was to collect high quality bedrock cores from selected intervals of the Mesozoic and Paleozoic strata in the area. The program of shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin was initiated from near- shore bedrock mapping project in the coastal Norwegian North Sea areas. This study was based on existing data, mainly conventional seismic, and was carried out by IKU in cooperation with NPD (Oljedirektoratet) and Statoil (Rokoengen et al. 1988). proposal for shallow drilling program was put forward to several companies of which seven supported the program as Early Participants. One company joined as an Early Late Participant before drilling started (and increased the budget) and one company has, so far, joined as Late Participant after drilling. NPD had observer status in the project. Following the intentions of the inaugural meeting in Stavanger on 19th August 1988, shallow seismic survey with 667 km of digital (2.5 sec.) and analog equipment was run in September 1988 (Figure 1.1). The data were collected and processed by A/S Geoteam. Based on the new seismic data, revised bedrock and Quaternary thickness maps were presented and possible coring sites proposed in February 1989 (Lippard and Rokoengen 1989). Dril- ling program and priorities were discussed and decided on Steering Committee meeting at Oppdal and applications sent to NPD in March 1989. First priority was given to the two drillsites 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 (Figure 1.1) located on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate Base Cretaceous and cover most of the Jurassic section in the area. Second priority was given to the drill- sites 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 located on the shallow seismic line IKU-0822SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate the oldest Mesozoic sediments (of supposed Triassic age) and give information from the Paleozoic rocks in the area. The drillings were done on the platform northeast of the Farsund Subbasin (Figure 1.2), where the drilled strata can be tied into the basin itself.

question: Do lab-measured thermal conductivity values for Rogn sandstone agree with log-derived thermal conductivity, and is the Rogn sandstone thermally anisotropic?
answer_text: No — log-derived values are too low compared to laboratory measurements for the Rogn sandstone, and thermal anisotropy in the Rogn sandstone was not measured.

context_snippets.text: PORE PRESSURE EVALUATION WHILST DRILLING Please note that all depths are in TVD. Prior to drilling this section, the well was displaced with g/cc Anco Tec. oil based mud. The drilling commenced with PDC-bit / mud motor. The top of this section consisted predominantly of claystones and sandstones to approximately 1320 metres. Sliding combined with the usage of PDC-bit / mud motor strongly affected the modified Dxc and the MLNDR, which made it very difficult to establish trendline, as the models are based on compaction sequences in claystones. Good shale points were picked by correlation of cuttings- and Gamma Ray data during rotary drilling. normal compaction trendline was thereby established by assuming normal pore pressure at the top of this hole section. However, lot of the drilling throughout this hole section was conducted in steering mode: therefore the Dxc and the MLNDR can not be considered to be reliable tools to detect abnormal pore pressure. The interpretation was therefore based on empirical data, i.e. appearance of trip- and / or connection gas. torque trends, background gas levels etc. While drilling this section, the mud weight was held at g/cc. Several gas peaks were observed, few of them quite large, but all gas is believed to be drilled gas associated with very high penetration rates. slight increase in drag on connections was recorded from approximately 1750 metres. but the increase is probably result of high hole inclination. No close to balance indicators, such as trip gas or connection gas were observed. Thus, interpretation of given data suggests normal pore pressure throughout the entire hole section. The static overbalance is assumed to be approximately 74 bar at TD. 8-2

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness. drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure. i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction. any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 8-1

Porosity Determination ELAN computes porosities taking the mineralogy and fluid effects into account automatically. The presence of mud filtrate (and possibly of light hc) and the effects of clay (and other) minerals are accounted for by the response equations simultaneously solved by the ELAN optimizer, ensuring accurate porosity and saturation calculations, provided the model and its end-points are also accurate. The main measurement controlling the porosity in ELAN's forward model is the bulk density. Its theoretical response equation takes into account the variable fluid mixture present in the invaded zone and the (also variable) mineralogy. This is achieved by using simultaneously all the relevant information extracted from the other available logs through their corresponding tool response equations. This ensures the use of the correct effective fluid density and matrix density on continuous depth by depth level basis. The forward model approach does not rely on prior calibration of the bulk density log with core data, which requires the knowledge of the reduction factor to be applied to the raw core porosities. What is critical instead, is the accuracy of the model and its parameters: fluids and minerals and their end-point values. Q:REPORTS\2511-10H.DOCAthm13/01/99 page 38

Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. LEVEL, DEPTH, TIME and PEAK/PEAK on each heading have the same meaning as for the surface breaks. TIME now displays the time of the geophone breaks relative to the start of recording. The definition of the breaktime on both surface and downhole sensors is the time instant indicated by drawing tangent through the point of inflection on the first departure and taking the intersection of this tangent with the trace zero line. STACKED DATA PLOT 11 displays STACKED DATA, i.e. data after application of median coherency stacking procedure, by which the good traces of each level are first selected according to their mutual coherency, and then subjected to median stacking procedure, ideally suppressing random noise completely. The break time of each trace is recomputed after stacking and displayed as TIME, which is the transit time from surface sensor to geophone. The definition of the breaktime on both surface sensors and stacked geophone traces Is the time indicated by drawing tangent through the point of inflection on the first departure and taking the intersection of this tangent with the trace zero line. COMMENTS o tube-wave component (with much steeper slope, i.e. slower velocity than the that of the first-breaks) is present in the data set. o The shallower levels are marred by casing arrivals (several depths around 2200 metres were tested to avoid this problem). o Else the data are noise-free data with generally clean first-breaks. o The Vertical Seismic Profile Processing Report describes the subsequent processing.

INTRODUCTION The report presents the results of petrographical evaluation of the cored section in Well 7122/2-1, that was drilled by Norsk Hydro within the PL179 licence during the Autumn 1992. Well 7122/2-1 provided eight cores from the depth intervals 1771-1784m (core to 3), 1812-1824m (core 4) and 1833-1932m (core to 8). The upper four cores represent the Early to Middle Barremian Kolje Formation, whilst the lower four represent the Valanganian to Heuterivian Knurr Formation. main objective of the present study is to provide detailed petrographical characterization of these cored intervals. Furthermore, an attempt is maid to decipher the diagenetic evolution in order to comment on the effect of rock composition and diagenetic evolution on the reservoir quality of the sandstones. The report presents 1) the results of standard petrographical analyses based on thin- section and XRD-analyses, and 2) the results of some more detailed mineralogical and textural analyses emphasising the diagenetic evolution of the sandstones. The discussion on the diagenetic evolution includes detailed modal analyses, fluid inclusion thermometry on inclusions in quartz cements and Cathodo-Luminescence (CL) and Back Scatter Electron Imaging (BSE) using Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). The report is organized as follows: The standard petrographical analyses of samples from the cored sections are presented in Part 2, and the results of the more detailed diagenetic analyses on the samples are presented in Part 3. summary of the findings of the present study and some recommendations for further work is given in Part 4. The cored section shows less mudstones upwards and change from very fine grained sandstone to fine grained sandstone upwards. The cored section can be subdivided into four facie associations. Offshore transition mudstone and sandstone. This facies association is seen in the lower meters of the cored section and comprises inter bedded well burrowed mudstones (Lithofacies and very fine grained wave rippled to micro hummocky cross-stratified sandstones (Lithofacies C). The bed thickness is typically to 15 cm. Burrows of chondrites type are recognized. The alternating lithology probably represent alternation of fair weather mud layers and storm sands within an offshore transition zone, e.g. deposition close to the storm weather wave base. Palynofacies characteristics are consistent with this interpretation. Lower shoreface sandstone and minor mudstone. The cored section from 3976,5m to 3967,25m can be subdivided into four minor fining upward sub units. Each unit consists of massive cross stratified fine grained sandstone (Lithofacies and minor C) with an erosive base which passes upward to burrowed, very fine grained sandstone and inter bedded sandstone/mudstone similar to the bedding in the lower meter of the cored section. The massive cross strata, hummocky or swaly, are typical of high energy middle shoreface setting. The interbedded sandstone and mudstone beds suggest more quiet or protected shoreface environment. The four units can also be seen defined as four parasequences within lower order (4th or 6th order) sequences. The gradual increase of mudstone in the two upper units may also indicate that this part of the cored section represents retrograding parasequence sets. The palynofacies characteristics of these parasequences are described below. Middle shoreface sandstone. From 3967,25m to 3954,75m massive cross stratified sandstone is the dominating sedimentary feature. The sandstones are fine grained to very fine grained (Lithofacies and rare and D) with few mudstone partings. The beds vary from few dm in thickness to more than meter. The hummocky/swaley cross stratified beds are commonly amalgamated. Erosive surfaces occur above few thin mudstone beds. Wave ripples and slightly more muddy sandstones occur in the upper 0,5m of the unit. Based on modem shelf studies, amalgamated hummocky, cross stratified, finer grained sandstones are associated with storm dominated shoreface and shelves. Typical water depth have been reported as 15-40 m. In association with the general overall coarsening upward trend of the cored section, middle shoreface environment is suggested. The lean kerogen obtained from these lithologies yield palynofacies types consistent with high energy depositional setting. Reworked shoreline and shoreface sandstone. This facies association is seen in the upper 1,8 meter of the cored section. Thin laminae of medium grained sandstones mark the erosive base of this unit. In contrast to the facies associations below, common plant remains, wood (coaly streaks) and leaves together with massive burrowed fine grained sandstones are seen. context_snippets.text: Palynological Examination of the 2/7-9X Well Summary The study analyzed the palynology of forty-three cutting samples of the 2/7-9X well. The sediments penetrated at the base of the well are interpreted to be Valanginian to Barremian in age. Conclusions The well passes through thick Albian to Neocomian sequence. The caving of Paleogene forms and the recycling of both Upper Jurassic and Permo-Triassic taxa complicate the basic age interpretation. Recommendations The findings of this study agree with the results of the EPS nannofossil data communicated in Report No. 2463A.

Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

QUATERNARY AND TERTIARY; SPUD - 3000m TVD SS The Quaternary and Tertiary sector is subdivided into three groups, which are the: 1) Nordland Group dominated by soft clays and sands which overlies the 2) Hordaland Group consisting mainly of claystones and interbedded carbonates which overlies the 3) Roaaland Group which contains tuffaceous shales and varicolored muds tones. RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group.
