question: How does FIS m/z≤180 data from 34/8-A-1 indicate hydrocarbon classes, paleofluid distribution, and exploration risks?
answer_text: FIS m/z≤180 from 34/8‑A‑1 detects low‑molecular‑weight organics (≤C13) and represents major hydrocarbon classes (aromatics, naphthenes, paraffins), yielding nearly continuous stratigraphic paleofluid logs for 2D/3D mapping. These logs delineate migration pathways, seal integrity and proximity to reservoired petroleum and highlight exploration risks such as bypassed pay and reservoir compartmentalization.

context_snippets.text: Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, includ- ing petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries through Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS) petroleum exploration and exploitation risk tool developed at Amoco, we obtain valuable and unique information on three major top- ics relevant to exploration: 1) Hydrocarbon Migration, 2) Seals and 3) Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum and two major topics relevant to production: 1) Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimitation and 2) Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy involves the rapid, complete analysis of volatiles trapped as fluid inclusions in rock samples using quadrupole mass analyzers. The technology documents the presence and relative bulk abundance of ionized volatile fragments with mass/charge ratio of m/z 180. This includes most geologically important inorganic species as well as organic species with less than or equal to 13 carbon atoms. The resulting analysis of the petroleum fraction is comparable to the low molecular weight fraction of whole-oil gas chromatographic mass spectrometric (GCMS) analysis (without devolatilization of the gas fraction); hence, the major classes of hydrocarbons (e.g., aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins) are represented. The Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy program at FIT is unique in several ways: 1) the method- ology and theoretical framework necessary for this unique technology are the result of long-standing research and development effort, 2) the cumulative experience and database of documented case histories are the most extensive in the world and 3) the technology rep- resents the most rapid analytical capability of its kind available. In its present configuration, FIS instrumentation has the potential to analyze all available samples for 2-4 wells in 24 hr period at total cost of approximately $4000-5000 per well, thus making it one of the most inexpensive and rapid geochemical techniques available. The resulting dataset can provide nearly continuous log of paleofluid chemistries through the stratigraphic section penetrated by well, and, given adequate sample coverage, the data can be mapped in two or three dimensions. 1.1 Organization of this Report Analytical results of the FIS analysis of 34 A1 BH are presented graphically in Sections and as series of profiles each illustrating the variation of particular atomic mass (m/z) or ratio of two masses with measured depth. general discussion of the interpretation of FIS data including the significance of particular features and trends (or their absence) is provided in Section A. Some of the calcite cemented stringers can apparently be correlated across the N1-segment. However, the calcite cemented zones in A-1 AH are probably associated with fault zones. Faulting has affected the Rannoch Formation in A-1 AH as seen from the common tectonized lamination on the cores (see Enclosure 1); hence the reduced Rannoch Formation thickness in A-1 AH, when compared to other Visund wells, is likely not fully representative for the area. The Etive Fm. on Visund mainly consists of medium-coarse sandstones (El, E3, E5), however, zones of fine-grained, micaceous Rannoch-type facies (E2, E4) occur and apparently thicken northwards on the field. The Etive zonation reflects this interlayering of coarser and finer facies. In Well A-1 AH the upper part of the Etive Formation (and likely also the lowermost Ni) is probably faulted out (possibly eroded, however, these zones appear to be present in Well A-1 BH near by). The thinning of particularly the Etive zones E4 and E3 when compared to the other Visund wells is believed to be due to condensation caused by syndepositional tectonic activity in the area (i.e. the southern triangle on the N2-segment). This is in line with the seismic which suggests thinning of the Brent isochore within the southern triangle on the N2-segment. The Ness Fm. on Visund consists for large part of sandy bay fill facies, with typical channel sandstones being rare. The Tarbert Fm. on Visund consists of very fine to fine-grained, micaceous, hummocky cross-laminated sandstones. The Ness/Torbert boundary may be difficult to pick on logs only because of often transitional facies changes. Displaced hole from casing shoe to SG OBM, no losses observed. Seawater and interface dumped while displacing to SG. POOH with 12 1A drilling BHA. Made up new 12 1/4 clean out BHA and RIH. Broke circulation every 20 stands towards TD with increasing flow rate gradually to 1500 1pm. Reamed through tight spot at 3172 meters, washed down to 3186 meters. Back reamed from 3186 meters and lost returns at 3183 meters. Filled top of hole with seawater and managed to stabilize hole after 18 m3 of seawater. Pumped 15 m3 LCM pill and displaced it with OBM. POOH to 2896 and pumped second LCM pill (15 m3) and displaced it with OBM.

DRILLING CAUTIONS: No abnormal pressure is expected in this hole section. The mud weight schedule illustrated in the drilling target curve is required for wellbore stability in the Hordaland Shale. The Hordaland Shale is weak shale section that has history of wellbore stability problems. Shale inhibition will be provided by the KCl/Glycol mud system. The mud weight schedule currently shown is based on prior wellbore stability analysis performed by Exxon Production Research Company (EPR). EPR is currently updating the Elli Wellbore Stability Model. An updated mud weight schedule may be issued upon completion of this work. The hole section will be logged according to the formation evaluation program. Depending on the actual mud weight selected, the amount of overbalance while logging and coring will be +1- 1200 psi. EXTREME CAUTION should be exercised to avoid sticking any logging tools. To the extent possible, tools should not be allowed to remain stationary. All calibrations and opening of arms should be done while the tools are moving at slow speed.

BIT RUN SUMMARY PAGE 11-2-10 RUN #11 BIT #7 BIT MANUFACTURER : HUGHES TOOL COMPANY BIT TYPE / JETS : ATM18 / 2x22, lx24 BIT SERIAL No. : M221853 DRILLING PARAMETERS TORQ: 0-2500 Amps MW : PPg DRILLING SUMMARY (2 1m) Bit #7 was picked up and RIH after surface testing both the MWD tools and the mud motor and adding drill collars and stabilisers to the BHA. The bit was washed to bottom from 2220m before drilling ahead, sliding from 2257 to 2265m, where increasing pipe drag required the use of surface rotation. At 2270m pump #1 failed and the pipe was worked while repairs were carried out before drilling ahead to 2272m where pump #1 failed again. After effecting repairs drilling continued, orientating from 2272m to 2275m and drilling conventionally between 2275 and 2301m, again due to excessive pipe drag. Due to the difficulties experienced trying to steer, it was decided that casing should be set. After circulating B/U and checking for flow, the bit was backreamed to 2010m before pulling back to the casing shoe. The hole was checked for flow before running in to 1869m and reaming back to bottom. The hole was found to be very tight between 2280 and 2301m. 75 bbl hi-vis pill was pumped and circulated out before dropping multi shot survey and POOH. The interval drilled by bit #7 was comprised mainly of interbedded sandstone and light to medium grey, soft, blocky claystone with dark grey platy shales grading to claystones in places. The sandstone was composed of medium to coarse, well sorted clear to translucent quartz grains. Thin beds of mottled white argillaceous limestone with fine black laminations were also present throughout the section.

question: What are the formation names, lithologies, and MSL depth ranges for Quaternary Units I–IV at PWL 25/8-17?
answer_text: Unit I – Witch Ground Fm: 127±1 m to 147±2 m (MSL): very soft clay with a thin silty fine sand at seabed; Unit II – Ferder Fm: 147±2 m to 156±2 m (MSL): soft to firm clay with lenses of coarse sediments (pebbles/cobbles/possible boulders); Unit III – Mariner Fm: 156±2 m to 293±8 m (MSL): very stiff clay and dense to very dense sand (possible sandy layers, boulders); Unit IV – Shackleton Fm: 293±8 m to 327±9 m (MSL): very stiff to hard sandy clay with occasional dense clayey sand layers.

question: Summarize processing applied to 9/2-1 VSP VA/VA(FK): CD stack, cross-corr align, gun-hydro deconv?
answer_text: Yes — the VA/VA(FK) data were common‑depth stacked after cross‑correlation trace alignment, with marine source‑signature deconvolution using the gun hydrophone applied.

context_snippets.text: VERTICAL SEISMIC PROFILE REPORT APPENDIX Description of V.S.P. Displays Vertical Well: Source at Well Head Display VA (Stacked Geophone Data at one-way time) This display indicates the quality of the data used in the subsequent VSP processing. The trace displayed for each geophone position is the result of editing, as appropriate, and summing common depth traces; the common depth traces having undergone trace alignment procedure (based on cross correlation) in order to obtain accurate alignment prior to summation. Source signature deconvolution will have been applied to marine data, unless otherwise stated, using the gun hydrophone signal as source signature. Wavelet stabilisation may optionally have been applied to the data to remove variations in source character due to changing source conditions, (particularly onshore) and/or variation in geophone coupling. A broad band filter will have been applied to this data in order to remove noise without compromising the usable bandwidth of the data. The polarity of this display is such that the first downgoing arrival is plotted as black peak. (SEC normal polarity) Display VA(FK) (F-K Display of Stacked Geophone Data at One-Way Time) This display shows the stacked geophone data (after source signature deconvolution, if appropriate) at one-way time transformed into F-K space. This data is displayed as wave number (K) against frequency, with variation in colour indicating amplitude in dB below the maximum amplitude. A velocity alignment in T-X space transforms to an alignment in F-K space, rotated through 90°; the various wavefields (i.e. velocity alignments) commonly observed in T-X space transform into F-K space as illustrated in Fig.1 The strongest wavefield will normally be the Downgoing wavefield and this transforms into an alignment from zero wave number, zero frequency sloping in the positive wave number direction. Significant velocity changes in wavefield will result in multiple alignments in F-K space; although in practice it may not be possible to differentiate between the different F-K alignments and the resulting event may be smeared. /Cont'd....

Displays VC and VD (Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time; before and after enhancement) These displays show the Primary and Multiple activity observed at the borehole location from the shallowest VSP geophone position to some way below the deepest VSP geophone position (and therefore, normally, some way below Total Depth of the borehole). The data shown on Display VD is that of Display VC after application of spatial filter; this spatial filter will be the result of various trials and will have been chosen to give the best enhancement of the upgoing events (horizontal and/or dipping) observed in the data. In marine data, if source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the input wavelet will be zero-phase and the wavelet contained in the data will be zero phase modified by earth absorption and transmission loss effects (i.e. mixed phase). In the case of onshore data, if neither wavelet stablisation nor source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the source signature remains in the data. Wavelet stabilisation can be carried out by shaping to any given wavelet; we would recommend, however, that all geophone data is transformed to the waveform of shallow geophone level. In this case then the source signature effectively remains in the data but is made consistent from level to level. Events that reach the time-depth curve are primary and their lithologic significance can be established unequivocally by reference to the calibrated velocity log. This comparison can be made using Display VG1 which contains the data from Display VF and the calibrated velocity log at the scale(s) of the seismic section. Multiples having their last bounce from primary within the range of the VSP may be identified by observing their termination in the data at the same depth point at which the primary cuts the time-depth curve. From this display, any dip across the well location can be recognised by move- out of the primary event to shorter time, as the geophone moves up the well and away from the lithology creating the reflection. No azimuth of dip can be computed from this display but true-dip can be computed from measurement of the LT against vertical depth increment. Unconformity may be recognised by an abrupt change of moveout of adjacent primary events. Topographical features up-dip away from the well may be recognised by an increase in the LT or in the termination of an event away from the time-depth curve. Dip increasing 'up-dip' away from the well can be observed in the data; however, if dip is decreasing 'up-dip' (i.e. crest of an anticline) then the event in question will disappear from the data. 6.3 Top and Fault Seal Top seal at the prospect is provided by the Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous shales overlying the Bryne Formation. In two nearby wells, 10/8-1 and 9/12-1, this shale interval is 331 in and 487 thick respectively. Within these wells the shale is generally silty with occasional interbedded claystone and limestone. Northwestward, toward to the basin center, the silt content of the interval decreases. At the TOTT prospect well location this interval is estimated to be 556 thick and to provide adequate top seal for the prospect. Esso's technique for fault seal analysis is based on the study of the vertical displacement of the stratigraphic sections along fault plane, the sealing characteristics of the resultant fault gouge and the changes in these factors laterally along fault. Displaced section analysis models have been constructed based on two wells, 9/2-1 and 10/8-1, providing range from sand-prone to shale-prone nature for the Jurassic section, respectively. These models suggest, in general, that for fault throws between 50 and 150 meters there will be cross leak only from the low-side to the high-side of fault. For fault throws less than 50 there will be cross leak whereas for throws greater than 150 the fault will be sealing. Fault plane profiles along the critical faults to the north of the prospect indicate that migration of hydrocarbons into the prospect from this direction is feasible (section 6.4). Fault plane profiles along the crestal faults on the prospect indicate that cross leak is probable, resulting in reservoir communication across the structure. Although these crestal faults cut through the top seal, they are not interpreted to have caused dip leakage. 6.4 Source The predicted source for hydrocarbons in the TOTT prospect is the Kimmeridgian Tau Formation. The formation was deposited on shallow-marine shelf. Restricted circulation in the Egersund Basin led to the deposition of organic-rich shales in the deep portions of the basin. In the vicinity of Block 9/5 the formation is 37 to 105 thick with 27 to 55 thick zone of high total organic carbon (TOC), the hot shale, in the upper part of the formation. The formation laps out on the basin margins and is absent in wells near Block 10/7, such as 10/8-1 and 9/12-1.

LOGGING A7.1 MWD Logs 17 Yz hole section A MWD service (Anadrill Schlumberger) including gamma ray sensor for picking the sandstone intervals, and survey measurements was run over the 17 Y2 section. Sand (Utsira Fm.) was detected at 405 with corresponding increase in penetration rate. At 600 severe shocks were recorded which led to failure of the gamma ray sensor (fractured crystal). Further increase in shock rate at 725 eventually led to the failure of the direction and inclination sensor package at 920 m. 12 '4 hole section The MWD tool over this section included gamma ray, resistivity and survey measurements package. The tool indicated the presence of unexpected sand packages in the upper part of the Hordaland Gp. from 1750 to 1850 m, shallower than the potential Frigg Fm. MWD failures were recorded over this section. The MWD stopped pulsing at 2708 due to seal problem in silicate(high pH) mud, and this caused significant amount of non-productive time as magnetic single shot survey had to be run to comply with internal surveying procedures. The second tool failure was related to the same mud related problems. Picking the next section TD for the 5/8 casing had to be done without the gamma ray support and the thinner than expected Cromer Knoll interval which was targeted as the casing seat was missed. Casing was set within the Upper Jurassic Draupne shale. 8 Y2 hole section Drilling continued with no response from the GST (geosteering motor with resistivity at the bit). Real time resistivity was critical for coring point selection so the GST tool was recovered for evaluation, with no problem identified at surface. The backup GST tool was picked up and attempts to shallow test were inconclusive (because of difficulties in transmitting the signal via mud rather than formation). GST#2 was run in the hole and drilling resumed with no response of the tool. These tool failures were due to insulation problems on some wires that are not regularly checked prior to tool dispatch. The bottom hole assembly was recovered to install MWD/CDR configured in rotary mode to bring the resistivity sensor as close to the bit as possible. Another MWD failure was recorded, related to the silicate mud, and magnetic single shot survey was attempted with no success. context_snippets.text: The shaker room on the Maersk Jutlander filled with steam from hot mud, making it difficult to see especially with safety glasses. This was partly caused by the crew leaving the doors open and disturbing the airflow pattern, of the HVAC system. A good proportion of the Drill-Reps time was spent on logistic issues, rather than on drilling ones. dedicated offshore logistics man would remove this load, in future. If severe balling problems occur, consideration to increase the frequency of BOP Function test should be given. As it was with the riser and wellhead so balled there would have been no guarantee that the BOPs could have been used in well control situation. The MWD failed after cumulative pumping time of 154 hours in the silicate mud. This could set the limit of MWD life in silicate WBM. However anaylsis performed by technicians in town suggest that the failure was not due to the silicate WBM, but coil in the turbine had melted and short circuited parts of the turbine, resulting in power cut to the MWD. 9 5/8 Casing the use of fast developing compressive strength cemCRETE plug could have been further investigated for the kick-off plug. The extra cost due to the nature of the cemCRETE blend, could have been saved on reduced WOC time. The manual override for the Deepsea Express cement head was found to be difficult to operate, after the hydraulic system had failed - most likely due to the suction below. The manual system needs to be confirmed to be adequate. Special attention should be paid to drifting of any casing XO and its design tolerances. In preference have the X0s pre-installed on casing joint to stop them being over looked in baskets. Even if the casing is drifted in town, ensure that it is re-drifted offshore. Ensure that if the XO are to be drifted in town they are done so with solid API or special made drift (depending on the required drift ID) rather than hand-held Have taper mill for polishing any XO used, on standby as contingency - in case of design tolerance problems. 1/3-9s T2 Drilling Completion Report Rev 72

question: How does swelling green clay and casing-stage lost circulation affect FIT evaluation, cement success, and squeeze planning?

question: In Y2H, which is more likely to cause high M-sand/C-sand: deeper-than-prognosed reservoir depth or heterolithic infill?
answer_text: Deeper-than-prognosed reservoir depth is the more likely cause; heterolithic infill may contribute but is uncertain.

In general, any deviation between prognoses and actual depths are caused by discrepancies in either the seismic picks, the velocity model used for depth conversion or combination of these. For dipping horizons, also difference between the planned and actual well track will influence the comparison. Top Sognefjord was penetrated meters deeper than prognoses in well 31/5-I-32 Y1H/Y2H. question: In the D85-J limestone unit, how do porosity and permeability compare, what controls their differences, and what are the reservoir implications?
answer_text: Porosity is locally high (moldic) while permeability is extremely low; the contrast is controlled by moldic pore types and lack of pore interconnection from cementation and remineralization, so the unit has little reservoir potential.

Mudclasts and traces of carbonaceous material are noted throughout the section. Predominant colours are light green, green and grey. Red colouration typically associated with the Triassic appears to be absent. At and below 4616m, the lithologies and log profiles are similar to those of the cored interval. Mudstones and siltstones recorded within this section are subordinate and predominantly dark grey or medium dark grey in colour, much of which is probably due to significant caving from the overlying Jurassic. Only traces of the characteristic pale to moderate reddish brown Triassic lithologies are recorded in ditch cuttings samples but, significantly, both the sidewall core samples at 4695.1m and 4704m from the 2/5-10A well comprise argillaceous siltstones which are entirely red.

In these shale-zones the porosity have been set to zero. 3.2 Log analysis method The Farsund Unit, Intra Farsund Sand and the Hegre Group have been analysed using computer model, based on the complex lithology method using the density log for porosity calculations with corrections for hydrocabon and shale effects. Shale volume has been determined from the gamma-ray log and the resistivity data using the R, value. In most sections the gamma-ray log has been used while the R, curve has been used in wash-out sections. In the pipeconveyed section the induction log is used to calculate the true resistivity of the uninvaded formation. The resistivity of the invaded zone is calculated from the microspherical focused log. The resistivity logs are corrected for borehole and invasion effects. In the MWD section the RACM curve (Resistivity Amplitude Ratio Corrected Memory) is used as the true resistivity of the formation while the RPCM curve (Resistivity Phase Difference Corrected Memory) is used as the resistivity of the invaded zone. Formation water resistivity and mud filtrate resistivity are varied with depth using temperature gradient established from Horner plots of temperature data.

4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( Tv-D vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has 'Tl-Tc' value of zero. From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity anclior lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

Ford (Ref. 6) attached environmental significance to occurrences of Oligosteginids (calcispheres), dominant in and practically restricted to the Maastrichtian part of the interval, and of Radiolaria occurring with varying grades of dominance in the remainder. He recognised the shallower, aragonitic realm of deposition to concur with an abundance of Oligosteginids and deeper, siliceous realm with dominant Radiolaria whereas the intermediate, calcitic realm would be characterized by predominance of planktonic Foraminifera. In summing up all microfossil data, definite open marine environment of deposition would apply to the major part of the carbonate sequence and in gross aspect most likely upper bathyal to outer neritic. Somewhat shallower conditions are thought to have prevailed towards the end of the carbonate regime during earliest Paleocene time when lime mud gave gradually way, through intermediate softer chalk, to marl. This is indicated by increased quantities of calcareous benthonic Foraminifera and the presence of bryozoan, echinoid and shell remains in these softer carbonates, which points more likely towards middle neritic environment. Paleocene The ensuing Cenozoic sequence of elastic sediments started during the Paleocene with the deposition of non-calcareous shales, in part vari- coloured (melange), followed by fine glauconitic sands and altogether amounting to relatively small thickness. The shales bear distinct deep-water arenaceous foraminiferal assem- blage equivalent to Brouwer's Rhabdammina fauna (Ref. 3) indicative for an abyssal environment. This rather drastic change from the pre- ceding shallower carbonate environment within relatively short space of time is thought to have been caused by last phase of considerable subsidence in the Central Graben structure. The occurrence of exotic blocks of Upper Cretaceous chalk within the Paleocene shales (e.g. well 1/3-1) would be in support of such movement. Eocene Deep water conditions prevailed subsequently throughout the Eocene on evidence of the continued presence of the all-arenaceous foraminiferal assemblage in largely non-calcareous shales, interrupted only by non- foraminiferal interval of late Paleocene sand deposition and the diatom associated tuffaceous sediments of the earliest Eocene. Oligocene The foraminiferal assemblage of the Oligocene sediments, largely non- calcareous pyritic shales with intercalations of claystone and dolomite, is predominantly arenaceous although some modification on generic and specific level took place accompanied by intermittent invasions of calcareous benthonic and planktonic Foraminifera, the latter sometimes in floods of small sized specimens as witnessed in sidewall samples.

question: What equations and corrections are used to derive porosity and water saturation, including hydrocarbon correction and Poupon→Archie condition?
answer_text: Porosity is calculated from the density log with hydrocarbon correction applied via a computed pseudo‑MSFL (microresistivity); water saturation is calculated from the Poupon‑Leveaux equation using the MHz phase resistivity log, which reduces to the Archie equation when shale volume is zero.

Although the continuity of the 3D data is not good at these levels, there is some correlation with the anomalies plotted from the site survey data. The Quaternary succession is expected to comprise an interbedded clay, sand and silt sequence. At the proposed location the base of the Quaternary probably occurs at about 530ms TWT (± 30ms), 480m MSL. Underlying the Quaternary units is thick succession of Tertiary sediments which are from early Palaeocene to Pliocene in age. The Tertiary units exhibit some structural features such as gentle folding/flexure and also an anticlinal structure can be observed on site where the Tertiary sediments drape over the older Cretaceous succession. The upper part of the Tertiary exhibits number of laterally continuous, sub-horizontal reflectors interpreted as sand-prone horizons (illustrated by the 16/10-1 completion well log). Chart 12 illustrates such reflector which dips gently towards the northwest (mapped reflector 4). At this level number of amplitude anomalies can be observed (see figures and 4.12.). These anomalies exhibit reversal of phase and at the proposed location such feature occurs at about 670ms TWT. They have been assigned low risk of gasification and may represent locations where the sand-prone horizon locally varies in thickness. Figures 4.19. and 4.20. are Time Map and Reflection Intensity attribute plot respectively. The latter indicates that the 3D data is resolving some significant localised anomalies at these depths, with one occurring to the northwest of the proposed Relief Well Location. These individual areas would carry higher risk of gas presence. As mentioned above, residual statics applied to the ES9401 data render the time map less reliable, for example, the apparent NE/SW trending ridge to the south of location is probably statics effect beneath shallower infilled channel. With depth, reflectors become more laterally discontinuous and it is believed that the Tertiary succession becomes more clay/shale rich down through the sequence. All depths on the core log are drillers depths. 2.2 Lithostratigraphy of the Palaeogene interval The Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession of the Viking Graben (Rogaland Group; lsaksen and Tonstad, 1989) comprises sandstones, mudrocks and tuffaceous deposits of highly variable thickness. In the central parts of the Viking Graben, the Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession reaches thicknesses in excess of about 1000m, whereas much thinner successions are found, for example on the Utsira High, where minimum succession thicknesses of about 100m are seen. Chalk deposits, of both autochtonous and allochtonous origin, of the Cretaceous-Danian Shetland Group, underlie the Palaeogene clastic succession. Two lithostratigraphic nomenclatures exists for the studied succession (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992). In recent studies it has been found to be most practical to use combination of the two nomenclatures, although with the main emphasis on the one by Isaksen and Tonstad (1989). lsaksen and Tonstad's subdivision of the Paleocene-Eocene into the Rogaland and Hordaland Groups is maintained, rather than the three-fold subdivision of Mudge and Copestake (1992). The Hordaland Group is not subdivided into formations, whereas the Rogaland Group consists of the Vale-, Lista-, Sele- and Balder Formations. number of other formation names were introduced by lsaksen and Tonstad in order to distinguish sandstone-rich intervals in the Palaeogene. However, as pointed out in Mudge and Copestake (1992), these refer to locally occurring sandstones, and should therefore not be given formation status. Major sandstones within the formations are seen as members, as will be discussed in the forthcoming paragraphs. The regional lithostratigraphic compilations (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992) provide set of criteria to distinguish between the four main formations. The Vale Formation is usually described as light grey calcareous R251122. SAM !MAC \RESBESK

Rock Characterisation 3.3 Characteristics of the Reservoir: Summary & Discussion The following summary and discussion is based on the combined analysis of 6305/8-1, 6305/7-1 and 6305/5-1. The strength and stiffness distribution within the reservoir is governed by the lithology and facies sequences. detailed sedimentological and lithological description is given in /ref. 5, 20 & 21/ and is summarised below together with the rock mechanic properties. 3.3.1 Reservoir lithology The reservoir sequence is represented by the Jorsalfare Formation of Maastrichtian age and the informal Egga member of the Lower Paleocene Vale Formation. The Jorsalfare Formation is characterised by interbedded sandstone and mudstone facies. The sandstones are generally medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses cemented either by quartz or occasionally abundant calcite. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from to 200 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show few internal structures other than occasional parallel lamination or bioturbation near their tops. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 30%. The Egga member of the Vale Formation is dominated by sandstone but both the top and base of the sequence have significant proportion of interbedded mudstone. The sandstone units in the lower and upper part of the sequence are generally fine to medium grained (occ. coarse), fining upward, moderately to occasionally poorly sorted subarkoses to sublitharenites which are slightly to moderately cemented with quartz (2 to 8% by volume) and occasionally abundantly cemented with carbonate. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from 10 to 350 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show some primary structuring such as horizontal or cross laminations. More massive sandstones (little or no interbedded mudstone) occur in or near the middle of the sequence and are characterised by relatively featureless, fine to medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses which are poorly to slightly cemented with quartz (& occ. calcite). The beds have sharp bases and range between 50 to 700 cm in thickness. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. so-called 'pinstriped' mudstone which contains mm-thick layers of siltstone occurs near the base of the Egga member and varies in thickness across the Ormen Lange field. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 35%. 3.3.2 Strength & Stiffness of the Reservoir formation The rock strength and stiffness varies with porosity, grain size distribution, volume of cement and silt/clay/shale content and the variation in strength clearly reflects the interbedded nature of the sandstone and mudstone units (including the erosive bases to the sandstone units) and their distribution within the Egga Member and Jorsalfare Formation (figures - 3.3). Within the thicker sandstone units, slight increases in strength and/or stiffiless (note: corresponding decrease in Poisson's ratio) from the base to the top of the unit can be associated with fming upward effects and/or the influence of bioturbation. Porosity is logically associated with strength and stiffness and the weakest most compressible layers are generally observed to have the highest porosity. 2.3 Summary of the well All depths in this programme are with reference to RKB (23,5 m) unless otherwise stated. Well 6305/1-1 will be drilled with the semi-submersible drilling vessel Transocean Leader. 6305/1-1 is vertical well with an estimated TD of 4500 m. Well TD criteria is 4500 meter or drilling into rocks of Cenomanian age. The objectives of the well are to: O Test the reservoir potential within the Paleocene/Eocene and Cretaceous sequences: - Vale (Egga Mbr.) as primary target - Balder as secondary target - Lysing and Lange as third targets O Test the hydrocarbon potential and the type of hydrocarbons O Secure an optimal seismic tie to the subsurface and to understand the seismic response to the rock properties and fluid fill O Have the well approved as commitment well Drilling Strategy The basic drilling strategy for this well is to have the required safety margins in all operations. And - at the same time have the flexibility to handle the underlying uncertainties (geology, pore pressure and formation integrity). To achieve this, mud density and ECD must be controlled and maintained higher than the pore pressure, but lower than the formation fracture gradient. The mud density during drilling shall be based solely on evaluated pore pressure and not the pore pressure prognosed in this programme. Fracture gradient data will be obtained through leak-off tests (LOT). ECD will be measured by Pressure-While-Drilling sub (PWD) with real-time surface read-out. Surge & swab guidelines for tripping will be established using software for hydraulic calculations. Well design The well is deep water well with 839 water depth. Temperature at seabed is -1°C. Potential high bending loads requires an extra heavy conductor string. Pore Pressure Due to lack of relevant correlation wells the uncertainty in the pore pressure prognosis is higher than normal. Pore pressure evaluation will be highly focused during drilling. In addition to the pore pressure evaluation performed by the mudlogging company, an independent evaluation will be performed by Hydro-assigned pore pressure specialists.

than on the 3D seismic data. However the complete coverage of the 3D seismic data in map view allows the shapes of the amplitude anomalies to be imaged. The Plio-Quaternary Unconformity is seen on seismic data as reflector of laterally variable amplitude. This is to be expected, as the unconformity brings different lithologies in contact with each other and the tuning effects on seismic amplitudes will vary from place to place. In addition, there are some anomalous areas which show indications of gas in the sediments. These indications are: reverse phase top reflector, normal phase basal reflector, highest amplitudes in subtle structural highs, phase reversed lateral truncation, localised edge diffractions, acoustic masking and velocity pull-down of deeper reflectors. The proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are both on the edge of an amplitude anomaly at the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity which is likely to be due to gas in the sediments. linear feature, which may be buried iceberg ploughmark with sandy infill, links the western and eastern parts of the anomaly. The thickness of the possible gas bearing interval is estimated to be less than 21 at the proposed 7122/7-2 location and less than 16 at the relief well location. There is no lithology or velocity data from the previous well 7122/7-1 at such shallow level, but realistic velocities would place the top of the possible gas bearing zone at somewhere between 55 and 75 below seabed (432 and 452 MSL). At such shallow level, any gas bearing sandy layer is likely to be normally pressured. The gas may not be moveable. The seismic data do not indicate the gas saturation and moderate to high seismic amplitudes can be produced by only or 10% gas saturation. None the less, due caution should be taken while drilling through the Plio-Quaternary Unconformity. Reference is made to the Askeladden West well 7120/7-1 which had gas bearing sand interval in the Quaternary, from 375 to 392 m. The Base Tertiary Unconformity is of variable seismic amplitude within the site survey area. These lateral changes are interpreted as mostly due to lithological variations and seismic tuning effects. The amplitudes at the proposed 7122/7-2 well location and the relief well location are not anomalously high and the chance of shallow gas at the Base Tertiary Unconformity is assessed as low. The interval in question is less than 10 thick. pilot hole will be drilled through this level and appropriate shallow gas procedures will be followed. Conclusions At the proposed location of well 7122/7-2 there may be boulders in the glacial sediments down to maximum of 100 below seabed. In the lower half of the same interval there may be gas in sandy layer up to 21 thick. The gas is likely to be normally pressured and the saturation may be low. The chance of gas at the Plio- Quaternary Unconformity level is assessed as high. Between 580 and 600 MSL there may be thin layer of gas bearing sand at the Base Tertiary Unconformity. Fluid Inclusion Technologies (FIT), Inc., is laboratory-based petroleum service or- ganization established in 1997 and offering variety of analytical services including some previously proprietary technologies. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. The procedure has major impact in the areas of both Petroleum Production and Exploration Applications providing informa- tion unattainable via more traditional methods and, has been instrumental in the discovery of significant petroleum reserves, influenced exploration and acreage acquisition decisions and provided innovative options for resource estimation, petroleum production and enhanced oil recovery operations. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphic Analysis, often in combination with other patented techniques, emerging geochemical methodologies and standard microscopic methods, all available through Fluid Inclusion Technologies, Inc., provides unique and un- equaled industry product boasting an impressive list of proven applications including deter- mination of Product Type, Hydrocarbon Migration, Seals and Seal Integrity, Fluid Contacts, Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum, Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimi- tation, Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization and Fluid Pressure Compartments. Further information regarding the application of FIS Analysis and the other technical ser- vices we provide to problems in petroleum exploration and production is available elsewhere in this report and on our website:www.fittulsa.com. 1.1 General Logistics of Initiating an FIS Analysis To Initiate an FIS Analysis: contact FIT' directly to discuss goals of the study, sample requirements, turnaround time, pricing, and other related aspects. New clients are particularly encouraged to consult with our staff during the early stages of project development to optimize sample selection, preparation and shipment. Rock materials for FIS Analysis are shipped directly to C&M Storage2, our sample handling facility, for sample preparation including any necessary crushing/sieving, subsampling and washing. The turnaround time for typical FIS Analysis is preliminary data in 1-2 weeks time following receipt of samples by C&M and final report 1-2 weeks following preliminary analysis. These times are approximate and depend on the amount of sample preparation required, job size and analytical backlog. At the time of issue of this report, the cost for obtaining an FIS Analysis was $5,500 U.S. for full-well analysis (up to 575 samples) and $3,000 U.S. for short-well analysis (up to 180 samples). The cost includes the automated mass spectrometric analysis, preparation of and fluid inclusion petrography on selected thin-sections sampled throughout the well, and interpretation in the form of annotated depth plots (see Figure 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest samples analysed are sands of the DuniIn Group, Cook Formation of Late Pliensbachian?-?Early Toarcian and Early Toarclan age, which were deposited in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment with the accumulation of Drake Formation claystones during Early Toarcian, Late Toarcian and Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times. A regional regressive event during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group, Broom?-Ness formations. Deposition of the Brent Group continued through Late Bajocian, Late Bajocian?-?Early Bathonian and Early-Middle Bathonian times with the deposition of the Ness and Ness?-Tarbert formations. During Early-Middle Bathonian times sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. stratigraphic break occurs at the top of the Early-Middle Bathonian interval. Heather Formation deposition continued during early Callovian through to Middle Oxfordian times in marine, inner shelf setting. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Late Oxfordian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in an inner shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. An unconformity exists within the Draupne Formation resulting from the absence of early Kimmeridglan to Early Volgian aged sediments. Accumulation of Draupne Formation sediments resumed during Middle-latest Middle Volgian times in marine, mid to outer shelf setting with dysaerobic to anaerobic bottom conditions. Deposition continued in similar environment throughout Early-Late Ryazanian times. Deposition continued, without apparent unconformity, with Cromer Knoll Group sediments of latest Late Ryazanian age. Deposition occurred in marine, inner to mid shelf environment and continued thorough Late Valanginian-Early Hauterivian times. Following period of erosion or non deposition during Late Hauterivian to Late Aptlan times, deposition of Cromer Knoll Group sediments resumed briefly during Early Albian times in marine, mid shelf setting. further unconformity at the top of Cromer Knoll Group sediments indicates period of erosion or non deposition during Middle and Late Albian times. Deposition resumed with transgression at the beginning of Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Early Cenomanian through to Late Maastrichtlan age. A period of erosion and/or non deposition during Early Palaeocene times possibly resulted in the absence of Rogaland Group, Vale Formation sediments. Deposition resumed with calcareous and non calcareous claystone of the Rogaland Group, Lista Formation which accumulated in marine, outer shelf to upper bathyal environment during Early to Late Palaeocene times. The stratigraphic succession observed in 34/11-2S is complicated by repeated faulting of Brent Group and Viking Group, Heather Formation sediments. Details of these fault repeats are discussed in the biostratigraphy and lithostratigraphy chapters of this report. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine to coarse grained sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marine, inner shelf environment during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian times. Following marine transgression during Sinemurian?-Early Pliensbachian to Late Pliensbachian times, deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen and Burton Formation occurred in marine, inner shelf conditions. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachian and Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of beginning of Aalenian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Broom Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Aalenian?- Early Bajocian times continued deposition of the Rannoch Formation was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during Aalenian?-Early Bajocian, Bajocian and Bajocian-?Bathonian and Early Bathonian times. The Early Bathonian, Middle? Bathonian and Late? Bathonian sediments of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu stricto accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition of claystones continued through to early Callovian times in similar environmental setting. Deposition was interrupted, possibly because of regional regressive phase, resulting in the absence of middle and late Callovian aged sediments. Heather Formation deposition continued during Early Oxfordian times and was followed by period of erosion or non deposition. Following renewed subsidence, the Late Jurassic transgressive phase resumed during Kimmeridgian?-?Ryazanian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of calcareous claystones of Early? Albian age and are succeeded, following short period of erosion or non deposition, by Late Albian sediments. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. High sedimentation and subsidence rates throughout the Late Cretaceous resulted in the accumulation of complete Shetland Group sequence of Cenomanian age through to Late Maastrichtian age. A period of erosion and/or non deposition during Early Palaeocene times resulted in the absence of Montrose Group, Vale Formation sediments. 1 INTRODUCTION This report is part of the research and development project “Mechanical effects of depletion of the Kristin field” carried out for Statoil. The main objective of the project is to study geomechanical issues related to the development of the Kristin field. The work consists of the following four specific topics: I. Behaviour of intact rock and faults A) Review on fault characterisation and properties B) Description and classification of core material, with focus on faults and fracture types C) Laboratory testing on reservoir and fault rock material D) Interpretation of existing laboratory tests, preliminary geomechanical analyses, and development of constitutive models for intact rock and faults II. Characterisation of shallow seismic horizons with focus on gas leakage, sand distribution and faults. III. Effects of stress changes due to production on fault properties in the reservoir and overburden. IV. Investigation of rock deformations and failure during production by geomechanical analysis. question: How do helium-injection (Boyle's-law) porosimetry and mercury-immersion/buoyancy measurements differ in estimating grain volume versus bulk volume?
answer_text: Helium-injection (Boyle's-law) porosimetry measures grain volume. Mercury-immersion with the weigh/buoyancy technique determines bulk volume.

In practical terms, this implies that an inclined well drilled at 90° to the maximum horizontal stress direction would be more stable than well of similar inclination drilled parallel to that stress direction. Well AO7B will be drilled along an azimuth of 322°N from the top of the Ekofisk Formation and will be quasi parallel to the direction of maximum horizontal stress for length of over 1800m MD. context_snippets.text: Geoservices Saga Petroleum A further drilling break was flowchecked at 4526m but proved negative. From this point there was no further evidence of increasing pore pressure gradient with both the d-exponent and background gas indicating, if anything, decreasing trend. At 4593m another drilling break occurred which was flowchecked at 4596m. The well was found to be flowing and total of 8m' was allowed into the trip tank before the well was shut in. Post kick analysis of the drilling data failed to yield any valid indicators that might have predicted this overpressured zone. The elapsed time from the drill break until the flow check was about four minutes and there were no indications of influx during this period. It was only after the pumps were shut down for the flowcheck that an increase in volume was noted. Following the kick an attempt was made to establish the bottom hole pressure but this failed due to breakdown of the formation. It was later determined that the well was flowing from TD and leaking out to the formation at between 3970 and 3950m. The hole packed off around the string at 3800m and it was necessary to back it off after setting cement plug on bottom. With the string free circulation was established with difficulty and the kick circulated out. Extremely high gas values were recorded while circulating. Gas composition showed large proportion of heavier components and good fluorescence was obtained from fluid samples suggesting that reservoir formation had been encountered. Later in the circulation the returns were seen to consist entirely of slightly brackish water for several minutes. It is therefore possible that the migrating gas bubble reduced the hydrostatic enough to produce water from one of the porous sand formations. Once well control had been re-established it was determined that the hole was in extremely poor condition with large, unstable washed out sections. It was therefore plugged back to below the 13 3/8 casing shoe prior to sidetracking. Following evaluation of the VSP log run in the 5/8 casing at the end of the 121/4 section of 6406/2- 3T2 it was determined that the kick originated in the Aptian sandstone of the Intra Lange formation and not in the Gam formation as had been originally thought.

Figures and are geoseismic sections of the NW-SE oriented seismic line NH9010-102 and the NE-SW oriented seismic line B-17-83. These lines illustrate the geological evolution of block 6507/2. The geological evolution of the area can be subdivided into four tectonic cycles. Each cycle started with major tectonic event which gave rise to structural relief and subsequent sedimentation controlled by tectonic lineaments. At later stage of each cycle, the sedimentation continued under tectonically quiet conditions with relief levelling, before new tectonic event initiated the next cycle. Structural elements mentioned in the text are shown in figure la. Cycle 1: Cambrian - Middle-Permian The collision of two continental plates, the Greenland/North America Plate and the Fennoscandian/Russian Plate initiated the first cycle which gave rise to the Caledonian Orogeny. Compressional episodes, combined with volcanic activity entailed deformation and metamorphism of sedimentary rocks involved in the orogeny. Early Devonian and older rocks are therefore expected to represent economic basement in the area. The Caledonian Mountain Chain is oriented in predominately NNE-SSW direction. 2.1 Classification Samples were classified using point-count results, according to the scheme of Pettijohn (1975). Quartz arenites are the dominant lithologies (Figure 2.1), with the following exceptions: lithic wacke at in the Lysing; subarkoses at m, and in the Lange; and sublitharenites at in the Lysing and and in the Tilje. It should be noted that in Jurassic samples, where feldspar dissolution is advanced, depositional arkosic component may have been diagenetically removed. Textural attributes are derived from grain size point-count data which are presented as histograms in Appendix and are summarised on Table 2.1. The Cretaceous Lysing and Lange Formation mass flow reservoirs are very fine (U) sands to coarse (L) sands, with the Lysing samples being comparatively slightly finer. In these formations sorting is moderate to moderately good and grain shapes vary from angular to rounded. Compaction is weak to moderate, which is less than would be expected under normal burial conditions for sandstones at this depth (2420-2940 below sea floor). Gam Formation sandstones are fine (U) to coarse (L) sands with good to moderately good sorting and subrounded to rounded grains. Compaction is moderate. Are/Tilje Formation sandstones comprise fine (L) to medium (L) sands, are well to moderately well sorted and subangular to subrounded. Compaction is moderately strong. Quartz, which is mostly monocrystalline and unstrained, is the dominant detrital component in Lysing/Lange samples except in the lithic wacke at m. Potassium feldspars are quite common (up to 4.0%) and generally only exhibit minor dissolution. Plagioclase feldspars and occasional microcline characterise lower Lange samples between and (3.7-5.3%). Rock fragments are widespread but generally quite minor (trace-4.3%); these comprise predominantly sedimentary clasts (mudrock, some containing calcispheres and chert fragments) with subordinate metamorphic clasts. Micas include relatively fresh muscovite (0.3-5.3%) and chloritised former biotite. Coaly carbonaceous fragments are locally common as is glauconite. Detrital illite/smectite clays are sparse but widespread, except for the uppermost lithic wacke (2822.54 m) and the subarkoses in the lower Lange (trace-2.7%). As they represent potential provenance indicators for the turbidites, heavy minerals were examined. 2 INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE OF WORK 2.1 GENERAL On the request of Det norske oljeselskap ASA, Fugro Survey AS was contracted to conduct high- resolution seismic site-survey, DA1202, at PL494, NCS Block 2/9, in the North Sea. The vessel MV Fugro Meridian, operated by Fugro Survey Ltd, carried out the survey in November 2012. The final geophysical survey program covered one km large template area (PWL 2/9-5 Alt 1). It consisted of 37 integrated survey lines, including one tie line towards existing well 2/9-3 which is the tie well for this survey. On all integrated lines data were acquired with multibeam echo sounders, dual- frequency side scan sonar (120 kHz and 400 kHz), hull-mounted pinger (sub-bottom profiler), mini air gun and 2DHR digital multichannel seismic system. Additional infill lines were run with sub bottom profiler, side scan sonar and mini sleeve gun only. The geotechnical Survey comprised Cone Penetration Tests at 10 locations at and around the PWL (Figure 2.1). The originally planned well location 2/9-5 was investigated and preliminary summary of the expected geohazards was issued. Because of shallow gas warning for that PWL at depth of 129 below seabed the planned well position was relocated and renamed PWL 2/9-5 B, 214 to the southeast of the original location. The position of the new location is given in Table 2.1. This report provides details of the conditions expected at the planned well location 2/9-5 B. It is based on results of the investigation of multibeam echosounder, sidescan sonar, subbottom profiler, mini sleeve gun and high resolution 2D seismic data, and the draft results of the geotechnical survey. 3D seismic data, delivered by det norske oljeselskap ASA has been investigated as background information, to aid the geohazard analysis of the 2DHR seismic data of this survey. context_snippets.text: The marine Jurassic sequences from the northern North Sea show several major changes in the general characteristics of the palynological constituents, represented essentially by an alternation of two types of preservation. Certain intervals are characterised by the relatively well preserved appearance of their constituents and include the common occurrence of material comparable to palynomacerals and 3, or in some cases structureless (sapropelic) organic matter, but with only infrequent blade- shaped palynomaceral 4. Such intervals are believed to represent relatively enclosed areas where energy conditions at the sea bottom may be relatively low because current activity from tides or open oceanic conditions is limited. Conversely, other intervals subject to higher oxygenation and current activity are characterised by poorly preserved constituents which are frequently darkened or bleached and dominated by high proportions of blade-shaped palynomaceral 4. These intervals can be correlated, using dinocysts, across the northern North Sea and appear to be relatively isochronous, and thus most likely reflect regional changes of depositional setting.

However, care most is taken in assigning one specific environment to this ichnofabric 'blindly' since it may resemble both ichnofabrics 5, 6, and even 7, without carefully analysing the trace fossils, sediment grain-size and what ever appears of the original lamination. This ichnofabric commonly occurs above the Ophiomorpha nodosa ichnofabric (Ichnofabric 7) in what appears to be in the upper part of prograding succession where the high degree of biogenetic reworking suggests reduced or slow accumulation of sediments. Martin and Pollard (1996) do not assign any particular environment to this ichnofabric, however the more clear observations of traces in addition to sediment grain-size and preserved lamination suggests middle lower- to-upper shoreface setting for this ichnofabric. Martin and Pollard (1996) describes the similar ichnofabric from the Kittiwake Field (UKCS) as rare and points out that some of the poorly outlined ellipsoidal burrows may in fact be de- watering structures. It should be noted however that 'classical' definition of lower upper to middle shoreface environments describes low angle lamination to cross- bedding as observed sparsely within the less bioturbated intervals of this ichnofabric. The cored section shows less mudstones upwards and change from very fine grained sandstone to fine grained sandstone upwards. The cored section can be subdivided into four facie associations. Offshore transition mudstone and sandstone. This facies association is seen in the lower meters of the cored section and comprises inter bedded well burrowed mudstones (Lithofacies and very fine grained wave rippled to micro hummocky cross-stratified sandstones (Lithofacies C). The bed thickness is typically to 15 cm. Burrows of chondrites type are recognized. The alternating lithology probably represent alternation of fair weather mud layers and storm sands within an offshore transition zone, e.g. deposition close to the storm weather wave base. Palynofacies characteristics are consistent with this interpretation. Lower shoreface sandstone and minor mudstone. The cored section from 3976,5m to 3967,25m can be subdivided into four minor fining upward sub units. Each unit consists of massive cross stratified fine grained sandstone (Lithofacies and minor C) with an erosive base which passes upward to burrowed, very fine grained sandstone and inter bedded sandstone/mudstone similar to the bedding in the lower meter of the cored section. The massive cross strata, hummocky or swaly, are typical of high energy middle shoreface setting. The interbedded sandstone and mudstone beds suggest more quiet or protected shoreface environment. The four units can also be seen defined as four parasequences within lower order (4th or 6th order) sequences. The gradual increase of mudstone in the two upper units may also indicate that this part of the cored section represents retrograding parasequence sets. The palynofacies characteristics of these parasequences are described below. Middle shoreface sandstone. From 3967,25m to 3954,75m massive cross stratified sandstone is the dominating sedimentary feature. The sandstones are fine grained to very fine grained (Lithofacies and rare and D) with few mudstone partings. The beds vary from few dm in thickness to more than meter. The hummocky/swaley cross stratified beds are commonly amalgamated. Erosive surfaces occur above few thin mudstone beds. Wave ripples and slightly more muddy sandstones occur in the upper 0,5m of the unit. Based on modem shelf studies, amalgamated hummocky, cross stratified, finer grained sandstones are associated with storm dominated shoreface and shelves. Typical water depth have been reported as 15-40 m. In association with the general overall coarsening upward trend of the cored section, middle shoreface environment is suggested. The lean kerogen obtained from these lithologies yield palynofacies types consistent with high energy depositional setting. Reworked shoreline and shoreface sandstone. This facies association is seen in the upper 1,8 meter of the cored section. Thin laminae of medium grained sandstones mark the erosive base of this unit. In contrast to the facies associations below, common plant remains, wood (coaly streaks) and leaves together with massive burrowed fine grained sandstones are seen. The wide range of lithotypes was reflected by highly variable TOC contents, from organic rich mudstones in the Nordmela Formation and upper part of the Fruholmen Formation (TOC content of up to 6.97%wt.), to organic lean grey brown sandstones of the Stoe Formation (TOC content 0.10%wt.). DISCOVERY REPORT WELL 7120/1-2 Suim_p_yar Well 7120/1-2 was spudded on 1st January 1989 as the second and final commitment well in Production Licence 108. The well was planned to test a Lower Cretaceous/Upper Jurassic wedge play immediately to the south of the Loppa High, and drilled to total depth of 2630 in bdf in rocks of Triassic age. The upper of the two seismically-defined wedges was found to comprise silts and shales of Early to Middle Albian age (Wedge In), whilst the lower wedge consisted of two contrasting clastic packages of Valanginian to latest Ryazanian (Wedge IIa) and Early Volgian (Wedge IIb) age respectively. Oil was recovered from RFT's at in (Wedge ha) and in (an isolated sand in the Kimmeridgian Hekkingen Formation). In addition, well-log interpretation revealed low hydrocarbon saturations in sands of the Triassic Fruholmen Formation. Subsequent testing revealed the Fruholmen to be tight and the hydrocarbons to be immovable, but total of 1600 litres light 31°API (0.87 g/cm3 ) oil was recovered from the hydrocarbon-bearing interval in Wedge ha. Evaluation of the test results was hampered by technical problems encountered during the testing. However, RFT pressures together with the petrophysical evaluation suggest single oil column of approximately 90 in in Wedge IIa (Valanginian) with an oil-water contact at about 1970 in bdf. Reservoir parameters in the hydrocarbon-bearing zone are generally poor, with extensive quartz overgrowth and calcite cementation resulting in an average porosity of only 13% and net/gross of 8%. By analogy with the Cod Field it is possible that these linear to lobeate sandstones will show rapid lateral thickness variations, and possible shale-outs. This could lead to complex fluid and contact distributions. Downstructure, local slump sheets are inferred and due to the sediment contortion and mixing during slumping, they are expected to have very poor reservoir characteristics. • Porosity variations are expected to parallel net to gross ratio trends. Superimposed on this pattern however, will be the trend of decreasing porosity with increasing burial depth due to compaction. • Permeability variations are also expected to parallel net to gross ratio and porosity trends. The importance of this is critical to the future viability of the field. Though it is preferable that future wells contact thicker sequences with higher net to gross ratio, the quality of the sand, must also increase. Therefore, higher permeability values than currently calculated must be encountered in order to achieve significantly higher flow rates. The presence of thicker and coarser grained sandstones in such lobeate sandbodies should provide better permeability values provided the depth of burial is not significantly deeper than that of the 1/3-6 well. 6.3 Reservoir Characteristics 6.3.1 Water Saturation Due to the difficulty in obtaining precise Rw value for Well 1/3-6, it is not possible to come to any firm conclusions when comparing Lomond and Cod Field saturations with Well 1/3-6 data. question: How do wellbore instability and fracture gradient differ when drilling quasi-parallel versus perpendicular (90°) to the maximum horizontal stress?
answer_text: Quasi-parallel drilling increases wellbore instability and produces a weaker (lower) fracture gradient, whereas drilling at 90° to the maximum horizontal stress is more stable and yields a stronger (higher) fracture gradient.

SPERRY - SUN PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) Sonic log: Can be used to calculate pore pressures, using Eaton’s formula, and subsequently confirm and/or revise any pore pressure calculations made whilst drilling. 6608/10-D-1 AH/BH

The Tarbert Formation, Unit II, represents lateral continuous, high quality reservoir zone of mainly clean, marine sands. The sands of the Tarbert Formation, Unit I, are also probably lateral continuous, but have some interfingering claystone intervals which may be laterally extensive, thereby creating vertical permeability barriers. The Ness Formation consists of alternating sands and shales, probably with low to moderate sand continuity. This formation is assumed to increase in thickness to the south and die out fairly rapidly northwards. The Etive Formation is assumed to exhibit very good reservoir properties, including high porosities and permeabilities, as well as extensive lateral sandbody continuity. However, this formation may show some thinning both towards south and north from the discovery well. Seismic data in the area does not show any consistent fault- ing that can be carried from line to line, but fault is identified on the higher frequency VSP data. The well is designed to drill through this fault. The fault is located at the end of the trajectory and will provide future data on the impact of drilling and producing near faults. This information will affect future horizontal wells that may be needed in areas with less seismic control and no VSP cover- age. In Valhall, faulting and fracturing is generally considered to provide paths for fluid flow, and so enhance well productivity. If any problems do occur as result of the fault, the location of the fault near the end of the well trajectory means that the problem can be isolated. These costs include: abandon- ing Well A-12(ST-2); drilling an 1/2 inch hole to +/- 10 meters above the Tor; installing 5/8 inch liner; drill- ing 500 meter horizontal section of 3/4 inch hole; logging; casing with inch liner; and completing. Well 2/8A-12A will be Amoco Norway's first horizontal well and as such, there are uncertainties in estimating opera- tional times. For that reason 10% contingency has been included in the intangible costs of the well. The completion will consist of 1/2 inch production tubing and inch cemented liner through the Tor with three perforated intervals 170 meters apart. propped fracture with resin coated proppant will be conducted in each perfo- rated interval. The finished completion will leave an open inch liner on bottom with no restriction to production. Total completion time is estimated to be 24 days. diagram of the expected completion is included as Attachment 5. LONG TERM STRATEGY The strategy behind drilling Well 2/8A-12A as the first horizontal well at Valhall is that it will be drilled in an area of the field with excellent control on the geology and reservoir properties. Well 2/8A-12A will be drilled between two wellbores (2/8A-12(ST-1) and 2/8A-12(ST-2)) which have known pay thickness, dip and petrophysical properties. In addition, vertical seismic profile (VSP) was shot in Well 2/8A-12(ST-1) which provides detailed interpretation of the Tor formation thickness between the two wells.

GEOPHYSICAL MAPPING GENERAL For general discussion on seismic data quality, geophysical setting and acoustic properties of the Valhall Chalk reservoir please refer to; 1990 VALHALL GEOLOGIC AND GEOPHYSICAL RE ANALYSIS AND RESERVE REASSESSMENT Text 2/2. A subsequent map revision based on the 2-D seismic database was released in March 1992. Since then the seismic data base has been upgraded by 3-D seismic dataset covering the field. This dataset is being interpreted and the generation of complete reservoir maps is in process. In order to support planning of South End development special wavelet processing and subsequent band-limited inversion has been applied to sub cube of the 3-D dataset. METHODOLOGY Interpretation of the seismic data and the mapping of those data has been done without preconceived geologic models. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

question: How did the roles and mixing practices of Max-Bridge and Max-shield differ during coring from 2385–2521.4m in well 16/1-11?
answer_text: Max-Bridge was added continuously throughout 2385–2521.4 m at the recommended mixing rate as a bridging/fluid‑loss control; Max‑shield was introduced as a base‑oil borehole sealant bled in via slug pit (not continuously) to reduce losses.

Consequently, the string was pulled to surface and the coring program could commence. Cut cores, each core barrel filled with 27 metres of formation, in the interval from 2385m to 2521.4m. question: Which SOGNEFJORD wells have formation tests (FMTs), and what fluids were recovered in their FMT and DST samples?
answer_text: FMTs were run in wells 31/6-6 and 31/6-A-11; the 31/6-6 FMT samples contained formation water and mudfiltrate, and Sognefjord DST samples (well 35/11-7) recovered oil.

context_snippets.text: 5.2 FMT and test summary 5.2.1 FMT results Prior to setting 5/8 casing, the formation multi tester (FMT) was run in hole to define reservoir pressure and pressure gradients. The pore pressure is equivalent to g/cc at the top reservoir (1561 RKB) decreasing to g/cc at the gas/water contact at approximately 1570 RKB. Below the contact the reservoir is normally pressured with water gradient of The gas column is too thin to establish gas gradient from FMT. The FMT results are illustrated in Fig. 5.2.1. Two single FMT samples were taken, one 3/4 gal. chamber at in RKB and gal. chamber at in RKB. Both contained formation water and mudfiltrate. 5.2.2 Test performance Two tests were performed in this well. In the first test, which was carried out in the Sognefjord formation, a gravel pack was installed in the well. The second test was carried out in the silt zone utilizing standard drill stem test string. When the well was perforated underbalanced, it was backflushed and cleaned up at low rate. Some formation sand was produced during the pre gravel pack test. Two attempts to kill the well from the SSTT was necessary. After the first attempt the well had to be put on production again.

4.2 DRILL STEM TESTS Two drill stem tests were carried out, one in the oil zones of each of the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formations. DST flowed oil and free gas from the Brent Group. DST flowed oil from the Sognefjord Formation. Bottom-hole sampling was carried out in DST and DST 2. Two samples were recovered from the Brent Group in DST 1, and samples were recovered from the Sognefjord formation in DST 2, for direct PVT analysis. Surface sampling was carried out in both DST's to obtain samples for recombination and PVT analysis. 4.2.1 Methodology for Interpretation The DST interpretations were carried out using the SAPHER PC interpretation package. All interpretations used the superposition method. The methodology used was: 1. Create Derivative/Log-Log plot to carry out diagnostics of the test, identify flow regions (early, middle and late time regions) and identify the reservoir and boundary models to be used in the analysis. This plot was used to identify the infinite-acting flow region and plot correct Homer straight line on the Semilog or Superposition plot. 2. Plot infinite-acting straight line on Superposition plot and identify main reservoir characteristics (permeability-thickness, skin). 3. Perform any supplementary plots that may assist in identifying character of late time flow (i.e., square-root of time plot for linear flow). 4. Return to Derivative/Log-Log plot and perform time and pressure match to dimensionless functions. Identify reservoir and boundary models to be used and generate synthetic dimensionless derivative and log-log functions for the model. Compare these with the test data. Iterate until good match is obtained. 5. Use the simulation capability to generate the synthetic pressure function from the final chosen model and the calculated reservoir parameters. Compare the synthetic pressure with the test pressure data to ensure that good match is obtained over the whole test, not just the portion being analyzed.
