Title: Standard Core Description, Well 25/11-22 No. 2 SEDIMENTOLOGY 2.1 Introduction A summary sheet of the core description is given in Enclosure 1. It contains the core log description with relative percentages of mud and sand. Gamma Ray curve with logger's depths is given for comparison and correlation with the graphical core log. At the left side of the summary sheet the stratigraphy is given with groups, formations and ages defined by the core facies, log patterns and biostratigraphic dating. The macro-biological content and degree of bioturbation are given according to internal Norsk Hydro procedure. The burrowing intensity scale runs from to 6, being virtually non-bioturbated, and being completely reworked by bioturbation. bathymetric curve is presented. This is an integrated interpretation based on the core description. On the right-hand side of the summary chart, comments are made on the processes and environments interpreted by the present authors. All depths on the core log are drillers depths. 2.2 Lithostratigraphy of the Palaeogene interval The Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession of the Viking Graben (Rogaland Group; lsaksen and Tonstad, 1989) comprises sandstones, mudrocks and tuffaceous deposits of highly variable thickness. In the central parts of the Viking Graben, the Palaeocene - Early Eocene succession reaches thicknesses in excess of about 1000m, whereas much thinner successions are found, for example on the Utsira High, where minimum succession thicknesses of about 100m are seen. Chalk deposits, of both autochtonous and allochtonous origin, of the Cretaceous-Danian Shetland Group, underlie the Palaeogene clastic succession. Two lithostratigraphic nomenclatures exists for the studied succession (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992). In recent studies it has been found to be most practical to use combination of the two nomenclatures, although with the main emphasis on the one by Isaksen and Tonstad (1989). lsaksen and Tonstad's subdivision of the Paleocene-Eocene into the Rogaland and Hordaland Groups is maintained, rather than the three-fold subdivision of Mudge and Copestake (1992). The Hordaland Group is not subdivided into formations, whereas the Rogaland Group consists of the Vale-, Lista-, Sele- and Balder Formations. number of other formation names were introduced by lsaksen and Tonstad in order to distinguish sandstone-rich intervals in the Palaeogene. However, as pointed out in Mudge and Copestake (1992), these refer to locally occurring sandstones, and should therefore not be given formation status. Major sandstones within the formations are seen as members, as will be discussed in the forthcoming paragraphs. The regional lithostratigraphic compilations (Isaksen and Tonstad, 1989; Mudge and Copestake, 1992) provide set of criteria to distinguish between the four main formations. Rock Characterisation 3.3 Characteristics of the Reservoir: Summary & Discussion The following summary and discussion is based on the combined analysis of 6305/8-1, 6305/7-1 and 6305/5-1. The strength and stiffness distribution within the reservoir is governed by the lithology and facies sequences. detailed sedimentological and lithological description is given in /ref. 5, 20 & 21/ and is summarised below together with the rock mechanic properties. 3.3.1 Reservoir lithology The reservoir sequence is represented by the Jorsalfare Formation of Maastrichtian age and the informal Egga member of the Lower Paleocene Vale Formation. The Jorsalfare Formation is characterised by interbedded sandstone and mudstone facies. The sandstones are generally medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses cemented either by quartz or occasionally abundant calcite. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from to 200 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show few internal structures other than occasional parallel lamination or bioturbation near their tops. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 30%. The Egga member of the Vale Formation is dominated by sandstone but both the top and base of the sequence have significant proportion of interbedded mudstone. The sandstone units in the lower and upper part of the sequence are generally fine to medium grained (occ. coarse), fining upward, moderately to occasionally poorly sorted subarkoses to sublitharenites which are slightly to moderately cemented with quartz (2 to 8% by volume) and occasionally abundantly cemented with carbonate. The sand units are reported to vary in thickness from 10 to 350 cm and have sharp (erosive) bases and show some primary structuring such as horizontal or cross laminations. More massive sandstones (little or no interbedded mudstone) occur in or near the middle of the sequence and are characterised by relatively featureless, fine to medium grained (fining upward), moderately sorted subarkoses which are poorly to slightly cemented with quartz (& occ. calcite). The beds have sharp bases and range between 50 to 700 cm in thickness. The mudstones are characteristically grey to greenish in colour and are variably bioturbated. so-called 'pinstriped' mudstone which contains mm-thick layers of siltstone occurs near the base of the Egga member and varies in thickness across the Ormen Lange field. The porosity reflects the facies variation and ranges from 10 to 35%. 3.3.2 Strength & Stiffness of the Reservoir formation The rock strength and stiffness varies with porosity, grain size distribution, volume of cement and silt/clay/shale content and the variation in strength clearly reflects the interbedded nature of the sandstone and mudstone units (including the erosive bases to the sandstone units) and their distribution within the Egga Member and Jorsalfare Formation (figures - 3.3). Within the thicker sandstone units, slight increases in strength and/or stiffiless (note: corresponding decrease in Poisson's ratio) from the base to the top of the unit can be associated with fming upward effects and/or the influence of bioturbation. Porosity is logically associated with strength and stiffness and the weakest most compressible layers are generally observed to have the highest porosity. And - at the same time have the flexibility to handle the underlying uncertainties (geology, pore pressure and formation integrity). 4.2.5 Continuously varying shift A continuously varying shift may be applied to tie the log times to the check shot times. best-fit curve is used, and its slope in microseconds per foot is applied as a continuously varying function. This correction is not related to lithological boundaries, and tends to smear errors over boundaries. The advantage of this method is that is the best-fit curve is well conditioned, at no point will the correction be greatly in error. It is applicable where the Tl-Tc curve shows series of short trends, which can not be easily interpreted as either linear or differential shifts. 5.0 EDITING OF SONIC AND DENSITY LOGS. Velocity and density logs can be incorrect due to borehole conditions, or acquisition errors, and should be edited before calibration, depth/time conversion and production of synthetic seismograms. READ has the following tools available: - Interactive log editing software - Plots of other logs, e.g. caliper, gamma ray, resistivity - Generation of synthetic velocity and density logs from other well logs - Generation of synthetic velocity logs from check shot first arrival times This processing stage is usually done in close cooperation with the client.

‘Minimum phase’ interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is recorded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse (ca. 25 kHz.), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal-to- noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no dispersion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough- to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrating the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismogram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

time over the logged interval can be obtained. This is not usually adequate, however, for detailed studies and the log requires calibration. The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmitted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognized, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attributed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the borehole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Checkshot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time with the check shot time at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate, the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. The different types of shifts are discussed in more detail in chapter 4.2.

The pressure log commences with the establishment of returns at the 30 casing shoe. These sediments may be assumed to be in full communication with the seabed, therefore showing normal pore pressure gradient of 1.03/1.04 SG equivalent mud weight (EMW). DXc trends over this section tend to be unreliable, since as measure of drillability of the formation, values are misleadingly low. In such unconsolidated sequences, drill rate is very strongly affected by the 'jetting' action of the bit nozzles. Hence DXc shows decreasingly negative anomaly until the formation is sufficiently lithified so as to be unaffected by bit washing. Gas levels are high, and relatively constant at 50 to 100 units, with occasional peaks from the minor sand horizons. These gas levels represent the immature, shallow gas zones commonly present in such sediments. Mud temperature readings show normal trends i.e. steadily increasing with depth although there is temporary but inconclusive increase in delta from 600 to 670 metres. Electric log plots of deep resistivity and sonic time show normal trends, although the resistivity plot displays negative trend from 600 to 800 metres. This is assumed to reflect the increasing sand content of the formation. In summary, the recent Pliocene sediments are interpreted as having constant 'normal' pore pressure gradient of 1.03/1.04 SG EMW. Miocene ( metres) This section comprises clays and claystones with major sand sequence, the Utsira formation, from 847 to 1062 metres. The pressure log for this sequence is characterised by major cutback in DXc, with corresponding increase in background gas. Both these changes are result of the Utsira sand member, and are not attributed to an increase in pore pressure gradient. Mud temperature plots show the normal trend established over long bit runs, as previously discussed. Sonic delta also displays normal trend, that is, a steady decrease with depth. Resistivity shows similar trend, although shifted negatively (but with the same gradient) across the sand sequence. Pore pressure gradient through the Miocene is assumed to be normal at 1.03/1.04 SG EMW.

question: Which fossils, rock‑fragment types, and accessory minerals differentiate claystone intervals from sand intervals?
answer_text: Claystones: common fossil fragments with sedimentary rock fragments and traces of micromica, carbonaceous material and glauconite. Sands: fossil fragments in quartz-rich grains with sedimentary and metamorphic rock fragments (including chert) and accessory biotite, pyrite, garnet, amphibole, phlogopite, feldspar and heavy minerals (zircon, rutile, anatase, apatite).

Figures and are geoseismic sections of the NW-SE oriented seismic line NH9010-102 and the NE-SW oriented seismic line B-17-83. These lines illustrate the geological evolution of block 6507/2. The geological evolution of the area can be subdivided into four tectonic cycles. Each cycle started with major tectonic event which gave rise to structural relief and subsequent sedimentation controlled by tectonic lineaments. At later stage of each cycle, the sedimentation continued under tectonically quiet conditions with relief levelling, before new tectonic event initiated the next cycle. Structural elements mentioned in the text are shown in figure la. Cycle 1: Cambrian - Middle-Permian The collision of two continental plates, the Greenland/North America Plate and the Fennoscandian/Russian Plate initiated the first cycle which gave rise to the Caledonian Orogeny. Compressional episodes, combined with volcanic activity entailed deformation and metamorphism of sedimentary rocks involved in the orogeny. Early Devonian and older rocks are therefore expected to represent economic basement in the area. The Caledonian Mountain Chain is oriented in predominately NNE-SSW direction. 2.1 Classification Samples were classified using point-count results, according to the scheme of Pettijohn (1975). Quartz arenites are the dominant lithologies (Figure 2.1), with the following exceptions: lithic wacke at in the Lysing; subarkoses at m, and in the Lange; and sublitharenites at in the Lysing and and in the Tilje. It should be noted that in Jurassic samples, where feldspar dissolution is advanced, depositional arkosic component may have been diagenetically removed. Textural attributes are derived from grain size point-count data which are presented as histograms in Appendix and are summarised on Table 2.1. The Cretaceous Lysing and Lange Formation mass flow reservoirs are very fine (U) sands to coarse (L) sands, with the Lysing samples being comparatively slightly finer. In these formations sorting is moderate to moderately good and grain shapes vary from angular to rounded. Compaction is weak to moderate, which is less than would be expected under normal burial conditions for sandstones at this depth (2420-2940 below sea floor). Gam Formation sandstones are fine (U) to coarse (L) sands with good to moderately good sorting and subrounded to rounded grains. Compaction is moderate. Are/Tilje Formation sandstones comprise fine (L) to medium (L) sands, are well to moderately well sorted and subangular to subrounded. Compaction is moderately strong. Quartz, which is mostly monocrystalline and unstrained, is the dominant detrital component in Lysing/Lange samples except in the lithic wacke at m. Potassium feldspars are quite common (up to 4.0%) and generally only exhibit minor dissolution. Plagioclase feldspars and occasional microcline characterise lower Lange samples between and (3.7-5.3%). Rock fragments are widespread but generally quite minor (trace-4.3%); these comprise predominantly sedimentary clasts (mudrock, some containing calcispheres and chert fragments) with subordinate metamorphic clasts. Micas include relatively fresh muscovite (0.3-5.3%) and chloritised former biotite. Coaly carbonaceous fragments are locally common as is glauconite. Detrital illite/smectite clays are sparse but widespread, except for the uppermost lithic wacke (2822.54 m) and the subarkoses in the lower Lange (trace-2.7%). As they represent potential provenance indicators for the turbidites, heavy minerals were examined. ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. The latter application suggests an operational and interpretational advantage in performing combined heat flow/surface geochemical surveys in the Barents Sea and elsewhere. context_snippets.text: Structural core description - Well 15/9-19SR 33 At MD RKB in the Triassic, fracture with oil patches was encountered in an otherwise dry Skagerrak Formation. This is probably fracture of dilatational nature, possibly late fracture. The same phenomenon has been seen in the Pismo Formation of California, where fractures are observed in_the field as both barriers and (more rarely) conduits. Brace (1978) showed that pore-volume increase, or dilitancy, accompanies failure of intact rock in the laboratory. Antonelli et al. (1993) found that dilatation is found in an early stage of deformation band development. (Furthermore, it should be noted that en echelon open induced fractures were encountered in thin section at MD RKB.) a2. Decreased porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis The thin section from MD RKB (Skagerrak Fm.) exhibits compaction in the fracture, but no grain crushing. At mesoscopic scale, the fracture is filled with grey material, and is probably syn-sedimentary. It is surrounded by some rotated bedding and clay clasts and may well be associated with slumping at low mean stress levels. a3. Unchanged porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis Such band was found at MD RKB (Triassic). This type seems to be easier to recognize at core scale that in the thin-section. b. Deformation bands with cataclasis In most thin sections the deformed zone has decreased porosity relative to the host rock. This is mainly due to tighter packing, grain size reduction (Figure 1, Appendix B) and possible pore-filling illite (Figures B5/B6, Appendix B). This type is represented in most of the thin sections. Porosity is decreased typically by one order of magnituded, from (roughly speaking) 20 % to 0-2 %. 6.3 Comparison of meso and micro scale observations The number of thin sections (15) is bit too small to make complete analysis of micro/meso scale relationships. question: Rank and classify Dxc, MLNDR, and gas as pore-pressure indicators, stating their relative reliability.
answer_text: Ranking (most→least): MLNDR > Modified Dc Exponent (Dxc) > gas levels. MLNDR is quantitative and reliable in shales; Dxc is moderately reliable only in claystones (unreliable in heterogeneous/reservoir sections); gas is qualitative except connection gas, which indicates pore pressure within 35 bar of hydrostatic.

context_snippets.text: PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

question: What are the purposes and typical corrections applied when using trough-to-trough first-arrival picking versus check-shot calibration?
answer_text: Trough‑to‑trough picking is used to pick first‑arrival times for aligning geophone traces and apply system‑delay compensation (here ~18 ±1 ms); check‑shot calibration ties log time to absolute depth and corrects sonic drift/velocity errors using linear or differential shifts so integrated sonic times match check‑shot interval times.

Appendix: Sonic Log Calibration The types of problem which occur with the sonic logs are most commonly either cycle skips, when one receiver fails to detect the true first arrival of the ultrasonic signal, or washouts, where the first arrival has been transmit- ted through the fluid column and not the formation. These types of errors can often be recognised, but cycle skip, in particular, is not obvious if the log has been filtered or is playback. Editing of known errors can remove some of these problems but not all. In the case of washouts, for example, the true formation velocity may not be known accurately. Another problem for the geophysicist is that the velocities measured by the sonic log are often different from seismic velocities, which are obtained by a study of acoustic waves of much greater wavelength. This can be attribut- ed to either the different ways of timing the sonic log waveforms and the seismic check shot arrivals, or to genuine velocity dispersion between the different frequencies. In addition, de-stressing or fluid invasion of the bore- hole wall caused by drilling may alter its acoustic properties. Lastly the sonic log rarely is made up to surface, and thus the velocity in this upper zone is unknown. The absolute travel time to particular depth is therefore not certain. 4.0 CHECK SHOT CALIBRATION Most of these problems can be removed by checkshot calibration. Check- shot calibration is performed in two stages: 1. Tying the log time with the check shot time at specific depth to give an absolute time below datum. This is done using single check shot value. Thus it is fixed that travel time is associated with depth D. 2. Modifying the recorded values so that the integrated travel times from the calibrated log are equal to the interval times from the checkshot levels. Stage is not so simple. It is possible to adjust the log so that all values over given section are changed by few microseconds per foot. This is known as linear shift and is usually applied when the velocities from the sonic log are too high. The assumption made is that the log is in error by constant amount at each reading. An alternative method of modifying log velocities is called differential shift and is usually applied when the log velocities are considered too low. In this case the error is often in low velocity values caused by washouts. To compensate the low velocities are adjusted more than high velocities. Appendix : Sonic Log Calibration- Page of - Mod. mercury immersion technique. Samples with large holes require special attention. Special tests such as com- pressive strength or static moduli require additional plugs (see Special Testing). Velocities are measured using the Pulse Transmission Technique (Schreiber, et al. 1973) with nominal frequencies of 300-500 KHz. Dry velocities are measured first, samples are then saturated with 25,000 ppm NaC1 brine for the saturated velocity measurements. Saturation is performed in separate pressure chamber where samples are main- tained at 1000 psi for 12 hours. Velocities are recorded to effective pressures equivalent to conditions corre- sponding to the depths from which the samples came. Specifically, with normal hydrostatic gradient of psi/ft, sample from depth of 10,000 feet would be subjected to maximum effective stress of 5,000 psi. Since we report on measurements on series of pressures up to this value and give the best fitting quadratic for each data set, you can calculate the velocities at any pressure below the maximum. This of course would be necessary if the reservoir of interest were over pressured. The data presented in the tables which follow has been subjected to number of quality control checks but when data, i.e. the raw information, appears sound but generates inconsistencies we elect to report the data. The inconsistencies are flagged in the tabular reports. An explanation of the data symbols and abbreviations used in the tables is given in Chapter 2. The velocity tables consist of measurements of Vp, Vsi and Vs2 for three possible saturation states; native, wet and dry. Vsi and Vs2 refer to two shear velocities having com- mon propagation direction. The particle motion or polarization used to measure Vsi is orthogonal to that used to measure Vs2. Thus the difference between Vsi and Vs2 at specific pressure reflects the amount of shear wave anisotropy or shear wave birefringence. It is quite common for both the horizontal and diagonal core plugs to display large differences. Velocities are reported in either ft/sec or rn/sec while effective pres- sure control points are reported in psi {14503 psi — 1Kbar — 100 MPa). April 21, 1995

ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. The latter application suggests an operational and interpretational advantage in performing combined heat flow/surface geochemical surveys in the Barents Sea and elsewhere. Corresponding thermal conductivity measurements were performed on gravity-core samples covering similar depth intervals (0 - meters). Technical Memorandum (John Cater and Andrew Taylor, lchron Limited) Introduction Slabbed core from wells 6507/7-3, 6507/7-A17 and 6507/7-A35 was logged at ResLab Laboratories, Stavanger, by John Cater and Andrew Taylor (lchron Limited), on March 25th-27th 2003. For each well, copy of the hand-drawn 1:50 scale core log and written log comments are presented here. Illustrative core photographs are shown on Plates to 5. The sedimentology of the cored intervals is summarised below. Detailed descriptions are contained in the log comments. The depositional environments recorded by the cored intervals are interpreted below. Recommendations for future work to investigate the likely distribution and facies of Late Cretaceous sandstones in the Heidrun area are made at the end of this memorandum. Note that the most recent biostratigraphic data are not available for this memorandum. All depths quoted are core depths. Summary of core descriptions and interpreted depositional environments The cored section comprises mid to late Coniacian siltstones of the Kvitnos Formation overlying 2.51m of medium grained sandstones of the mid-Coniacian Lysing Formation (2367.55m-2370.06m), which in turn overlie fine grained sandstones of the late Aalenian Garn Formation. 2360.00m - 2367.55m This interval is dominated by laminated siltstones displaying local, weak bioturbation by pyritised Chondrites and sand-filled Sabularia (Plate 1A and 1B). The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

This was necessary in order to increase the build rate in Area of the reservoir, and thereby maximise the sands above the OWC. After circulating the hole clean at TD the BHA was pulled without pumping or backreaming to the shoe, where high-vis pill was pumped and the casing circulated clean. The BHA was then pulled to surface, the MWD data dumped and the tool broken down. The rest of the BHA was broken down after waiting for crane for one hour. Due to quick drilling the Western Atlas equipment only arrived onboard as the MWD was being laid down, so there was delay while the FMT tool and spear were made up and tested. The FMT was being rigged up on drillpipe when the decision came from town to run the log on wireline, so the PLC equipment was laid down and the CHT/GR/FMT combination was run on wireline. Minor hang-ups occurred at 2059, 2245, and 2415 mMD; the tool was unable to go beyond 3068 mMD. The top three pressure points were taken before, again, attempting to pass 3068 mMD, but without success. The tool was pulled to surface and rigged down. It was decided not to run in on drillpipe to take the five lower points. A 121/4 hole opening assembly was made up, including bull nose, 81/2 hole opener, followed by 121/4 hole opener 825 behind the bull nose. The well was opened up to 121/4 from 1960 - mMD, working tight spots at 3197 and 3239 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean. short wiper trip was performed back to 3100 mMD without pumping, and then the hole was backreamed from 4 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean again with 121/4 hole opener at 1955 mMD. A 95/8 liner string was run to 3272 mMD. The predominance of Rannoch sands was expected, and with TVT of 57.6m it must have been affected by downfaulting, thickening the better quality sands in the upper part of the Rannoch Formation.

This section coincides with carbonaceous claystones of the Viking Group, which produced significantly higher gas readings in the range - 0.30% CI to nC4. The lower part of the Draupne Formation and the entire Tarbert Formation were cored. Because of reduced returns during coring, absolute gas values were moderately, but qualitative paraffin ratios were significant. Background gas ranged from - 0.23% C1 to nC4 over this interval which represents the upper part of the Tarbert Formation. Mud weight was maintained at rd throughout the 8 1/2 hole section. In this middle to lowermost part of the Tarbert Formation, gas values were generally reduced, apart from peaks associated with coal seams. Background gas ranged from - 0.07% C1 to C3. Most significantly, nC4 values were reduced to zero, although traces were recorded on penetrating coals. Background gas averaged to - 0.08% C1 to C3 through this section, with isolated peaks of up to 1.14% C1 to nC4, corresponding to the penetration of coal seams. Generally much lower gas readings resulted from the Etive / Rannoch Formation and gas values averaged -0.04% C1 to C3.

5 FORMATION EVALUATION 5.1 Logging The logging programme included runs with wireline logs and run with CDR/CDN- tool (LWD), see Figure 4.3. The logs are of good quality and only minor problems occurred during the logging operations. Due to only minor differences between measured depth (MD) and true vertical depth (TVD), deviation corrections have not been applied. The Top Brent Group at 2455,5 mRKB (MD) is 0,1 deeper compared to the TVD, for the Top Dunlin Group the difference is 0,2 m. The logs have been analyzed using computer based model applying complex lithology method. The Brent Group net sand intervals have been defined using porosity cut-off corresponding to ml), which for the Tarbert Formation is 16 %, the Ness and Etive Formations 12 %, and the Rannoch Formation 15 %. shale volume cut-off of 40% has been applied. The main results from the preliminary log analysis are summarized in Table 5.1. For further details and final interpretation, reference is made to the Petrophysical Report. The resistivity logs indicate oil down (ODT) to 2477 mRKB and water up to (WUT) 2483 mRKB. The OWC is located within very fine grained, bioturbated and argillaceous, calcite cemented sandstone, and cannot be exactly defined from the resistivity logs. However, an OWC is from the formation pressure measurements (RFT) estimated within the Tarbert Formation at 2478 mRKB (2460 mSS). 5.2 Conventional Core Analysis A total of 10 cores were cut in the interval 1 mRKB Driller's. Core No.1 contained only marl and shaly claystone belonging to the Cromer Knoll Group and to the Heather Formation. Cores - 10 were cut in the Brent Group and 12 into the Dunlin Group. The total Brent core recovery was 186,05 (95,7%). Conventional core analysis was performed on all cores, except cores nos. 1, and 10 due to very high content of claystone. Horizontal air permeability, helium porosity and grain density were measured every 0,25 meter, while vertical permeability, summation porosity and pore saturation were measured every meter. The results are shown in Table 5.2.

4.2.2 1/2” Drilling Phase 34/10-M-4 AH T2: The section was planned as short correction run with DLS's of approximately 5.5º. With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. In the future there are two main things to be investigated further before drilling similar type of well/section. The first being the necessity of such high mud weight, which clearly initiates sticking, and drag problems. Secondly, if water based mud is to be used, clarify to what extent the graphite additives will affect Schlumberger 13 Drilling & Measurements 34/10-M-4

3.2 Well 34/7-19 The interpretation has been performed interactively by correlation on normalized images generated from conductivity curves of the FMS tool. For the following description, the reader is referred to the Composite Log (Enclosure 2). The Composite Log provides the following tracks; Petrophysical log (GR), depth annotation with formation tops and cores implemented (depthshifts included), dip-azimuth tadpoles, correlation lines superimposed on normalized images, and conductivity raw-curves. The interpretation is further supported by detailed sections where important features are described and examplified, and Schmidt stereograms projected to the upper sphere in order to evaluate the structural orientations throughout the Brent Group. Hole quality has been evaluated from caliper logs to be fair to good for the entire investigated section. The Rannoch Formation, as expressed in this well, mainly consists of parallel laminated, fine to medium grained coarsening upwards sequence. The FMS interpretation generated from correlated surfaces within the Rannoch Formation is shown in Figure 3.2.1. The lower, fine grained (silty) part of the section displays nearly uniform structural trend of laminae. For the interval between 2605.00m and 2640.00m the calculated mean orientation equals 268/4.8 (Fig. 3.2.2). The close clustering of poles seen from the Schmidt plot reflects the parallel nature of the laminae which probably was close to horisontal during deposition, and therfore is considered to represent the present structural rotation for this part of the Brent Group. The upper part of the Rannoch Formation (above 2605.00m) is characterised by larger spread of tadpoles which is partly caused by an increased occurrence of steep dipping laminations. The mean dip of the planar structures between 2595.00m and 2604.50m is calculated to be 286/5.2. From Figure 3.2.3 the spread of poles due to cross-lamination is obvious. In spite of the orientation variations, the mean structural orientation for this interval is close to the interval below 2605.00m. In addition, tadpoles are present which display dips in excess of 30 - 40 degrees (Fig. 3.2.1). With the exception of the surface at ca 2585.00m which is interpreted to represent carbonate cemented lense, these steep dipping surfaces are related to fractures (faults and joints). The two lowermost of these tadpoles at 2604.50m represent the carbonate cemented joints at core depth 2600.80m (Fig. 3.2.4). At approximately 2590.00m another pair of tadpoles which relate to steep dipping surfaces appear. These are correlated to the faults observed in the cores at 2585.30m - 2586.30m (core depth). Based on core observations (thin fault surfaces within the same lithology which do not affect the orientation of the layering within the sequence), this faulting is regarded unimportant with respect to throw. These fault surfaces dip at 72 degrees towards northeast. Structural Dipmeter Interpretation of Wells 34/7-12, 19 and 20

• 3 LOG ANALYSIS 3.1 Log data and quality The 13 3/8 casing was set at mRKB (drillers depth). Both the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group was evaluated during the TD-logging in the 12 1/4 borehole section. HTHP mud with density of g/cc was used in this borehole section. The logs run in well 2/2-5 are shown in figure 3.1. The wireline and pipeconveyed logging service was performed by Schlumberger and the Triple Combo MWD service was performed by Teleco. For further information, see operational report (chapter 5). Log data from the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group are partly from logs run on drillpipe (3352.0- 3629.0 m), partly Triple Combo MWD data (3550.0-4080.0 m). Bad hole conditions made it impossible to run logs on wireline or on drillpipe below approximately 3600 m. Below this depth Teleco resistivity/density/neutron sub was used. After logging with Triple Combo MWD, the well was plugged back to m. In the petrophysical interpretation data from wireline logs have been used in the interval to m. From to Triple Combo MWD data have been used. Both the wireline logs and the MWD logs are highly influenced by washouts which especially is reflected in poor quality density/neutron logs. It is especially the shales which are washed out. From log calculation the shales of the upper Farsund Unit, interval 3426.0-3550.0, have erratic high effective porosities. In these shale-zones the porosity have been set to zero. 3.2 Log analysis method The Farsund Unit, Intra Farsund Sand and the Hegre Group have been analysed using computer model, based on the complex lithology method using the density log for porosity calculations with corrections for hydrocabon and shale effects. Shale volume has been determined from the gamma-ray log and the resistivity data using the R, value. In most sections the gamma-ray log has been used while the R, curve has been used in wash-out sections. In the pipeconveyed section the induction log is used to calculate the true resistivity of the uninvaded formation. The resistivity of the invaded zone is calculated from the microspherical focused log. The resistivity logs are corrected for borehole and invasion effects. In the MWD section the RACM curve (Resistivity Amplitude Ratio Corrected Memory) is used as the true resistivity of the formation while the RPCM curve (Resistivity Phase Difference Corrected Memory) is used as the resistivity of the invaded zone. Formation water resistivity and mud filtrate resistivity are varied with depth using temperature gradient established from Horner plots of temperature data.

The prognosed target location was situated in crestal position some 700 metres to the north west of the Ula platform. The well trajectory was planned to follow the local stratigraphical dip at the base of Unit 1A1, where — meter zone of slightly higher permeability had been identified. The main objective was to drill maximum of 700 metres of horizontal reservoir section, placing 100% of the wellbore in Units 1A1 and 1A2, which are collectively 10 — 15 metres thick in this area. The proposed well trajectory in the reservoir section was to follow relatively straight course along azimuth 325°N, turning gently to an azimuth of 311°N by the planned TD of the well. A risk to the reservoir integrity was to avoid penetrating the base of Unit 1A2, where previously identified thin shale bed was known to act as pressure barrier between the target zone and lower units that had been influenced by the effects of water injection. The commercial objective of the target zone was to deliver oil at stabilised production rate of 4000 BOPD. Gyda - Breakout Analysis, Addis & McLean, 1989, which also applies for the Ula Field). In practical terms, this implies that an inclined well drilled at 90° to the maximum horizontal stress direction would be more stable than well of similar inclination drilled parallel to that stress direction. Well AO7B will be drilled along an azimuth of 322°N from the top of the Ekofisk Formation and will be quasi parallel to the direction of maximum horizontal stress for length of over 1800m MD. context_snippets.text: Palynological Examination of the 2/7-9X Well Summary The study analyzed the palynology of forty-three cutting samples of the 2/7-9X well. The sediments penetrated at the base of the well are interpreted to be Valanginian to Barremian in age. Conclusions The well passes through thick Albian to Neocomian sequence. The caving of Paleogene forms and the recycling of both Upper Jurassic and Permo-Triassic taxa complicate the basic age interpretation. Recommendations The findings of this study agree with the results of the EPS nannofossil data communicated in Report No. 2463A.

The subsidence curve with maturity path based on the present day geothermal gradient of degree F/100' is shown on Fig. 1-2. The Pliocene/Miocene boundary was placed in the section which was drilled without returns in an attempt to follow the sub- sidence pattern established in the Miocene and to avoid unrealistically rapid subsidence in the Pliocene. The Miocene - Pliocene boundary was not defined in the 2/7-9 well, biostratigraphy started below 4,000'. As shown in the subsidence graph, vitrinite reflectance in excess of 1.3% would have been expected in the well at TD. Figure 1-3 shows the actual measured maturity which reaches only - 0.87% for the in-situ vitrinite at TD. To match the observed maturity with paleogradient, thermal modelling was carried out (Fig. 1-4). paleogradient between and 1.5° appears to give the best match. For the burial history shown on Fig. 1-5 geothermal gradient of F/100' was assumed which gives more realistic maturity distribution. The observed phenomenon can be interpreted as follows: The high geothermal gradient observed in the well near TD has been established relatively recently. If the high tem- peratures would have acted on the vitrinite for longer period of time, higher vitrinite reflectance values would have been observed. The reason for this anomaly is unknown. Changes in the local or regional heat flow regime are the likely causes.

1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

I. STRATIGRAPHIC PROGNOSIS The stratigraphic prognosis for the 2/11-9 well is described below and shown in Figure 9. This prognosis is based primarily on wells 2/7-20, 2/7-9, 2/11-8, Kim-1 and Lone-1 Additionally, information from various papers on North Sea geology have been used, including C.E. Deegan and B.J. Scull's standard lithostratigraphic nomenclature for the Central and Northern North Sea, as well as NPD Bulletins No. and 5. This combined information provide good source from which stratigraphic conclusions have been drawn for the 2/11-9 well. QUATERNARY AND TERTIARY; SPUD - 3000m TVD SS The Quaternary and Tertiary sector is subdivided into three groups, which are the: 1) Nordland Group dominated by soft clays and sands which overlies the 2) Hordaland Group consisting mainly of claystones and interbedded carbonates which overlies the 3) Roaaland Group which contains tuffaceous shales and varicolored muds tones. RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group. GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. A value of 1.38sg was obtained for the leak-off after drilling out the 13 3/8” casing and drilling 12 1/4” hole commenced. Drilling was halted at 2730 mBRT when pore pressure was seen to have reached 1.25sg and the bit was pulled into the casing shoe. In an attempt to carry on drilling an open-hole leak-off was performed that confirmed the 1.38sg value obtained earlier. Having insufficient kick tolerance to drill ahead, the decision was made to run 5/8” liner. triple-combo wireline log was run to acquire data over the drilled section. Liner was set and 1.47sg leak-off was obtained. Drilling commenced in 1/2” hole. No reservoir horizons were identified and the well was TD’d at 02:45 hrs on the 20th February at depth of 3650 mBRT. Three wireline logging runs were performed. The 6404/11-1 well was plugged and abandoned as dry hole at 22:00 hrs on the 10th March 2002 and the rig released to Norsk Hydro. RESULTS The shallowest primary target (Early Eocene T50 sandstones) was absent at the well location. Upper Cretaceous (K90 sandstones) were absent and K80 (Nise Formation) sandstones were poorly developed. The well was not extended to penetrate the deeper, K72 (Lysing Formation) secondary target.

2.3 Carbon Isotope Analysis of test/mud gas (Figures 2.1a-d) The carbon isotope analysis was performed on 25 IsoTubes samples selected following the main trend obtained from the headspace gas data. The results can be seen in appendix 1, table 3. The values of carbon isotope for methane vary from -72 ‰PDB to -37 ‰PDB. In other words the values vary from biogenic origin to thermogenic origin down hole. It seems that the interval comprises from 1550 to 2925 (Brygge to Blålange formation) may correspond to genetic trend mainly responding to transition zone from biogenic to thermogenic process. The interesting and more important interval is from 3050m to 3992m (Intra Blånge to Åre formation) where the values reflect more mature thermogenic gas with almost the same signature, suggesting possible same origin. Using the Schoell plot (see figure 2.1b) these gases can be related with sapropelic kerogen type II. 2.4 Deuterium δD on Methane Analysis (Figures 2.2a-b) This analysis was performed on the same 25 IsoTubes samples as the analysis above to be able to correlate them at certain depth. The values vary from -209 ‰ SMOW to -162 ‰ SMOW. Again the results show the same trend obtained from carbon isotope analysis confirming the same origin for the gases found between 3050 to 3992 with most likely sapropelic kerogen type II by using the Whiticar, 1996 diagram (see figure 2.2a-b, and table 3). 2.5 Lithology Description, TOC/Rock-Eval (Figure 2.3a-c and table 4) Lithology Description/TOC. question: How do palynological assemblages, depositional environments, and ages differ between the Sleipner and Hugin formations?
answer_text: Sleipner: virtually non‑marine palynofloras deposited in non‑marine conditions during Early–Mid Callovian. Hugin: restricted marine palynofloras deposited in restricted marine conditions of Mid–Late Callovian.

Stewart (1987) in an important paper on the stratigraphy of S the Early Paleogene of the central North Sea documents series of depositional sequences providing valuable framework that, combined with lithostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data allow detailed stratigraphic analysis of the sedimentary basin. Somewhat similar studies have also been carried out on the Frigg Field (Conort 1986). Stewart (0p.cit.) recognised total of 10 seismically defined sequences based on study of over 300 wells. Each depositional sequence (Stewart p. 559) is regarded as an essentially chronostratigraphic unit that can be correlated on regional scale. The sequence boundaries are frequently associated with characteristic wireline log responses which locally permit recognition of the sequence by well data alone.

1. Introduction This report presents results of palynological analyses of Mid-Late Jurassic and base Cretaceous sediments in well 15/9-F-1B (3160m-3440m). Results are summarised in Figure and detailed in the range and abundance chart (Figure 2). These include all key bioevents, together with chronostratigraphic and biostratigraphic interpretations. Lithostratigraphic boundaries and wireline logs were provided by Statoil. Age interpretations are based on the recognition palynological biozones (Appendices 1-4). Where recovery allows, the Statoil palynological counting procedure (PCP) includes two separate counts; Count includes 100 identifiable palynomorphs, including pollen, spores, microplankton, acritarchs and miscellaneous forms. Count is of 100 marine taxa, miscellaneous microplankton and acritarchs, with further scanning for rare taxa. All sample depths are given in mBRT (drilled). The following abbreviations may be used in this report; LO last occurrence (top, extinction, first downhole occurrence) LFO last frequent occurrence LCO last common occurrence LAO last abundant occurrence LSAO last superabundant occurrence FO first occurrence (base, last downhole occurrence) FFO first frequent occurrence FCO first common occurrence FAO first abundant occurrence FSAO first superabundant occurrence PRES present FREQ frequent CMN common ABNT abundant SA superabundant Main conclusions The interval assigned to the Sleipner Formation does not contain typical Sleipner microfloras. These sediments were deposited under virtually non-marine conditions during Early-Mid Callovian times. They are succeeded by the Hugin Formation, which contains restricted marine microfloras of Mid-Late Callovian age. The palynological evidence indicates that the upper boundary of the Hugin Formation is unconformable, with Mid Oxfordian Heather Sandstone Formation above. The overlying Heather Formation is of Mid to latest Oxfordian age and the upper surface is also truncated by significant unconformity which omit the entire Kimmeridgian and Tithonian Stages. Deposition of the Draupne Formation commenced during Early Berriasian times in an open marine, periodically anoxic environment.. The youngest Draupne Formation preserved in the well is of Early Berriasian age, with any Late Berriasian sediments being eroded at BCU.

context_snippets.text: Well 25/11-G-21 is the second well to be drilled from the predrilling template on Grane Well 25/11-G-21 will be located west of the Grane platform, and the well will produce oil from the Heimdal formation. The horizontal section of the well will be drilled above the OWC, and have horizontal completed length of 620m in the Heimdal formation. The well is located in an area with shallow top Heimdal formation. The gas cap will first be formed in this area, and the gas cap pushes oil down into the water zone. The water production in the well is therefore reduced, and the oil production increases. The well will be extended with 50-100m, in the toe of the well, out of the Heimdal reservoir. The purpose of this extention is to reduce the geological uncertainties, and identify the western extent of the reservoir The 24” and 17 1/2” sections of this well were drilled with conventional steerable motor assemblies, with full set of backup equipment on board. In the 12 1/4” section the PowerDrive®, PD900 rotary assembly was run to land the well as planned. In the 1/2” section PowerDrive Xtra® 675 was run to guide the well path along the reservoir section of the well through use of real time inclination, azimuth and steering setting values at the bit. Two directional drillers were on location the whole time directional services were being run. The Drilling & Measurements IDEAL Well-site Information System (IWIS) provided the surface interface between the acquisition of data obtained from Measurements While Drilling (MWD), or Logging While Drilling (LWD) tools and the real-time outputs needed for Directional Drilling and Logging services. Software versions used were IDEAL version C10. PowerPulse MWD - The PowerPulse MWD tool was used to measure the well-bore direction and inclination (D&I) throughout the well. In addition, the PowerPulse measured downhole tool temperature and incorporated shock sensor for use in monitoring rough drilling conditions. Turbine RPM, which is also transmitted by the tool, was monitored as an aid in the early detection of drill string washouts. All data were transmitted to the surface in real time at 6 bits per seconds, providing full raw-value surveys, continuous inclination, shocks, temperature and turbine RPM measurements. Interpretation Summary 16 pressure measurement stations were evaluated and given quality grading from 1-10 as described in Section 2. Test analysis resulted in: ■ 12 good quality formation pressures (quality=10) These tests built up to stable pressure on both pretests at each station (test lost seal after stable pressure was reached). Example of high permeability effects Anytime the pressure decreases rather than increases during buildup, the derivative curve will take sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (log of negative number -infinity). Typically, such buildup is considered un- interpretable. If this occurs for short period, then the final shut-in pressure may still be good estimate of formation pressure, depending on permeability. When the permeability is high, the total pressure changes seen during the buildup are small. The derivative calculation becomes more sensitive as the magnitude of the pressure changes gets near the resolution of the pressure gauge. The derivative curves may have the above wavy appearance. The true shape of the derivatives are often unclear. Good estimates of extrapolated formation pressure are still possible using simple straight line fit to the time function plots. Permeability estimates will be reasonable if the straight line fits reflect the true flow regime.

GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-22 & B-22 INTRODUCTION Well 25/8-B-22 was an observation well for potential horizontal oil producer. Well 25/8-B-22 was pilot hole for potential horizontal oil producer. Both wells were drilled in the Sindre Structure. The pilot hole was kicked off from B-22 at 4282m MD All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. These involve plotting the pressure as function of the spherical and radial time functions. The slopes of the straight-line sections are used to compute the formation parameters such as the spherical mobility, the radial mobility-thickness product, and extrapolated pressure at infinite shut-in. Drawdown Mobility During the drawdown, most of the fluid movement takes place in small volume immediately surrounding the probe. Thus , steady-state conditions are usually obtained very quickly. Using the spherical flow equation of slightly compressible fluid in homogeneous medium, the drawdown mobility, (k/µ) d, could be expressed as follows; (k/µ)d = ( Cpf / ∆pss ) Where ∆pss = steady-state drawdown pressure drop Cpf = drawdown proportionality factor q = pretest flow rate. The drawdown proportionality factor depends on the packer-probe configuration. The figure shows an example of mobility profile obtained using the sink probe. As this mobility is mainly that of drilling-damaged zone, it may not be representative of the virgin formation. question: How do the GWR and LHR definitions differ in terms of numerator and denominator components used in calculating gas–water ratio versus liquid hydrocarbon ratio?
answer_text: GWR = (C2 + C3 + C4 + C5) / total (×100%); LHR = (C1 + C2) / (C3 + C4 + C5) (often expressed ×100).

In the event these assumptions proved erroneous as an FMT point at 4653m gave pressure gradient of 1.97sg. The mud weight was increased to 2.05sg at 4661m before performing formation integrity test. The formation, however, broke down at only 2.18sg EMW. further mud weight increase was made to 2.07sg before proceeding with the coring program. The calculated ECD with 2.07sg mud at 1000 litres per minute was over 2.16sg which left very small margin for operations. The possibility of setting an intermediate liner was discussed but in the event was not necessary. Coring continued and close watch was kept on trip gas levels as these were the only available indicators of pore pressure with the d-exponent rendered useless by the sandstone formation and coring operation. The following peaks were observed: 1.62% (0.02%) at 4671m, 2.12% (0.30%) at 4699m, 4898m. These no longer showed an increasing trend which was to be expected if the pore pressure gradient was decreasing in line with the fluid gradient in the porous reservoir formation. Connection gas peaks were seen at 4864m and 4873m with values of 0.44% (0.29%) and 0.41% (0.29%) respectively. This time there was little doubt that these were the result of formation ballooning/flushing. Further FMT logs at 4926m confirmed maximum pore pressure gradient of 1.97sg at 4634m, declining to 1.91sg at 4926m. The actual reservoir fluid gradient was 0.044bar/m which should have produced gradient of 1.88sg at this depth, therefore it was apparent that there was not complete communication between all horizons within the reservoir. The d-exponent did not provide any useful information until the Lower Ror formation was entered at 5015m. Similarly, background gas was masked by frequent formation related peaks and provided little in the way of pressure indications in the overlying formations. close watch was kept for pump off and connection peaks since these provided the only useful pressure tool. In the event none were seen until the base of the Tofte formation. Thereafter connection gas peaks were regular feature until the end of the well. Once again these were thought to be the result of the high overbalance and not increasing pore pressure.

Estimating the pore pressure from the Dxc was fraught with errors due to the scatter of its values. Since the trend was was largely not discernible, compromising start was made in the attempt to set trendline. From the pressure prognosis (derived from offset data) in the Hasselmus well programme, the pressure was assumed to have pressure dropped back to normal in the claystones above the reservoir, and stayed normal until TD. Two clusters of Dxc points for claystones were identified — one starting from c. 1640m to c.1700m in the Shetland Group and the other below the reservoir, from c. 1840m (Top Ror formation) to c. 1870m (Top Tilje formation) where the pressure was normal hydrostatic, as per the prognosis. Connecting these two clusters and extending the line provided the only trend. Despite the litter, Dxc points are seen to shift to the left from approximately 1150 m. From calculations, it was found that at 1300m, the pressure was SG, at c. 1350m SG, from c.1470m to 1570m it peaked to SG, at 1600m SG, and at 1625m SG, before returning to normal at 1640m. There is scatter of Dxc points even further to the left, between 1500m to 1570m which would give theoretical values of up to SG, but these have been rejected from being useful or reliable, for there were no indications from the well to suggest pressures higher than those prognosed. As the hole packed off while in the reservoir and the string got stuck there, the meachanism was believed to be differential sticking . The high overbalance/differential pressure was thought to be the cause of this, as the mud weight was SG and the ECD went up to maximum of SG. The pressure profile in the sidetrack followed the same pattern as in the original well. 8-2
