question: How do lithology and depositional characteristics differ between NORDLAND GP and HORDALAND GP in well 1/5-4S?
answer_text: Nordland GP: Recent–Pleistocene thick glacial sands with interbedded clays and Late Miocene–Pliocene very soft, silty claystones with minor sand and limestone stringers; Hordaland GP: Mid Eocene–Mid Miocene firmer, micromicaceous silty claystones grading to siltstone/argillaceous sandstone with rare limestone/dolomite stringers and local ash tuffs.

context_snippets.text: 3 of 16 lithological interpretation and the placing of formation boundaries, supported by the biostratigraphic analyses provided by Microstrat Ltd. A 7/8” pilot-hole, was drilled riserless (returns to seabed), down to 928 and later opened-up to 26” to enable the 20” casing to be run and set at 923m. First returns were from 928m within the Nordland Group Claystones. NORDLAND GROUP (Undifferentiated) Nordland group formation from 93 to 928 was not collected as that section was drilled riserless and all returns were to the seabed. Note: Bed thicknesses are not reported as the well was inclined and the dip of the beds was not known. Interval: to MD BRT (93 – 571 TVD) Age: Recent - Pleistocene Thick glacial deposited sands with interbedded clays characterised this section, as identified from MWD logs. Interval: to MD BRT (571 – TVD) Age: Late Miocene - Pliocene This interval consisted of massive Claystones with minor Sand and Limestone stringers. The claystone was variably medium greenish grey to greenish black, olive grey to olive black, light to medium grey & occasionally medium bluish grey. It was very soft & sticky in the topmost part of the hole, becoming more indurated with depth, although there were localised zones of soft, sticky, hydrophilic clay. It was generally not calcareous, (locally moderately - very calcareous and grading to Marl), was silty, often with matrix supported fine quartz sand grains. Traces of very fine mica were present along with very fine glauconite grains, finely crystalline to disseminated pyrite, common very fine dark brown laths of organic material, fragments of bivalve shells and microfossils (foraminifera). There was evidence of bioturbation in the form of pyritised burrow infills.

4 of 16 The Limestone stringers were soft to firm, very pale orange brown, pale orange or off-white to pale orange grey cryptocrystalline to microcrystalline lime mudstones with porcelainous or pasty texture. They were often slightly argillaceous and rarely dolomitic towards the base of the interval. Dolomite stringers were moderate yellowish brown colour microcrystalline lime mudstones, were very hard, brittle and slightly argillaceous. Rare Sand flasers comprised loose, clear to translucent, colourless to pale yellow & pale pink quartz and sparse moderate orange-pink K-feldspars. These were very fine to fine grained, subangular & subspherical in shape. HORDALAND GROUP (undifferentiated). Interval: - MD BRT (1699.7 – TVD) Age: Mid Eocene - Mid Miocene This was massive Claystone with minor Limestone and rare Dolomite stringers. The Claystones were series of interbedded brownish grey to locally brownish black, olive grey to greenish grey, light to medium grey, light bluish grey. The formations were firm to moderately hard producing subfissile, blocky (locally splintery or platey), bit cuttings that were commonly silty and graded to Siltstone. They were often micromicaceous, generally non to slightly calcareous (locally moderately calcareous), locally had waxy texture and contained traces of very finely crystalline to disseminated pyrite. Traces of very fine quartz sand were also present and the claystone locally graded to Argillaceous Sandstone. In the lower section of the Hordaland (from 2840m-2864m) there were traces of reddish brown sediments considered to represent volcanic ashfall tuffs. A silty sandy interval was seen between 2560-2598m and was considered to be of Oligocene age. The rare Argillaceous Sandstone horizons were firm, moderately consolidated and

10 of 16 The Claystone laminations were dark grey to olive black and locally medium to dark green and greenish grey. They were micromicaeous, non to slightly calcareous, locally were moderately to very calcareous and graded Calcareous Claystone. They were firm to moderately hard and produced subblocky drilled cuttings. Zechstein Group Interval: – MD BRT (2584.2 – TVD) Age: Permian This was massive Anhydrite with thin Limestone & Claystone interbeds. The Anhydrite was white in colour, microcrystalline (locally with sucrosic texture) and produced soft to moderately firm, subblocky to friable cuttings. Limestone stringers were very pale orange to off white, occasionally very light grey to white in colour and were firm to moderately hard. They produced sub-blocky to blocky (locally brittle or crumbly) cuttings. They were occasionally argillaceous and only rarely exhibited chalky texture. Thin Claystone stringers were dark grey to olive black and occasionally medium to dark greenish grey in colour, were firm to moderately hard, micromicaeous and were non to slightly calcareous.

15 of 16 Våle Formation limestone at 2981m had slight light brown stain, poor dull bluish white direct fluorescence and slow streaming dull bluish white fluorescent cut, which left faint residue. The chalk of the Tor and Hod Formations displayed trace of bright blue white fluorescence giving slow streaming milky blue white cut. There was no visible oil staining present. 7.5.1 Geochemistry. Geolab Nor was requested to propose an analytical program in order to investigate possible shows occurring in two intervals of K1T1well NOCS 1/5-4S, this well being drilled with organic mud additives (mud XP07) causing strong masking of any free hydrocarbons. The two intervals of interest comprise an upper interval (spls 2480 – 2590 m) representing Oligocene lithologies; and lower interval (spls 2942 – 2954 m) representing the Andrew Fm. Shows were suspected in the Oligocene at 2480 – 2590 by fluorescence, including possible fault-associated hydrocarbons at 2560 m. An FMT in the Andrew Fm. at 2945 was reported to have an oily film. Analyses of cuttings, mud and FMT samples from the Oligocene and Andrew Fm. sections of well NOCS 1/5-4S were performed in order to assess the possibility for the presence of migrated hydrocarbons. The well samples were heavily impregnated with contaminant additives from the XP07 mud system used. All samples were analysed by thermal extraction GC (GHM). This included the FMT samples, which were analysed by injecting the (mainly water) samples onto pre-cleaned sand substrate which was then gently dried sufficiently for analysis. This allowed more direct comparison between all samples. Traces of migrated hydrocarbon staining are considered to occur around 2560 and 2590 in the Oligocene section. These support the report of shows in the 2480 – 2590 section, including hydrocarbons associated with faulting around 2560 m. Traces of hydrocarbons are also considered to occur around 2942 and 2945 in the Andrew Fm., although the FMT from 2945 m was only of water with mud additive components, this also being evident from visual inspection of the FMT samples. Full details of the analysis are available in the Geolab Nor report of well 1/5-4S.

0 GARDLINE SURVEYS 4.4 Shallow Soils Pinger data acquired over the survey area were mostly of good quality (see figs to 4.8). A sweep of 80ms was utilised and provisional interpretation was done using an assumed seismic velocity of 1600m/s Penetration across the site was at times marginal, with an average depth of approximately 8m and maximum of approximately 20m. The pinger records show an uppermost unit that consists of bright horizontal reflectors, possibly indicating clays with sand prone interbeds. This unit is approximately 2m thick and is found site wide. On the western side of the survey area directly below the clay drape, poorly imaged unit with discontinuous and chaotic reflectors can be seen to approximately 5-6m. It is believed that this unit is the upper part of the Forth Formation and, as such, represents the Whitethorn Member. The base of this sequence is unclear and this may be due to limited penetration rather than lithological change. The underlying sequence is not clear although some faint dipping reflectors can be seen - these may be poorly imaged channel deposits. The central and eastern part of the survey area is dominated by sequence of steeply dipping reflectors and channel fill deposits. The pinger records indicate the presence of more than one channel and areas of floodplain between. This unit has been delineated and extends between 4m and 20m below the seabed. The observable extents of the channel features have been plotted on chart 6. However, the base of the unit in the central eastern area appears to be beyond the limit of penetration and coincides with frequent masking and diffractions. It is believed that this unit is the lower part of the Forth Formation and thus represents the Fitzroy Member. The observed masking is not thought to be associated with gas seeps. Diffractions near the seabed from two pipelines running across the northeast part of the survey block were also evident. No hazards or obstructions to drilling activity have been observed within the shallow sedimentary sequence.

question: For Naust Units I–VII near wells 6406/12‑3 and 6406/12‑4, what are the detailed lithologies including grain size, interbeds, and boulders?
answer_text: Units I–II: very soft to soft clay, interbedded with coarser material including loose gravel and with boulders possible. Units III–VII: hard sandy, silty clay (Units III–IV) interbedded with sand and silty claystone and occasional conglomerate up to pebble size, and Units V–VII hard sandy, silty clay with minor sand interbeds and occasional pebble‑size conglomerate.

INTERPRETATION OF FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY (FIS) DATA A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context Fluid inclusions are the only direct records of paleofluids existing in the subsurface, and as such, have the potential to record conditions accompanying geologic processes, including petroleum migration. By studying the subsurface distribution of paleofluid chemistries with FIS, one can obtain valuable and unique information on three major exploration topics: 1. Petroleum migration or paleocharge 2. Seals 3. Proximity to undrilled pay and two major production topics: 1. Pay zone and bypassed pay delimitation 2. Reservoir compartmentalization. The previous discussions have concentrated on identifying spectral types in FIS data. This is necessary first interpretive step. The next task is to evaluate the significance of FIS depth trends in their own right (now knowing their spectral origins), and eventually, in light of other available information to answer specific questions, such as were enumerated above. Petrographic data from anomalous fluid inclusion zones are often critical elements of these higher order interpretations, as will be seen, which why petrographic follow-up work is conducted as routine part of every FIS analysis (see Table of Petrographic Observations). A.3.1 Significance of FIS petroleum indications The most basic question that FIS can address is Is there any evidence for present or past petroleum in this borehole? Documentation of an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly generally pro- vides positive answer to this question, but could indicate other processes as well. Possible explanations for an FIS hydrocarbon anomaly are discussed in the following paragraphs. Migration without trapping A migration pathway may be indicated when FIS responses are low or moderate, when contamination and recycled inclusions can be discounted, when quoted visual petroleum inclu- sion abundances are rare or several (see Table of Petrographic Observations), and when no other petrographic or log evidence of current petroleum charge is identified in the zone. There are number of factors that influence inclusion abundance and, consequently, raw FIS response strength, including geologic setting, extent of diagenesis, rock type and permeability. However, it has been demonstrated that both visual petroleum inclusion abundance and FIS strength within many porous reservoir rocks is proportional to hydrocarbon saturation or pa- leosaturation in relative sense. Because migration occurs at average bulk-volume petroleum saturations below those encountered in charged reservoirs, FIS signal strength and visual in- clusion abundance are generally lower along migration pathways than in charged reservoirs from the same area. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 43 gas) and the relative abundance of these inclusions will influence the bulk spectra. Addi- tionally, total inclusion abundance will affect the spectra insofar as higher molecular weight species represent smaller volumetric proportion of petroleum and are also less volatile, hence decrease below instrumentation detection limits before low molecular weight species. Conse- quently, some samples with low oil inclusion abundance generate wet gas mass spectra, for instance. Optical inclusion abundance and characteristics should be consulted, where pro- vided, to verify the interpreted petroleum type (see Table of Petrographic Observations). With the above limitations in mind, the following petroleum types are identified on the basis of spectral characteristics: Dry gas: mostly C1 with lesser C2-C3 and no higher hydrocarbons. Wet gas: C1-C9 may be present, but C6+ species are in minimal abundance. The alkane slope is extreme. Gas-condensate: C1-C11 may be present. The alkane slope is quite steep, reflecting very gas- enriched phase. Volatile oil: C1-C13 present. Slight gas-range enrichment is observed and the alkane slope is mod- erate to steep. Oil: C1-C13 is present. The alkane slope may be flat to moderate. Biodegradation is suggested if sulfur compounds such as H2S, COS, CS2, S2 (+/- SO2) and/or thiols are present in addition to petroleum species. Ratios of paraffins to naphthenes may be low as well, as bacteria typically prefer to metabolize alkanes compared to other classes of petroleum compounds. Petrographic data may provide further evidence for biodegradation in the form of low-gravity petroleum inclusions. Bacterial activity is generally restricted to maximum burial temperatures below 65-70°C; hence FIS evidence of biodegradation is most commonly observed in rocks that are currently below this temperature. Thermal alteration of liquid petroleum species can produce spectra very similar to those generated from biodegraded hydrocarbons, because the products of two common processes, bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR) and thermochemical sulfate reduction (TSR), are essentially identical. The best distinction is made from current bottom-hole temperature data, which, if above 140°C or so may be indicative of TSR, and if below 70°C or so is more consistent with BSR. Potential interpretive problems arise in the intervening temperature range, when deeply buried sediments are unroofed or when petroleum altered at shallow depths becomes buried to greater depth. Petrographic data may help, as pyrobitumen frequently accompanies TSR, while low-gravity liquid petroleum inclusions often occur in association with bacteri- ally altered oils. Additional temperature or thermal maturity data (including fluid inclusion homogenization temperatures) may also be useful. The presence of significant amounts of sulfur species can indicate sour petroleum phase, where the souring process may in some cases be reflection of the source rock, but could also reflect BSR or TSR. study of TSR sour gas pools in Canada suggests that evaluating the relative proportion of products and reactants can provide measure of sour gas potential. As TSR progresses, long-chain alkanes decrease while low molecular weight petroleum species increase along with CO2, aromatics organic acids and the various sulfur compounds enumer- ated above. Ironically, H2S alone may not be as accurate an indicator of H2S content, as it is scavenged naturally (e.g., to form pyrite in iron-rich rocks) and by the metallic internal surfaces of the analytical system.

Interpretation of Logs From Esso Exploration Norway 25/10-1 In reply to request from Esso Exploration Norway Inc., well logs recorded in the Norway 25/10-1 well have been reexamined for quality and log scaling. Our log interpretation report, dated November 25, 1969, included section on log quality as follows: Log Quality Log quality is fair to poor for the well logs run in the 25/10-1 well. Several discrepancies were observed on the induction electric log which are the result of the logging engineer's ineptitude. The SP curve shale base line was improperly located on Run so that the SP curve went off scale to the left at 4090 ft where the base of thick sand was logged. Apparently the logging engineer noted this, and shifted the SP curve to the right so that the log would appear on the film. comparison of the SP shale base line above and below the sand indicates shift of to 10 millivolts which should have been noted on the log. better technique would have been to relog with proper SP shale base line setting. There is also depth discrepancy of ft between Runs and which adds repeat section of 4 ft from 4500 to 4504 ft on the composite log. The BHC sonic log was very noisy and cycle skipping was especially severe on Run 4. Cycle skipping can be caused by faulty surface or downhole instrumentation, improper operational technique, or possibly by gas in the mud. We suggest that the sonic log be rerun in the event the well is reentered. Excessive borehole rugosity and enlargement prevented the effective use of the microlaterolog and compensated formation density log for forma- tion evaluation. Therefore, data from these logs was not relied upon for calculating resistivity indexes. The possibility that the SP base line shift between 3900 ft and 4090 ft was the result of formation change rather than an SP shift made by the logging engineer has been considered. If the shale beds above and below the thick sand from 3955 ft to 4090 ft have interstital waters which are much different in their chemical composition, then there is possibility that an SP change could occur. There is some evidence to support this possibility since the shale above the sand has an average induction log resietivity of ohm-m, whereas the shale below the sand has an average resistivity of ohm-m. resistivity gradient is present from the base of the sand to about 5400 ft. Also, transit time gradient is noted on the sonic log. These gradients suggest the possibility of an abnormal formation pressure condition in which case the change in shale resistivity could be accounted for by the degree of compaction of the shale beds. rather than by change in the chemical composition of the interstital water.

Purpose of Well: Esso 25/10-3 was located 1) to test the Lower Eocene oil sands encountered in Esso wells 25/10-1, 25/11-1 end 25/8-1 in lower structural position to accurately establish the oil/water contact in the area; 2) to determine the lnteral continuity of the thin Lower Eocene oil sands; and 3) to test the theory that the Lower Eocene sands thicken towards the northwest. III. Results of Well: Esso 25/10-3 drilled to total depth of 6304 feet and bottomed in Paleocene sediments. The 394 feet of Paleocene penetrated was composed primarily of sands with beds of grey green shale between. From top to bottom the Paleocene sands were respectively 98 feet thick, with 35% porosity, 111 feet thick with 35% porosity, and 30 feet thick with 30% porosity. These sands were water-bearing. The 1700 foot thick Eocene section was chiefly grey to grey green clay shales with 22 feet of wet sand in the interval 4595-4635 feet, 13 foot oil-bearing sand from 5741 to 5754 feet, and foot wet sand just above the Eocene-Paleocene contact at 5910 feet. The 13 foot oil sand had 32-36% por- osity and tested 26° API gravity oil on wire line formntion test. The Oligocene to Recent sediments consisted of clays and sands with no indications of hydrocarbons.

-3- INTRODUCTION Norsk Hydro's well 7117/9-2 is the second well drilled on main structure called the Senja Ridge, situated in the north-western parts of the Troms-1 exploration area. The first well, 7117/9-1, was also operated by Norsk Hydro, with IKU as biostratigraphic consultant. The biostratigraphy of well 7117/9-2 is based on the analysis of cuttings, sidewalls and core samples. Fossil material obtained from the first set of sidewall cores does not seem to match the fossil material obtained from cuttings. This is particularly evident across the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary and in the Paleocene/Eocene, though difficult to demonstrate in the thick sequence of Albian deposits. Sidewall cores down to 1695 are therefore considered unreliable. We have documented this in the text and, as sidewall analysis was well underway before discovering the anomaly, we have plotted out the SWC results on the log sheets. Analyses carried out during drilling (hot shots) indicated an unusually thick sequence of Albian and Aptian deposits. Following consultation with the client it was decided that some reduction in the density of analyses should be made. Fairly complete palynological analysis were to be carried out, based primarily on sidewall cover, but with sample density somewhat less than the standard detailed palynology (1 sample/15 m). Micropaleontological analyses should also be reduced though the primary net should be supplemented if results warrented this. In the lower part of the well most samples analysed for micropaleontology were barren. Preservation of palynological material is also extremely poor (below ca 3400 m). In view of the interest expressed in this part of the section we have nevertheless attempted to locate workable samples. These are few and far between, though an assemblage recorded at 4798 gave reliable Barremian or younger age. Moreover, circumstantial evidence for the whole of this section points to more likely Aptian age. G45/c/3/ems

ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. The latter application suggests an operational and interpretational advantage in performing combined heat flow/surface geochemical surveys in the Barents Sea and elsewhere. INTRODUCTION As part of the 1985 IKU Barents Sea heat flow program, reconnaissance shallow-probe heat flow measurements were performed at nine site locations, Saettem et al (1985). Corresponding thermal conductivity measurements were performed on gravity-core samples covering similar depth intervals (0 - meters). The intent of these measurements was to combine the shallow thermal data with the deeper downhole data to assess the feasibility and limitations of future shallow-probe surveys in the Barents Sea as cost effective means of increasing data density. The well was drilled and steered from 1960 mMD to the TD at 3280 mMD in one run, taking hours in total. The hole angle was built up from 27.34° at 1938 mMD, to 60.53° at 2883 mMD, just above the top of the reservoir at 2887.0 mMD, and continued to build up to 68.82° at 3250 mMD. The natural build tendency of the BHA was generally sufficient to keep the wellpath on the planned line and only one short section, 1 mMD, was steered in the reservoir section. This was necessary in order to increase the build rate in Area of the reservoir, and thereby maximise the sands above the OWC. After circulating the hole clean at TD the BHA was pulled without pumping or backreaming to the shoe, where high-vis pill was pumped and the casing circulated clean. The BHA was then pulled to surface, the MWD data dumped and the tool broken down. The rest of the BHA was broken down after waiting for crane for one hour. Due to quick drilling the Western Atlas equipment only arrived onboard as the MWD was being laid down, so there was delay while the FMT tool and spear were made up and tested. The FMT was being rigged up on drillpipe when the decision came from town to run the log on wireline, so the PLC equipment was laid down and the CHT/GR/FMT combination was run on wireline. Minor hang-ups occurred at 2059, 2245, and 2415 mMD; the tool was unable to go beyond 3068 mMD. The top three pressure points were taken before, again, attempting to pass 3068 mMD, but without success. The tool was pulled to surface and rigged down. It was decided not to run in on drillpipe to take the five lower points. A 121/4 hole opening assembly was made up, including bull nose, 81/2 hole opener, followed by 121/4 hole opener 825 behind the bull nose. The well was opened up to 121/4 from 1960 - mMD, working tight spots at 3197 and 3239 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean. short wiper trip was performed back to 3100 mMD without pumping, and then the hole was backreamed from 4 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean again with 121/4 hole opener at 1955 mMD. A 95/8 liner string was run to 3272 mMD. The logs are of good quality and only minor problems occurred during the logging operations. Due to only minor differences between measured depth (MD) and true vertical depth (TVD), deviation corrections have not been applied. The Top Brent Group at 2455,5 mRKB (MD) is 0,1 deeper compared to the TVD, for the Top Dunlin Group the difference is 0,2 m. The logs have been analyzed using computer based model applying complex lithology method. The Brent Group net sand intervals have been defined using porosity cut-off corresponding to ml), which for the Tarbert Formation is 16 %, the Ness and Etive Formations 12 %, and the Rannoch Formation 15 %. shale volume cut-off of 40% has been applied. The main results from the preliminary log analysis are summarized in Table 5.1. For further details and final interpretation, reference is made to the Petrophysical Report. The resistivity logs indicate oil down (ODT) to 2477 mRKB and water up to (WUT) 2483 mRKB. The OWC is located within very fine grained, bioturbated and argillaceous, calcite cemented sandstone, and cannot be exactly defined from the resistivity logs. Core No.1 contained only marl and shaly claystone belonging to the Cromer Knoll Group and to the Heather Formation. Cores - 10 were cut in the Brent Group and 12 into the Dunlin Group. The total Brent core recovery was 186,05 (95,7%). Conventional core analysis was performed on all cores, except cores nos. 1, and 10 due to very high content of claystone. Horizontal air permeability, helium porosity and grain density were measured every 0,25 meter, while vertical permeability, summation porosity and pore saturation were measured every meter. The results are shown in Table 5.2.

4.2.2 1/2” Drilling Phase 34/10-M-4 AH T2: The section was planned as short correction run with DLS's of approximately 5.5º. With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. In the future there are two main things to be investigated further before drilling similar type of well/section. The first being the necessity of such high mud weight, which clearly initiates sticking, and drag problems. This variability was perhaps surprising in view of the fact that applying a simple time delay of about 20 msec to the BP processed section makes it appear very similar to the G.S.I. processed data, apart from exhibiting reduced legginess in character. Data from an earlier survey carried out by Western was also to hand and this exhibited other differences. Here the G.S.I. synthetics fitted best under the compression as black' convention, though from previous experience we believe the convention used by this contractor is also compression as white'. In the new synthetic seismogram construction it was decided to check carefully the basic well data on which the G.S.I. synthetics had been based, and to incorporate the effects of dip unconfornities into the model, in an effort to resolve (a) the true polarities of the recordings, (b) the effect of multiple reflections, if any, and (c) the nature of the differences between the results of G.S.I., Western and BP processing. Using the oil and water density data that you supplied me, have estimated maximum column heights for the two 15/9-A22 samples. The wackestone can support an oil column of 400 ± 100 meters, while the argillaceous siltstones can support columns of 1200 ± 300 meters. Looking at your sketch, it looks like the siltstone is unstained, while the lower Hod Formation wackestones are stained. This implies one of the following: • If the siltsones are continuous over the closure, 1200m oil column (unlikely). • If the siltstones are discontinuous, 400 meter column is still necessary to stain the wackestone. Alternatively, if the staining is along fractures, the interval could have been stained with smaller oil column, and the oil would never have intruded the matrix pores. This seems more likely. Is it possible to examine the core and determine, in detail, where the staining occurs? • If the staining is in coarser-grained carbonates than the ones you sampled in this well, the stained intervals may have been fed by fractures. Depending on the underlying column height in the trap, you will see selective staining in the coarsest intervals. In this scenario, the column height can be bracketed by the entry pressures of the best stained and worst unstained seals. However, this also seems unlikely, since all Hod samples from this well appear to be Type seals. Without looking at any more data, it appears that the stain distribution in the 15/9-A22 makes the most sense if staining occurs only along fractures, or is selective and restricted to coarser-grained intervals than the ones you ssent to EPR for analysis. question: Can m/z/track and petrographic criteria reliably distinguish pore‑filling bitumen causing anomalous FIS with low inclusions?
answer_text: Yes — combined m/z/track anomalies and petrographic evidence of abundant pore‑filling bitumen can be used to infer bitumen‑sourced FIS responses in zones with low visible inclusions, although the interpretation is not always definitive.

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 Current Charge A zone that displays strong FIS hydrocarbon indications and high visual petroleum in- clusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) may reflect penetrated pay, but could also indicate paleo-charge or, in some cases, migration pathway (e.g., where inclusion abundance is enhanced by extensive microfracturing). provisional interpretation of current charge is strengthened if residual petroleum (especially live oil stain) is identified in thin section, and particularly if water-soluble petroleum species (so-called proximal pay indicators; see below) are recorded in FIS data (e.g., in the seal overlying the anomaly, in the water leg underlying the anomaly, or in low permeability zones within the reservoir section itself). Any independent indications (e.g., from electric logs or mudlog gas shows) provide further encouragement. Paleo-charge Intervals of strong FIS response, high visual inclusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) and significant bitumen (e.g., dead oil stain or asphaltic residue) without accompanying water-soluble anomalies or independent evidence of current charge, may represent paleo-column, but could also represent current charge or in rare cases migration pathway. The interpretation of paleo-charge is favored if valid DST has shown the interval to be currently wet. Recycled inclusions Very rarely, detritus that is generated from previous sedimentary rock may contain inher- ited petroleum inclusions. These inclusions must be recognized, as they clearly do not provide any useful information about the current petroleum system(s). Petrographic or microther- mometric criteria can often be used to argue the origin of these inclusions, for instance, the presence of petroleum inclusions along recycled quartz overgrowths, or measured homogeniza- tion temperatures that are too high to have been produced during the current burial history. Associated FIS depth trends are usually erratic and poorly compartmentalized, and inclusion abundance is typically low. Inherited inclusions may be restricted to specific geologic units that derived detritus from particular provenance, and are not found in intercalated chemical precipitates (e.g. bedded carbonates or diagenetic cements). Heavy bitumen stain In some instances, pore-occluding bitumen may contribute to FIS signals. Here, solid petroleum behaves as any other cement, and is capable of trapping residual hydrocarbons as bitumen-hosted fluid inclusions. These may be invisible due to the opacity of the solid petroleum host. Petroleum species may also desorb from pore-occluding bitumen during crush- ing, much as they do from mature kerogen (see below). Bitumen-sourced FIS responses may be inferred when strongly anomalous zones contain low visible petroleum inclusion abundance but have significant amounts of bitumen (e.g., common, abundant or extremely abundant). Abundant pore-filling bitumen in porous rock implies significant petroleum saturation at some time, so low visual petroleum inclusion abundance is unexpected (and not commonly encoun- tered). In such cases it is possible either that the size of the inclusions are below the resolution of the light microscope (< micron), that grain surface conditions (e.g., wettability) did not favor trapping of inclusions, or that the section was diagenetically quiescent during and after charging (i.e., little or no cementation or microfracturing).

A.4 Individual Track Plots A.4.1 Explanation and Significance of Individual Track Plots The following is synopsis of the significance of the different patterns of mass abundances and abundance ratios shown in Tracks 1-25. Note that not all species are quantified using their parent or molecular peaks (e.g., methane at m/z = 15) in order to minimize interfering contributions from other species. A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. Track 2: m/z = 44 Dominant peak for carbon dioxide (CO+2 ), with possible minor contribution from C+3 hydrocarbon fragments and acetic acid. StatoilHydro ASA Gardline Report ref: ST0873 Site Survey, PL327, NCS 6705/10-1 Asterix StatoilHydro supplied no nearby well information. For wells 6605/1-1 Obelix and 6605/8-1, no useful lithological data were available from the NPD website, although drilling history and formation tops were available for tie well 6605/8-1. The ST0873 survey area is an extended grid, measuring 5km and covering the proposed well location. Due to the depth of the water, only Single Beam Echo Sounder and 2D high resolution seismic data were acquired. No coring was undertaken. The survey comprised 28 lines of the integrated survey with mainlines orientated 024°/204° and crossline orientated 114°/294°. StatoilHydro provided the GRE02STR05-3530 3D cube. The 3D data, as supplied, covers the Asterix survey area and extends 26km to the SSW providing some coverage over the 6605/1-1 Obelix well. The supplied volume has record length of seconds TWT to which static offset of 993ms was added to provide match with the 2D data. No well logs were supplied by StatoilHydro, neither was shallow gas evaluation. However, the previous report for the Obelix location, situated 24km to the SSW of the Asterix site was made available to which the stratigraphy was tied (see section 9).

A.2 FIS Mass Spectra 43 is inferred (but not demonstrated) only in the presence of other sulfur species. The m/z 32 would appear to be good one for indicating sulfur presence; however, this ion location suffers major potential interference from atmospheric oxygen (O+2 ). Care must be taken when interpreting sulfur-enriched FIS spectra, because at first glance they resemble the water-soluble enriched spectra. Ideally, the distinction lies in the location of CS2 at m/z 76 (as opposed to benzene at 78), H2S at m/z 34 and S+2 and/or SO2 at m/z 64. SO2 presence can be verified by the presence of paired anomaly at 64 and 48. In practice, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between sulfur-enrichment and water-soluble species enrichment when these species are not strongly anomalous, and combinations of the two spectra occur as well. A.2.3 Summary of the Five Spectral Types The above is relatively detailed account of the characteristics of the five major classes of FIS mass spectra. In the end, however, the best way to recognize and distinguish among spectral types is to compare them to the end-member examples presented herein and categorize them by eye. After examining few examples of each, pattern recognition will become easy. Understanding the complexities outlined in the previous sections is important, but usually unnecessary for first-order interpretation of FIS mass spectra. To summarize: Non-hydrocarbon Spectra: Characterized by four peak clusters centered on m/z 15, 28, 42 and 55; the first three being dominant. Most peaks are attributable to water and carbon dioxide. Gas-range enriched: Characterized by strong responses on C1-C5 (m/z 12-72) and lesser intensities on higher molecular weight ion locations. Peak clusters may be more broad at m/z 12-30 and 37-46. Predominance of masses 15 and 16, and high 57/55 ratios is possible. Liquid-range enriched: Characterized by the presence of C7-C13+ species as regularly-spaced peak clusters in the m/z 95-180 range, which are dominated by ions from paraffinic and naph- thenic compounds. Aromatic species contribute subordinate peak clusters between the paraffin- naphthene peaks (although, typically only benzene, toluene and xylenes are resolved). Water-soluble enriched: Characterized by methane, ethane, organic acids, benzene and toluene. Acetic Acid (m/z 60) and aromatic peak clusters (m/z 78, 91, 105) attain intensities near or greater than those of adjacent paraffin-naphthene peak clusters. Sulfur-compound enriched: Characterized by the presence of H2S, COS, CS2 and SO2 and/or native sulfur gas as indicated by anomalies on some combination of the m/z peaks 34, 48, 60, 64 and 76. A.2.4 Combinations of Spectral Types Combined FIS spectra are common, and appear as superimposed end member types. Although combinations of all end member spectra have been noted, the most common are gas + liquids and liquids + water-solubles. Recall that FIS is bulk technique and samples the entire fluid history of the pore system. Hence, mixed FIS spectra might be expected if the sample has experienced temporally distinct charges of petroleum (or brine) types or contained heterogeneous (immiscible) fluid in the pore system at some time.

LONG TERM STRATEGY The strategy behind drilling Well 2/8A-12A as the first horizontal well at Valhall is that it will be drilled in an area of the field with excellent control on the geology and reservoir properties. GEOPHYSICAL MAPPING GENERAL For general discussion on seismic data quality, geophysical setting and acoustic properties of the Valhall Chalk reservoir please refer to; 1990 VALHALL GEOLOGIC AND GEOPHYSICAL RE ANALYSIS AND RESERVE REASSESSMENT Text 2/2. A subsequent map revision based on the 2-D seismic database was released in March 1992. Since then the seismic data base has been upgraded by 3-D seismic dataset covering the field. This dataset is being interpreted and the generation of complete reservoir maps is in process. In order to support planning of South End development special wavelet processing and subsequent band-limited inversion has been applied to sub cube of the 3-D dataset. METHODOLOGY Interpretation of the seismic data and the mapping of those data has been done without preconceived geologic models. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

question: Can the depositional setting and ichnofabrics in the Heimdal Formation support a palaeodepth estimate of ≥200 m?
answer_text: Yes — the Zoophycos/Chondrites ichnofabrics and deep-marine depositional interpretation indicate a palaeodepth of at least 200 m.

Tuffs and tuffaceous shales are also present and these are greenish grey with characteristic white mottling. Lower in the unit, hard, yellowish grey, finely crystalline limestone and chalky limestone occur as thin beds. Sele Formation: 2334m (log) - 2410m (log) This unit is identified by the log pattern. One hundred and thirty-nine samples were described and sixty-one indivi- dual lithologies were analysed for TOC content. The samples are described in stratigraphic context below. Palaeocene Rogaland Group (2 m) Heimdal Formation (2307 - ?) Sixteen samples were described from the Rogaland Gp. interval between 2361 and 2697 m. Down to 2595 these contained overwhelmingly loose white to light grey sands, with moderately abundant greenish to brownish grey shales. Below this, the greenish grey/olive grey micaceous shales become dominant until 2670 m, below which loose sands similar to those above again become dominant. None of Palaeocene sands were analysed for TOC content, being analysed directly by thermal extraction/pyrolysis gas chromatography.

( HYDRO kia Depositional environments The environment of deposition is interpreted as deep marine basin. The almost constant degree of bioturbation indicates steady rate of sedimentation during the deposition of the shale intervals. The Zoophycos/Chondrites ichnofabric indicates sea depth at least 200m during deposition. The colour of the shale may reflect the quality of the bottom waters. Red colour indicates more oxygenized conditions. However, the change from red and brown colours to bluish green in well track 25/11-18T2 indicates that the colour also is influenced by diagenesis. The varicoloured nature of the shale may as whole be the result of volcanic input to the area. The thin sand beds (10-20cm) are very contorted and mixed up with clay clasts. and, as the sand also occurs in fissures in the shale, the most possible explanation is that this sand has been injected into the shale. The pore water in the sand has been trapped by the growing overburden of clay. The sand/pore water has been fluidized and this sand/water fluid has been injected into the overlying clay. The 1-2.5m thick sandstones have two possible interpretations: One interpretation is that the sand was injected into the shale due to the processes mentioned above. The clay was torn loose from the side rock and mixed into the sand. The faint lamination may be ascribed to water movement within the sand during or after injection. Another interpretation is that these sands are separate turbidites that settled between the main 40-60m thick turbidite bodies in the area, and that the - 2.5m thick sands seen in 25/11-18/T2 are the thinner outer parts of these turbidites. Then the main parts of these sands should exist between the thicker sand ridges penetrated by wells 25/11-15 and 25/11-18/T2. The faint lamination described above may then be ascribed to dewatering of the sand soon after deposition (dish structures). The lamination seen in the upper 10cm of the sand at 1721.4m in well track 25/11-18 may indicate exposure to bottom currents after the settling of turbidite, or, perhaps more likely, reworking from the dilute tail of the depositing turbidity current. The high angle of this lamination may be caused by later movements of the sandbody within the clay. 2.3.2 The Heimdal Formation (1741.5-1798 mRKB, log) The formation belongs to the Rogaland Group and is represented by cores 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 in well track 25/11-18T2. The top of the Formation was recovered in core # 16 in well track 25/11-18T2, see Enclosure 1. The entire formation consists of homogeneous sandstone almost void of sedimentary structures, except in the lower parts of cores and and also in core # 16 where very faint lamination can be seen. Above 1770.6m (core) the sand is very fine to medium grained, below the sand is fine to coarse grained. In the entire formation the sand is moderately sorted.

Experimental Procedures All procedures follow NIGOGA, 4th Edition. Below are brief descriptions of procedures/analytical conditions. Sample preparation Cuttings samples are washed in water to remove mud. When oil based mud is used, soap (Zalo) is added to the sample and the sample is washed thoroughly in warm water to remove mud and soap. Extraction A Soxtec Tecator instrument is used. Thimbles are pre extracted in dichloromethane with 7% (vol/vol) methanol, 10 min boiling and 20 min rinsing. The crushed sample is weighed accurately in the pre extracted thimbles and boiled for hour and rinsed for hours in approximately 80 cc of dichloromethane with 7% (vol/vol) methanol. Copper blades activated in concentrated hydrochloric acid are added to the extraction cups to cause free sulphur to react with the copper. An aliquot of 10% of the extract is transferred to pre weighed bottle and evaporated to dryness. The amount of extractable organic matter is calculated from the weight of this 10% aliquot. Deasphaltening Extracts are evaporated almost to dryness before small amount of dichloromethane (3 times the amount of EOM) is added. Pentane is added in excess (40 times the volume of EOM/oil and dichloromethane). The solution is stored for at least 12 hours in dark place before the solution is filtered or centrifuged and the weight of the asphaltenes measured. TOC A Leco SC-632 instrument is used. Diluted HCl is added to the crushed rock sample to remove carbonate. The sample is then introduced into the Leco combustion oven, and the amount of carbon in the sample is measured as carbon dioxide by an IR-detector. Rock-Eval A Rock-Eval instrument is used. Jet-Rock was run as every tenth sample and checked against the acceptable range given in NIGOGA. Temperature programme Pyrolysis: 300 °C (3 min.) - 25 °C/min. - 650 °C (0 min.) Iatroscan An Iatroscan MK-5 (TLC/FID Analyser) instrument is used. µl of extract or diluted oil is spotted on Chromarod S-III rods before elution in hexane (25 min), toluene (8 min) and dichloromethane with % methanol (vol/vol). The solvent is allowed to evaporate before the rods are placed into the next eluation chamber. Before running the rods in the analyser, the rods are heated for 90 sec. in heating chamber at 60 °C. Density An Anton Parr instrument is used. Air and distilled water is used to calibrate the instrument. All measurements are done at 15°C. NSO-1 is used as reference sample, and is run in each series of density measurements. If the viscosity of the oil is very high at 15°C, gravimetric method is used. API gravity is calculated from the density. API Gravity (°) = 141.5/Density (g/cm3) – Page 95

5 SEABED CONDITIONS AND INSTALLATION CONSTRAINTS This section describes the seabed and near-seabed conditions and includes maps of the bathymetry and seabed features (Figures and 2.3, Appendix Chart and 2). The information presented is based on data acquired, processed and interpreted by Gardline Geosurvey Ltd (2007a and b) and Gardline Environmental Ltd (2007). 5.1 Bathymetry A bathymetry extract around the Planned Well Location is presented in Figure and 5.1, based on data from single-beam and multi-beam echo sounders. The water depth is displayed with color coding and contoured at intervals of 1.0m and 5.0m, respectively. Water depth at the Planned Well Location 6407/8-5 is 252.5m ± 1.5m below Mean Sea Level (MSL). Within the surveyed site (5km 5km), depths vary between 243 ± 1.5m MSL and 307m ± 1.5m MSL, range of 64m. In general the investigated area deepens from NE to SW. At the Planned Well Location the seafloor gradient is dipping with 0.4° gradient to the SE. larger depression/trench is situated 100m to SE of Location into which the gradient is 13° to the SE. The trench shows relative relief of 14m is 300m wide and can be tracked 3000m. Inside this depression/trench are several ploughmarks. The northern part of the investigated area, including the Planned Well Location, is characterized mainly by an NW-SE trending large moraine bank that is over 8km in width. The moraine bank is extending over the whole investigated area, with exception of the and SW (see inset in Figure and Appendix Chart 2). Several SW – NE ice- scoured ploughmark depressions are oriented perpendicular to the moraine bank. These depressions are up to 20m deep and 75m – 125m wide, locally reaching over 300m in width. The most noticeable ploughmarks appear to be the youngest, but numerous older ones are also identifiable. The older ploughmarks have more random orientation. The ploughmark density is greatest to the NE of the Planned Well Location with fewer ice- scours to the SW. Within the ploughmarks the gradient can reach up to 14° (Figure 2.2). 5.2 Seabed Sediment and Features The seabed in the investigated area is very irregular and heavily ice-scoured, and the reflectivity of the seabed reflects the topography rather than the lithology. Generally, the investigated area shows thin cover of very soft CLAY and SILT overlying moraine deposits with somewhat coarser material, including bands of SILT / SAND. The moraine bank is extending over the whole site area with the exception of the west and southwest, where the moraine tails out with thickness less than 5m. The soft substrate varies in thickness and may increase within ploughmarks. At the Planned Well Location the superficial cover comprises very loose sandy silt and this is underlain by very soft to soft CLAY to depth of approximately 7m (Figure and Table 5.1). The moraine material underlying the very soft to soft CLAY cover, displays higher variability with higher sand content, and with shear strength from soft to hard. The variability is typical of morainic deposits although the sediments are predominantly argillaceous. Page 22 of 56

question: Which offset wells are cited for check-shot use versus for sonic-log calibration for well 2/7-20?
answer_text: Check-shot use: not specified in the provided context; Sonic-log calibration: Embla wells (notably 2/7-20) and other offsets such as 2/11-8, Kim-1 and Lone-1.

context_snippets.text: associated with limestone stringers, sand stringers and fault zones but will usually be seepage type losses. Mud weight should therefore be maintained at the optimum level and close attention is required to detect losses. Several of the offset wells experienced losses of some type, e.g. 2/7-20 and Chevron's Kim-1. Pore Pressure, Overburden and Fracture Gradients The general overburden pressure gradient for the area has been based upon the offset density values (where available) and the sonic derived bulk density values using the AGIP method. Regional overburden gradients have been reviewed and are generally very consistent across the Central Graben. While the shallower sediments typically have lower gradients, the deeper sections overburden gradients approach psi/ft. Typically, the shallower intervals in the offset wells had no density data, therefore, the sonic information can be utilized. In the deeper sections, density logs are normally run and that data can be utilized in predicting the overburden. The density values, both calculated from sonic and measured by logs, are then integrated as function of depth taking into account water depth and air gap to give the overburden pressure gradient curve. The overburden curve for Well 2/11-9 will be adjusted accordingly, if necessary, following intermediate logging. The Fracture gradients have been predicted based upon the following classical stress ratio method: FG = FP + * (OBG - FP) where, FG = Fracture Gradient, ppg FP = Formation Pressure, ppg K = Horizontal to Vertical Stress Ratio for the North Sea OEG = Overburden Gradient Pore Pressure Notes The pore pressure gradient is based on sonic derived pore pressures from Embla and other offset wells through the Chalk. Onset of overpressure is expected to occur within 8-June-93 Page 58

S. PRESSURE PROFILE AND CASING POINTS The planned pressure profile and casing points for well 2/11-9 are included in Figure 1. The pressure profiles were developed based on offset well data and seismic velocity evaluations. The major offsets are Phillip's Embla wells (in particular 2/7-20), Chevron's Kim-1 and Lone-1 in Danish waters and Norsk Hydro's 2/11-8. Several Central Graben HPHT wells have been drilled nearby and have been used to form the basis for HPHT drilling practices for Amoco Norway. Of particular interest are ANOC's 2/8-14, 2/8-12, 2/5-9, Norsk Hydro's 2/12-1 and Saga's 2/4-14. The specific pressure environments and drilling conditions for these wells have helped in developing this program. The pressure regime from the surface through the base of chalk has been well defined regionally where no uplift of the chalk is evidenced. Pore pressures through the Tertiary and Upper Cretaceous sections are seen to be consistent across the offset well data set. Accordingly, overburden gradients and fracture gradients are also fairly well defined and consistent across the offset well data set. Weak zones are generally not anticipated down to the base of the chalk assuming no major faulting has occured through the interval. The beginning of the major overpressure zone is anticipated to occur within the Lower Cretaeous (Cromer Knoll Group). The pressure transition is anticipated to increase from +-14.0 ppg at the base of the chalk section to +-17.3 ppg at the anticipated Pre- Cretaceous objective. Repeat Formation Tester (RFT) data from the nearby offset wells, i.e. 2/7-20, 2/11-8, Kim-1 and Lone-1 have been evaluated and included as Figure 1A to this program. The evaluation of the RFT data indicates that the 2/7-20 and the Kim-1 are at the same pressure gradient in the Pre- Cretaceous prospective section although they are over 20 km apart. Both wells are located on Horst block structures adjacent and upthrown to the regional Skrubbe fault. These Horst blocks exhibit significant relief and the potential for extended hydrocarbon columns (Reference Section 3: Well Overview Report). The subject well, 2/11- 9, is geologically very similar to 2/7-20 and Kim-1 as it will be positioned to evaluate the so called central horst block structure adjacent to the Skrubbe fault. Based on these geological similarities and the pore pressure results from 2/7-20 and Kim-1, the 2/11-9 is expected to be similarly pressured, i.e. - ppg. Both the 2/11-8 and the Lone-1 are off structure and their pore pressures have been measured between and ppg within the Pre-Cretaceous section. Draft 21-May-93 Page 51

Exlog provided DMS logging service on well 2/7-27S, from seabed to 15750 ft Total Depth. In addition to formation evaluation and conventional mud logging, automatic real-time data monitoring and recording, combined with pressure progress, provided an aid in optimizing drilling costs, and ensured that drilling continued with maximum safety to personnel, well and equipment. 1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

Procedure No. 128/90 Section Date: July 26, 1990 Page The South Eldfisk Field is believed to be highly faulted. Core analysis indicates that normal or wrench faulting associated with extensional rift tectonics of the late Jurassic dominate. This model is complicated by the combination of younger strike slip and inversion tectonics that formed the Lindesnes Ridge. These movements occured during the late Cretaceous and Early Tertiary, and are expected to be superimposed on the earlier Jurassic fault pattern. series of down to the west normal faults are suspected within the structure itself. The seismic survey covering the field has not provided the definition expected within the reservoir interval. Attempts are underway to try to improve the quality of the data volume and hopefully help resolve the internal geometry of the reservoir interval and the fault patterns. Hydrocarbons within the gross reservoir interval are trapped by combination of two sealing mechanisms. Overlying the reservoir are siltstones and shales of late Jurassic and /or early Cretaceous age, forming vertical barier to hydrocarbon migration. Lateral migration of hydrocarbons from the closure is restricted by both the structural dip and faulting against the overlying seal. Reservoir Interval comprised of at least two To- sections separated by silty mudstone interval. ion of these sands is complicated by intervening faults of various magnitudes. Nonetheless, it is believed the upper sand in both the 2/7-9 and 2/7-20 forms the main reservoir. The same sand is present but much thinner, and fault cut at the base, in the 2/7-21S. <'‹ 41k \ The reservoir interval is interpreted to be Available cores are interpreted to be of continental red bed sequence exhibiting the characteristics of an alluvial fan environment. Four facies associated with alluvial fan deposition have been described. They are: Facies A: Proximal pebbly braided/sheetflood sediments. Facies B: Distal alluvial plain sediments. Facies C: Floodplain/Lacustrine sediments Facies D: Alluvial fan sediments. The sands are texturally immature and locally conglomeratic reflecting high energy environment. Due to the nature of an alluvial fan deposit, the lateral continuity of these sands can vary from isolated wedges to contineous bodies of coalescing fans. Additionally, the reservoir properties may also vary significantly both vertically and laterally.

SPERRY - SUN PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) Sonic log: Can be used to calculate pore pressures, using Eaton’s formula, and subsequently confirm and/or revise any pore pressure calculations made whilst drilling. 6608/10-D-1 AH/BH

CHAPTER Summary 1. The youngest strata examined are mudstones assigned to the 'Lark Formation Equivalent' of Early Oligocene age. These deposits which accumulated under upper bathyal depths rest with minor unconformity upon the Eocene 'Horda Formation Equivalent'. Throughout the Eocene and Paleocene the NSPg sequence framework of RRI has been applied to assist regional/local correlations. 2. The Late Eocene is relatively thin and is considered, at least in part, to be condensed, as reflected in the higher gamma ray mudstone unit within Sequence NSPg180. 3. The Middle Eocene comprises stacked retrogradational sequences of NSPg140 through to NSPg170. The older sequences, especially NSPg140 and NSPg150, are significantly sand- prone. Throughout the Middle Eocene progressive reduction in both sand content and thickness of the sequence is evident reflecting gross retrogradational package. The sands, equivalent to the Grid Formation and the Caran Sandstone in the UKCS, were deposited via gravity flow processes into an upper bathyal or deeper setting being sourced off the Malloy Terrace area to the east. Contemporaneous sands exist in blocks 35/3 and 35/8. Recycled taxa suggest some erosion of the shelf/slope break. 4. minor hiatus separates the Middle and Early Eocene. Within the Early Eocene part of the Hordaland Group gravity flow sands occur in Sequences NSPg120-100, being time equivalent to the Frigg Formation as seen to the south in the Viking Graben. Minor erosion of the underlying Rogaland Group is indicated in Sequence NSPg100. It is considered likely that the 35/4-1 well was located close to the westward pinch-out of Eocene sands, with little or no easterly derived sands occurring further west beyond the Marflo Ridge. 5. The Rogaland Group part of the Early Eocene comprises the Balder Formation and Sele Formation, deposited under upper bathyal depths. 6. Available biodata suggest the possibility of minor hiatus at the base of Sequence NSPg70. with Sequence NSPg60 possibly missing. 7. Sequences NSPg55 to NSPg10 comprise an essentially conformable Late - Early Paleocene section, with trace sand development. Page

Pilot well 15/9-F-11 and injector 15/9-F-1 have already proven oil (i.e. oil-down to situation) in the NW segment so steering according to resistivitiy is not required. Instead the focus is on obtaining maximum reservoir interval, using gamma ray (GR) and density (DEN) images to understand and control the stratigraphic position of the wellbore. Active geosteering is most important when drilling across faults, where drilling into Heather Formation in the hanging wall is likely. The aim is to avoid / miminise drilling non-productive Heather Formation sections by steering down before the prognosed faults to mitigate the effect of the throw. The largest prognosed fault has throw of ca. 40 TVD and is at 3470 MD along the planned wellpath. Different sandstone and shale facies within the Hugin Formation have sufficient GR and DEN contrasts which will allow for good quality images. F-11 and F-15 have previously been geosteered successfully in the Hugin Formation. Uncertainty in Hugin thickness in the up-flank area of the NW may make it necessary to begin geosteering soon after entering Hugin, based on the stratigraphy present. For example, should thinner than expected Hugin reservoir be encountered, due to erosion, it may be necessary to build immediately to avoid drilling directly into Sleipner Formation below. Reservoir The IVING Paleocene Prospect reservoir is the Lower Heimdal (ET4) and Ty Formation (ET2-3) sands (Figure 7), which are interpreted to have been deposited within deep-water depositional environment, transported from the western side of the Viking Graben . The sands were deposited after the sediment-gravity currents encountered the adverse slope associated with the western margin of the Utsira High The Ty/Heimdal Formation sands at the WING Prospect are believed to be mixture of high- density turbidites and sandy debrites deposited through feeder channel from the north. The sands can be correlated to the north (i.e. 25/8-7) of the prospect (Figure 8). The map pattern and cross-sectional geometry are seismically well defined. debris-flow origin for the majority of the sands are supported by mounded geometry of the thickest reservoir interval along the western margin of the prospect, while more sheet-like deposits to the east could be deposited by turbidity currents. The Grane Field located to the south is suitable analog with thick sandstone deposition by high-density gravity currents and high reservoir quality continuing undiminished over the mounded parts of the field. Trap Definition/Spill Point In the current interpretation the Ty/Heimdal Formation sands pinch out along the NE-SW fault trend which defines the eastern margin of the lying Terrace (Figure 9). The trap is defined based on the assumption that the sands pinch out along the mapped fault. There is some seismic evidence for this, but the quality of the Top Ty seismic pick is sometimes relatively weak, and where the Ty/Heimdal Formation gets thin interference with the Top Chalk reflector complicates the interpretation. Trap definition in the eastern part of the prospect is therefore somewhat weak (Figure 10a, and c). The oil-water contact is believed to be identical to Tau West (2091 TVDSS), as the sands at WING probably are in communication with Tau West. The current mapping of Jotun shows that the Tau West structure does not spill structurally, and therefore has to be controlled stratigraphically or by structural spill point in an older reservoir in communication with Paleocene reservoirs.
