question: For wells 9/2-7, 9/2-3, and 3/7-5, what are the Bryne Formation depositional environments and corresponding Jurassic age(s)?
answer_text: 9/2-7: fluviodeltaic — Bajocian–Bathonian (±Bathonian); 9/2-3: deltaic/paralic — Bajocian–?Bathonian (Middle Jurassic); 3/7-5: fluvio-deltaic — Aalenian–Bathonian (Middle Jurassic).

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

Halliburton Geo Consultants Limited IV. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

Cretaceous and Tertiary times provided period of relative tectonic quiescence. The basin-fill was primarily affected by regional basin downwarp, resulting in gently westward thickening wedge of Cretaceous and Tertiary strata. Reactivation along the pre-Cretaceous fault systems, resulting from an Alpine N-S compressional field during early Tertiary times, and continuing salt movements, generated some inversion features and localised thickening of the overlying stratigraphic sequence. Halokinetic movements have occurred from Triassic times onwards, with particularly important episode coinciding with, and possibly triggered by, the Late Kimmerian tectonic event. 2.2 Regional Stratigraphy and Basinal Development (Fig. 4) The oldest sedimentary strata penetrated in the area are coarse clastic sediments of the Rotliegendes Formation (Lower Permian in age). Volcanic intercalations are found in the basinal area (well 3/7-2). Marine incursions during late Permian times led to the deposition of thick evaporites (salt together with anhydrite and carbonates) in the subsiding SOgne Basin. After the sea receded thick Triassic sequence was deposited over the Zechstein evaporites and carbonates. This phase of sedimentation continued into Late Triassic/Early Jurassic times: possible Lower Jurassic strata have been reported only from the well 3/5-2. At the end of Early Jurassic times rifting phase took place. Block faulting, accompanied by drop in sea level and subsequent erosion of the emerged blocks, led to the deposition of fluvio-deltaic sediments of Aalenian to Bathonian age (the Bryne Formation, within the Vestland Group). These comprise alternating shales and sandstones with occasional laterally persistent coals. The potential sediment source areas were the Mandel High and the Southern Vestland Arch. A second phase of uplift and non-deposition occurred at the end of the Middle Jurassic, expressed in the Callovian Unconformity. This

Cretaceous times: the associated faulting affects mainly the lower part of the Chalk. Carbonate sedimentation was terminated during the Early Palaeocene by increased clastic input. Sedimentation during Palaeocene and Eocene times is characterised by series of marine transgressions and regressions. Claystones and limestones constitute the greater part of the Paleogene sequence, with locally well developed sandstones at the base. Volcanic tuffs and tuffaceous shales of the Balder Formation indicate widespread volcanic event at the Palaeocene - Eocene boundary. Subsidence in the North Sea continued at an uniform rate in Neogene times, resulting in the deposition of fine grained marine clastics. thin Quaternary cover completes the stratigraphic column. 2.3 Previous Exploration Results (Fig. 1) Within PL 147, the wells 3/7-1, -2 and -3 were all dry. Well 3/7-4, drilled on combined fault/truncation trap, found gas/condensate column of 135 metres within sandstones of the 'Lindesnes' and Bryne Formations (Upper and Middle Jurassic respectively). production test over the Bryne Formation flowed 626 Sm3/d condensate and 755,365 Sm3/d gas, and second commingled test over the Bryne and 'Lindesnes' Formations 604 Sm3/d condensate and 838,535 Sm3/d gas, both on 3/4 choke. Other neighbouring wells in Norwegian acreage were all dry (3/5- 1, -2). A number of hydrocarbon discoveries have also been made in adjacent Danish acreage. In the Lulu-1 well, gas and oil shows were reported within the greater part of the Middle Jurassic reservoir section. However, petrophysical evaluation and test data indicate that any hydrocarbons are likely to be residual, and only formation water was produced on test. Oil and gas were, however, successfully tested from the overlying Chalk. ( Note: In normal oil based mud system, the effect of the mud system on total gas readings is effectively constant) What is the relationship between increased formation gas and increased mud effects? Why should the use of PDM produce negligible background gas values', but high proportion of mud effect? This quicklook appraisal of mud/gas effects was undertaken to establish if potential problem exists in identifying small formation gas peaks above the mud effects. It would appear that formation gas can be isolated from the mud effects, although degree of masking ought to be considered possible, including an unpredictable mud effect base line. This subject would probably benefit from more detailed appraisal and referral to Baroid for their comments. MUD COMPRESSIBILITY The PETROFREE mud system demonstrated curious response to compression during the casing test on the 13-3/8. The pressure increased in linear fashion while pumping at bbl/min until 3550 psi. Despite maintaining the pump rate the pressure was observed to bleed off to 3400 psi, at first giving the impression of casing integrity problem. The pumps were shut off and the pressure stabilised at 3280 psi in 12 minutes. Pumping was resumed at the same rate and the pressure increased lineally until the casing test pressure of 5000 psi had been reached. Though the pumps were off, the holding pressure was observed to rise slightly. It was felt that gas/liquid phase change occurred at around 3500 psi in the temperature regime under which the casing test was conducted. It was also noted that although bbls were pumped, only 20 bbls bled back. The elastic properties of this mud system clearly require some investigation to enable well control and fracture pressures to be established at range of temperatures and mud weights. -39- 6. DESCRIPTION OF BOREHOLE CORES 0 up. The following chapter gives description of each borehole. The lithologies are described and the boreholes are divided into lithozones. Boundaries between lithozones and foraminifera assemblage zones are rarely penetrated by cored sample and the exact location of these boundaries is uncertain. In cases where log response or information from the drilling suggest more accurate boundary depth this level has been chosen. 6.1 Core 7317/10-U-01 6.1.1 Lithology and structures The stratigraphy of this borehole is summarized in Figure 6.2. The samples from this site generally comprise nonstratified, very silty clay with varying, but low content of sand and fine gravel. The clay content is typically 40-50% and the silt content typically 35%. The remaining constituent is sand and fine gravel. It has been noted that clasts of rounded clays tone observed in bulk samples is absent in the coarse fractions of the split sample. These clasts are mechanically weak and are apparently worn down during sample splitting. The clast content is therefore underestimated in the recorded grain size parameters. The main exceptions are samples between and which partly comprise sands, and samples between and which comprise silty clays. The content of coarse sand and gravel is lower in the latter interval and comprises pyritized burrows (30% of the gravel fraction at m). Eight lithozones, named Li - L8, are distinguished in this borehole based on variations in colour, petrography, structures and grain size variation. Some of the variations are rather faint. Statistical work on the petrography is not done, and comments given below are limited to particular observations that appear diagnostic for the different intervals. background content of rock fragments throughout most of the hole comprises various undifferentiated angular - subrounded sedimentary rocks dominated by mudstones and sandstones. Rounded to well rounded clasts form very common constituent of most of the samples. The roundedness of these clasts is striking. They disintegrate, however, when the samples are disperged for grain size analysis (causing an error in grain size analysis) and appear mechanically weak. Once the different flow regimes have been identified in the derivative curve, localized mobilities can be estimated using the corresponding specialized plots. These involve plotting the pressure as function of the spherical and radial time functions. The slopes of the straight-line sections are used to compute the formation parameters such as the spherical mobility, the radial mobility-thickness product, and extrapolated pressure at infinite shut-in. The proper straight-line sections for these specialized plots are the data subsets that exhibit horizontal line in the derivative curves. Example of high permeability effects Anytime the pressure decreases rather than increases during buildup, the derivative curve will take sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (log of negative number -infinity). Typically, such buildup is considered un- interpretable. If this occurs for short period, then the final shut-in pressure may still be good estimate of formation pressure, depending on permeability. When the permeability is high, the total pressure changes seen during the buildup are small. The derivative calculation becomes more sensitive as the magnitude of the pressure changes gets near the resolution of the pressure gauge. The derivative curves may have the above wavy appearance. The true shape of the derivatives are often unclear. Good estimates of extrapolated formation pressure are still possible using simple straight line fit to the time function plots. Permeability estimates will be reasonable if the straight line fits reflect the true flow regime.

GEOLOGY OF WELL 25/8-B-22 & B-22 INTRODUCTION Well 25/8-B-22 was an observation well for potential horizontal oil producer. Well 25/8-B-22 was pilot hole for potential horizontal oil producer. Both wells were drilled in the Sindre Structure. The pilot hole was kicked off from B-22 at 4282m MD All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. answer_text: Seven Isotube samples from 7321/8-2 ST2 dominated by N2 and O2+Ar (and CO2) indicate atmospheric air contamination; Isotube samples at 690m, 750m and 790m (7322/7-1) indicate thermogenic gas (vitrinite reflectance ~1%), implying the former are contaminated air and the latter are indigenous thermogenic gas.

context_snippets.text: 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

Chapter INTRODUCTION The well under consideration in this report is exploration well NCS 7124/4-1 from the South-East Barents Sea. The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. Normal procedures for removal of these compounds, i.e. water washing cannot remove these compounds from smectite-rich claystones. Instead, mild acid solution (10% HCl) was added to an aliquot of claystone (it is not necessary to analyse sandstones or limestone this way, as only clay minerals are badly affected by glycol) and then washed with methanol/acetone and then water, before drying and analysis, by thermal extraction and pyrolysis GC and Rock-Eval. 1 SUMMARY Petroleum geochemical analyses of Isotube mud gas and drill cuttings samples from the interval 499m to 797m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7322/7-1 have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. Drill cuttings samples from the Nordland Group (484m to 540m) mainly poor to minor source potential, mainly for gas. The shallowest sample 499m has good organic carbon content and marginally good source potential, mainly for gas, but is unlikely to have generated significant hydrocarbons in attaining the present level of maturity. Drill cuttings samples from the Kolmule Formation (540m to 661m), the Kolje Formation (661m to 677m) and the unspecified reservoir section (677m to 797mTD) have mainly poor to marginally fair source potential, mainly for gas. Extracts of selected samples the Nordland Group and unspecified reservoir are dominated by polar fractions, attributed mainly to polyglycols from the drilling fluid. Alkane fractions include suspected base oil, possibly from the drilling fluid. Biomarker ratios indicate that all extracted samples are immature for oil generation with vitrinite reflectance no more than 0.6%. The regional unconformity at the base Nordland Group is not evident from the data. Most biomarker ratios indicate slightly lower maturation level for the two deeper samples 763m and 790m from the unspecified reservoir than for the three shallower samples 499m, 505m and 517m form the Nordland Group. This may be related to combination of organic facies variation and reworking of organic material into the shallower section. The 763m and 790m samples contain mainly terrestrial higher plant derived organic material consistent with the rather low HI values throughout the interval. The 499m, 505m and 517m samples contain mainly marine organic material and type II or mixed type II/type III kerogen. The rather low HI values throughout the Nordland Group could be related to oxidation during reworking of the organic material. Isotube mud gas samples are dominated by N2 and also O2+Ar with N2/(O2+Ar) ratios indicative of air and with low CO2 concentrations. Samples from 690m, 750m and 790m comprise thermogenic gas generated from gas mature source rock with vitrinite reflectance around 1%. Samples from 510m and 530m are suggested to have leaked, indicated by low gas wetness and anomalously heavy carbon isotope ratios. Interpretation of samples from 550m, 590m and 630m is less clear but these do not appear to have leaked. Relatively heavy C2 and C3 carbon isotope ratios could suggest biodegradation, although this is not supported by molecular composition ratios, and it is unclear why biodegradation should affect shallow gases within the claystones of the Kolmule Formation but not the underlying unspecified reservoir section.

CALIBRATION Though they both measure times of propagation through the rocks, the sonic and seismic tools are affected by various and complex phenomena (environmental effects, frequency content of the signal...) that create discrepancy between the two types of information. To enable the comparative interpretation of log data and seismic sections,we need to adjust (or calibrate) one measurement to the other. Our basic assumption will be that times of propagation measured on the seismic data are correct within certain precision depending on the shot quality, precision of the breaktimes picking etc... The new method presented here with CALIFE avoids problems in case of deviated wells and complex seismic acq. geometry by working in model that can describe both types of measurements and their geometry. What is generally used to compute synthetic responses in seismics is subsurface description in flat layers of constant velocity. To describe the sonic in such way, we have employed the squaring (or zoning ) techniques used for lithofacies identification. This gives us partition of the log data in zones of low variations. In the case of the sonic, those zones can be seen as layers of constant velocity. The methodology employed to calibrate the sonic is the following: • Take the squared sonic as initial solution (or initial model). • Compute in this model synthetic arrival times for each source-receiver couple with ray tracing method. • Compute the drift i.e. the difference between those synthetic arrival times and the times measured on the VSP or check shots.

question: What LDT core-calibrated porosity method, net-sand selection criteria, and Archie/Rw determination were applied to well 35/11-2?
answer_text: LDT porosity was calculated using the LDT calibrated to core; net sands were selected where the Dual Laterolog–Micro SFL indicated permeable zones with a 10% porosity cutoff; Archie parameters and apparent Rw were determined from Pickett plots with Rw from DST fluid analysis (value: Not in context) referenced to 130°C.

context_snippets.text: 2.8 PETROPHYSICS 2.8.1 Introduction The 35/11-2 well encountered hydrocarbons in the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formation. Evaluation with RFT's and log data indicated the Brent contained producible hydrocarbons. The Sognefjord Formation has low net/gross, is tight and was not tested. 2.8.2 Summary The petrophysical evaluation for well 35/11-2 was performed using open hole wireline logs. Matrix parameters were established using core data when possible (Figure 2.10).The dual laterolog was used for resistivity, and the LDT calibrated to core was used to calculate porosity. Net sands were picked where the Dual Laterolog-Micro SFL log indicated permeable zones. Core data further indicated 10% porosity cutoff should be applied to the net sands. The petrophysical results along with the parameters used in the evaluation are summarized in Figure 2.11. For reserves and mapping purposes the upper Ness and the Tarbert are grouped into one unit, the lower Ness is in separate unit. The Etive and Oseberg are each separate units. The Archie parameters and apparent Rw used to calculate water saturation were determined using Pickett plots. The above method compensates for errors which could result from using incorrect Rw. The Rw obtained from analysis of a fluid sample from DST is ohm/m. The reference temperature for the Rw value is 130°C.

S 4.3 PORE PRESSURE Introduction Figure is composite plot of formation pressures against depth for well 35/11-3. Wireline pre-test data (FMT pressures) were obtained in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. Over the remainder of the well the pore pressure profile has been derived from empirically calculated data. Figure is composite plot of drilling exponent (Dxc), wireline and gas data for the well. Shale factor data for the Tertiary interval has been included to llustrate the influence of clay mineralogy changes on the data plots. The interpretation of pore pressures has been largely based upon the Dxc and Delta data plots, supplemented by gas data and well bore conditions. However, for the most part, the 35/11-3 well was drilled with significant overbalance which has minimized the use of these parameters. Well Summary Normal pore pressures equivalent to ppg EMW (equivalent mud weight) are assumed for the top hole section of Quaternary to Tertiary (Pliocene) age claystones and sandstones. There was no evidence of shallow gas as was tentatively interpreted at 479 to 497m and 573 to 634m on the shallow site survey. The Miocene Utsira Formation sandstones ( m) are overpressured to ppg EMW, and resulted in salt water flow into the well. Similar overpressured environments were encountered in the Utsira Formation in the Mobil operated 35/11-1 and 35/11-2 wells, and in the adjacent Gulf operated block, 35/8. Both of the previous Mobil wells in block 35/11 were drilled on, or adjacent to, seismically disturbed zones in the basal Nordland and uppermost Hordaland

Group sediments. This chaotic seismic character has been interpreted as being result of plastic deformation and/or slumping of the sediments. If is believed to have genetic link with the origin of the abnormal pore pressures in the Utsira Formation (see Well 35/11-2, Final Well Report, section 4.3). The 35/11-3 well, however, was drilled at location free from disrupted zones with only slight chaotic seismic structure, yet was still overpressured. This questions the previously argued causitive link between the disrupted zones and the development of abnormal pore pressures. Below the base of the Utsira Formation, pore pressure is believed to return to normal in the claystones and sandstones of the Nordland Group, and to remain so down to approximately 1400m in the Hordland Group. Below this depth the Dxc and wireline data plots indicate an increase in pore pressure up to maximum of to ppg at approximately 1660m. It should be noted however, that the observed shifts in the data plots are coincident with change from mixed layer to smectite clays and it is difficult to quantify accurately how much of the shift is due to changes in clay mineralogy and how much to increased pore pressure. I Below 1700m, the data plots indicate regression in pore pressure to normal (i.e approximately ppg BMW) by 1800m. Pressure remains close to normal throughout the Upper Cretaceous Shetland Group to 2600m. Below this depth, the data plots suggest that pore pressure increases slowly with depth down into the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Group, reaching maximum overpressure of around 9.5ppg BMW by the base Cretaceous. A marked shift in the compaction data plots, together with an increase in gas levels, marks the transition to higher pore pressures at the top of the Jurassic Viking Group at 2821m. •

- 204 - GAFFNEY, CLINE & ASSOCIATES CASED HOLE DST-2 Perforations 3 5m Commentary The zone perforated for this test was in the lower section of the Upper Jurassic Heather Formation. Log interpretation carried out by Schlumberger and Gulf had indicated that hydrocarbons could be present within the section though only limited intervals of moveables were postulated, water saturations seemingly being high and hydrocarbons possibly being reduced to residual for the most part. The log interpretation was hampered by lack of information pertaining to water resistivity and also by problems of mineralisation and therefore was considered only in semi-quantitative fashion. It was understood that sidewall core analysis had supported the view that hydrocarbons were present, possibly in the liquid phase. Prior to testing, the mud weight was taken down from ppg to 12.7 ppg in order to reduce the differential pressure across the APR-N tester . valve to an acceptable level, internal pressure being provided by only partial water cushion of some 2133 metres. full water cushion was not used since reservoir pressure of around 5300 psig was expected from RFT data and it was considered necessary to maintain an underpressure of around 0 psig if the formation was to be given fair chance to flow. The well began to clean up very quickly when opened for the main flow period and some 45 bbl of water cushion was recovered in 40 minutes. However, another 15 minutes were required to seemingly recover bbl of viscous gel that had been spotted above the APR-N valve and with all other flowing conditions unaltered this seemed to indicate more recovery than could be accounted for.

• The density and neutron logs show small gas effect in the Ness Formation and in some thin, clean sand stringers in the Etive. The gas effect is not seen in the other formations due to the thin sand and shale sequences. The increased liquid yield as seen in DST in the Tarbert Formation could reduce the gas effect on the density and neutron logs in this part of the well. The logs were reviewed to identify potential gas/oil contact in the Tarbert,but no contact is apparent. 2.8.4 Sognefjord Formation 2 The Sognefjord Formation was found to have of net reservoir rock. Log data indicate the formation has thin sand/shale laminations and low porosity. Core data from the base of the zone shows it to be micaceous. Fourteen RFT pressure readings were attempted in the Sognefjord Formation. Figure is summary of the RFT results. A segregated RFT sample taken from this interval required 2 hours, 41 minutes to fill the and gallon chambers. Gas with mud filtrate was recovered from both chambers. test was not conducted in this interval due to the poor reservoir characteristics. 2.8.3 BRENT GROUP 1 The evaluation of the Brent Group indicates pay section with an average porosity of 16.7%, and an average water saturation of 32.7%. Drill stem tests produced oil, gas and condensate at various rates from zones between 3370-3542 m.

question: How did AutoTrak doglegs (0.037–0.067; ≈0.07) affect torque limits, rate of penetration, and MWD reliability?
answer_text: The AutoTrak doglegs (0.037–0.067; ≈0.07) increased torque demand, causing torque-limited operations and reduced ROP, and the MWD generally performed well with high‑speed telemetry though occasional decoding problems occurred after connections.

question: Which HORDALAND GP sand layers at wells 2/4-22S and 2/4-23 have slight/moderate gas risk?
answer_text: 2/4-22S: Sand Layers 3a, 4a and 5 (slight risk). 2/4-23: Sand Layer 3b (slight risk) and Sand Layers 3a and 4a (moderate risk).

Generally shallow drilling conditions are expected to be similar to those encountered at offset wells (Section 3.1). 7.1 Shallow Water Flow There is no mention of shallow water flow within the available information for the tie wells. ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. The latter application suggests an operational and interpretational advantage in performing combined heat flow/surface geochemical surveys in the Barents Sea and elsewhere. INTRODUCTION As part of the 1985 IKU Barents Sea heat flow program, reconnaissance shallow-probe heat flow measurements were performed at nine site locations, Saettem et al (1985). Corresponding thermal conductivity measurements were performed on gravity-core samples covering similar depth intervals (0 - meters). The intent of these measurements was to combine the shallow thermal data with the deeper downhole data to assess the feasibility and limitations of future shallow-probe surveys in the Barents Sea as cost effective means of increasing data density. The main problem associated with shallow penetration (less than 10 meters) heat flow measurements in shallow water areas is due to periodic fluctuation in bottom water temperature. This disturbing effect is generally absent in abyssal plain areas where most marine heat flow measurements are confined. context_snippets.text: Technical Memorandum (John Cater and Andrew Taylor, lchron Limited) Introduction Slabbed core from wells 6507/7-3, 6507/7-A17 and 6507/7-A35 was logged at ResLab Laboratories, Stavanger, by John Cater and Andrew Taylor (lchron Limited), on March 25th-27th 2003. For each well, copy of the hand-drawn 1:50 scale core log and written log comments are presented here. Illustrative core photographs are shown on Plates to 5. The sedimentology of the cored intervals is summarised below. Detailed descriptions are contained in the log comments. The depositional environments recorded by the cored intervals are interpreted below. Recommendations for future work to investigate the likely distribution and facies of Late Cretaceous sandstones in the Heidrun area are made at the end of this memorandum. Note that the most recent biostratigraphic data are not available for this memorandum. All depths quoted are core depths. Summary of core descriptions and interpreted depositional environments The cored section comprises mid to late Coniacian siltstones of the Kvitnos Formation overlying 2.51m of medium grained sandstones of the mid-Coniacian Lysing Formation (2367.55m-2370.06m), which in turn overlie fine grained sandstones of the late Aalenian Garn Formation. 2360.00m - 2367.55m This interval is dominated by laminated siltstones displaying local, weak bioturbation by pyritised Chondrites and sand-filled Sabularia (Plate 1A and 1B). The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

-73- 3.4.3 Sedimentology The core (179.8 - m) is subdivided into three main lithostratigraphical units (Figure 3.4.3), which are interpreted to be lateral developments of the Tofte Formation, the Lange Formation and the Kvitnos Formation. Core description 179.8 - m: Tofte Formation, Late Toarcian The Tofte Formation displays one single facies association. It consists of erosive cycles of graded, poorly sorted, medium grained, micaceous sandstones (0.2 - m) that are interbedded with silty claystones and gravel, and contain few rootlets and abundant coal fragments. Apart from a few darker clayey intervals, and numerous thinner (5 - 15 cm) light brownish grey intervals, most of the unit displays greenish grey to light greenish grey colour. The light brownish grey intervals contain some coaly material (plant debris). The whole unit shows an overall upward fining trend. There is dominance of gravel and conglomeratic material in the lower part, and medium and finer grained sandstones in the upper part. Sedimentary structures comprise horizontal lamination, large scale cross lamination, some ripple lamination and slumping structures. The graded units generally have large scale cross lamination in the coarse grained parts, and horizontal lamination and ripples in the finer parts. Most of the unit is poorly cemented, but some intervals are completely calcite cemented. This is especially noteworthy from 169 to 165 m, but there are also calcite cemented intervals at 136 in, in and 101 in. These intervals are generally associated with zones of coarse sand, gravel or conglomeratic material, and they vary in thickness between and in. They are homogeneous and show hardly any sedimentary structures apart from few intervals with low angle, large scale cross lamination.

After having drilled of new formation, the assembly stopped drilling due to malfunction in the bearings on the motor and the BHA was pulled. A second motor assembly was run in the hole and the section was drilled from 4282 MD to TD at 4926 MD in one run. Tight hole was encountered in the lower part of this section. but the section was drilled without any problems. The 5- liner shoe was run, and set with the shoe at 4926 mMD (2990.4 TVD RT). No major problems were experienced while running the liner. The initial 121/4 hole section (Track1=T1) encountered problems with tight hole and lost circulation, and some elongated - cm cavines were produced by the Brygge. Tare and Tana formations. Partial loss of returns occurred while drilling at 2925 MD. in the Brygge Formation, and at 3176 MD in the Tare Formation. While tripping out of the hole, tight hole was encountered at 3725 and 3640 in the Sprinear Formation, and the hole packed off at 3472 (Springar Formation) and 3100 (Brygge Formation). The string was worked / reamed from 3300 with occasional packing off / mud losses to 3927 where the pipe became irretrievably stuck after being left static for 12 minutes while changing out worn saver sub. The hole problems encountered during tripping in T1 were due, at least in part, to inefficient hole cleaning, as copious quantities of Springar Formation cuttings were circulated out of the hole even when the problem occurred above the Springer Formation. Mud losses of this magnitude suggest that the formation is very fractured, and it is possible that the sidetrack encountered fault which was missed by the first well. When drilling out the 95/s casing shoe. mud losses occurred instantaneously. After having squeezed cement and drilled it out the mud losses continued, although to lesser extent. second cement job was done by squeezing cement with the cement retainer set at 2781 MD. When drilling out the retainer and cement no cement was found below 2857 m, suggesting that the losses were occurring around the 95/i casing shoe. which was set in the uppermost part of the Brygge formation. The density log showed two zones of anomalously low. (approximately se to sg) bulk density in the upper part of the Brygge Formation. The first was immediately below the 95/g casing shoe. from 2844 MD to 2885 MD. and the second was from 2955 to 2972 m. The cuttings from these areas contained light to very light grey, soft, hydrated claystone. Drilling and steering the hole section showed drag on connections over the last hundred meters drilled, from the middle part of the Tilje Formation and downwards.

ABSTRACT Analyses performed on shallow probe and downhole heat flow data from the 1985 Barents Sea survey define the seasonal variation in the shallow (less than 10 meters) thermal regime. Based on these data an operationally feasible scheme for calibrating shallow probe measurements using downhole data has been developed. Analyses of test data generated from the 1985 measurements suggest that high density shallow probe/shallow penetration heat flow surveys can be used to map salt related thermal anomalies, the ocean/continent heat flow transition, and fluid flow related anomalies such as might be due to active hydrocarbon seepage or migration in the Barents Sea. INTRODUCTION 1.1 INTRODUCTION A Sperry Drilling Mudlogging Unit was contracted by AkerBP for the drilling of the wells 35/4-3 and 35/4-U-2 using the semi-submersible drilling rig the DeepSea Nordkapp. The well is designed as vertical exploration well. The well is classified as HPHT. The objective of the well is to explore the hydrocarbon potential in the lower Jurassic Cook formation. A 35/4-U-2 1/2” pilot hole was spudded on the 7th April 2022 at 430.5m MD / 430.5m TVD, reaching the well TD at 1163m MD / 1163m TVD on the 7th April. A 35/3 was spudded on the 8th April 2022 at 431.2m MD / 431.2m TVD, reaching the well TD at 4707m MD / 4706.25m TVD on the 4th May. Depths refer to RKB DeepSea Nordkapp at 32.65m. This report is intended as summary of the information and data collected, monitored and analysed as part of the service. The work was carried out by the following engineers, whose responsibility was to provide an Applied Drilling Technology and Geological Engineering service. DATA ENGINEERS LOGGING GEOLOGISTS Tomas Mockus Heine Helland Paulius Grigas Jurgis Merkelis Wojciech Bilan Oda Fossan-Waage David Trend Andreas Waage Løyning Andrew Horeckyj Gunnar Hellesund Kestutis Gasperavicius Hans Harald Berge Lukasz Wojcik Elena Martin Casamayor Surface Data Logging End of Well Report

Five objects with heights up to m, have been interpreted from the side scan sonar data as possible methane derived authigenic carbonates (MDAC). Two further objects were identified, by photograph and video, as potential MDAC during the environmental survey. MDACs are seabed structures, such as rock-like slabs or pavement, formed by leaking gases at seabed when the carbonates cement the sands. Bacterial mats were also identified within the vicinity of the MDAC as observed on the environmental photographs. Two objects with heights of up to are interpreted as possible boulders. summary of all the objects located within the survey area are presented in Table 3.6. No anomalies on the magnetometer data have been identified that correspond to these objects. Thirteen magnetic anomalies, with readings ranging from to 41 nT, have been identified within the survey area. The anomalies are not related to any known infrastructure or seabed contacts identified on the side scan sonar or MBES data and may therefore represent buried ferrous metal objects. summary of the magnetic anomalies is presented in Table 3.7. Nine areas of possible gas in the water column have been identified and delineated on the Seabed Features chart (Appendix A.2). These areas have been mapped from acoustic anomalies observed above the seabed on the chirp data. In the case of the three largest areas of possible gas seepage, there are possible MDAC identified within 100 of these areas. Seven of the nine areas identified overlap with areas mapped from the 2DHR data as possible shallow gas in Quaternary Units and 2. At one of these locations the SSS data shows possible evidence of gas in the water column. There is no evidence in the MBES data to support possible gas discharge above seabed. Several seabed scars, interpreted primarily to be trawl scars, extend from the northern to the southern limits in the east of the survey area. These scars are orientated 175° / 355° and span corridor approximately 350 wide. FSLTD/Report No. 120161.1V1.3 Page 15

3.6.3 Potential Sensitive Habitats and Species Submarine Structures Made by Leaking Gases ‘Submarine structures made by leaking gases’ are defined by the EC Habitats Directive as comprising ‘methane derived authigenic carbonate’ (MDAC) that forms rock-like slabs, pavements and pillars formed through process of precipitation where the carbonate cements the sand (Judd, 2001). They have restricted distribution in European waters, due-in-part, to their relationship to sources of shallow gas. MDAC is often found in conjunction with pockmarks, and are protected as Annex habitats within the EC Habitats Directive. While Norway is not party to the EC Habitats Directive and these habitats are not protected by other Norwegian legislation, it was still considered important to establish whether any MDAC occurred within the survey area. As result, of the original 10 proposed transects were located over pockmarks, hard contacts and areas of high reflectivity. Further information on these features is provided in Appendix B. Possible shallow gas accumulations close to seabed, with hard contacts within seabed depressions above them, were identified across the survey site from geophysical data. Environmental groundtruthing supported this assertion, with visual identification of potential structures indicative of MDAC. These structures were found on the camera transects ES1 and ES3, and were accompanied by bacterial mats growing on the surface of the surrounding sediment. The presence of potential MDAC indicates that hydrocarbon seep is currently active or has occurred in the past; while the presence of the bacterial mats suggests that seeping of hydrocarbon-rich water may be currently active. It is possible that other hard contacts in similar pockmark depressions across the site represent MDAC structures. 3.6.4 Conclusion General Habitats / Biotopes A review of the geophysical and environmental data suggested that three habitats occurred within the survey area. These habitats were defined by the EUNIS habitat classification as ‘circalittoral mixed sediments’ (A5.44), ‘circalittoral muddy sand’ (A5.26), and MDAC which is analogous to ‘communities on soft circalittoral rock’ (A4.23). These habitats were characterised by fine to medium silty sand with varying densities of shell fragment mosaics. Potentially Sensitive Habitats and Species Potential MDAC structures with associated Beggiatoa sp. bacterial mats and cold-water seeps were found in two locations. These findings indicate the likely presence of these structures elsewhere. MDAC structures are noteworthy as they are protected by the EC Habitats Directive. However these habitats are not described under any legislation relevant to the Norwegian Sea. No Norwegian Red List species or other vulnerable environmental resource (as defined by Section 51 of ‘The Activities Regulations’) were recorded within the survey area. context_snippets.text: OPERATOR A/S Norske Shell WELL 3/7-4 SECTION 17 1/2 Hole The cement was drilled with seawater, then the hole was displaced with sg mud. The leak off test gave sg mud weight equivalent. When drilling commenced, it was necessary to dump the header tank on each connection as it was full of cuttings. From 892 to 1011 meters, the formation consisted of very soft clays. The string tended to hydraulic; that is to say it was lifted by pump pressure from the bottom of the hole. The soft clays were extremely hydratable and the MBT showed that the clay content of the mud rose sharply. This problem was compounded by the use of PDC bit. PDC bits produce cuttings that are powder size. This powder is difficult to remove from the system. After being circulated second time, the clay particles are dispersed and begin to affect rheology. Drilled ahead to 1182 meters. The string continued to hydraulic in the soft clays. At 1182 mete-L's it was necessary to pump the string out of the hole. Drilled ahead to 1853 meters. The MBT continued to rise, and eventually reached 38 ppb. This again was due to the powdered cuttings that hydrated and made extraction with the solids control equipment impossible. Prior to this point, the centrifuge was being run to reduce solids. Only the high rpm machine was available for use, so that barite was being dumped in addition to clay solids. That barite was being dumped in addition to solids created other problems. The mixing equipment could not maintain the required weight in the active so the centrifuge was eventually stopped. The barite mixing system was monitored and mixed approximately 10 metric tonnes per hour. Speeds in excess of this caused blockages in the screw conveyor troughs or the drive belts to break. Reducing clay content in the mud is also achievable through dilution with premix. This was difficult on the Hunter. Mixing 50 cubic meters of premix required hours. Weighting up the premix to 1,5 sg required an additiond hours. During this time it was not possible to add barite to the active system as required.

The direct pressure measurement data were used to calibrate the semi-quantitative indications from Corrected Drilling Exponent (Dxc), Sonic and Resistivity data. In this context these are all termed 'porosity logs' as their use here is to indicate porosity which is related to abnormal pore pressure. The procedure for calculation of PP from porosity log and, where possible, calibration using actual pressure values, is as follows: - Where good gamma ray or spontaneous potential log data are available they are used for determination of shale intervals. series of shale baselines is drawn on the lithology log and shale determination analysis run to create dataset of shale points (prefix SHPT) which are applied to the porosity logs to define all shale intervals on the porosity logs. - The porosity shale points are then filtered using boxcar filter to produce continuous shale porosity trend dataset (called for example 'DT shale f39') for each porosity log. If no shale points analysis is done, then the raw log is smoothed using 39-point box car filter. In either case the resulting smoothed curve is used as basis for quantitative pore pressure estimation. - normal compaction trendline (NCT) is established on the porosity log. - The exponent method is used to create pore pressure dataset, in this case by applying the standard exponents of for sonic and for Dxc and Resistivity. The shallower or Upper Lange sand was higher quality but in lower pressure regime; whilst the deeper or Lower Lange was of lower quality and overpressured with relation to the shallower sand. The upper sand yielded hydrocarbon contact whilst the lower sand is believed to be hydrocarbon filled. The Upper Lange sands warrants some discussion as at this time the phase of the hydrocarbon is debatable. A sample was taken at 3055m. Due to the low permeability of the formation at this depth, the drawdown exerted on the sample was of the order of 1000psi (probably below any oil bubble point if it had been single phase oil in the formation); however there was no evidence from the MDT OFA that the hydrocarbon flowing through the tool was ever liquid during the early stages of pumpout. Subsequent PVT analysis indicates that the sample taken at this depth (with the excessive drawdowns) was very light and condensate. From log analysis, there is no obvious excavation effect on the neutron logs to indicate that the hydrocarbon phase is gas; such an effect may have been masked by mud invasion (there was 500psi mud overbalance at this depth) but this is considered unlikely. An alternative explanation is the thinly bedded nature of the beds may smooth out such an effect on the nuclear logs. The saturation calculation dependency of the Upper Lange (and probably Lysing and Lower Lange) sands on knowledge of the water resistivity is reduced as the water samples taken from the water leg at 3083m have been interpreted to yield an unequivocal formation water resistivity as follows. The ionic chemistry, water resistivity and mud contamination (by way of the tritium mud tracer) yielded the following data that are stored in spreadsheet called Lange Water Chemistry. Measurements of type (1)-(4) are always needed. The amount of type (2)-(5) data will vary, but the engineering disciplines Reservoir, Production, Flow Assurance, and Process should be able (forced) to specify specifically the number and type of measurements required at any given phase of exploration, delineation, and field development. From reservoir point-of-view, most sample information can be obtained immediately and does not require “wait-and-see”; with one exception. Special gas-injection measurements (5) may be needed, but the design and interpretation of such studies are not usually needed until relatively late stage in field development. It is almost impossible to obtain too much type (1) “basic” compositional data and, sometimes, saturation pressures. These data are also inexpensive and can be measured almost immediately after the samples are obtained. Furthermore, such basic data is always used as basis for deciding whether to use the samples in other measurements (2)-(5). A limited number of samples should be stored long-term, for (a) unexpected and “confirmation” data requirements, and (b) for studying processes which may first be defined later in field development, e.g. type (5) data. Recommendation – Cost-Effective Sample Storage The recommended practice for cost-effective sample storage is based on the observations that: 1. Storing large number of samples for extended periods of time has high associated cost while providing little or no information. 2. Only limited number of samples are usually required for long-term storage – i.e. for “later” usage (usage dependent on longer-term assessment of the field development). 3. Most samples can provide useful and timely information “immediately” at cost significantly less than “wait-and-see” long-term storage practice. 4. “Immediate” basic analysis of all samples provides: a. basis for whether the sample should be used for further testing (few samples), or whether the sample should be discarded (most samples). b. Information which can be used for on-going engineering, including correlation of statistically-significant data base. 5. Each engineering discipline (reservoir, production, flow assurance, and process) should be forced to define the type and number of samples required for their needs, and time-frame for usage.

question: What are the limitations of CRA evaluations and which data and methods are required to complete a final petrophysical evaluation?
answer_text: CRA evaluations are preliminary and limited by reliance on environmentally corrected log curves and standard input parameters/exponents (and can be degraded by high gas in the mud). A final petrophysical evaluation requires laboratory-derived parameters and properly tested evaluation models plus core data (horizontal/vertical air permeability, helium porosity, pore saturation, fluid summation porosity, grain density).

They are usually recognized by identifying sharp boundaries followed by sequence of gradationally related beds or facies. question: At what temperature and depth do Johan Castberg FIS microseeps terminate, and what percentage overlie productive reservoirs?
answer_text: They terminate at about 65–70°C (typically within the upper 1–3 km of the rock column) and overlie ~75–80% of productive reservoirs.

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 51 A.3.4 Seals FIS seals are inferred at boundaries marking abrupt changes in FIS species strength or chem- istry. The underlying assumption is that detected fluids are more or less synchronous on either side of the boundary and that some process has prevented free mixing of species across this barrier. In detail the boundary may represent change in lithology, poroperm or structural element. In the case of in-situ generated petroleum the boundary might represent transi- tion from poor to better source rock, or immature to mature source intervals. In the case of migrated petroleum the boundary might represent the extent of petroleum migration through porous rock, or the top seal to present or past petroleum column. Basal compartment limits may represent seals or, in some cases, fluid contacts or paleocontacts (see below). In general, only the tops of FIS compartments are identified on interpreted FIS depth plots. If fluids were not synchronous on either side of the compartment boundary (e.g. post-migration unconformity) then the seal interpretation would be in error. Seals may be selective or chro- matographic, in which case low molecular weight species may migrate across the boundary, while higher molecular weight species do not. A.3.5 Microseepage FIS microseeps are analogous to gas chimneys seen in seismic data, and surface manifestations of deeper charge identified in surface geochemical surveys. They are interpreted to result from near-vertical migration of light hydrocarbons followed by bacterial alteration in the shallow subsurface at temperature-depth conditions permissible for bacterial activity. Most bacteria are restricted to temperatures below 65-70°C; hence, anomalies may be observed in the up- per 1-3 km of rock column, depending on the prevailing geothermal gradient. Key indictor species include light hydrocarbons, CO2, possibly organic acids and aromatic compounds, and sulfurous volatiles, including H2S, COS, CS2, S2 ( /- SO2) and in some cases thiols. H2S is often sequestered within pyrite in iron-rich siliciclastics, hence is less common in shale-bearing lithologies. Inclusion formation in such low temperature environments may be aided by pre- cipitation of bacterial carbonate. FIS microseeps are geometrically distinct, often beginning at the surface and abruptly disappearing at the appropriate temperature-controlled depth. The presence of an FIS microseep appears to be good indicator of deeper charge in the immediate vicinity, although weak seeps may represent regional signals within shallow aquifers. Data suggest that these anomalies overlie 75-80% of productive reservoirs, while only 10% of non-productive areas display similar signals. Hence, the presence of strong seep within dry hole might indicate deeper or nearby lateral charge in the area. A.3.6 Fluid Contacts The basal boundary (abrupt or transitional) of any strong FIS compartment is candidate for present or past fluid contact, although the interpretation is often equivocal. The most compelling evidence for present day contact occurs where hydrocarbon-dominant FIS signals (the petroleum leg) give way to water-soluble dominant signals (PTP in the water leg) and where visual petroleum inclusion abundance displays parallel decrease. When inclusion abundance is high in the petroleum zone but PTP signals are not present in the water leg, it is possible that paleo-charge is recorded. A FIELD TECHNIQUE - FRACTURE STIMULATION OF THE TOR FORMATION The following is representation of Appendix III in ref. (3). The permeability in the Tor Formation of the Valhall Field varies significantly. Consequently, fluid loss varies significantly. Therefore, a pump-in/pressure decline test is required prior to each fracture stimulation treatment to obtain fluid loss data. This necessitates the design of the pad volume and sand schedule to be carried out in the field just prior to each treatment. To save time and to facilitate the treatment design, field technique(3) was derived to design the required pad volume and pump time, +At, to achieve triple width for certain fracture radii without having to run the PENNY frac program on location. This technique is particularly applicable for highly permeable reservoirs (k > md) where fluid loss is dominated by permeability. It is valid for both oil and gas reservoirs but to certain extent limited to those cases where the difference in pressure inside the fracture and reservoir fluid pressure is sufficient to establish fluid loss rate that is inversely proportional to the square root of time. For penny - shaped system, the calculation of fluid efficiency is dependent on pump rate (Q) and Young's modulus (E). Gel viscosity (4) has an insignificant impact on the accuracy of the analysis, and per- forating height (h) has no impact at all. After complete loss of returns the annulus was filled with base oil, and 10 ppg mud was pumped to reduce the losses. question: How do overpressure and consolidation state compare between the Hordaland Group, Paleocene, and down to the Utsira Sands?
answer_text: The Hordaland Group and Paleocene show minor overpressure, while down to and including the Utsira Sands the formations are fairly unconsolidated and predominantly normally pressured.

Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The sediments penetrated at the base of the well are interpreted to be Valanginian to Barremian in age. Conclusions The well passes through thick Albian to Neocomian sequence. The caving of Paleogene forms and the recycling of both Upper Jurassic and Permo-Triassic taxa complicate the basic age interpretation. Recommendations The findings of this study agree with the results of the EPS nannofossil data communicated in Report No. 2463A.

If the high tem- peratures would have acted on the vitrinite for longer period of time, higher vitrinite reflectance values would have been observed. The reason for this anomaly is unknown. Changes in the local or regional heat flow regime are the likely causes.

1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group. question: How does the pressure-derivative curve behavior differ during pressure-decrease buildup compared to ideal spherical and radial buildup?
answer_text: During pressure-decrease buildup the derivative curve exhibits a sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (often wavy and un-interpretable), while ideal spherical and radial buildups show horizontal/straight-line sections in the derivative indicating the respective flow regimes.

context_snippets.text: General Summary This report presents an evaluation and interpretation of StethoScope675 Formation Pressure While Drilling data. Interpretation Summary 16 pressure measurement stations were evaluated and given quality grading from 1-10 as described in Section 2. Test analysis resulted in: ■ 12 good quality formation pressures (quality=10) These tests built up to stable pressure on both pretests at each station (test lost seal after stable pressure was reached). The calculated drawdown mobilities were of good quality and within range from 10 mD/cp to 452 mD/cp. ■ tests building near formation pressure (quality=7) Test 16 was building and not fully stabilized at the end of both pretests. Test did not draw down below formation pressure on pretest invest. Final pretest built up to near stable pressure before seal was lost. ■ poor quality tests (quality=0) Test and test did not draw down below formation pressure on either of the pretests and not able to build up to formation pressure. All pretest interpretation plots are found in Section 5. 34/10-C-51 T2

Example of high permeability effects Anytime the pressure decreases rather than increases during buildup, the derivative curve will take sharp downward dip toward negative infinity (log of negative number -infinity). Typically, such buildup is considered un- interpretable. If this occurs for short period, then the final shut-in pressure may still be good estimate of formation pressure, depending on permeability. When the permeability is high, the total pressure changes seen during the buildup are small. The derivative calculation becomes more sensitive as the magnitude of the pressure changes gets near the resolution of the pressure gauge. The derivative curves may have the above wavy appearance. The true shape of the derivatives are often unclear. Good estimates of extrapolated formation pressure are still possible using simple straight line fit to the time function plots. Permeability estimates will be reasonable if the straight line fits reflect the true flow regime.

The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. question: How do the lithology, sandstone occurrence, and reservoir potential compare between the Draupne Formation and Sognefjord Formation?
answer_text: Draupne is dominantly claystone/shale with possible lower sandstone interbeds and limited reservoir potential, while Sognefjord consists of interbedded clean sandstones and micaceous siltstones with proven excellent reservoir-quality sands (notably in the USO interval).

Discovery Evaluation Report PL 055 Well 31/4-11 Bowmore structure 5 GEOLOGICAL INTERPRETATION 5.1 Stratigraphy The Brent interval 2644 m(log) - 2785 m(log) (mdRKB) has been studied closely resulting in dating of the various strata and identification of palyno zones and lithostratigraphical reservoir units. Some complications have been encountered, however, regarding potential caving, which has reduced the ability to confidently pick the top of the Late and the Early Bajocian intervals. This has consequently, from biostratigraphic point of view, reduced the level of confidence regarding top and base of the Tarbert Formation. 5.2 Biostratigraphy The consultant company Ichron Ltd. performed the biostratigraphic routine work on this well. Analyses within the interval top Brent Group - TD are based on ditch cutting samples, exclusively. Ditch cuttings were sampled every 2+3m. The interval was not cored, neither conventional nor sidewall cores were taken. Results from the routine analyses are further evaluated and interpreted according to Norsk Hydro standard biozonation system and presented in Fig.5.2-1. Interval 2644mRICB(log)-2654mRKB(log) Age: Late Bajocian (Zone PJ4D/E) The highest occurrence of Nannoceratopsis gracilis, pellucida and Kallosphaeridium spp. (Batiacasphaera spp.) together with with co-occurring common Cerebropollenites macroverrucosus and Alisporites spp. indicates Late Bajocian age at 2650m. minor downhole increase in sporomorph diversity is also noted at this horizon, represented by the downhole appearance of Baculatisporites comaumensis, Callialasporites microvelatus, Cyathidites australis, Ischyosporites crateris, Spheripollenites psilatus, Staplinisporites caminus and Striatella spp. together with downhole increase in the frequency of Deltoidospora (Cyathidites) minor. These latter two features can also be indicative of Brent Group style assemblages. Several other dinocyst forms which are characteristic of both Early Bathonian and younger sediments, were present. The frequent occurrence ofDurotrigia daveyi at 2650m may indicate support for in situ latest Bajocian deposits or caving from immediately overlying strata of earliest Bathonian age. This is further supported by the frequent, caved occurrence of D. vesiculata and D. filapicata at 2670m. The degree to which caving is affecting palynomorph record in this well, is little uncertain.

Core description 179.8 - m: Tofte Formation, Late Toarcian The Tofte Formation displays one single facies association. It consists of erosive cycles of graded, poorly sorted, medium grained, micaceous sandstones (0.2 - m) that are interbedded with silty claystones and gravel, and contain few rootlets and abundant coal fragments. Apart from a few darker clayey intervals, and numerous thinner (5 - 15 cm) light brownish grey intervals, most of the unit displays greenish grey to light greenish grey colour. The light brownish grey intervals contain some coaly material (plant debris). The whole unit shows an overall upward fining trend. There is dominance of gravel and conglomeratic material in the lower part, and medium and finer grained sandstones in the upper part. Sedimentary structures comprise horizontal lamination, large scale cross lamination, some ripple lamination and slumping structures. The graded units generally have large scale cross lamination in the coarse grained parts, and horizontal lamination and ripples in the finer parts. Most of the unit is poorly cemented, but some intervals are completely calcite cemented. This is especially noteworthy from 169 to 165 m, but there are also calcite cemented intervals at 136 in, in and 101 in. These intervals are generally associated with zones of coarse sand, gravel or conglomeratic material, and they vary in thickness between and in. They are homogeneous and show hardly any sedimentary structures apart from few intervals with low angle, large scale cross lamination.
