Sandstones with predominantly intergranular porosity have high permeabilities and Sw of <25%. Sandstones with mostly intragranular and microporosity have relatively low permeabilities and Sw >25%. The major factors controlling the pore types is the presence or absence of microquartz cement, clay matrix and the grain size. 6.9 The Ula Formation has been divided into poroperm units which are comparable with the reservoir zones in other 7/12 wells. 6.10 There is close correspondence between the poroperm zones and the coarsening and fining upwards depositional units. The highest porosities and permeabilities occurring over the coarser-grained parts of the depositional sequences. In these intervals the sandstones are fine to coarse-grained, moderate well sorted and have predominantly intergranular porosity. In the lower poroperm intervals the sandstones are fine-grained and argillaceous with modertely high clay and microquartz content. 6.11 Highest porosity and permeability occurs in reservoir Zone 2A with mean porosity of 20% and geometric mean permeability of 676 mD (arithmetic mean 854 mD).

This will give an indication of mono phasic or diphasic flow by measuring light reflected from the flowing formation fluid and fluid density reading. With respect to formation damage, TCP guns will be used to achieve optimum perforation performance. The water based mud will be designed for minimum invasion. Underbalance perforation will be considered. Initial clean up is critical. 3.4 TEST ON SECOND ZONE The DST is designed for top quality fluid sampling of oil in the GARN formation and one zone only. If the well comes in as expected there will be no test of second zone. However, there are scenarios where the PL212 license might want testing of second zone, however at an extremely low probability. For such test work has already been done to close out couple of issues: A second test would be separate from the first, ie. no commingled test and separate test string. A design will be based on the equipment being used for the original test. Formation parameters and test design will be refined during the first test based on data acquired during the DA programme.

5.2 Technical 5.2.1 Jurassic Primary Targets To determine the presence or absence and phase of any hydrocarbon columns in the Jurassic Garn, lie and Tile Formations. It is most important to prove the presence of oil in the Garn Formation. To gather information to allow confident resource estimates to be made for the block part of the structure. This will require: • identification of hydrocarbon contacts (gas-oil, oil-water and gas-water) for each formation. Most critical is to define the oil volume in the Garn Formation. • reservoir parameters : porosity, permeability, sedimentology, diagenesis (petrology). • pressure and pressure gradients. • fluid samples gas , oil and water. • biostratigraphic information for correlation. • data necessary for tying seismic to the subsurface. a). Prove oil in the Gam Formation (This is the most important of all objectives listed): In addition the aim is to gather sufficient information to be able to quantify the volume of oil in the Gam Formation in the structure. • Well Location - Location is selected to give the best possible chance of placing an oil leg in the Gam Formation. It is placed downdip on the block within the amplitude anomaly in position where, even with the possible errors in depth conversion, there is the best chance of placing the Gam in the oil leg. The location should not be below the structural spill to the east. (note: this is achieved on some of the depth map versions but not all). This means that the well location does NOT specifically target the Gas oil contact or the Oil water contact . • Be able to sidetrack updip or downdip, 1000 laterally. • Prove oil in Gam based on shows, logs, MDT/RFT pressure b). Define gas/oil contact in Gam • If gas/oil contact present or can be confidently calculated from MDT/RFT then requirements are met. • If gas/oil contact uncertain - optional sidetrack c). BP Amoco Norge AS Report No. 8321/Id 6.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY SUMMARY 6.4.1 Melke Formation The Melke Formation is uncored in the 6507/5-2 well and has no si___ nificant reservoir potential in the Skary area. The Melke is dominated by mudstones, possibly with minor component of very fine grained argillaceous sandstones, and forms regionally extensive seal to reservoirs in the underlying succession. To the north of the Skary area lower parts of the Melke locally contain progradational wedges of sandstone which were derived from the north. These sandstones do not, however, extend much further south than the Nome Field. Wealdy progradational log signatures within lower parts of the Melke Formation in the Skary area may be distal equivalent of these progradational wedges. 6.4.2 Garn Formation The Gam Formation as whole in the 6507/5-2 well has mean porosity of 19.03%, an arithmetic mean permeability of 1529.75mD and geometric mean permeability of 944.3mD. This formation is by far the best quality reservoir encountered in the 6507/5-2 well, but is marginally poorer than the equivalent interval in the 5-1 well. Although of good quality throughout, the Garn is internally heterogeneous with some marked internal variations in reservoir characteristics associated with changes in depositional facies. Detailed facies description and correlation of the Garn Formation suggests that the interval as whole is likely to be laterally extensive with sheetform external geometry, although there is some potential for significant thickness variations over distances of few tens of kilometres, particularly in response to syn-depositional variations in subsidence rate. In addition, there is potential for lateral pinch-out of the upper parts of the Gam Formation to the south of the Skary area, although the minimal variation between the 5-1 and 5-2 wells suggests that this may occur over significantly greater distance than the well spacing and potentially at some location beyond the licence boundary. The local presence of bitumen stain within the Gam Formation may suggests relatively complex history of hydrocarbon emplacement. It is possible that relatively early hydrocarbon charge could be partially responsible for the preservation of excellent reservoir quality. The greatest uncertainty concerning the reservoir potential of the Gam Formation at the field scale is possible variations in the degree of cementation rather than continuity of the sandbody. 6.4.3 Not Formation The Not Formation has mean core analysis porosity of 10% and an arithmetic mean permeability of 69.38mD with low geometric mean permeability of only 1.43mD. Reservoir quality is highly variable and is primarily controlled by the depositional facies of the sediment, being at maximum in the coarsest parts of the formation and specifically in the unit of 'Gam facies' corresponding to the lower part of Reservoir Subzone JS11. In this interval the arithmetic mean permeability is 208mD (geometric mean 69.3mD) with mean porosity of 14.3%. Local carbonate cementation in this part of the Not Formation has detrimental effect on reservoir quality and in large part accounts for the difference between the rock quality of this unit and the overlying sandstones of the Gam Formation. Carbonate cementation, in the form of irregular diagenetic nodules, was also noted at similar level in the 6507/5-1 well but the discrete nature of these 'doggers' in the previous well suggests they that are unlikely to have significant effect on the overall permeability of the units which contain them. The more diffuse cements in the 'Gam facies' unit appear to have greater overall impact on reservoir quality, although the presence of sandstones in this interval with permeabilities in excess of 1000mD indicates the potentially excellent reservoir quality that might be expected in the absence of carbonate cements. Page 82

1.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY The Garn Formation and uppermost Not Formation represent the primary reservoir in the 6507/5-4 well. good visible oil stain was observed in the core with probable gas cap in the upper part of the Garn. The cored interval of the Garn Formation in 6507/5-4 has mean porosity of 17.89%, with a relatively low standard deviation of 2.41, but has wide range of permeability values with maximum of 9870 mD and minimum of mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is 1739.33 mD, with slightly lower geometric mean permeability of mD, and relatively high standard deviation of highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals only weak positive correlation. There is moderate relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Reservoir quality is influenced by variations in the abundance of kaolinite, the main authigenic mineral. Although quartz overgrowth cement has reduced porosity, it does not appear to control variations in reservoir quality. The cored interval of the Tilje Formation is in the water leg and has poor to only rarely moderate reservoir quality. In view of the broad similarity in terms of depositional character between the Tilje Formation between Skarv wells, diagenetic influence on this reduction in reservoir quality needs to be considered. The Tilje Formation has mean measured porosity of 16.01%, with standard deviation of 0.35, and limited range of permeability values with minimum of mD and maximum of 1290 mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is mD, with geometric mean permeability of only mD, and standard deviation of 198.33, highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals positive correlation and there is good relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Authigenic kaolinite has significant deleterious effect on reservoir quality. Other authigenic minerals have also reduced reservoir quality, as has compaction, which is likely to be most important in the less well sorted and ductile-rich sandstones. significant proportion of the macroporosity in the Tilje is of secondary, grain dissolution origin and secondary porosity tends to be common in sandstones rich in detrital albite and lithic grains. The reservoir geology of the remaining Jurassic succession is variable but is generally lower than that in either the Garn or Tilje Formation. Moderately good quality sandstones occur in the upper part of the Not Formation whereas much poorer quality is prevalent in the micaceous, very fine sandstones in the lower part of the formation. The micaceous sandstones also tend to be rich in kaolinite and carbonate cements. The Ile Formation is sand prone relative to the enclosing Ror and Not Formations but is particularly thin and condensed in the 6507/5-4 well. The highly bioturbated and typically argillaceous nature of these sandstones results in generally poor reservoir quality. 1.5 ZONATION AND CORRELATION The Lower to Middle Jurassic sediments examined in the study well contain complete succession of the constituent formations recognised in earlier wells (6507/5-1 and 6507/5-2) which penetrated this interval in the Skarv area (see RRI Reports Nos. 8150/Id and 8321/Id, respectively). As result of regional work in the Mid Norway area, Robertson erected broadly chronostratigraphic zonation scheme for the entire Lower to Middle Jurassic which was defined in ‘The Lower to Middle Jurassic reservoirs of Mid Norway’ study (RRI Report No. EM079, 1997). This zonation scheme has been extended into the 6507/5-4 well as part of this report, the zones being given the appropriate suffixes (e.g. Tilje 1, Ror 4, etc.). All of the constituent zones are recognised in the present study well although, in common with the successions in these earlier wells, subdivision of the Melke Formation is difficult and the usable wireline log data terminate in the upper part of the Åre Formation, making correlations below this depth impossible.

2.3 COMPARISON OF 2D AND 3D DATA There is difference in resolution between the 2D and 3D data. The higher resolution offered by the 2D data is of significant importance in the interpretation of the Pleistocene and Upper Pliocene deposits, which comprise sediments deposited during greatly varying conditions. High-resolution 2D data also increase the possibility of detecting thin features, such as sand layers and ploughmarks. The 2DHR data set is of adequate to good quality. However, the majority of the energy is reflected in the upper part. From approximately 1000ms TWT the loss of energy starts to significantly affect data quality, and below 1300ms TWT only high amplitude events can be discerned. The 3D data set TO06R06M1 was provided by Total EP Norge AS. comparison between TO06R06M1 and the 2DHR data set is presented in Figure 2.2. It can be concluded that the high- resolution 2D seismic data set displays significantly better resolution and quality in the upper sequence compared to the 3D survey TO06R06M1. High-resolution 2D data is essential for the detection of amplitude anomalies and small-scale features in the shallow part. 2.1 VSP PROCESSING 2.1.1 Velocity Survey Computations The digital VSP data were reformatted and displayed. source signature deconvolution was performed on the vertical and horizontal geophone components using operators derived from the first 600 ms of the reference hydrophone The reference hydrophone and vertical geophone components were then timed on the first trough arrival, representing the primary direct arrival from the source. The hydrophone traces were examined and the first-maximum time was picked establishing consistent reference hydrophone picks. Each downhole geophone trace was subsequently shifted by the first- maximum time value of the corresponding reference hydrophone trace. time correction of ms to account for the time from hydrophone to source, at water velocity (1500 m/sec), so that all downhole geophone traces were referenced back to the source. The downhole geophone traces for each depth level were then stacked using mean summation technique. Noisy traces were rejected prior to stacking. The stacked reference hydrophone component and stacked geophone data for all levels of each component are shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, & 7. The measured slant times were then geometrically converted to vertical times below the source and then corrected to the datum of MSL using static correction of ms, at water velocity 1500 m/sec. These time-depth pairs were then used as the input data for the final velocity survey computations to give the average, RMS and interval velocities listed in Section and displayed as Enclosure 1. Good downgoing shear energy can be seen in the horizontal components as indicated by Figures & 5. This shear arrival could be timed and used to calibrate shear log data and provide detailed VP:VS ratio. 2.1.2 Acoustic Log Calibration The acoustic log was supplied in LAS format and has been input to the calibration procedure. The depth range is – MD below DF. For the calibration, the acoustic log was integrated to produce a time-log, which is depth-indexed. The discrepancy between the corrected checkshot time of the shallowest checkshot level (within the logged interval) and the corresponding log-derived time was then computed. The time-log was next shifted by adding this value to all the time-log values, thus tying the log to the shallowest checkshot. A drift curve was then generated, showing the difference between the corrected checkshot times and the corresponding times from the shifted time-log. Calibration points fixing the drift at certain depths (including the top and bottom of the logged interval) were then chosen. Such that they divide the drift curve into intervals of approximately linear drift, and also so that they occur at velocity contrasts. The calibration points are indicated with triangular marks on the drift curve displayed on Enclosure 1. The shifts applied to the log are considered reasonable with maximum shift of 14us/m (4.3us/ft). For each interval between consecutive calibration points, the ratio between the difference in the fixed drift of these calibration points and the interval thickness was computed, and this constant was added to all acoustic log values of the interval, thus shifting the acoustic log in this interval by this amount. The whole acoustic log was calibrated by repeating this procedure for all calibration point intervals. After calibration, the calibrated time-log was computed by integrating the calibrated acoustic log and tying it to the shallowest checkshot. The residual drift curve, shown on Enclosure 1, was generated using the corrected checkshot times and the calibrated time-log. The tables in Section contain details of the acoustic log calibration, including the residual drift before and after calibration and the tabulated time-depth values listed in linear depth and linear time. The depth- indexed calibrated acoustic log and associated logs are displayed as Enclosure 2.

answer_text: Run 3A: 27 pre-tests (24 dry, 3 valid); Run 4B: 15 pre-tests (13 dry, 2 valid) — total 42 pre-tests with 5 valid pressures (four in the Egga target interval and one in the Kyrre). The primary causes of dry tests were lost seal and very tight (low‑permeability) formation.

context_snippets.text: Page: 23 of 35 MDT static pressures / sampling résumé: Wireline formation testing was carried out with the objectives of obtaining true formation pressures and fluid gradients from the reservoir as well as fluid samples. The tool used was an MDT, Modular Formation Dynamics Tester. The MDT was as normal run with both strain gauge and COG quartz gauges. Fig. -1, contains both formation- and hydrostatic- (mud) pressures, to illustrate the particular conditions while conducting the MDT surveys in this well. Two runs of MDT was carried out, runs 3A and 4B. Below is summary of these. Run 3A: 27 pre-tests attempted out of which 24 dry tests due to lost seal or tight formation. The operation took 16 hrs 25 min out of which hr 10 min were lost time due to software problems. After reinterpreting the pre-tests, good tests were identified as can be seen in the table below Run 4B: 15 pre-tests attempted out of which good and 13 dry tests. The dry tests were again due to lost seal or tight formation. The whole operation took 20 hr 50 min, including fluid sampling at 2567.7m. 20 min were reported as lost time, again due to software problems. Due to the very tight nature of the Egga unit reservoir in this well only four pre-tests giving valid formation pressures were obtained in the target interval. In addition one assumed valid formation pressure was acquired in the Kyrre Formation. context_snippets.text: Depth conversion was achieved by isopaching down from Top Chalk. Nine wells were analyzed for velocity information and the following methodology was applied. Where the Cretaceous interval is greater than 20 msecs constant interval velocity of 3500 in/sec was used. Where the interval was less than 20 msecs the following formula was applied Cretaceous Isopach (m) = *Cretaceous Isochron (m sec) + 4357 The proposed well intersects the Base Cretaceous just east and outside of nearby closure. The closure has previously been intersected by the 25/11-5 well. The Lower Jurassic, Statfjord Formation sands intersected in this well are water wet with no shows. 5.3 RESERVOIR 5.3.1 Summary Seismic interpretation and well log correlations provide the framework for the reservoir mapping. The Balder Field sands are interpreted to have been deposited in deep water submarine fan environment by high-density turbidity currents. All mounds penetrated to date contain both massive and some thinner sands. High-relief mounded geometries are believed to have been caused by complex interaction between deposition and syn- and post- depositional deformation processes. Associated sand injections into overlying shales occurred during the soft-sediment deformation processes which predominantly took place during early Eocene. The lower Tertiary section is split into main reservoir zones. (Eocene Zone III, Paleocene Zones II, D3 and IA2). The definition of the main biostratigraphic zones established in 1991 is anchored in top/base occurrence of palynomorphs from cores and sidewall cores (Figure 13). The sandbody geometry is complex and total sand thickness can vary from few to over 100 meters. Reservoir properties are excellent with average porosity of 33%, permeability of 1-10 Darcies and 85-90% average oil saturation. MOOIRPM.DOC - 23.02.95 / Pg 13

question: What is the relationship between Sandnes FM petrography in well 9/2-1, reservoir quality, and regional YME stratigraphy?
answer_text: Sandnes sandstones in well 9/2-1 are an arenaceous, high-energy shallow‑marine deposit whose primary composition and diagenesis principally control reservoir porosity and permeability (GECO plug analyses). Stratigraphically, the Sandnes FM represents the Middle Jurassic arenaceous phase (late Callovian–earliest mid‑Oxfordian) within the Vestland Group of the regional YME succession.

5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

Abstract This report contains mineralogical and microstructural descriptions of Middle Jurassic sandstones from the Sandnes Fm cored in well 9/2-1. Petrographic modal analysis and x-ray diffraction mineralogical data are reported for 22 sandstones together with estimates of grain size and sorting and GECO's plug analysis on porosity and permeability. In addition, x-ray diffraction analysis of the clay fraction of selected samples from drill stem test intervals are reported. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

question: What is the eroded thickness between Naust Fm (base Nordland Gp) and the top Kolmule unconformity at 528 m in well 7321/8-2 ST2?
answer_text: Approximately 600 m ± 90 m (although regional comparisons suggest it may be closer to ~1500 m).

context_snippets.text: 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. If representative of claystones within the Fruholmen Fm, the observation would suggest that any source potential was mainly for gas. The Fruholmen Fm is late mature for oil generation but no more than marginally mature for gas generation, so the bulk of any original gas source potential may remain to be generated at more advanced maturation level. • Seven mud gas (Isotube) samples analysed are dominated by N2, O2+Ar and CO2 with compositional ratios indicative of atmospheric air, and with very low concentrations of Page 83

The aims of the analytical program were to evaluate the composition and characteristics of the source rocks and migrated hydrocarbons and where possible correlate these with possible source rocks. Cuttings from 830 to 2813 were received for analysis. Two sets of samples were received, these were • set of samples for geochemical analyses • Canned samples for headspace gas analysis The first set of samples after washing proved to be too small individually for some of the screening analysis, mainly those in the interval including the Snadd formation and the upper part of the Kobbe Formation. The canned sample material was sufficient to cover this part of the well. A water-based mud system was used in drilling the well. However, the composition of the mud contained certain organic mud additives, particularly glycols. These cause problems in the interpretation of source potential, particularly in low maturity shales. 1 SUMMARY Petroleum geochemical analyses of Isotube mud gas and drill cuttings samples from the interval 499m to 797m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7322/7-1 have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. Drill cuttings samples from the Nordland Group (484m to 540m) mainly poor to minor source potential, mainly for gas. The shallowest sample 499m has good organic carbon content and marginally good source potential, mainly for gas, but is unlikely to have generated significant hydrocarbons in attaining the present level of maturity. Drill cuttings samples from the Kolmule Formation (540m to 661m), the Kolje Formation (661m to 677m) and the unspecified reservoir section (677m to 797mTD) have mainly poor to marginally fair source potential, mainly for gas. Extracts of selected samples the Nordland Group and unspecified reservoir are dominated by polar fractions, attributed mainly to polyglycols from the drilling fluid. Alkane fractions include suspected base oil, possibly from the drilling fluid. Biomarker ratios indicate that all extracted samples are immature for oil generation with vitrinite reflectance no more than 0.6%. The regional unconformity at the base Nordland Group is not evident from the data. Most biomarker ratios indicate slightly lower maturation level for the two deeper samples 763m and 790m from the unspecified reservoir than for the three shallower samples 499m, 505m and 517m form the Nordland Group. This may be related to combination of organic facies variation and reworking of organic material into the shallower section. The 763m and 790m samples contain mainly terrestrial higher plant derived organic material consistent with the rather low HI values throughout the interval. The 499m, 505m and 517m samples contain mainly marine organic material and type II or mixed type II/type III kerogen. The rather low HI values throughout the Nordland Group could be related to oxidation during reworking of the organic material. Isotube mud gas samples are dominated by N2 and also O2+Ar with N2/(O2+Ar) ratios indicative of air and with low CO2 concentrations. Samples from 690m, 750m and 790m comprise thermogenic gas generated from gas mature source rock with vitrinite reflectance around 1%. Samples from 510m and 530m are suggested to have leaked, indicated by low gas wetness and anomalously heavy carbon isotope ratios. Interpretation of samples from 550m, 590m and 630m is less clear but these do not appear to have leaked. Relatively heavy C2 and C3 carbon isotope ratios could suggest biodegradation, although this is not supported by molecular composition ratios, and it is unclear why biodegradation should affect shallow gases within the claystones of the Kolmule Formation but not the underlying unspecified reservoir section.

5 SEABED CONDITIONS AND INSTALLATION CONSTRAINTS This section describes the seabed and near-seabed conditions and includes maps of the bathymetry and seabed features (Figures and 2.3, Appendix Chart and 2). The information presented is based on data acquired, processed and interpreted by Gardline Geosurvey Ltd (2007a and b) and Gardline Environmental Ltd (2007). 5.1 Bathymetry A bathymetry extract around the Planned Well Location is presented in Figure and 5.1, based on data from single-beam and multi-beam echo sounders. The water depth is displayed with color coding and contoured at intervals of 1.0m and 5.0m, respectively. Water depth at the Planned Well Location 6407/8-5 is 252.5m ± 1.5m below Mean Sea Level (MSL). Within the surveyed site (5km 5km), depths vary between 243 ± 1.5m MSL and 307m ± 1.5m MSL, range of 64m. In general the investigated area deepens from NE to SW. At the Planned Well Location the seafloor gradient is dipping with 0.4° gradient to the SE. larger depression/trench is situated 100m to SE of Location into which the gradient is 13° to the SE. The trench shows relative relief of 14m is 300m wide and can be tracked 3000m. Inside this depression/trench are several ploughmarks. The northern part of the investigated area, including the Planned Well Location, is characterized mainly by an NW-SE trending large moraine bank that is over 8km in width. The moraine bank is extending over the whole investigated area, with exception of the and SW (see inset in Figure and Appendix Chart 2). Several SW – NE ice- scoured ploughmark depressions are oriented perpendicular to the moraine bank. These depressions are up to 20m deep and 75m – 125m wide, locally reaching over 300m in width. The most noticeable ploughmarks appear to be the youngest, but numerous older ones are also identifiable. The older ploughmarks have more random orientation. The ploughmark density is greatest to the NE of the Planned Well Location with fewer ice- scours to the SW. Within the ploughmarks the gradient can reach up to 14° (Figure 2.2). 5.2 Seabed Sediment and Features The seabed in the investigated area is very irregular and heavily ice-scoured, and the reflectivity of the seabed reflects the topography rather than the lithology. Generally, the investigated area shows thin cover of very soft CLAY and SILT overlying moraine deposits with somewhat coarser material, including bands of SILT / SAND. The moraine bank is extending over the whole site area with the exception of the west and southwest, where the moraine tails out with thickness less than 5m. The soft substrate varies in thickness and may increase within ploughmarks. At the Planned Well Location the superficial cover comprises very loose sandy silt and this is underlain by very soft to soft CLAY to depth of approximately 7m (Figure and Table 5.1). The moraine material underlying the very soft to soft CLAY cover, displays higher variability with higher sand content, and with shear strength from soft to hard. The variability is typical of morainic deposits although the sediments are predominantly argillaceous. Page 22 of 56

Experimental Procedures All procedures follow NIGOGA, 4th Edition. Below are brief descriptions of procedures/analytical conditions. Sample preparation Cuttings samples are washed in water to remove mud. When oil based mud is used, soap (Zalo) is added to the sample and the sample is washed thoroughly in warm water to remove mud and soap. Extraction A Soxtec Tecator instrument is used. Thimbles are pre extracted in dichloromethane with 7% (vol/vol) methanol, 10 min boiling and 20 min rinsing. The crushed sample is weighed accurately in the pre extracted thimbles and boiled for hour and rinsed for hours in approximately 80 cc of dichloromethane with 7% (vol/vol) methanol. Copper blades activated in concentrated hydrochloric acid are added to the extraction cups to cause free sulphur to react with the copper. An aliquot of 10% of the extract is transferred to pre weighed bottle and evaporated to dryness. The amount of extractable organic matter is calculated from the weight of this 10% aliquot. Deasphaltening Extracts are evaporated almost to dryness before small amount of dichloromethane (3 times the amount of EOM) is added. Pentane is added in excess (40 times the volume of EOM/oil and dichloromethane). The solution is stored for at least 12 hours in dark place before the solution is filtered or centrifuged and the weight of the asphaltenes measured. TOC A Leco SC-632 instrument is used. Diluted HCl is added to the crushed rock sample to remove carbonate. The sample is then introduced into the Leco combustion oven, and the amount of carbon in the sample is measured as carbon dioxide by an IR-detector. Rock-Eval A Rock-Eval instrument is used. Jet-Rock was run as every tenth sample and checked against the acceptable range given in NIGOGA. Temperature programme Pyrolysis: 300 °C (3 min.) - 25 °C/min. - 650 °C (0 min.) Iatroscan An Iatroscan MK-5 (TLC/FID Analyser) instrument is used. µl of extract or diluted oil is spotted on Chromarod S-III rods before elution in hexane (25 min), toluene (8 min) and dichloromethane with % methanol (vol/vol). The solvent is allowed to evaporate before the rods are placed into the next eluation chamber. Before running the rods in the analyser, the rods are heated for 90 sec. in heating chamber at 60 °C. Density An Anton Parr instrument is used. Air and distilled water is used to calibrate the instrument. All measurements are done at 15°C. NSO-1 is used as reference sample, and is run in each series of density measurements. If the viscosity of the oil is very high at 15°C, gravimetric method is used. API gravity is calculated from the density. API Gravity (°) = 141.5/Density (g/cm3) – Page 95

Few data are available from the lower part of the Cretaceous, creating uncertainties about the actual strength of the formation at this level. However, experiences from the wells drilled on the field so far indicates decrease in the fracture gradient from approx. 3200 mTVD RT down to approx. 3500-3600 mTVD RT (lower Cretaceous) where it again increases (related to the pore pressure gradient). The minimum fracture pressure in this interval (Shetland/Cr. Knoll Group) is not identified, but is most likely in the range 1.90-2.00 g/cm3 EMW. It is assumed that the fracture initiation pressure in the sandstones are at the same level as the surrounding shales due to anticipated sealing mud filter cake. 5 Collapse Calculations Collapse pressures are calculated by using the in-house Statoil programme STABIL, which is simple linear elastic model. Input parameters are pore pressure, overburden, fracture pressure, well inclination and compressive strength (calculated from Sonic ΔT). • Due to the high wellbore inclination (>50°) in the 17 1/2 section the calculated collapse pressure have maximum value of g/cm3 EMW in the Rogaland Group. This section will be drilled with high mud weight to ensure stable well conditions (MW of g/cm3 down to approx. 1900 mTVD and g/cm3 from this depth and to TD of the section). • From the top of the Shetland Group and down to TD of the well the collapse pressure more or less follow the pore pressure gradient. • From the lower part of the Cretaceous (below the Tryggvason Formation) the pore pressure is expected to increase rapidly until it reaches maximum of g/cm3 EMW at prognosed top reservoir. In this interval the collapse pressure is lower than the pore pressure gradient, and the latter will dictate the mudweigth. • High collapse pressures are expected if the Draupne Formation is present, but the calculated collapse pressure is lower than the predicted pore pressure. Thus the mud weight selected to balance the pore pressure in the lower part of the 12 1/4 section should be sufficient to prevent hole collapse. • If the Draupne Formation is present in the well this may create unstable hole over time. It should therefore be considered to drill into the Heather Formation below in order to case off the Draupne Formation with the 5/8 casing.

question: In well 6201/11-1 what explains the Dxc cut-back, the gas spike to 18.29% at 1323 m, and the mud weight changes after the 1293 m limestone?
answer_text: A limestone seal at ~1293 m caused a rapid pressure build-up beneath it, producing the Dxc cut-back and the 18.29% gas spike at 1323 m, and the mud weight was increased to balance the elevated pore pressure.

Fluid Inclusion Technologies (FIT), Inc., is laboratory-based petroleum service or- ganization established in 1997 and offering variety of analytical services including some previously proprietary technologies. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS), the most widely applicable of these technologies is rapid analytical technique that involves the automated analysis of volatile compounds trapped within micron-sized cavities in rock material taken from well cuttings, core or outcrop samples. These fluid inclusions are representative sam- ples of subsurface fluids, and are not subject to fractionation during sampling or evaporative loss during sample storage for any length of time. The procedure has major impact in the areas of both Petroleum Production and Exploration Applications providing informa- tion unattainable via more traditional methods and, has been instrumental in the discovery of significant petroleum reserves, influenced exploration and acreage acquisition decisions and provided innovative options for resource estimation, petroleum production and enhanced oil recovery operations. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphic Analysis, often in combination with other patented techniques, emerging geochemical methodologies and standard microscopic methods, all available through Fluid Inclusion Technologies, Inc., provides unique and un- equaled industry product boasting an impressive list of proven applications including deter- mination of Product Type, Hydrocarbon Migration, Seals and Seal Integrity, Fluid Contacts, Proximity to Reservoired Petroleum, Pay Zone/By Passed Pay Delimi- tation, Reservoir-Scale Compartmentallization and Fluid Pressure Compartments. Further information regarding the application of FIS Analysis and the other technical ser- vices we provide to problems in petroleum exploration and production is available elsewhere in this report and on our website:www.fittulsa.com. 1.1 General Logistics of Initiating an FIS Analysis To Initiate an FIS Analysis: contact FIT' directly to discuss goals of the study, sample requirements, turnaround time, pricing, and other related aspects. New clients are particularly encouraged to consult with our staff during the early stages of project development to optimize sample selection, preparation and shipment. Rock materials for FIS Analysis are shipped directly to C&M Storage2, our sample handling facility, for sample preparation including any necessary crushing/sieving, subsampling and washing. The turnaround time for typical FIS Analysis is preliminary data in 1-2 weeks time following receipt of samples by C&M and final report 1-2 weeks following preliminary analysis. These times are approximate and depend on the amount of sample preparation required, job size and analytical backlog. The main reservoir targets in 6507/5-4 were the Lower and Middle Jurassic sandstones of the Fangst and Baat Groups (the Garn, Ile and Tilje Formations) and high risk secondary reservoir target in the Cretaceous (Lysing and Lange Formations). question: Define Δtdrift when calibrating TVDSS compressional sonic to ZOVSP/checkshot travel times, and identify causes of positive versus negative Δtdrift.
answer_text: Δtdrift = ΔtVSP − Δtsonic. Positive Δtdrift is usually caused by velocity dispersion or frequency‑dependent velocity differences (seismic vs sonic bandwidths); negative Δtdrift is typically due to hole rugosity or local effects where formation velocity > borehole‑fluid velocity.

9 Conclusions Summarised below are the key points and conclusions drawn from the acquisition and processing of the Walkaway VSP for well 25/2-17 in the Frigg Delta Field. ■ Both surface and downhole data performed well during the survey, with very good quality data being recorded. Good vector fidelity was achieved by the 3C recording and both compressional and converted back-scattered wavefields could be effectively separated using full wavefield elastic separation. ■ Vp, Vs, and Anisotropy in Hordaland Gp was the primary objective of the project, while any imaging was secondary objective. ■ No strong shear observed in WAVSP dataset and any oblique shear energy would be affected due to the effect of anisotropy and so, the best technique for estimating vertical Vs profile would be from rig-source dataset. ■ Both deconvolution and wavefield separation were computed after the data was converted into the Tau-P domain. The main advantage of processing in this domain is that multiple periodicity becomes time-invariant and hence robust deconvolution operator was derived to effectively attenuate the multiples in the dataset. ■ 1D VTI model was built utilising the ZOVSP travel times and well log data, and inverting the WAVSP travel times to estimate anisotropy parameters. ■ Good coherency was observed in the 20 fold common image point domain after migration, giving confidence in the processing to obtain an upgoing wavefield and the 1D VTI model. ■ 3D migration volume was computed utilising the VTI model and the upgoing Pp Wavefield. The image was visualised in 3D along with the surface seismic and ZOVSP corridor stack.

Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction On the 5th of October 2009, Zero Offset VSP survey was carried out for Statoil on the 25/2- 17 Frigg Delta exploration well, offshore Norway. The survey was acquired in the final open and cased hole sections of the well. The survey was acquired in comjunction with Walkaway survey that is documented in separate report, and the objective was to generate corridor stack and vertical time-depth curve for 3-way tie (surface seismic, corridor stack and synthetics). This report describes the time picking of the checkshot data, sonic calibration and synthetic seismogram generation and the processing of the Zero Offset VSP data. The data was processed using Borseis proprietary software as implemented on Geoframe commercial baseline 4.0.3. The polarity convention adopted in this report ( Except the 3-Way-Tie plot, which is in Statoil polarity convention) is as follows. In normal polarity an upgoing compressional wave, reflected by an increase in acoustic impedance with depth, is displayed as white trough (negative number). The raw x, y, z, surface sensor data, intermediate and final processing results are provided in SEGY format on the accompanying CD-ROM. All plots, cgm and/or PDS, digital data and the processing report are also provided on the CD-ROM.

4 Sonic Calibration The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the sonic slowness log to match the vertical VSP transit times. 4.1 Compressional Sonic Calibration Prior to sonic calibration, the log data (compressional- and shear sonic, density, caliper and gamma ray logs) were validated (including depth-matching and environmental corrections) by StatoilHydro. Compressional sonic was available from 997.0m MD DF to 2169.87m MD- RKB . This was corrected to true vertical depth using the well deviation and bulk shifted by - 22.0m to the Seismic Reference Datum, to give compressional sonic log from 974.96m- 2147.02m TVDss. All accompanying logs were also corrected to TVDSS. As the water depth for this well was 120.3m it was decided to add checkshot level at seabed in order to help guide the sonic calibration. The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the integrated sonic slowness to match the vertical VSP travel times for given reference depth. The difference in time defines the drift (tdrift =tVSP-tsonic), which can be either positive or negative. positive drift is usually caused by velocity dispersion or the frequency dependant nature of the velocities as measured by the seismic bandwidth and the sonic bandwidth. negative drift can be due to hole rugosity where Vformation > Vborehole-fluid and is generally very local effect. In order to minimize the residual drift function, user defined smoothed drift curve has been designed to honour the raw drift curve as closely as possible with view to generating “calibrated” sonic log that should be used as time to depth relationship for the well only and NOT used for Acoustic Impedance generation. For AI generation, the raw sonic, correctly time indexed using the calibrated velocity function has been used for input to synthetic reflectivity generation. The compressional sonic was calibrated using the geometrically corrected, vertical Time/Depth relationship from the Zero Offset VSP survey. comparison of the sonic slowness log and the ZOVSP interval velocities is shown in Figure 26 and an initial visual inspection shows the character appears similar with major lithological boundaries tying well. Figure 27 shows the drift correcting applied during calibration of the sonic log. The sonic, VSP interval, RMS and average velocities after calibration are shown in Figure 28 and are available as digital logs on the CD-ROM accompanying this report. The velocity information and calibrated time depth curves are tabulated in Well Seismic Repor, Drift & Sonic Adjustment Report & Velocity Report.

2.2 Seismic interpretation versus well results Sonic logs (both compressional and shear) were acquired in the two pilot wells 15/9-F-11 T2 and 15/9-F-11 A. Checkshots and VSP were acquired in 15/9-F-11 T2. 2.2.1 15/9-F-11 T2 pilot Volve North prospect Top and Base Hugin Formation depth prognosis in the North prospect were initially very uncertain. The seismic reflectivity in this area is very poor in all datasets and together with the presence of an undrilled thick Upper Jurassic package in this downfaulted segment the uncertainties on Top and Base Hugin Formation prognoses were set to ±70 TVD. Top Hugin Formation came in +29 TVD deeper and Base Hugin Formation came in +33 TVD deeper than prognosis. Checkshot pairs and VSP (normal incident and rig source) were acquired. The synthetic seismic from well logs confirmed poor seismic signal on Top Hugin Formation and weak seismic signal on Base Hugin Formation compared to Base Hugin Formation on the main field (Figure 2-5). Using checkshots as time depth curve deeper time interpretation of Top and Base Hugin Formation is initiated. This information has been implemented in the updated maps. VSP image data is processed by Schlumberger and preliminary results indicate more northern placement of the large main bounding fault compared to initial seismic interpretation. These preliminary observations have also been implemented in the updated maps. It was not observed any improvement of Top and Base Hugin reflectors on the preliminary results. Final imaging results of VSP processing are estimated to be delivered during November 2013. Classification: Internal Status: Final Expiry date: 2010-12-30 Page 23 of 110

The results from the calculations showed that the upper part of Ile and parts of the top of Ile can theoretically be completed with 300 micron screen in an open hole without facing the risk of sand production or screen plugging. Calculations performed on data from the remaining sieve analysis of Ile zones indicated that no screen size is particularly suitable for open hole completion without the possibility for sand production or screen plugging. Discussions have indicated certain conservatism in the “Sand12” program. The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

Core description 179.8 - m: Tofte Formation, Late Toarcian The Tofte Formation displays one single facies association. It consists of erosive cycles of graded, poorly sorted, medium grained, micaceous sandstones (0.2 - m) that are interbedded with silty claystones and gravel, and contain few rootlets and abundant coal fragments. Apart from a few darker clayey intervals, and numerous thinner (5 - 15 cm) light brownish grey intervals, most of the unit displays greenish grey to light greenish grey colour. The light brownish grey intervals contain some coaly material (plant debris). The whole unit shows an overall upward fining trend. There is dominance of gravel and conglomeratic material in the lower part, and medium and finer grained sandstones in the upper part. Sedimentary structures comprise horizontal lamination, large scale cross lamination, some ripple lamination and slumping structures. The graded units generally have large scale cross lamination in the coarse grained parts, and horizontal lamination and ripples in the finer parts. Most of the unit is poorly cemented, but some intervals are completely calcite cemented. This is especially noteworthy from 169 to 165 m, but there are also calcite cemented intervals at 136 in, in and 101 in. These intervals are generally associated with zones of coarse sand, gravel or conglomeratic material, and they vary in thickness between and in. They are homogeneous and show hardly any sedimentary structures apart from few intervals with low angle, large scale cross lamination.

‘Minimum phase’ interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is recorded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse (ca. 25 kHz.), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal-to- noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no dispersion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough- to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrating the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismogram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

Formation top interpretation can be checked in both time and depth domains: lines drawn at constant two way time can be 'reflected' at the first break line on the VSP and continued as lines of constant depth to the linear depth scale logs. This binder contains the results of the WSC/GEO processing of your well 34/10-32. COMMENTS: The quality of this job was in general good. The rigshots from the VSP was used to calibrate the sonic. DENSITY LOG The density log was corrected so that the badhole effects would not generate any false reflections. Where density log is absent synthetic density log is computed from sonic log. CALIBRATION Though they both measure times of propagation through the rocks, the sonic and seismic tools are affected by various and complex phenomena (enviromental effects, frequency content of the signal...) that create discrepancy between the two types of information. To enable the comparative interpretation of log data and seismic sections,we need to adjust (or calibrate)one measurement to the other. Our basic assumption will be that times of propagation measured on the seismic data are correct within certain precision depending on the shot quality, precision of the breaktimes picking etc... The new method presented here with CALIFE avoids problems in case of deviated wells and complex seismic acq. geometry by working in model that can describe both types of measurements and their geometry. What is generally used to compute synthetic responses in seismics is subsurface description in flat layers of constant velocity. To describe the sonic in such way, we have employed the squaring (or zoning ) techniques used for lithofacies identification. This gives us partition of the log data in zones of low variations. In the case of the sonic, those zones can be seen as layers of constant velocity. The methodology employed to calibrate the sonic is .the following: • Take the squared sonic as initial solution (or initial model). • Compute in this model synthetic arrival times for each source-receiver couple with ray tracing method. • Compute the drift i.e. the difference between those synthetic arrival times and the times measured on the VSP or check shots. • Modify the initial model iteratively (by changing the layers velocities) until the dif- ference between synthetic and measured times is smaller than certain threshold.

Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction A multiple-offset, boat source Walk-Away Vertical Seismic Profile (WAVSP) was recorded in the deviated well 34/10-52A on the 29th of July 2011. The drilling rig was the DeepSea Atlantic semi submersible. The objective of the survey was to image the fault below BCU top formation marker, to generate 2D/3D image to be tied to the surface seismic and to estimate anisotropy parameters. The WAVSP survey was planned to be shot with the fault imaging in mind. The 16 receivers were positioned far above BCU top formation to have big enough coverage to image the fault. Anisotropy estimation was only decided some time after the acquisition and so the survey was not accurately designed for this purpose. Nevertheless, good values and interesting results were obtained. This report describes the anisotropy estimation, the construction of the borehole calibrated 1D VTI model and the 3-component processing workflow used to compute the Pp image. Zero Offset VSP survey was also acquired during acquisition operations, the processing of this dataset is detailed in separate report, which can be found on the accompanying data CD-ROM The WAVSP was processed using Q-BorSeis baseline 2.7.1, which is the next generation borehole seismic package built on top of WesternGeco‟s Omega surface seismic processing system. Petrel 2011 was also used for 3D visualisation of the final results. The raw downhole x,y,z data, surface sensor data, intermediate and final processing results are provided in SEGY format on CD-ROM accompanying this document. All plots, gif and/or PDS, digital data and the processing and acquisition reports are also provided on CD-ROM. Throughout this report all plots adhere to the polarity convention set out by SLB, where an increase in acoustic impedance with depth is displayed as white trough and negative number on tape (except migrations and tie-in displays which adhere to Statoil polarity convention: increase in acoustic impedance is displayed as positive number and blue peak)

Note that all plots were produced in Petrel software with an increase in Acoustic Impedance with depth displayed as blue horizon (peak). The full processing sequence for the walkaway imaging is shown in Table 5. 5.2 Tie to ZOVSP Results Figure 111 and Figure 112 show the 2D visualization of the WAVSP images respectively for line #1 and line #2 with the ZOVSP 5-85 Hz corridor stack projected along the well trajectory. Both views show good tie between the two datasets. The small mismatches can be explained by many reasons with among them the 3D effect. 5.3 3D Velocity Model As per Statoil request, the latest version of the 3D anisotropic velocity model generated by WesternGeco (Vp, Epsilon and Delta 3D property grids) was tested within the 3D Pp migration. Figure 113 shows the Vp property grids in 3D view along with the well path. Figure 114 and Figure 115 display the Pp images, respectively for WAVSP line #1 and line #2, migrated using the 3D anisotropic velocity model provided by WesternGeco. The images generated using either the 1D VTI model or the 3D model are very similar but with shift of about 20-25msec between the two models. As for the migration with the 1D VTI model, CIP gathers were computed as QC of the 3D migration and shown in Figure 116 for WAVSP line #1 only. Generally the CIP gathers have lower quality than the ones using the 1D VTI model. When comparing the CIP gathers migrated from the two models with WAVSP lines #1, squeeze-stretch effect from the velocities or the anisotropy parameters is visible and seemed to be the explanation for the shift mentioned previously. Indeed, if comparing the CIP gathers close to zero offsets, reflector around 2.3km moves upward using the 3D model, while reflector around 3.2km moves downward and the reflectors around 2.75km are more or less at the same position. Based on WesternGeco information, it seems that the surface seismic model was not calibrated for the checkshot velocities. The checkshot time-depth function was used only for the anisotropy tomography inversion and then, only the anisotropy parameters were updated in the final 3D velocity model. Figure 117 and Figure 118 display the tie-in plots for the Pp images using the 3D anisotropic velocity model with surface seismic, respectively for WAVSP line #1 and line #2. Again it is clear that the image from the 1D VTI model matches the surface seismic better than the image from the 3D model in terms of times. In terms of structural features the images are not very different from each other. Statoil 34/10-52A June 2012

2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.

above, the boundary marks change from the deposition of shaly sands to cemented clean sands, and is also an erosional surface. From analogy with similar environments elsewhere it was postulated that this surface may have been the site of soil development and possibly related cementation. On logs the surface coincided with thick tight zone (figure 4), and in order to match both pressures and water cut it was found necessary to make the surface a complete barrier to vertical permeability in all updip areas, where maximum erosion of the lower unit had taken place (figure 5). Thus, in this case, the cross section was used to test geological hypotheses such as the existence of permeability barriers and possible Kv/KH ratios, which were then used in full field simulation. 4. Full Field Modelling The use of full field modelling is natural extension of the cross-section work described above. However, layers are coarser, and due to the size of the model, changes are more difficult and more expensive to make. However, certain facets of the reservoir model such as areal variability can be tested. In the field under study the net/gross ratio shows marked changes areally. This is caused by the natural feature of fluviatile systems where zones located on, or near, the major axis of the drainage system tend to be sand rich, while those on the periphery are sand poor. Figure shows diagramatically this relationship. In sand-rich zones, where channels erode into one another, the overall transmissibility is good, as is the vertical permeability. However, in sand-poor zones both these parameters are drastically lowered. In order to account for this effect, the net/gross ratio was introduced as multiplier for the two horizontal gridblock permeabilities. It was found that for an effective match, the vertical grid block permeability had to be multiplied by power of the net/gross ratio because the interbedded shales parallel to reservoir layers will always have more pronounced impact on vertical fluid movement (figure 7). Research is continuing into more realistic ways of modelling such parameters as the effective vertical permeability, but it is hoped that the above discussion indicates that it is possible to improve reservoir modelling by iterative use of simulation models. CONDENSATE FIELD WITH NO PRODUCTION DATA. One of the major exploration plays in the North Sea currently is for condensate in Mesozoic sandstone reservoirs of the Central and Northern North Sea. Clearly, development of reservoirs of this type could involve markedly different development programmes from those currently in operation on the oilfields. Compositional changes, gas/liquid relative relationships and the possibility of cycling are important factors that require consideration and, as this paper demonstrates, the system becomes very complex making the prediction of the optimum configuration for maximum liquid recovery difficult. In order to analyse the problem, simple model was built using realistic reservoir properties. The model was then used to test various production strategies and the sensitivity of these to the reservoir geological model. Geological Model The geological model is illustrated in figure and represents an average Brent Sand package with three layers of high permeability representing the Etive Formation, low permeability layer at the Rannoch/Etive boundary and four layers of intermediate permeability representing the Rannoch and Broom Formations. Since this was preliminary study the model was kept as simple as realism allowed, and such features as very high permeability zones in the Etive Formation were not introduced.

BP Amoco Norge AS Report No. 8321/Id 6.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY SUMMARY 6.4.1 Melke Formation The Melke Formation is uncored in the 6507/5-2 well and has no si___ nificant reservoir potential in the Skary area. The Melke is dominated by mudstones, possibly with minor component of very fine grained argillaceous sandstones, and forms regionally extensive seal to reservoirs in the underlying succession. To the north of the Skary area lower parts of the Melke locally contain progradational wedges of sandstone which were derived from the north. These sandstones do not, however, extend much further south than the Nome Field. Wealdy progradational log signatures within lower parts of the Melke Formation in the Skary area may be distal equivalent of these progradational wedges. 6.4.2 Garn Formation The Gam Formation as whole in the 6507/5-2 well has mean porosity of 19.03%, an arithmetic mean permeability of 1529.75mD and geometric mean permeability of 944.3mD. This formation is by far the best quality reservoir encountered in the 6507/5-2 well, but is marginally poorer than the equivalent interval in the 5-1 well. Although of good quality throughout, the Garn is internally heterogeneous with some marked internal variations in reservoir characteristics associated with changes in depositional facies. Detailed facies description and correlation of the Garn Formation suggests that the interval as whole is likely to be laterally extensive with sheetform external geometry, although there is some potential for significant thickness variations over distances of few tens of kilometres, particularly in response to syn-depositional variations in subsidence rate. In addition, there is potential for lateral pinch-out of the upper parts of the Gam Formation to the south of the Skary area, although the minimal variation between the 5-1 and 5-2 wells suggests that this may occur over significantly greater distance than the well spacing and potentially at some location beyond the licence boundary. The local presence of bitumen stain within the Gam Formation may suggests relatively complex history of hydrocarbon emplacement. It is possible that relatively early hydrocarbon charge could be partially responsible for the preservation of excellent reservoir quality. The greatest uncertainty concerning the reservoir potential of the Gam Formation at the field scale is possible variations in the degree of cementation rather than continuity of the sandbody. 6.4.3 Not Formation The Not Formation has mean core analysis porosity of 10% and an arithmetic mean permeability of 69.38mD with low geometric mean permeability of only 1.43mD. Reservoir quality is highly variable and is primarily controlled by the depositional facies of the sediment, being at maximum in the coarsest parts of the formation and specifically in the unit of 'Gam facies' corresponding to the lower part of Reservoir Subzone JS11. In this interval the arithmetic mean permeability is 208mD (geometric mean 69.3mD) with mean porosity of 14.3%. Local carbonate cementation in this part of the Not Formation has detrimental effect on reservoir quality and in large part accounts for the difference between the rock quality of this unit and the overlying sandstones of the Gam Formation. Carbonate cementation, in the form of irregular diagenetic nodules, was also noted at similar level in the 6507/5-1 well but the discrete nature of these 'doggers' in the previous well suggests they that are unlikely to have significant effect on the overall permeability of the units which contain them. The more diffuse cements in the 'Gam facies' unit appear to have greater overall impact on reservoir quality, although the presence of sandstones in this interval with permeabilities in excess of 1000mD indicates the potentially excellent reservoir quality that might be expected in the absence of carbonate cements. Page 82

1.4 RESERVOIR GEOLOGY The Garn Formation and uppermost Not Formation represent the primary reservoir in the 6507/5-4 well. good visible oil stain was observed in the core with probable gas cap in the upper part of the Garn. The cored interval of the Garn Formation in 6507/5-4 has mean porosity of 17.89%, with a relatively low standard deviation of 2.41, but has wide range of permeability values with maximum of 9870 mD and minimum of mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is 1739.33 mD, with slightly lower geometric mean permeability of mD, and relatively high standard deviation of highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals only weak positive correlation. There is moderate relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Reservoir quality is influenced by variations in the abundance of kaolinite, the main authigenic mineral. Although quartz overgrowth cement has reduced porosity, it does not appear to control variations in reservoir quality. The cored interval of the Tilje Formation is in the water leg and has poor to only rarely moderate reservoir quality. In view of the broad similarity in terms of depositional character between the Tilje Formation between Skarv wells, diagenetic influence on this reduction in reservoir quality needs to be considered. The Tilje Formation has mean measured porosity of 16.01%, with standard deviation of 0.35, and limited range of permeability values with minimum of mD and maximum of 1290 mD. The arithmetic mean permeability is mD, with geometric mean permeability of only mD, and standard deviation of 198.33, highlighting the variability in measured horizontal permeabilities. Cross plotting of the core analysis porosity against permeability values reveals positive correlation and there is good relationship between reservoir quality and both facies and grain size. Authigenic kaolinite has significant deleterious effect on reservoir quality. Other authigenic minerals have also reduced reservoir quality, as has compaction, which is likely to be most important in the less well sorted and ductile-rich sandstones. significant proportion of the macroporosity in the Tilje is of secondary, grain dissolution origin and secondary porosity tends to be common in sandstones rich in detrital albite and lithic grains. The reservoir geology of the remaining Jurassic succession is variable but is generally lower than that in either the Garn or Tilje Formation. Moderately good quality sandstones occur in the upper part of the Not Formation whereas much poorer quality is prevalent in the micaceous, very fine sandstones in the lower part of the formation. The micaceous sandstones also tend to be rich in kaolinite and carbonate cements. The Ile Formation is sand prone relative to the enclosing Ror and Not Formations but is particularly thin and condensed in the 6507/5-4 well. The highly bioturbated and typically argillaceous nature of these sandstones results in generally poor reservoir quality. 1.5 ZONATION AND CORRELATION The Lower to Middle Jurassic sediments examined in the study well contain complete succession of the constituent formations recognised in earlier wells (6507/5-1 and 6507/5-2) which penetrated this interval in the Skarv area (see RRI Reports Nos. 8150/Id and 8321/Id, respectively). As result of regional work in the Mid Norway area, Robertson erected broadly chronostratigraphic zonation scheme for the entire Lower to Middle Jurassic which was defined in ‘The Lower to Middle Jurassic reservoirs of Mid Norway’ study (RRI Report No. EM079, 1997). This zonation scheme has been extended into the 6507/5-4 well as part of this report, the zones being given the appropriate suffixes (e.g. Tilje 1, Ror 4, etc.). All of the constituent zones are recognised in the present study well although, in common with the successions in these earlier wells, subdivision of the Melke Formation is difficult and the usable wireline log data terminate in the upper part of the Åre Formation, making correlations below this depth impossible.
