question: What are the lithology, thickness, and mineralogy of the Early Bajocian–Middle Bathonian and Late Bathonian–Middle Callovian intervals in well 35/3-1?
answer_text: Early Bajocian–Middle Bathonian: ~240 m of medium– to dark‑grey (locally brown/black) non‑calcareous, silty, fissile shale with occasional thin siltstone and fine–very fine sandstone stringers; mineralogy includes pyrite, mica, calcite (in sand cements), rare dolomite and organic (lignite) fragments. Late Bathonian–Middle Callovian: ~70 m of dark brown–dark grey, subfissile, silty micromicaceous and partly carbonaceous highly pyritic shale with occasional thin fine–medium sandstone beds (calcite and minor silica cement); minerals include pyrite, mica, calcite, minor silica and organic matter.

context_snippets.text: STRATIGRAPHY Based on well cuttings, electrical logs and sidewall cores, the lithology of the various formations are as follows: Bajocian - Early Bathonian - Middle Bathonian, 0 in (240 m) Shale, medium to dark grey, partly becoming brown grey to black with black lignite fragments showing woody textures. The shale is generally noncalcareous, fissile, silty and grades occasionally to siltstone. The sequence is occasionally interrupted by thin stringers of sand- stone, fine to very fine grained, light brown, dirty, with calcite cement and calcareous, silty matrix. The sand is pyritic and micaceous and generally tight. The interval includes rare stringers of limestone, light grey to brawn grey, dolomitic, dirty and partly carbonaceous. Late Bathonian - Middle Callovian, 0 (70 m) Shale, dark brown to dark grey, occasionally black, subfissile, silty micromicaceous, partly carbonaceous with traces of lignite, highly pyritic. Occasional thin beds of sandstone, white to light brown. fire to medium grained, subangular to subrounded with calcite and minor silica cementation, partly with muddy calcareous matrix, poor porosity. The sands appear predominantly in the bottom (Bathonian) part of this interval. The sequence is interrupted by thin lime- stone stringers, light brown, dirty, argillaceous, increasing in number upwards.

3.2 Syn-sedimentary and tectonic deformation Although structural analysis was not specifically part of this study, intervals affected by possible faulting or slump/slide deformation (oversteepened units) were highlighted adjacent to the facies column ('dashed' and `‘,' shading respectively). In some cases, it was not possible to provide facies breakdown for these deformed intervals. Without detailed dip processing and core integration it is difficult, in some cases, to determine whether deformation is syn-depositional or tectonic, though some intervals of probable syn- sedimentary deformation can be correlated between adjacent wells. 3.3 Orientation data A basic interpretation of orientation data was carried out, mainly to contrain correlations and to determine any overall palaeotransport/palaeoslope trends for the studied wells. This data also has important implications for predicting the orientation of sand-prone fairways, and sandbody geometry/connectivity. It should be emphasised that interpretation was brief, and much more information could be gained on sediment body geometries with more thorough analysis. Two types of data are summarised: 1. Mean dip of bedding: this is shown as dip/strike symbols on the Enclosures, giving an indication of bedding dip and the presence of angular unconformities 2. Axes of bedding rotation: these indicate intervals of bedding steepening which may be related to fault drag, shale compaction at sandstone contacts, drape/fill features or slump/slide deformation. The symbol shows the trend of the axis, the plunge direction and sense of deflection of bedding from horizontal. 4. DEPOSITIONAL SETTING Using the facies association scheme discussed above, it is possible to characterise the likely depositional setting and sandstone geometries for the genetic sequences of interest (K51-54). These are shown on correlation panel (Enclosure 6). 4.1 51 Sequence This sequence varies in thickness from c. 115m in well 35/3-5 to c. 50-60 metres in wells 35/3-1 and 35/3-2. It is shale-dominated, though 35/3-5 contains several 'lower gamma' blocky to serrated sandstone units from few- to c. 10 metres thick. Thinner (metre-scale) sandstones are recorded in 35/3-1 and 35/3-1. Shales are regularly bedded in all wells, though sandstone/heterolithic units show steep dips (massive/chaotic to discordantly bedded), with the exception of stratified/laminated sandstones from 3604-3587 metres in 35/3-5. Interpretation Basin-plain sedimentation dominated, with isolated sandstones of probable poor lateral continuity encased in shale. Steep dips at sandstone bases, and compaction of adjacent shales indicate possible channelisation, though internal character of sandstones is chaotic suggesting infilling of channels/depressions by sandy slumps or mass-flows. Oversteepened units in this sequence are restricted to the sandier middle to upper part. Consistent N-S trending axes of deformation are recorded in 35/3-5 and 35/3-2, though ENE-WSW trends are present in 35/3-2. Z & Geologi a.s / BP Norge UA /Agat Field/April 1996

STUDY OBJECTIVE The objective of this study was to carry out facies analysis of the Lower Cretaceous and Jurassic section in the 35/3-1 well to assist the location of better exploration targets in the 36/1 and 35/3 blocks. TECHNIQUES EMPLOYED The techniques of integrated fades analysis used in this report are based on the DOUBLE C*method. This necessitates the careful identification of glauconite and carbonaceous detritus in borehole samples. -23- environments Dorag dolomitization (Badiozamani, 1973) may have occurred and sideritization by remobilization of iron may have taken place. Several clastic grains (quartz and feldspar) were also partly replaced by carbonates at this time. Consequently, we believe the main diagenetic formations of the Jurassic sediments to have taken place before the overlying Aptian sediments were deposited. 2. The Cretaceous System In Aptian time the sea transgressed the Jurassic rocks, the paleoslope was towards west and erosion of the Jurassic highs took place. The break, succeeded by the Lower Cenomanian transgression, marks the transition from Lower to Upper Cretaceous. Generally, marine clays were deposited during the rest of Mesozoic. Probably shortly after or together with deposition of the Aptian sediments, early diagenetic formation of framboidal pyrite took place, in addition clay minerals and organic matter act as cementing agents. As far as only one of the Albian sandstones have been analysed, the general aspects of Albian diagenesis are only tentative. In the analysed sample kaolinite is the dominating cement, in addition to quartz-overgrowth. Kaolinite was formed after the quartz overgrowing, seen by kaolinite books surrounding quartz overgrowth. The diagenetic formation mechanisms of quartz and kaolinite were probably similar to those described for the Jurassic rocks. Probably due to higher permeability and porosity than underlying clays, Si- and Al-enriched solutions may have percolated through the rocks and precipitated as quartz-overgrowth and kaolinite cement. At the boundary between Lower and Upper Cretaceous there is regional hiatus in the area. The Jurassic/Cretaceous boundary is, however, marked by much larger break which resulted in crhonate cementation of Jurassic sediments. The much shorter Mid-Cretaceous break may be the reason why only minor amounts of diagenetic carbonates have been observed in Cower Cretaceous rocks. Maturity analyses (Q/F ratio, fig. 7) show the Albian and Cenomanian sandstones to be the most mature beds, while the strata from Cenomanian to Palaeocene display two steps of decreasing maturity. This may reflect minor changes in the source areas, e.g. by fault block movements at the Turonian/Senonian transition. At that boundary another transgressive development started.

CONCLUSIONS The oldest examined material is of Early Bajocian age and there is probably conformable sequence of Early and Mid Bajocian sediments which were deposited in restricted marine environment. There is an unconformity between 4217m and 4214m with Early Oxfordian deposits overlying those of Mid Bajocian age. There is evidence for both restricted marine and non-marine depositional environments during the Early Oxfordian. Marine deposits of Late Aptian age overlie the Early Oxfordian, and they are succeeded by thick sequence of Late Albian marine sediments.

question: For well 25/5‑3 (2430–2384.2m), list ELAN input tools and wireline logs used to derive porosity and saturation.
answer_text: ELAN inputs: bulk density (RHOB), photoelectric factor (U), neutron porosity (NPHU), compressional slowness (DT), uninvaded/invaded conductivity (CUDC, CXDC), Thorium (THOR) and Potassium (POTA); wireline logs used for porosity and saturation: density and neutron logs (RHOB, NPHU), induction/conductivity logs (DLL/DIL/CNL/CXDC/CUDC, MSFL) and gamma ray (GR).

question: For well 34/7-8, were cores from the Upper Jurassic (Dunlin/Statfjord/Lunde) depth-shifted to CDL prior to Corelab porosity and permeability analyses?
answer_text: Yes — the cores were depth-shifted to match the density log (CDL) prior to the Corelab porosity and permeability analyses.

context_snippets.text: Norsk Agip Report No. 5084/Ia Lithostratigraphy The results presented in this report are based on the analysis of ditch cuttings, sidewall cores and selected core pieces. The lithostratigraphic terminology is based on Vollset and Dore (1984) and Cameron (1993). Descriptions of colour conform to the 'Rock Color Chart' distributed by the Geological Society of America. For detailed lithological comments, the relationship between the lithological units, biostratigraphy and graphic lithology column, refer to Enclosure (1:500 scale summary log). LITHOSTRATIGRAPHIC UNITS HEGRE GROUP: 4584.8m(core)-4704m(SWC) (TNS); Age: Upper? - Middle? Triassic Examination of all available data suggests lithostratigraphic assignment to the Skagerrak Formation, Joanne Sandstone Member, discussed in full below: Skagerrak Formation, Joanne Sandstone Member: 4584.8m(core)-4704m(SWC) The Triassic section in this well comprises thick sequence of interbedded sandstones, siltstones and mudstones. The upper section (4575m-4591m) is cored and details have been supplied in the form of 1:50 scale core log. Lithologies from the remaining section have been examined from ditch cuttings and two sidewall cores. The cored section is dominated by sandstones which are predominantly fine to medium grained and locally coarse grained or pebbly representing sequence of ephemeral channels, sheetflood and channel lag deposits deposited in distal alluvial plain environment. Mudclasts and traces of carbonaceous material are noted throughout the section. Predominant colours are light green, green and grey. Red colouration typically associated with the Triassic appears to be absent. At and below 4616m, the lithologies and log profiles are similar to those of the cored interval. At 4616m the colour of the sandstones is generally very light grey or pinkish grey. They are mainly disaggregated, fine to locally coarse grained and commonly micaceous. Mudstones and siltstones recorded within this section are subordinate and predominantly dark grey or medium dark grey in colour, much of which is probably due to significant caving from the overlying Jurassic. Only traces of the characteristic pale to moderate reddish brown Triassic lithologies are recorded in ditch cuttings samples but, significantly, both the sidewall core samples at 4695.1m and 4704m from the 2/5-10A well comprise argillaceous siltstones which are entirely red.

• 3 LOG ANALYSIS 3.1 Log data and quality The 13 3/8 casing was set at mRKB (drillers depth). Both the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group was evaluated during the TD-logging in the 12 1/4 borehole section. HTHP mud with density of g/cc was used in this borehole section. The logs run in well 2/2-5 are shown in figure 3.1. The wireline and pipeconveyed logging service was performed by Schlumberger and the Triple Combo MWD service was performed by Teleco. For further information, see operational report (chapter 5). Log data from the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group are partly from logs run on drillpipe (3352.0- 3629.0 m), partly Triple Combo MWD data (3550.0-4080.0 m). Bad hole conditions made it impossible to run logs on wireline or on drillpipe below approximately 3600 m. Below this depth Teleco resistivity/density/neutron sub was used. After logging with Triple Combo MWD, the well was plugged back to m. In the petrophysical interpretation data from wireline logs have been used in the interval to m. From to Triple Combo MWD data have been used. Both the wireline logs and the MWD logs are highly influenced by washouts which especially is reflected in poor quality density/neutron logs. It is especially the shales which are washed out. From log calculation the shales of the upper Farsund Unit, interval 3426.0-3550.0, have erratic high effective porosities. In these shale-zones the porosity have been set to zero. 3.2 Log analysis method The Farsund Unit, Intra Farsund Sand and the Hegre Group have been analysed using computer model, based on the complex lithology method using the density log for porosity calculations with corrections for hydrocabon and shale effects. Shale volume has been determined from the gamma-ray log and the resistivity data using the R, value. In most sections the gamma-ray log has been used while the R, curve has been used in wash-out sections. In the pipeconveyed section the induction log is used to calculate the true resistivity of the uninvaded formation. The resistivity of the invaded zone is calculated from the microspherical focused log. The resistivity logs are corrected for borehole and invasion effects. In the MWD section the RACM curve (Resistivity Amplitude Ratio Corrected Memory) is used as the true resistivity of the formation while the RPCM curve (Resistivity Phase Difference Corrected Memory) is used as the resistivity of the invaded zone. Formation water resistivity and mud filtrate resistivity are varied with depth using temperature gradient established from Horner plots of temperature data.

RESULTS Well 6305/12-1 was drilled to T.D. at 4302m in Triassic Hegre Group Equivalent Conglomerates on 12th September 1991 and then plugged and abandoned as dry hole on 18th September 1991. Thinly developed, hydrocarbon bearing, sandstones were encountered in the Late Cretaceous.Svarte Formation, and Early Cretaceous which generally displayed poor direct and cut fluorescences while being drilled, which later proved to be oil-bearing, though tight, in subsequent cased-hole RFT's. The Middle Jurassic Unit exhibited interbedded thin sand- stones, coals and claystones. trace of oil was observed to be seeping from fractures in thin coal band (see core#1). Chromatographic analysis of drilled gas showed C4's to be present from the Late Cretaceous Blodoks Formation through to the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, where they gradually diminished towards the base, and being absent below 3970m. A summary of the Petrophysical Evaluation indicates 144.6m net sand within the Paleocene Sand Unit is water bearing, with an average porosity of 19.7%. Moveable hydrocarbons were detected in thin Svarte sandstone stringers with 3.75m net pay, and an average porosity of 14.4% was interpreted. No reservoir potential was encoutered below the Cretaceous. Two cased-hole RFT runs were performed, obtaining two sets of fluid samples from the Svarte Formation. No reliable pressures were obtained, however small volumes of oil were recovered. The results of these tests may be found in Appendix III, whilst further discussion may be found in Norsk Hydro report Petrophysical Evaluation Report, Well 6305/12-1.

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

Halliburton Geo Consultants Limited IV. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

Cretaceous and Tertiary times provided period of relative tectonic quiescence. The basin-fill was primarily affected by regional basin downwarp, resulting in gently westward thickening wedge of Cretaceous and Tertiary strata. Reactivation along the pre-Cretaceous fault systems, resulting from an Alpine N-S compressional field during early Tertiary times, and continuing salt movements, generated some inversion features and localised thickening of the overlying stratigraphic sequence. Halokinetic movements have occurred from Triassic times onwards, with particularly important episode coinciding with, and possibly triggered by, the Late Kimmerian tectonic event. 2.2 Regional Stratigraphy and Basinal Development (Fig. 4) The oldest sedimentary strata penetrated in the area are coarse clastic sediments of the Rotliegendes Formation (Lower Permian in age). Volcanic intercalations are found in the basinal area (well 3/7-2). Marine incursions during late Permian times led to the deposition of thick evaporites (salt together with anhydrite and carbonates) in the subsiding SOgne Basin. After the sea receded thick Triassic sequence was deposited over the Zechstein evaporites and carbonates. This phase of sedimentation continued into Late Triassic/Early Jurassic times: possible Lower Jurassic strata have been reported only from the well 3/5-2. At the end of Early Jurassic times rifting phase took place. Block faulting, accompanied by drop in sea level and subsequent erosion of the emerged blocks, led to the deposition of fluvio-deltaic sediments of Aalenian to Bathonian age (the Bryne Formation, within the Vestland Group). These comprise alternating shales and sandstones with occasional laterally persistent coals. The potential sediment source areas were the Mandel High and the Southern Vestland Arch. A second phase of uplift and non-deposition occurred at the end of the Middle Jurassic, expressed in the Callovian Unconformity. This

Cretaceous times: the associated faulting affects mainly the lower part of the Chalk. Carbonate sedimentation was terminated during the Early Palaeocene by increased clastic input. Sedimentation during Palaeocene and Eocene times is characterised by series of marine transgressions and regressions. Claystones and limestones constitute the greater part of the Paleogene sequence, with locally well developed sandstones at the base. Volcanic tuffs and tuffaceous shales of the Balder Formation indicate widespread volcanic event at the Palaeocene - Eocene boundary. question: How does the mineralogy of Plug10 NiseFm (illite-dominated, ferroan calcite, siderite, plagioclase-rich) compare to SkalmenFm?
answer_text: Plug 10 (Nise Fm.) is illite‑dominated with prominent ferroan calcite replacement, minor siderite and relatively high plagioclase (≈11–13%), whereas the Skalmen Fm. is comparatively more kaolinitic with notable glauconite/chlorite and lower plagioclase.

This biogenic fabric is well seen as the mudrocks transform to green colour and clean medium grained sand-filled burrows are preserved, presumably piping down sand from the overlying unconformity surface of the Skalmen Formation. This uppermost green mudrock contains glauconite /chlorite and phosphatic shell fragments (Fig. 3A,D), whilst the mudrocks as whole appear to be of mixed clay composition (illite with subordinate smectite or chlorite-smectite and kaolinite; Fig. 3E). The more kaolinitic nature of the clay-fraction in the single Skalmen sample analysed by XRD (Plug 2; Fig. 3E) adds weight to the argument that the mudrock interval may be of different provenance. Interpretation: as with the Skalmen sandstones, the combination of glauconite/chlorite and burrowing (especially the Chondrites-type) suggests a marine setting. The association of reddening, intense bioturbation and sand-filled burrows piping down from the overlying unconformity all point to reduced sedimentation rates and the existence of submarine hiatal surface at the mudrock /sandstone interface. Collectively therefore sand- starved site below wave base is implied, arguably associated with depositional high. However, the thrust of this interpretation would be undermined if all the burrowing were associated with the hiatal surface; this would open up other possibilities for the mudrock origin (see End. 1). Wireline log characteristics: over the cored interval the Nise Formation mudrocks have very distinctive log signature: • high gamma (c.105API), and • widely separated mudrock-style neutron/density cross-over with density values of c.2.20gm/cm3 and neutron values of c.35-45PU. Below this interval the gamma profile is bowed with the lowest values being c.75API whilst the neutron/density traces have persistent mudrock-type cross-over, not significantly dissimilar from the Skalmen Formation; mudrock to dirty sandstone type of elastic succession is therefore suggested. Mineralogy and reservoir quality Only single mudrock sample (Plug 10, 1759.80m dd) has been reviewed in thin-section, although XRD analysis has been performed on an additional three samples (Fig. 3E). The modal and textural results for Plug 10 are presented on Figure 3A. Note that as the sample is mudrock, the textural data reflects the grain size and sorting characteristics of the sand fraction. In thin-section, the sample appears to support disrupted /bioturbated predominantly illitic matrix (63.6%; green, ?smectitic/?chloritic clays are also present, 11.5%), now extensively replaced by ferroan calcite and to more minor extent microcrystalline siderite (Fig. 3A,D). Interspersed within the matrix are sand grade framework and ductile grains. The framework grains (13%) comprise quartz, K-feldspar, plagioclase, igneous rock fragments and scarce phosphatic shelly debris. The ductile grains include large, green, microporous clasts of probable smectitic composition (?tuff; 3.5%), glauconite / chlorite beads (2.5%) and mica (2.5%, principally biotite). Ferroan calcite (displaying pseudo-beef textures) constitutes the dominant authigenic mineral but since it is primarily replacive of mud it has been recorded as such. Other trace authigenic components include kaolinite (after mica), microcrystalline siderite, and pyrite. XRD analysis of the red/brown mudrocks lower down in the succession indicates significant compositional differences with the overlying Skalmen Formation (Fig. 3E). question: How do Utsira reflectors in loose sand/clay affect drilling vibration, anchoring, shallow-gas and stratigraphic interpretation?
answer_text: They have caused high drilling vibration/shock (observed at wells 31/7-1 and 30/9-23) and reduce anchor holding due to loose sand with thin clay layers; they produce high‑amplitude, complex reflectors that complicate stratigraphic interpretation (possible extrusive sand vents or gravity‑flow deposits), but no shallow gas is expected at the appraisal location to the limit of interpretation.

These appear to be part of wider sand deposit which is present across much of the eastern corner of the survey area, including at the Appraisal Well Op location. Similar features have been noted within the Utsira Formation in the wider region around the survey area and several published studies outline conflicting mechanisms for the creation of the feature. question: For well 30/6-E-6, which slim PDC/AutoTrak BHA components are used, and what mud, tripping, or connection mitigations correspond to each?
answer_text: BHA components: PDC bit, 8-1/4 AutoTrak, MAP sub, CSDP, 6-1/2 jar and HWDP. Mitigations: keep mud specs within limits (low filter‑loss/LGS), adjust mud viscosity to milling spec and displace to s.g. OBM as required, minimize connection/survey time, rotate the string before pumping to break gel, be careful when tripping through shale/clay and avoid rotating the BHA in the casing window.

However, this high mud weight cause significant hydrostatic overbalance drilling the pressure depleted formation. Due to the lower pore pressure and the reduced fracture-gradient, the risk of lost circulation has increased. In addition, due to the potential high hydrostatic overbalance the risk of differential sticking has increased. The following measures shall be emphasised drilling E-7 A: Drilling BHA to be optimised to avoid differential sticking, e.g. include only CSDPs, no DCs. Always keep the mud specifications within the given limitations. Keep the filter-loss and the LGS-parameters at the lower end of specifications. Plan the operations in order to minimise the time used when making connections and taking surveys. • Also be careful when initiating pumping, especially after trip. Rotate the drillstring prior to start pumping carefully to break the gelstrength of the mud. • Always be careful when tripping through shale/clay, and be aware of the increased risk of hole pack-off when tripping from clay/shale into sandstone. • Use the annular pressure sub to ensure good hole cleaning and avoid pressure pulses in the wellbore. • Evaluate wiper trips in the horizontal sections if signs of poor hole cleaning, and in case of intervals with clay/shale or rapid changes between sand and shale. question: Across NORNE wells, how do petrophysical log responses, pore-pressure indicators, and formation-pressure trends compare?
answer_text: Petrophysical logs show normal compaction in the upper Nordland and anomalous responses below ~1650 mRKB; pore-pressure indicators (gas, hole conditions, cavings, flowline temperature, modified Dxc, sonic and RFTs) consistently detect overpressure. SPERRY - SUN PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) Sonic log: Can be used to calculate pore pressures, using Eaton’s formula, and subsequently confirm and/or revise any pore pressure calculations made whilst drilling. 6608/10-D-1 AH/BH

Good reservoir properties in the Tofte Formation and the lower part of the Tilje Formation gave reliable pressure measurements in these intervals. SUMMARY: This shallow drilling project has been run in the Skagerrak area, northeast of the Farsund Subbasin. In September 1988, 667 km of shallow seismic data were collected. Subcropping bedrock units and Quaternary thickness were mapped and potential drillsites selected. Four holes have been drilled: 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88 and 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 on line IKU-0822SK-88. The drilling was carried out with M/S Bucentaur in May 1989. The water depth for the localities varied from 505 to 525 and the Quaternary overburden from to m. The holes were drilled from 90 to below sea bed (603.7 to 817.5 below sea level). The four cores comprise about 420 of diamond (piggyback) drilling in bedrock of Paleozoic and Mesozoic age. The coring yielded 370 of samples representing 88.5% recovery in average. This report presents seismic interpretation, sedimentology, petrophysical logs and core measurements, biostratigraphy and organic geochemistry. In addition, special studies have been made including trace fossil analyses, thermal conductivity, oedo- meter and apatite fission track analysis. The depositional environment, bedrock subcrop distribution, stratigraphy, regional correlations and burial history are discussed. KEYWORDS: Shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin North Sea Paleozoic Skagerrak Mesozoic SkOries

As they give information about maximum temperature and timing, another two samples were picked from core 13/2-U-2 and submitted to Geotrack International, Australia. Even if the most promising intervals of the core were selected, the two samples did not yield single grain of apatite or zircon. Unfortunately, it was therefore not possible to proceed further with the fission track analysis. 4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Good bathymetric maps are of great help in interpreting the outcropping geology between seismic lines. On Figure the previous geological inter- pretation is combined with the new bathymetric map. The steep slope in southwest along the - fault is very striking. On the SW - NE line IKU- 101SK-88, sp 3000-3200, topographic high of about 50 was found and the form was discussed in the Main Report. From the bathymetric map it is clear that the high is not local dome but more the easternmost seen extension of WNW - ESE trending ridge. This trend can also be seen on the three dimensional perspective view (Figure 2.3). The bathymetric map has thus limited the discussion about volcanic intrusions by showing that dome structure probably does not exist. No clear evidence of outcropping volcanic rocks is seen near the drill site. In combination with the seismic evidence of possible subcropping volcanic rocks (e. g. the strong disturbance and loss of reflection continuity on line IKU-0822SK-88, sp 2700-2900) there might be subcropping dike system in the area as indicated on Figure 4.1. From the shallow drilling program in 1989 it seems probable that also the Paleozoic rocks found outcropping east of 9°E in the Skagerrak area is of mainly Cambro-Silurian age. Core 13/2-U-2 was postmature, but evaluating the above suggested existence of volcanic dike, we still find it very probable that this was caused by later Paleozoic intrusions. This is also supported by the supposed migrated hydrocarbon content in the core. We therefore find it highly valuable to continue the investigation of the Paleozoic rocks in the Skagerrak area. Our recommendation is to acquire shallow seismic data between 9° and 10° and then continue with shallow drilling based on the results of the seismic.

INTRODUCTION 5_Eg , _INTEF-GRUPPEN The joint industrial research and development program SHALLOW DRILLING FARSUND SUBBASIN 1988/89 had the objective to carry out shallow seismic, shallow drilling and laboratory examination of the subcropping bedrock in the Skagerrak area northeast of the Farsund Subbasin and to evaluate these data. The main target was to collect high quality bedrock cores from selected intervals of the Mesozoic and Paleozoic strata in the area. The program of shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin was initiated from near- shore bedrock mapping project in the coastal Norwegian North Sea areas. This study was based on existing data, mainly conventional seismic, and was carried out by IKU in cooperation with NPD (Oljedirektoratet) and Statoil (Rokoengen et al. 1988). proposal for shallow drilling program was put forward to several companies of which seven supported the program as Early Participants. One company joined as an Early Late Participant before drilling started (and increased the budget) and one company has, so far, joined as Late Participant after drilling. NPD had observer status in the project. Following the intentions of the inaugural meeting in Stavanger on 19th August 1988, shallow seismic survey with 667 km of digital (2.5 sec.) and analog equipment was run in September 1988 (Figure 1.1). The data were collected and processed by A/S Geoteam. Based on the new seismic data, revised bedrock and Quaternary thickness maps were presented and possible coring sites proposed in February 1989 (Lippard and Rokoengen 1989). Dril- ling program and priorities were discussed and decided on Steering Committee meeting at Oppdal and applications sent to NPD in March 1989. First priority was given to the two drillsites 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 (Figure 1.1) located on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate Base Cretaceous and cover most of the Jurassic section in the area. Second priority was given to the drill- sites 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 located on the shallow seismic line IKU-0822SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate the oldest Mesozoic sediments (of supposed Triassic age) and give information from the Paleozoic rocks in the area. The drillings were done on the platform northeast of the Farsund Subbasin (Figure 1.2), where the drilled strata can be tied into the basin itself.

Apart from rutile, zircon and garnet, tourmaline is the most commonly occurring heavy mineral these samples. Tourmaline which is common to variety of metamorphic and magmatic (pegmatitic) rocks except for granulites, has been recorded in 15 sections from wells. As for the other minerals mentioned of possible importance to provenance, the distribution of tourmaline does not show any geographical trends. A mineral separation is clearly needed to concentrate the heavy minerals to produce statistically significant provenance information. Well 6407/9-1 stand out in this context. Of the detailed minerals garnet, Ti-Bt, RNQ and tourmaline samples from this well contained few grains of garnet only, and no members of the other three minerals. Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions (liquid-dominated as well as gas-dominated inclusions) have been observed hosted in overgrowth zones of both quartz and feldspar in some of the samples of this study. However, as this is point-coint study, fluid inclusion have not in any way been mapped as would have been the case in hydrocarbon fluid inclusion screening. Nevertheless, the use of microthermometry on the samples studied may well constrain the temperature (and time?) aspect of the major pore volume altering reactions which in this study are quartz overgrowth and feldspar dissolution. 41) Conclusive remarks The two overall most important diagenetic reactions responsible for pore volume alterations in the samples studied are quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) reducing porosity and (K-) feldspar dissolution which definitely is the major contributor to the formation of secondary pore volumes (PVSC). The table in Appendix shows positive correlation of quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) with depth of 0.65. K-feldspar (FSKF) shows negative correlation with depth of (feldspar dissolution). (The formation of PVSC shows positive correlation with depth of 0.34.) Though samples show grain sizes up to 500 microns practically no samples have been found to contain rock fragments as to be suitable as provenance indicators. The heavy minerals zircon and rutile are recorded in trace amounts in nearly every sample. Heavy minerals or detrital minerals (or mineral inclusions) that represent specific metamorphic facies do not give any consistent geographical distribution or clustering. Hence, no suitable provenance indicators have been recorded apart from the possible use of zircons for radiometric dating.

This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. context_snippets.text: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS 1. Samples and Fluids Used in the Testing Core Samples The core material used for this work was obtained from Ringhome Field Wells 25/11-23, 25/8-12S, and 25/8-12A (a sidetrack of 25/8-12S), Norwegian North Sea. These wells were cored with oil-based mud during ENAS's 2Q1999 appraisal drilling campaign. The core was stabilized with gypsum and transported to ResLab's laboratory in Stavanger, Norway. Plug samples were cut using rotary bit cooled with air and packaged with double screens (fine and coarse) on the ends and wrapped in TeflonTm tape and tin sheet. These plugs were first preserved in ProtecCoreTM heat-sealable laminate pouches. In order to stabilize them for shipping, they were later re-preserved by wrapping in plastic wrap and dipping in CoreSealTM (wax). Details of procedures used are reported elsewhere (Conventional Core Analysis Reports for Wells 25/11-23, 25/8-12S, and 25/8-12A, ResLab 2000). total of 184 plugs were shipped in this state to URC in July, 2000. Testing began shortly thereafter. All samples were imaged by Westport Technology Center Intl. (Houston) using X-Ray computerized tomography (CT). The resulting images, provided in Appendix A, were used to identify samples that were not good candidates for testing because of heterogeneities, fractures, or insufficient length.' Ninety-six of the most suitable plugs were sent to Omni Laboratories (Houston) for measurements of as-received permeability to oil. These data were used for selecting samples for specific core analysis tests. Omni's results are presented in Appendix B. Nine samples were provided to PIS Labs International, Inc. in Houston for electrical property and capillary pressure measurements by the porous plate method. The porous plate capillary pressure data are reported elsewhere (PTS Laboratories, Inc.: File No. 21964, December 2001). The porous plate capillary pressure measurements are compared to the centrifuge capillary pressure measurements made at URC in Section 3. The PTS report is presented in Appendix C. Samples used in each test, along with their properties, are listed in Tables 1-1 to 1-4. Fluids Used Two synthetic brines, formulated for use with Eocene and Jurassic core samples in testing at URC, had total dissolved solids (TDS) of 50,587 and 68,007 mg/L, respectively. Detailed compositions of these brines are given in Table 1-5. The composition of the brine used in testing the Jurassic core samples was based on formation water analysis from well 25/8-11. For the Eocene cores, the brine was based on formation water analyses from Balder. Also presented in Appendix are sieve analysis, laser particle size analysis (LPSA), and high pressure mercury injection results (Integrated Core Consultancy Services, 1999) on selection of samples from each well, not including the test samples. These data are presented in lieu of measurements on the actual test samples, for future reference. question: Which FIS signatures, bitumen/inclusion observations, and DST wetness indicate paleo-charge in hydrocarbon-bearing intervals?
answer_text: Strong FIS response with high visual inclusion abundance (common/abundant/extremely abundant), significant bitumen (dead oil stain or asphaltic residue), absence of water‑soluble anomalies or other independent current‑charge indicators, and a valid DST showing the interval to be currently wet.

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 Current Charge A zone that displays strong FIS hydrocarbon indications and high visual petroleum in- clusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) may reflect penetrated pay, but could also indicate paleo-charge or, in some cases, migration pathway (e.g., where inclusion abundance is enhanced by extensive microfracturing). provisional interpretation of current charge is strengthened if residual petroleum (especially live oil stain) is identified in thin section, and particularly if water-soluble petroleum species (so-called proximal pay indicators; see below) are recorded in FIS data (e.g., in the seal overlying the anomaly, in the water leg underlying the anomaly, or in low permeability zones within the reservoir section itself). Any independent indications (e.g., from electric logs or mudlog gas shows) provide further encouragement. Paleo-charge Intervals of strong FIS response, high visual inclusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) and significant bitumen (e.g., dead oil stain or asphaltic residue) without accompanying water-soluble anomalies or independent evidence of current charge, may represent paleo-column, but could also represent current charge or in rare cases migration pathway. The interpretation of paleo-charge is favored if valid DST has shown the interval to be currently wet. Recycled inclusions Very rarely, detritus that is generated from previous sedimentary rock may contain inher- ited petroleum inclusions. These inclusions must be recognized, as they clearly do not provide any useful information about the current petroleum system(s). Petrographic or microther- mometric criteria can often be used to argue the origin of these inclusions, for instance, the presence of petroleum inclusions along recycled quartz overgrowths, or measured homogeniza- tion temperatures that are too high to have been produced during the current burial history. Associated FIS depth trends are usually erratic and poorly compartmentalized, and inclusion abundance is typically low. Inherited inclusions may be restricted to specific geologic units that derived detritus from particular provenance, and are not found in intercalated chemical precipitates (e.g. bedded carbonates or diagenetic cements). Heavy bitumen stain In some instances, pore-occluding bitumen may contribute to FIS signals. Here, solid petroleum behaves as any other cement, and is capable of trapping residual hydrocarbons as bitumen-hosted fluid inclusions. These may be invisible due to the opacity of the solid petroleum host. Petroleum species may also desorb from pore-occluding bitumen during crush- ing, much as they do from mature kerogen (see below). Bitumen-sourced FIS responses may be inferred when strongly anomalous zones contain low visible petroleum inclusion abundance but have significant amounts of bitumen (e.g., common, abundant or extremely abundant). Abundant pore-filling bitumen in porous rock implies significant petroleum saturation at some time, so low visual petroleum inclusion abundance is unexpected (and not commonly encoun- tered). In such cases it is possible either that the size of the inclusions are below the resolution of the light microscope (< micron), that grain surface conditions (e.g., wettability) did not favor trapping of inclusions, or that the section was diagenetically quiescent during and after charging (i.e., little or no cementation or microfracturing).

A.4 Individual Track Plots A.4.1 Explanation and Significance of Individual Track Plots The following is synopsis of the significance of the different patterns of mass abundances and abundance ratios shown in Tracks 1-25. Note that not all species are quantified using their parent or molecular peaks (e.g., methane at m/z = 15) in order to minimize interfering contributions from other species. A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. However, the previous report for the Obelix location, situated 24km to the SSW of the Asterix site was made available to which the stratigraphy was tied (see section 9).

A.2 FIS Mass Spectra 43 is inferred (but not demonstrated) only in the presence of other sulfur species. The m/z 32 would appear to be good one for indicating sulfur presence; however, this ion location suffers major potential interference from atmospheric oxygen (O+2 ). Care must be taken when interpreting sulfur-enriched FIS spectra, because at first glance they resemble the water-soluble enriched spectra. Ideally, the distinction lies in the location of CS2 at m/z 76 (as opposed to benzene at 78), H2S at m/z 34 and S+2 and/or SO2 at m/z 64. SO2 presence can be verified by the presence of paired anomaly at 64 and 48. In practice, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between sulfur-enrichment and water-soluble species enrichment when these species are not strongly anomalous, and combinations of the two spectra occur as well. A.2.3 Summary of the Five Spectral Types The above is relatively detailed account of the characteristics of the five major classes of FIS mass spectra. In the end, however, the best way to recognize and distinguish among spectral types is to compare them to the end-member examples presented herein and categorize them by eye. After examining few examples of each, pattern recognition will become easy. Understanding the complexities outlined in the previous sections is important, but usually unnecessary for first-order interpretation of FIS mass spectra. To summarize: Non-hydrocarbon Spectra: Characterized by four peak clusters centered on m/z 15, 28, 42 and 55; the first three being dominant. Most peaks are attributable to water and carbon dioxide. Gas-range enriched: Characterized by strong responses on C1-C5 (m/z 12-72) and lesser intensities on higher molecular weight ion locations. Peak clusters may be more broad at m/z 12-30 and 37-46. Predominance of masses 15 and 16, and high 57/55 ratios is possible. Liquid-range enriched: Characterized by the presence of C7-C13+ species as regularly-spaced peak clusters in the m/z 95-180 range, which are dominated by ions from paraffinic and naph- thenic compounds. Aromatic species contribute subordinate peak clusters between the paraffin- naphthene peaks (although, typically only benzene, toluene and xylenes are resolved). Water-soluble enriched: Characterized by methane, ethane, organic acids, benzene and toluene. Acetic Acid (m/z 60) and aromatic peak clusters (m/z 78, 91, 105) attain intensities near or greater than those of adjacent paraffin-naphthene peak clusters. Sulfur-compound enriched: Characterized by the presence of H2S, COS, CS2 and SO2 and/or native sulfur gas as indicated by anomalies on some combination of the m/z peaks 34, 48, 60, 64 and 76. A.2.4 Combinations of Spectral Types Combined FIS spectra are common, and appear as superimposed end member types. Although combinations of all end member spectra have been noted, the most common are gas + liquids and liquids + water-solubles. Recall that FIS is bulk technique and samples the entire fluid history of the pore system. Hence, mixed FIS spectra might be expected if the sample has experienced temporally distinct charges of petroleum (or brine) types or contained heterogeneous (immiscible) fluid in the pore system at some time.

context_snippets.text: GEOLOGICAL COMPLETION REPORT 6404/11-1 SUMMARY GENERAL PL 254 was awarded to consortium comprising BP Amoco, TotalFinaElf, Norske Conoco and the SDFI (now Petoro AS) as part of the 16th Licencing Round on the 20th May 2000. BP Amoco operate the licence. The pre-drill objective of well 6404/11-1 was to test three primary reservoir targets at T50, K90 and K80 levels and have an option to test one secondary target at K72 level in the Havsule Prospect. The prospect is seismically defined north - south trending structural dome located in the north of the Møre Basin in the Norwegian Sea that is thought to have developed during the Tertiary Period in response to compression during opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. OPERATIONS BP Amoco took over the dynamically positioned (DP) semi-submersible rig, Scarabeo 5, at 19:00 hrs on 14th November 2001 with the rig arriving at the Havsule location at 15:00 hrs on the 24th November 2001. DP trials were undertaken and after the seafloor transponders were deployed, the 6404/11-1 well was spudded at 21:30 hrs on the 1st December 2001. A 12 1/4” pilot hole was drilled from seabed to 2195 mBRT in one bit run. No indications of shallow gas or abnormal pore pressures were observed from drilling data or on LWD. After drilling to section TD the bit was pulled and the hole opened to 36” to 1629 mBRT. While repositioning one of the subsea marker buoys it was inadvertently dropped into the hole necessitating re-spud of the well 28.6m to the north-north west of the original hole location. The well was re-spudded at 13:30 hrs on the 6th December 2001 using 42” 36” hole opener assembly. 26” hole was drilled to 2175 mBRT with seawater and hi-vis sweeps. After displacing to seawater, circulating the hole clean and pulling to 1870 mBRT bubbles were seen flowing from the wellhead. Drillpipe was run to bottom and the hole was made static with 1.20sg mud. Casing was run and cemented without problem, however weather delayed running the BOP’s and riser. The 17” hole section was TD’d 15m shallow to prognosis due to concerns over increasing pore pressure. After running and cementing the 13 3/8” casing it was necessary to run piggy-back casing hanger to allow the seal assembly to seat in the correct position. A value of 1.38sg was obtained for the leak-off after drilling out the 13 3/8” casing and drilling 12 1/4” hole commenced. Drilling was halted at 2730 mBRT when pore pressure was seen to have reached 1.25sg and the bit was pulled into the casing shoe. In an attempt to carry on drilling an open-hole leak-off was performed that confirmed the 1.38sg value obtained earlier. Having insufficient kick tolerance to drill ahead, the decision was made to run 5/8” liner. triple-combo wireline log was run to acquire data over the drilled section. Liner was set and 1.47sg leak-off was obtained. Drilling commenced in 1/2” hole. No reservoir horizons were identified and the well was TD’d at 02:45 hrs on the 20th February at depth of 3650 mBRT. Three wireline logging runs were performed. The 6404/11-1 well was plugged and abandoned as dry hole at 22:00 hrs on the 10th March 2002 and the rig released to Norsk Hydro. RESULTS The shallowest primary target (Early Eocene T50 sandstones) was absent at the well location. Upper Cretaceous (K90 sandstones) were absent and K80 (Nise Formation) sandstones were poorly developed. The well was not extended to penetrate the deeper, K72 (Lysing Formation) secondary target.

The Base Cretaceous Unconformity and the Intra Are Coal Marker were used as guides for the structural interpretation. The characteristics of Cretaceous and Tertiary reflectors will not be commented upon here, as they have limited influence of the reservoir level. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flowline temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. question: For VSP at well 33/9-18, which displays—VC/VD, F-K, or AT versus depth—most reliably yield true dip?
answer_text: The AT versus depth display (measurement of the AT against vertical depth increment) most reliably yields true dip.

context_snippets.text: BSD/VSP/VC.2 DISPLAY VC Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display describes the primary and multiple reflection responses of the subsurface at the borehole location, within and below the depth range of the VSP. This data is filtered using the 'maximum bandwidth' filter designed after F-K analysis to determine the usable bandwidth of the upgoing wavefield. In marine data, if source signature deconvolution has been applied, then the input wavelet is zero phase and the wavelet contained in the data is zero phase modified by earth absorption and transmission loss effects (ie mixed phase). Events that reach the time-depth curve are primary and their lithologic significance can be established unequivocally by reference to the calibrated velocity log. Multiples having their last bounce from primary within the range of the VSP may be identified by observing their termination in the data at the same depth point at which the primary cuts the time-depth curve. From this display, any dip across the well location can be recognised by moveout of the primary event to shorter time, as the geophone moves up the well and away from the lithology creating the reflection. No azimuth of dip can be computed from this display but true dip can be computed from measurement of the AT against vertical depth increment. Unconformities may be recognised by an abrupt change of moveout of adjacent primary events. Topographical features up-dip away from the well may be recognised by an increase in the AT or in the termination of an event away from the time-depth curve. Dip increasing up-dip away from the well can be observed in the data; however, if dip is decreasing up-dip (ie crest of an anticline) then the event in question will disappear from the data. Dip can be calculated using the method described in the Appendix contained in this report. DISPLAY VC(FK) F-K Display of Upgoing Wavefield at two-way time before enhancement This display is used in the design of the 'maximum bandwidth' filter in conjunction with the F-K display of the deconvolved upgoing wavefield and filter trials. It shows the data from the upgoing wavefield at two-way time transformed into F-K space. Any filter applied to the data before transformation is noted on the display. Since the upgoing wavefield is aligned horizontally, or near horizontally, in T-X space (unless there is steep dip across the well location) it is aligned vertically, through zero wavenumber, in F-K space. The 'maximum bandwidth' filter is the least restrictive filter that can be applied to the upgoing wavefield to remove noise whilst retaining resolution of the data in the zone of interest. The F-K analysis is therefore performed on data within window around the zone of interest. Additionally, the data is windowed in time so that data analysed is close to the time-depth curve, where we would expect better resolution. If the zone of interest is not known, it is assumed to be just above T.D. of the well.

S Abstract The dipmeter from the Jurassic and part of Cretaceous of 33/9-18 is of high quality and only degraded in sections of irregular borehole. Irregular borehole sections are found in brecciated, fractured or strongly sheared zones, often subhorizontal. The mode of drilling is not related to quality of hole. The absence of borehole breakout indicates low horizontal stress anisotropy. This can only be explained by low macroscopic strength due to densely spaced dislocation planes. The Jurassic is of extreme complexity but can be understood if it is subdivided into four structural domains: 1) huge block of lower Jurassic sliding off the Statiford crest during early rifting in Upper Jurassic collapses under its own weight. Albeit strongly deformed internally, the gross stratigraphy is preserved 2) series of smaller slides are emplaced, forming pile of imbrication sheets with varying internal bedding orientation 3) turbidites are deposited on strongly sculptured surface, enclosing occasional allochthonous slide blocks, and sliding into local swales to form slightly reoriented sheets or wedges 4) deposition of Draupne shale as the basin floor rotates due to continued main fault activity. Changes in the plunge of deformation axes are ascribed to syndepositional activity of large transverse fault. Gravitational instability of the talus wedge led to the formation of low angle thrusts, thought to affect also the Cretaceous, causing minor reorientation of lamination.

A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 9/2-7S is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are claystones, sandstones and carbonaceous siltstones of the Vestland Group, Bryne Formation which accumulated in fluviodeltaic environment during Bajocian-Bathonian and ?Bathonian times. An unconformity is present between the Bryne Formation and the overlying Sandnes Formation with the absence of Bathonian?-?Callovian sediments. A marine transgression during Early?-Middle Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of claystones, sandstones and coals of the Sandnes Formation in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment. Further transgression during Late Oxfordian times resulted in the deposition of the silty claystones of the Boknfjord Group, Egersund Formation initially in marginal marine to marine, inner shelf environment and then in marine, inner shelf conditions. Deposition of the Egersund Formation continued throughout Late Oxfordian and early Kimmeridgian times. The Egersund Formation was succeeded by the claystones of the Tau Formation at the onset of Kimmeridgian times, representing further transgression. The Tau Formation was deposited during Kimmeridgian and Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times in marine, outer shelf environment. The uppermost section analysed has been assigned to the Sauda Formation and was deposited in similar environment during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times.

Abstract This report contains mineralogical and microstructural descriptions of Middle Jurassic sandstones from the Sandnes Fm cored in well 9/2-1. Petrographic modal analysis and x-ray diffraction mineralogical data are reported for 22 sandstones together with estimates of grain size and sorting and GECO's plug analysis on porosity and permeability. In addition, x-ray diffraction analysis of the clay fraction of selected samples from drill stem test intervals are reported. The relationship between primary sand composition, diagenesis, and reservoir quality is discussed with reference to selected photomicrographs of petrographic thin sections and scanning electron microscope photomicrographs, with special emphasis on the reservoir properties of the drill stem test intervals. GEOLOGICAL HISTORY The deepest sediments encountered in the Statoil 9/2-3 well were claystones and coals attributed to the Bryne Formation (Vestland Group). general Middle Jurassic age is suggested by the long-ranging miospore assemblages present although regionally the Bryne Formation is considered to be of Bajocian to ?Bathonian age. Deltaic/paralic environments of deposition are indicated for this sequence. A stratigraphical hiatus separates the Bryne Formation from the overlying Sandnes Formation (Vestland Group). The Sandnes Formation is predominantly sandstone sequence representing deposition in relatively high energy, shallow marine environment close to terrestrial source. This arenaceous depositional phase is considered to have been initiated by a late Callovian transgression which continued into earliest mid Oxfordian times. Sand deposition was terminated in the Oxfordian and replaced by claystones attributed to the Egersund Formation (Boknfjord Group). These argillaceous sediments represent deposition in relatively nearshore shelf setting and are dated as Oxfordian. An intraformational palynofacies break manifested by reduced terrestrial influences within the late Oxfordian is interpreted as the horizon of the pseudocordata Zone transgressive event. Egersund Formation shelf claystone deposition continued through the early Kimmeridgian into the late Kimmeridgian. A further transgressive event associated with the eudoxus Zone (late Kimmeridgian) was responsible for water mass stratification and the development of anoxic bottom waters which resulted in the deposition of the sapropelic Tau Formation (Boknfjord Group) claystones. Tau Formation sediments are dated as Kimmeridgian to early Volgian in this well. The Tau Formation is conformably overlain by claystones of the Sauda Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as early Volgian to early Ryazanian in age. They are envisaged to have been deposited in generally regressive shelf palaeoenvironment with dysaerobic bottom waters. The Sauda Formation is overlain with apparent conformity by identical claystones of the Flekkefjord Formation (Boknfjord Group) which are dated as late Ryazanian in age. They represent deposition in low energy, ?sub wavebase shelf setting under overall regressive conditions. The Flekkefjord Formation - Valhall Formation (Cromer Knoll Group) boundary which regionally is coincident with the major stenomphalus Zone (intra-late Ryazanian) transgressive event could not be recognised lithologically in this well, although palaeontological and palvnofacies changes were observed. The contact is inferred to equate with the biostratigraphically determined late - latest Ryazanian boundary.

DISCOVERY REPORT WELL 7120/1-2 Suim_p_yar Well 7120/1-2 was spudded on 1st January 1989 as the second and final commitment well in Production Licence 108. The well was planned to test a Lower Cretaceous/Upper Jurassic wedge play immediately to the south of the Loppa High, and drilled to total depth of 2630 in bdf in rocks of Triassic age. The upper of the two seismically-defined wedges was found to comprise silts and shales of Early to Middle Albian age (Wedge In), whilst the lower wedge consisted of two contrasting clastic packages of Valanginian to latest Ryazanian (Wedge IIa) and Early Volgian (Wedge IIb) age respectively. Oil was recovered from RFT's at in (Wedge ha) and in (an isolated sand in the Kimmeridgian Hekkingen Formation). In addition, well-log interpretation revealed low hydrocarbon saturations in sands of the Triassic Fruholmen Formation. Subsequent testing revealed the Fruholmen to be tight and the hydrocarbons to be immovable, but total of 1600 litres light 31°API (0.87 g/cm3 ) oil was recovered from the hydrocarbon-bearing interval in Wedge ha. Evaluation of the test results was hampered by technical problems encountered during the testing. However, RFT pressures together with the petrophysical evaluation suggest single oil column of approximately 90 in in Wedge IIa (Valanginian) with an oil-water contact at about 1970 in bdf. Reservoir parameters in the hydrocarbon-bearing zone are generally poor, with extensive quartz overgrowth and calcite cementation resulting in an average porosity of only 13% and net/gross of 8%. 7 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS Petroleum geochemical analyses of mud gas (Isotube) and drill cuttings samples from the interval 888m to 1898m in the Norwegian Barents Sea well 7321/8-2 ST2 (Sandia) have been carried out on behalf of Spirit Energy Norge. 7.1 Conclusions The following conclusions are reached: • total of 14 drill cuttings samples were submitted for maturity evaluation by both vitrinite reflectance (reflected light microscopy) and spore colour index (with visual kerogen description, transmitted light microscopy), the analysed sample depths ranging from 900m within the Kolje Fm to 1898m within the Snadd Fm and close to the well TD (1899m). The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. The Hekkingen Fm is late mature for oil generation (SCI ~7.0-7,5, vitrinite reflectance ~0.75-0.80%). Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. The lower part of the Kolje Fm may have had some source potential, mainly for gas, although probably minor compared to the Hekkingen Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the claystone-dominated lower part of the Fruholmen Fm (1663m to 1787m) have fair TOC values and apparently fair source potential although evaluation is complicated by polyglycol contaminant. Kerogens (assumed to be isolated predominantly from claystones within drill cuttings samples) are dominated by coaly OM (inertinite macerals) with minor woody (vitrinite) and amorphous OM. question: How are increased pump pressure, motor/MWD losses, under-reamer nozzle anomalies, and WOB/torque readings interrelated during drilling?
answer_text: Higher-than-expected pump pressure and motor/MWD pressure losses pointed to under-reamer nozzle anomalies (some nozzles blocked, some washed out). These hydraulic inefficiencies reduced effective nozzle flow, raising torque (up to ~12 kft·lbs) and constraining usable WOB (kept low in context).

Ranges of petrophysical parameters are presented in Table 5.4. 5.3.3 Reservoir Engineering The formation fluid is lean gas condensate with gas to liquid ratio of 188 m3/MMscm. An oil rim is encountered within one of the wells (Robertson ERC, 1990b). Pressure data show that each well lies in separate compartment. This is supported by log data which shows different hydrocarbon water contacts in each well. Many tests prove difficult to interpret unambiguously due to poor formation permeability, multiphase flow and the presumed isolated nature of the sands. However, two of the wells showed good flow rates and permeability thickness values. Test permeabilities averaged between - 10 mD with core data averaging 10 mD. 5.3.4 Volumetrics and Reserves A wet gas initially in place of approximately 25 Bcm has been established for Lomond and an approximate recovery factor of 70 per cent. applied, giving reserves of the order of 17 Bcm. As Lomond is relatively lean gas condensate, liquid dropout may be small and condensate recoveries of around 35 per cent. are therefore expected. 5.4 Conclusions On the basis of the descriptions above, the following key points can be made, which are of direct relevance to the inferred Well 1/3-6 reservoir model. • Intrafield shale out of reservoir sandstones can be used to model the distribution of fluids and contacts. • Top structure mapping and pressure data indicate that the reservoirs at Cod and Lomond are possibly faulted. • Complex fluid and contact distribution may therefore be controlled by one or combination of reservoir sand shale outs and faulting. • Gross reservoir thickness in the nearest analogue (Cod Field) is directly related to structural position, whereas at Lomond it is not. • Net to gross ratio variation tends to parallel gross thickness trends and is controlled by the detailed distribution of reservoir sandstones facies. • Porosity variations are controlled by primary facies type and depth of burial. question: How do seal failure, migration evidence, and reservoir quality in Skagerrak FM compare between wells 1/3-8 and 2/1-11?
