1. Conclusions • Well 1/3-8 was dry because of seal failure. The vertical seal failed by fracturing induced by excess overpressure. Flexural stress caused by Tertiary halokinetic inversion may have contributed to fracturing and leakage, but this was not the primary cause. • Hydrocarbons did migrate into the 1/3-8 structure. This is evident from the shows at the top of the reservoir sands, from bulk fluid inclusion (FIS) and petrographic fluid inclusion indicators, and from the condensate that was encountered in the Lower Cretaceous. • Reservoir sandstones were encountered in the Basal Sandstone interval of the well. This was the secondary reservoir objective interval. The sands are of poor quality, but they are capable of producing and receiving oil or gas as indicated by conventional core, petrographic, and capillary pressure analyses. No sands were encountered in the younger Volgian primary reservoir objective interval. • The Kuskjell and BI5skjell prospects are no longer valid prospects because of increased risk associated with reservoir presence, reservoir quality, and seal. • The Flyndre Deep Prospect is longer valid prospect because of increased risk associated with (at the very least) seal. • The Boreskjell Prospect is no longer valid prospect based on confirmation of poor Triassic reservoir quality by the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The reservoir objective is the Triassic Skagerrak Formation, which was penetrated by both the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The formation has very poor reservoir properties in Well 1/3-8. In well 2/1-11, the formation is very sandy, but reservoir quality is poor. • The seal failure at 1/3-8 underscores the risk of seal failure at 7/11-N, similar prospect in terms of depth and predicted stratigraphy and pressure. Seal is the primary Risk at 7/11-N. Based on revised pore pressure prediction model with 1/3-8 data as calibration, the chance of seal failure (vertical or lateral) was increased significantly. This was reviewed by the PQT in January, 1998. consensus total chance of success of 18% was arrived at. This substantiated the team's concerns regarding seal failure and justified ANOC's very recent decision to try to trade or swab its interest in PL070 for an interest in more prospective acreage. • Deep Jurassic prospects can succeed. There are several examples in the UK sector of the Central Graben where commercial discoveries have been made, and several of these are being developed (e.g. Elgin, Franklin, Shearwater, Erskine). The downsides of these prospects are higher risks associated with seal failure and high drilling and production costs. The upside of high pressure Jurassic prospects is significant: higher deliverabilities even through poor reservoir rocks, greater storage capacities for given trap size, and positive impacts on porosity preservation in certain cases (up to 30% porosity at Shearwater!). To date, this play has not proven to be commercial in the Norwegian sector.

question: What is OSEBERG FM's stratigraphic order and relative age versus Drake, Rannoch, and Brent in well 30/2-3?
answer_text: Oseberg FM is younger than the Drake and Brent (Drake = Early–Late Toarcian; Brent = end‑Late Toarcian) and was deposited in the Aalenian. It is coeval with the lower Rannoch (Aalenian) while Rannoch continues into the Early Bajocian.

context_snippets.text: 5. STRATIGRAPHIC SYNTHESIS The stratigraphic and geological history of well 30/2-3 is depicted in the stratigraphic summary diagram (Fig. 1). This figure illustrates the burial history, unconformities, transgressions, regressions and lithostratigraphy against chronostratigraphic time scale. The oldest sediments analysed are very fine sandstones of the Statfjord Formation which accumulated in fluvial to marginal marine environment during Rhaetian?-?Hettanglan times. Following period of non deposition, marine transgression during Late Pliensbachian times resulted in the deposition of the Dunlin Group, Amundsen Formation in marine, inner shelf conditions. These sediments were succeeded during Late Pliensbachlan times by the Burton Formation. Sands of the Cook Formation accumulated in marine, inner shelf environment during Late Pliensbachlan to Early Toarcian times. These sands were succeeded during Early Toarcian to Late Toarcian times by the Drake Formation. A regional regressive event at the end of Late Toarcian times led to the development of fluviodeltaic-marginal marine conditions and the accumulation of the Brent Group. Initial deposition of the Oseberg Formation and the lower part of the Rannoch Formation took place during Aalenian times. During Early Bajocian times continued Rannoch Formation deposition was succeeded by the Etive Formation and more argillaceous deposits of the Ness Formation. The uppermost Ness Formation and Tarbert Formation were deposited during ?Late Bajocian times. The Early Bathonian claystones of the Viking Group, Heather Formation sensu strict° accumulated during transgressive phase in marine, inner shelf setting with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Deposition continued through Middle Bathonian to early Callovian times in similar environmental settings. Deposition was interrupted during mid Callovian times, possibly because of regional regressive phase. Subsidence and sedimentation of the Heather Formation resumed during late Callovian?-Early Oxfordian times although further, major unconformity separates the Early Oxfordian Heather Formation sensu stricto from the overlying Draupne Formation. The Late Jurassic transgressive phase continued during Kimmeridgian-Early Volgian times with the accumulation of claystones of the Draupne Formation in mid to outer shelf environment with dysaerobic to anaerobic sea floor conditions. Sedimentation continued through to Middle Volgian times in similar environmental conditions, although major unconformity is present at the top of the Draupne Formation. The Early Cretaceous sequence is characterised by major condensation and unconformities. The oldest Cromer Knoll Group sediments consist of Early Hauterivian calcareous claystones assigned to the Valhall Formation which accumulated in marine, inner shelf setting. These sediments are overlain unconformably by Early Barremian calcareous claystones of the Tuxen Formation following regional transgressive phase. further unconformity separates the Tuxen Formation from the overlying Early Albian Sola Formation. The Soia Formation accumulated in marine, mid shelf environment with dysaerobic sea floor conditions. Following period of non deposition, transgressive phase during Late Albian times resulted in the deposition of calcareous claystones of the Rodby Formation in marine, outer shelf setting. The transgressive phase continued into Late Cretaceous, Cenomanian times when claystones of the Shetland Group, Formation 'A' were deposited in marine outer shelf to upper bathyal environment. Boyle’s law: When the temperature remaines constant, the volume of given mass of ideal gas varies inversely with its absolute pressure. Extention of the equation to account for temperature variation and nonideal gas behavior is required for accurate grain volume determination The method is direct measurement of Grain Volume using helium gas expansion porosimeter. Prior to measurements, the porosimeter was calibrated. This is done by performing standard measuring sequence using various combinations of steel-plugs with known volumes. Based on these measurements, function for grain volume is calculated from P1/ P2 : The calibration equation is determined by linear regression (last squares method) of disc volumes versus P1/ P2 Grain volume = + * P1/ P2 Porosity and pore volume are then calculated from grain volume and bulk volume. Bulk volume was measured by immersing the sample in mercury (the weight balance/ buoyancy technique). The dry weight of the core plug divided by grain volume gives grain density of the core plug. Well 25/8-B-22 was pilot hole for potential horizontal oil producer. Both wells were drilled in the Sindre Structure. The pilot hole was kicked off from B-22 at 4282m MD All the depths in this report refer to the RKB. The lithological boundary was interpolated between two neighbouring cutting samples if no significant change in drilling parameter was observed. Analyses of the cuttings were conducted at the well site using binocular microscope. The interpreted lithology is based on cuttings and drilling parameters such as rate of penetration, weight on bit, torque and background gas values and MWD (gamma and resistivity log). Gas was monitored by means of Total Hydrocarbon Gas detector (Flame Ionisation Detector - FID), calibrated such that 50 API units are equal to % total gas in air. Gas Chromatograph was used for detailed breakdown of the gas into its different components and was calibrated to analyse C1, C2, C3, iC4, nC4. Gas Chromatograph values are reported in ppm. Below is brief explanation to the use of the different gas ratios in the enclosed Gas Ratio Plot. C1 Ratios (C1/C2, C1/C3, C1/C4) display the fraction of each component compared to the fraction of C1. The ratios will decrease with depth as more mature sediments are encountered. Mature source rocks and hydrocarbon reservoirs show low ratios. Productive dry gas zones may only show C1, but very high shows of C1 are usually indicative of salt water. If the C1/C2 ratio is low in the oil section and the C1/C4 ratio is high in the gas section, the zone is probably non-productive. If C1/C4 is less than C1/C3 the zone is probably water bearing. As rule of thumb the following ratio values can be used to evaluate the C1 Ratios (these ratios may not be definitive for low permeability zones): OIL GAS RESIDUAL/ NON-PRODUCTIVE However, if the GWR ratio is higher than 48 there is probability of heavy or dead oil. Light to Heavy Ratio (LHR): C1 + C2 / C3 + C4 + C5 100. The LHR is expected to decrease with depth. It is also good coal indicator (as coal gas is very high in C1 and C2). If the LHR ratio falls below then they are probably non-productive gasses and if the LHR is equal or greater than 100 then they are probably light and non-productive gasses. However, if the LHR ratio is less than the GWR ratio Gas Wetness Ratio (GWR): C2 + C3 + C4 + C5 / total 100. The GWR gives an indication of maturity. It will increase with depth, as the C1 fraction will represent smaller part of the total light HC there is probability of dead residual oil. Oil Character Qualifier (OCQ): C4 + C5 / C3. Under some circumstances, high amounts of C1 will mask the presence of oil. This may be in water wet zones or in gas cap reservoir. GWR and LHR could then be misinterpreted. However, in the presence of oil, C4 + C5 will increase relative to C3 and therefore the OCQ would increase. Generally OCQ values greater than would indicate higher probability of productive oil. Note that as C3, C4 and C5 are the least abundant components, areas with low gas readings will give unreliable ratios. question: For 1" CCA plugs, how do helium-expansion porosimeter and mercury-immersion methods compare in measured porosity and grain density?
answer_text: Helium-expansion porosimetry measures grain volume (used to calculate porosity), while mercury immersion measures bulk volume by buoyancy; porosity is then computed from grain and bulk volumes and grain density is dry weight divided by grain volume.

Boyle’s law: When the temperature remaines constant, the volume of given mass of ideal gas varies inversely with its absolute pressure. Extention of the equation to account for temperature variation and nonideal gas behavior is required for accurate grain volume determination The method is direct measurement of Grain Volume using helium gas expansion porosimeter. Bulk volume was measured by immersing the sample in mercury (the weight balance/ buoyancy technique). The dry weight of the core plug divided by grain volume gives grain density of the core plug. 4 CORE HANDLING AND SAMPLING Following above described studies the core was removed from the core inner barrel and wiped clean using dry rags before being measured and marked with way up lines and depth markings. Plug samples for routine analyses were drilled from all cores. These plugs were collected by drilling with inch inch bore, using simulated formation brine (constructed to standard concentration of 50 000 ppm NaCl) as cooling agent. In order to characterise the petrophysical properties parallel to bedding, horizontal plugs taken every 25 cm. To represent vertical data, plug samples were drilled approximately every 50 cm, perpendicular to apparent bedding. The inch samples were cut to one inch lengths and the end faces were lightly brushed using the same fluid, to remove any fines induced by trimming. Plug off cuts were labelled and retained for possible further use. Prior to measurements the inch plug samples were cleaned in hot soxhlet extractor using alternating sequences of methanol and toluene. Toluene was used to remove any residual hydrocarbons and methanol to remove water and salt. The plug samples were dried in hot oven at 60 °C between the toluene and methanol extraction to avoid mixing of the solvents. In order to ensure the complete removal of all pore contaminations the salt content in methanol was checked using silver nitrate (forms silver chloride in presence of chloride ions) The presence of hydrocarbons was gauged from visual inspection of the solvent used and UV fluorescence. Finally the samples were dried in hot oven at 60 °C in 48 hours prior to the measurements. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D.

7 SATURATION 7.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 7.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 14

Due to the absorptive and dispersive properties of the earth, it is observed in most wells that the time between first break and first trough increases with depth. The first trough, however, still retains its meaning as travel time characteristic of the group velocity of the medium. The first break, however, will characterize the arrival of the various phase velocities. The position of the first break in time will depend on the amplitude and gain downhole. Higher frequencies will be detectable with higher gain. In the presence of broad band noise, detectability becomes yet more complex problem. 'Minimum phase' interpretation of surface seismic data deals essentially with breaks, though velocity analysis deals essentially with peaks and troughs (though at much lower resolution). The timing of identifiable events on the surface seismic will thus be break measurement. The 'tie' between the VSP and the surface seismic will depend on both data sets having the same temporal bandwidth. This can be arranged by using the same deconvolution and bandpass filter parameters on the VSP as were used on the surface seismic. If the surface seismic is 'zero phase', this will often mean, in the marine case, that some sort of phase correction process has been run on the data. similar process can be applied to the VSP data set. One important use of check shot data is the calibration of sonic logs. The sonic log is re- corded with single ultra-sonic sound pulse ( ca. 25 kHz. ), and the transit time measured by the signal crossing detection threshold. The threshold varies according to the signal- to-noise conditions at the receiver, and although some adjustment is made, the 'pick' is neither first break nor first trough. The single frequency means there will be no disper- sion, and there is relatively little absorption over the short travel path. The well geophone data includes possibly dispersive and certainly absorptive effect better estimated by the trough-to-trough method and not removed by picking break-to- break. Thus by calibrat- ing the sonic log with trough-to-trough picked check shot values, the synthetic seismo- gram will have included in it the effects of dispersion and absorption. This will then tie well with the surface seismic data. Sonic derived interval velocities are often used for quite detailed formation analysis, and in these cases it is wise to investigate the way in which the sonic log has been calibrated.

question: How do two valid StethoScope tests differ from lost-seal, dry, and tight tests in pressure response, mobility, and seal assessment?
answer_text: Valid StethoScope tests show stable, repeatable drawdown and buildup pressure responses with measurable formation mobility and confirmation of communication/seal integrity. Lost‑seal tests show no communication and seal failure, dry tests show no formation response, and tight tests show only limited, non‑stabilizable response (low or unmeasurable mobility).

1. Conclusions • Well 1/3-8 was dry because of seal failure. The vertical seal failed by fracturing induced by excess overpressure. Flexural stress caused by Tertiary halokinetic inversion may have contributed to fracturing and leakage, but this was not the primary cause. • Hydrocarbons did migrate into the 1/3-8 structure. This is evident from the shows at the top of the reservoir sands, from bulk fluid inclusion (FIS) and petrographic fluid inclusion indicators, and from the condensate that was encountered in the Lower Cretaceous. • Reservoir sandstones were encountered in the Basal Sandstone interval of the well. This was the secondary reservoir objective interval. The sands are of poor quality, but they are capable of producing and receiving oil or gas as indicated by conventional core, petrographic, and capillary pressure analyses. No sands were encountered in the younger Volgian primary reservoir objective interval. • The Kuskjell and BI5skjell prospects are no longer valid prospects because of increased risk associated with reservoir presence, reservoir quality, and seal. • The Flyndre Deep Prospect is longer valid prospect because of increased risk associated with (at the very least) seal. • The Boreskjell Prospect is no longer valid prospect based on confirmation of poor Triassic reservoir quality by the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The reservoir objective is the Triassic Skagerrak Formation, which was penetrated by both the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The formation has very poor reservoir properties in Well 1/3-8. In well 2/1-11, the formation is very sandy, but reservoir quality is poor. • The seal failure at 1/3-8 underscores the risk of seal failure at 7/11-N, similar prospect in terms of depth and predicted stratigraphy and pressure. Seal is the primary Risk at 7/11-N. Based on revised pore pressure prediction model with 1/3-8 data as calibration, the chance of seal failure (vertical or lateral) was increased significantly. This was reviewed by the PQT in January, 1998. consensus total chance of success of 18% was arrived at. This substantiated the team's concerns regarding seal failure and justified ANOC's very recent decision to try to trade or swab its interest in PL070 for an interest in more prospective acreage. • Deep Jurassic prospects can succeed. There are several examples in the UK sector of the Central Graben where commercial discoveries have been made, and several of these are being developed (e.g. Elgin, Franklin, Shearwater, Erskine). The downsides of these prospects are higher risks associated with seal failure and high drilling and production costs. The upside of high pressure Jurassic prospects is significant: higher deliverabilities even through poor reservoir rocks, greater storage capacities for given trap size, and positive impacts on porosity preservation in certain cases (up to 30% porosity at Shearwater!). To date, this play has not proven to be commercial in the Norwegian sector.

context_snippets.text: Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction On the 20th August 2005, Vertical Incidence Vertical Seismic Profile (VIVSP) was carried out for Norsk Hydro on the deviated well 31/2-N-11-H in the Troll field, offshore Norway. The objective of the survey was to obtain an accurate time depth profile and VSP image to tie to surface seismic. This report describes the time picking of the checkshot data and processing of VIVSP data which was performed using Borseis proprietary software as implemented on Geoframe commercial baseline 4.0.3. The polarity convention adopted in this report is as follows. In normal polarity an upgoing compressional wave, reflected by an increase of acoustic impedance with depth, is displayed as a white trough (negative number). A4 figures in this report are plotted at vertical time scale of 20cm/sec. The raw x,y,z, surface sensor data, raw stacked x,y,z data and migrated datasets have been provided in SEGY format on CD-ROM accompanying this document. All digital data and the processing reports is also provided on CD-ROM.

After careful analysis of the spectral content, zero phase third order Butterworth filter with bandpass frequency interval of 5-95Hz was applied to both the TRY and TV. The choice of bandpass was made to preserve the maximum frequency content in the data at this early stage of the processing and at the same time to remove the higher frequency noise. The data was then normalized and corrected to vertical one way travel time below MSL by subtracting the transit time from hydrophone to geophone and adding the vertical travel time using straight ray assumption and water velocity of 1480 m/s. Applying normalization turns the downgoing wavefield into plane wavefield, which later will provide more robust computations.

Commercial In Confidence 4 Sonic Calibration The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the sonic slowness log to match the vertical VSP transit times. 4.1 Compressional Sonic Calibration Prior to sonic calibration the log data (compressional & shear sonic, density, calliper, gamma ray, neutron porosity, resistivity and Photo-Electric Factor logs) were petrophysically validated (including depth-matching and environmental corrections) by Norsk Hydro. Compressional sonic was available from 1699m MD DF to 3200m MD DF. This was corrected to true vertical depth using the well deviation and bulk shifted by -35.5m to the Seismic Reference Datum, to give compressional sonic log from 1508.5m to 2085.9m TVDSS. All accompanying logs were also corrected to TVDSS. The sonic logs had some sections that were straight line interpolated where data were missing. The calibration of the sonic log is an adjustment of the integrated sonic slowness to match the vertical VSP travel times for given reference depth. The difference in time defines the drift (Δtdrift =ΔtVSP-Δtsonic), which can be either positive or negative. postitive drift is usually caused by dispersion in the seismic wavefield with depth or distance. negative drift (too slow sonic slowness) can be due to hole rugosity where Vformation > Vborehole-fluid and is generally very local effect. In order to minimize the residual drift function, the user defined smoothed drift curve has been designed to honour the raw drift curve as closely as possible with view to generating “calibrated” sonic log that should be used for time to depth conversion only and NOT used for Acoustic Impedance generation. For AI generation, the raw sonic, correctly time indexed using the calibrated velocity function has been used for the input to the synthetic reflectivity generation. The compressional sonic was calibrated using the geometrically corrected, vertical Time/Depth relationship from the Vertical Incidence VSP survey. comparison of the sonic slowness log and the VIVSP interval velocities is shown in Figure 23 and an initial visual inspection shows the character appears similar with major lithological boundaries tying very well. The sonic, VSP interval, RMS and average velocities after calibration are shown in Figure 25 and are available as digital logs on the CD-ROM accompanying this report. The velocity information and calibrated time depth curves are tabulated in Velocity Report, Time to Depth Report and Depth to Time Report.

The optimally-designed well trajectory and overall thick Tor section present in the wells provide the maximum amount of security in case unexpected variations in Tor thickness or Tor depths occur. Well 2/8A-12A will be Amoco Norway's first horizontal well and as such, there are uncertainties in estimating opera- tional times. For that reason 10% contingency has been included in the intangible costs of the well. LONG TERM STRATEGY The strategy behind drilling Well 2/8A-12A as the first horizontal well at Valhall is that it will be drilled in an area of the field with excellent control on the geology and reservoir properties. Well 2/8A-12A will be drilled between two wellbores (2/8A-12(ST-1) and 2/8A-12(ST-2)) which have known pay thickness, dip and petrophysical properties. In addition, vertical seismic profile (VSP) was shot in Well 2/8A-12(ST-1) which provides detailed interpretation of the Tor formation thickness between the two wells.

GEOPHYSICAL MAPPING GENERAL For general discussion on seismic data quality, geophysical setting and acoustic properties of the Valhall Chalk reservoir please refer to; 1990 VALHALL GEOLOGIC AND GEOPHYSICAL RE ANALYSIS AND RESERVE REASSESSMENT Text 2/2. A subsequent map revision based on the 2-D seismic database was released in March 1992. Since then the seismic data base has been upgraded by 3-D seismic dataset covering the field. This dataset is being interpreted and the generation of complete reservoir maps is in process. In order to support planning of South End development special wavelet processing and subsequent band-limited inversion has been applied to sub cube of the 3-D dataset. METHODOLOGY Interpretation of the seismic data and the mapping of those data has been done without preconceived geologic models. However, the following general guidelines has been applied in the interpretation of the seismic data: Evaluation of well control reveals that the total Palaeocene thickness varies laterally slowly, observed values are between 30-50m. Furthermore it has been demonstrated that the Tor formation on the crest of the reservoir expresses very low acoustic impedance, in fact lower than the overlying Lista formation. Off the flanks, water wet Tor formation is characterised by high acoustic impedance. This effect is seen in the seismic data by the presence of polarity reversal observed when climbing structurally from the flank area on to the crestal area. Sufficient well control and reservoir characteristics now exist across most of the field to adequately tie into the seismic database and make general correct seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk horizon. However significant challenges are related to the presence of high gas saturation in the overburden causing significant distortion in the seismic images in the crestal area both with respect to structure and phase characteristics. The recent 3-D seismic interpretation of the Top Chalk reflectors has been based on consistent picking on phase/polarity reflecting the observed presence of low acoustic impedance rock in the crestal area. The polarity reversal effect is easily observed on north, east and west flank areas and conforms fairly well with well observations. Observation from the south flank, however, could reflect the possible presence of porous Tor formation further south of well 2/11-1.

3 Geological Programme 3.1 Purpose of the Well The vertical exploration well 2/6-5 will be drilled on the Chalk Prospect which is situated in the central eastern part of PL 008 (Figs. and 3.2). The main purpose of well 2/6-5 is to test the presence of hydrocarbons and the reservoir properties within the Shetland Group in the Chalk Prospect. The planned TD of the well is 25 into Basement, or prognosed TD at 3185 mRKB. The well will be planned as possible future producer. Secondary purpose of the well is to test possible sediment fill in the interval between the Shetland Group and the basement topography. For well 2/6-5 the primary target of Cretaceous age is prognosed at 2843 mRKB, below approx. 40 of the Ekofisk Tight zone causing the laterally consistent seismic reflector mapped as the Top Shetland horizon. The primary target interval consists of the total Shetland package below the tight zone mentioned above. Target interval belongs to the Ekofisk-, Tor- and Hod Formations (or their time equivalents). Reservoir zones are expected in several intervals, some in pressure communication and some not. A distinct change in ROP is expected when drilling from the Ekofisk Formation tight zone into the primary target of prognosed highly porous carbonates. The porosity in the Shetland Group is expected to be more than 35%, locally more than 50%. Open reservoir structure and or zones with large number of small fractures are expected. Secondary target is the section mapped below the Shetland Group. This interval is of unknown age, but probably belonging to Jurassic/Triassic infill of the faulted basement topography of the Mandal High. However, the interval might show up as only representing intra basement reflectivity within metamorphic rocks. The well is located high on structural closure defined on Top Shetland Group (Figs. and 3.2). The trapping mechanism is partly caused by structuring reflecting the Paleotopography of the underlying crystalline Mandal High, and partly due to stratigraphical component within the Shetland Group (Fig. 3.3). The latter is supported by the observation of anomally low seismic stacking velocities for parts of this interval draping the Mandal High. A possible seismic direct hydrocarbon indicator (flatspot) is observed in the Shetland Group at approx. 2965 mRKB (2.855 sec TWT.). The total depth of the well is estimated to 3185 mRKB (with an uncertainty of +/- 175 m), or 25 m within basement, whatever comes first. 1:\FELLESTORINGLETEBOR\2_6_5\PROGRAM\265WP.DOC 17

question: For well 35/3-1, what were the leak-off test pressure build-up increments and the final-stage pressure range?
answer_text: Pressure was built up in 50–200 psi increments, with final-stage increments of 25–100 psi.

context_snippets.text: FORMATION PRESSURE TEST After drilling out casing strings the formation below the shoe will be subjected to pressure leak off test. 1. Depending on the type of formation and estimated future drilling conditions this test will be run either to predetermined pressure or to actual bleedoff. If predetermined maximum pressure is to be used, the pressure will be advised by the Stavanger Office. It will be calculated from the following: (a) Maximum mud weight anticipated to next casing point. (b) Maximum pressure anticipated when cementing the next casing string. (c) Estimated formation fracture graients. 2. Clean out cement below the shoe and make three meters of new hole. 3. Pick up into the casing and close blow out preventor. 4. Pump slowly down the drill pipe with the cementing pump pressuring up the casing and the exposed formation. Maximum pump rate is to be bbl/min. 5. The pressure is to be built up in 50 to 200 psi stages depending on the estimated fracture pressure. When the surface pressure reaches first level, shut the pump down and check for bleed off. Increase surface pressure, shut the pumps down and check again, and so on until reaching final pressure. It may be desirable to use 25 to 100 psi increments during final stages. 6. An accurate measurement of pressure build up and volume pumped is to be recorded on the form provided. If the formation begins to take mud, shut the pump down immediately and record the surface holding pressure. 7. Release the pressure, open the blow out preventor and drill ahead. 8. The results of the formation pressure test are to be reported on the Daily Drilling Report.

question: What are the MDT-measured JU2 reservoir pressure and corresponding MD RKB depth for well 2/7-29?
answer_text: 11209 psia at 4463.2 m MD RKB (TVD ss).

context_snippets.text: Notes: No stable pressures recorded on run 4B due to stability problem on the pressure gauges. Hydrostatic Pressures A straight line fitted through the hydrostatic pressure points gives hydrostatic gradient of 2.62 psi/m which corresponds to SG mud. The mud density measured at surface prior to running the MDT was SG. The difference of SG might be explained by barite settling. The MDT mud hydrostatic pressures are presented in Figure 3.18. Formation Pressures Obtaining formation pressures in JU2 proved to be difficult due to relatively low permeability sands. In the two JU7 sands and the Permian sand no formation pressures were obtained due to low permeability. The reservoir pressure in JU2 was measured to be 11209 psia at MD RKB ad) (4463.2 TVD ss) The valid MDT pressure points obtained in the upper part of the JU2 reservoir section defines two possible gradients, however this is with very few points. One MDT gradient is 0.59 psi/m which correspond to reservoir fluid density of SG. The other is gradient of psi/m which corresponds to reservoir fluid gradient of SG. This last gradient compare reasonably well with the hydrocarbon density of SG from preliminary PVT analysis. One explanation for the different gradients is reservoir fluid segregation. This is however not considered very likely as pump-out was done at the upper point and the optical fluid analyser showed similar signature as the one obtained at MD RKB ad), where 37° API oil was sampled (API gravity from preliminary PVT analysis). The most likely explanation for the two different gradients is that the upper pressure point (4499.1 MD RKB (1d)) is affected by hysteresis and temperature as the reading was taken when pulling out of hole. The magnitude of the hysteresis/temperature affect is approximately psi which is higher than the tool specifications of psi. The hysteresis/temperature effect is supported by the fact that also the mud pressure is approximately 10 psi higher compared to the dry test at MD RKB (1d) running in hole. The increase in mud pressure can not be explained by fluid loss or barite settling as these would tend to decrease the mud pressure. However, an increase in fluid level could explain the difference. It should also be noted that small depth discrepancies between running in and coming out of hole is possible. Figure shows is plot of the formation pressures and the two gradients. Based on the above mentioned uncertainties with respect to the formation pressure measured coming out of hole, MDT reservoir fluid gradient of psi/m (0.68 SG) is believed to be the most accurate. A comparison between the MDT on 2/7-29 and the RFT run on 2/7-22 showed very similar pressure behaviour. The oil gradient in 2/7-22 (0.41 SG) is identical to the smaller gravity gradient found in 2/7-29 and the pressures are within psi of each other. The pressure regime of 2/7-29 was expected to be very similar to 2/7-22 and the small difference seen in pressure is believed to be coincidental. Geological models rule out pressure communication between 2/7-29 and 2/7-22 (ref 2). Page 19

3.3 MDT Pressures The MDT pressure tool was run in 3/8 open hole to take PVT samples and to establish formation pressures. The MDT was run before conventional logging in order to have all essential information available at an early stage so decisions with respect to testing could be made. The MDT mud hydrostatic pressures are presented in Figure 3.9. • Obtaining formation pressures in JU2 proved to be difficult due to relatively low permeability sands. question: Did the site-survey for Njord 6407/7-6 report no shallow gas warning, thereby justifying omission of a pilot hole?
answer_text: Yes. The site survey reported no shallow gas warning, so a pilot hole will not be drilled.

context_snippets.text: HYDRO E&P Division Grading: Internal Title: Well Programme 6407R-6 Page4of 61 2 PRESENTATION All depths in the program refer to RKB unless otherwise stated, RKB - MSL is 26 m. Well 6407/7-6 is an exploration well which will test the hydrocarbon potential of the B-segment on the NW-flank of the Njord field. The primary target is the Tilje Formation and the secondary target is the Ile Formation. There is also possibility of encountering hydrocarbons in the Upper Jurassic Melke Formation and in the Lower Cretaceous Lange Formation. Figure shows the well location. No shallow gas warning is given in the site survey report for well 6407/7-6 (ref. Cap. & Site Survey At Location 6407/7-6), hence pilot hole will not be drilled. The seabed is at 361m MD / ND. All LWD memory data was dumped and logs produced as per requirements. The first wireline run became stuck at 4782m, 4720m, 4555m and 4350m whilst logging up so the second run was cancelled and wiper trip was performed before running the 5/8” casing. A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Where it is found that sliding is unavoidable towards the end of the 12 1/4” section it may be worthwhile to have Dogsub available on the Rig in case a trip is made where it could be picked up, although it would probably not be worth making special trip for it. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. The rotary BHA consisted of full gauge double nearbit roller reamer followed by float sub and variable gauge Andergauge stabilizer. This was followed by CDR, ILS stabilizer and MWD tools, as well as the ADN tool for porosity and density logs. After drilling out the float collar, shoe track and shoe, the hole was displaced to 1.32sg Versavert oil based mud. Very moderate drilling parameters were used to drill out the shoe, plugs and cement in an effort to protect the bit from excessive wear. Consequently 4.5hrs were used before drilling on new formation. The second target at TVD of 4264m had been extended to the north to take into account the significant walk rates seen in the previous 12 1/4 section. This extension allowed the 1/2 section +/- 0.5deg/30m right hand walk rate as well as 0.5/30m build or drop rate, dependant on actual walk rates experienced. Hence, ideally, maintaining the inclination and azimuth would hit the middle of the target extension.

question: How do seismic shallow-gas/amplitude and coarse‑unit signals correlate with seabed bathymetry for rig emplacement and anchoring suitability?
answer_text: Medium shallow‑gas amplitude anomalies (Kai Fm.) and coarse‑unit signals (cobbles/boulders in Undifferentiated Naust T/A) coincide with boulder‑rich seabed zones, reducing anchoring suitability and increasing rig emplacement risk.

context_snippets.text: 1 INTRODUCTION This report describes the sea-floor conditions and shallow geology within an approximately km area covering the Planned Well Location Idun (Figure 1.1). Potential installation and drilling hazards have been evaluated and special attention has been given to: • Seabed conditions, including water depth, sea-floor slope, seabed sediments and potential obstructions or hazards • Near-seabed sediments and likely anchoring conditions • Top hole sediments and well bore stability • Shallow water flow potential • Shallow gas • Boulders The report covers the interval from seabed down to the top of the Kai Formation at depth of 1341 meters Mean Sea Level (MSL). The report is divided into nine sections. The introduction, Section 1, is followed by summary of the main results and conclusions in Section 2. short description of the well and seismic data applied in the study is given in Section 3. In Section the criteria for horizon picking and anomaly definitions with its associated resolutions are presented. In Section description of the conditions for rig emplacement is given, including bathymetry, seabed and near-seabed sediments, potential obstructions and anchoring. Section deals with the shallow geology of the survey area, including brief geological history of the region from Miocene to present, details of the seismic interpretation and depth conversion, and geological prognosis for the well. Potential drilling hazards such as shallow gas and shallow-water flow is addressed in Section 7. Both sections, and 7, include examples from the seismic data to illustrate pertinent features. Section contains maps summarizing time structures and amplitude anomalies for the interpreted intervals. Section 8, recommendations, gives details of two possible relief well locations. Section contains full list of references. All positional data is referenced to ED50, Zone 32, Central Meridian 9° East. All depths are relative to Mean Sea Level (MSL), unless stated otherwise.

Figure 2.5-d Anomaly Level – Medium risk of shallow gas within Unit (Kai Fm.) 2.5.2 Coarse deposits Cobbles and boulders are expected to be present within Unit (Undifferentiated Naust T), Unit (Undifferentiated Naust T) and Unit (Undifferentiated Naust A). During the drilling of Well 6507/3-3 boulders were reported within Unit from 30 to 32 below seabed (421 to 423 MSL) and also at 56 below seabed (447 MSL). Completion report for Well 6507/3-3 reported slow interval during drilling within Unit 2, from 113 to 131 below seabed (504 m to 522 MSL), caused by boulders. During the drilling of Well 6507/3-7 boulders were reported within Unit from 53 to 54 below seabed (430 to 431 MSL), with possible boulders also reported between 84 and 86 below seabed (461 to 463 MSL). Revision : RA – Approved Issue Page 56 of 57

V Executive Summary for well: 6507/3-7 Petroleum Indications, Type and Quality: There are three main intervals displaying hydrocarbon anomalies in this well. The sections above 1530 and at 2895-3195 consist of mostly dry gas responses, with the exception of single sample from 3201 displaying an oil-like spectrum. thin section from 2943 contains several to common, white-fluorescent, and rare, yellow-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. Inclusion abundance is marginally high enough to suggest the presence of an oil column or paleo-column at this depth. No visible petroleum inclusions are documented at 1330 or 3201 m. The section below 3546 reveals dry gas to oil-like spectra. The most significant responses are gas-condensate to oil indications noted intermittently at 3546-3600 m. Thin sections from 3549 m, 3632 m, 3717 and 3840 contain rare to several, white-fluorescent, moderate gravity liquid petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz grains. Thin sections from 3549 and 3840 also contain rare to several, blue-fluorescent, upper-moderate gravity petroleum inclusions in fractured detrital quartz. The remainder of the analyzed interval contains sub-anomalous hydrocarbon concentra- tions. No petroleum inclusions are recorded in thin sections from 1910 m, 2420 or 3339 m. Shales contain moderate amounts of gas-prone kerogen and rare to several occurrences of immature to mature oil-prone kerogen in most samples (apparently oil-mature below about 3000 m). Highest visual kerogen abundance is noted at 3339 m. Proximal Pay Indications: Anomalous concentrations of acetic acid and, in general, more prominent benzene anomalies are identified at 3546-3588 and 3651-3654 m. Samples containing acetic acid anomalies usually suggest the nearby presence of reservoired liquid petroleum (oil or condensate), while more prominent benzene anomalies can indicate nearby gas. This well is reportedly gas discovery, thus it is probable that these features are sensing penetrated charge. Anomalies within reservoirs can indicate elevated Sw (for instance in relatively tight or impermeable reservoirs). Potential Seals: Possible seals are identified at 2898 m, 3340 m, 3546 and 3690 m. Evidence for Bacterial or Thermal Alteration: Sulfur species of probable bacterial origin are noted at 1230-1250 m, 2010 and 2340 m. These compounds generally indicate migration or microseepage of light, thermogenic hydrocarbons from depth followed by bacterial sulfate reduction at temperatures below 65°C. FIS microseeps are considered encouraging for deeper liquid petroleum exploration in the vicinity, and are consistent with deeper charge in the wellbore. Other: Nothing of note.

2 1. OVERVIEW OF FIT, INC. AND FLUID INCLUSION STRATIGRAPHY as can samples of any age (i.e., fresh cuttings or those warehoused for many years). Our suggested sampling interval for general well studies is 30 ft (10 m). Pay-delineation studies, reservoir-scale studies or other applications involving rapidly changing fluid chemistries should be sampled at the tightest possible spacing, depending on sample availability (e.g., 1-3 ft). A maximum of 575 samples can be analyzed for given well. Approximately gm of clean rock material is needed for each sample. In most cases, some amount of additional washing is required - even for washed samples, thus, it is best to send enough to ensure ample material after final wash. It is further recommended that clean lith cuts be provided to minimize costs associated with additional sample preparation as all sample washing and preparation costs will be charged back to the client. The quoted price for an FIS Analysis is exclusive of sample preparation, handling and shipping; estimates for these project-specific services are available upon request. 1.2 Organization of this Report Analytical results of the FIS analysis of 6507/3-7 are presented graphically in Sections and as series of profiles each illustrating the variation of particular atomic mass (m/z) or ratio of two masses with measured depth. general discussion of the interpretation of FIS data including the significance of particular features and trends (or their absence) is provided in Appendix A. The remaining information provided in subsequent sections includes: 1) ref- erence spectra, collected on internal standards and used to monitor inter- and intra-analytical consistency of the quadrupole analyses which are presented and discussed in Appendix B; and 2) mass spectra from all samples which are listed individually by depth in Appendix C. 1.3 Output Formats Analytical results of the present study are available in electronic format as described below. The first five items are included on the floppy diskette provided with each color hard- copy of the final report. The remaining file, FI090135a-1.pdf, is available upon request for nominal fee. 1. FI090135a-1.las - LAS-format, 26-column file containing recorded depth and Tracks 1-25 from the FIT Analysis of 6507/3-7 2. FI090135a-1.txt - TXT-format, 26-column file containing recorded depth and Tracks 1-25 from 3. FI090135a-2.las.Z - LAS-format (compressed), 181-column file containing recorded depth and background corrected, normalized, standardized individual mass spectra (m/z 2-180) from the FIT Analysis of 6507/3-7 4. FI090135a-s.pdf - PDF format, electronic file of the summary tracks and annotations from the 5. FI090135a-c.pdf - PDF format, electronic file of the poster containing 90% of all FIS Data from the FIT Analysis of 6507/3-7 6. 3 Discussion 3.1 Hydrocarbon quantity The hydrocarbon detection limit or threshold for the HCSTM is set to 800 counts which is comparable to concentration of ≈ 100 ppm HC. At the opposite end of the scale, wells with an Imax higher than 10,000 counts have been known to produce commercially elsewhere. Hydrocarbon contents are rather regularly distributed as shown in Figure 3, fluctuating between Imax 2000 – 6000 counts, only rarely up to Imax 6000-12000 counts. 3.2 Hydrocarbon quality Comparison with API gravity using range of reference petroleums gives correlation with HCSTM Q580 of R2 = (90 different oils) and (112 different oils) for CUSC. (HCSTMQ580 = Figure 1, lower insert, unpublished data and CUSC Q580 = Figure 2.) Hydrocarbon HCSTM measurements of the cored section show variation in Q580 within the range – corresponding to light oil to heavy oil compositions. The restricted presence of Q580 scattering is indicative of overall good vertical fluid communication. However, there are three depths that stand out in this respect: 3557.3 Discrete shift from light to medium oil compositions 3565.3 Local shift medium-heavy-medium oil compositions 3580.3 Overall shift from medium to heavy oil compositions. The shift close to is readily observable, whereas the other shifts are subtle accompanied by an overall decrease in grain size with depth. However, even below 3600 m, in those few segments were poro-perm performance suddenly shifts from poor to good medium oils can be detected in an otherwise heavy oil environment (Figure 6). Overall there seems to be good vertical fluid communication, from the top of the cored section down to approximately 3608 m, the shifts from light through medium to heavy oil composition possibly due to gravitative segregation. In this respect the HCSTM spectral information (Figure 5) from light/medium oil at 3549 (Q580 0.27) to light/medium oil some 20 deeper at 3568 (Q580 0.24) is pointing towards common source for this petroleum. The light to medium oil compositions occurring above 3580 correspond to API values close to 35-40. Q580 values of to reflect predominantly PAH of 2-3 ring isomers (Lakowitz, 1991; Parr & Hanson-Parr, 1988, Khorasani 1987; Dumke & Teschner 1988; Barker & Kopp 1991; Kihle 1995; Zhu & Mullins 1992; Stasiuk & Snowdon, 1997). And they all confirmed the prognosed pressure prediction in the well program. The pressure gradient showed normal trend down to approximately 1500m TVD where rapid increase was detected. The pore pressure gradient reached maximum of EMW at 1990m TVD in the Hordaland Group. From 1937m MD pore pressure increased rapidly throughout the lower Hordaland Group to reach maximum of 1.40sg at the base of the Hordaland Group at 2560m MD (1964m TVD). Prior to drilling the overpressured zone mud weight was increased from sg to sg. The increase in pore pressure from 1937m MD/1537m TVD was seen as rapid decrease in the d-exponent trend, without any noticeable change in formation. Throughout this pressure build-up section gas levels remained very low at - 0.05% indicating that considerable overbalance exsisted. Large and frequent variations in d-exponent values were due to lithological effects and frequent periods of steering, but gradual shift to the right indicated reduction in pore pressure. large overbalance exsisted during this reduction in pore pressure and background levels remained low in the range - 0.02%. question: How do drying, incomplete coring, bed‑boundary, and vertical‑resolution effects produce core‑log porosity gaps in Ness, Rannoch, and Broom?
answer_text: Drying/cleaning of cores inflates porosity in shaly sands and incomplete coring leaves intervals unrepresented, biasing core averages. Bed‑boundary effects smear log responses and limited vertical resolution causes thin laminations or very thin sands to be missed on logs, producing lower or differing log porosities.

The cores have been depth shifted to match the density log (CDL) depth (Table 5.1). Conventional core analyses have been carried out by Corelab and consist of measurements of porosity, air-permeability, grain density and fluid saturation. complete list of core analysis data is given in the Petrophysical Report well 34/7-8 (Ref. 1). Shale volume is defined as the minimum value calculated from the GR and the neutron-density crossplot.

There is, however, significant difference between average porosities from cores and logs in the Ness, Rannoch and Broom Formations, as is also in the Dunlin Group. This is believed to be mainly an effect of too high core porosities in shaly sands caused by the cleaning and drying process, and is known effect also in other Brent wells (Statfjord Field and Statfjord Ost). Note that the intervals are not completely represented by cores, and the average values are not necessarily comparable. Also note that bed boundary effects on logs may affect average log values. Due to the difference in core and log porosities in the Rannoch and Broom, the core porosity corresponding to permeability of mD could not be used as cutoff to evaluate net sand averages from logs. Above this depth no zones of particular interest were encountered. The interpretation is based on suite of Schlum- berger logs with listing of the different logging runs given in table I/7.1. The reservoir is interpreted to be gas bearing from to ca. 1574 m. This is confirmed by the graph of RFT pressures versus depth shown as figure 1/8.2 and from separation between porosity logs in the cleaner sand intervals. Below 1574 m, the clean sands, where log interpretation is most reliable, appear to be water bearing. In the less clean zones between 1574 and 1622 some oil saturation exists as seen in cores. The hydrocarbon saturation as estimated from log data varies between a maximum of 40% and zero in the interval 1574 to 1622 m. This would be consistent with the presence of residual oil. The oil bleeding from cores as noted at surface could be interpreted as extremely low formation permeability rather than the presence of producible oil. An RFT sample taken at 1597 in permeable interval recovered no hydrocarbons although it was heavily contaminated with mud filtrate. Core analysis shows that some intervals between 1574 and 1622 contained high percentages of mica which may affect standard log interpretation. However, the presence of mica in these quantities re- sults in very low permeabilities and the net effect would be that any hydrocarbons would be non-producible. When developing the porosity/permeability relationship from core ana- lyses shown as fig. 7.2, it was found that shale and mica have similar effect. It is important to note that this relationship is proba- bly pessimistic as an average trend since it is indicative of the tighter intervals and not the cleaner sands which were too unconsoli- dated to be analysed. 2 Source rock study 2.1 Upper Jurassic Shales The source rock potential and maturity of the Upper Jurassic shales have been assessed on sidewall cores between RKB. The following results are to be emphasized (Table and Figures 2, & 4): Tau formation Excellent potential and very good organic fades, oil-prone marine organic matter of type 11 (400 HI in average), deposited in restricted and reducing environment. The anoxicity as well as the marine influence increase upwards throughout the formation as indicated by the continuous and stepwise decrease of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). The vitrinite reflectance is around % Ro (Cf. Appendix). This formation is geochemically similar to the hot shales from the top Draupne formation (Unit according to EPN subdivision). Egersund formation High source potential and fair organic facies, mainly wet gas-condensate prone mixed organic matter dominated by terrestrial influence, variable in properties, but dominantly of type ifi (180 HI in average), deposited in rather high energy environment. The continental influence and oxic conditions increase downwards as indicated by the continuous and stepwise increase of the pristane/phytane ratio (Figure 4). This formation is geochemically rather similar to the Heather formation with however clear higher input of material derived from terrestrial organic matter. The maturity is about the same as in the Tau Formation (0.63 % Ro, value at % is questionable). The source rock properties of both formations are graphically illustrated in Figure and summarized below where mean values of the main geochemical parameters are calculated based on the screening analyses (number of samples analysed indicated). TOC Tmax Si S2 +S2 HI OI EOM Yield Sat 2.2 Sandnes Formation Coals Several layers of coals and coaly shales have been sampled from the cores (2 coals and coaly shales) and analysed. These source rocks are typical of coals from the North Sea with very high S2 and EOM constituted mostly by NSO compounds. The pristane/phytane is very high and the saturates/aromatics very low. The hydrogen index is 180-240, corresponding to dominant type HI kerogen (Table and Figure 2). The potential is mainly for gas/wet gas generation. The vitrinite reflectance is around 0.64-0.67 % Ro, i.e. slightly higher than in the Upper Jurassic Tau and Egersund formations. It should be stressed that the maturity of the Jurassic section (Upper and Middle) from this well, measured by reliable vitrinite reflectance, is clearly higher than the regional trend observed so far for the northern Quadrant 25 at equivalent depths (report EP/P/EXP/GDP 94-022 RP).

For each well, copy of the hand-drawn 1:50 scale core log and written log comments are presented here. Illustrative core photographs are shown on Plates to 5. The sedimentology of the cored intervals is summarised below. Detailed descriptions are contained in the log comments. The depositional environments recorded by the cored intervals are interpreted below. Recommendations for future work to investigate the likely distribution and facies of Late Cretaceous sandstones in the Heidrun area are made at the end of this memorandum. Note that the most recent biostratigraphic data are not available for this memorandum. All depths quoted are core depths. Summary of core descriptions and interpreted depositional environments The cored section comprises mid to late Coniacian siltstones of the Kvitnos Formation overlying 2.51m of medium grained sandstones of the mid-Coniacian Lysing Formation (2367.55m-2370.06m), which in turn overlie fine grained sandstones of the late Aalenian Garn Formation. 2360.00m - 2367.55m This interval is dominated by laminated siltstones displaying local, weak bioturbation by pyritised Chondrites and sand-filled Sabularia (Plate 1A and 1B). The siltstones contain rare pinstripe laminae of silt and very fine to fine grained sandstone and are intercalated with cm-scale beds of medium-grained sandstone. The latter are generally moderately poorly sorted, sparsely to moderately bioturbated by Sabularia, Planolites and Taenidium, and contain angular pebbles of locally sideritised mudstone and clasts of green, swelling claystone and glauconite. The siltstones record offshore marine conditions with episodic dilute gravity flows. The common occurrence of sand-filled burrows isolated within siltstones suggests sediment by-pass, perhaps in slope setting. lchron Ref no: 03/605/S Statoil AS

Core description 179.8 - m: Tofte Formation, Late Toarcian The Tofte Formation displays one single facies association. It consists of erosive cycles of graded, poorly sorted, medium grained, micaceous sandstones (0.2 - m) that are interbedded with silty claystones and gravel, and contain few rootlets and abundant coal fragments. Apart from a few darker clayey intervals, and numerous thinner (5 - 15 cm) light brownish grey intervals, most of the unit displays greenish grey to light greenish grey colour. The light brownish grey intervals contain some coaly material (plant debris). The whole unit shows an overall upward fining trend. There is dominance of gravel and conglomeratic material in the lower part, and medium and finer grained sandstones in the upper part. Sedimentary structures comprise horizontal lamination, large scale cross lamination, some ripple lamination and slumping structures. The graded units generally have large scale cross lamination in the coarse grained parts, and horizontal lamination and ripples in the finer parts. Most of the unit is poorly cemented, but some intervals are completely calcite cemented. This is especially noteworthy from 169 to 165 m, but there are also calcite cemented intervals at 136 in, in and 101 in. These intervals are generally associated with zones of coarse sand, gravel or conglomeratic material, and they vary in thickness between and in. They are homogeneous and show hardly any sedimentary structures apart from few intervals with low angle, large scale cross lamination.

Note that not all species are quantified using their parent or molecular peaks (e.g., methane at m/z = 15) in order to minimize interfering contributions from other species. A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. A Interpretation of Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy (FIS) Data A.1 FIS Analysis A.1.1 Introduction to FIS Analysis Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy involves the rapid, complete analysis of volatiles trapped as fluid inclusions in rock samples using quadrupole mass analyzers attached to an automated, high- vacuum sample introduction system. The technique documents the presence and relative bulk abundance of ionized volatile fragments with mass/charge ratio of m/z 180 that have been released from fluid inclusions by crushing of natural samples. This includes most geologically important inorganic species as well as organic species with less than or equal to 13 carbon atoms. The resulting analysis of the petroleum fraction is comparable to the low molecular weight fraction of whole-oil gas chromatographic - mass spectrometric (GCMS) analysis (without devolatilization of the gas fraction); hence, the major classes of hydrocarbons (e.g., aromatics, naphthenes and paraffins) are represented. Unlike GCMS, where the quadrupole is front-ended with GC, boiling point separation is not achieved and all species are analyzed simultaneously. Hence, significant interference can occur among species with the same mass to charge ratio. However, what FIS lacks in compound specificity, it makes up for in sensitivity and speed, allowing detection of petroleum in samples that are well beyond the reach of standard GCMS methodologies. Prior to analysis, samples of rock material are freed of significant interfering contamina- tion by washing, picking and magnetic separation as necessary to remove drilling fluids, lost circulation materials, other solid mud additives such as gilsonite, and metallic particles from the drillstring. Cleaned samples are loaded with appropriate standards into specially designed autosamplers and are heated in vacuum oven for minimum of 24 hours. This is done to remove adsorbed organic and inorganic volatile material that could interfere with the analysis. The autosampling device is placed in the vacuum system and evacuated to appropriate high vacuum. Bulk fluid inclusion volatiles are afterwards instantaneously released from each sam- ple in sequential manner by automated mechanical crushing. Volatile organic and inorganic species are dynamically pumped through quadrupole mass analyzers where they are ionized, separated according to their mass/charge and recorded. Fluid Inclusion Stratigraphy is unique in several ways: 1) the methodology and theoretical framework are the result of long-standing research and development effort, 2) the cumulative experience and database of documented case histories are the most extensive in the world and 3) the technology represents the most rapid analytical capability of its kind available. The resulting dataset can provide nearly continuous log of present and past pore fluid chemistry through the stratigraphic section penetrated by well, and, given adequate sample coverage, the data can be mapped in two or three dimensions. question: In MUNIN wells, how do MWD and GST failures compare regarding primary causes, sensors typically failed, and reliance on magnetic SS survey as fallback?
answer_text: MWD failures were mainly mud-related (silicate/high‑pH seal problems) and shock/fracture damage affecting gamma‑ray and direction/inclination sensors, with magnetic single‑shot surveys used as the fallback (sometimes successfully). GST failures were mainly due to insulation/wiring and signal‑transmission problems that lost resistivity‑at‑bit/geosteering response, and magnetic single‑shot surveys were attempted as fallback but sometimes failed.

question: How does moldic porosity compare to effective permeability in D85-J's dolomitized limestone, and what are the implications for reservoir potential?

question: Can FIS tracks, key m/z, and petrography distinguish current, paleo, and recycled fluid inclusions in well 6705/10-1?
answer_text: Yes. Current charge is indicated by water‑soluble petroleum species and live oil stain; paleo‑charge by bitumen/asphaltic residue (dead oil stain) with no water‑soluble anomalies and/or DST showing the interval wet; recycled inclusions are identified petrographically (e.g., in recycled quartz overgrowths or by anomalously high homogenization temperatures).

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 45 Current Charge A zone that displays strong FIS hydrocarbon indications and high visual petroleum in- clusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) may reflect penetrated pay, but could also indicate paleo-charge or, in some cases, migration pathway (e.g., where inclusion abundance is enhanced by extensive microfracturing). provisional interpretation of current charge is strengthened if residual petroleum (especially live oil stain) is identified in thin section, and particularly if water-soluble petroleum species (so-called proximal pay indicators; see below) are recorded in FIS data (e.g., in the seal overlying the anomaly, in the water leg underlying the anomaly, or in low permeability zones within the reservoir section itself). Any independent indications (e.g., from electric logs or mudlog gas shows) provide further encouragement. Paleo-charge Intervals of strong FIS response, high visual inclusion abundance (i.e., common, abundant or extremely abundant) and significant bitumen (e.g., dead oil stain or asphaltic residue) without accompanying water-soluble anomalies or independent evidence of current charge, may represent paleo-column, but could also represent current charge or in rare cases migration pathway. The interpretation of paleo-charge is favored if valid DST has shown the interval to be currently wet. Recycled inclusions Very rarely, detritus that is generated from previous sedimentary rock may contain inher- ited petroleum inclusions. These inclusions must be recognized, as they clearly do not provide any useful information about the current petroleum system(s). Petrographic or microther- mometric criteria can often be used to argue the origin of these inclusions, for instance, the presence of petroleum inclusions along recycled quartz overgrowths, or measured homogeniza- tion temperatures that are too high to have been produced during the current burial history. Associated FIS depth trends are usually erratic and poorly compartmentalized, and inclusion abundance is typically low. Inherited inclusions may be restricted to specific geologic units that derived detritus from particular provenance, and are not found in intercalated chemical precipitates (e.g. bedded carbonates or diagenetic cements). Heavy bitumen stain In some instances, pore-occluding bitumen may contribute to FIS signals. Here, solid petroleum behaves as any other cement, and is capable of trapping residual hydrocarbons as bitumen-hosted fluid inclusions. These may be invisible due to the opacity of the solid petroleum host. Petroleum species may also desorb from pore-occluding bitumen during crush- ing, much as they do from mature kerogen (see below). Bitumen-sourced FIS responses may be inferred when strongly anomalous zones contain low visible petroleum inclusion abundance but have significant amounts of bitumen (e.g., common, abundant or extremely abundant). Abundant pore-filling bitumen in porous rock implies significant petroleum saturation at some time, so low visual petroleum inclusion abundance is unexpected (and not commonly encoun- tered). In such cases it is possible either that the size of the inclusions are below the resolution of the light microscope (< micron), that grain surface conditions (e.g., wettability) did not favor trapping of inclusions, or that the section was diagenetically quiescent during and after charging (i.e., little or no cementation or microfracturing).

A.4 Individual Track Plots A.4.1 Explanation and Significance of Individual Track Plots The following is synopsis of the significance of the different patterns of mass abundances and abundance ratios shown in Tracks 1-25. Note that not all species are quantified using their parent or molecular peaks (e.g., methane at m/z = 15) in order to minimize interfering contributions from other species. A.4.2 Ratios vs. Absolute Abundance Both ratios of key ionized compounds as well as absolute abundances of key compounds (rel- ative to natural oil inclusion standard) are used in interpretation. Absolute abundances of species can be influenced by the efficiency of inclusion formation, the size distribution of the inclusions, the saturation and residence time of the fluid within the pore system and the relative proportion of fluid of given composition that moved through that stratigraphic com- partment. Chemical ratios, on the other hand, are not as susceptible to lithologic/diagenetic controls on inclusion formation/distribution, hence, may be better suited for displaying chem- ical compartments in some cases. They are also useful for enhancing some of the subtle trends within the data, and for characterizing chemical variability among petroleum inclusion com- partments, which could be related to source, timing, or migration process. Ratio plots are not completely independent of inclusion abundance, as the intensity of mass spectrometer re- sponses is somewhat non-linear with respect to ion concentration. Both types of plots should be considered during interpretation. Track 1: Total Response - This represents the sum of the positive responses on all measured masses from < m/z < 180. These data are potentially useful for some data normalization schemes, or for estimating the relative percentage of given compound in the analyzed sample. Note that responses are generally dominated by water and carbon dioxide, and that absolute quan- tification is not possible because water cannot be quantitatively analyzed with this system. The polar nature of water causes it to adhere to metallic surfaces inside the instrument resulting in false readings by the detector. However, two characteristics of the total response are notewor- thy. First, total responses are often orders of magnitude greater for samples yielding proximity spectra than for other samples originating outside the hydrocarbon zone, even though the lithologies are usually clay rich, hence low in natural inclusion abundance. This is one line of evidence that leads us to hypothesize that proximity samples are dominated by drilling induced inclusions which trap some of the present day formation fluid. Secondly, inferred petroleum migration compartments are often characterized by high total responses. This suggests that both organic and inorganic inclusions are anomalously represented within these compartments. The significance of this correlation is not fully understood, but may document fracture form- ing process occurring during focused movement of basinal fluids, including petroleum. If so, it may eventually provide additional information about the nature and mechanisms of secondary petroleum migration. Track 2: m/z = 44 Dominant peak for carbon dioxide (CO+2 ), with possible minor contribution from C+3 hydrocarbon fragments and acetic acid. Anomalous values have been noted associated with pan-evaporative dolomitization of limestones in China and Oman. CO2 response is often

For wells 6605/1-1 Obelix and 6605/8-1, no useful lithological data were available from the NPD website, although drilling history and formation tops were available for tie well 6605/8-1. The ST0873 survey area is an extended grid, measuring 5km and covering the proposed well location. Due to the depth of the water, only Single Beam Echo Sounder and 2D high resolution seismic data were acquired. No coring was undertaken. The survey comprised 28 lines of the integrated survey with mainlines orientated 024°/204° and crossline orientated 114°/294°. StatoilHydro provided the GRE02STR05-3530 3D cube. The 3D data, as supplied, covers the Asterix survey area and extends 26km to the SSW providing some coverage over the 6605/1-1 Obelix well. The supplied volume has record length of seconds TWT to which static offset of 993ms was added to provide match with the 2D data.
