However, the previous report for the Obelix location, situated 24km to the SSW of the Asterix site was made available to which the stratigraphy was tied (see section 9).

A.2 FIS Mass Spectra 43 is inferred (but not demonstrated) only in the presence of other sulfur species. The m/z 32 would appear to be good one for indicating sulfur presence; however, this ion location suffers major potential interference from atmospheric oxygen (O+2 ). Care must be taken when interpreting sulfur-enriched FIS spectra, because at first glance they resemble the water-soluble enriched spectra. Ideally, the distinction lies in the location of CS2 at m/z 76 (as opposed to benzene at 78), H2S at m/z 34 and S+2 and/or SO2 at m/z 64. SO2 presence can be verified by the presence of paired anomaly at 64 and 48. In practice, it is sometimes difficult to distinguish between sulfur-enrichment and water-soluble species enrichment when these species are not strongly anomalous, and combinations of the two spectra occur as well. A.2.3 Summary of the Five Spectral Types The above is relatively detailed account of the characteristics of the five major classes of FIS mass spectra. In the end, however, the best way to recognize and distinguish among spectral types is to compare them to the end-member examples presented herein and categorize them by eye. After examining few examples of each, pattern recognition will become easy. Understanding the complexities outlined in the previous sections is important, but usually unnecessary for first-order interpretation of FIS mass spectra. To summarize: Non-hydrocarbon Spectra: Characterized by four peak clusters centered on m/z 15, 28, 42 and 55; the first three being dominant. Most peaks are attributable to water and carbon dioxide. Gas-range enriched: Characterized by strong responses on C1-C5 (m/z 12-72) and lesser intensities on higher molecular weight ion locations. Peak clusters may be more broad at m/z 12-30 and 37-46. Predominance of masses 15 and 16, and high 57/55 ratios is possible. Liquid-range enriched: Characterized by the presence of C7-C13+ species as regularly-spaced peak clusters in the m/z 95-180 range, which are dominated by ions from paraffinic and naph- thenic compounds. Aromatic species contribute subordinate peak clusters between the paraffin- naphthene peaks (although, typically only benzene, toluene and xylenes are resolved). Water-soluble enriched: Characterized by methane, ethane, organic acids, benzene and toluene. Acetic Acid (m/z 60) and aromatic peak clusters (m/z 78, 91, 105) attain intensities near or greater than those of adjacent paraffin-naphthene peak clusters. Sulfur-compound enriched: Characterized by the presence of H2S, COS, CS2 and SO2 and/or native sulfur gas as indicated by anomalies on some combination of the m/z peaks 34, 48, 60, 64 and 76. A.2.4 Combinations of Spectral Types Combined FIS spectra are common, and appear as superimposed end member types. Although combinations of all end member spectra have been noted, the most common are gas + liquids and liquids + water-solubles. Recall that FIS is bulk technique and samples the entire fluid history of the pore system. Hence, mixed FIS spectra might be expected if the sample has experienced temporally distinct charges of petroleum (or brine) types or contained heterogeneous (immiscible) fluid in the pore system at some time.

context_snippets.text: Palynological Examination of the 2/7-9X Well Summary The study analyzed the palynology of forty-three cutting samples of the 2/7-9X well. The sediments penetrated at the base of the well are interpreted to be Valanginian to Barremian in age. Conclusions The well passes through thick Albian to Neocomian sequence. The caving of Paleogene forms and the recycling of both Upper Jurassic and Permo-Triassic taxa complicate the basic age interpretation. Recommendations The findings of this study agree with the results of the EPS nannofossil data communicated in Report No. 2463A.

1 - 23 C. Maturation History - Thermal History Maturity modelling was carried out using Phillips proprietory software in Stavanger. The subsidence curve with maturity path based on the present day geothermal gradient of degree F/100' is shown on Fig. 1-2. The Pliocene/Miocene boundary was placed in the section which was drilled without returns in an attempt to follow the sub- sidence pattern established in the Miocene and to avoid unrealistically rapid subsidence in the Pliocene. The Miocene - Pliocene boundary was not defined in the 2/7-9 well, biostratigraphy started below 4,000'. As shown in the subsidence graph, vitrinite reflectance in excess of 1.3% would have been expected in the well at TD. Figure 1-3 shows the actual measured maturity which reaches only - 0.87% for the in-situ vitrinite at TD. To match the observed maturity with paleogradient, thermal modelling was carried out (Fig. 1-4). paleogradient between and 1.5° appears to give the best match. For the burial history shown on Fig. 1-5 geothermal gradient of F/100' was assumed which gives more realistic maturity distribution. The observed phenomenon can be interpreted as follows: The high geothermal gradient observed in the well near TD has been established relatively recently. If the high tem- peratures would have acted on the vitrinite for longer period of time, higher vitrinite reflectance values would have been observed. The reason for this anomaly is unknown. Changes in the local or regional heat flow regime are the likely causes.

1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

I. STRATIGRAPHIC PROGNOSIS The stratigraphic prognosis for the 2/11-9 well is described below and shown in Figure 9. This prognosis is based primarily on wells 2/7-20, 2/7-9, 2/11-8, Kim-1 and Lone-1 Additionally, information from various papers on North Sea geology have been used, including C.E. Deegan and B.J. Scull's standard lithostratigraphic nomenclature for the Central and Northern North Sea, as well as NPD Bulletins No. and 5. This combined information provide good source from which stratigraphic conclusions have been drawn for the 2/11-9 well. QUATERNARY AND TERTIARY; SPUD - 3000m TVD SS The Quaternary and Tertiary sector is subdivided into three groups, which are the: 1) Nordland Group dominated by soft clays and sands which overlies the 2) Hordaland Group consisting mainly of claystones and interbedded carbonates which overlies the 3) Roaaland Group which contains tuffaceous shales and varicolored muds tones. RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group. question: What was the sequence of operations after the 7" liner stuck at 5720m, including cut, fishing/RIH attempts, and the 200m cement plug (5720–5520m)?
answer_text: The 7″ liner was cut at 5720 m, RIH with fishing assemblies to engage and work the fish (unsuccessfully), POOH with the fishing assembly, then RIH with a cement stinger and set a 200 m cement plug from 5720–5520 m.

question: How do vertical permeability values of the micaceous siltstone core compare with those from the Fensfjord formation, and what are the trapping implications?
answer_text: Both are very low (<1 mD vertical permeability) and therefore act as vertical barriers/seals that can trap hydrocarbons.

context_snippets.text: above, the boundary marks change from the deposition of shaly sands to cemented clean sands, and is also an erosional surface. From analogy with similar environments elsewhere it was postulated that this surface may have been the site of soil development and possibly related cementation. On logs the surface coincided with thick tight zone (figure 4), and in order to match both pressures and water cut it was found necessary to make the surface a complete barrier to vertical permeability in all updip areas, where maximum erosion of the lower unit had taken place (figure 5). Thus, in this case, the cross section was used to test geological hypotheses such as the existence of permeability barriers and possible Kv/KH ratios, which were then used in full field simulation. 4. Full Field Modelling The use of full field modelling is natural extension of the cross-section work described above. However, layers are coarser, and due to the size of the model, changes are more difficult and more expensive to make. However, certain facets of the reservoir model such as areal variability can be tested. In the field under study the net/gross ratio shows marked changes areally. This is caused by the natural feature of fluviatile systems where zones located on, or near, the major axis of the drainage system tend to be sand rich, while those on the periphery are sand poor. Figure shows diagramatically this relationship. In sand-rich zones, where channels erode into one another, the overall transmissibility is good, as is the vertical permeability. However, in sand-poor zones both these parameters are drastically lowered. In order to account for this effect, the net/gross ratio was introduced as multiplier for the two horizontal gridblock permeabilities. It was found that for an effective match, the vertical grid block permeability had to be multiplied by power of the net/gross ratio because the interbedded shales parallel to reservoir layers will always have more pronounced impact on vertical fluid movement (figure 7). Research is continuing into more realistic ways of modelling such parameters as the effective vertical permeability, but it is hoped that the above discussion indicates that it is possible to improve reservoir modelling by iterative use of simulation models. CONDENSATE FIELD WITH NO PRODUCTION DATA. One of the major exploration plays in the North Sea currently is for condensate in Mesozoic sandstone reservoirs of the Central and Northern North Sea. Clearly, development of reservoirs of this type could involve markedly different development programmes from those currently in operation on the oilfields. Compositional changes, gas/liquid relative relationships and the possibility of cycling are important factors that require consideration and, as this paper demonstrates, the system becomes very complex making the prediction of the optimum configuration for maximum liquid recovery difficult. In order to analyse the problem, simple model was built using realistic reservoir properties. The model was then used to test various production strategies and the sensitivity of these to the reservoir geological model. Geological Model The geological model is illustrated in figure and represents an average Brent Sand package with three layers of high permeability representing the Etive Formation, low permeability layer at the Rannoch/Etive boundary and four layers of intermediate permeability representing the Rannoch and Broom Formations. Since this was preliminary study the model was kept as simple as realism allowed, and such features as very high permeability zones in the Etive Formation were not introduced.

Based on porosity logs, the Etive Formation may be subdivided into three separate units. The upper has porosity ranging from 8% at 2656 to 25% at 2665 meters. The middle unit (2 5m) has nearly constant porosity around 20%. The lower unit (2 6m) has porosity increasing with depth, from 1796 to 20%. The Etive Formation appears to have an overall coarsening upwards trend.

Because of the surprisingly low heat flow values that were calculated quite some effort was put into investigations to look for any errors in the heat flow calculation. The first to be checked was the thermal conductivity, and from theoretical calculations based on input of mineral composition, water content and gas voids (in some cores) it was found that the originally used values for thermal conductivity should have been multiplied by factor of about 1.81. Further analyses of the needle probes used for the field measurements showed that the correct factor is 1.799, which therefore should be applied to all values given in the first report. Other effects which were investigated were possible changes in thermal conductivity due to pressure and temperature changes from in situ conditions to the laboratory, gas influence, anisotropy and possible influences on the temperature gradient due to Quaternary glaciations. The thermal conductivity was measured in the laboratory on board and it is concluded that neither the temperature nor the pressure change itself influenced significantly. secondary but significant effect of pressure release has occurred at sites D85-N, D85-0 and D85-V, because samples from the depths in question from these sites were found to contain gas dissolved in the pore water. This resulted in gas voids being formed in the laboratory which influenced the thermal conduct- ivity measurements. The necessary correction for this is found to be an increase in the average measured thermal conductivity from these sites by 16%, 8% and 4% respectively. 28 representative samples have been subjected to measurement of both vertical and horizontal thermal conductivity and these values were found to differ in average by 13%. question: Do migration-edge distortions, pick/velocity uncertainties, or diplog stress preclude resolving Ness Formation fault throw using VSP and 3D walkaway data?
answer_text: Yes — migration-edge distortions and pick/velocity uncertainties prevent defining exact Ness Formation fault throws from the VSP and walkaway data; diplog stress perturbations do not preclude fault identification and can support the interpretation.

context_snippets.text: Compared to the 3D seismic data, the Normal Incidence VSP has better intra-Brent resolution and shows more details. A minor fault displacing the reservoir sequence down to the west (Figure 3-3), is hardly detectable on the ordinary seismic lines. Also for the Brent unit the VSP image shows good seismic continuity and justify the picking of seismic horizons tied to the well. The main results shown on the Walkaway image (Figure 3- 4), is that the existence of the faults originally mapped to the east and the west of the well, are confirmed by the walkaway VSP. possible minor fault in the middle to lower Jurassic sequence is indicated as well. Due to migration effects along the edges, the exact throws can not be defined. The line also indicates that faulting has occurred in late Jurassic deposits above the main reservoir. Time/Depth Well Results The actual depths and transit times for 30/9-12 and -12A have been compared to the prognosis (Tables 3-3 and 3-4). For some of the markers the discrepancies between the prognosis and the actual results are outside the range of the estimated uncertainties. Deviations between prognosed and actual values are caused by discrepancies in either the seismic picks, the velocity model used for depth conversion, or combination of these. Also difference between the prognosed and final well track will influence the results. Location maps for Base Cretaceous Unconformity, Top Ness Formation and Base Brent Group are shown in Figures 3-5 through 3-7.

the reservoir in the first section, drill through the lagoonal event, and drain the lower part of the reservoir in the last part of the well section. The TD criteria will be to have at least 100 meter reservoir section in the lower reservoir. In order to avoid the weaker, coarse-grained sands of T2B4, which are considered to be prone to sand production as reservoir pressure drops, optimal position of the drain is in reservoir zone T2B5 (below the hot shale separating T2B5 from T2B6, and above the hot shale indicating the top of the lagoonal event (T2B3). Below the lagoonal event position as close to the middle of the sandy interval as possible should be sought after. The actual target location might be shifted outside given limitations if results during drilling should demand so. 5.2 Geophysical Prognosis Seismic quality and well database The Tune Field is covered by the NH9802R99 and NH9304 surveys. The NH9802R99 is reprocessed data from NH9802 while NH9304 is merge of NH9304, VG91 and SH9004. The NH9802R99 data set has normal polarity display (SEG standard), i.e. an increase in acoustic impedance is represented by negative pulse (red trough on all enclosed seismic line examples). The wavelet is close to zero phase. The data quality for the survey NH9802R99 varies from good to poor. In the central parts of the field the target sequence, Middle Tarbert and Ness Formations, are clearly defined with good seismic character. In structural complicated areas, like the relay ramp area in the southeast and the drag-zone in the north-east (A-North) and the southern part of A-Main, the definition of key seismic horizons and faults are poor. In addition, the poor data quality appears to be related to shale diapirism in the Tertiary and/or the possible presence of gas in the Cretaceous and Jurassic sections. Ray-path distortion in the Terti- ary section is another factor that deteriorates the data quality. The NH9802 survey and the reprocessed NH9802R99 data set are definitely an improve- ment from the earlier data sets. The seismic reflectors are better defined, the resolution is higher and the fault definition has higher confidence. The main well database for the seismic calibration and depth conversion consist of the used to establish the velocity field for depth conversion. Seismic horizon definition along the well path Five seismic reflectors are used in the well prognosis. The reflectors Top Cretaceous and Base Cretaceous Unconformity are taken from the Tune PDO 1999, whereas Top Balder Formation, Top Tarbert 2B6 and Top Ness Formation were reinterpreted on the survey NH9802R99 in 2000. Figure shows seismic profile along the planned well path while Figure shows the planned well path in the target area. Table lists the geophysical prognosis for the different markers based on seismic picks from these. The well is expected to penetrate only few smaller faults along the track.

IrakIII this interval. There is strong evidence for an intra-Etive fault, possibly oriented E-W, which has cut out part of the Etive interval and caused subtle structural rotation of the upper Brent relative to the lower Brent. separate structural dip (159/04°) has therefore been removed from the upper Brent. There is zone of penecontemporaneous faulting within the Ness Fm at around 4100m. There is probably fault immediately above top reservoir but the distinction between faulting and unconforrnity over this zone is difficult to establish. We would recommend that diplog data be re-displayed in the time domain to overlay large-scale seismic displays in order to resolve this. We would be pleased to work with Statoil to produce suitable plots if required. 4.2 STRESS FIELD Knowledge of stress field anisotropy and orientation can yield important tectonic insights, enable prediction of the orientation of natural and induced rock fractures and assist in the correction of core petrophysical parameters to subsurface conditions. Fracture systems and breakouts are not directly observable on diplogs (c.f. image logs, such as the CBIL) but valuable information can be obtained from calliper data alone. Boreholes in an anisotropic horizontal stress field tend to become elliptical, with the long axis of the ellipse oriented parallel to the minimum horizontal principle stress. The borehole walls will tend to fail and spall away in this direction, producing vertical grooves known as breakouts (e.g. Hillis & Williams, 1992). The four-arm diplog provides two orthogonal calliper measurements. One calliper will tend to lodge in the long-axis of the borehole ellipse, so that the callipers give an indication of the orientation of borehole elipticity, and hence an insight into the stress field. The borehole in 34/11-1 is only slightly elliptical. Data on borehole eccentricity were obtained by comparing the maximum and minimum calliper values every 0.5m, seeking eccentricities greater than 1.01, ignoring hole sections greater than out of gauge, interpreted as washouts. 1:200 plot of ellipse orientations (in-situ stress analysis) is included in Volume 2. The most obvious feature of these data is strong WNW-ENE preferred orientation (Fig. 11), indicating SSW-NNE orientation for the maximum horizontal principal stress. This orientation is consistent with regional observations on the stress field of the North Viking Graben (Cowgill et al. 1993) but is orthogonal to much of the data for the Tampen Spur (Jorgensen & Bratli, 1995). Open faults/fractures are known to cause local perturbations in the stress field (Bell et al., 1992). Such perturbations provide additional support for fault interpretations from diplogs and some insight into fault orientation. The inferred faults at 4170m and 4040m both show perturbations in the stress field consistent with approximately E-W faulting. Page 18

question: Which primary measured outputs and sample requirements distinguish STT triaxial tests from Dean-Stark saturation analyses?
answer_text: STT triaxial: measures triaxial compressive strength (MPa) on 1×2‑inch vertical natural‑moisture core plugs under a 2 MPa confining pressure. Dean–Stark: measures extracted water volume / water saturation (Sw) on onshore‑drilled inch plugs via toluene extraction with salt correction.

context_snippets.text: 2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (Clairsol) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. 3 SPECTRAL CORE GAMMA LOG A spectral core gamma log of the cores was performed by recording the natural gamma radiation from the cores using NaI crystal scintillator. The signals were detected and amplified through photo multiplicator tube, and recorded by computer connected multi channel analyser. The different radioactive minerals emit gamma rays of characteristic energy levels, and based on these levels the contributions from the minerals, potassium, uranium and thorium are specified. The quantitative description of the mineral content is based on calibration with standard calibration cores supplied by IFE, Institutt for Energiteknikk, Kjeller (Norway). The total and spectral core gamma log are reported in 1:200 scale, the total gamma is plotted in counts/minute (c/min), the concentration of potassium is plotted in %, and the concentrations of thorium and uranium in ppm. Spectral core gamma log plots are included in Appendix of this report.

7 TRIAXIAL STRENGTH (STT) Simplified triaxial compressive strength tests were performed on 1x2 inch vertical samples. The tests were performed on natural moisture samples. The core plug compressive strength was determined by loading axial pressure to the sample in compression bi-axial core holder to sample failure (collapse). The triaxial compressive strength of the sample is defined as the highest pressure reading value before failure. A constant axial hydraulic (hand pump) pressure was applied, at constant radial (2 MPa) confining pressure. The time for hydrostatic loading up to MPa and time for consolidation was minimum minute. The confining pressure was kept constant at MPa and the axial pressure was increased until plug collapse. The time for loading in the shear phase upon rock failure is minimum minutes. The manometer (max. peak memory) read the failure pressure directly in MPa, the only adjustment required was small correction factor for the difference in piston and sample areas. A calculated correction factor of was required in this experiment to correct the compressive strength gauge reading. Ccorr = meas. * Results from the triaxial compressive strength tests are presented in Appendix of this report. Results are also included on the Final report CD. Restricted 13

8 SATURATION 8.1 Dean & Stark Fluid saturation analyses were performed by Dean-Stark method on inch plugs drilled onshore: Plugs for Sw were drilled with Clarisol oil as cooling agent. Water was extracted from the plugs using toluene, giving direct water volume readings. The amount of water extracted from each sample was recorded. Method: Toluene has boiling point of approx. 110°C. When the toluene reaches the boiling point, heat from the toluene vapor causes the water in the sample to evaporate. The toluene- and water vapor both condense in water cooler. The water is collected in water-trap. The toluene in its liquid state flows back and soaks the sample, extracting the oil in the sample. See Figure 8.1, standard D&S equipment setup. The water in the water collector is distilled. Dissolved salts in the formation water are not dissolved by the toluene, and, therefore, remain in the core sample. Subsequent to the Dean&Stark extraction the sample is placed in the soxhlet apparatus using methanol to remove salt deposits in the sample. The extracted water volume is corrected for salt content. correction factor for each depth zone is found using total water volume and total salt weight from all plugs covering each depth zone. Where: w = Distilled water density (g/cm3) b = Brine density (g/cm3) Cs = Dissolved salt concentration (g/l) The salt weight is the plug weight difference prior and after Methanol extraction. Density of brine is based on all salt being NaCl (Sodium Cloride). Complete removal of hydrocarbons was confirmed by visual checking the solvent discoloration, and by examine the sample using UV light. Chemical checks, using Silver Nitrate solution, were made to ensure that all salt had been removed. The samples were dried at 60 0C, for 48 hours and the weight recorded. Restricted 15

The CT scan also helps locating any fractured areas of the core, identify density variations and can be used as tool for orientation of the core prior to slabbing or subsequent plug sampling. The core still in unopened core inner barrels was CT-scanned to evaluate core quality. One overview picture (topogram) and four slice pictures were produced every 100-cm of core. The topogram is standard X-ray Scan taken from above, covering the length of the preserved core sample. context_snippets.text: 2.5.2 CORE DESCRIPTION AND INTERPRETATION Introduction Three whole cores were recovered in the 7321/7-1 well, amounting to 16 of section in the Knurr, StO, and Snadd Formations. Cores of the Knurr and StO were photographed following cleaning prior to any further core work, in order to differentiate between natural fractures and those produced during slabbing and plugging. Cores of all three formations were photographed following slabbing in order to facilitate sedimentological analysis. Core descriptions were made in November of 1988, soon after slabbing. Samples were taken for special studies on diagenesis and for comparison to petrophysical measurements. The special studies will be the subject of separate report to be completed in 1989. This section is devoted to an objective description of the rocks and their reservoir quality. Knurr Formation Approximately three (3) meters of shale in the Knurr Formation were obtained at core depth of 1907-1909,5 (Fig. 2.5). Log-core comparisons indicate depth shift of (core is high to the log). The rock is dark grey silty shale, containing numerous disarticulated bivalves. The shale is not calcareous and shows color change to light grey at 1908 core depth. The shale contains cubic forms of the mineral pyrite with the degree of pyritization increasing downward. Chondrites-type burrows are present. A few open fractures were observed on the slabbed and unslabbed cores. It is likely that these are natural fractures, although the fissility of the shale in the lower part of the core makes fracture interpretation more tenuous. Paleoenvironmental Interpretation: The presence of Chondrites-like burrows and thin-walled bivalves suggests marine, low-oxygen, reducing environment well below fairweather wave base. This is

AlII HYDRO 1. INTRODUCTION The report presents the results of petrographical evaluation of the cored section in Well 7122/2-1, that was drilled by Norsk Hydro within the PL179 licence during the Autumn 1992. Well 7122/2-1 provided eight cores from the depth intervals 1771-1784m (core to 3), 1812-1824m (core 4) and 1833-1932m (core to 8). The upper four cores represent the Early to Middle Barremian Kolje Formation, whilst the lower four represent the Valanganian to Heuterivian Knurr Formation. main objective of the present study is to provide detailed petrographical characterization of these cored intervals. Furthermore, an attempt is maid to decipher the diagenetic evolution in order to comment on the effect of rock composition and diagenetic evolution on the reservoir quality of the sandstones. The report presents 1) the results of standard petrographical analyses based on thin- section and XRD-analyses, and 2) the results of some more detailed mineralogical and textural analyses emphasising the diagenetic evolution of the sandstones. The discussion on the diagenetic evolution includes detailed modal analyses, fluid inclusion thermometry on inclusions in quartz cements and Cathodo-Luminescence (CL) and Back Scatter Electron Imaging (BSE) using Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). The report is organized as follows: The standard petrographical analyses of samples from the cored sections are presented in Part 2, and the results of the more detailed diagenetic analyses on the samples are presented in Part 3. summary of the findings of the present study and some recommendations for further work is given in Part 4. Figure shows the location of Licence PL179 and of Well 7122/2-1. Seismic section crossing the well location is presented in Fig. 1.2. Schematic litho-logs and sample depths from the cored intervals are presented in Figs. and 1.4.

SCREENING ANALYSES A total of 339 samples, covering the depth interval 9 m, was supplied by A.S. Norske Shell. The cuttings samples were washed, and all samples lithologically described (Table 1), and all relevant source rock lithologies analysed by LECO TOO. (Table 1). Eighty-two selected lithologies were, based on the TOO data analysed by Rock-Eval (Table 2). Figure is lithological column with relevant stratigraphic information and TOO values. Figures 3, 4, and show the S2, the hydrogen index, the petroleum potential and the production index plotted as function of depth respectively, while Figure shows Tmax versus depth plot. 2.1.1 Lithology and Source Rock Potential The samples from the Lower Cretaceous undifferentiated Nordvestbanken Gp. and the Knurr Fm. (1 m) consist mainly of medium to dark grey silty claystone and shale. The samples from the undifferentiated part of the section have typically fair TOO contents (0.44 - %), while the samples from the Knurr Fm. have good contents (1.45 - %). Only three samples from the latter were analysed by Rock-Eval, all having low hydrogen indices (57 - 76 mg HC/g TOO) suggesting organic matter of type IV kerogen with at best poor potential (< mg HC/g rock) foi.generation of very small amounts of gas.

HYDRO CORE DESCRIPTION - WELL 7122/2-1 Page: 10 of 13 2.2 The Kolje formation Cores no. 1, 2, and were cut in the Kolje Formation comprising the interval between 1771 - in the lower half of the formation. The age is Early Barremian to Early Albian. Core - are dominated by very hard claystones cemented by siderite, calcite and pyrite. This caused very slow drilling rate. Core consist of claystones interbedded with siltstones and sandstones. Figure shows detailed stratigraphic log from core 4. The lower half is dominated by dark brown and black pyritic claystone with thin stringers of siltstone. The claystones are very organic rich. Siderite, pyrite and calcite occurs in nodules and layers. The upper part of the core contains alternating sandstone layers and claystones. The sandstones are massive with small fining upwards sequences. It is fine to coarse grained with a grey to dark grey colour. Soft sedimentary structures including convolute lamination and water escape structures are observed. No trace fossils are identified. Organic rich claystones reflects regional transgressive event in the Barremian. The Knurr Formation was overlain by shaly deposits. transgressive development caused shift in facies from submarine fan systems to open marine pyritic shales in the Kolje Formation.

2.4 STRATIGRAPHY 2.4.1 Biostratigraphy The biostratigraphical study of well 7122/7-2 was carried out by Eni S.p.A. Di visione Agip. Fig. 2.4.1 shows summarised chronostratigraphic and lithostratigraphic subdivision of the well. Further details may be found in the report Norsk Agip Well 7122/7-2, Biostratigraphic analysis of the interval 900m — 1418m. 2.4.2 Lithostratigraphy The following summary is compiled predominantly from LWD data in the pilot hole from seabed at 395m (-377m TVDSS) to the 13 3/8 casing shoe at 900m. This section was drilled with return to seabed and Gamma ray, resistivity and ROP were used for interpretation. From 900m (-882m TVDSS) cuttings and cores were used in addition to wireline data for the interpretation. Nordland Group (395m — 448) Age: Tertiary/Quaternary Based on GR and resistivity the Nordland Group comprises undifferentiated siltstones. Sotbakken Group (448 — 600m) Age: Tertiary Sandstone becoming silty and argillaceous with occasionaly limestone stringers. Nygrunnen Group (600 — 638m) Age: Cretaceous Siltstone with claystone beds. Nordwestbanken Group ( 638 — 986m) Massive claystone, initially with sandstone stringers. Claystone with thin Limestone and Dolomite stringers is the dominant lithology below the 13 3/8 shoe where cuttings were available for description. The Claystone is dark grey, soft to firm occasionally silty, with glauconite and pyrite. The Limestone is pale red brown to dusty yellow brown, hard, brittle in parts, very argillaceous grading to marl. Knurr Formation (984m — 1021m) Age: Early Cretaceous Upper Boundary: Shows slightly increasing gamma ray combined with general drop and less spiky resistivity. The lithology is massive claystone with two dolomitic limestone stringers around 1000m. The claystone is dark grey, earthy, firm to hard. occasionally soft and sticky, fissile in parts, amorphous to sub blocky, occasionally calcareous with abundant pyrite. question: How do turbine plug, DICV leak, and OH at 3350m differently affect BHA changes and kill operations?
answer_text: Turbine plugging caused very high, fluctuating pressure losses that made BHA rotation and stripping unsafe and compromised well control. A leaking DICV (loss of isolation) and the open hole in very bad shape below 3350 m forced pulling the BHA back to the 5/8 window, installing valves and bullheading premixed kill mud (SG 2.10–2.20) to kill the well.

question: How does VSP compare with surface seismic in resolving Brent fault throws and imaging the impact of migration edges?
answer_text: VSP provides superior intra‑Brent resolution and reveals/validates faults that ordinary surface seismic often misses, but migration effects along edges prevent precise definition of fault throws.

context_snippets.text: Compared to the 3D seismic data, the Normal Incidence VSP has better intra-Brent resolution and shows more details. A minor fault displacing the reservoir sequence down to the west (Figure 3-3), is hardly detectable on the ordinary seismic lines. Also for the Brent unit the VSP image shows good seismic continuity and justify the picking of seismic horizons tied to the well. The main results shown on the Walkaway image (Figure 3- 4), is that the existence of the faults originally mapped to the east and the west of the well, are confirmed by the walkaway VSP. possible minor fault in the middle to lower Jurassic sequence is indicated as well. Due to migration effects along the edges, the exact throws can not be defined. The line also indicates that faulting has occurred in late Jurassic deposits above the main reservoir. Time/Depth Well Results The actual depths and transit times for 30/9-12 and -12A have been compared to the prognosis (Tables 3-3 and 3-4). For some of the markers the discrepancies between the prognosis and the actual results are outside the range of the estimated uncertainties. Deviations between prognosed and actual values are caused by discrepancies in either the seismic picks, the velocity model used for depth conversion, or combination of these. Also difference between the prognosed and final well track will influence the results. Location maps for Base Cretaceous Unconformity, Top Ness Formation and Base Brent Group are shown in Figures 3-5 through 3-7.

the reservoir in the first section, drill through the lagoonal event, and drain the lower part of the reservoir in the last part of the well section. The TD criteria will be to have at least 100 meter reservoir section in the lower reservoir. In order to avoid the weaker, coarse-grained sands of T2B4, which are considered to be prone to sand production as reservoir pressure drops, optimal position of the drain is in reservoir zone T2B5 (below the hot shale separating T2B5 from T2B6, and above the hot shale indicating the top of the lagoonal event (T2B3). Below the lagoonal event position as close to the middle of the sandy interval as possible should be sought after. The actual target location might be shifted outside given limitations if results during drilling should demand so. 5.2 Geophysical Prognosis Seismic quality and well database The Tune Field is covered by the NH9802R99 and NH9304 surveys. The NH9802R99 is reprocessed data from NH9802 while NH9304 is merge of NH9304, VG91 and SH9004. The NH9802R99 data set has normal polarity display (SEG standard), i.e. an increase in acoustic impedance is represented by negative pulse (red trough on all enclosed seismic line examples). The wavelet is close to zero phase. The data quality for the survey NH9802R99 varies from good to poor. In the central parts of the field the target sequence, Middle Tarbert and Ness Formations, are clearly defined with good seismic character. In structural complicated areas, like the relay ramp area in the southeast and the drag-zone in the north-east (A-North) and the southern part of A-Main, the definition of key seismic horizons and faults are poor. In addition, the poor data quality appears to be related to shale diapirism in the Tertiary and/or the possible presence of gas in the Cretaceous and Jurassic sections. Ray-path distortion in the Terti- ary section is another factor that deteriorates the data quality. The NH9802 survey and the reprocessed NH9802R99 data set are definitely an improve- ment from the earlier data sets. The seismic reflectors are better defined, the resolution is higher and the fault definition has higher confidence. The main well database for the seismic calibration and depth conversion consist of the used to establish the velocity field for depth conversion. Seismic horizon definition along the well path Five seismic reflectors are used in the well prognosis. The reflectors Top Cretaceous and Base Cretaceous Unconformity are taken from the Tune PDO 1999, whereas Top Balder Formation, Top Tarbert 2B6 and Top Ness Formation were reinterpreted on the survey NH9802R99 in 2000. Figure shows seismic profile along the planned well path while Figure shows the planned well path in the target area. Table lists the geophysical prognosis for the different markers based on seismic picks from these. The well is expected to penetrate only few smaller faults along the track.

IrakIII this interval. There is strong evidence for an intra-Etive fault, possibly oriented E-W, which has cut out part of the Etive interval and caused subtle structural rotation of the upper Brent relative to the lower Brent. separate structural dip (159/04°) has therefore been removed from the upper Brent. There is zone of penecontemporaneous faulting within the Ness Fm at around 4100m. There is probably fault immediately above top reservoir but the distinction between faulting and unconforrnity over this zone is difficult to establish. We would recommend that diplog data be re-displayed in the time domain to overlay large-scale seismic displays in order to resolve this. We would be pleased to work with Statoil to produce suitable plots if required. 4.2 STRESS FIELD Knowledge of stress field anisotropy and orientation can yield important tectonic insights, enable prediction of the orientation of natural and induced rock fractures and assist in the correction of core petrophysical parameters to subsurface conditions. Fracture systems and breakouts are not directly observable on diplogs (c.f. image logs, such as the CBIL) but valuable information can be obtained from calliper data alone. Boreholes in an anisotropic horizontal stress field tend to become elliptical, with the long axis of the ellipse oriented parallel to the minimum horizontal principle stress. The borehole walls will tend to fail and spall away in this direction, producing vertical grooves known as breakouts (e.g. Hillis & Williams, 1992). The four-arm diplog provides two orthogonal calliper measurements. One calliper will tend to lodge in the long-axis of the borehole ellipse, so that the callipers give an indication of the orientation of borehole elipticity, and hence an insight into the stress field. The borehole in 34/11-1 is only slightly elliptical. Data on borehole eccentricity were obtained by comparing the maximum and minimum calliper values every 0.5m, seeking eccentricities greater than 1.01, ignoring hole sections greater than out of gauge, interpreted as washouts. 1:200 plot of ellipse orientations (in-situ stress analysis) is included in Volume 2. The most obvious feature of these data is strong WNW-ENE preferred orientation (Fig. 11), indicating SSW-NNE orientation for the maximum horizontal principal stress. This orientation is consistent with regional observations on the stress field of the North Viking Graben (Cowgill et al. 1993) but is orthogonal to much of the data for the Tampen Spur (Jorgensen & Bratli, 1995). Open faults/fractures are known to cause local perturbations in the stress field (Bell et al., 1992). Such perturbations provide additional support for fault interpretations from diplogs and some insight into fault orientation. The inferred faults at 4170m and 4040m both show perturbations in the stress field consistent with approximately E-W faulting. Page 18

context_snippets.text: Formation Pressures affecting the temperature out readings. The temperature data showed continuation of the previously established geothermal gradient of degC/100m. The temperature gradient exhibits slight negative trend from 3450m to 3530m and then increases at the normal geothermal gradient to TD. Sonic data shows compactional trend to the top of the chalk when the data shows trend of 163 usecs/ft. As the chalk grades to mudstones the travel time increases to 190 usecs/ft by 3400m. Between 3400m and 3520m the data shows an increasing trend in mudstones suggesting an increase in pore pressure. Resistivity data indicates normally compacting sequence to the top of the chalk with values then becoming scattered. As mudstones are encountered the trend decreases to TD. 3.2 THE PRESSURE LOG — DISCUSSION Formation pressures were continuously evaluated from the 18 5/8 casing shoe until T.D. at 3710m. The following measured and calculated parameters were used in the pore pressure evaluation:- Corrected Drilling exponent Shale Density Mud Temperature In/Out MWD Tool Temperature Total Gas Observations of hole condition, cavings, trip gas and connection gas also furnished valuable data for overpressure evaluation, as did data obtained from wireline logs. The well can be divided pressure profile :- into the following sections with regard to the pore 1. 547m to 1400m Normal pore pressure (possible transition zone below 1000m) 2. 1400m to 1650m Rise in pore pressure to SG. 3. 1650m to 2050m Stable pressure SG. 4. 2250m to 2500m Rise in pore pressure to SG 5. 2500m to 3405m Stable or slight reduction in pressure 6. 3405m to T.D. Rapid rise stabilizing at SG.

- 23 -_ DISCUSSION OF THE PRESSURE LOG ( continued ) Flowline temperature was not available through this section due to the sensor being continuously buried in cuttings in section of the shaker box not readily accessible for maintenance. Gas levels were generally low to moderate in this section, ranging between 0.3% - 1.0%, with only occasional isolated peaks above the background level. Trip gases were all in the range - % (total) which were only slightly above the drilled gas levels. Overpull of 75 Klbs was encountered whilst reaming at 1700m, mainly due to packing of cuttings in the annulus during periods of continual very fast drilling; however the mud weight was raised from 1.28 sg to sg prior to drilling ahead. Through most of this section, data from logs of previous wells in the field was used in aiding in the estimation the pore pressure gradient. SECTION : 1/2 HOLE FROM 3203 TO 4375 I. The lithology in this section was variable; initially tuffaceous mudstone before small sandstone section, then siltstone, limestone and mudstone sections before the main body of hard chalky limestone with chert nodules. The base of the interval from about 4030m onwards consisted of calcareous mudstone. The lithology being so variable and the use of PDC bits in this section meant that no usable DXc Exp- onent trend was obtained although slight cutback was observed in the mudstone at the base of the section which was judged to be indicative of an increase in formation pore pressure. Drilling gas levels were very low, generally below %, down to 4200m where tenfold increase in background level was seen. This increased background level plus connection gases of up to % and wiper trip gases of up to % also were indicative of increased pore pressure in the section from 4200m to 4375m. Mud temperatures were not available over the first part of the interval due to the sensor being buried by accumulated cuttings, and the short bit runs made after clearing the sensor gave highly variable values. From 3800m stable trend was seen with slight cutback shown from 4100m. Delta temperature showed an increasing trend from 4200m. The pore pressure estimate was maintained at sg down to 4050m where indications from gas, temperature and DXc trends led to this being raised to sg in the MANDAL formation after 4300m. SECTION : HOLE FROM 4375 TO 4550 The lithology in this section consisted of the bottom part of the MANDAL formation and the main GYDA SANDSTONE reservoir. Most of the section was cored so no useful formation pore pressure evaluation information was recorded. The pore pressure estimate of sg seen in the MANDAL formation was maintained until the top of the GYDA sandstone was encountered where it was lowered to sg.

Authority J. Gamblen The pore and fracture pressures in this section are primarily based on the Gyda wells. Normal pore pressure (1.04 SG) will be evident until c. 1300m where it gradually increases to SG at c. 1700m. It gradually increases to 1.45 SG by section TD at 3200m. The 5/8 LOT at 3200m is expected around SG EMW. The 1/2 hole will be drilled to top reservoir, and possibly to well TD (4523m BRT) if mud weights allow. If the Mandal formation is not overpressured, the mud weight in use at top reservoir is SG or below, and there are no indications of hole problems, drilling/coring will continue to well TD, provided the error bar on top salt remains deeper than TD. If the Mandal formation is overpressured, the liner will be committed having tagged top sand, and the reservoir interval will be drilled in hole. The 1/2 hole will be initially drilled in the Chalk group. The upper Chalk, in the top Ekofisk formation, is expected to contain chert. The amount of chert is difficult to predict, however the lithology logs produced following 1/3-3 and 2/1-6 both indicated chert in the Ekofisk formation. Also, traces of blue grey chert were reported in the upper and mid Tor formations from well 1/3-3. Occasional pyrite was reported in the lower Tor formations on well 2/1-6. This cherty limestone is difficult to drill and will require conical insert drilling bits to efficiently drill the interval. As well as the hard drilling conditions in the Chalk Group there is also the possibility of stuck pipe due to differential sticking in the Tor. Careful attention will be made to monitoring mud properties and minimising overbalance. BP's extensive stuck pipe guidelines will be strictly adhered to throughout this section. of BP Norway Limited U.A.

SUMMARY This is the first time the PP/FG TM service has been used offshore Norway real-time. The well was drilled without significant problems and the reservoir pressure was close to that prognosed in the drilling programme. The PP/FG calculated pore pressure results calculated by the model can only be verified in permeable formations from formation tests and well control incidents. Pore pressure transition zones always occur in impermeable formations and here results can be contentious when compared to traditional methods of pore pressure prediction. However, the results do have value if they can aid in the prediction of pressure when entering permeable formation. There were only two depths in the well where it was possible to verify the PP/FG results: 1. possible small influx at 4387m implied that the pressure PP/FG result was close to the actual formation pressure. 2. Below the Mandal Formation we had to interpolate the resistivity through hydrocarbon-rich formations. Using this corrected resistivity curve we predicted the reservoir pressure gradient at 4500m to be 1.81g/cc. The measured pressure gradient was I.75g/cc from the MDT. A calculated pore pressure maximum of 2.09g/cc was reported during drilling of the Cromer Knoll Group. This was revised down to 2.00g/cc when the wireline data became available. The difference was mainly due to miscalibrated MWD resistivity run which was consistantly reading values 30% more conductive than the wireline, but also slightly due to the model interpreting the lithology from the gamma ray as too calcareous. The PP/FG calculated fracture pressure results were within 0.03g/cc of the actual LOT's at 13 3/8 and 7/8 shoes. This indicates that we have an accurate fracture propagation pressure gradient. Considerable valuable information and experience was gained as result of this work which will improve the PP/FG service and future pore and fracture pressure prediction in this area. It has allowed us to assess the updates and improvements to the program which have recently been added to the software, and has suggested additional improvements which are now being implemented. I. INTRODUCTION The Sperry-Sun PP/FG service is based on software model that calculates pore and fracture pressures on an incremental basis through all major lithologies in normally compacted sedimentary sequences. It requires calibration to offset wells. The two closest wells to the 2/7-29 location, 2/7-19 & 2/7-22, were studied and calibration for the real-time job was derived. This was described fully in previous report. This final report for BP Norway describes the pore and fracture pressure results using the PP/FG service on the Mmrsk Guardian for well 2/7-29. The service commenced from the 7/8 casing point at 3124m on the 16th October until the Permian at 4850m on the 21st December. Results from real- time MWD data whilst drilling arc compared to the wircline data for this post well analysis. question: Which geochemical species and temperature-depth ranges characterize FIS microseeps associated with near-vertical light hydrocarbon migration?
answer_text: Light hydrocarbons, CO2, organic acids, aromatic compounds and sulfurous volatiles (e.g. H2S, COS, CS2, S2, SO2, thiols); temperature <65–70°C and typically in the upper ~1–3 km of the rock column.

context_snippets.text: A.3 Interpreting FIS Track Plots and Petrographic Data in Geologic Context 51 A.3.4 Seals FIS seals are inferred at boundaries marking abrupt changes in FIS species strength or chem- istry. The underlying assumption is that detected fluids are more or less synchronous on either side of the boundary and that some process has prevented free mixing of species across this barrier. In detail the boundary may represent change in lithology, poroperm or structural element. In the case of in-situ generated petroleum the boundary might represent transi- tion from poor to better source rock, or immature to mature source intervals. In the case of migrated petroleum the boundary might represent the extent of petroleum migration through porous rock, or the top seal to present or past petroleum column. Basal compartment limits may represent seals or, in some cases, fluid contacts or paleocontacts (see below). In general, only the tops of FIS compartments are identified on interpreted FIS depth plots. If fluids were not synchronous on either side of the compartment boundary (e.g. post-migration unconformity) then the seal interpretation would be in error. Seals may be selective or chro- matographic, in which case low molecular weight species may migrate across the boundary, while higher molecular weight species do not. A.3.5 Microseepage FIS microseeps are analogous to gas chimneys seen in seismic data, and surface manifestations of deeper charge identified in surface geochemical surveys. They are interpreted to result from near-vertical migration of light hydrocarbons followed by bacterial alteration in the shallow subsurface at temperature-depth conditions permissible for bacterial activity. Most bacteria are restricted to temperatures below 65-70°C; hence, anomalies may be observed in the up- per 1-3 km of rock column, depending on the prevailing geothermal gradient. Key indictor species include light hydrocarbons, CO2, possibly organic acids and aromatic compounds, and sulfurous volatiles, including H2S, COS, CS2, S2 ( /- SO2) and in some cases thiols. H2S is often sequestered within pyrite in iron-rich siliciclastics, hence is less common in shale-bearing lithologies. Inclusion formation in such low temperature environments may be aided by pre- cipitation of bacterial carbonate. FIS microseeps are geometrically distinct, often beginning at the surface and abruptly disappearing at the appropriate temperature-controlled depth. The presence of an FIS microseep appears to be good indicator of deeper charge in the immediate vicinity, although weak seeps may represent regional signals within shallow aquifers. Data suggest that these anomalies overlie 75-80% of productive reservoirs, while only 10% of non-productive areas display similar signals. Hence, the presence of strong seep within dry hole might indicate deeper or nearby lateral charge in the area. A.3.6 Fluid Contacts The basal boundary (abrupt or transitional) of any strong FIS compartment is candidate for present or past fluid contact, although the interpretation is often equivocal. The most compelling evidence for present day contact occurs where hydrocarbon-dominant FIS signals (the petroleum leg) give way to water-soluble dominant signals (PTP in the water leg) and where visual petroleum inclusion abundance displays parallel decrease. When inclusion abundance is high in the petroleum zone but PTP signals are not present in the water leg, it is possible that paleo-charge is recorded. SHALLOW GEOLOGY AND WELL PROGNOSIS 6.1 Background The proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location is situated in NCS block 7219/8. The interpreted stratigraphy is based on information from tie wells. Interpretation is limited to the top Cretaceous, 1847m MSL (1646ms TWT) at the PWL. Two figures are presented, figures and 6.2, illustrating the geological profiles at the proposed 7219/8-2 Iskrystall location. Time-Depth conversion is based upon velocities derived from seismic processing of the 2D data (figure 10.1). All depths are quoted in metres MSL and two way time in milliseconds at the proposed location. The time-depth conversion is expected to be accurate to ±2m at seabed increasing to around ±10m at second TWT. 6.2 Sub-seabed Conditions The geological section to the top Cretaceous has been split into units as tied to offset wells, previous surveys (section 3.4) and in accordance with interpretation provided by Statoil. Quaternary - Nordland Group (Unit 1): Unit is expected to comprise very soft to firm clay with rare gravel becoming firm clay with sand layers and silt with depth. The base is marked by moderate amplitude, phase reversed, approximately sub-horizontal reflector reaching 458 to 506m MSL (589 to 639ms TWT) across the site, deepening gently to the north. The base of Unit represents sand layer and gas level (section 7) and is an angular unconformity. At this horizon slight risk of gas is assigned at the PWL (section 7). Within unit several possibly erosional events are observed. At 426m MSL (555ms TWT) at the PWL weak possibly reverse phase horizon is seen possibly representing sand layer. Possible boulders may be expected throughout this unit and specifically at the base as seen in offset wells. Well 7220/8-1 confirms the base of Unit as sand layer and also encountered boulders. Problems with boulders are also reported at the base Quaternary in the 7219/9-1 well (section 7.4); this is referenced from the 7220/7-1 drilling program and the problems are not specified. The 7220/5-1 well also encountered boulders at the base Quaternary. Tertiary (Palaeocene to Eocene) - Sotbakken Group (Units and 3): Unit forms thick sequence, the upper part is seismically well layered, with horizons dipping to the northwest, while the lower part is possibly less so though it becomes obscured by the seabed multiple. Sediments are expected to comprise predominantly silty claystone. Sand layers may be present in the upper part, as suggested by seismic character.

RELIEF WELL CONTINGENCY PLANS: WELL 217-29 Stimulation vessels Rig(s) Selection • Rig specifications • Deck layout for kill equipment • Special kill equipment Kill spools Long co-flexip hoses High pressure riser, etc. Relative Position Uncertainty One of the first steps in relief well geometry planning is to estimate the relative position uncertainty between the blowout and the proposed relief well(s). This is essential for determining the initial magnetic search depth, the number of relief wells required, and the angle of approach. Both the uncertainty in the surface positions and the borehole trajectory must be analyzed. Sulface Uncertainty More than one relief well has missed its intended target do to errors and/or misunderstanding surrounding the surface coordinates and/or azimuth reference system of the two wells. To avoid this costly mistake, redundant surveys should be taken between the blowout and the relief well wellheads using different measuring techniques. The primary objective is to assure that no gross errors exist in the primary positioning system. The secondary objective is to fix the relative distance and true north bearing between the two surface locations with an uncertainty of +/- lm, with high degree of confidence (if reasonably possible). For relief well drilling purposes only the relative position of the two wells is important (as opposed to UTM coordinates or Latitude/Longitude). Additionally, it is important to assure that common azimuth and depth reference system is being used. This has caused many directional drilling problems in the past, particularly when switching between grid systems and magnetic/true north reference systems. Normally three independent measurements are sufficient to assure reasonable confidence in relative positioning, with one using geodetic surveying techniques and sun-shots for true north reference if possible, to eliminate any remote grid errors. question: If upper Rannoch is downfault-thickened by 57.6 m TVT, how would reservoir thickness and sand quality be affected?
answer_text: Reservoir thickness would be increased by about 57.6 m TVT, yielding thicker, better-quality sands in the upper Rannoch Formation.

The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. STRUCTURAL GEOLOGY GROUP IG,UiB/NRSC REPORT NO.: REVISION NO: TITLE: Cap-rock qualities of the Teistengrunnen Group, southwestern Barents Sea with emphasis on its fracture pattern AUTHORS(S): Roy H. Gabrielsen NUMBER OF PAGES: 129 NUMBER OF COPIES: DISTRIBUTION: Norsk Hydro a.s.; restricted ABSTRACT: The cap rocks of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations in wells 7321/9-1, 7219/9-1, 7120/2-2, 7120/6-1, 7120/12-1, 7228/2-1, 7228/9-1 and 7125/1-1 have been investigated from structural geological and rock mechanical point of view. The study has demonstrated that the fracture geometry and fracture frequency vary within the study area. The following preliminary conclusions are drawn: 1) The shales of the Fuglen Formation reveal higher vertical shear strengths (16-40 MPa) than the shales of the Hekkingen Formation (7-22 MPa). If erosion of approximately 1000 metres of rocks is assumed, the bulk of the cap rock may have been fractured. The present data, however indicate that the fracture frequency attributed to this deformation, is low. 2) The wells in the western part of the study area are characterized by high fracture frequencies and low-angle fractures. This deformation is probably associated with post early Tertiary compressional reactivation of some of the master fault complexes. Accordingly, the master fault complexes associated with the large basins in the west (Tromso Basin and Bjornoya Basins) are potentially most exposed to leakage through microfractures. However, since the shales of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations seem to have different rock mechanical properties the continuity of these units should be mapped in detail, and the problems with diffusion characteristcs of the units should be addressed.

question: How do the petrophysical properties (resistivity and porosity) of upper Heimdal sands compare to the underlying sandstones?
answer_text: The upper Heimdal sands are low-resistivity, high-porosity intervals, whereas the underlying sandstones have adequate porosity but distinctly higher resistivities.

context_snippets.text: Introduction This report contains the results of detailed petrographic analyses on 44 thin sections from inch core plugs taken from conventional core of well 25/8-8 and 46 thin sections from inch core plugs from well 25/8-B 2. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

The logs used in the analysis were then borehole corrected as necessary. The Spectral Gamma was corrected for potassium content in the mud and hole size corrected, the Densilog was hole size corrected, the Dual Laterolog resistivity curves were corrected for borehole effects, and the Compensated Neutron curve was corrected for all borehole effects. The analysis of this well was done as part of multi-well study, which also included the 25/8-5S, 25/8-6, 25/8-6 T2, and the 25/8-8S, all of which are in the Elfi / Tau discovery area. The analysis focused on the Heimdal sands, as they were the only ones containing hydrocarbons, however the analysis was done over the Sele - Ty interval. All corrections and analyses were done using Logstar, the in-house Conoco evaluation program. The analysis for well 25/7-3 was not straightforward in that the upper part of the Heimdal Fm. contains shale clasts and lenses which depressed the resistivity response. Even the two primary sand units are too thin for the deep laterolog to resolve correctly. To account for this, form of resistivity forward modeling was applied. Petrophysical Model The overall petrophysical model consists of combination of several different models. Schlumberger Volan' type logic was applied in the computation of clay and silt volumes. Using information from the core analysis, porosity was computed which provided the best fit to the core data. Fluid saturation and permeability were computed using the Archie equation, capillary pressure relationships, and sound geologic reasoning. Clay and Shale Volume Computation Clay volume was computed from weighted average of non-linear transform of the gamma ray, linear transform of the gamma ray divided by bulk density, and density / neutron. The average is Hodges-Lehmann weighted average, which is described in an 1982 SPWLA paper by Coates, et al'. According to whole core descriptions of the Heimdal sands in the 25/7-3, they consist of mix of high-density turbidites, muddy sandstones, low-density turbidites, carbonate-cemented sandy shale, injected/slumped sands, and shales. They range in grain size from medium to very fine, and in sorting from well to poorly sorted'. The top five meters is heterolithic mix of each of these facies, and as such was fairly poorly resolved by the logging tools. The sampled sandstones are dominantly sublithic arenites and wackes, with variable grain sizes (silt-fsU) and detrital clay abundances (5.5-38.5%). Diagenetic overprinting is largely restricted to replacive pyrite and locally significant quartz overgrowths. • reservoir quality is variable (0 = 6.0-30.7%, Kh = 0.03-1350mD), reflecting the observed textural and mineralogical variability of the cored interval. The best reservoir quality is observed in the clean, fine grained sands of lithotype Sd-d, where dewatering has remobilised detrital clay. Increasing ductile contents (especially detrital clay) and finer grain sizes in lithotypes DF and Si/Sr impart lower reservoir quality to these samples. Patchy solid cements (quartz in the single cemented sample examined) degrade porosities, but have less impact on permeabilities as pore throats generally remain open. VESTLAND GROUP The main conclusions related to the Vestland Group are: • in 25/8-9 the Vestland Group comprises relatively thick (86.0m It), heterogeneous but sand-prone succession that can be readily divided into a series of discrete, genetically-related depositional packages and subpackages. The sedimentology of these suggests that the entire Vestland Group belongs to the Hugin Formation. • the genetically-defined depositional packages range in nature from fluvial sandstones through bay-fill deposits to estuarine deposits to marine shoreface sandstones. The stratal arrangements however, favour these deposits infilling series of stacked incised valleys, the contacts between which have the characteristics of (candidate) sequence boundaries. The depositional evolution of the Vestland Group is pulsed rather than progressive therefore with each incised valley fill representing discrete, 'detached' series of depositional subenvironments separate from those above and below. • whilst the Vestland Group succession is 'layered' in 25/8-9 both the nature of some of the facies, and the probable existence of incised valleys means that the layering may well be breached within the scale of the prospect. • the Vestland Group comprises texturally variable, quartz-dominated sandstones whose detrital clay content is <16.5%. Mica is also relatively abundant in these sandstones (≤7.0%). Authigenic phases are essentially replacive and are dominated by kaolinite and pyrite although locally ferroan carbonate cement is abundant (eg. core 2). • reservoir characteristics in the cored Vestland interval are highly variable (7.8-42.5%, Kh 0.32-16000mD), reflecting the textural variability. The best overall reservoir quality is encountered in the cleaner and overall coarser grained fluvial sandstones (packages Al and B2), whilst the generally fine grained and argillaceous nature of the lagoonal mudrock (subpackage C2) means that they are of non-reservoir quality.
