• This binder contains the results of the WSC/GEO/GEO-A processing of your well 25/5-2. COMMENTS: The VSP was acquired by SCHLUMBERGER. 155 cu.in. clustered airguns was used. DENSITY LOG The Density is correceted for badhole effects. CALIBRATION Though they both measure times of propagation through the rocks, the sonic and seismic tools are affected by various and complex phenomena (environmental effects, frequency content of the signal...) that create discrepancy between the two types of information. To enable the comparative interpretation of log data and seismic sections,we need to adjust (or calibrate) one measurement to the other. Our basic assumption will be that times of propagation measured on the seismic data are correct within certain precision depending on the shot quality, precision of the breaktimes picking etc... The new method presented here with CALIFE avoids problems in case of deviated wells and complex seismic acq. geometry by working in model that can describe both types of measurements and their geometry. What is generally used to compute synthetic responses in seismics is subsurface description in flat layers of constant velocity. To describe the sonic in such way, we have employed the squaring (or zoning ) techniques used for lithofacies identification. This gives us partition of the log data in zones of low variations. In the case of the sonic, those zones can be seen as layers of constant velocity. The methodology employed to calibrate the sonic is the following: • Take the squared sonic as initial solution (or initial model). • Compute in this model synthetic arrival times for each source-receiver couple with ray tracing method. • Compute the drift i.e. the difference between those synthetic arrival times and the times measured on the VSP or check shots.

question: For well 34/10‑M‑3 H, what HSE, QA, and reporting measures apply to shallow‑gas, mud‑mixing, and cementing operations?
answer_text: HSE measures: drill with special focus on shallow‑gas controls, avoid oil‑based mud spillage to sea, prohibit personnel in riding belts during cement jobs, involve service companies in HSE campaigns, ensure supervisors are familiar with the SBP procedure, and give special attention to crane operations and heavy lifts. QA/reporting: plan and execute logistics and mud‑mixing for the section, verify HC contacts and casing‑shoe setting, perform a pre‑start risk evaluation, and report all downtime in Synergi‑99 with entries logged on a separate Time Planner sheet.

The well was drilled and steered from 1960 mMD to the TD at 3280 mMD in one run, taking hours in total. The hole angle was built up from 27.34° at 1938 mMD, to 60.53° at 2883 mMD, just above the top of the reservoir at 2887.0 mMD, and continued to build up to 68.82° at 3250 mMD. The natural build tendency of the BHA was generally sufficient to keep the wellpath on the planned line and only one short section, 1 mMD, was steered in the reservoir section. This was necessary in order to increase the build rate in Area of the reservoir, and thereby maximise the sands above the OWC. After circulating the hole clean at TD the BHA was pulled without pumping or backreaming to the shoe, where high-vis pill was pumped and the casing circulated clean. The BHA was then pulled to surface, the MWD data dumped and the tool broken down. The rest of the BHA was broken down after waiting for crane for one hour. Due to quick drilling the Western Atlas equipment only arrived onboard as the MWD was being laid down, so there was delay while the FMT tool and spear were made up and tested. The FMT was being rigged up on drillpipe when the decision came from town to run the log on wireline, so the PLC equipment was laid down and the CHT/GR/FMT combination was run on wireline. Minor hang-ups occurred at 2059, 2245, and 2415 mMD; the tool was unable to go beyond 3068 mMD. The top three pressure points were taken before, again, attempting to pass 3068 mMD, but without success. The tool was pulled to surface and rigged down. It was decided not to run in on drillpipe to take the five lower points. A 121/4 hole opening assembly was made up, including bull nose, 81/2 hole opener, followed by 121/4 hole opener 825 behind the bull nose. The well was opened up to 121/4 from 1960 - mMD, working tight spots at 3197 and 3239 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean. short wiper trip was performed back to 3100 mMD without pumping, and then the hole was backreamed from 4 mMD (bull nose depth), and the hole circulated clean again with 121/4 hole opener at 1955 mMD. The logs are of good quality and only minor problems occurred during the logging operations. Due to only minor differences between measured depth (MD) and true vertical depth (TVD), deviation corrections have not been applied. The Top Brent Group at 2455,5 mRKB (MD) is 0,1 deeper compared to the TVD, for the Top Dunlin Group the difference is 0,2 m. The logs have been analyzed using computer based model applying complex lithology method. The Brent Group net sand intervals have been defined using porosity cut-off corresponding to ml), which for the Tarbert Formation is 16 %, the Ness and Etive Formations 12 %, and the Rannoch Formation 15 %. shale volume cut-off of 40% has been applied. The main results from the preliminary log analysis are summarized in Table 5.1. For further details and final interpretation, reference is made to the Petrophysical Report. The resistivity logs indicate oil down (ODT) to 2477 mRKB and water up to (WUT) 2483 mRKB. The OWC is located within very fine grained, bioturbated and argillaceous, calcite cemented sandstone, and cannot be exactly defined from the resistivity logs. However, an OWC is from the formation pressure measurements (RFT) estimated within the Tarbert Formation at 2478 mRKB (2460 mSS). 5.2 Conventional Core Analysis A total of 10 cores were cut in the interval 1 mRKB Driller's. Core No.1 contained only marl and shaly claystone belonging to the Cromer Knoll Group and to the Heather Formation. Cores - 10 were cut in the Brent Group and 12 into the Dunlin Group. The total Brent core recovery was 186,05 (95,7%). Conventional core analysis was performed on all cores, except cores nos. 1, and 10 due to very high content of claystone. Horizontal air permeability, helium porosity and grain density were measured every 0,25 meter, while vertical permeability, summation porosity and pore saturation were measured every meter. The results are shown in Table 5.2.

4.2.2 1/2” Drilling Phase 34/10-M-4 AH T2: The section was planned as short correction run with DLS's of approximately 5.5º. With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. In the future there are two main things to be investigated further before drilling similar type of well/section. The first being the necessity of such high mud weight, which clearly initiates sticking, and drag problems. question: How does sample depth 4798 in well 7117/9-2 compare to deeper samples for evidence of Barremian-or-younger age?
answer_text: The sample at 4798 yielded a reliable Barremian-or-younger assemblage, whereas deeper samples are mostly barren or poorly preserved and do not provide such age evidence.

-3- INTRODUCTION Norsk Hydro's well 7117/9-2 is the second well drilled on main structure called the Senja Ridge, situated in the north-western parts of the Troms-1 exploration area. The first well, 7117/9-1, was also operated by Norsk Hydro, with IKU as biostratigraphic consultant. The biostratigraphy of well 7117/9-2 is based on the analysis of cuttings, sidewalls and core samples. Fossil material obtained from the first set of sidewall cores does not seem to match the fossil material obtained from cuttings. This is particularly evident across the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary and in the Paleocene/Eocene, though difficult to demonstrate in the thick sequence of Albian deposits. Sidewall cores down to 1695 are therefore considered unreliable. We have documented this in the text and, as sidewall analysis was well underway before discovering the anomaly, we have plotted out the SWC results on the log sheets. Analyses carried out during drilling (hot shots) indicated an unusually thick sequence of Albian and Aptian deposits. Following consultation with the client it was decided that some reduction in the density of analyses should be made. Fairly complete palynological analysis were to be carried out, based primarily on sidewall cover, but with sample density somewhat less than the standard detailed palynology (1 sample/15 m). Micropaleontological analyses should also be reduced though the primary net should be supplemented if results warrented this. In the lower part of the well most samples analysed for micropaleontology were barren. Preservation of palynological material is also extremely poor (below ca 3400 m). In view of the interest expressed in this part of the section we have nevertheless attempted to locate workable samples. These are few and far between, though an assemblage recorded at 4798 gave reliable Barremian or younger age. Moreover, circumstantial evidence for the whole of this section points to more likely Aptian age. G45/c/3/ems

question: For Vestland and Skagerrak wells, what are the proposed coring depths, expected core counts, and hydrocarbon-show contingency measures?

context_snippets.text: Structural core description - Well 15/9-19SR 33 At MD RKB in the Triassic, fracture with oil patches was encountered in an otherwise dry Skagerrak Formation. This is probably fracture of dilatational nature, possibly late fracture. The same phenomenon has been seen in the Pismo Formation of California, where fractures are observed in_the field as both barriers and (more rarely) conduits. Brace (1978) showed that pore-volume increase, or dilitancy, accompanies failure of intact rock in the laboratory. Antonelli et al. (1993) found that dilatation is found in an early stage of deformation band development. (Furthermore, it should be noted that en echelon open induced fractures were encountered in thin section at MD RKB.) a2. Decreased porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis The thin section from MD RKB (Skagerrak Fm.) exhibits compaction in the fracture, but no grain crushing. At mesoscopic scale, the fracture is filled with grey material, and is probably syn-sedimentary. It is surrounded by some rotated bedding and clay clasts and may well be associated with slumping at low mean stress levels. a3. Unchanged porosity relative to host rock and no cataclasis Such band was found at MD RKB (Triassic). This type seems to be easier to recognize at core scale that in the thin-section. b. Deformation bands with cataclasis In most thin sections the deformed zone has decreased porosity relative to the host rock. This is mainly due to tighter packing, grain size reduction (Figure 1, Appendix B) and possible pore-filling illite (Figures B5/B6, Appendix B). This type is represented in most of the thin sections. Porosity is decreased typically by one order of magnituded, from (roughly speaking) 20 % to 0-2 %. 6.3 Comparison of meso and micro scale observations The number of thin sections (15) is bit too small to make complete analysis of micro/meso scale relationships. However, the following may be stated: i. No relationship between infill colour and microstructure seems to exist.

WELL 9/2-7S INTRODUCTION The exploration well 9/2-7S was drilled in the northern segment of the Beta Vest structure, with the Sandnes formation as target horizon. Baker Hughes INTEQ provided the Teleco MWD service on well 9/2-7S. 1/2 Dual Propagation Resistivity tool (DPR) was used for the 17 1/2 hole section, two 1/4 Modular Dual Propagation Resistivity tools and one Dual Propagation Resistivity tool for the 12 1/4 hole section. For the 1/2 section one 3/4 Dual Propagation Resistivity tool was used. Included in this End of Well report are final logs for the above mentioned hole sections. The logs provided are Recorded While Drilling (RWD). The depth scales of the logs are 1:500 MD, 1:200 MD and 1:500 TVD. This section was drilled in one run utilising 1/2 DPR MWD tool as directional indicator and to record formation data. This section was drilled with sea water with hi-vis pills for hole cleaning. TOOL PERFORMANCE The DPR-TF4 tool (S/N 970-28) performed to specifications for circulating hours and gave clear picture of the formation changes. LOGGING CONDITIONS New formation was logged from immediately below the 30 conductor shoe at 162m and continued to section TD at 1192m MD. Penetration rate was high, but good real-time log was transmitted giving clear view of the formation tops while drilling. No decoding problems were encountered, and at surface the memory was downloaded, giving high resolution log for the hole section. The section was drilled with sea water with density of SG. The DPR resistivity was corrected for mud resistivity (Rm), tool/hole size, downhole temperature and formation dielectric properties by use of the CRIM model. The Gamma Ray was normalised to MWD- API units. The time between the formation being drilled to the time the DPR sensor passed can be seen on the Time Since Drilled curve. Memory data is processed with Gamma Ray Dark Current OFF.

During water sampling, the MDT tool failed, and the sampling had to be aborted. In Run 2D, the sampling programme was completed with extra hydrocarbon samples from the same level as in Run 2C, and water samples from two levels. Pumping of fluid through the Optical Fluid Analyser of the MDT tool to verify water filled reservoir was done at two additional levels. Extra pressure tests were also attempted, especially in the upper part of the Tilje Formation. Of the 10 new attempts, all were either tight or supercharged. Good reservoir properties in the Tofte Formation and the lower part of the Tilje Formation gave reliable pressure measurements in these intervals. In the upper part of the Tilje Formation, the pressure measurements either showed tight reservoir or were affected by supercharging and hence not reliable. The pressure gradient in the hydrocarbon interval in Tofte Formation shows reservoir fluid density of g/cm3. The good pressure measurement in the water filled intervals of the Tofte, Tilje and Are Formations indicates common pressure regime with fluid density, at reservoir conditions, of g/cm3. This also means that one gradient through the entire water filled interval is not fully representative. The water sample from had total salinity of 144000 mg/1, while the sample from had salinity of 103000 mg/l. An increasing background gas and trip gas trend were also noted but were thought to be due to the proximity of the reservoir formation. In the event these assumptions proved erroneous as an FMT point at 4653m gave pressure gradient of 1.97sg. The mud weight was increased to 2.05sg at 4661m before performing formation integrity test. The formation, however, broke down at only 2.18sg EMW. further mud weight increase was made to 2.07sg before proceeding with the coring program. The calculated ECD with 2.07sg mud at 1000 litres per minute was over 2.16sg which left very small margin for operations. The possibility of setting an intermediate liner was discussed but in the event was not necessary. Coring continued and close watch was kept on trip gas levels as these were the only available indicators of pore pressure with the d-exponent rendered useless by the sandstone formation and coring operation. The following peaks were observed: 1.62% (0.02%) at 4671m, 2.12% (0.30%) at 4699m, 4898m. These no longer showed an increasing trend which was to be expected if the pore pressure gradient was decreasing in line with the fluid gradient in the porous reservoir formation. Connection gas peaks were seen at 4864m and 4873m with values of 0.44% (0.29%) and 0.41% (0.29%) respectively. This time there was little doubt that these were the result of formation ballooning/flushing. Further FMT logs at 4926m confirmed maximum pore pressure gradient of 1.97sg at 4634m, declining to 1.91sg at 4926m. The actual reservoir fluid gradient was 0.044bar/m which should have produced gradient of 1.88sg at this depth, therefore it was apparent that there was not complete communication between all horizons within the reservoir. The d-exponent did not provide any useful information until the Lower Ror formation was entered at 5015m. Similarly, background gas was masked by frequent formation related peaks and provided little in the way of pressure indications in the overlying formations. close watch was kept for pump off and connection peaks since these provided the only useful pressure tool. In the event none were seen until the base of the Tofte formation. Thereafter connection gas peaks were regular feature until the end of the well. Once again these were thought to be the result of the high overbalance and not increasing pore pressure.

CONCLUSION & RECOMMENDATIONS The MWD and CDR tool failures and damage to the MWD collars in the 12 1/4 hole section is consistent with extremely rough drilling conditions. The use of PDC bits with an aggressive cutting action and packed bottom hole assemblies produced high and cyclic torque. On both MWD runs and this caused the ten pin coverplate torx head screws to back off allowing the coverplate to fall away. The exposed MWD collar wiring was stripped away causing the real time communication failures between the MWD and CDR tools and hence the loss of real time Gamma Ray and Resistivity data. Anadrill has had previous experience of drilling in Chalk in this area, notably on well 2/11-8 where five MWD tool failures occurred in the 12 1/4 hole section. The failed tools all exhibited the following damage eaused by rough drilling: black dust on electr- ical connections, worn and loose shock sleeves and pressure activated pads and electrical components parted from circuit boards. Anadrill had recommended the use of roller reamers and the inclusion of 12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools to reduce the high and cyclic torque levels. The recommended config- uration of 12 1/4 bit-12 1/4 near bit roller reamer-8 CDR-12 1/4 In-Line Stabilizer-8 MWD-12 1/4 stabilizer would have provided more protection for the CDR and MWD tools, but this was not utilised. On future vertical wells drilling in Chalk, Anadrill recommends the use of an In-Line Stabilizer between the CDR and MWD tools and the use of either roller reamers or turbine in the bottom hole assembly to reduce torque levels.

The core was well consolidated: Core no. 1: - PREPARATION: The plug samples for analyses were collected by drilling with one inch bore in the horizontal and vertical planes using brine as cooling agent. They were then cut to lengths of one inch, cleaned in an extractor and dried at 600C and 40% relative humidity under controlled conditions. MEASUREMENTS: AIR PERMEABILITY Standard air permeability is measured with nitrogen gas as net confining sleeve pressure of 15 bar. The gas flow rate, the pressure drop, p, over the plug sample, and the back pressure, P2, is measured. The air permeability, Kg, is then calculated using Darcy's law. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability value, -el, is determined empirically for each sample. Our empirical correction is based on permeability measurements using different back pressures. Our statistical measurements have been performed on sandstone samples from different fields in the North Sea area with different lithologi. The permeameters used are designed by GECO Petroleum Laboratory. To get complete permeability curve, we also report the Ka-value, defined as the extrapolated air permeability at 1/Pm = (see figure), together with the Klinkenberg corrected permeability, Kal. Measured air permeability, Kg, and 1/Pm (where Pm is average pressure in the sample) for each measurement are also reported. WELL: 2/11-8

With 1.5º motor bend set-up, this meant sliding intervals of 18 to 20 per stand. However, after having drilled the first two stands, as well as following the continuous reading from the AIM tool, one found that the desired doglegs were not achieved and it was decided to pull out of hole. The reason for not yielding 5.5º doglegs was not believed by the Schlumberger DDs to be due to insufficient capabilities of the assembly. It is rather considered that the high friction (drag) downhole caused by the large overbalance, created problems for sliding efficiently enough in order to get 5.5º DLS. Therefore it was suggested to pump graphite additives into the mud to reduce the drag and, thus, be able to slide efficiently. It was decided to give it shot, and 15 kg graphite/m3 mud was pumped into the well before starting to drill again. Sliding was hereafter effortless, rotary torque was reduced by approximately 30%, and drag was reduced by 10% from what was recorded earlier. The assembly yielded 8º plus for dogleg capability, and the section was drilled successfully, landing 3.2m deeper TVD than initially planned for - 0.8m within the maximum accepted TVD limit. One was now at 96° inclination and 3409.2m TVD, so one had to drop down to 88° and then flatten out at 3401m, which was the planned TVD for the producing zone. However, it was found that the formation layers weren't quite as predicted, and the Rannoch formation below the Etive formation was drilled into. Therefore, the well had to be brought 4m shallower and 10° to the left before one was once more back into the producing layers of the Etive. Throughout the run, the PD675Xtra took all the commands as expected, tool face offset of approximately 25-30° right of PD tool face set point was observed, and stick-slip and shocks were found to be kept at its lowest at RPM's around 140 to 145. In the future there are two main things to be investigated further before drilling similar type of well/section. The first being the necessity of such high mud weight, which clearly initiates sticking, and drag problems. question: How does measured gas permeability Kg compare to Klinkenberg-corrected Kl, and how do iterative correction parameters m and Pm influence the correction?
answer_text: Kl is the Klinkenberg-corrected permeability derived from the measured Kg (e.g., Kl = Kg^1.06 for Kg 0–2.0 mD or via the iterative relation Kln+1 = Kg - mn/Pm); increasing m increases the correction magnitude while increasing Pm reduces the correction.

question: How do rig-source velocity estimates compare to vertical-incidence survey-derived velocities in predicting true vertical times, and what are their calibration roles?
answer_text: Rig‑source data provide the best estimate of velocity along the well and are used to calibrate the acoustic log velocities. Vertical‑incidence surveys give the best estimate of true vertical times and are used to time‑tie the calibrated log to the surface seismic.

context_snippets.text: 1.3.2 Acoustic Log Calibration Acoustic and density logs were supplied by the client over the depth range to 5224.1m MDKB. Due to the configuration of the survey the rig source data is thought to give the best estimate of the velocity along the well; while the vertical incidence survey yields the best estimate of the true vertical times of the geophones. Thus the rig source times were used to calibrated the acoustic velocities and then this calibrated log was time tied to the vertical incidence data to give the best match to the surface seismic dataset. For the calibration, the acoustic log was integrated to produce time-log, which is depth-indexed. The discrepancy between the corrected checkshot time of the shallowest checkshot level (within the logged interval) and the corresponding log-derived time was then computed. The time-log was next shifted by adding this value to all the time-log values, thus tying the log to the shallowest checkshot. A drift curve was then generated, showing the difference between the corrected checkshot times and the corresponding times from the shifted time-log. Calibration points fixing the drift at certain depths (including the top and bottom of the logged interval) were then chosen such that they divide the drift curve into intervals of approximately linear drift and also so that they occur at velocity contrasts (typically formation boundaries), thus avoiding false reflectivity. The calibration points are indicated with triangular marks on the drift curve displayed on Enclosure 1. For each interval between consecutive calibration points, the ratio between the difference in the fixed drift of these calibration points and the interval thickness was computed, and this constant was added to all acoustic log values of the interval, thus shifting the acoustic log in this interval by this amount. The whole acoustic log was calibrated by repeating this procedure for all calibration point intervals. After calibration, the calibrated time-log was computed by integrating the calibrated acoustic log and tieing it to the shallowest checkshot. The residual drift curve, shown on Enclosure 1, was generated using the corrected checkshot times and the calibrated time-log. The tables in Section contain details of the acoustic log calibration, including the residual drift before and after calibration, and the calibration points used, together with tabulated time-depth values listed in linear depth and linear time. The depth-indexed calibrated acoustic log and associated logs are displayed at scale of 1:1000 as Enclosure 2.

The siemic data cube supplied by BP Norge was input and change of direction points defined along random line which closely follows the well trajectory. The random line was output at 12.5m spacing. Next the VSP was interpolated on offset to 12.5m spacing along the wellpath. The VSP was then spliced into random line to show the match between VSP and sesimc datasets; the best match was obtained by shifting the Surface seismic up by 15 ms. The displays have been produced scale of 20 cm/s and both polarities using North Sea polarity convention (Normal Polarity: an increase in acoustic impedance is plotted as trough). 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

Gabrielsen NUMBER OF PAGES: 129 NUMBER OF COPIES: DISTRIBUTION: Norsk Hydro a.s.; restricted ABSTRACT: The cap rocks of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations in wells 7321/9-1, 7219/9-1, 7120/2-2, 7120/6-1, 7120/12-1, 7228/2-1, 7228/9-1 and 7125/1-1 have been investigated from structural geological and rock mechanical point of view. The study has demonstrated that the fracture geometry and fracture frequency vary within the study area. The following preliminary conclusions are drawn: 1) The shales of the Fuglen Formation reveal higher vertical shear strengths (16-40 MPa) than the shales of the Hekkingen Formation (7-22 MPa). If erosion of approximately 1000 metres of rocks is assumed, the bulk of the cap rock may have been fractured. The present data, however indicate that the fracture frequency attributed to this deformation, is low. 2) The wells in the western part of the study area are characterized by high fracture frequencies and low-angle fractures. This deformation is probably associated with post early Tertiary compressional reactivation of some of the master fault complexes. Accordingly, the master fault complexes associated with the large basins in the west (Tromso Basin and Bjornoya Basins) are potentially most exposed to leakage through microfractures. However, since the shales of the Fuglen and Hekkingen Formations seem to have different rock mechanical properties the continuity of these units should be mapped in detail, and the problems with diffusion characteristcs of the units should be addressed.

The hydrocarbon composition of the reservoir fluid was determined to decanes plus using combination of low temperature and high temperature fractional distillation. This is reported on page two of the report in terms of mol and weight percent, together with the molecular weight and density of the heptanes through decanes plus cuts. The reservoir fluid was charged to high pressure visual cell and thermally expanded to the reservoir temperature of 183°F. During constant mass expansion the fluid was found to have bubble-point of 3383 psig. The results of the pressure volume measurements at reservoir temperature may be found on pages three and four. When subjected to differential pressure depletion at the reservoir temperature the fluid evolved total of 611 cubic feet of gas at psia and 60°F. per barrel of residual oil at 60°F. The resulting relative oil volume factor was 1.316 barrels of saturated fluid per barrel of residual oil at 60°f. The oil density and the properties of the evolved gases were measured at each point during the differential pressure depletion and this data is included in the summary of the differential depletion data on page five and represented graphically on pages seventeen and eighteen.

Continuously monitored torque has also been valuable aid, in deter- mining bit wear. 11) Bit run summary reports were printed after each bit run and sent to the STAVANGER office.

The section was drilled successfully within budget time in one run, penetrating several sedimentary rock groups, including the tuffaceous Balder formation, without problems. The Carbo-Sea oil based mud system proved once more to be of high quality, contributing to excellent hole cleaning and an effective drilling operation. Also, being able to run casing continuously to bottom with miniscule problems, reflects good quality in regards to hole cleaning. The 500 kg salt sacks appeared well sealed, resulting in dry salt that was easily added via hopper to the active system. Emphasis must be made on continuous quality control of the mentioned salt sacks, to avoid shipment of flocculated salt which has devastating effect on salt hopper equipment. Focus should be set on improving measuring devices on bulk tanks, as these have proven inaccurate at times.

Apart from rutile, zircon and garnet, tourmaline is the most commonly occurring heavy mineral these samples. Tourmaline which is common to variety of metamorphic and magmatic (pegmatitic) rocks except for granulites, has been recorded in 15 sections from wells. As for the other minerals mentioned of possible importance to provenance, the distribution of tourmaline does not show any geographical trends. A mineral separation is clearly needed to concentrate the heavy minerals to produce statistically significant provenance information. Well 6407/9-1 stand out in this context. Of the detailed minerals garnet, Ti-Bt, RNQ and tourmaline samples from this well contained few grains of garnet only, and no members of the other three minerals. Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions Hydrocarbon fluid inclusions (liquid-dominated as well as gas-dominated inclusions) have been observed hosted in overgrowth zones of both quartz and feldspar in some of the samples of this study. However, as this is point-coint study, fluid inclusion have not in any way been mapped as would have been the case in hydrocarbon fluid inclusion screening. Nevertheless, the use of microthermometry on the samples studied may well constrain the temperature (and time?) aspect of the major pore volume altering reactions which in this study are quartz overgrowth and feldspar dissolution. 41) Conclusive remarks The two overall most important diagenetic reactions responsible for pore volume alterations in the samples studied are quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) reducing porosity and (K-) feldspar dissolution which definitely is the major contributor to the formation of secondary pore volumes (PVSC). The table in Appendix shows positive correlation of quartz overgrowth (CMQZ) with depth of 0.65. K-feldspar (FSKF) shows negative correlation with depth of (feldspar dissolution). (The formation of PVSC shows positive correlation with depth of 0.34.) Though samples show grain sizes up to 500 microns practically no samples have been found to contain rock fragments as to be suitable as provenance indicators. The heavy minerals zircon and rutile are recorded in trace amounts in nearly every sample. Heavy minerals or detrital minerals (or mineral inclusions) that represent specific metamorphic facies do not give any consistent geographical distribution or clustering. Hence, no suitable provenance indicators have been recorded apart from the possible use of zircons for radiometric dating.

question: What could cause an approximately 20–25 ms WAVSP Pp time shift between WG 3D Vp/Eps/Del synthetics and borehole‑calibrated 1D VTI?
answer_text: Because the WG 3D surface model was not calibrated to the checkshot/borehole velocities, differences in Vp and anisotropy (ε/δ) between the 3D model and the borehole‑calibrated 1D VTI, plus squeeze‑stretch and 3D imaging effects, caused the ~20–25 ms shift.

This binder contains the results of the WSC/GEO processing of your well 34/10-32. COMMENTS: The quality of this job was in general good. The rigshots from the VSP was used to calibrate the sonic. DENSITY LOG The density log was corrected so that the badhole effects would not generate any false reflections. Where density log is absent synthetic density log is computed from sonic log. CALIBRATION Though they both measure times of propagation through the rocks, the sonic and seismic tools are affected by various and complex phenomena (enviromental effects, frequency content of the signal...) that create discrepancy between the two types of information. To enable the comparative interpretation of log data and seismic sections,we need to adjust (or calibrate)one measurement to the other. Our basic assumption will be that times of propagation measured on the seismic data are correct within certain precision depending on the shot quality, precision of the breaktimes picking etc... The new method presented here with CALIFE avoids problems in case of deviated wells and complex seismic acq. geometry by working in model that can describe both types of measurements and their geometry. What is generally used to compute synthetic responses in seismics is subsurface description in flat layers of constant velocity. To describe the sonic in such way, we have employed the squaring (or zoning ) techniques used for lithofacies identification. This gives us partition of the log data in zones of low variations. In the case of the sonic, those zones can be seen as layers of constant velocity. The methodology employed to calibrate the sonic is .the following: • Take the squared sonic as initial solution (or initial model). • Compute in this model synthetic arrival times for each source-receiver couple with ray tracing method. • Compute the drift i.e. the difference between those synthetic arrival times and the times measured on the VSP or check shots. • Modify the initial model iteratively (by changing the layers velocities) until the dif- ference between synthetic and measured times is smaller than certain threshold.

Commercial In Confidence 1 Introduction A multiple-offset, boat source Walk-Away Vertical Seismic Profile (WAVSP) was recorded in the deviated well 34/10-52A on the 29th of July 2011. The drilling rig was the DeepSea Atlantic semi submersible. The objective of the survey was to image the fault below BCU top formation marker, to generate 2D/3D image to be tied to the surface seismic and to estimate anisotropy parameters. The WAVSP survey was planned to be shot with the fault imaging in mind. The 16 receivers were positioned far above BCU top formation to have big enough coverage to image the fault. Anisotropy estimation was only decided some time after the acquisition and so the survey was not accurately designed for this purpose. Nevertheless, good values and interesting results were obtained. This report describes the anisotropy estimation, the construction of the borehole calibrated 1D VTI model and the 3-component processing workflow used to compute the Pp image. Zero Offset VSP survey was also acquired during acquisition operations, the processing of this dataset is detailed in separate report, which can be found on the accompanying data CD-ROM The WAVSP was processed using Q-BorSeis baseline 2.7.1, which is the next generation borehole seismic package built on top of WesternGeco‟s Omega surface seismic processing system. Petrel 2011 was also used for 3D visualisation of the final results. The raw downhole x,y,z data, surface sensor data, intermediate and final processing results are provided in SEGY format on CD-ROM accompanying this document. All plots, gif and/or PDS, digital data and the processing and acquisition reports are also provided on CD-ROM. Throughout this report all plots adhere to the polarity convention set out by SLB, where an increase in acoustic impedance with depth is displayed as white trough and negative number on tape (except migrations and tie-in displays which adhere to Statoil polarity convention: increase in acoustic impedance is displayed as positive number and blue peak)

Note that all plots were produced in Petrel software with an increase in Acoustic Impedance with depth displayed as blue horizon (peak). The full processing sequence for the walkaway imaging is shown in Table 5. 5.2 Tie to ZOVSP Results Figure 111 and Figure 112 show the 2D visualization of the WAVSP images respectively for line #1 and line #2 with the ZOVSP 5-85 Hz corridor stack projected along the well trajectory. Both views show good tie between the two datasets. The small mismatches can be explained by many reasons with among them the 3D effect. 5.3 3D Velocity Model As per Statoil request, the latest version of the 3D anisotropic velocity model generated by WesternGeco (Vp, Epsilon and Delta 3D property grids) was tested within the 3D Pp migration. Figure 113 shows the Vp property grids in 3D view along with the well path. Figure 114 and Figure 115 display the Pp images, respectively for WAVSP line #1 and line #2, migrated using the 3D anisotropic velocity model provided by WesternGeco. The images generated using either the 1D VTI model or the 3D model are very similar but with shift of about 20-25msec between the two models. As for the migration with the 1D VTI model, CIP gathers were computed as QC of the 3D migration and shown in Figure 116 for WAVSP line #1 only. Generally the CIP gathers have lower quality than the ones using the 1D VTI model. When comparing the CIP gathers migrated from the two models with WAVSP lines #1, squeeze-stretch effect from the velocities or the anisotropy parameters is visible and seemed to be the explanation for the shift mentioned previously. Indeed, if comparing the CIP gathers close to zero offsets, reflector around 2.3km moves upward using the 3D model, while reflector around 3.2km moves downward and the reflectors around 2.75km are more or less at the same position. Based on WesternGeco information, it seems that the surface seismic model was not calibrated for the checkshot velocities. The checkshot time-depth function was used only for the anisotropy tomography inversion and then, only the anisotropy parameters were updated in the final 3D velocity model. Figure 117 and Figure 118 display the tie-in plots for the Pp images using the 3D anisotropic velocity model with surface seismic, respectively for WAVSP line #1 and line #2. Again it is clear that the image from the 1D VTI model matches the surface seismic better than the image from the 3D model in terms of times. In terms of structural features the images are not very different from each other. Statoil 34/10-52A June 2012

The Balder Field sands are interpreted to have been deposited in deep water submarine fan environment by high-density turbidity currents. Associated sand injections into overlying shales occurred during the soft-sediment deformation processes which predominantly took place during early Eocene. SUMMARY: This shallow drilling project has been run in the Skagerrak area, northeast of the Farsund Subbasin. In September 1988, 667 km of shallow seismic data were collected. Subcropping bedrock units and Quaternary thickness were mapped and potential drillsites selected. Four holes have been drilled: 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88 and 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 on line IKU-0822SK-88. The drilling was carried out with M/S Bucentaur in May 1989. The water depth for the localities varied from 505 to 525 and the Quaternary overburden from to m. The holes were drilled from 90 to below sea bed (603.7 to 817.5 below sea level). The four cores comprise about 420 of diamond (piggyback) drilling in bedrock of Paleozoic and Mesozoic age. The coring yielded 370 of samples representing 88.5% recovery in average. This report presents seismic interpretation, sedimentology, petrophysical logs and core measurements, biostratigraphy and organic geochemistry. In addition, special studies have been made including trace fossil analyses, thermal conductivity, oedo- meter and apatite fission track analysis. The depositional environment, bedrock subcrop distribution, stratigraphy, regional correlations and burial history are discussed. KEYWORDS: Shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin North Sea Paleozoic Skagerrak Mesozoic SkOries

As they give information about maximum temperature and timing, another two samples were picked from core 13/2-U-2 and submitted to Geotrack International, Australia. Even if the most promising intervals of the core were selected, the two samples did not yield single grain of apatite or zircon. Unfortunately, it was therefore not possible to proceed further with the fission track analysis. 4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Good bathymetric maps are of great help in interpreting the outcropping geology between seismic lines. On Figure the previous geological inter- pretation is combined with the new bathymetric map. The steep slope in southwest along the - fault is very striking. On the SW - NE line IKU- 101SK-88, sp 3000-3200, topographic high of about 50 was found and the form was discussed in the Main Report. From the bathymetric map it is clear that the high is not local dome but more the easternmost seen extension of WNW - ESE trending ridge. This trend can also be seen on the three dimensional perspective view (Figure 2.3). The bathymetric map has thus limited the discussion about volcanic intrusions by showing that dome structure probably does not exist. No clear evidence of outcropping volcanic rocks is seen near the drill site. In combination with the seismic evidence of possible subcropping volcanic rocks (e. g. the strong disturbance and loss of reflection continuity on line IKU-0822SK-88, sp 2700-2900) there might be subcropping dike system in the area as indicated on Figure 4.1. From the shallow drilling program in 1989 it seems probable that also the Paleozoic rocks found outcropping east of 9°E in the Skagerrak area is of mainly Cambro-Silurian age. Core 13/2-U-2 was postmature, but evaluating the above suggested existence of volcanic dike, we still find it very probable that this was caused by later Paleozoic intrusions. This is also supported by the supposed migrated hydrocarbon content in the core. We therefore find it highly valuable to continue the investigation of the Paleozoic rocks in the Skagerrak area. Our recommendation is to acquire shallow seismic data between 9° and 10° and then continue with shallow drilling based on the results of the seismic.

INTRODUCTION 5_Eg , _INTEF-GRUPPEN The joint industrial research and development program SHALLOW DRILLING FARSUND SUBBASIN 1988/89 had the objective to carry out shallow seismic, shallow drilling and laboratory examination of the subcropping bedrock in the Skagerrak area northeast of the Farsund Subbasin and to evaluate these data. The main target was to collect high quality bedrock cores from selected intervals of the Mesozoic and Paleozoic strata in the area. The program of shallow drilling Farsund Subbasin was initiated from near- shore bedrock mapping project in the coastal Norwegian North Sea areas. This study was based on existing data, mainly conventional seismic, and was carried out by IKU in cooperation with NPD (Oljedirektoratet) and Statoil (Rokoengen et al. 1988). proposal for shallow drilling program was put forward to several companies of which seven supported the program as Early Participants. One company joined as an Early Late Participant before drilling started (and increased the budget) and one company has, so far, joined as Late Participant after drilling. NPD had observer status in the project. Following the intentions of the inaugural meeting in Stavanger on 19th August 1988, shallow seismic survey with 667 km of digital (2.5 sec.) and analog equipment was run in September 1988 (Figure 1.1). The data were collected and processed by A/S Geoteam. Based on the new seismic data, revised bedrock and Quaternary thickness maps were presented and possible coring sites proposed in February 1989 (Lippard and Rokoengen 1989). Dril- ling program and priorities were discussed and decided on Steering Committee meeting at Oppdal and applications sent to NPD in March 1989. First priority was given to the two drillsites 13/1-U-1 and 13/1-U-2 (Figure 1.1) located on the shallow seismic line IKU-8608SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate Base Cretaceous and cover most of the Jurassic section in the area. Second priority was given to the drill- sites 13/2-U-1 and 13/2-U-2 located on the shallow seismic line IKU-0822SK-88. These drillings were intended to penetrate the oldest Mesozoic sediments (of supposed Triassic age) and give information from the Paleozoic rocks in the area. The drillings were done on the platform northeast of the Farsund Subbasin (Figure 1.2), where the drilled strata can be tied into the basin itself.

Note also that no significant timing discrepancies were encountered between such duplicated levels, implying that reasonable depth control was maintained throughout the survey. DATA TIMING AND COMPUTATIONS Noise transmitted through casing sections caused severe problems in timing the majority of the data, particularly for shallowest levels where casing noise arrivals are evident before the expected direct arrivals. In an attempt to identify direct arrivals throughout the bulk of the data, several noise attenuations were carried out. The data was first filtered using restrictive 2,5-40,45 Hz bandpass filter designed to retain most of the signal bandwidth (as seen by F-K analyses) whilst attenuating the casing noise of higher frequencies. Further to this, remaining casing noise has been attenuated through an enhacement and subtraction technique (after coarse downwave subtraction, casing noise was then estimated using a short median operator, this estimate finally being subtracted from the raw data). An automated trace alignment method was used on resultant direct arrival data, improved times generally being obtained as result. However, no usable times could be obtained for the levels at and above 2180m, these levels having to be disregarded due to the contamination from noise transmitted through the casing, nor for the level at 3944m. Final times were therefore obtained for 151 of the levels, although all those seen to be affected by casing noise should still be treated with caution. The check levels have been selected at vertical depth intervals of either 90m (for shallower levels) or 45m (for the deepest levels) in the calculation of interval velocities and for the sectional display of well geophone signals. The analysed well section is interpreted to be early mature for oil generation from 900m to about 1100m, middle mature from 1100m to about 1500m and late mature for oil from 1500m to 1898m. • The base Nordland Gp (Naust Fm) – top Kolmule Fm unconformity at 528m represents an uplift and erosion event. Based upon the vitrinite reflectance data for the 7321/8-2 ST2 well considered in isolation, the thickness of section removed due to uplift and erosion is estimated at 600m ± 90m. Comparisons with nearby wells together with regional studies of the Norwegian Barents Sea suggest that this is an under-estimate, probably consequence of the limited thickness of section drilled by the well and possibly also the absence of samples from the shallow part of the well section, particularly the uppermost part of the Kolmule Fm. The thickness of section removed is more likely closer to 1500m, comprising any Torsk Fm deposited was removed, together with an uncertain thickness of Kolmule Fm. • Drill cuttings samples representative of the Hekkingen Fm (1545m to 1610m) have good TOC values and fair to good source potential. Although complicated to some extent by polyglycols that could not be completely removed from the samples, the TOC and HI values are probably reasonably representative; these will be significantly lower than original (i.e. immature) values, due to the generation and expulsion of HCs. • One sample from 1502m, corresponding to an interval of slightly increased gamma response within the lower part of the Kolje Fm (835.5m to 1516m), has fair source potential. Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. 3.6.3 Potential Sensitive Habitats and Species Submarine Structures Made by Leaking Gases ‘Submarine structures made by leaking gases’ are defined by the EC Habitats Directive as comprising ‘methane derived authigenic carbonate’ (MDAC) that forms rock-like slabs, pavements and pillars formed through process of precipitation where the carbonate cements the sand (Judd, 2001). They have restricted distribution in European waters, due-in-part, to their relationship to sources of shallow gas. MDAC is often found in conjunction with pockmarks, and are protected as Annex habitats within the EC Habitats Directive. While Norway is not party to the EC Habitats Directive and these habitats are not protected by other Norwegian legislation, it was still considered important to establish whether any MDAC occurred within the survey area. As result, of the original 10 proposed transects were located over pockmarks, hard contacts and areas of high reflectivity. Further information on these features is provided in Appendix B. Possible shallow gas accumulations close to seabed, with hard contacts within seabed depressions above them, were identified across the survey site from geophysical data. Environmental groundtruthing supported this assertion, with visual identification of potential structures indicative of MDAC. These structures were found on the camera transects ES1 and ES3, and were accompanied by bacterial mats growing on the surface of the surrounding sediment. The presence of potential MDAC indicates that hydrocarbon seep is currently active or has occurred in the past; while the presence of the bacterial mats suggests that seeping of hydrocarbon-rich water may be currently active. It is possible that other hard contacts in similar pockmark depressions across the site represent MDAC structures. 3.6.4 Conclusion General Habitats / Biotopes A review of the geophysical and environmental data suggested that three habitats occurred within the survey area. These habitats were defined by the EUNIS habitat classification as ‘circalittoral mixed sediments’ (A5.44), ‘circalittoral muddy sand’ (A5.26), and MDAC which is analogous to ‘communities on soft circalittoral rock’ (A4.23). These habitats were characterised by fine to medium silty sand with varying densities of shell fragment mosaics. Potentially Sensitive Habitats and Species Potential MDAC structures with associated Beggiatoa sp. bacterial mats and cold-water seeps were found in two locations. These findings indicate the likely presence of these structures elsewhere. MDAC structures are noteworthy as they are protected by the EC Habitats Directive. However these habitats are not described under any legislation relevant to the Norwegian Sea. No Norwegian Red List species or other vulnerable environmental resource (as defined by Section 51 of ‘The Activities Regulations’) were recorded within the survey area. question: What are for 16/1-14 PWL each Unit I–III dominant lithology, thickness, and any conflicting thickness measurements?
answer_text: Unit I: very dense silty sand (occasional silt/clay), ≈13.6 m at the PWL (no conflicting PWL thickness reported); Unit II: stiff–hard silty clay with occasional dense sand/gravel and boulders, PWL thickness reported as ≈28 m but conflictingly reported as ≈39 m with local ranges ~11–56 m and 26–130 m within 2 km; Unit III: interbedded sands and clays (Fisher Formation), ≈85 m at the PWL (nearby max ~87 m, no other PWL conflict).

context_snippets.text: Shallow Soils Shallow soil conditions across the study area have been inferred from CPT information and sub-bottom profiler interpretation. The CPT results suggest homogeneous Unit (Witch Ground Formation) composition comprising very dense silty sand, with occasional silt and clay layers. Unit is overlain by Top Seabed Layer (TSL), typically ~ to thick, of loose to dense, silty, clayey sand. Unit thickness is relatively uniform in the vicinity of the PWL, but thickens slightly south-westwards. Unit is expected to be ~13.6 thick at the PWL. Unit is underlain by Unit II deposits interpreted to represent Coal Pit Formation deposits. Unit II is expected to comprise stiff clay with clayey sand layers. Coarse material such as gravel and boulders may occur within this unit. Unit II thickness ranges from ~11 in the south-westernmost part of the study area to ~56 about km south- west of the PWL. Unit II is expected to be ~39 thick at the PWL. Potential Geohazards General The PWL is located in part of the North Sea where shallow gas is potential geohazard, especially at the Crenulate Reflector and within the Pliocene deposits. blowout occurred at 494 RKB corresponding to the Upper Unit VI level (upper part of Pliocene deposits, ‘Crenulate Reflector’) at well 16/4-1 located in the south-western part of the Luno II area. Gas was encountered at wells 16/1-6 S, 16/1-4, 16/1-8, 16/1-9, 16/1-10, 16/1-13, 16/1-14 and 16/4-5 in the Pliocene deposits. Formation gas reaching maximum of more than 3% at depths probably corresponding to the top and upper Unit VII level (Late Miocene deposits) was observed in wells 16/4-4 and 16/5-5. Shallow Gas at the PWL Shallow gas cannot be excluded at Upper Unit VI level (upper part of Pliocene deposits, ‘Crenulate Reflector’). slight gas warning is issued for the interval from Shallow Water Flow at the PWL Due to the interbedded sand/clay nature an structural complexity of the Fisher and Ling Bank Formations, there is general potential for shallow water flow in the study area. The seismic data does not indicate any particular structural closures within these deposits at the PWL. Hence, the probability of shallow water flow events at the PWL is considered to be low. Boulders at the PWL The nearest boulder (height: m) on the seabed has been identified on sidescan sonar data ~460 NNE of the PWL. Coarse material and scattered boulders may occur throughout the Quaternary deposits below Unit down to the base of Unit at the PWL (113.5 ± to 412 ± 13 MSL, 152 ms to 473 ms TWT). Faulting No major faulting has been identified in the vicinity of the PWL down to the limit of interpretation at 1203 ± 45 MSL (1238 ms TWT).

1.1 INTRODUCTION On the instructions of Lundin Norway AS, Fugro Survey AS (FSAS) performed an integrated geophysical survey over the 16\1-14 well site and extended region during the period to 16 May 2010. The survey vessel M/V Birkeland was used for the purpose of the integrated survey. The geophysical survey was required to provide information for the location, emplacement and operation of a semi-submersible drilling rig at the proposed well location and also to give an extended regional survey over the area to the east of the proposed well site. Proposed Location Co-ordinates Proposed Well Location 16\1-14 International 1924 Spheroid, ED50, UTM Zone 31N, 3°E Longitude Latitude Easting Northing This survey comprised two different types of grid. The densely spaced lines of the main survey grid consisted of km km grid orientated 359° / 179° and 089° / 269°. second larger grid covered this site survey and extended both east and west. The larger grid had the same line orientation but covered an area approximately km km. The survey programme is presented in Figure 1.1. The survey spread consists of: • Multibeam echo sounder (MBE) • Side Scan Sonar (SSS) • Sub Bottom Profiler (SBP) • Mini Air Gun (MAG) • 2D High Resolution multichannel Seismic (2DHR) The survey was performed as integrated acquisition, i.e. SSS, MBE, MAG, SBP and 2DHR simultaneously. Unit II (Swatchway and Coal Pit Formations) Unit II contains deposits of the Swatchway and Coal Pit Formations and comprises stiff to hard silty clay with occasional layers of dense sand and gravel. Scattered boulders may occur throughout the unit. glacial channel filled with Coal Pit Formation sediments runs from NE to SW through the north- western part of the survey area. The channel’s slope is located about 600m NW of PWL. Additionally numerous small-scale erosional channel features are observed on sub-bottom profiler data in the upper part of Unit II, some extending only few metres (Appendices and 6.5). The thickness of Unit II is expected to be about 28m at the PWL. The unit thickness varies within 2km radius around PWL between 26m in the SW and 130m within the channel in the NW. Within 2km radius around PWL the depth to the base of Unit II varies from 142m MSL in the SW to 247m MSL in the NW. Figure 4.3: 2D seismic line LN1052-313 through PWL 16/1-14 showing the Quaternary sequence (Units I to V). Unit III (Fisher Formation) The Fisher Formation is absent in the eastern part of the survey area and in the northwest, where it has been eroded by glacial channels filled with Coal Pit and Ling Bank Formation deposits. Where the Unit is present it shows parallel to sub-parallel reflectors with high amplitudes. The Fisher Formation is interpreted to comprise interbedded sands and clays. Water filled sand layers at this level were reported for wells 16/1-9, 16/1-8 and 16/1-13. Scattered boulders may occur throughout the unit. The thickness of Unit III is expected to be about 85m at the PWL. Within 2km radius of the PWL the maximum unit thickness is 87m NE of PWL. FSAS Report No. 9059.V00 Page 15

Potential Geohazards General The study area is located in part of the North Sea where shallow gas frequently occurs at the Crenulate Reflector (top of Unit VII) and in Lower Pliocene deposits (near top of Unit VIII), as results from nearby wells show. Shallow water flow is well-known problem in this region and several nearby wells have experienced this. Shallow Gas at the PWL The presence of shallow gas cannot be excluded at the PWL. slight shallow gas warning is issued at Anomaly Level (top of Unit VII), 372 ± 12 to 396 ± 13 MSL (431 to 457 ms TWT). General precautions are recommended at Anomaly Level (616 ± 21 MSL, 684 ms TWT) due to regional experience. Shallow Water Flow at the PWL Problems with shallow water flow were experienced at wells 16/1-9 (Opseth et al 2009), 16/1-13, 16/1-8 and 16/1-14 at the top of the Fisher Formation (Part of Unit IV) The vertical path of the PWL leads through interpreted channel deposits (Ling Bank and possible Fisher Formation). The seismic data suggests possible structural closure where shallow water can be trapped. Therefore moderate probability of encountering shallow water flow has to be considered at the PWL, between 203 ± MSL and 223 ± MSL (250 – 271 ms TWT). Boulders at the PWL Scattered boulders may occur within the Quaternary deposits below Unit (Units II to V,115.5 ± to 372 ± 12 m). Coarse deposits are most likely to be associated with the base of channels filled with Unit II to Unit IV deposits. Channels The PWL is located within channel, filled with Ling Bank Formation deposits (and possible Fisher Formation deposits. The base of the channel is expected to be penetrated by vertical well path at 223 ± MSL (271 ms TWT). Faulting Minor faulting has been observed within the Quaternary units associated with erosional events and sediment loading. No major fault is observed to intersect vertical path of the PWL. Environmental Considerations No environmental survey has been performed for PWL 16/1-27. Environmental investigations have been undertaken in 2012 for the near-by route surveys to the Edvard Grieg platform (FSLTD Reports No. 00911.1, and 00911.3). No indications of corals or potential protected habitats have been identified on the sidescan sonar data near PWL 16/1-27.

Both the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group was evaluated during the TD-logging in the 12 1/4 borehole section. HTHP mud with density of g/cc was used in this borehole section. The logs run in well 2/2-5 are shown in figure 3.1. The wireline and pipeconveyed logging service was performed by Schlumberger and the Triple Combo MWD service was performed by Teleco. For further information, see operational report (chapter 5). Log data from the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group are partly from logs run on drillpipe (3352.0- 3629.0 m), partly Triple Combo MWD data (3550.0-4080.0 m). Bad hole conditions made it impossible to run logs on wireline or on drillpipe below approximately 3600 m. Below this depth Teleco resistivity/density/neutron sub was used. From to Triple Combo MWD data have been used. Both the wireline logs and the MWD logs are highly influenced by washouts which especially is reflected in poor quality density/neutron logs. It is especially the shales which are washed out. From log calculation the shales of the upper Farsund Unit, interval 3426.0-3550.0, have erratic high effective porosities. In these shale-zones the porosity have been set to zero. 3.2 Log analysis method The Farsund Unit, Intra Farsund Sand and the Hegre Group have been analysed using computer model, based on the complex lithology method using the density log for porosity calculations with corrections for hydrocabon and shale effects. Shale volume has been determined from the gamma-ray log and the resistivity data using the R, value. In most sections the gamma-ray log has been used while the R, curve has been used in wash-out sections. In the pipeconveyed section the induction log is used to calculate the true resistivity of the uninvaded formation. The resistivity of the invaded zone is calculated from the microspherical focused log. The resistivity logs are corrected for borehole and invasion effects. In the MWD section the RACM curve (Resistivity Amplitude Ratio Corrected Memory) is used as the true resistivity of the formation while the RPCM curve (Resistivity Phase Difference Corrected Memory) is used as the resistivity of the invaded zone. Formation water resistivity and mud filtrate resistivity are varied with depth using temperature gradient established from Horner plots of temperature data.

context_snippets.text: 104( I-IYDRO It ii When modelling the temperature history of sedimentary sequence one of the most important parameters to match is the heat-conductivity of the rocks. For this purpose the rock composition and porosity should be carefully analysed. In the actual case where in addition to the temperature also the pore pressure history is needed, it was also important to match the rock-permeability as close as possible. To get around this problem we had to make use of certain assumptions. In both wells modelled, the Tertiary sequence is composed at the base of thin and compact shaly Paleocen and Early Eocene sequence with some sandy stringers at Late Paleocene level. Above this sequence follows thick sandy and silty Plio- and Pleistocene sequence that evidently is fairly loose and unconsolidated. If it is assumed that this sequence has an equivalent permeability that is an order or two above what is found in the Paleocene - Eocene sequence below where overpressures start to build up, then this may be used as basis for the modelling. There has been performed one dimensional models in the area; one in each of the wells and one at shotpoint 2500 of line E-17-83 (Fig. 4). In the modelling of well 6507/2-1, the hydrostatic pressure was first subtracted from the pore pressure profile in Fig.l. This gave us the size of the over pressure in the well. Next suitable permeability value for the sediments around 1000 depth was chosen to match the measured pressure buildup at this level. The permeability of the Eocene - Paleocene sequence was then varied till good match between the measured and modelled pore pressures was obtained also for this level and down to Late Cretaceous. These permeabilities and those chosen for the remaining part of the well are shown Fig. 5; and the corresponding over pressures modelled and measured are shown in Fig. 6.

All LWD memory data was dumped and logs produced as per requirements. The first wireline run became stuck at 4782m, 4720m, 4555m and 4350m whilst logging up so the second run was cancelled and wiper trip was performed before running the 5/8” casing. A.2.3.1 12 1/4” Section Recommendations Three runs were needed to complete the 12 1/4” section as result of higher than expected walk and drop rates in the tangent section. The first run was terminated to pick up an Andergauge Stabiliser to give better inclination control without time consuming sliding. In the Lange Formation degree lead angle was initiated to counteract the expected righthand walk rates, this proved insufficient and time was again spent sliding to the left. Thought should perhaps be given to utilising an Andergauge VGS from the first run and being more aggressive on the Lead angle from an earlier point in the section. Where it is found that sliding is unavoidable towards the end of the 12 1/4” section it may be worthwhile to have Dogsub available on the Rig in case a trip is made where it could be picked up, although it would probably not be worth making special trip for it. Once the Spekk and Melke were penetrated sliding did become noticeably easier than in the Lange, so if any required azimuth turn can be left until this stage it would be most efficient in terms of rig time. A.2.4 1/2” Hole Section The 1/2” section was drilled with the one bit run using Hycalog DS94 PDC bit. The rotary BHA consisted of full gauge double nearbit roller reamer followed by float sub and variable gauge Andergauge stabilizer. This was followed by CDR, ILS stabilizer and MWD tools, as well as the ADN tool for porosity and density logs. After drilling out the float collar, shoe track and shoe, the hole was displaced to 1.32sg Versavert oil based mud. Very moderate drilling parameters were used to drill out the shoe, plugs and cement in an effort to protect the bit from excessive wear. Consequently 4.5hrs were used before drilling on new formation. The second target at TVD of 4264m had been extended to the north to take into account the significant walk rates seen in the previous 12 1/4 section. This extension allowed the 1/2 section +/- 0.5deg/30m right hand walk rate as well as 0.5/30m build or drop rate, dependant on actual walk rates experienced. Hence, ideally, maintaining the inclination and azimuth would hit the middle of the target extension.
