context_snippets.text: Norsk Agip Report No. 5084/Ia Lithostratigraphy The results presented in this report are based on the analysis of ditch cuttings, sidewall cores and selected core pieces. The lithostratigraphic terminology is based on Vollset and Dore (1984) and Cameron (1993). Descriptions of colour conform to the 'Rock Color Chart' distributed by the Geological Society of America. For detailed lithological comments, the relationship between the lithological units, biostratigraphy and graphic lithology column, refer to Enclosure (1:500 scale summary log). LITHOSTRATIGRAPHIC UNITS HEGRE GROUP: 4584.8m(core)-4704m(SWC) (TNS); Age: Upper? - Middle? Triassic Examination of all available data suggests lithostratigraphic assignment to the Skagerrak Formation, Joanne Sandstone Member, discussed in full below: Skagerrak Formation, Joanne Sandstone Member: 4584.8m(core)-4704m(SWC) The Triassic section in this well comprises thick sequence of interbedded sandstones, siltstones and mudstones. The upper section (4575m-4591m) is cored and details have been supplied in the form of 1:50 scale core log. Lithologies from the remaining section have been examined from ditch cuttings and two sidewall cores. The cored section is dominated by sandstones which are predominantly fine to medium grained and locally coarse grained or pebbly representing sequence of ephemeral channels, sheetflood and channel lag deposits deposited in distal alluvial plain environment. Mudclasts and traces of carbonaceous material are noted throughout the section. Predominant colours are light green, green and grey. Red colouration typically associated with the Triassic appears to be absent. At and below 4616m, the lithologies and log profiles are similar to those of the cored interval. At 4616m the colour of the sandstones is generally very light grey or pinkish grey. They are mainly disaggregated, fine to locally coarse grained and commonly micaceous. Mudstones and siltstones recorded within this section are subordinate and predominantly dark grey or medium dark grey in colour, much of which is probably due to significant caving from the overlying Jurassic. Only traces of the characteristic pale to moderate reddish brown Triassic lithologies are recorded in ditch cuttings samples but, significantly, both the sidewall core samples at 4695.1m and 4704m from the 2/5-10A well comprise argillaceous siltstones which are entirely red.

• 3 LOG ANALYSIS 3.1 Log data and quality The 13 3/8 casing was set at mRKB (drillers depth). Both the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group was evaluated during the TD-logging in the 12 1/4 borehole section. HTHP mud with density of g/cc was used in this borehole section. The logs run in well 2/2-5 are shown in figure 3.1. The wireline and pipeconveyed logging service was performed by Schlumberger and the Triple Combo MWD service was performed by Teleco. For further information, see operational report (chapter 5). Log data from the Farsund Unit and the Hegre Group are partly from logs run on drillpipe (3352.0- 3629.0 m), partly Triple Combo MWD data (3550.0-4080.0 m). Bad hole conditions made it impossible to run logs on wireline or on drillpipe below approximately 3600 m. Below this depth Teleco resistivity/density/neutron sub was used. After logging with Triple Combo MWD, the well was plugged back to m. In the petrophysical interpretation data from wireline logs have been used in the interval to m. From to Triple Combo MWD data have been used. Both the wireline logs and the MWD logs are highly influenced by washouts which especially is reflected in poor quality density/neutron logs. It is especially the shales which are washed out. From log calculation the shales of the upper Farsund Unit, interval 3426.0-3550.0, have erratic high effective porosities. In these shale-zones the porosity have been set to zero. 3.2 Log analysis method The Farsund Unit, Intra Farsund Sand and the Hegre Group have been analysed using computer model, based on the complex lithology method using the density log for porosity calculations with corrections for hydrocabon and shale effects. Shale volume has been determined from the gamma-ray log and the resistivity data using the R, value. In most sections the gamma-ray log has been used while the R, curve has been used in wash-out sections. In the pipeconveyed section the induction log is used to calculate the true resistivity of the uninvaded formation. The resistivity of the invaded zone is calculated from the microspherical focused log. The resistivity logs are corrected for borehole and invasion effects. In the MWD section the RACM curve (Resistivity Amplitude Ratio Corrected Memory) is used as the true resistivity of the formation while the RPCM curve (Resistivity Phase Difference Corrected Memory) is used as the resistivity of the invaded zone. Formation water resistivity and mud filtrate resistivity are varied with depth using temperature gradient established from Horner plots of temperature data.

RESULTS Well 6305/12-1 was drilled to T.D. at 4302m in Triassic Hegre Group Equivalent Conglomerates on 12th September 1991 and then plugged and abandoned as dry hole on 18th September 1991. Thinly developed, hydrocarbon bearing, sandstones were encountered in the Late Cretaceous.Svarte Formation, and Early Cretaceous which generally displayed poor direct and cut fluorescences while being drilled, which later proved to be oil-bearing, though tight, in subsequent cased-hole RFT's. The Middle Jurassic Unit exhibited interbedded thin sand- stones, coals and claystones. trace of oil was observed to be seeping from fractures in thin coal band (see core#1). Chromatographic analysis of drilled gas showed C4's to be present from the Late Cretaceous Blodoks Formation through to the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, where they gradually diminished towards the base, and being absent below 3970m. A summary of the Petrophysical Evaluation indicates 144.6m net sand within the Paleocene Sand Unit is water bearing, with an average porosity of 19.7%. Moveable hydrocarbons were detected in thin Svarte sandstone stringers with 3.75m net pay, and an average porosity of 14.4% was interpreted. No reservoir potential was encoutered below the Cretaceous. Two cased-hole RFT runs were performed, obtaining two sets of fluid samples from the Svarte Formation. No reliable pressures were obtained, however small volumes of oil were recovered. The results of these tests may be found in Appendix III, whilst further discussion may be found in Norsk Hydro report Petrophysical Evaluation Report, Well 6305/12-1.

The results are documented in the report Well 34/8-12ST2 Biostratigraphy report, Reference 3. 11 ditch cuttings samples and 18 sidewall core samples were analysed for palynology. Assemblages known to indicate mid and basal parts of Tarbert, Upper Ness, Basal Ness and Basal Rannoch are clearly observed. - Assemblages known to indicate Upper and Lower parts of the Drake Formation. are observed. - Assemblages known to indicate Cook, Burton, Amundsen and uppermost Statfjord Formations are observed. - All stratigraphical units (Formations) appear to be in sequence. 1. Conclusions • Well 1/3-8 was dry because of seal failure. The vertical seal failed by fracturing induced by excess overpressure. Flexural stress caused by Tertiary halokinetic inversion may have contributed to fracturing and leakage, but this was not the primary cause. • Hydrocarbons did migrate into the 1/3-8 structure. This is evident from the shows at the top of the reservoir sands, from bulk fluid inclusion (FIS) and petrographic fluid inclusion indicators, and from the condensate that was encountered in the Lower Cretaceous. • Reservoir sandstones were encountered in the Basal Sandstone interval of the well. This was the secondary reservoir objective interval. The sands are of poor quality, but they are capable of producing and receiving oil or gas as indicated by conventional core, petrographic, and capillary pressure analyses. No sands were encountered in the younger Volgian primary reservoir objective interval. • The Kuskjell and BI5skjell prospects are no longer valid prospects because of increased risk associated with reservoir presence, reservoir quality, and seal. • The Flyndre Deep Prospect is longer valid prospect because of increased risk associated with (at the very least) seal. • The Boreskjell Prospect is no longer valid prospect based on confirmation of poor Triassic reservoir quality by the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The reservoir objective is the Triassic Skagerrak Formation, which was penetrated by both the 1/3-8 and 2/1-11 wells. The formation has very poor reservoir properties in Well 1/3-8. In well 2/1-11, the formation is very sandy, but reservoir quality is poor. • The seal failure at 1/3-8 underscores the risk of seal failure at 7/11-N, similar prospect in terms of depth and predicted stratigraphy and pressure. Seal is the primary Risk at 7/11-N. Based on revised pore pressure prediction model with 1/3-8 data as calibration, the chance of seal failure (vertical or lateral) was increased significantly. This was reviewed by the PQT in January, 1998. consensus total chance of success of 18% was arrived at. This substantiated the team's concerns regarding seal failure and justified ANOC's very recent decision to try to trade or swab its interest in PL070 for an interest in more prospective acreage. • Deep Jurassic prospects can succeed. There are several examples in the UK sector of the Central Graben where commercial discoveries have been made, and several of these are being developed (e.g. Elgin, Franklin, Shearwater, Erskine). The downsides of these prospects are higher risks associated with seal failure and high drilling and production costs. The upside of high pressure Jurassic prospects is significant: higher deliverabilities even through poor reservoir rocks, greater storage capacities for given trap size, and positive impacts on porosity preservation in certain cases (up to 30% porosity at Shearwater!). To date, this play has not proven to be commercial in the Norwegian sector.

Uphole there is transition to mixed sandy-silty and limestone lithologies, again laid down in shallow shelf environment. An Early Paleocene age can be confirmed for these deposits from the lowermost sidewall core at 2549.1m upto 2515.8m. These deposits are overlain by series of Late Paleocene deposits of the Rogaland Group (Lista and Ileimdal Formations). The lowermost part of the sequence at 2495.0m consists of medium to coarse and fine to medium sandstones but uphole from 2478.0m the lithologies consist primarily of claystone and sandstone. Reworked material of Late Jurassic age is abundant at several levels in the Late Paleocene. Reworked early Middle or Early Jurassic and occasionally older materials have also been identified at all levels in the \ veil. There was deepening of the basin; these deposits were laid down in an outer shelf or bathyal environment, probably with good circulation though there may have been periods of restricted circulation. This is most marked in the uppermost sample at 2030m(dcs). This thick sequence of claystones and sandstones extends uphole for almost 500m and tops at about 2030m (dcs). This is coincident with the top of the Lista Formation (2028m, clients data). In the uppermost parts of the well section there are indications of one or more condensed or non-sequences. Palynozone Tp5a is represented by only one sample (2030m dcs) and palynozone Tp4b has not been identified. The Late Paleocene is overlain by deposits of Early Eocene-Late Paleocene age. The lowermost part of this sequence is assigned to the Sele Formation and the upper part to the Balder Formation (Balder/Sele boundary is at 1991m, clients data). Lithologies consist of grey and greenish grey claystones. These deposits were laid down in bathyal or outer shelf environment, probably with some restriction in circulation. Early Eocene deposits are identified uphole of 1956.5m at which level there is major change in the assemblages. The depositional environment was outer shelf to bathyal but marine event is recognised between 1870-1900m; the deposits around this level were probably outer shelf. The Balder Formation continues uphole to 1939m (clients data) and the top is coincident in this well with palynozone Tp6a2 (= top Deflandrea oebisfeldensis). Lithologies of the available Balder samples consisted of dark grey claystone. Stratlab a.s/ P904/2/95 Esso Norway Well 25/8-6: Main hole and 12 sidetrack

NORSK PETROPHYSICAL FIELD STUDY, HERMOD AREA, Page: 16 4 GEOLOGY AND STRATIGFtAPHY 4.1 Structural framework and tectonic setting Blocks 25/11 and 25/8 lie on the western flank of the Utsira High along the eastern flank of the Southern Viking Graben. The Utsira High has been positive feature since the initial opening of the Southern Viking Graben in Permian times. During the Middle to Late Jurassic, large scale, extensional block faulting resulted in extensive erosion of the high and the removal of large volumes of earlier deposited sediments. The Statfjord Fm. was heavily eroded but appears to be present over most of the licence area and pinches out to the south of the 25/11-17 well. transgression in the Late Jurassic resulted in the formation of shallow marine platform and the deposition of shallow marine sandstones which can be correlated over large part of the high. During the early Cretaceous the area remained positive feature and received only thin deposits which were probably exposed and eroded during low-stand times. During the late Cretaceous the area received little clastic input and thick sequence of limestones were deposited on shallow marine platform. From the Late Cretaceous to the present day the Southern Viking Graben has been characterised by regional subsidence. During the Paleocene the East Shetland Platform was raised in response to the spreading period which had commenced in the Norwegian Greenland sea. This combined with number of relative sea-level changes resulted in the erosion of the Shetland Platform and the deposition of a number of large submarine fans in the Southern Viking Graben. Since deposition of the Paleocene and early Eocene sands the Utsira High has been stable and the deposits appear only to have been affected by compactional effects in the shales and associated sliding, slumping and small scale faulting. The sands appear to have been isolated as a result rapid deposition resulting in retention of high volumes of pore water. Compaction and possibly early emplacement of hydrocarbons causing pressure build up within the sands probably shortly after deposition. This pressure appears to have exceeded the strength of the surrounding shales resulting in injection of the sand into the shales. The extent of this injection is not well defined at present, but large number of wells in the Hermod, Balder and Jotun area exhibit various amounts of sand injections into the surrounding shales. 4.2 Depositional environment An overview of the depositional environment of the Rogaland Group is presented here. more detailed description can be found in Ref. /4.1/. Vale Fm The Vale Fm. marks the return to clastic deposition after the shallow marine chalk deposition of the Shetland Group. The Vale Fm. lies unconformably on the calcareous Tor Fm. or the Ekofisk Fm depending on the amount of erosion of the Chalk. The lower few meters of the formation are strongly calcareous reflecting the mixing of the hemi-pelagic/pelagic clays with the underlying chalk. There is sharp but conformable break between the lower calcareous part of the formation and the upper non-calcareous part.

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. It is possible to be underbalanced without getting significant gas readings though if the formation has very low porosity and permeability. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness, drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure, i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction, any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 4-

Page 24 of 29 11.0 PETROPHYSICAL REPORT 11.1 Log analysis (CPI 1:200 scale attached as enclosure) All wireline logs were acquired and edited, including depth shifts, by Western Atlas. The logs used in the analysis were then borehole corrected as necessary. The Spectral Gamma was corrected for potassium content in the mud and hole size corrected, the Densilog was hole size corrected, the Dual Laterolog resistivity curves were corrected for borehole effects, and the Compensated Neutron curve was corrected for all borehole effects. The analysis of this well was done as part of multi-well study, which also included the 25/8-5S, 25/8-6, 25/8-6 T2, and the 25/8-8S, all of which are in the Elfi / Tau discovery area. The analysis focused on the Heimdal sands, as they were the only ones containing hydrocarbons, however the analysis was done over the Sele - Ty interval. All corrections and analyses were done using Logstar, the in-house Conoco evaluation program. The analysis for well 25/7-3 was not straightforward in that the upper part of the Heimdal Fm. contains shale clasts and lenses which depressed the resistivity response. Even the two primary sand units are too thin for the deep laterolog to resolve correctly. To account for this, form of resistivity forward modeling was applied. Petrophysical Model The overall petrophysical model consists of combination of several different models. Schlumberger Volan' type logic was applied in the computation of clay and silt volumes. Using information from the core analysis, porosity was computed which provided the best fit to the core data. Fluid saturation and permeability were computed using the Archie equation, capillary pressure relationships, and sound geologic reasoning. Clay and Shale Volume Computation Clay volume was computed from weighted average of non-linear transform of the gamma ray, linear transform of the gamma ray divided by bulk density, and density / neutron. The average is Hodges-Lehmann weighted average, which is described in an 1982 SPWLA paper by Coates, et al'. According to whole core descriptions of the Heimdal sands in the 25/7-3, they consist of mix of high-density turbidites, muddy sandstones, low-density turbidites, carbonate-cemented sandy shale, injected/slumped sands, and shales. They range in grain size from medium to very fine, and in sorting from well to poorly sorted'. The top five meters is heterolithic mix of each of these facies, and as such was fairly poorly resolved by the logging tools. The high sample rate density, neutron and spectral gamma tools, with their meter resolution, described the clay volume the best. detailed grain size description was used as guide in File: DEW.095.710-B3.98Rev:

Finally, formation water was flooded to obtain 100% water saturated core plugs. Water permeability, kw was determined. At 100% water saturation, the core plugs were flooded with nitrate based water and Mohrs titration was performed on the effluents in order to determine the pore volume. The plugs were then flooded with formation water. Confining pressure measurements The test was performed at ambient conditions on 100% water saturated core plugs. Pore volume reduction, kw and formation resistivity factor, (FRF), were determined at six different hydrostatic confining pressures, using 20 bar as the starting pressure. Produced water from the pores was collected at each pressure step in fine graduated pipette connected to the outlet of the core holder. The pressure was kept constant until stable conditions occured, typically after one hour. The following pressure steps were used: 20 - 50 - 75 - - 200 bar. The results are presented in Figures 3.4.1 through 3.4.23. illesLab

question: How do helium porosimeter measurements (with Boyle's law calibration) and mercury immersion porosimetry determine porosity and grain density?
answer_text: Helium porosimetry measures grain volume by helium expansion (Boyle’s law) with a P1/P2 calibration and porosity/pore volume are calculated from grain volume and measured bulk volume. Bulk volume is measured by mercury immersion and grain density = dry weight / grain volume.

2 OFFSHORE SERVICES 2.1 Mud Tracing Weatherford was requested to perform water saturation study on the cores from the subject well. This involved using Tritium as tagger for the mud system. Tritium is radioactive isotope of hydrogen and is added to the mud system in the form of tritiated water. Weatherford representative was present at the well site undertaking the tritium tracer adding, the associated tritium activity measurements and the drilling of core plugs. Tritium tracer was added to the active mud system on the rig prior to coring. To achieve an activity level in the water phase of the mud giving approximately 100 Bq/ml, tritium tracer with an activity level of total of 34 Gbq was added. Calculations of required tracer amount were based on the mud system volumes. Volumes provided by the service company mud engineer offshore. The tracer was added to the mud by dripping slowly into the mud flow line over minimum of one full circulation. Analysis of the mud offshore after adding tracer and prior to coring showed that the desired tracer concentration was obtained. The depth intervals for plugging were selected by customer. 2.2 Offshore Sampling Offshore plug drilling The well site plug sampling programme consisted of the following: Drill inch horizontal priority plugs (hot shot) for permeability and porosity measurements. Drill inch vertical centered plugs for Water saturation/invasion determination and additional analysis. The plugs were cut using an air driven plug drill and refined oil (MedicWay-15) as drillbit lubricant. To prevent any drying of the plug samples the plugs were wrapped in cling film, Aluminium-foil and sealed using ProtecCore laminate immediately after drilling. Number of plugs and sample depths are listed in Analysis Results, Appendix D. Restricted 10

11.2.3 Helium porosity and grain density on CCA plugs Grain volume was measured in helium porosimeter on the cleaned and dried core plug using Boyle’s law to reference volume. Boyle’s law: When the temperature remaines constant, the volume of given mass of ideal gas varies inversely with its absolute pressure. Extention of the equation to account for temperature variation and nonideal gas behavior is required for accurate grain volume determination The method is direct measurement of Grain Volume using helium gas expansion porosimeter. Prior to measurements, the porosimeter was calibrated. This is done by performing standard measuring sequence using various combinations of steel-plugs with known volumes. Based on these measurements, function for grain volume is calculated from P1/ P2 : The calibration equation is determined by linear regression (last squares method) of disc volumes versus P1/ P2 Grain volume = + * P1/ P2 Porosity and pore volume are then calculated from grain volume and bulk volume. Bulk volume was measured by immersing the sample in mercury (the weight balance/ buoyancy technique). The dry weight of the core plug divided by grain volume gives grain density of the core plug. Number of plugs and results from the analysis are listed in Appendix D. Restricted 17

At steady state conditions, the gas flow rate, the pressure drop over the plug sample and the upstream pressure were recorded. The confining pressure applied during the measurement was 20 bar. Ambient temperature was applied during the measurements. The gas permeability Kg was calculated using Darcy's law. The Klinkenberg corrected permeability value, Kl, was determined empirically, based on the measured Kg and the corresponding average pore pressure, Pm. Empirical Klinkenberg correction: 1. Kg range 0-2.0 mD Kl = Kg1.06 2. Two iterations are found to give proper result, giving Kl3 = Kl Symbols: Kg : Measured permeability to gas, Nitrogen Kl : Klinkenberg corrected gas permeability m : Klinkenberg correction (gas slippage effect). The samples are cleaned in soxhlet extractor using alternating sequences of methanol and toluene. Cleaned sample are dried at 60 0C for at least 48 hours prior to further preparing. The samples are disaggregated sufficient to reduce the sample to individual grains, without crushing grains or otherwise artificially create fines. The aim of this analysis is to determine grain sizes and distribution of the grain sizes in unconsolidated/loose sand. Grain size distribution analysis was performed on cleaned, dry and disaggregated samples using sonic sifter sieve apparatus. Appendix: VSP Deconvolution DECONVOLUTION DURING VSP PROCESSING 1.0 SOURCE SIGNATURE DECONVOLUTION In some situations it may be necessary to perform source signature deconvolution on the data set before stack. This occurs when there is significant variation in the source signature from shot to shot, caused by large variations in gun depth, variation in the pressure of the air supplied to the gun, or with sources consisting of several guns, failure of the synchronization system. In these situations, the geophone traces will be potentially dissimilar, and cannot be stacked without severe loss of signal quality. Source signature deconvolution is performed by designing filter which shapes each near field hydrophone signal into suitable standard output wavelet (e.g. bandlimited spike), and applying this filter to the corresponding geophone trace. Another technique, which can be applied to cases where the source signature varies, but is still essentially minimum phase, is predictive deconvolution using window from the geophone trace alone. Software for performing both these types of deconvolution is in available at RWS. It should be noted that the near field hydrophone data is usually not of the same quality as the geophone data. The severe operating environment requires an instrument built for robustness rather than high fidelity. The signal is also dominated by high frequencies which do not penetrate the earth to the geophones. Hence it is recommended to employ gun flotation system, good air supply, and reliable gun control system to ensure repeatable source signature. Then the source signature may be removed from the data together with downgoing multiples during the VSP deconvolution process. 2.0 VSP DECONVOLUTION In order to remove the downgoing multiple response and source signature from the upgoing wavefield, there are two main options available: Deterministic deconvolution: This is applicable to zero offset, vertical incidence, and with less accuracy to offset geometry’s. The assumption is that measured upgoing wavefield is the convolution of the reflection series beneath the geophone with the downgoing wavefield measured at the geophone. Thus if we design filter which collapses the measured downgoing wavefield to bandlimited spike, applying the filter to the measured upgoing wavefield will produce the bandlimited reflection coefficient series beneath the geophone. The window input to the Wiener filter will be chosen to include significant multiples. In the case of offset geometry’s, the main assumption made above is invalid, as the downgoing energy has different ray-path to the upgoing at given receiver. 5.1 LITHOLOGY DESCRIPTIONS . 36 HOLE SECTION As all returns were to the seabed, the lithology may only be inferred from the steady ROP with low WOB as moderately soft, uniform sequence. The relatively low torque would suggest clays with marked absence of boulder beds. 26 HOLE SECTION This section was predominantly argillaceous sequence with minor interbedded SAND horizons. The CLAYSTONE was medium to light grey,silty and was associated with abundant shell fragments and microfossils. The shell type was essentially molluscs (bivalves and gastropods) with occasional echinoids, foraminifera and bryozoa. The SAND appeared colourless or milky,although some grains were stained orange or grey.It was very coarse and angular to subround, coarse or medium grained and subround, and also fine grained. This very poorly sorted quartz was associated with abundant Lithic fragments especially black, very hard, cryptocrystalline volcanics and traces of biotite mica. Many of the coarse granular quartz grains were veined with heavy minerals and contained muscovite inclusions.There were also traces of white, fine grained SANDSTONE which was sorted and well consolidated by calcareous matrix. 17 1/2 HOLE SECTION The section commmenced as light to medium grey CLAYSTONE which was silty, finely sandy, soft and amorphous. It appeared slightly swelling, very sticky and calcareous. It was associated with traces of very fine to fine grained SAND and SHELL FRAGMENTS together with minor traces of PYRITE NODULES and LITHIC FRAGMENTS. By 500m the CLAYSTONE became increasingly silty, occasionally grading to an argillaceous SILTSTONE and also showed scattered disseminated GLAUCONITE and PYRITE. The SAND became locally consolidated into fine, sorted SANDSTONE while the loose quartz increased in size to dominantly coarse grain.

question: How do porosity, permeability, and diagenetic origins compare between Sto and Snadd gas sands?
answer_text: Sto: low porosity and poor permeability with mostly primary porosity from deep burial (chemical and mechanical compaction); Snadd gas sand: good porosity but low permeability with secondary-porosity origins.

context_snippets.text: 8 PETROPHYSICAL EVALUATION SUMMARY The petrophysical evaluation of the well shows the primary and secondary objectives have low porosity, poor permeability and are wet. RFT's in the objectives recovered mud filtrate with some solution gas. The only hydrocarbons found are in gas sand at 2385 in the Snadd Formation. The sand has good porosity but RFT pressure tests and fluid sampling indicate low permeability. A small volume of gas and mud filtrate were recovered from RFT samples. The decision was made to P&A the well without testing. WELL DATA The petrophysical evaluation was performed using logs recorded on intermediate logging run (1 m) and the final logging run (1425 - TD). The sections of hole logged above 1425 do not have hydrocarbon potential. Log quality is generally. good with two exceptions, both on the final logging run. The first is the result of poor hole conditions which complicate the evaluation of the interval from 2450-2800 m. The second is an SFL tool failure that occurred at 2478 m. Logging run 5A has good SFL recorded from 1425-2450 m. The result is 28 meter gap in SFL data. It was decided not to relog as the missing data was not in a critical zone and several hours would have been required to relog. Conventional cores were taken in the StO Formation and the Snadd gas sand. The grain densities measured on core plugs are high in the gas sand apparently due to the presence of heavy minerals. A sand/shale model was used for lithology identification and porosity calculation. Density, neutron, sonic and gamma-ray logs were the primary input for the model. The matrix density used to calculate porosity is gm/cc in the primary objective, in the Snadd gas sand, and in the Carnian sands. Appropriate limestone or dolomite densities were used when doing hand calculations on the Carnian limestone section. Water saturation (Sw) was calculated using the Archie equation. 2.10 GEOCHEMISTRY 2.10.1 Geothermal Gradient Figure gives summary of log derived bottom hole tem- peratures (BHT's) corrected to equilibrium formation temperature. The first temperature data, from logging suite number one was not suitable for correction to equilibrium using Horner type extrapolation. Instead it was corrected using the empirically derived graphs used by Robertson Research in their Geothermal Database of the North Sea', (1986). Data from the three other logging suites was corrected using Horner type extrapolation and gave geothermal gradient for the well of degrees Celcius per Kilometer (see Figure 2.23). An estimate based on vitrinite reflectance data gives an effective gradient of approximately 36 degrees Celcius per Kilometer. 2.10.2 Source Rock Potential The greatest source rock potential is found in the Hekkingen Formation. There is rich total organic carbon (TOC) content in the claystones, varying between and 7.8% and comprising of kerogen type II. It is basically marine source rock with some input of terrestrial organic material. Source rock potential also exists in both the Snadd and Kobbe Formations but it is highly variable in nature. In terms of it's source rock potential the Snadd Formation can be split into three intervals. From the top of the Formation at 1523 mMD down to 2000 mMD there is fair potential for predominantly gas generation (mainly kerogen type III). Down to 2250 mMD the potential is highly variable, ranging from poor to rich and predominantly gas prone ( kerogen type III) to almost oil prone (kerogen type II). Down to the base of the Snadd at 2438 mMD the formation contains Kerogen type III with poor to fair potential for mainly gas generation but with occasional thin beds of more oil-prone source rocks. Total organic carbon content of the claystones varies from 0.03 to 12.67%, but averages 1% with the highest values asso- ciated with coals around 2100 mMD. From the base of the Snadd Formation to TD the maturity is such that the original kerogens have been converted to hydrocarbons so that the present potential for hydrocarbon generation is much reduced. From 2438 mMD to approximately 3000 mMD the Kobbe Formation is thought to have had good to rich potential for petroleum generation. It also appears to have had mixed potential for oil and gas generation. Based on the relatively large amounts of triterpanes compared with steranes this appears to have been strongly terrestrially influenced source producing a predominantly waxy oil. Total organic content of the claystones varies from to 3.27%. Below 3000 mMD there was originally much poorer potential and was more gas prone.

The top of the formation, down to 1220, is marked by an increase of the gas show with C1=6000 ppm, C2=180 ppm and C3-05 <10ppm. Below 1220, the gas decreases until the interval 1281-1283 where moderate gas show is recorded (Cl max 2300 ppm but presence of heavier components to iC5). Only in the upper, more drillable part (down to 1420), slight increase of BGG is recorded. like the Sto. Plots of reservoir properties versus present burial depth do not exhibit the same depth-related linear trend, instead displaying general scatter in the 1000 to 2000 range (Fig. 11). The lack of well-defined porosity (permeability)-depth trend confirms the importance of adjusting present burial depths for removed section. Interestingly, the Sto Formation in 7321/7-1 displays the greatest maximum burial depth and the lowest average porosity and permeability (Fig. 10). Petrologic analyses demonstrate that the Sto displays all the characteristics of deeply buried, highly compacted sandstone. The period of maximum burial prior to uplift must have been long enough for the rock to reach equilibrium with its subsurface en- vironment. When the Snadd Formation is plotted on the porosity-depth curve, it departs from the normal compaction trendline, instead deviating toward the higher porosities (Fig. 12). Such elevated porosities in deeply buried sandstones are characteristic of reservoirs with secondary porosity (Schmidt and McDonald, 1979). The petrographic evidence of secondary porosity further confirms this interpretation. SUMMARY: IMPLICATIONS FOR EXPLORATION IN THE BARENTS SEA Petrologic examination of the cored reservoirs in the 7321/7-1 well identified two types of sandstone with dissimilar reservoir properties. The Sto Formation represents compositionally mature sandstone with mostly primary porosity. Deep burial of the rock resulted in highly reduced porosity and permeabil- ity. Diagenetic processes influencing this rock, including chemical and mechanical compaction, are depth-sensitive. Exploration should be confined to areas experiencing minimum amounts of uplift when the Sto and similar compositionally mature sandstones are the primary reservoir objectives. Unfortu- nately, the trend of eastward decreasing uplift, as interpreted by MENI , is accompanied by concurrent decrease in the thickness of the Sto and other units (Gjelberg and others, 1987; Snedden and others, 1989). However, there may be central fairways where the reservoir thickness and estimated maximum burial depths fall within acceptable limits.

question: What log porosity cutoffs should be used for Tarbert, Ness/Etive, and Rannoch in the Dunlin GP/Brent Group rock/core evaluation?
answer_text: Tarbert: 16%; Ness/Etive: 12%; Rannoch: 15%.

FORMATION EVALUATION 5.1 Petrophysical Analysis The petrophysical interpretation of well 34/7-8 is based on available log, core and test data. 5.1.1 Conventional Core Analysis A total of cores were cut in the Upper Jurassic reworked sand, Dunlin Group, Statfjord Formation and Upper Lunde Unit (Fig 4.3). The cores have been depth shifted to match the density log (CDL) depth (Table 5.1). Conventional core analyses have been carried out by Corelab and consist of measurements of porosity, air-permeability, grain density and fluid saturation. complete list of core analysis data is given in the Petrophysical Report well 34/7-8 (Ref. 1). To define the net sand averages, the porosities have been plotted versus horizontal air permeabilities (Fig. a-d). Based on this analysis net sand cutoffs have been defined (Table 5.2). 5.1.2 Log Analysis Methods The well 34/7-8 has been analysed using modified version of Logcalc CAM model. This model calculates porosity from the neutron-density crossplot, with correction for hydrocarbon effects. Shale volume is defined as the minimum value calculated from the GR and the neutron-density crossplot.

There is, however, significant difference between average porosities from cores and logs in the Ness, Rannoch and Broom Formations, as is also in the Dunlin Group. This is believed to be mainly an effect of too high core porosities in shaly sands caused by the cleaning and drying process, and is known effect also in other Brent wells (Statfjord Field and Statfjord Ost). Note that the intervals are not completely represented by cores, and the average values are not necessarily comparable. Also note that bed boundary effects on logs may affect average log values. Due to the difference in core and log porosities in the Rannoch and Broom, the core porosity corresponding to permeability of mD could not be used as cutoff to evaluate net sand averages from logs. Plotting core permeability versus depth shifted log porosities in these intervals gives porosity cutoff of 16% (Fig. 3.8). Log analysis gives some metres more net sand in Rannoch than does the cores. By visual inspection of the cores, this interval proved to be thinly laminated, and was decided not to contribute to net. Note, however, that very thin sands may have permeabilities in the range of - 10 mD (Chapter 9), and that this lithology can not be registered by logs (vertical resolution effects).

Underpressure or sub-normal pressure may be defined as being any fluid pressure that is less than the hydrostatic pressure exerted by column of water (commonly assumed to have density of ppg) in communica- tion with the surface. There are several possible mechanisms for the origin of underpressures that might be applicable to the geological conditions and burial and thermal histories previously described for the two wells. 1 : Erosion and uplift involving temperature decrease. The effects of temperature changes on pore pressure are significant within closed or semi-closed fluid system. As temperature increases with burial, pore waters may expand as much as 300 times more than typical rock matrix, resulting in rapid pore pressure increases with depth. Assuming paleo-geothermal gradient of 50 degrees C/km during burial of the Jurassic reservoirs, aquathermal pressure gradients of up to psi/m during burial could result, based upon pressure-temperature- density relations established by Barker (1972). question: Which Mobil 35/11 wells and which Gulf-operated block exhibited Utsira Formation overpressure in the VEGA dataset?
answer_text: Mobil wells 35/11-1 and 35/11-2; Gulf-operated block 35/8.

context_snippets.text: 2.8 PETROPHYSICS 2.8.1 Introduction The 35/11-2 well encountered hydrocarbons in the Brent Group and Sognefjord Formation. Evaluation with RFT's and log data indicated the Brent contained producible hydrocarbons. The Sognefjord Formation has low net/gross, is tight and was not tested. 2.8.2 Summary The petrophysical evaluation for well 35/11-2 was performed using open hole wireline logs. Matrix parameters were established using core data when possible (Figure 2.10).The dual laterolog was used for resistivity, and the LDT calibrated to core was used to calculate porosity. Net sands were picked where the Dual Laterolog-Micro SFL log indicated permeable zones. Core data further indicated 10% porosity cutoff should be applied to the net sands. The petrophysical results along with the parameters used in the evaluation are summarized in Figure 2.11. For reserves and mapping purposes the upper Ness and the Tarbert are grouped into one unit, the lower Ness is in separate unit. The Etive and Oseberg are each separate units. The Archie parameters and apparent Rw used to calculate water saturation were determined using Pickett plots. The above method compensates for errors which could result from using incorrect Rw. The Rw obtained from analysis of a fluid sample from DST is ohm/m. The reference temperature for the Rw value is 130°C.

S 4.3 PORE PRESSURE Introduction Figure is composite plot of formation pressures against depth for well 35/11-3. Wireline pre-test data (FMT pressures) were obtained in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. Over the remainder of the well the pore pressure profile has been derived from empirically calculated data. Figure is composite plot of drilling exponent (Dxc), wireline and gas data for the well. Shale factor data for the Tertiary interval has been included to llustrate the influence of clay mineralogy changes on the data plots. The interpretation of pore pressures has been largely based upon the Dxc and Delta data plots, supplemented by gas data and well bore conditions. However, for the most part, the 35/11-3 well was drilled with significant overbalance which has minimized the use of these parameters. Well Summary Normal pore pressures equivalent to ppg EMW (equivalent mud weight) are assumed for the top hole section of Quaternary to Tertiary (Pliocene) age claystones and sandstones. There was no evidence of shallow gas as was tentatively interpreted at 479 to 497m and 573 to 634m on the shallow site survey. The Miocene Utsira Formation sandstones ( m) are overpressured to ppg EMW, and resulted in salt water flow into the well. Similar overpressured environments were encountered in the Utsira Formation in the Mobil operated 35/11-1 and 35/11-2 wells, and in the adjacent Gulf operated block, 35/8. Both of the previous Mobil wells in block 35/11 were drilled on, or adjacent to, seismically disturbed zones in the basal Nordland and uppermost Hordaland

Group sediments. This chaotic seismic character has been interpreted as being result of plastic deformation and/or slumping of the sediments. If is believed to have genetic link with the origin of the abnormal pore pressures in the Utsira Formation (see Well 35/11-2, Final Well Report, section 4.3). The 35/11-3 well, however, was drilled at location free from disrupted zones with only slight chaotic seismic structure, yet was still overpressured. This questions the previously argued causitive link between the disrupted zones and the development of abnormal pore pressures. Below the base of the Utsira Formation, pore pressure is believed to return to normal in the claystones and sandstones of the Nordland Group, and to remain so down to approximately 1400m in the Hordland Group. Below this depth the Dxc and wireline data plots indicate an increase in pore pressure up to maximum of to ppg at approximately 1660m. It should be noted however, that the observed shifts in the data plots are coincident with change from mixed layer to smectite clays and it is difficult to quantify accurately how much of the shift is due to changes in clay mineralogy and how much to increased pore pressure. I Below 1700m, the data plots indicate regression in pore pressure to normal (i.e approximately ppg BMW) by 1800m. Pressure remains close to normal throughout the Upper Cretaceous Shetland Group to 2600m. Below this depth, the data plots suggest that pore pressure increases slowly with depth down into the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Group, reaching maximum overpressure of around 9.5ppg BMW by the base Cretaceous. A marked shift in the compaction data plots, together with an increase in gas levels, marks the transition to higher pore pressures at the top of the Jurassic Viking Group at 2821m. •

- 204 - GAFFNEY, CLINE & ASSOCIATES CASED HOLE DST-2 Perforations 3 5m Commentary The zone perforated for this test was in the lower section of the Upper Jurassic Heather Formation. Log interpretation carried out by Schlumberger and Gulf had indicated that hydrocarbons could be present within the section though only limited intervals of moveables were postulated, water saturations seemingly being high and hydrocarbons possibly being reduced to residual for the most part. The log interpretation was hampered by lack of information pertaining to water resistivity and also by problems of mineralisation and therefore was considered only in semi-quantitative fashion. It was understood that sidewall core analysis had supported the view that hydrocarbons were present, possibly in the liquid phase. Prior to testing, the mud weight was taken down from ppg to 12.7 ppg in order to reduce the differential pressure across the APR-N tester . valve to an acceptable level, internal pressure being provided by only partial water cushion of some 2133 metres. full water cushion was not used since reservoir pressure of around 5300 psig was expected from RFT data and it was considered necessary to maintain an underpressure of around 0 psig if the formation was to be given fair chance to flow. The well began to clean up very quickly when opened for the main flow period and some 45 bbl of water cushion was recovered in 40 minutes. However, another 15 minutes were required to seemingly recover bbl of viscous gel that had been spotted above the APR-N valve and with all other flowing conditions unaltered this seemed to indicate more recovery than could be accounted for.

• The density and neutron logs show small gas effect in the Ness Formation and in some thin, clean sand stringers in the Etive. The gas effect is not seen in the other formations due to the thin sand and shale sequences. The increased liquid yield as seen in DST in the Tarbert Formation could reduce the gas effect on the density and neutron logs in this part of the well. The logs were reviewed to identify potential gas/oil contact in the Tarbert,but no contact is apparent. 2.8.4 Sognefjord Formation 2 The Sognefjord Formation was found to have of net reservoir rock. Log data indicate the formation has thin sand/shale laminations and low porosity. Core data from the base of the zone shows it to be micaceous. Fourteen RFT pressure readings were attempted in the Sognefjord Formation. Figure is summary of the RFT results. A segregated RFT sample taken from this interval required 2 hours, 41 minutes to fill the and gallon chambers. Gas with mud filtrate was recovered from both chambers. test was not conducted in this interval due to the poor reservoir characteristics. 2.8.3 BRENT GROUP 1 The evaluation of the Brent Group indicates pay section with an average porosity of 16.7%, and an average water saturation of 32.7%. Drill stem tests produced oil, gas and condensate at various rates from zones between 3370-3542 m.

question: Do connection gas peaks, slight torque/drag from ~1750, and held mud weight indicate normal pressure?
answer_text: Yes; the interpretation of those indicators suggests normal pore pressure throughout the entire hole section.

context_snippets.text: PORE PRESSURE EVALUATION WHILST DRILLING Please note that all depths are in TVD. Prior to drilling this section, the well was displaced with g/cc Anco Tec. oil based mud. The drilling commenced with PDC-bit / mud motor. The top of this section consisted predominantly of claystones and sandstones to approximately 1320 metres. Sliding combined with the usage of PDC-bit / mud motor strongly affected the modified Dxc and the MLNDR, which made it very difficult to establish trendline, as the models are based on compaction sequences in claystones. Good shale points were picked by correlation of cuttings- and Gamma Ray data during rotary drilling. normal compaction trendline was thereby established by assuming normal pore pressure at the top of this hole section. However, lot of the drilling throughout this hole section was conducted in steering mode: therefore the Dxc and the MLNDR can not be considered to be reliable tools to detect abnormal pore pressure. The interpretation was therefore based on empirical data, i.e. appearance of trip- and / or connection gas. torque trends, background gas levels etc. While drilling this section, the mud weight was held at g/cc. Several gas peaks were observed, few of them quite large, but all gas is believed to be drilled gas associated with very high penetration rates. slight increase in drag on connections was recorded from approximately 1750 metres. but the increase is probably result of high hole inclination. No close to balance indicators, such as trip gas or connection gas were observed. Thus, interpretation of given data suggests normal pore pressure throughout the entire hole section. The static overbalance is assumed to be approximately 74 bar at TD. 8-2

PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION Whilst drilling this well the following factors were used in the detection of abnormal pore pressures: 1) Gas levels: Background gas and trip gas are qualitative indicators of pore pressure. Connection gas can be used effectively as quantitative measurement as it is considered that it's presence indicates that pore pressure is within 35 bar of the drilling fluids hydrostatic pressure. 2) Hole conditions: Tightness. drag and fill can be used as qualitative indications of abnormal pore pressure. 3) Cavings appearance: Spalling cavings is good indicator of higher pore pressure than the hydrostatic pressure from the drilling fluid. 4) Flow line temperature: A qualitative indicator which, can display rapid increases on entering over-pressured zones. 5) Modified Dc Exponent: The modified drilling exponent (Dxc) can be used to calculate pore pressures in claystones using Eaton's formula. Having established trend line for normal pore pressure. i.e. increasing with depth as the formation drillability decreases due to normal compaction. any cutbacks away from the trendline whilst drilling claystone indicate increasing pore pressure. 6) MLNDR: The Modified Log Normalised Drill rate is one of the Sperry Sun Logging Services drilling model for pore pressure prediction, based on original work by Bourgoyne and Young (1974). The LNDR contains controllable mechanical parameters and the MLNDR predicts the behaviour of the in-situ formation characteristics related to the borehole. The observed and modified results can be equated to produce value for the pore pressure. The plotted results show that in normally compacted shale sequence MLNDR should decrease with depth - being directly proportional to ROP - and thus an increase in MLNDR can be associated with higher pore pressure. 8-1

Porosity Determination ELAN computes porosities taking the mineralogy and fluid effects into account automatically. The presence of mud filtrate (and possibly of light hc) and the effects of clay (and other) minerals are accounted for by the response equations simultaneously solved by the ELAN optimizer, ensuring accurate porosity and saturation calculations, provided the model and its end-points are also accurate. The main measurement controlling the porosity in ELAN's forward model is the bulk density. Its theoretical response equation takes into account the variable fluid mixture present in the invaded zone and the (also variable) mineralogy. This is achieved by using simultaneously all the relevant information extracted from the other available logs through their corresponding tool response equations. This ensures the use of the correct effective fluid density and matrix density on continuous depth by depth level basis. The forward model approach does not rely on prior calibration of the bulk density log with core data, which requires the knowledge of the reduction factor to be applied to the raw core porosities. What is critical instead, is the accuracy of the model and its parameters: fluids and minerals and their end-point values. Q:REPORTS\2511-10H.DOCAthm13/01/99 page 38

•1 Interpretation, Continued Sampling • It is best to sample well from top to bottom rather than to examine strategy small interval of interest only. The amount of money saved by analyzing part of well is usually offset by having insufficient data to make good interpretations. • Generally, the top of the well is sampled at coarser intervals, ranging from 30 to 90 ft., decreasing to 10 ft. intervals in areas of interest. These areas of interest include the reservoir and seal, perhaps faults and unconformities, and any potential migration pathways. Very thin sand/shale packages also require tighter sampling. • When conventional core is available and detailed analysis is required, such as locations of fluid contacts, sampling is commonly done on foot- by-foot basis. Analytical Cuttings or core samples from potential reservoir zones may be analyzed in technique two different ways using the FIV technique. Where rock samples are available from core or cuttings: Step Action I Samples are placed in chamber and pumped down to high vacuum. Compounds that are liberated from the pore space during pump down are monitored with mass spectrometer. 9 Samples are crushed under vacuum to release fluids trapped within the rocks. Each sample is squeezed under vacuum three times, each step being at higher pressure. Total final pressure on the sample is about 2000 psi. The gas released at each increase in pressure is analyzed separately with the mass spectrometer. 3 Zones with high responses are targeted for follow-up optical examination. Doubly-polished sections of core chips or cuttings are used. These petrographic observations confirm if the geochemical anomalies are related to fluid inclusions, and if the anomalies are due to burial processes related to migration or if they are due to inherited inclusions derived from provenance erosion. If the inclusions relate to burial processes, then all of the optical and geochemical techniques described in the toolkit can be applied to gain additional information. Continued on ;text page

Whole (Bulk) Rock XRD Analysis Sample Requirements: 1. Clean, preferably de-oiled samples ( although samples can be cleaned in-house if necessary) 2. At least 2g sample, we can work with less, even very small samples, but may need to use an amorphous backing powder. 3. Information with regard to any samples e.g. evaporites, that may be affected by the micronisation process (wetting/drying). If necessary samples can be prepared by dry crushing to fine powder in an agate mortar and pestle or micronised using acetone. 4. Information with respect to any rare/trace minerals which may be present and any particular minerals which we should look for. Method: To obtain semi-quantitative measurement of the mineral components of rock or soil sample, it is gently disaggregated using pestle and mortar and then „micronised‟ using McCrone Micronising Mill to obtain an x-ray diffraction „powder‟ with mean particle diameter of between - 10 microns. The slurry is then dried and packed into an aluminium cavity mount, producing randomly orientated sample for presentation to the x-ray beam. Each sample is analysed between 3° to 60° 2Θ (theta) at step size of 0.05°/sec using x-ray radiation from copper anode at 35kV, 30mA. Interpretation and Limitations: Identification of unknown minerals is achieved by using our “TRACES” software to compare the x-ray diffraction pattern from the unknown sample with an internationally recognised database containing reference patterns for more than 70,000 phases. The maximum intensity of each mineral identified is measured and compared to standard intensity for pure sample of that mineral. The method does not take into account any amorphous content and the results are normalised to 100% based on the assumption that the complete mineral content of the sample is accounted for in the diffractogram. Where feasible, mineral determination will include more detailed interpretation, particularly with respect to feldspar and carbonate compositions. Restricted 13

The tests were performed in the period 20/4-12/5-96, and the objectives were to: • collect pressure and temperature data for determination of reservoir properties and productivity • obtain representative fluid samples • investigate lateral boundary effects • determine the minimum horizontal stress (minifrac test) The first test was two stage test designed to investigate the productivity of the low permeability Etive Formation and the lower part of the Ness Formation. The Etive Formation (DST 1A) was perforated from to MD RKB, and the well was opened on 16/64 adjustable choke. The choke was increased several times, and the well produced mud to surface after approximately three hours. After hours the annulus pressure was lost and the PCT (Pressure Controlled Tester) valve shut in the well dovvnhole. The test was aborted when communication between tubing and annulus was discovered. The well was killed and the test string was pulled out of hole. No analysis was performed from the pressure data from DST 1A, and no fluid sample was collected. question: How do BHA motor pressure losses, MWD failures, and under-reamer nozzle anomalies differ in causes, diagnostic indicators, and operational impacts?
answer_text: Motor pressure losses — cause: higher‑than‑expected motor internal loss (motor tested individually); indicator: elevated surface/downhole pump pressure (surface loss >1830 psi); impact: required testing and BHA changes/pulls. MWD failures — cause: tool failure or pump‑pressure spikes knocking telemetry out of sync; indicator: loss of pulses/decoding errors and tool failures at 4076m and 4009m; impact: trips, BHA retrievals and drilling delays. Under‑reamer nozzle anomalies — cause: blocked or washed‑out nozzles; indicator: actual pump pressure ≈1.4× theoretical (theoretical ~70% of recorded) with conflicting surface jet wear; impact: higher pump pressures, reduced ROP and extended reaming time (40 hrs).

question: What method and sequence were used to measure formation factor (FF) and saturation exponent (n) on 33/9-19 S plugs at 20 bar confining pressure?
answer_text: FF was measured on clean plugs before the porous‑plate capillary pressure test, and RI versus Sw was measured during the porous‑plate capillary test at 20 bar confining pressure to determine the saturation exponent n.

context_snippets.text: 4. Capillary Pressure Test 4.1 Introduction and Key Results Capillary pressure measurements were performed at ambient conditions by use of the single porous plate method. For porous medium the capillary pressure will be dependent on wettability, saturation and very complex pore structure and must therefore be determined experimentally. In this test oil was displacing brine and the endpoint pressure applied was bar. Table Endpoint saturations, capillary pressure test State Plug no. Sw,endpoint kel (frac.) (mD) Fresh 1241 Clean 1215 Fresh 806 Clean 966 Fresh 462 Clean 488 Clean 612 Fresh 530 Clean 484 Fresh 501 Clean 352 Fresh 330 Fresh 444 Clean 456

5. Resistivity Test 5.1 Introduction and Key Results To aid the interpretation of electrical logs, formation factor (FF) and resistivity index (RI) measurements were made in the laboratory on rock samples taken from the formation of interest. In this study, RI versus water saturation (Sw) were measured in conjunction with the porous plate capillary pressure test. As result the saturation exponent (n) could be determined. The Formation factor was measured before the capillary pressure test for the clean core plugs. The fresh samples were tested after the capillary pressure test in clean state. The resistivity measurements reported have been performed with net confining pressure of 20 bar. Table Formation factor and saturation exponent State Plug no. FF at S, endpoint Ice (mD) Fresh 1241 Clean 1215 Fresh 806 Clean 966 Fresh 462 Clean 488 Clean 612 Fresh 530 Clean 484 Fresh 501 Clean 352 Fresh 330 ' Fresh 444 Clean 456 A graph showing the results of FF as function of Porosity is presented in section 3. The results for the clean plugs in particular indicate range of values for the cementation factor from to and for the fresh plugs from to 1.81.

Schlumberger 10.1 Procedures 10.1.1 Porosity Prior to the porosity test, the samples were dried at 60°C and 40% humidity. Grain volume was measured with Boyle's law porosimeter using helium gas. Bulk volume was measured by immersing the sample in mercury and weighing the displaced mercury. Knowing also the weight of the sample, it was possible to calculate the porosity, the pore volume and the grain density. 10.1.2 Klinkenberg Corrected Gas Permeability Gas permeability was determined by flowing nitrogen gas through the sample. moderate flow rate was used to minimize any «turbulence» effect. At steady state conditions, flow rate, back pressure and differential pressure were recorded. Thus the gas permeability and the mean pressure in the sample could be calculated. The gas permeability was determined at different back pressures allowing calculation of the Klinkenberg corrected gas permeability. During the measurements the samples were exposed to 20 bar net confining sleeve pressure. 10.1.3 Liquid Permeability The samples were exposed to net confining sleeve pressure of 20 bar to avoid water leakage along the sleeve and the sample. Liquid permeability was measured by flooding liquid through the samples at constant rate until the differential pressure stabilized. Flow rate and differential pressure were recorded, thus the permeability could be calculated. 10.1.4 Formation Resistivity Factor, Ambient Condition Each sample, saturated with simulated formation water, was placed in device specially designed for electrical measurements and exposed to known current frequency of kHz. The impedance and the phase angle were recorded, allowing calculation of the electrical sample resistivity. Knowing the resistivity of the simulated formation water, FF was calculated for each sample. Also, knowing the porosity of the samples, the parameters and in Archies formula were determined for the sample set by use of the least squares method both forced through (FF = 1.0, to = 1.0) and with free fit. Both curves are presented graphically in Figure 3.4. Archies formula: FF = = a.(1) r„,

4.2 PORE PRESSURE DISCUSSION. The following indicators of changes in formation pore pressure were continuously monitored throughout the drilling of the well 33/9-19S Corrected drilling exponent Gas levels Connection, trip, or swab gas Flowline and differential temperature Overpull during drilling and on trips Torque Cavings All measured depths quoted based on driller's depth BRT. All TVD depths referred to have been calculated using the raw well-site MWD surveys. For the purposes of the discussion the Pore pressure regime has been analysed within each hole section. This is to remove the necessity of shilling data trends and making comparisons of data derived from different hole sizes with Background gas, Dc exponent and Temperatures all being noticeably affected by changes in bit size. When bit runs are referred to in the text i.e. first second etc., this is usually referring to the number of runs within specific section and not the well bit record numbers Similarly TD refers to the section TD and not that of the well. All depths quoted in the pressure regime discussion are TVD BRT unless otherwise stated. SECTION NUMBER HOLE SECTION DEPTHS (TVD) Meters BRT. 4.2 Pore Pressure Discussion Pore pressure estimates were based on interpretations from recorded data such as ROP, gas, torque and flowline temperature combined with results from D-Exponent calculations. Information from MWD sources is used, when available, to help in these estimations. The 17 %2” hole was drilled using seawater and high viscosity sweeps every 15m, with returns going to seabed. No signs of shallow gas was noted and it was assumed to be normally pressured. Background gas values: The hole was displaced to 1.45sg Novatec oil based mud at the start of the 12 1/4” section. The mud weight was then increased in two steps, 1.48sg at 2006mMD and 1.55sg at 2080mMD, and was 1.56sg at the end of the section. FIT was performed to 1.61sg EMW at 1108mMD (1094.6mTVD). Using d’exponent trend set in the 17 %2” section leftward shift of the d’exponent relative to the trend are seen at around 1250m, possibly indicating the start of an increasing pressure regime. general leftward departure is seen to depth of around 1650mMD from where the d’exponent stays close to the trend throughout this section. The maximum gas recorded was 1.5% at 1153mMD, with 0.3% background gas at the start of the section rising slightly to 0.5% at the end of the section. No connection or trip gasses were observed indicating good overbalance was being maintained. From the d’exponent it would seem that the pore pressure increased over the section from hydrostatic to around 1.40sg EMW (d’exponent calculated) at the end of the section. No pressure related hole problems were experienced while drilling the section. No cavings were seen at the shakers. It would seem therefore that the mud weights in this section were sufficient to supply safe overbalance and maintain hole integrity. question: For well 6506/12-7, confirm that seawater, Hi‑Vis bentonite slugs, and seawater‑gel mud were used to drill the 36″ hole?
answer_text: Yes — the 36″ hole was drilled with seawater using Hi‑Vis bentonite slugs and seawater‑gel mud.

context_snippets.text: DISCUSSION BY INTERVALS The well (6506/12-7) was spudded in on 24th March 1985. The• 36 hole was drilled to total depth of 357 metres. The ROP was - metres per hour to prevent any deviation. At 312 metres, the bit was changed and drilling continued on to 356 metres. The hole was drilled with sea water using Hi-Vis bentonite slugs to clean the hole. The bentonite was pre-hydrated with 99-113 Kg/M3 and then flocculated with seawater (2:1 ratio) and lime to make Hi-Vis mud. At 356 metres, the hole was displaced to Hi-Vis mud and short trip was made with no fill. Because of sea conditions the rig had to wait on weather before the 30 casing could be run. When the weather improved, the hole was drilled one metre to 357 metres and circulated clean. short trip showed that the hole was in good shape. It was then displaced to Hi-Vis mud prior to running 30 casing. The 30 casing was run and set at 356 metres with no problems on 20th March 1985.

The dominant fluid phase within the reservoir is not definite at this time. It is likely that some two phase flow occurs in both reservoir and tubing. The analysis has been conducted here assuming oil as the dominant phase. Wellbore generated features are prominent in the first hour of the build-up. During this time decreasing well-bore storage effects are evident perhaps caused by fluid segregation and an increasing liquid level. This is followed by flat derivative profile from about delta = hours attributed here to radial flow response. It should be noted that any estimates are well-site calculated and should be regarded as initial results. They should not be regarded as the findings of rigorous interpretation. Steve RODGERS 27-JULY-87

4.1 DRILLING SUMMARY 36 HOLE: Well 6506/12-7 was spudded on May 4th 1987 with 17 1/2 bit. The pilot hole was drilled to 410m. The hole was opened tO 36 using 17 1/2 bit/ 26hole-opener/36hole-opener assembly.The MWD tool was not incorporated in the spudding assembly. seawater-gel mud was used to drill this section, which was completed in two runs. The 30 casing shoe was set at 406.5m. 26 HOLE: The 26 hole was first drilled as 7/8 pilot hole, using an MWD tool. The MWD collar was modified by the removal integral standoffs from the resistivity sub at the request of Statoil. Statoil considered that any stabiliser or standoff on the pilot hole assembly would increase the risk of swabbing if shallow gas sands were encountered. Anadrill Data processing centre were able to demonstrate that although total packing off of 8 mwd standoffs would cause higher swab pressures the effect would still be less than partially balled bit of slick assembly. The advice given was that the best way to control swabbing was to control tripping speed. Where swabbing is particular danger tripping speed should be strictly managed. One bit run was required to reach the 20casing point using seawater-gel mud of 1.04-1.38sg. One sand was identified at 589m. The hole was opened using bullnose/ 12 1/4 hole- opener/ 17 1/2hole-opener/ 26hole-opener assembly. The bullnose was lost in the hole at 557m. cement plug was set back to 523m. The fish was sidetracked using 17 1/2bit/ 26hole-opener assembly. MWD tool was incorporated in this assembly to provide directional control. This assembly continued to drill to the casing depth of 596m. The 20 casing shoe was set at 589m.
