question: Could a seismic polarity change misinterpretation cause the Top Sognefjord seismic pick to be placed 296 m deeper?
answer_text: Yes — a polarity change on the seismic reflection (not interpreted) caused Top Sognefjord to be penetrated 296 m deeper than prognosed.

context_snippets.text: A- 11 2 GEOPHYSICAL EVALUATION 2.1 VSP Data No VSP data was recorded in the well. 2.2 Velocity Log Calibration No Sonic log was run in the well. 2.3 Well Results The actual formation top depths are compared to the prognosis in Table A-1a. In general, any deviation between prognoses and actual depths are caused by discrepancies in either the seismic picks, the velocity model used for depth conversion or combination of these. For dipping horizons, also difference between the planned and actual well track will influence the comparison. Top Sognefjord was penetrated meters deeper than prognoses in well 31/5-I-32 Y1H/Y2H. This was due to polarity change on the seismic reflection of Top Sognefjord not interpreted in the prognosis. As Top Sognefjord was penetrated in the horizontal section of the build-up, the measured depth was 296 metres more than prognosed. Seismic profiles extracted from the 3D cube (NH0102M) along the drilled well tracks is shown in Figure A-2a and A-2b. Depth map for Top Sognefjord is shown in Figure A-2c. The depth map has been updated based on the 31/5-I-32 Y1H/Y2H results.

A- 20 The quality of the logs in wellbore I-32 Y2H is also regarded good, except o That no density data is presented from 4618 MD to TD, due to ORD sub failure. 4.3 Petrophysical log interpretation results Tables A-4c,d and figures A-4a,b,c present the petrophysical interpretation results (CPI) for the I-32 Y1H build up section, and the 1/2horizontal sections from wellbores Y1HT2 and Y2H, respectively. There is most probably no significant drift in the wellbore. No contacts were penetrated in the build-up section or in the horizontals, but the OWC seems to be at initial level. No indications of contact movement along the wellpaths, please see Fig A-4d. 4.4 Evaluation Method True vertical depths and thicknesses are calculated in Recall. The petrophysical evaluation is done with the Recall program Prototype. The calculation parameters including parameter sources are listed in Table A-4b. The formation temperature is estimated from the temperature gradient for the Troll Field. Water saturation is calculated using the MHz phase resistivity log and the Archie equation. Porosity is calculated from the density log. As this log may be heavily affected by hydrocarbons present, hydrocarbon correction is applied based on computed pseudo MSFL (microresistivity). For detailed information and equations of porosity, water saturation and formation temperature, please refer to 'Final well report, well 31/5-H-6 H', Norsk Hydro 1996. 4.5 Definition of Net Reservoir To obtain the best values for net sand in the well the calcites have been manually picked on the density log (BDCM) and by applying cut off on the density log.

Page: 41 Geosteering will be important during drilling of the horizontal sections to keep the well paths close to the target level, and to obtain as much C-sand as possible. Target tolerances are described in Chapter 4.3. 4.3.8 Draupne Draupne is interpreted in the Interval ~2000m – ~2300m MD. The most critical part is in the end of the interval due to the low angle between the well path and Draupne. 4.3.9 Azimuthal Gamma-Ray Prior to the drilling, no special needs for Azimuthal Gamma Ray (AGR) investigations seems to be necessary. However, if any unexpected M-sand should appear, Troll PeTek or geologist on duty will decide the use of AGR. 4.3.10 Drift problems Some tool-drift is expected, but drift more than +/- 1,0m should be prevented. 4.4 Formation evaluation and data acquisition The formation evaluation program for 31/5-I-32 Y1H/Y2H is summarized in Figure 4.5. 4.4.1 Logs In the 36” and 24” sections no logging are required by Troll PeTek. In the 17 1/2” section the MWD logging should consist of GR, Multiple Propagation Resistivity (MPRlite) and directional survey. If the GR or MPR tool should fail in these sections, it will not be necessary to pull out for tool change. Troll PeTek or geologist on duty will decide upon the need for later MWD logging over possible lost log intervals. For depth control purposes, logging of the radioactive marker (“piptag”) or thorough logging of the casing shoe should be performed when drilling out of the shoe. In the 12 1/4” build-up section MWD shall comprise the Real-time Directional, GR, Resistivity, Neutron and Density logs (Auto Track + Triple Combo). All tools shall function properly or be replaced before drilling continues in order to pick the fluid and stratigraphic contacts accurately. When drilling through important intervals like contacts and formation tops, the drilling speed should not exceed the rate where the number of measure points is at the minimum of what is necessary to achieve the required accuracy (see Chapters and 5.7). In the 1/2” horizontal sections, the same MWD requirements as in the 12 1/4” section is to be used. All logs shall as principle function properly. If not, they must be replaced before drilling continues. Logs of good quality must be acquired for geosteering and petrophysical purposes. If the nearbit inclination readings fail, drilling shall not continue until the tool is replaced by another tool. Decision to continue drilling if log fails shall be made by Troll PeTek or geologist on duty. In addition, the azimuth GR tool must be calibrated and ready for use if needed in the 1/2” horizontal section.

3.3 17 1/2” Hole Section Hole Summary The 17.5” Hole section was drilled with single bit run in drilling hours and an average ROP of m/hr. An AutoTrak was used to drill the hole. Directional Objective Build and turn with 2.8°/30m to 1071m. Hold 54° inclination and 186.8°AZ down to 1541m. Build and turn with 4.0°/30m to section TD at 1974m. L.O.T./F.I.T. formation integrity test was performed after drilling out the 18 5/8” casing shoe at 898m and 3m of new formation from 905m to 908m MD 876.9m TVD.The formation was tested to surface pressure of bar with mud weight of SG giving an FIT of 1.40SG EMW (Equivalent Mud Weight). The formation was not pressured to leak off. Lithology Claystone Mud type Glydril mud with weight of SG was used. Hi Visc sweeps were pumped at intervals to optimise hole cleaning. Cavings None observed. 873.8 – 910 1.03(0.99) Normal trend. No indication of abnormal pressure. 910 – 1040 - (0.99 – 1.13) Pressure transition zone. No overpressure gasses observed. Hole conditions good. No overpressure gasses observed pore pressure assumed as prognosed 1.17SG. 1140 – 1180 – 1.20(1.13 – 1.16) Further increase in pore pressure to SG High pressure zone with pore pressure stable at 1.20SG 1 – 1.15(1.16 – 1.12) Pressure regresion zone. Pore pressure returning towards normal trend line. Hole Condition/Cleaning The green clays of the Eocene along with the claystones of the Balder were drilled with relative ease. Mud losses due to new hole volume were slightly

A- 15 3 GEOLOGY 3.1 General The 31/5-I-32 Y1H well was drilled with the objective of producing the Sognefjord 4Dc/4Dcd, 4Bc and 4Ac sands. The total amount of C-sand interval along the well is 1585m (C-sand/total horizontal length is 0.69). For details see petrophysical evaluation in Chap. A-4 below. The 31/5-I-32 Y2H was drilled with the objective of producing the Sognefjord 4Dc/4Dcd sand. The Sognefjord Formation was found deeper than prognosed and resulted in drilling of the well stratigraphically shallower than planned – including 80 meters interval of Draupne. The last 1/3 of the horizontal section was targeted to follow the 4Dc sand - the well was therefore turned right towards the I-23 well. See Fig. A-3c. The total amount of calcite in the two branches were 3%. 3.2 Lithostratigraphic subdivision The prognosed and actual depth of formation tops is given in Table A-1a/b. Figure A- 3a and figure A-3b shows the geological cross-section of the Sognefjord Formation along the wellpaths, and Figure A-3c shows the updated subcrop map. Due to change in the geological model after the drilling program was written, the U- heterolithic has replaced the 5-series sands. The main reason for this is that the 5- series seismic event, seen on the western part of the Troll, not can be followed over to the southeastern area of Troll. Poor biostratigraphy in the area can not either prove the presence of the 5-series sands. These doubts have resulted in the changes in the geological model mentioned above. The relative high M-sand/C-sand ratio in the first 2/3 of branch Y2H is mainly caused by that the reservoir was found deeper than prognosed causing the well to be located in the overlying M-sand. The deeper than prognosed structural depth was also the reason for the presence of Draupne over interval 4100-4180m. The sedimentological content of the seismically interpreted heterolithic infill is somewhat uncertain, but can contribute to the relative high M-sand/C-sand ratio mentioned above. Geomodel used for planning:2001update/lay/I-32_rms_1211.lay. The model was locally updated after drilling.

question: For Nordland, Hordaland, and Roaaland GPs, what are the dominant lithologies and respective stratigraphic positions?
answer_text: Nordland Group — dominated by soft clays and sands, uppermost (Quaternary–Top Upper Miocene; SPUD–1490 m TVDSS); Hordaland Group — mainly claystones with interbedded carbonates, middle unit (Upper Miocene–Top Paleocene; 1490–2864 m TVDSS); Roaaland Group — tuffaceous shales and varicolored mudstones, lowermost (below ~2864 m TVDSS).

context_snippets.text: Palynological Examination of the 2/7-9X Well Summary The study analyzed the palynology of forty-three cutting samples of the 2/7-9X well. The sediments penetrated at the base of the well are interpreted to be Valanginian to Barremian in age. Conclusions The well passes through thick Albian to Neocomian sequence. The caving of Paleogene forms and the recycling of both Upper Jurassic and Permo-Triassic taxa complicate the basic age interpretation. Recommendations The findings of this study agree with the results of the EPS nannofossil data communicated in Report No. 2463A.

The subsidence curve with maturity path based on the present day geothermal gradient of degree F/100' is shown on Fig. 1-2. The Pliocene/Miocene boundary was placed in the section which was drilled without returns in an attempt to follow the sub- sidence pattern established in the Miocene and to avoid unrealistically rapid subsidence in the Pliocene. The Miocene - Pliocene boundary was not defined in the 2/7-9 well, biostratigraphy started below 4,000'. As shown in the subsidence graph, vitrinite reflectance in excess of 1.3% would have been expected in the well at TD. Figure 1-3 shows the actual measured maturity which reaches only - 0.87% for the in-situ vitrinite at TD. To match the observed maturity with paleogradient, thermal modelling was carried out (Fig. 1-4). paleogradient between and 1.5° appears to give the best match. For the burial history shown on Fig. 1-5 geothermal gradient of F/100' was assumed which gives more realistic maturity distribution. The observed phenomenon can be interpreted as follows: The high geothermal gradient observed in the well near TD has been established relatively recently. If the high tem- peratures would have acted on the vitrinite for longer period of time, higher vitrinite reflectance values would have been observed. The reason for this anomaly is unknown. Changes in the local or regional heat flow regime are the likely causes.

1 - SECTION - GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY 1. Objectives/Well History The objective of the 2/7-20 well was to test sands on the South Eldfisk structure below the Upper Jurassic shales of the Mandal Formation, and to establish economic flow rates. At the time of drilling the cost for subsea completion had been estimated to be US$ 12 million which meant that flow rates in excess of 1,800 BOPD were con- sidered economic. Presence and hydrocarbon content of these sands on the South Eldfisk structure had been established in the 2/7-9 well drilled in 1973. This well established 363 feet pay section with an average porosity of 13%, average oil saturation of 55% and well defined oil-water contact at 14,394 feet subsea. Test results were disappointing with a maximum rate of only 226 BOPD. review of the 2/7-9 well in 1986 revealed that the poor test results might have been due to mechanical problems and that the well could have had a flow potential of up to 2000 BOPD. Based on this eva- luation the 2/7-20 was spudded. The reservoir section in the 2/7-20 was encountered 712 feet higher than in 2/7-9 due to faulting. This resulted in higher average oil saturation of 81% and might have contri- buted to somewhat higher average porosity of 15%. Following the encouraging test result (3,700 BOPD through 24/64 choke with positive skin of 12), the main question was whether this test rate could be maintained for any length of time, how far the skin factor could be reduced on a future completion, and whether problems with sediment or water production would occur after some time. It was planned to address these questions in long term test to be carried out by subsea completion. However, detailed cost evaluation resulted in US$ million estimate which made the project expensive compared to potential full field development. In addition an economic analysis has shown that the project would result in negative cash flow if seen in the context of an overall field development assuming rising oil prices; a US$ 32 million expenditure would produce oil at lower price that could be recovered at essentially no additional cost later at higher oil prices. For these reasons it was decided to shelve the subsea completion project. Present plans call for the next well to be drilled after the 3-D seismic survey has been evaluated.

I. STRATIGRAPHIC PROGNOSIS The stratigraphic prognosis for the 2/11-9 well is described below and shown in Figure 9. This prognosis is based primarily on wells 2/7-20, 2/7-9, 2/11-8, Kim-1 and Lone-1 Additionally, information from various papers on North Sea geology have been used, including C.E. Deegan and B.J. Scull's standard lithostratigraphic nomenclature for the Central and Northern North Sea, as well as NPD Bulletins No. and 5. This combined information provide good source from which stratigraphic conclusions have been drawn for the 2/11-9 well. QUATERNARY AND TERTIARY; SPUD - 3000m TVD SS The Quaternary and Tertiary sector is subdivided into three groups, which are the: 1) Nordland Group dominated by soft clays and sands which overlies the 2) Hordaland Group consisting mainly of claystones and interbedded carbonates which overlies the 3) Roaaland Group which contains tuffaceous shales and varicolored muds tones. RECENT - TOP UPPER MIOCENE Nordland Group; SPUD - 1490m TVDSS The Nordland Group consists of light to medium grey amor- phous clay. The clay is usually soft and sticky and con- tains loose sand grains, shell fragments and traces of pyrite, mica and glauconite. Sand grains in thin sand lenses are milky white to yellowish-brown in color, fine- to medium-grained and subrounded to subangular. These sands are not considered prospective reservoirs, but may contain biogenic gas. Siltstones, limestones and lignite are also present in trace amounts. Wood fragments have been observed in soft Quaternary sediments. Rare stringers of limestone may occur and are pale to dark yellow brown, blocky, firm, cryptocrystalline, locally argillaceous. UPPER MIOCENE - TOP PALEOCENE Hordaland Group; 1490m TVDSS - 2864m TVDSS The Top Lower Miocene marks the transition from the overlying unconsolidated clays and silts of the Nordland Group to the firmer claystones of the Hordaland Group. TEST PROCEEDURE The Test string was run using Schlumberger Tubing Conveyed guns with SPF at 60 deg. phasing, Haliburton Bottom Hole Assembly and 6 downhole Pressure/Temperature recorders in Carriers above Packer. The well was perforated, by operating the pressure activated firing head, against closed choke manifold and immediately opened on an adjustable choke to the surge tank. The initial build up was made with the well shut in at the LPR-N valve. The first clean up flow was then performed with the well flowing to the separator on 12.7mm. (32/64) fixed choke so that rates could be determined. The well was then shut in at the LPR-N for the 2nd. build up and during this time the wireline equipment was rigged up to run in and release the perforating guns. After releasing the guns the well was opened up for the second clean up flow and flowed to both separators through 11.11mm. fixed chokes on both choke manifolds,this gave an effective choke size of 15.71mm. but did not give any better separation or back pressure on the burner. The well was then shut in at the choke manifolds for the 3rd. build up and during this time the monoconductor wireline equipm ent with the Schlumberger Production Logging Tool was rigged up and the tool was run in the hole. A pre-test flow was then carried out with the well flowing to one separator on various choke sizes to obtain rate measurements and at the same time making several passes across the perforations with the P.L.T. to measure the transients of each layer. The well was then shut in at the choke manifold for build up and during this build up passes were made with the P.L.T across the perforations and then at various static depths to obtain pressure data. The well was then opened on 12.7mm. (32/64) fixed choke. The choke was then changed to 14.29mm. (36/64) fixed choke for the extended flow period. During this flow period sets of separator PVT samples were taken and set of passes across the perforations was made with the P.L.T. which was then set at depth below the bottom zone to take measurements of pressure/temperature. During this flow period the test string was lifted out of the wear bushing due to problem with the rig heave compensators, Sc' short shut in was made at the choke manifold and the P.L.T was pulled up above the LPR-N valve until the problem was solved. The well was then opened up again on mm (36/64) fixed choke and pased straight to the separator for the 2nd. Extended Flow Period. During this flow periiod sets of P.L.T. passes across the- perforations were made, one at the beginning, one around the mid-point and one at the end. Three sets of PVT samples from the separator and three monophasic samples from the wellhead (standpipe) were also taken. The well was then shut in at the choke manifold for the final build up with ELT recording pressure data. One pass was then made across the perforations to record any sign of crossflow. The well was then killed according to the SAGA program and the test string pulled out, at wich time the downhole Pressure/Temperature gauges were recovered from the carriers.

END OF GEOLOGICAL SUMMARY WELL REPORT Page : II-1-1 17 SECTION 1545 ft - 5034 ft MD 1545 ft - 5032 ft TVD All of this section is part of the Nordland group. It primarily consists of CLAYSTONE with some minor interbedded SAND and rare minor LIMESTONE stringers. The CLAYSTONE is light grey to dark grey, soft and sticky, but increasingly firmer with depth. It is sandy and silty, and micaceous in almost the whole section, and it varies between calcareous to non calcareous, becoming less to non calcareous, less to non micaceous and less sandy towards section TD. It also becomes darker with depth. Occasionally some Glauconite and Pyrite is present within the CLAYSTONE and there is trace of shell fragments and LIMESTONE. SAND is present in short intervals down the section, the amount varying from traces to 20 % and is comprised of clear translucent loose Quartz. The grains vary from very fine to medium fine grained, angular to rounded, moderate sphericity and are very well sorted. No cementation is seen. The SAND becomes increasingly rare with depth and from 3840 ft no SAND is seen. The LIMESTONE is milky white to very light brown, firm, argil- laceous and cryptocrystalline. The shell fragments occur mainly in the upper part of the section. Background gas throughout this section remained between % and % total hydrocarbon gas equivalent with the highest background gas around 3000 ft, and peak of % Total gas at 2230 ft.

Page 36 UNIT: 23 BURROWED HOMOGENEOUS CHALK THICKNESS: 7'4 SEDIMENTARY PETROGRAPHY: Throughout the unit, the matrix material is generally off-white to, less commonly, light-gray (photo A). In zones where the chalk is oil-stained such as 10472'2 - 10471', it is tan (photo B). Very thin, often undulatory, wispy, dark colored laminae are present throughout the section, but become progressively less frequent upward. Burrowing is pervasive becoming somewhat less so upward. Argillaceous layers, 1/8 - 1/2 thick are observed at 10474'11, 10472'11 and 10471'. Black specks correspond to skeletal debris and are observed commonly. Glauconite is observed occasionally. In general the layer is very soft (ave. B.H. = 7). Stylolites are present throughout the section and are generally oriented parallel to bedding. Some are laterally discontinuous. Small, stylolite-associated fractures are also present and are sometimes oil-stained. SEM photomicrographs were taken of sample from 10473'. Very small (< micron) calcite crystals are most abundant and are mixed in with scattered coccolithic debris (primarily rings and partial rings) (photos & D). Bedding and fracture dip data have been presented on separate dip tracks on the composite summary log (Enclosure 1) and their classifications are summarised below: o Bedding: This occurs as alternating lighter and darker beds or laminae (Plate 5) according to the relative proportions of micritic calcite versus fine grained terriginous siliceous material, and the effects of bioturbation. True bedding of this type is visible throughout much of the core except within debris flow units. Slumped bedding planes have been included in the bedding classification. Where noted, siliceous rich beds have been distinguished from bedding and shale bedding (Plates 11, 15) • Shale bedding: Shale bedding occurs as distinct and individual dark grey to black shale laminations and beds ranging in thickness from 3-4 mm to greater than cm (Plate 6). They display very sharp contacts with the adjacent chalk lithologies and locally appear to occur at regularly spaced intervals. • Zoophycos burrows: Several horizons contain these characteristic pelagic-hemipelagic feeding traces (Plate 2). They generally comprise bedding-parallel and slightly discordant, frequently discontinuous traces of up to mm in thickness with well developed spreiten. The traces trend to be clay enriched and thus also defined by colour. It is relatively common for these traces to depart from the plane of bedding and consequently they have only been used to define the bedding orientation where other bedding types are absent. Burrows (other): Indeterminate bedding parallel to discordant burrows, frequently clay enriched. o Stylolites: Stylolites are common feature within the cored interval. They comprise sub- mm to sub-cm thick, near black, sub-planar, meandering to strongly sutured dissolution planes (Plate 4) that are generally parallel to near-parallel to bedding (Plate 1). They are used to define bedding attitude in the absence of well defined bedding or shale bedding. Z&S Geology Ltd. ZSL-95-227

context_snippets.text: Of major concern must be the origin of the abnormal pressure. As has been seen, the area that the Odin field occupies has been subject to very little structural deformation as indicated on the seismic log which shows all major reflectors to be near horizontal lines. It is thought that the method of pore pressure formation here is due to the compactional effect of geostatic loading of sediment whereby the sediment is deposited far too quickly for all the water to escape during compaction. The presence of gas indicates that the formation has little vertical permeability. •

If pit volume increase or flow occurs the driller should proceed as follows: 1. Shut down pump. 2. Pull kelly above rotary and tool joint clear of Shaffer Big. 3. Open subsea choke valve with manifold chokes open. 4. Close Shaffer Bag. 5. Close hand adjustable chokes. 6. Haag drill pipe on top pipe rams and connect chiksan hose. 7. Observe drill pipe and annulus pressures and notify tool pusher, super- intendent and Esso Supervisor. The well will not be shut in with only 20-inch casing set to avoid formation breakdown and the possibility of an uncontrolled blowout through fracture ex- tending to the ocean floor. The main bore (P-23 Y1H) starts after this 100 and follows roughly down-dip direction, in way, that it climbs gradually upwards through the 4-series’ stratigraphy towards the main north-south trending fault (see Figure 4.2a, fault no. 5). Fault-effects in the seismic survey around this fault cause major interpretation uncertainties, which might result in an actual well path, which runs high up in the 5Ac sand before passing the fault. After passing the fault the well is expected to be set back in the 4Cc sand. Hereafter the well is planned to follow trajectory, which runs sub- parallel to the dip direction, so that it will climb stratigraphically upwards through the overlying 4-, 5- and 6-series into the Draupne formation, where TD will be set. The neutron logs are thus not implemented in quantitative calculations, but just applied qualitatively as lithology indicators. All resistivity logs are borehole corrected. Invasion corrections were attempted for both induction and laterologs. Laterologs are known to read too high in low resistivity formations. Induction logs however, often fail to provide correct resistivity values in high resistivity (hydrocarbon bearing) zones (Ref./5.10/). common approach is therefore to splice :i.1e..ologs and induction logs at the OWC in wells where both services are available. 4.1 THE CALIBRATION CURVE An example is given in Fig 1. To display the relationship between check level times and integrated sonic log times, cal- ibration curve is produced. This is plot of true vertical depth against the difference be- tween integrated log time and check level time at each check level depth( TVD vs TI-Tc)). The sonic log integrator is time-tied to the corrected time of the shallowest check level in- cluded in the depth range covered by the log. Then the first point on the calibration curve has `Tl-Tc' value of zero. From the calibration curve, single or series of drift 'shifts' will be indicated by the points implying that the velocities require correction. The points will define both the direction and the magnitude of the shift to be applied to the velocity log. The shifts can be applied from check level to check level but are more often interpolated to change at significant changes of velocity and/or lithology. The danger of not changing drift at significant boundaries is of changing the local character of the log and introducing artificial velocity interfaces. By changing at the ends of lithological units, the reasonable assumption is made that the source of the error is related to lithology.
